To the Director and to the Whole Teaching Staff of the “Yavneh” Gymnasium in Będzin

[Będzin — education; letter to the editor.] A Purim ball was organised for the children of the “Yavneh”. Very well: let the little children rejoice, and let their childish joy engrave itself in their souls for long, long years, and let the memories of their childhood joy sweeten, in later years, the moments of despair and bitterness...
So children and fathers and mothers eagerly set about preparing for this ball, each in his own way: rich fathers, for whom spending tens of złoty, and perhaps more than tens of złoty, on one evening plays no particularly great role, assigned money, and mothers with untroubled heads ran to the seamstresses and the tailors and turned their little Chanas into marquises, into “Day and Night” and the like, and the little Moshes — into medieval knights, into historical or symbolic figures and the like. Other fathers, on the other hand, for whom a few dozen złoty play quite a large role in today's hard times, and other mothers, whose heads are not light and who, besides the hard work at home, often have to work with their husband in the shop as well — made it simpler. They told themselves: “Chanele must have a new little dress for Passover and Moishele must have a new little suit for Passover. Let us make them for Purim, and they will have them for the Purim ball too.”
On the day of the ball the children's excitement reached its highest pitch: in their rich childish fantasy they had already lived through in advance the whole joy that was still to come.
But soon after crossing the threshold of the ball the joy turned into a tragedy: two friends met, Chanele and Chayele. For several years now they have been going to the “Yavneh” together and even sit on one bench. But Chanele came only in a new dress, and Chayele was a “marquise”. Chanele stood there dumbfounded, a stream of the poison of envy poured into her childish little heart, and in her throat the spasms of weeping began to choke her.
Mr Director and teachers of the “Yavneh”! Should you not, in your pedagogical foresight, have foreseen that such a division of children at a ball into “pretty” and “ugly”, into “rich” and “poor”, is inadmissible, that it is anti-pedagogical, that it can only demoralise the children? Or is this perhaps a system with you? Perhaps you want to make of the “Yavneh” an “Institute for Noble Maidens” [in Russian; preceded by an unclear word “apalinen” [?]]? Then we parents must know it and draw the necessary consequences.
So, already at the threshold of the ball some of the children carried bitterness instead of joy. And further on come splendid little flowers of a special kind of “pedagogy” and “fairness”. The children were divided into two categories: the privileged “with costumes” and the “rightless” without costumes. The “privileged” were attended to, danced with and made merry with, and the “plain” ones were left to the side and hardly attended to at all; the privileged received gifts — pretty balloons, and the plain ones — a “fig” (I beg a thousand pardons for the vulgarity of the expression). And when a little boy with a tearful little heart ran up to one of the teachers and asked for a balloon, he got from the teacher the answer: “You, without a costume — clear off from here”...
Mr Director and teachers! My children went off to the ball cheerful, happy, in new little dresses and suits but without “costumes”, and they came back in tears, embittered, full of righteous indignation at the specific “fairness” that befell them at their ball. And the children sharply criticised their teachers and counsellors, who treated them so “fairly”. And we, father and mother, had to act so far “unpedagogically” as to side with the children against the teachers, “because covering up the truth, muddling the children's little heads with lies, would have been even less pedagogical.
Mr Director and teachers of the “Yavneh”, after the holidays my children will cross the threshold of the “Yavneh” again. But they will cross it with bitterness, and towards your teachers they will carry in their little hearts, instead of respect and trust, contempt and hidden hatred. So I ask you: how do you intend to repair the enormous sin you have committed against the children and against the whole school? What do you have in mind to do to win back the trust and respect of the children — or perhaps you will even let yourselves slide down the slippery road of searching out the “informers” — the children who dared to tell tales out of school [lit. “out of the cheder”], or the father who “dared” to write these few words — in order to punish them? An answer must be given, because this is a question not of an individual but of the community, and the manner of education at the “Yavneh” concerns first of all the parents of the children, who want the school to bring up their children as healthy people and not to make spiritual cripples of them.
Respectfully,
A Father
(of non-costumed children).
A Guest for a While... (From the Polish Press)

[Będzin — press; a visitor's impressions.] The contributor to the “Kurier Warszawski”, Mr J. Parowski [?] — by the way one of the best Polish feuilletonists — has lately been making a journey across the whole country. Among other places he also visited “our” Zagłębie. His impressions, printed in the “Kurier Warszawski”, have been reprinted in the Sosnowiec “Kurier Zachodni”. The writer gives rather little space to Sosnowiec, but on the other hand he writes at length about Będzin, sparing no “compliments” to the Jewish population, which happened to be strolling on the streets of Będzin on a Sabbath day. And here is what he writes:
“Będzin was once an old town of Casimir [King Casimir the Great]. From the centre, from which the outskirts of the town began to spread some decades ago, the ruined castle still stands to this day, and the tradition of the great king lives there. Będzin is a very old town, and the surrounding towns of Zawiercie, Sosnowiec and Dąbrowa are still quite ‘young’ compared with it.
And besides that? It is the only town in the region that possesses a well-worked-out regulation [town-planning] plan. It does not develop ‘just anyhow into the world’, but with a certain ‘discipline’.”
Here the author takes on the Jews, being unable, it seems, to bear that a Jewish young man or girl should for once in the week allow themselves to stroll through the street.
“In Będzin — Mr P. writes further — I was on the Sabbath. On the streets wandered a crowd of resting people [?], and because the ‘Sabbath-keepers’ here amount to over 40 per cent, the mass of people was large enough... It does not matter that, owing to the thaw, water poured from the roofs onto the strollers. Nor does it matter that the ‘shower’ from under the wheels of the electric transport [the tram] drenched them completely. The people wandered, their eyes were raised to heaven and from their hearts burst a ‘mute cry’: hey [?], spring, you must come at last after all”?
The author quotes several more “Jewish” [printed “yurishe”] exclamations, which, for all my earnest and strenuous effort and with my poor wits, I could by no means work out what he meant by them. He then enumerates the merits of the town of Będzin and arrives at the conclusion that:
“Będzin is definitely similar to a town in Upper Silesia. The multi-storey houses are very nicely painted, which compared with other towns is a great ‘plus’. The population has room to move, the transport is broad enough, there is no lack of greenery either, and in some ten years Będzin will become a ‘Leit’ [?].”
As the saying goes: “A guest for a while...” — but in this case, it seems, the guest was a little mistaken...
(Sh.)
Hooligan Attack on a Young Man

[Będzin — antisemitism; Purim.] On Tuesday evening the management of Public School No. 2 in Będzin held a Purim ball in the hall on the "Góra Zamkowa" (Castle Hill).
At 11 p.m., when 16-year-old Szmul Jaskowicz left the hall, he was attacked at the exit onto the street by a Christian hooligan, who inflicted a serious knife wound in his left side.
Jaskowicz, covered in blood, went with several other pupils to the municipal hospital for urgent help; but, as the father of the wounded boy tells us, the staff refused to give help, demanding money first; only when a policeman was brought was hospital help given.
The attack at the above-mentioned spot is not the first; several times already Jewish visitors going to support Jewish undertakings have been attacked there.
Educational Methods in the Będzin "Talmud Torah"

[Będzin — education; charity.] The poor boys, the little pupils of the Będzin "Talmud Torah", are used by the "management" for various purposes that bring income into the Talmud Torah's treasury.
If there is a rich deceased in town and the family of the departed wants to arrange a "fine" funeral, they turn to the Talmud Torah's gabbaim, come to terms with them, the "deal" is closed, and the poor boys in torn underpants cry out "Charity saves from death"...
This income is apparently still too little, so the gabbaim have "invented" a new means from which one can earn a few złoty.
A group of boys has been engaged — the poorest, naturally, with long coat-tails [?], so as to impress the donors — and they, the boys that is, have been given the mission of going from house to house with Purim cards...
"How much do you get, little boy, when you hand over such a card?" I ask the little beggar.
"Whatever they give, I take; one gives 30 groszy, another 50 groszy. With donations one mustn't haggle..."
Commentary is superfluous.

Katowice. — Exhibition of the first Katowice artists' group
On Sunday the 24th of this month the first exhibition of the Katowice artists' group was opened.
The exhibition was received by the Katowice elite, chiefly by the Germans, with warm applause; the German press declared that this is the first time Katowice sees an exhibition where artists group together not just for the sake of the little shop [i.e. commerce], like the exhibitions so far, but for the sake of spreading art in Upper Silesia. Moshe Appelbaum, the initiator of the group, which consists of Sikora, Myśliwiec and Neumann, was heartily congratulated by the Katowice German intelligentsia for his initiative.
The exhibition, located in the house at Jana 10, 2nd floor, remains open until 4 April, from 9 a.m. to 8 p.m.

Away with the Beggary!

All our public work rests on beggary. Not a single Jewish public institution has a sound financial foundation. The institution's expenses are usually covered by staging a more or less makeshift[?] evening, "academy" or ball. Then couples form and start going from house to house selling tickets. In the high season one is often blessed daily with several such couples. From time to time emissaries (meshulachim) turn up as well, collecting money either to maintain or to build a yeshiva.
These are almost the only revenues from which our public institutions cover their most essential expenses. The method of collecting money in people's homes has taken root so deeply that no one even tries to find other ways. And yet this beggary — I regret I cannot call it anything else — has a demoralizing effect both on the takers and on the givers.
It is true that we must turn to Jewish society and demand money from it so as to be able to maintain our schools, orphans, charitable associations, etc., when the government understands only how to burden us with taxes but wants to know nothing of other cultural needs. On the one hand we must wage a struggle for our institutions to be maintained by the government; on the other hand, until our demands are accepted, we must maintain our cultural and charitable institutions with our own money. These are facts we must reckon with.
It is from this standpoint that our public institutions proceed when they assert that they have every moral right to demand money from Jewish society for cultural and charitable purposes. With that I fully agree; what I do not like at all is the way in which the money is taken from society, because collecting money in people's homes demoralizes, as I have already mentioned, both the taker and the giver.
The taker is not, of course, the chance couple, but the institution for which it collects. Every institution must first and foremost cover its expenses from regular revenues. If any institution is entitled to exist at all, it has a certain number of members whose duty it is to maintain the institution with their monthly dues. It is very interesting to see what the state of monthly payments looks like in our public institutions: do the boards take care to act educationally on their members and accustom them to pay their dues voluntarily every month — which is the first duty of every member of an association? No, unfortunately they do not, and precisely this has a demoralizing effect on the members. That is why we cannot record anywhere the flourishing of any Jewish institution at all. All Jewish associations merely vegetate, and this will go on until the beggary for public institutions stops. The honour of the institution must be as dear to every member as his own honour. When the members understand this, they will know that just as it is a disgrace to beg for oneself, so it is a disgrace for a public institution to beg.
There are, however, institutions that could by no means cover their expenses from membership dues alone, and that have the full right to turn to the wider public and demand money from it in order to relieve the need of the poor and of the sick, to bring up orphans, to found Jewish schools, etc. Such an institution should not turn directly to the public; rather, the Jewish community (gmina) must subsidize such institutions — on the one hand by raising the community taxes, and on the other by forbidding once and for all any institution that receives a subsidy to collect money from the public.
But loneliness, need, the sick, the summer colonies, the schools, the orphans cannot wait until we reform our Jewish communities; they must be helped now. Quite true, but that still does not in the least entitle us to stage dance balls in order to relieve need.
"Res sacra miser" [Latin: "the unfortunate is a sacred thing"] you can read in Warsaw on the building of the Polish charitable society — that is to say, need is a sacred thing. What a corrupt, shameless society it must be that finds no other way to support the most wretched of its wretched than by arranging low entertainments: so that the poor man may get a little warm tea in winter, whole bottles of champagne must be drunk, a large hall must be hired[?] for a few hundred złoty a night, a first-class band must be engaged. Flowers, serpentines and confetti are bought; the committee ladies get the chance to spend money with a lavish hand so as not to have to be ashamed of the buffet at the ball. How much is spent at home on preparing for the ball — of that I would rather not speak: the fancy-goods trade is astir, in the tailors' workshops the gowns are being finished, the magistrate (city council) collects the high tax on the entertainment — and all this so that the poor man may receive a glass of tea. Is there no shorter and more fitting way to relieve need?
And one more thing: who supports whom? You keep shouting that society supports the poor man. That is a lie — the poor man supports society: of the whole celebration he barely gets a glass of tea, while the good morsel goes to society.
Nor is it understandable why we do not receive a cash report after every entertainment. The figures would — speaking for themselves — teach us to look for other ways of relieving need, not in such a brutal manner.
This way of collecting money is also wrong because only a very small part of society is burdened with this unpleasant tax, while the rest is entirely free of it. Usually the ladies call on the old wealthy men who still live in the principal streets, of whom it was said during the war: had it not been for the old wealthy men, there would have been no poor people[?]. Those who are actually able to must maintain the public institutions. Free of any burden are precisely those who are actually well-off. They have not yet been brought up to take upon themselves a share of the public expenses.
Only the community (gmina) is the one body that can and must put an end to the crude method used until now of "taxing" the public for cultural and charitable institutions. As long as we have not won from the government and the municipal authority equal rights for our social and cultural needs, we must see to it that the community is the only institution entitled to tax the entire Jewish population for social and cultural purposes. For that the community need not be reformed at all; one need only see to it that people with a public sense sit in the community board. I shall return to this matter.
But one thing must happen right now: dancing for the benefit of need must stop unconditionally, because it demoralizes the whole of society, it embitters the needy person who still has a little self-respect, it humiliates him.
Wounds must be healed in a delicate[?] manner. Our public institutions must act educationally on the whole of society. Therefore the beggary for public institutions must stop once and for all.
Dr. P. Wiederman.
The Rebbe's Son (27)

[Serialized historical novel — „The Rebbe's Son“ by Yaakov Zimmerman, instalment 27; the time of the 1648 (Chmielnicki) massacres, the synagogue of Kraków.]
A historical Jewish novel by Yaakov Zimmerman.

"Now that we are leaving this place and do not ourselves know where to, whether it will ever be our lot to come back here and when that will happen, we must take our holy Torah with us on our way, so that its merit may protect us, as it has until now..."
The heads of the community and the synagogue gabbaim had now gathered around the rabbi. Each of them held in his hand a Torah scroll which they had taken out of the Holy Ark. Each scroll was adorned with its „crown“, „breastplate“ and „pointer“.
"We are now beginning to go on a dangerous road; the future lies dark before all of us, and we do not yet know where we must turn for protection and help. Therefore, as long as we are all still together, let us sanctify and proclaim the unity of the Name, as we are accustomed to do in public on Yom Kippur, the holiest day of the year, and as every Jew is obliged to do before his soul departs, before he leaves this world — let us all call out together:
Shema Yisrael, the Lord is our God, the Lord is One!"
A thousand-voiced voice now filled the synagogue. All those present repeated these holy words after him.
Outside, too, in the street, it now thundered and lightninged, and just as the rabbi called out his „Shema Yisrael“, a strong flash of lightning lit up the whole synagogue and for a single moment filled it with a sea of light.
All those assembled took this as a sign from Heaven that the Master of the Universe was with them and was answering them. A cry arose:
„The Lord is God! The Lord is God!“
— — — — — —
With his „pralnik“ [?] (hammer), with which he gave his signals, the shammes had quieted the congregation completely, and things were already at the point where the rabbi would go on speaking, when suddenly a loud knocking was heard at the synagogue doors, which were locked from inside.
Suddenly they heard a rider approaching outside, calling out over and over „heira“ and „hallo“, and when a minute later the rider was already at the synagogue doors, he began to pound on them with his fists, so that they would open for him as quickly as possible.
All those present were terribly frightened. They, who had already had their fill [?] this whole evening of so much grief and mortal terror, were now firmly convinced that the rider knocking at the doors was a Cossack, the first one come to announce to them the terrible news that the other Cossacks had already burst into the town and that everyone's last hour was now so near.
To many of them it now seemed that this very „Shema Yisrael“, which they had all just called out here in public, would also be their last...
Only R' Yom Tov Lipman Heller, the Kraków rabbi, was the one man who did not now lose his head. He gave the shammes an order to let in the person knocking out there and to ask him why he was disturbing the prayers of those assembled here.
Hardly had the old shammes carried out the rabbi's order when a soldier appeared in the doorway, armed with a sword and a gun, and went straight up to the bimah, where the rabbi stood, surrounded by the heads of the community and the gabbaim with the Torah scrolls in their hands.
All those assembled were silent and very curious to hear what the soldier had to say — good things, or, God forbid, bad?
But suddenly a cry was heard, coming from the women's gallery:
"Shimon!!"
That single but bone-shaking word was cried out by Sarah, the daughter of our acquaintance Chaim the wagon-driver.
As our readers will probably remember, Sarah was not indifferent to the handsome, middle-aged [?] Shimon, and in the several months since he had gone off with the others to war with Prince Wiśniowiecki's Jewish soldiers, she had not forgotten him for even a single minute; it is therefore no wonder that she was the first to recognise him at once, although he was now greatly changed and was dressed in soldier's clothes, in which nobody here had ever seen him before.
The rabbi, too, now recognised him.
He grew even calmer than he had been a little earlier. No enemy, no Cossack had burst in here now, but one of our own, a friend, who had surely brought with him good tidings, salvation and consolation.
"Sholem aleichem, Shimon!" the rabbi now began, stretching out his hand to the soldier, who stood before him with great respect. "What good news have you now brought us?"
"Good and joyful tidings, dear Rebbe!" Shimon answered, looking around the synagogue at all those assembled. "The Blessed Name has helped His people Israel! After a hard and bitter battle our men today won a great victory over the enemy."
Hardly had Shimon uttered these few but meaningful words when it was as if a heavy burden had fallen from the hearts of all those present; all at once everyone felt lighter. In this short moment they had already forgotten all the troubles and the great fear they had had to endure before. Everyone — so it seemed — wanted to catch a little air and unburden his heart of what he had suffered and had had to endure lately.
(To be continued).

Responsibility Toward the Community.

[Sosnowiec — municipality; budget; Jewish institutions.] (The budget of the Sosnowiec municipal self-government amounts to 15 million złoty. What do we get from it?)

The municipal self-government in Sosnowiec has already prepared [?] its budget for a sum of 15 million zł. One cannot say otherwise: the sum is quite a respectable one, and when one wants to draw such a considerable sum out of a town, it is worth pausing over it.

It is a plague: at a time when from various sources we are shown the practical necessity of saving money, at that very same time our public institutions do not understand this with regard to their citizens. And here we see that our self-government now understands precisely how to enlarge its budget, regardless of the fact that with the previous budget the town was already burdened heavily enough. And the question arises: what is the reason for the enlargement? Is the town really better off? Has the economic situation improved? Have the broad strata of the population grown richer? Have its affairs improved, grown and risen to a wider scale? Was the previous budget collected so easily that it was considered necessary to enlarge it?

It seems that it is neither this nor that: neither has business improved, nor was the budget collected so easily and well that the town's leaders should have seen the necessity of enlarging the budget to 15 million złoty.

They know how to tell the population that it must save and economise and not spend too much money; why do not these leading institutions themselves set the example, from which the population could draw a moral lesson? Why do they not show that with good management one can save money and live more economically?

And if we set all this aside, if we disregard everything, the question also arises: what does our self-government give us as Jewish citizens? After all, it is well known that when it comes to apportioning the taxes, we Jews are counted among the first-class citizens; so how do we benefit from the taxes that are meant to be spent for the welfare of our local interests?

For we hear that it has not been provided at all that the charitable institutions be properly subsidised. Only the Jewish hospital is to receive 15 thousand zł. Everything else is to be treated with the greatest apathy. Yet we have enough institutions that find themselves in quite difficult conditions; many of them are barely, barely breathing, and they need someone to blow a breath of life into their souls. The Talmud Torah is in the cruellest conditions, and all the other institutions cannot maintain themselves on the municipal obligations [?]; so why should they not be supported by a local self-government? And if 15 thousand zł. is allocated for the hospital, is that a respectable subsidy? That means tossing a little bone, just to discharge an obligation, to such a useful institution; otherwise it should have received a respectable subsidy, since other institutions were not taken into consideration at all.

We do have our representatives in the city council. True, they are a minimal number, but they need not reckon with that; they need remember only one thing: these four councillors represent the whole of Jewish Sosnowiec, and as such they have the full right to speak in the name of the entire Jewish population. Therefore a sacred duty lies upon them to fight so that the institutions that need support are properly subsidised, and on no account may it be allowed that they be tossed a little bone just to discharge an obligation. A self-government that can allow itself to draw up such a gigantic budget of 15 million zł. can allow itself to subsidise respectably the institutions from whose citizens it receives a large part of its income; and not only philanthropic institutions must be subsidised, but also cultural, economic and professional institutions.

At the magistrate there is a municipal library with all sorts of newspapers and journals, but not a single Jewish newspaper is ever to be seen there. So why should the Jewish newspapers not have equal rights there? Why should a Jewish worker and intellectual not be able to come in there and read a Jewish newspaper?

One must not pass over such a phenomenon with indifference; our representatives must not forget that, after all, they represent the municipal interests, and they have the right and the duty to demand and to claim what is due to Jewish Sosnowiec.

With pride our representatives can demand that we be given what is due to us, what our public institutions need. It is an old rule that those who give also have the right to demand that the institutions they need be subsidised.

Our councillors must not forget what an obligation lies upon them, since they are the representatives of the entire Jewish population of the town, and as such they speak in the name of all Jews and have the right to demand what is due to them.

Let our councillors not take this very important matter lightly, and let all the councillors be present in the city council at the session when the debates on the budget take place.

Dr. Popuri.

A Letter to the Editor

[Sosnowiec — letter to the editor.] Most esteemed editors!
I ask you kindly to give space in your esteemed paper to the following statement:
A terrible villainy has taken place in Sosnowiec. The "Nayer[?] Undzer Tog" collected poor people's money from the "coal-ring" (coal fund?) and raised an outcry against me that I had supposedly taken it.
I declare categorically that I have fallen victim to a base lying libel out of personal revenge on the part of the editors.
I appeal to all to whom truth and justice are dear not to pass over the matter in silence. A commission of respected householders must be created to investigate the matter, track down the lost money and take up the wrong done to the poor and oppressed.
I turn to those who have already managed to convince themselves of my innocence that they should react to this properly[?]. There must be a public protest against such lawlessness, and everyone must shake himself free of this irresponsible rag.
Not a single decent person may subscribe to or support a newspaper that has puffed itself up in an ugly way through lies and libels.
Dr. Ch. Kaufman.

A Fit of Madness in a Jewish Girl.
For 6 weeks the 34-year-old K. had been working as a maidservant with the L. family on Jana [?] Street.
She had previously held such a post with the Kramałowska family as well, and at the funeral of Mrs. Kramałowska the girl went to pay the last respects to her late "madame" [mistress].
After coming back from the cemetery the girl was melancholy, did not sleep at night and often said that "the end of man is a very ugly one, and would that the Messiah came already — then surely 'death will be swallowed up forever'".
Last Tuesday at 5 in the morning the girl suddenly went up onto the courtyard balcony, where she shouted in wild cries: "Father, the Messiah has come!"...
The terrible cries woke the surrounding residents, who ran out into the street in fright, thinking that something terrible had happened to one of the neighbours.
A doctor was called to the woman who had suddenly gone mad; he gave the necessary help, and a few hours later the girl calmed down.

May a Beadle Be a "Posek" [Halakhic Authority]?

[Będzin — kehilla; synagogue.]
The local kehilla "muddle" [?] has been enriched by one more "little flower"...
It happened last Saturday after the Torah reading in the town synagogue (Shtot-shul), where not a single Sabbath goes by without a "sensation" occurring.
Last Sabbath's "sensation" consisted of an incident between the dozór [kehilla board member] Mr. Bożykowski and the synagogue beadle Mr. Mendel Kapłan.
The course of the incident was as follows:
The Sabbath fell on the 9th yahrzeit of Joseph Trumpeldor, who perished in the sad events at Tel Hai. The local "Brit Trumpeldor" therefore applied to the kehilla board to allow it to hold a memorial prayer (hazkara) on Sunday in the synagogue, since on the Sabbath of the Four Portions (arba parshiyot) no hazkara may be held.
When the letter of "Brit Trumpeldor" was dealt with at a meeting of the kehilla board, the rabbinate happened to be present as well, and the president, Mr. Prawer [printed "Prakher"], turned to the heads of the rabbinate, with the chief rabbi at their head, asking them to state whether one may hold a hazkara this Sabbath.
To this a member of the rabbinate declared that "nowhere is there a prohibition against it", and on that basis permission was given to hold the hazkara.
The mission was taken on by Mr. Bożykowski, who is at the same time on the synagogue committee; but when Mr. B. asked the cantor to recite "El Malei Rachamim", the beadle Mr. Kapłan tried to prevent it, explaining that there is an explicit ruling in the "Magen Avraham" that "on the Sabbaths of the Four Portions no hazkara may be held".
The dozór B. prevailed and the hazkara was held. But Mr. B. insisted on obtaining satisfaction and intervened with the kehilla board that the incident be dealt with at once and that Kapłan be severely punished.
The matter was indeed dealt with the next day, Sunday, but when Mr. Kapłan proved to the dozórs "in black and white" that he had carried out the instruction of the "Magen Avraham", he was let off a severe punishment.

Sosnowiec
A stormy meeting of the Kehilla Council.
(Sh.) The news that a meeting of the Kehilla Council was taking place on Sunday evening aroused great interest in the town. Already an hour before the meeting began a large "gallery" had assembled, which later "helped" the chairman conduct the meeting and took part in the "lexicon of abuse". The speeches of the "Agudah" councillors were delivered in a tone of a certain forcefulness; the reason for this is said to be a secret agreement between the Agudah and the artisans, who in their speeches did their best to be good contracting partners.
———
An hour late, the vice-president Mr. Szwajcer opens the meeting and announces that there are 2 points on the agenda: 1) the balance sheet for the year 1928 and 2) the approval of the budget for the year 1929. The first point passed peacefully: the secretary Mr. Lehegof [?] reads out all the budget items and gives explanations about all the moneys that were paid out by the community (gmina).
On proceeding to the second point a real brew starts boiling in our "homely little parliament". The air smells of gunpowder. The first to take the floor is councillor Kupferminc, who comes out sharply against the board, which ignored the budget committee and prepared the budget on its own responsibility. President L. Zendel replies that the community received a demand from the starosta to prepare the budget, and that within the course of this month it must still be submitted for approval. Mr. Zendel therefore asks that the council proceed to consider the budget. Councillor Zylberberg proposes sending the budget to the committee for consideration. A heated discussion develops over this, in which Messrs. Cwajghaft, Kalisz, Kupferminc, Nachemia [?] and others take part. Several speakers point out that such a committee does not exist at all and a new committee must be elected. Councillor Orman takes the floor and wants to begin speaking, but he is not allowed to get a word in. Interjections are heard from the gallery: "In whose name are you speaking? You have no right to speak in the name of the artisans!" "After all, we are not electing a rabbi now".
In the end the speaker does get his word. He proposes expressing the sharpest protest over the fact that Dr. Meladista [?] does not come to the meetings. During Mr. Orman's speech a sharp exchange of words occurs between councillors Brojger [?] and B. Sieciemski [?]. The latter, wishing to defend his attacked colleagues on the council, says: we have come together to deal with the budget, and meanwhile one councillor besmirches the other like street women. (Here a terrible uproar breaks out; the gallery shouts: "Shame on you, Agudah representatives, are such speeches made at a meeting of the Kehilla Council? Phooey!") The chairman is at his wits' end. The uproar grows stronger from minute to minute. Only after Mr. Sieciemski withdraws his words do people calm down a little and proceed to elect a budget committee. By secret ballot Messrs. Bergman, Szwajcer, Englard, and Feldman as deputy, were elected. Amid a tremendous uproar the chairman closes the meeting.
The gallery, however, is in no great hurry to leave the hall, and groups form which hurl mutual grave sins at one another. Most active of all are the Left Poale Zion, who demand that the council and the board dissolve themselves. Also worth noting is the accusation that Mr. Y. Grynfeld threw at the artisans' representative on the board, Mr. Bergman, that he took 1800 zł. from the community and has given nobody any account of it. Mr. G. shouts: "You are a public swindler; take me to court, I will say it to you again".
Nor were there lacking "merry" moments at the meeting. While people were arguing whether to elect a committee or not, and the temperature was rising with every minute, a certain Dazar [?] stood up and declared in a raised voice:
"Gentlemen, perhaps it really would be fair to cut the budget in half"!
Drawing up the bottom line, one must come to the conclusion that if the meetings of the Kehilla Council continue to take place in such an atmosphere, the council stands at a very low level.
—o—
"Fishing in troubled waters"...
Last week the committee for the distribution of coal to the poor held a meeting, at which it was also discussed how to react to the villainy committed by the editorial board of "Nekhtiger Tog" ("Yesterday's Day"), which took money from the coal ring [?] and does not want to give it back.
At the meeting it was resolved to give them a warning through the newspaper, and if these people do not return the poor people's pennies they snatched, the committee is to hand the matter over to the public prosecutor.
The gentlemen of the above-mentioned newspaper, however, are "sly fellows" and hit upon a fine invention: to cry out before the public "Stop thief!"... and almost every day there appear in the said "Tog" demands to their former collaborators that they "repay the editorial moneys they collected"...
Such a demand was also the lot of Dr. Kaufman. Because of this the latter posted a declaration in the "Mizrachi" synagogue that, since the above newspaper is at its last gasp and the "editors", wishing to wash themselves clean of their sins, are making do with demands, he therefore declares that he has no connection whatsoever with the villainy".
— A symbol of the wild lawlessness that prevails [?] so much at the present time...

Along with the PPS (Polish Socialist Party) rule over the municipal economy, the PPS member Dr. Michałowski had also held, for 2 years, the office of commissioner of the sickness fund (Kasa Chorych) in Zagłębie.
By an order of the Minister of Labour and Social Welfare, Dr. Michałowski is being removed from his post held until now.
A former major has been appointed commissioner, and he will already take office from 1 April.
—o—
6 passengers injured in a railway accident
At Maczki station a goods train ran into a carriage of the Warsaw–Kraków express train.
In the collision six passengers were injured.
—o—
A dangerous bandit caught.
The local police arrested in these days a well-known safe-breaker and bandit, who had been "touring" for a long time in Upper Silesia and the Zagłębie district.

Away with the Filthy Deeds! (A Letter to the Editor)

[Letter to the editor — Sosnowiec; local press.] Esteemed Editors!
Allow me to print the following lines in your esteemed paper, in order to point out to the public the wild lawlessness that prevails on the social ground.
However dreadfully unpleasant the matter may be to me, however much disgust and revulsion I may feel at the mere mention of the name of that scandalmonger and public troublemaker, I must nevertheless touch upon the matter and hold up his face, like a picture of horror, above everyone's head, because it has already taken on far too scandalous a character, and one would have to be insincere with oneself to keep silent about it.
On the foam of the muddy vermin-swarm that bears the name "Nayer Unzer Tog" (Our New Day) there has lately appeared a person — better said, a symptom of a contagious disease — who calls himself Mr. Z. Until now this person was completely unknown to us. After the "black exchange" spat him out, he conceived a craving to carry in his pocket a card as "editor-in-chief" of a newspaper as well.
Unfortunately he has succeeded, and by the power of that very card the greatest abominable deeds and public scandals are committed.
Here is a small picture:
When I was still working at the paper, I happened to write an article about a respectable middle-class family that had been ruined in a tragic way. The next day people turned up at the editorial office [printed "gemandn", probably a misprint for "gemeldn"] with considerable donations for this purpose. I informed the family of it, but how astonished I was to hear recently from the poor unhappy woman that at the editorial office she is met with "shehi pehi"[?] [apparently: evasions].
— Does this not exceed every measure of blackmail and robbery? And now what about the poor people's coal money?
And more, and more money that nobody even knows about. For example, some time ago a woman from Olkusz who came to Sosnowiec to visit her ancestors' graves left a rather large sum for the benefit of the "Dobroczynność" [charity society] — well, who knows about it? It would be interesting [Polish "ciekawe"] to know whether the "Dobroczynność" has even an inkling of it.
So, whose fault is this? As it happens, I believe too much in the innocence and honesty of the actual[?] editor, Mr. Kahan [Kohn], to accuse him too of the above; therefore one wants to ask him: how can you breathe in such a polluted air? Why don't you slam the door behind you, so that the public scandal may explode once and for all.
Yechiel Feiner.
Hatchalat Sefer Celebration in Königshütte

[Upper Silesia — Königshütte; community life.] This past[?] Tuesday a festive evening for the beginning of the writing of a Torah scroll (hatchalat sefer) took place in the beautifully decorated hall of the "Mizrachi" in Königshütte [Królewska Huta, today Chorzów].
The chairman, Mr. Waksman, welcomes those present, the guests from Będzin — Messrs. Oppenheim, Granek, Dafner — and Mr. Zimberknap[?] from Pabianice. The floor is given to Rabbi Dr. Kalberg, who speaks on current affairs; then the floor goes to the rabbinical judge (moreh tzedek) R' Yosele Blumenfeld, who stresses that the hatchalat sefer is celebrated on Shushan Purim because in the Megillah we read "kiymu ve-kiblu" (they confirmed and accepted), so today one must fulfil the last commandment of the Torah, "And you, write for yourselves this Torah" [as printed; the verse reads "Now therefore write ye this song for you"].
On behalf of the "B'nai B'rith Lodge" Mr. Pluch greets the gathering, and Cantor Zhupovitch [Żupowicz?] beautifully sings several compositions.
After the writing of the letters there is a banquet with the participation of "select individuals"; Mr. Granek (Będzin) as well as Cantor Zhupovitch entertain[?] the company at richly laid tables until 2 o'clock at night.
Yitzchak.

Thursday's session of the city council opens with honouring the late French Marshal Foch.
Then the interpellation of the PPS [Polish Socialist Party] club is dealt with, which demands that Councillor Żelawski [?] be excluded from the city council, because he allowed himself, at a time when a PPS councillor left the hall, to shout: “Thieves are going out!”

Olkusz — Eretz Israel Evening.
[Olkusz — Zionism.]
On Monday evening, in the beautifully blue-and-white decorated hall of the “Artisans' Association”, a meeting took place with the Eretz Israel delegate of the Keren Kayemet, Advocate Banfeld. The hall was overfilled with members of “Tzeirei Mizrachi”, “HaShachar”, older Zionists and plain listeners. Mr. Zylberberg gave the opening address and gave the floor to the distinguished guest, Advocate Banfeld of Tel Aviv.
For 3 hours the speaker gave a lecture rich in content, depicting Jewish life in the Diaspora in the past, present and future. After the lecture a Keren Kayemet “gdud” [unit] was founded of representatives of “HaShachar”, “Tzeirei Mizrachi” and older Zionists.

Dąbrowa—Hakoach 3:1.
The Będzin "Hakoach" played on Sunday for the first time this season. Its opponent was the second-class "Dąbrowa". "Hakoach" took the field with three reserve players in place of Szyszek [?] and Jankielewicz, and still had a great advantage over its opponent, winning the match 3:1.
After a fine combination by Goldsztajn, Wekslman shoots the first goal in the 20th minute. From a similar position Gutman shoots the second goal. The half-time ends 2:0 for "Hakoach". After the start of the second half "Hakoach" had an even greater advantage, but without result.
During a fatal run-out by the goalkeeper, the inside-right shoots one goal for the visitors.
Soon afterwards "Hakoach" gets a penalty kick, which Bechman converts very nicely. Goldsztajn is technically good, but he is a lazy player. Referee Szyszek [?] indecisive.
Policja—Makkabi 1:0.
A draw would better have expressed the course of the game, which was very exciting and interesting. After attacks on both sides the first half ends without result.

Despite the greatest effort "Makkabi" did not manage to equalize.
Distinguished for Makkabi were Prachcehajn [?], Chariton and Szmidt.

Esteemed Editor of the "Zaglembier Tsaytung".
Allow us, through your esteemed paper, to express our sharpest protest against the owners of the theatres "Nowości" and "Korso" [?] for allowing themselves to charge an illegal 20 groszy extra for tickets to the Yiddish theatre performances.
As if it were not enough that tickets here are dearer than in other towns in Poland, they also allow themselves, in an unheard-of manner, to take a gratuitous 20 groszy extra.
We hereby point out that the Będzin Jewish theatre-goer is not yet fair game and will not let himself be exploited twice over, but will find his rights another way, to compel the sale of tickets at the fixed price set by the Magistrate.

Lawlessness, Lawlessness on All Fronts!

[Sosnowiec and Będzin — local press; the "coal campaign" money; polemic.] (What has become of the vanished people's groszy? — How is this outrage being answered?)
Once they would not have had the strength to raise themselves to the level of existence; they would not have had the courage to show their face to the public, and had they had the nerve to go out into the street, they would have been stoned, they would have been wiped out of society, people would have shunned these unscrupulous persons for their ugly[?] deeds, for the boundless[?] humiliations they inflict with their acts on the Jewish public and on Jewish honour.
It began in Będzin: a "star" rose on the shining horizon, salvation came to the whole of Israel, the Torah was rescued; they proclaimed themselves Torah-loyal, an organ of the "Agudah" [Agudat Israel] that would not allow the "sinners", who had become so naturalised in the Jewish street, to keep Jews from being pious. And at the very time when they took upon themselves[?] with such fervour [the role of] "God's kushyure"[?] and shouted that vengeance must be taken on the Jews who do not walk in God's righteous ways, at the time when they demonstrated with signs and wonders that the "Zaglembier Tsaytung" preaches hatred and enmity against those who are not ashamed to be called by the name Jew, that we want to uproot everything that is Jewish — just then the bought souls stumbled, and the poor things were caught printing their holy organ on the Sabbath; and after every inquiry and investigation, after the whole bunch of "drapshchesy" [rogues] had tried to wriggle out, the truth was confirmed after all and the glitter vanished. And whoever had a good eye could see that the bought souls began to drift onto another line and pretended to forget the holy "little Torah"; but since they could not get through to the masses, they ran back into their [home?] — yet by then it was already too late: the genuine, sincere pious Jews had seen their face and had distanced themselves from that rag.
When they saw that things were bitter, that people no longer wanted to give even the monthly gulden [złoty] as a donation, they sent for an editor "from a big place", and perhaps with the help of the Blessed Name he will save the honour of the Torah — I really meant to say: of the "newspaper".
Then[?] what did we actually come to talk about? Who cares that some rag lives on beggarly foundations? In essence the question is a fair one; but the trouble is precisely this, that beggary is a contagious disease that drags along people who never imagined they would sink to such a disgusting level.
We too have in Sosnowiec a newspaper which in fact pretended to be founded on other foundations, although it was launched at once without knowing itself in what manner.
For what role can a newspaper play among the population when it does not itself know what it wants and what it came for? Who can reckon with such an organ, which has nothing to say to anyone, or the opposite — which perhaps promises everyone everything... But what are those promises worth, written yesterday by people who the very next day found themselves on the other side of the door, their places taken by others? For there the editors are thrown out and replaced every day with the speed of cinematograph pictures. There is already a saying in Sosnowiec that only young men with dowries have a place there, and as soon as the dowry has been buried they are thrown out and other applicants are needed in their place.
And when no "dowry young men" turn up, subsidies are sought from anyone at all. They were already on the point of taking in the "Agudah" together with the whole God-fearing Będzin "editorial staff", but as soon as it was seen that someone wanted to marry without a dowry, the match fell through... So off they run "kame-kame-tir"[?], now to the Zionists and Mizrachists, now to the artisans, and to whomever will have them. And therein lies the secret of why every issue has a different face. Every issue cries: you can buy me. We will give you everything in the world, only hand the coin over[?] here; give [it] there — whoever places an advertisement thereby earns the privilege of seeing his articles printed entirely free of charge. You understand: articles are now thrown in with advertisements, and everyone can praise himself to the skies...
This too would not have concerned us, even though the printed word has fallen to such a low state that every creature of flesh and blood who has not suffered or ached for it, who cares nothing for its birth pangs and labour pains, comes along, touches every holy thing and defiles it.
But they went further still. They laid hands[?] on public money — and what money? Money that had been designated to warm, in the great frosts, the poorest of the poor, the widows and orphans who cannot afford to buy a piece of coal.
During the severest frosts the public workers of Sosnowiec joined together and created a campaign to supply the freezing poor with coal. And now the editorial board informs us that it is not responsible for this or that member who took the coal money, since they have already been removed[?] from the editorial board. And those removed declare that they did not take the money. It goes without saying that even if they had taken it, the editorial board would still be responsible for its people.
But the question arises: to whom did the committee entrust this sacred money, which was taken from the people? How does the committee dare at all to allow such money to be touched and to let itself be used with it? After all, very respectable people were occupied with the campaign — so how did they let themselves be compromised like this? To us, to the town, the young men of the rag — whom, by the way, nobody knows, and who are already far from honesty by the very fact that they dared to touch such people's groszy — are not the ones responsible; responsible to the town are the people who stood at the head of this useful campaign. Why then do we not hear what measures they are taking against this shameful outrage, which must not be hushed up?
Naturally, in the old days such persons would themselves have fled into a mouse-hole the moment[?] they were caught at such a piece of work, from which every honest person recoils.
But today it is a different world. Today people have, on top of that, the courage and the nerve to come and preach morals to others and give their opinion, regardless of the fact that they themselves sit in the dock.
Yes, we have lost all shame in our present times, so that everything in the world is permitted; and therefore the committee of the coal campaign must come forward here and tell the town what happened and how it is responding to this shameful deed.
Selekt.
Trifles

[Satirical feuilleton — Russian Jews; Einstein; Lenin.] By Pini Baal-Lashon.

1.
Matzos for Russian Jews.
And since we are already talking about matzos, it is impossible to keep silent about our Russian brethren.
And precisely towards them there still prevails among us a merciless coldness.
When the "Matzah Fund" for Russian Jews was announced, we thought that so much money would immediately start flowing that there would not be enough hands to count it.
But meanwhile we do not yet see it; the public is still cold.
The public has in general grown cold to giving.
The "Yevseks" [members of the Yevsektsiya, the Jewish section of the Communist Party] in Russia will not suffer over it. They cannot stand the sight of this "counter-revolutionary matzah" anyway, and it will give them great pleasure when Russian Jews have to eat chametz.
But we know the truth, that Russian Jews have no chametz either.
So if one is sending — better matzos, and indeed right away — quickly! quickly!...

2.
Poor Professor Einstein!...
A real pity on poor Professor Albert Einstein, bless him.
A whole world goes and pounces on one man and wants — may it befall the enemies of Zion — to shorten his days.
What do they have against him and what do they want from him, a "Steiner" [?] [possibly a pun on his name, "stone"]?!
A man sits there in his innermost chambers making calculations about the earth, the heavens, stars and planets — whom, God forbid, is he harming? What has that to do with the simple world?
And out of curiosity [?] they give him no peace; he cannot drink a glass of tea calmly.
And now, when he turns fifty, they did not even let him stay at home and celebrate his birthday with his household, and he had to flee somewhere else.
This proves to us once again that the less the public understands someone, the more highly he is esteemed.
Many great men became great only because they said things the public did not understand.
Many have toiled to say incomprehensible things in order to become famous.
And that, it seems, is why we have so many incomprehensible authors and poets today, because they think that this will make them great.
The trouble is, however, that the public does understand them — that they themselves do not understand themselves.
The proof: all those incomprehensible authors and poets are left in peace, so they may celebrate even their hundredth birthday.
And that is why it is really better to speak like a human being, so that everyone understands.
Professor Einstein, poor man, has no other choice. God punished him with a great mind, so he cannot speak otherwise.
Well, so for that one must make his life a misery? An injustice, truly. People have no fairness...

3.
The Embalmed Lenin.
The newspapers tell us that the two doctors who embalmed Lenin four years ago uncovered and examined him this week, and it turned out that Lenin is still as fresh and strong as on the first day after his death.
Well then, we will not ask any questions as to why the Communists, who always mocked the bourgeois custom of deifying a person, themselves went and embalmed their leader Lenin, just like Pharaoh once in Egypt, and laid him in a glass case, so that the little goyim may come to bow down and pray to his holy body.
For they, the Communists, did not do only this. They have done, and "are doing", other, worse things, just like the tsars of old.
They have an excuse: for the sake of Communism everything is permitted!
But I wonder why the gang embalmed only Lenin and not "Leninism". Above all they should have embalmed "Leninism" and laid it in a glass case, because in a few years probably not a trace of it will remain.
But, it seems, they have not yet invented such a "balm" there...
