The Chaos (Tohu va-vohu).

(What do the prospects for the future look like in the Będzin City Council?)
When one reads the reports of the Będzin City Council, and one watches the debates and the all-sorts of votes, which are all annulled at one go; when one stands at a distance and watches the various intrigues, tricks and super-contrivances — at such a moment one wants to run away far, far, because the air is stifling and it becomes hard to breathe...
We understand that one may engage in politics; we also understand that one sometimes has to conduct behind-the-scenes politics — but all this is said [?] for when one knows how to do it, when one understands it. But when one understands nothing of all this, when one has not yet gone through any school, when one is not yet experienced, one makes mistakes constantly and meets failure at every step.
Half the councillors are Jews, so it was only sensible to try to take the upper hand — the Jewish councillors did indeed try to play first fiddle in the City Council. But what do we see? We see a defeat at every opportunity, the greatest failure in all negotiations. The question arises: what is the reason? Why do constant losses arise? One need not go far, however; no great erudition is required to get to the bottom of it all. It is plain and simple: most of our councillors have no idea how to run a municipal economy; they have learned nothing at all and want to learn nothing at all. On top of that they are torn and split on every question, and each one acts on his own hand, does things on his own responsibility, and they take no account whatever of the community. These people have no awareness at all that as representatives they must reckon with the public, must remember those who sent them there. They are under the impression that they were sent into the City Council and entrusted with the seats in order to sit on them and do whatever they please and whatever is more comfortable and pleasant for them.
And this with such colossal weight [?] — with a fifty-percent share of Jewish councillors.
Before every election to the municipal self-government we pointed out that we need conscious, intelligent representatives more than many people taken off the street, who understand nothing of municipal affairs and have no idea how to run a local economy — yet they do have the sense to count themselves among those who must play a role in public life, and they want nothing less than to measure themselves against great men, never noticing that one cannot even call them "little men".
We understand that it is good to get people from the street who are something, who let themselves be taught and want to understand, so that in time they will learn. But they come as ignoramuses (amei ha-aretz) and say that it is they who are the useful elements we need, that it is they who have been called to bring us salvation. And when we take, on the one hand, the arrogance and the coarseness of these representatives of ours, and on the other the mistakes they make — it weighs constantly on the heart.
It goes without saying that this helplessness and lack of sophistication of our municipal emissaries is exploited on the spot by the Christian councillors, who thus win position after position.
We know perfectly well that we have sunk socially when we sometimes look at who represents the Jewish community; we also know how far we have fallen when we consider by what [?] means people have pushed their way in there. We would overlook all of that if these people wanted to learn something — then at least we would know that eventually we would have some satisfaction from them. But the worst of it is that they persuade themselves that they are already the top of the heap, that all they do is good and fine, and that they bear no responsibility towards the public. Therein lies our tragedy. And if it goes on like this, if these people keep acting on their own responsibility just as they please, then the prospects are anything but brilliant, and we have every chance of sinking in the field of the municipal economy.
Our better representatives must by no means allow things to go on like a ship without a rudder, where everyone can do as he likes. These people must be taught by force and convinced that constant defeats are not permissible; and however little they may wish to look at themselves, they must be told that they are fully responsible to the whole town, and that otherwise a day will come when they will have to render an account to all the Jewish voters.
Let them draw a moral lesson; let them see how the Christian councillors unite, how black and red go together tied as one when it is a matter of [?] breaking through a Jewish position.
If one is not ashamed before oneself, if these people do not act like our [?], if they take no account of the defeats caused because of them — let them then be ashamed before their Christian colleagues, who exert themselves at every opportunity so that we lose position after position, and they themselves accordingly gain.
Let the people who have been seated on their public chairs be reminded that, after all, they are not sitting in a shtibl somewhere at home in their association, where they consider themselves rulers. Let them be told that, sitting in the City Council, one must have a little awareness and responsibility towards the voters, and on top of that also a little tact...
R. Les.
Before the Wedding and After the Wedding

[Humour — dialogue feuilleton; love and marriage.]
Before the wedding.
He: My dearest, my sweet, my most beautiful!
She: My beloved, my good one, my fine one, my faithful one!
He: How happy I am when I see you!
She: I waited for you the whole day. Every moment I looked at the clock and out of the window; I could not wait so long.
He (embracing her): My dearest! Early this morning, when I opened my eyes, I thought: oh, if only I could run off to you now, come into your room quietly... you are asleep, and I lay my hand lightly on your eyes, and you wake with a start, and I say: "Who is it?" And you say at once: "It's Benny." And I say: "You guessed it, indeed."
She: So why didn't you do it?
He: Child. I had to go to work, after all.
She: But if you hadn't had to go to work today, would you have done it? Wouldn't you have been ashamed in front of my mother to come into my bedroom so early, while I was still asleep?
He: I don't know whether I would have gone, but in the morning, just when I had to go to work, such a thought came to me. But I immediately said to myself: "No, Benny, you must wait until the evening to see your Pesele. You must work, you must save money so that you can get married and make a life with your Pesele."
She: You know, Benny, I often think that we won't need any money; the main thing, after all, is that one feels happy even without a penny. What is money anyway? It's only a means of buying pleasures with it. But when we have so much pleasure when we are together, what do we need money for?
He: You speak like an angel, Pesele. But it is not angels who go about in this world, only ordinary people, and when one lives among people, one has to have a little money.
She: Don't mention the word "money", I beg you.
He: You are right, Pesele, why talk about money when we can talk about our love, which is stronger and better than anything!

After the wedding.
He: Take the child. I must go out for a little air; I've worked the whole day.
She: Go to blazes [Yiddish curse; lit. "I have you in the ground"] — you lack air? You can't live without air? The whole day I hold the child,
He: And the whole day I work, after all!
She: You should see other people's husbands, how they wash the floors and polish up the house.
He: If I do all those things, what will you do then?
She: Right away he tells me that he works! What do I get from your working? The great sums you earn! Other people's husbands earn...
He: I don't want to hear what others earn. I do what I can. I — — —
She: And the pleasures I have with you! I don't even have a coat with you!
He: What do you mean? You only just bought yourself a coat!
She: You took me[?] — such a pauper, such a nothing. Why, I could have had the richest bridegroom! I — — —
He: You're a shrew, a harpy[?], you make my life a misery. Go to your rich bridegroom, do what you like, only leave me in peace. Good night!
She: Good night — go and be buried!
Tuvia Shmeykhl.
His New Landlady

[Literature — short story.]
(A story).
By Yitzchak Blum.

After living for a few weeks in his new room, Steinman began to suspect that his landlady lived alone, without her husband. The suspicion came to him when he noticed in the mornings that apart from him no other man went out to work. At the washstand hung two toothbrushes — a woman's and a child's — and this confirmed his suspicion.

To convince himself still further that he was not mistaken, on a few evenings, coming from work, he did not go straight to the restaurant to eat but went home instead. All that time [in the evening] the men are at home, and so it is the best time to find out.

Why he actually cared so desperately ["it goes into his life," as the Yiddish idiom has it] to find out whether she did or did not live with her husband was not clear even to himself. Possibly [?], had he known that they lived together, he would not have thought about it at all. But the uncertainty troubled him, as if he had some connection with her private life.

* * *

Steinman had not yet even taken a good look at his new landlady. His room was entirely separate. Right at the entrance from the corridor were the door and the washroom, so that he had not even had a chance to meet her. But the impression of her that had remained with him from the minute she opened the door for him when he rented the room was enough to "captivate" him, to stir his indifference, to fill his heart with a longing to see her as much and as often as possible.

She was somewhat taller than middle height, her figure full of lively feminine charm, her face clear and bright with a summer-blossoming grace, eyes blue, laughing and alluring, lips juicy, sensuous, and her hair golden blond.

Since then he had not seen her again.

Whenever he came to his room everything was in order: the bed made nicely and cleanly, the towels clean, so that he was completely satisfied.

The door of his room he always found shut, although a few times he had deliberately left it open. He could not understand why she did this, and it annoyed him. "After all, he is not living in a prison" — he thought — "the door may surely stay open sometimes"...

It often occurred to him that she did this only as a pretence — that she shut the door every time he left it open, also on purpose, [so that] he would become curious [one word damaged in print: "[—]t"]; closedness [?] and concealment arouse a desire to find out what is going on there on the other side of the door. It intrigued him greatly; but sure that she did it for this reason he was not. He could just as well think that by shutting his door she was giving him to understand, in a delicate way, that apart from the room in which he lived he had no further connection with the house.

That apart from him there was no other man in the house he was by now certain, because he had never heard a man's voice. Her voice he did hear. She talked to her child, and often sang it little songs. She had a soft, warm voice. She sang mostly Russian songs, which would seize him to the depths of his soul. Something of such sadness and longing was felt in them that they would wring his heart, rouse romantic feelings in him, so that he often wanted to open the door, run in to her, catch her in his arms [printed "zeyge" for "zeyne"] and cover her with kisses. He had to exert strong self-control to hold himself back and not actually do it.

* * *

Once he happened to meet her at the entrance to the house. Her little boy, blond and charming like his mother, was standing at her side.

When she saw him she was glad.

"Good that you have come just now," she said contentedly. "I forgot to take the key with me and cannot get into the house."

"I am truly sorry for the unpleasantness you have had," he said with regret, while in his heart he felt happy that he could meanwhile get a good look at her and exchange a few words with her.

He unlocked the door and they went into the house together.

"Thank you!" she said cheerfully [? printed "freygligh"], and went off with the child to her rooms.

Steinman remained standing, bewildered, not knowing what to do — whether to follow her or not. The long corridor that stretched to her rooms was dark, and he did not see her again.

Downcast, he went into his room and thought with pain that he had perhaps [missed] the only opportunity to talk to her in a friendlier and closer way [the verb is missing in print].

What the devil had brought him here [?] — he was angry [?] with himself — so he is to live here, so near her, and yet remain isolated and a stranger; what kind of punishment is that? How will he be able to bear it?

* * *

In the evening Steinman packed his things and got ready to move out. He felt that he could not and need not live here any longer.

He considered how, in what way, he should tell her of his decision to move out. He could actually go in and simply explain to her that he had to go away, or tell her some other excuse.

But it at once occurred to him that he should tell her nothing at all: he would leave without even leaving her a note — and let it annoy her, perhaps hurt her a little.

Having decided to act thus, he felt a certain sense of revenge, although it seemed strange even to himself that he — a stranger who had moved into a strange house because he needs somewhere to live, and who gets for his money a comfortable room to sleep in and spend his time in — should still be thinking of revenge. What did he actually have against her? What wrong had she ever done him?

"Such a young, pretty woman, who lives [printed "saoynt"] alone besides, without her husband, may not take in a man as a lodger" — he tried to answer himself.

When he was already about to leave, he noticed on his little table a letter addressed to him.

He quickly tore open the envelope and found the following lines:

"Dear Sir! —
I hereby let you know that you should look for another room. Your unfriendliness and your constantly hiding yourself in your room, your avoiding any encounter with the woman at whose place you live, make me believe that you do not feel at home here.
Helene Winer."

Steinman opened his eyes wide, broke into a smile, and slowly began to unpack his things again.
Our Panorama

[Zagłębie — satirical feuilleton; Pilica, Königshütte, Dąbrowa.]
(Pharaoh's decree is annulled. — A "mill" occupied [a pun on "mohel"]. — "Vekharos" sung in exile. — Three categories of Jews. — Sabbath "concerts". — A search by the "Tse'irey Emuney" — Eating chocolate before prayers. — A mirror of a "hefker-yung" [a lawless type]. — Dancing with "Kraft".)

Every town has its own worries, every place its own troubles ["klopotn", kłopoty]. For instance, the magistrates [town councils] in Zagłębie have "taken fright" at the danger of a flood, merchants tremble at the deluge of protests [protested bills], and Pilica [Pilica] has the same worry as our Pharaoh of old...
The only difference is this: Pharaoh decreed "every son that is born ye shall cast into the river" — a boy! — throw him into the water; whereas the Pilica Hasidim have ruled that "no circumcision may take place if the rabbi is to be sandek [godfather]"...
For quite a long time now the Ger Hasidim in Pilica have been waging a fierce battle against the local rabbi — incidentally a very decent Jew, a scholar, of distinguished lineage; he has only one "blot" on him, on account of which the Ger Hasidim cannot bear him.
— The rabbi travels to Aleksander [Aleksandrów, the Aleksander Hasidic court]...
The "war" against the rabbi is being waged with full force, following the system of the coalition in its day [?]: the war leaders have "occupied the munitions factories", taken the mohel "prisoner" ["plen", niewola], and barricaded the "enemy" — the rabbi — so that he could not get to the Chair of Elijah the Prophet...
And it came to pass, on a bright, fine morning, that the "terrible" news spread through the shtetl like lightning: "a male child has been born"...
The news caused an uproar on the "war fronts" [?]; the general staffs went into action, and it was immediately ordered that a guard be posted at the mohel's house to watch whether he would secretly hand over his "weapon" to the "enemy"... But unexpectedly, on Friday afternoon, the rabbi received "reinforcements": from Będzin [Będzin] came the father of the ba'al brit [the baby's father's father], also a Ger Hasid, but on the matter of the sandek honour he was as neutral as the Swiss state during the last war, so that the chances of the rabbi being sandek grew stronger...
The Ger general staff held an urgent consultation on the situation after Kabbalat Shabbat, at which it was resolved that "if their comrade, the guest from Będzin, does not change his decision that the 'enemy' should receive the sandek honour, none of the Ger fellowship shall come to the [Shalom] Zakhar"...
The "rozkaz" [order] was carried out: instead of "Shalom Zakhar" there was "Milchama [war] Zakhar". But that could still be endured; the situation grew worse on the day of the circumcision, when the Ger Hasidim "did not let them pray in their place". So the ba'al brit, with the young mother's father, an Aleksander Hasid, went off to the Aleksander shtibl — and there, too, they were not let in. "How so! — the Aleksander Hasidim argued — the Ger people are on bad terms with you, and you come to us? That won't do"...
Having no choice, the ba'al brit went [?] with his relatives to the beis medresh, and with a mohel from Wolbrom [Wolbrom] brought in by the police they sang "Vekharos" [the circumcision hymn] "in a foreign place"...
— — —
About "the same Yente, only veiled differently" they write to us from Königshütte [Królewska Huta, today Chorzów].
The Jewish community in Königshütte consists of three categories: German "Yahudim" [Juden], who "vollen" [sic, wollen — want] to have no community with the "Polish swine"; Galician Jews, known for their "fine qualities and good deeds"; and last but not least — Polish Jews, emigrants from Wolbrom, Pilica, Żarnowiec [Żarnowiec] and other similar "residences".
The Polish ones have "acclimatised" to some extent in the new settlement and become "European", especially the women, who do business on the Sabbath; but they do not, God forbid, forget that on this holy day one must wear the special Sabbath wigs on one's head.
Between the last two categories of Jews, the Galician and the Polish, there is no peace. They have rented a large hall for a house of prayer, where they gather [?] every Sabbath, when there is a little time to make merry...
So that the "entertainment programme" should be amusing enough ["amvirnd", sic], the worshippers have divided themselves into two camps:
— on the right the Galician wing, and on the left — the Polish.
Each camp has its own gabbai, whose office is to "naznaczać" [appoint] who shall lead the prayers before the amud. This point is guarded by the following system: whoever leads Shacharit may not lead Musaf. Well, the Polish camp is tolerant — even the biggest "drąg" [pole; i.e. lout] may lead the prayers at the amud, and they swallow it in silence; but conversely, when a prayer-leader from the "Kongresówka" [Congress Poland] takes his place at the amud, the heavens open: all sorts of miniature voices of cats, crows and similar "snakes" are heard from the Galician camp.
The only consolation — writes our correspondent — is that the moreh hora'ah [rabbinic decisor] R' Yosele is at last becoming a permanent resident there, and it is hoped that he will finally call off the "Sabbath concerts"...
— — —
Since we have come to speak of "Sabbath concerts", one must also mention the heroes of the "Tse'irey Emuney" in Dąbrowa [Dąbrowa Górnicza].
The "leadership" of the local "Tse'irey Emuney" had long been receiving secret information that some of their members were infected with "civilisation".
So the leadership held a consultation to find a way of establishing whether the suspicions were well founded.
At the consultation opinions were divided. Some said there was no need for any investigation and inquiry — it is an explicit law that "at the mouth of two witnesses shall a matter be established": if two young members testify that So-and-so son of So-and-so sang the tune of "Bubliczki" [a popular street song], he must be put outside the camp.
But the "democratic" tendency won, which held that one should not behave like the zealots of old, but that the matter must be "zbadać" [examined].
— How? A stroke of genius! On the Sabbath, after the Torah reading, a search of the coat-skirts and pockets ["poltns"] shall be carried out.
And so it was. Last Sabbath, after the "Chok" [?], a special commission searched all the pockets, and — be astonished, O heavens! — they did indeed find on one young member
? ?
— half a bar of chocolate...
The young man tried to defend himself [printed "fertayrinen"]: it is a sample, his own work; but it helped little; there was a "gevalt", a racket as at a fire. At first there was shouting, later slaps were counted out, and the end of it was that because of that piece of chocolate Musaf was not prayed at all...
But it was all worth it — what else? Allow a lawless world? Come to prayers with full pockets?!...
— — —
The Żarki [Żarki] Hasidim in Dąbrowa come into the "shtibl" on the Sabbath with empty pockets, and nevertheless their Sabbath rest has been disturbed.
Their Oneg Shabbat was disturbed by none other than our master "Reb Hefker" [Mr. Lawlessness], who dances about our little world free and easy — everywhere: in the synagogue, the kehilla, the editorial offices — and reaches even the Żarki Hasidim in Dąbrowa.
"Reb Hefker", in the person of a landlord who is a real "gem", cast his sly eyes on the Żarki "shtibl" and took a fancy to evicting them.
How? Rent — they pay; harmful [?] tenants? — not that either; so what is to be done?
But never fear for "Reb Hefker". He — when he wants to, he can. On the Sabbath after prayers he went into the "shtibl", opened the Holy Ark and "took" the Torah scroll.
— No Torah, no Hasidim..
Sabbath at dusk, the Hasidim are saying Ashrei and U-va le-Tziyon with devotion; the prayer-leader opens the Holy Ark with the sweet chant of "Va-yehi bi-n'soa".
— Huh? The scroll isn't there?...
With curious looks everyone runs to the Holy Ark and sees — it is the bitter truth: the Torah has been stolen...
The poor Hasidim had to do the same [printed "selbe"] as when "the congregation has no etrog", while "Reb Hefker" sat somewhere rolling with laughter — hee, hee, hee, "I played a trick on them, I took away their little Torah"...
— — —
Hasidic Jews, and especially those of the Żarki dynasty, swallowed such a villainy like pills, in silence; but the Dąbrowa "Kraft" cannot stand for pechules [?] to happen, and the culprits get their sentence with "koach and Kraft" [might and main; Kraft = strength]...
The members of "Kraft" are very observant of two commandments: the commandment of eating a great deal on the eve of Yom Kippur, and of rejoicing on Purim "until one cannot tell the difference"...
So "Kraft" organised a "Purim ball" and invited the dancing youth of the neighbouring towns — Sosnowiec [Sosnowiec], Będzin and so on — and there was gladness, "for the Jews"...
At the ball the decree of Ahasuerus was put into effect:
— "that every man should bear rule in his own house"!
That is, assimilation must not prevail: young people from each town are to dance with their own engaged "Vashtis"...
But the reactionary decree provoked a "social revolution", and
— a fight broke out...
It was no petty little quarrel, but on a broad scale, in the "European" manner; there was no lack of "all good things" — even revolver shots rang out in the streets...
Quite right, upon my life: let the nations of the world not boast that revolvers go off at their celebrations — their monopoly is over; "Kraft" has already outdone them in this respect...
— Bravo "Kraft"!
Ben Amotz.
The Rebbe's Son (28)

[Serialized historical novel — the 1648 massacres, Chmielnicki and the Cossacks; installment 28.]
A historical Jewish novel by Yankev (Jakub) Cymerman.

But a bang of the shammes's hand on the lectern [?] silenced everyone in one single second. The synagogue was now quiet again, and the grey-haired [?] rabbi, the "Tosafot Yom Tov" [R. Yom Tov Lipmann Heller, rabbi of Kraków], gave Shimshon a nod to go on with his story:

"For six days," Shimshon began in his strained [?] and ringing voice, "we lay in the field facing Chmielnicki's bands, not far from Kraków, all in all eight hours' journey away, but it still did not come to open war. Neither of the two sides wanted to start a general battle. The enemy did not do it because he was still waiting for the arrival of his haidamaks, who were still in Ukraine; we, for our part, felt that we did not have enough men to be able to overcome the foe, and so we had to wait for fresh troops. By vile and shameful machinations and political intrigues the enemies of our beloved prince Wiśniowiecki managed to arrange that not he, the best and ablest commander Poland now possesses, should become the commander of all the soldiers, but Prince Dominik Zasławski and his two lieutenants, Koniecpolski and Niklas [Mikołaj] Ostroróg. These three noblemen, quite incompetent men, who had now been placed at the head of the entire Polish fighting force, helped our beloved prince very little, or better said, not at all, and sent him no soldiers to reinforce his troops against the enemy's great numerical superiority. When our prince realized the situation he was in, he decided that, come what may, even if it should cost him his own life, he would not withdraw from here until he had first fought a battle with the enemy and tried to destroy him.

"This morning at dawn," Shimshon continued after a short pause for breath, "we noticed that the enemy camp was suddenly coming alive, and we already understood that they were preparing for an open battle. We ourselves were also glad of it, because we all wanted what must and inevitably will come to be over as quickly as possible. We were not mistaken. Soon we saw the enemy drawing up his army and his men taking up their positions. Our prince Wiśniowiecki did the same. Beforehand he had spoken to all of us with few, but true and heartfelt warm words, and had given us endurance [printed "with an endurance", probably for "courage and endurance"] for the war awaiting us. We, the Jews, were a camp six thousand men strong, and we were led by the young prince Wiśniowiecki. We formed the right wing of the battle order; the left wing was commanded by the old prince himself. Right against the centre the enemy had from the very start directed his entire fighting force. He did it with such speed and such great pressure that only after a terrible struggle could he be driven back to his earlier positions. But the enemy did not rest; he repeated his attack along the whole line, yet his main force he still directed against the centre. Now a dreadful battle developed, but the enemy's superior force was much greater than ours. It cracked and banged on all sides. Their muskets and cannons kept up a ceaseless fire on our soldiers. There was such terrible smoke and fumes that one could hardly bear it, and on top of that there was incessant stabbing, striking and breaking with swords and spears; it was so terrible that I cannot possibly retell it with my own mouth. So passed the first two hours of the war. A good many of our men already lay dead or wounded on the battlefield, but one still could not tell where in the world one stood, whether we were winning or losing. And then suddenly our middle point, the centre, began to fall back, and we all began to feel that we were losing and would all soon be annihilated.

"But at that very minute," Shimshon turned to the rabbi of Kraków, "your son, David, seized the banner, and in a mighty voice he cried out to us, the Jews of Kraków, whose leader he was: 'After me! We must win or die!' At a sharp gallop we all charged the enemy's left wing; they received us with terrible fire. Several of us fell dead or were wounded. But that could not stop us; we fell upon the enemies with a wild, superhuman fury of slaughter and heroic courage. We so cut them down and smashed them that the whole thing lasted only a few minutes, and we saw them turn their backs on us and begin to flee in wild haste. In this way the enemy's centre broke up. When our men saw this, they gained fresh courage and new endurance. From thousands of throats burst cries of victory, which confused and frightened the enemy still more. When our prince saw what we Jews had now accomplished, he hurled himself with his troops with such force upon the enemy's centre that the enemy, although he was in very great numerical superiority, could not withstand this terrible onslaught and began to fall back with heavy losses. But the prince understood well what he now had to do. He did not let go of the enemy any more. He promptly joined both wings with his centre, and with united force pressed the enemy so hard that he had to withdraw in order [?] from his positions.

"Now a terrible panic broke out among the enemy," Shimshon went on joyfully. "There they did nothing but run; they lost their heads so completely that all order and discipline ceased at once. They did not retreat in any kind of order, they did not pull back so as to be able to regroup and perhaps once more put up resistance or even become the attackers — they simply scattered in all directions."

Mother and Child in the Tram

[Essay — attitude to women; manners.] There are customs in the life of society which at first sight seem outdated. One senses in them a forcedness, a manicured artificiality, a submission to a dead fetish — and yet it is not always so. The very same customs, applied in the right place and at the desired time, are turned into a virtue, into an act of pure humanity.
This preface concerns the courtesy which we men show to women. We always give the woman precedence. In society, in the street, in the theatre, in all public places we clear the way for the woman, we open the door for her so that she may go out first.
We yield her our place at the window in the post office, in the bank, in the office. We pick up her dropped handkerchief so that she should not have to bend and overstrain her supple, elastic body — in short, we do all sorts of things which are not always necessary, and more than once they betray blind submission, empty foppishness [?] and idolatry in our attitude to the woman that goes beyond the bounds of ordinary politeness. [But] when the "readiness to serve" really turns into a kindness to the woman — oh, then we are in no such hurry to display our refinement, and our "chivalry" hides somewhere under our skin.
What has been said applies especially to us Jews, an old oriental race with firmly rooted habits, customs and manners, a people too serious to be superficial and affected [?] in its attitude to women. A people whose conception of woman as mother, human being and wife has been crystallised and formed in its culture of thousands of years, and finally a people whose language is too simple, too plain and intimate to be used for polished rhetorical bombast in the relation between man and woman.
No; we Jews were never used to this, but — here comes the big "only". All this was once. Nowadays, when Jewish life is changed and altered as in a kaleidoscope and does not lag behind fashion, behind time and place — nowadays, when we adapt ourselves with such fervour and exaggeration to the customs of Europe — nowadays our attitude to women has become exaggerated in an unnatural way, and everything unnatural inevitably takes on caricatured forms.
Our youth already knows, thank God, the art of bowing before a woman, of kissing her hands with the falseness of a servant — only one thing our youth still does not have, or has lost — yes, lost, because once, once Jewish youth did have it — that sense, that understanding — for the woman as mother.
We get into the tram; the car is packed, there is nowhere to sit, all the seats are taken. Well, we stand, there is no choice. But now, at the next stop, a woman with a child in her arms climbs onto the tram. Everyone stays seated, nobody makes room. Among the passengers sit young people — they stay seated. The mother with the child remains standing, the tram shakes, the mother grabs now at one person [?], now at another, she nearly falls — but the public stays seated, nobody gives up a place to her. Finally an elderly man thinks better of it — and a Christian, a Christian of all people, and be it even for a Jewish mother with a Jewish child in her arms — he gets up, yields his place to the woman and invites her simply, humanely, to sit down. The woman thanks him, she sits down, the old man remains standing and is shaken about, and only the youth, the fine, polished young men with stiff cuffs, dressed in suits after the latest fashion, the dandies, the intellectuals and whatnot — they stay seated.
And let it not be counted to our shame, we shall say it openly: in 90 cases out of a hundred it is precisely Jewish young men who stay seated, even, as said, if the woman with the child are Jewish. Christian young men, by contrast, will hesitate to stand up for the "żydówka" [Jewess], but — in 90 cases out of a hundred they will nevertheless get up and give the place to the woman, the mother with the child.
Where does this come from? It is the result of our exaggerated chasing after European customs; courtesy towards women turns among us into such a meaningless, empty habit that it makes one sick [?], and only from this stems the fact that it was once different among Jews [sic; apparently meant: that things are no longer as they once were among Jews]. To this bears witness the wonderful Talmudic legend about Rabbi Tarfon, who used to spread his hands on the floor so that his aged mother might tread softly. In this legend we see the reverence for the mother of the best of our people. This is not mere "courtesy", empty customs — this is humanity, exactly what the young people of our generation lack.
P. A.

The Life of the Jewish Students in Vienna
[Vienna — Jewish students; letter.] After the World War, Austria in general and the city of Vienna in particular lost much of their political authority. What remained were only the well-organised educational institutions in all fields, which still rank among the best in the world. — It goes without saying that the good institutions attract a large number of students from all over the world. More than 30 thousand students attend the Viennese colleges, among them 15—17 per cent Jews. The latter are organised among themselves exactly like the Christian students, in an organisation named the General Union of Jewish University Students "Judea" ("Judea"), to which belong all the professional associations, such as: medical students, technicians, world-trade students etc., the fraternities (corporations): Libanonia, Maccabaea, Unitas etc., and plain associations. Besides these there are also liberal organisations, to which the assimilationists belong; about the latter, however, we shall not speak now.
As we have already mentioned, professional associations belong to the general union, and they carry on a very successful cultural activity. In this field the "world traders" have lately especially distinguished themselves. A series of lectures held — on Hebrew and Yiddish literature, politics and political economy, science and art, as well as on the situation of the Jewish student body in other countries — was organised in exemplary fashion and had great success; this also caused the rector to begin to value highly the only Jewish representative at the "College for World Trade" [Hochschule für Welthandel]. The semester was concluded with a festive academy and a representative ball, attended by: the rector, Professor Ziegler, the professorial corps, the president of the Zionist Organisation Dr. L. Goldhammer, representatives of the Vienna kehilla and other prominent persons.
About the activity of other academic associations, as well as about the situation of the Jewish academic, we shall report in a second letter.
Z. L.
Vienna, 2 April 1929.

"The Seduced Woman" — a novel, a very gripping one, based on historical facts.
In the novel the writer depicts the inner experiences of a converted (apostate) woman who was led astray by missionaries. Their whole ugly activity throughout the entire past is masterfully painted here. The whole net that the Catholic soul-catchers have spread over Europe is described in the novel in a warm, many-coloured, splendid language.
Whoever loves a true Jewish novel, a novel whose plot is not based on cobwebs but is permeated with logic, with ardent Jewish patriotism, with facts — let him not forget to start reading this novel, which reads with tremendous suspense and arouses enormous interest.
Concert recital by Lucjan Barenblat

[Culture — concert.]
On Thursday, 21 March, a concert-recital by the 18-year-old violin artist Lucjan Barenblat took place in the hall of the „Nowości“ theatre, before his departure abroad to continue his studies. On the programme — the finest works of the masters of music: Vitali, Bach, Wieniawski, Schubert, Dvořák–Kreisler, Saint-Saëns, Chaminade–Kreisler, Nachéz, as well as „Eli Eli“ by Mischa Elman, „Kol Nidre“ by Erdenko, and an original composition by the young artist himself.
The performance was masterly; the whole auditorium was enchanted and the hall simply thundered with applause. The young artist is gifted with a very rich technique. This showed best in his performance of Nachéz's „Gypsy Dances“; he also has a sweet, heartfelt tone, much routine and a sure, well-studied bowing. One can tell from his playing that he is a faithful pupil of his music professor Bukowiński. Yet in the performance of the Jewish pieces one felt a little too little Jewishness. Very successful was his own composition „Capriccio“ à la mazurka, and it would be very desirable for the young artist to pay attention to composing, in which a brilliant future awaits him. At the piano sat his brother Heniek, a student of the conservatory, who distinguished himself with his accompaniment; he too has an adequate[?] technique and strong routine. The impression — extraordinarily strong and pleasant, and the audience left satisfied.
It is only to be regretted that the hall was so sparsely filled and that only a handful of connoisseurs enjoyed the rich concert.
Y. Abramczyk.

Będzin — The kehilla board members at the starosta's

Because the starosta (district head) fined every member of the kehilla board 100 zł. each for not submitting the kehilla budget on time, the board decided that a delegation should intervene with the starosta, asking him to cancel the fine and to make it possible to extend the deadline so that the budget could be completed properly.
The delegation, consisting of M. Y. Prawer, A. Liwer and G. Landner, went to the starosta on Tuesday. He did not receive the delegation properly, spoke with them about the matter and then left his office for another room, from where he informed the kehilla board members through his secretary that he would give them a precise answer within a few days.
The delegation left very dejected.
Converted to Judaism because of a Jewish girl

A few weeks ago a young Christian from Katowice approached the local rabbinate and declared that he wished to convert, and that the rabbinate should help him on his way to embracing Judaism.
The young man told that his father was of Jewish descent, but[?] as a freethinker he had married a Christian woman and had two sons with her — himself and his brother, who is a priest...
In Katowice he had met, by chance, the girl Schneiman, who worked there as a seamstress, and fallen in love with her.
The rabbinate referred the young man to the Kraków rabbinate, where the necessary operation (circumcision) was performed and he was given the name Avraham ben Avraham Gross.
The wedding of the convert to Miss Schneiman was celebrated last Sunday in the apartment of Mr. Rodaler with great pomp. Besides relatives, hundreds of local people came to watch the wedding, which was a genuinely[?] Jewish one. The groom is religious and did not even allow young men and girls to dance together, because "the Rebbe didn't permit it"...
The father is very angry with his son the convert, whereas the mother gave her consent and presented him with bedding.
From the Keren Kayemet 'academy' in Będzin

In connection with the campaign for the Emek Akko (Acre valley), a festive "academy" (gala meeting) took place last[?] Thursday in the "Nowości" cinema, organised by the Zionist women's association "WIZO". After the playing of the state anthem and "Hatikvah" by Rapaport's orchestra under the direction of Mr. Lustig, Mrs. Ratner, chairwoman of "WIZO", delivered the opening speech, in which she greeted in Hebrew the distinguished guests, Dr. Hindes of Warsaw and Dr. Lubrani of Haifa, and then switched to Yiddish, speaking about the great importance of redeeming the Emek Akko and about the duty that lies on the Jewish woman, the Jewish mother, to instil in their children the knowledge that every grosz saved must be dropped into the Keren Kayemet box, which is the symbol of our renaissance. In every Jewish home where the eternal light has not yet gone out, the Keren Kayemet box must occupy a place of honour.
Dr. Lubrani describes the 3 women personalities in Eretz Israel — Miss Szold, Mrs. Shahar[?] (probably Manya Shochat) and Hanna Maisel, head of Nahalal — who are no longer just names but a concept, and who through their great self-sacrifice will remain immortal in Jewish history. He calls on the Jewish woman to be active for the Keren Kayemet.
Councilman Dr. Hindes appears with a splendid speech in Polish. With sound, logical arguments he shows that Zionism is no longer a legend but a reality, which must be made use of by the whole Jewish people. He characterises Lord Melchett, Louis Marshall and Einstein, who, pen in hand, calculated that the Zionist ideal must and can be realised, if only the Jewish people wills it.
In the second part Miss Plessner (Sosnowiec) recites, in beautiful Hebrew, Tchernichovsky's "Se'u nes Tziyona"; "Hashomer" presents a living tableau of historical types of women, beginning with Sarah and ending with the modern halutza (pioneer woman). The procession is closed by a little shomeret (girl scout) dressed in many collection boxes, symbolising the Keren Kayemet. All the tableaux pass across the stage singing Hebrew songs.
The successful academy brought in an income of 1700 zł.

Sosnowiec
The fight between the Kehilla board and council over the budget.
Under the chairmanship of the vice-president of the Kehilla council, the second session of the Kehilla council, to fix the Kehilla budget for this year, took place on Saturday night.
The session was, as the first time, "interesting": once again "parliamentary" expressions were heard addressed to the gallery, which took a lively part in the budget discussion.
After the reading of the minutes of the first session it is explained that the budget committee reduced the budget by a sum of 57 thousand zł. below the resolution of the board, which had drawn up the budget at 264 thousand zł.
The vice-president of the board, Mr. L. Zendel, supports the board's budget and points out that the committee took the liberty of reducing the subsidy for the free-loan (g"ch) fund from 10 thousand zł. to 5 thousand; treatment of poor sick people, instead of 25 th. — 20 th.; 3600 zł. for urgent medical aid; 4500 zł. support for transients, etc.[?]
Board member Mr. Zaks demands that the council fix the item of 12 thousand zł. for renovating the synagogue (the committee had set 8 thousand zł. for this purpose).
Then the following proposals are submitted by council members: from Mr. Secemski[?], to increase the subvention for the "Talmud Torah", which is in a very critical state; from Mr. Binkowski, to set 2 thousand zł. for buying professional books for the artisans' library; from Mr. Ch. Unger, to subsidise the "Yeshivat Chachmei Lublin"; and from the representative of the Left Poale Zion, Mr. Nachemja, who demands that the item of 12 hundred zł. be increased to 2000 zł. for the "evening courses" of the Poale Zion.
A "fine" reception awaited Mr. Orman when he took the floor. Not only from the gallery is he met with protests, but also from the artisans' dozór member Mr. Braner, who protests that Mr. Orman permits himself to speak in the name of the artisans.
Finally, when Mr. Orman declares that he speaks in the name of "plain Jews", the hall grows quieter and he is able to get to his point. Mr. Orman, speaking about the rabbis question, comes out with a hard question that absolutely must be cleared up. The hard question is: where does the board of the artisans' association have the 9 thousand zł. which they received from the gmina (municipality) to open evening courses for artisans?
A storm of laughter breaks out among the gallery visitors when Mr. Bergman is given the floor. The latter turns to the troublemakers with the words: "Wet boys!" [a Yiddish insult: brats], for which the chairman calls him to order.
Mr. Secemski proposes that, since the gallery is preventing the conduct of the session, a committee should meet to consider the above-mentioned proposals.
The proposal is adopted. At its meeting the committee resolved: to subsidise the "Yeshivat Chachmei Lublin" with 500 zł.; evening courses from 12 to 15 hundred zł.; mikveh from 1000 to 1200 zł.; professional books from 1000 to 1500 zł.
Then the budget is adopted en bloc.
The Zionist and "Mizrachi" parnassim did not take part in the session.
The Kehilla board is dissatisfied with the Kehilla council's budget and does not want to consent to the vote.
—o—
The kimcha campaign begins on Sunday.
The kimcha [Passover flour relief] campaign, which is organised as every year, begins this Sunday. The city has been divided into districts, where the kimcha collectors have been authorised[?].
The number of registered needy has grown greatly this year, therefore everyone must bear this in mind and give according to his means.
—o—
Delegation of Kehilla representatives at the vice-starosta's.
Vice-president Mr. L. Zendel and board member Mr. Weinreb conferred this Wednesday with the vice-starosta, Mr. Kandyszewski, to whom they turned with the request that he cancel the fine of 100 zł. imposed on the Kehilla representatives because they had not drawn up the budget in time, and also that he state his position regarding the fact that the Kehilla council had struck out important items in the budget.
On the first question the vice-starosta declared that concerning the fine the Kehilla representatives should apply to the voivode; as regards the second question, the vice-starosta declared that the budget should be drawn up according to the approval of the Kehilla council.
—o—
Support for Russian Jews.
The Kehilla board has allocated 300 zł. for the matzah campaign for Russian Jews.

Proposal to raise rents — shelved.

Yesterday the board of the "Tenants' Association" in Będzin received a communication from the Central Committee in Warsaw, announcing that following the intervention of almost all the Sejm clubs, the proposal to raise rents has been shelved.
—o—
Tram cuts off the head of a young Christian woman.
Yesterday morning the tram killed a 30-year-old Christian woman on Kościelna [?] Street.
The woman, walking on the pavement, saw her friend walking on the other side and wanted to cross over to her. When she was in the middle, a car came racing along, and trying to save herself she ran back — but at that moment the tram arrived and cut off the girl's head.
—o—
Conference of Jewish and Polish artisans in Sosnowiec
The elections to the Chamber of Crafts in the Kielce voivodeship will take place on Sunday, 27 June [czerwiec]. In this connection, a conference will be held next Sunday at the Sosnowiec Artisans' Association in order to find a way to put forward a joint list of candidates of Jewish and Christian artisans.
—o—
Ministry declines to intervene in the rabbinate question.
Rabbi Englard's side applied to the Ministry with a request to intervene in order to hasten the confirmation of Rabbi Englard's candidacy.
Last week the Ministry rejected the request, because the matter is before the State Tribunal.
Leivick's "Golem" at the Sosnowiec Municipal Theatre.

This coming Tuesday and Wednesday the famous Vilna Troupe will appear at the Sosnowiec Municipal Theatre with Leivick's "The Golem" and A. Tolstoy's "Rasputin and the Tsarina".
The appearance of this troupe in our region is of great significance for all lovers of true stage art. The troupe's guest performances in Będzin passed with extraordinary success. At the head of the artistic direction stands Mark Arnshteyn.

Meeting of the Sosnowiec hospital committee

[Sosnowiec — Jewish hospital.] On Tuesday evening a meeting of the hospital committee took place in the premises of the Sosnowiec gmina [municipality]. At the meeting, which lasted over 4 hours, the question was discussed of deciding finally who should take the post of chief physician at the Jewish hospital.
A sharp discussion developed over this, which took on a stormy character. Finally the proposal of advocate Fryks[?] was adopted, to approach Dr. Meladysta[?] with a proposal that he take over the chief management of the hospital.
—o—
Stupidity or irresponsibility?
[Będzin — press; coal money.] In yesterday's issue of „Unzer Tog“ [„Our Day“] another oily statement appeared, bearing the signatures of Icchak Waks and A. Mangel, who declare that regarding the coal money not accepted at „Unzer Tog“ there was a misunderstanding (?) and that everything is now in the best order.
Well, if the gentlemen of „Unzer Tog“ want to wriggle out of the swamp they have sunk into, that is still understandable; but when a public figure such as Mr. Icchak Waks comes to help cover up such a public theft and to shame the very thing he besmirched yesterday — to that we truly have no words...
—o—
Sharp conflict between the Będzin cantor and his conductor.
[Będzin — community.] For a few weeks now, thanks to various intrigues, a strong hatred has reigned between the Będzin cantor, Mr. Żupowicz, and the conductor [of the choir], Mr. Kalmus. How far this blind hatred has gone is shown by the following fact: this Wednesday Mr. Kalmus was removed from a wedding at the demand of Mr. Żupowicz.
Such deeds, which desecrate the honour of the community, must not be tolerated, and the community leaders must liquidate this undesirable conflict as quickly as possible.
—o—

[Sosnowiec — labour.] The Ministry of Labour and Social Welfare intends to build in Sosnowiec a building to house the offices of the labour exchange, of government [unemployment] relief, and the concentration point where workers and employers will meet.

Something Has Stirred...

(Voices about the "fine" deeds of those who hang around the so-called[?] newspaper "Unzer Tog" ["Our Day", a Yiddish paper in Sosnowiec].)
A few weeks ago we printed in our paper, in the name of the coal committee in Sosnowiec, a demand to the editors of "Unzer Tog" that they return the money paid in by a number of donors who had supported the "coal ring" (koyln-ring).
The demand — as it turned out — had little effect on the editorial board (at least, so to say[?]), and there was neither voice nor answer: they made themselves deaf and wanted to hear nothing.
For some time, in our paper's column "From the Public to the Public", we gave space to former staff members of "Unzer Tog", Messrs. Dr. Kaufman and Y. Feiner, who made clear to the public various low deeds being done around the said newspaper.
The revelations naturally caused a stir in Sosnowiec, so much so that even the few dozen loyal readers of the said newspaper dared[?] to take the little paper in hand... Messrs. the "editors", seeing that they were "in a trap"[?], fell back on the well-known invention — "Stop thief!"...
And so the heroes[?] came out with a reply under the title "The vile lies and slanders of the 'Zagl. Tsaytung'". In the reply they stagger about like a drunkard. Gentlemen — they shout — "we are not guilty; the guilty one is precisely the coal committee, which out of negligence or ill will did not want to collect the money at the administration office. Then[?] they tell stories that the coal money was "grabbed" by Messrs. Dr. Kaufman and Feiner, who, poor things, are slandering them"...
Until now we have not taken a position on this question, because we have not yet, God forbid, sunk to the level of polemicising with "international businessmen"; above all we refrain from it so that nobody should get the impression that we are doing it for the sake of competition (woe to such means of competition). We therefore turned to the coal committee, asking them to speak out on the question.
And here is what they write:
To the hypocritical statement printed in "N. Unzer Tog" no. 52, that the coal committee out of negligence and ill will did not want to collect the 67 zł. that donors had paid in with them, we declare that this is a base lie. We, the undersigned, were at the editorial office of "U. T." 5 weeks ago, where we demanded that they deposit the sum of the coal ring in the "Bank Kupiecki" [Merchants' Bank], and to this day they have not done so.
By the way, it is worth noting that according to the information we have, the editors took a larger sum from the "ring", and they deny it.
Respectfully,
Itshke Zaks [Iczke Saks], Reuven Tshapnik [Czapnik].

Theatre and Music

Leivick's "The Golem".
Last week the Jewish theatre-goers of Będzin and Sosnowiec had a true artistic holiday: the well-known artists of the Vilna Ensemble, such as Nachama, Kash, Kadish, Shriftzetser and others, performed Leivick's mystery play in 3 acts "The Golem", staged and directed by Mark Arnshteyn. The performances were a huge moral and material success. The artists carried the whole audience along with their acting. Although the theatre was overfull and the "gallery" was heavily "occupied", the performances passed in exemplary order and complete quiet, which is a rarity in the Yiddish theatre.
Finally, heartfelt thanks to the artists Kadish (the Maharal), Kash (Tanchum), Grodner (the Golem), Shriftzetser (Tadeusz), Litvina (the Rebbetzin), Yedina (Dvorele) and others, for the figures they created so masterfully in Leivick's "Golem".
Worth mentioning too are the mass scenes with the participation of the Będzin "Muza", which came off brilliantly.
"Parisian Love".
The same artists gave in Będzin the operetta "Parisian Love" (Bayadère) and this time too enchanted with their versatility. Particularly outstanding were Mr. Kash and the temperamental, gifted Malwina Rapel. The splendid sets and costumes — a sensation of their own.
Today — "The Thought".
The famous Jewish artists Ida Kamińska and Zygmunt Turkow, who toured in Będzin last week with colossal success, give a farewell performance today in Będzin at the "Karso" theatre. "The Thought" by Andreyev will be played.
In the leading role Zygmunt Turkow has no rival. His acting electrifies the spectators.
It is therefore to be hoped that, as every time, the artists will be warmly received.
Concert by Kranelli.
Next Monday a concert will take place in Będzin at the "Karso" theatre with the participation of the singer Mr. Kranelli, well known in Zagłębie, who appears with a rich programme of European musical works and Yiddish folk songs.

I.
Esteemed Mr. Editor!
The management of the "Yavne" gymnasium in Będzin most politely asks you to give room in the next[?] number of your esteemed paper to the following statement:
In connection with the open letter by an anonymous author, which appeared in the "Zaglembier Tsaytung" No. 13 of 29 March of this year, the management and the pedagogical council of the "Yavne" gymnasium in Będzin declare the following:
We find that the open letter of the "father of non-'kastituirte'[?] children" is a highly unpedagogical way of criticising the school, because it frivolously undermines the authority of the teaching staff in public opinion and among the children; and precisely for pedagogical reasons we do not intend to conduct a polemic in the press about the matters touched upon in the above-mentioned open letter.
Were we to pay measure for measure, i.e. to answer on the merits the reproaches, which were written perhaps in a moment of anger, we would commit the same pedagogical error as the author of the open letter, and we would then provoke the same negative consequences for the youth in the school that the writing of the above-mentioned author has no doubt provoked.
And therefore, taking into account the above-mentioned reasons and striving to preserve and cultivate the atmosphere of harmonious living together at home as well as at school — we wish to avoid any discussion on the merits in the press and announce that the director of the "Yavne" gymnasium is ready to give all interested parents, or groups of parents, detailed explanations concerning the matters touched upon in the open letter.
For the above reasons we will also not answer further voices, should such appear in the press.
The management and pedagogical council of the "Yavne" gymnasium.
II.
Esteemed Editors!
For the sake of truth I am compelled to return to the sad affair of the charity money at the "Nayer Tog":
Wishing to wash themselves clean, the gentlemen of "Unzer Tog" keep confusing[?] the public's minds, as if I were the one to blame for everything, and the proof: I have already "made a name for myself" at "TOZ" and the Jewish hospital.
First, everyone knows that working both in the hospital and in "TOZ" I committed, God forbid, no abuses whatsoever; the boards of both institutions can confirm this.
And second — what has the Sabbatical year to do with Mount Sinai? What connection does the hospital have with the charity money that vanished in the editorial office?
It seems clear enough to everyone how badly the gentlemen of the "Nayer Tog" have come out of it; they are already seeking to return "all the money", even that which I supposedly took.
But that is not the main thing — even if one were to force[?] the editorial office to cover the money, the ugly affair[?] will still not be healed thereby.
There is therefore a duty on our communal representatives in general and on the Coal Committee in particular to take measures so that in future such a thing should not occur.
Let them as quickly as possible create a commission and establish how much money was collected and by whom, and also why it was not handed over at once. Otherwise suspicion must fall on the above-mentioned institutions or on the persons connected with this or that campaign that "their hand too was in it" and that they are interested in smearing the matter over...
At long last the matter must become clear, and honest people should finally know where the truth begins and where the lie ends.
Dr. Ch. Kaufman.
