The two girls, too — Blumele, Isaac the baker's daughter, and Sarah, Chaim the coachman's daughter, the two inseparable friends — were among those assembled. Their patience, too, was put to a very hard test, but for the time being their efforts had no effect whatever. Still none of the soldiers coming home had been seen.

But all through that time nobody stood idle [printed "leyder", apparently for "leydik"]. People kept talking and talking, and the main topic of the whole long day was the Jewish heroes of Kraków, who had distinguished themselves so greatly, and to whom alone was owed the great victory and the defeat of Chmielnicki's robber bands.

The greater part of all the talk was about Dudl, the handsome and heroic son of the Rabbi of Kraków, the "Tosafot Yom-Tov". Shimon did not tire all day of telling, and telling over again and again, of the great deeds of heroism that Dudl had shown yesterday on the battlefield, and that it was to him, and to him alone, and to the courage he had put into the hearts of his comrades, the Jewish soldiers of Kraków, that it was owed that the victory had been so great and so complete; had it not been for him, who knows how the battle would have turned out and — let us not open our mouths to Satan! — the murderers, the robber bands, would have won...

Among the circles of people who stood constantly around Shimon and never tired of hearing his stories were also the two girls, Blumele and Sarah. Among other men they would certainly not have had the boldness to join in, but since Shimon was the leader of the whole circle here, they felt at home and allowed themselves to linger. But while nearly every one of the men standing around could not contain his curiosity, and they kept bombarding Shimon with their questions and queries, which he kept answering with a smile on his lips, the two girls stood the whole time with flaming cheeks, just as if they were mute, and did not utter a single word. Only the gleam of their eyes showed the strength of the feelings that stirred their hearts...

Suddenly a great shout was heard from the end of the street, not far from the gate; the joy suddenly swelled, and everyone kept calling and shouting!
— They are coming! They are here!

Who the lucky one was [printed "gliklíber"] who spotted the riders, nobody knows even to this day... Shimon, however, always held to his own, even years later, that he had been the first, and nobody wanted to argue with him over it — he could get very angry about it — and deny it to him...

Soon the first riders appeared in the street. The voices and shouts of joy reached the heart of heaven, almost up to the sky. People did not stop shouting and greeting the heroes returning home.

At the head of the whole procession rode the old Prince Wiśniowiecki, on his left side his son, the young prince, and on his right side Dudl, the son of the Rabbi of Kraków, the "Tosafot Yom-Tov".

By Isaac the baker's little house the procession of riders halted; the old prince waved his hand as a sign that he wished to say something.

As if by magic the great crowd fell silent all at once, so silent that in every corner of the street one could hear the prince's words.

— Friends, Jews of Kraków — the prince began in his mighty voice — my messenger Shimon already told you last night about the great victory we won over Chmielnicki and his robber bands, and that almost all of it is owed to the great heroism of our Dudl, the son of your beloved rabbi. I wish now to confirm here before you all that all this is true, and that he alone saved the whole situation, and we, who were already so close to being the losers, became the victors through his heroic courage.

What I said after the battle was won before my whole army, I repeat here today once again before all of you: young David is as dear, precious and rooted in my heart as my own son; and to show him my love, esteem, gratitude and recognition, I present him with my great estate of Dmitrowa [?], with all the manor farms (folwarks) that belong to it, and I ask him to accept this gift from me!...

Dudl even wanted to wave it away with his hand and say something — that the gift was too great for his small merits and that he was therefore unable to accept it — but in that very second the old prince made a movement with his horse, rode up close to Dudl, embraced him with both arms and kissed him on the face. This came upon Dudl so quickly and so expectedly [sic; printed "ervartet", evidently for "umervartet", unexpectedly] that he could no longer speak at all or protest against the great gift the prince had just given him. He could not get out a word; only tears, hot tears of joy, kept running down his cheeks.

When Dudl came to himself, he saw that not far from him stood his father, the Rabbi of Kraków. He leapt from the horse, embraced his father and kissed him.

But when he saw that not far off stood Blumele, the dear girl to whom his heart was so drawn and whom he had not been able to forget for a single minute even in the stormiest war, he could no longer control and restrain himself; he ran up to her, embraced her and kissed her.

— Blumele! — was the only word he could now get out.

— Dudl! — was her answer, and forgetting where they were and paying no heed to the great crowd of people around them, she pressed herself tightly to him and wept bitterly..

The voices again reached the heart of heaven; everyone present shouted and strained their throats for great joy. With their jubilant cries they wanted to show their approval and consent to the extraordinary match that had just been concluded here, so suddenly and unexpectedly, before all their eyes...

And Isaac son of Yekele ["Ayzik Yekeles"]?...

His joy now knew no bounds at all. With his own eyes he had seen that his dream had not been an empty one, idle words!

He ran about like a madman for great joy. "Esther!" — he kept calling — "you see, half of the dream has already come true, and the same will surely happen with the other half!.."

(Conclusion follows).

What's Happening in Zagłębie? — Będzin: Around the Dispute between the Cantor and the Choir Conductor

[Będzin — Kehilla.]
(Slogan line above the page head: "By buying a shekel you help build our national home in the Land of Israel.")
What's happening in Zagłębie?
(Date boxes: Friday, 9 Nisan 5689 — 19 April 1929.)
Będzin
Around the dispute between the cantor and the conductor.
On Sunday a meeting took place of members of the kehilla board and council, who considered the dispute prevailing between the cantor Mr. Żwaczycz[?] and the conductor Mr. Kalmus.
It was resolved that Mr. Kalmus shall give a written undertaking that he will accept the regulations which the board will present to him, and also[?] that Mr. Kalmus shall not demand a compensation sum in case he has to leave his post as conductor.
Threatening with Knives...

[Będzin — Beit midrash.]
There is no peace among the gabbaim of the town beit midrash. It has gone so far that the gabbai Mr. Salomonowicz received a threatening letter with the following content:
"In the name of our organisation we warn you and caution you not to come into the beit midrash, because an attempt has been prepared against you — to stab you with knives."
Mr. S. handed the letter over to the police.
Tea for Philanthropic Institutions.

[Zagłębie — Charity.]
As every year, the well-known tea firm "W. Wissotzky" has sent us 4 kilos of tea for us to distribute among the philanthropic institutions in Zagłębie.
We pointed out to the local representative that we cannot give such a small portion of tea to all the institutions, and the representative accordingly turned to the above-mentioned firm, asking them to increase their donation.
Since the holiday is already near, we are distributing the tea according to this allotment: for "Linat ha-Cholim" three quarters of a kilo; the orphans' ochronka (children's home) three quarters of a kilo; "Beit La-Em" half a kilo; the Jewish hospital in Sosnowiec 1 kilo; the women's society in Dąbrowa half a kilo; "Dobroczynność" (charity society) in Zawiercie half a kilo.
The institutions listed are requested to collect the tea at our editorial office.
Conscription of the 1908 Class.

[Będzin — Military.]
On 2[?] May the conscription (pobór) of those born in 1908 begins. To each of those liable for conscription the magistrate sends a summons stating when he must report, and those who do not receive such summonses must report at the magistrate, military department, second floor.
On 2 and 4 May those with deferments (odroczenia) from the years 1906 and 1907 and part of 1908 must report.
The conscription will last until 16 May.
The magistrate asks us to draw the attention of young men who are not permanent local residents and are not on the local conscription lists that they must report in their places of birth.
Excursions to the National Exhibition in Poznań.

[Będzin — Municipality.]
The town administration has taken the initiative to organise excursions to the National Exhibition in Poznań. Professional, economic and social institutions are to take part in the excursions.
For this purpose a meeting will take place this Sabbath, to which representatives of the above-mentioned organisations have been invited, who will have to decide how the excursions are to be organised.
Saved from Death

[Będzin — Accident.]
On Wednesday in the daytime a young Christian tried to jump onto the tram while it was going at full speed on Małachowskiego[?] Street.
The Christian received a strong blow, from which he fell down right by the tram line. A few minutes later he got up. From the fall his face was covered in blood.
The Price of Matzah Has Risen

[Będzin — Passover / Cost of living.]
In the last days of the week the price of matzah rose by 30 groszy per kilo. Instead of 1.50 [złoty] the price has gone up to 1.80 per kilo.
The rise comes about because the bakers, seeing that no matzah is being brought in from the nearby small towns, have raised the price.
Wholesale Merchants Must Submit Applications Regarding the 1 Percent

[Będzin — Taxes and trade.]
The Merchants' Association asks us to draw the attention of the wholesale merchants: those who wish to benefit from the 1 percent turnover tax must, after receiving the assessment notices (nakazy), submit applications to that effect at the Urząd Skarbowy (Tax Office).
Water-supply plan being carried out

[Będzin — municipality; water supply.] These days the town administration [of Będzin] held a meeting at which the tender for awarding the work on the water-supply system throughout the whole town was drawn up. The tender will be published in the next few days.
Injured by the tram
[Będzin — tram accident.] On Kościuszki Street the tram struck Mr. Shloyme (Szlama) Gutman on his left hand. The latter went to the municipal hospital, where he is under treatment.
Suicide

[Będzin — suicide.] On Tuesday night the 42-year-old Żak, a resident of Warpie [a quarter of Będzin][?], hanged himself on the door. When the members of the household saw it, the suicide was already dead.
Sosnowiec — Suicide attempt of a young Jewish man

[Sosnowiec — attempted suicide.] In the night from Friday to Saturday (Shabbat) the 28-year-old Ch. Weinblum from „Pradle“[?] shot himself with the intention of committing suicide.
The bullet struck him in the lungs, in a place where it is impossible to perform an operation. The would-be suicide is lying in the local Jewish hospital [in Sosnowiec].
The suicide happened on romantic grounds. Mr. Ch. had for about a year been matched to Miss Y., whom he considered his bride.
But a day before the suicide, when Ch. asked for the consent of the young lady's mother, the latter refused him and advised him „to knock this foolishness out of his head“.
In despair at this answer, Ch. went up to the hotel „Wiktoria“ and wanted to put an end to his life.
A new Jewish bank

[Sosnowiec — economy; Jewish credit institution.] Last week a new Jewish credit institution was opened here [in Sosnowiec] under the name „Sosnowiec Mutual Credit Institution“.
At the head of the institution are Messrs. Leybish Zenrel[?], Shimon Mendel Tabiasz, Feivel Estri, L. Szwajcer, Simcha Estreicher, M. Zederman, Sh. Mencer, Y. Szwarcbaum and others.
Heavy sentences for trading in railway tickets

[Sosnowiec — court; railways.] On Monday the trial began in the local district court [in Sosnowiec] against several Jewish women and men who had been arrested on 5 May 1927 at Wolbrom station for carrying passengers on the Kielce—Strzemieszyce line „na gapę“ [Polish slang: without tickets].
In the dock sat: Rivka Ratner, Zisl Ratner, Pinchas Ratner, Pinchas Boym, Sheyndl Boym, Yekl Raskowski and 8 railway officials.
36 tickets were also found on those arrested.
To the trial, which lasted until Wednesday evening, 60 witnesses were summoned, who supported the charges against the Jews.
After the speech of the prosecutor, who demanded punishment for all the accused, the court withdrew for deliberation and then delivered the following verdict:
the 19-year-old Rivka Ratner is sentenced to a year in prison, the 20-year-old P. Ratner to 6 months in prison, the 24-year-old Zisl Ratner to 3 months; the 17-year-old P. Boym to 4 months and Rakowski — 3 months.
On the basis of the amnesty the sentences are reduced by half.
The remaining accused were fully acquitted.
Not for the League, only for his own pocket..

[Sosnowiec — court; embezzlement.] The well-known engineer Borkowski[?], who at one time committed abuses in the labour exchange office, sat again these days in the dock at the district court [in Sosnowiec].
This time he was accused that, while chairman of the „League of Seas and Rivers“ [Liga Morska i Rzeczna], he had collected the money at various private schools and collections, to the sum of a thousand złoty.
The „Seas“ chairman was sentenced to 8 months in prison.
Demands of the mine workers

[Zagłębie — miners; labour.] On Sunday a large meeting took place of the workers in the Zagłębie coal mines. At the meeting the question was presented of intervening with the Minister of Labour so that he should annul the agreement between the workers and the industrialists, who had added from 2 to 6 per cent (to wages), while soon afterwards they raised the price of coal by 10 per cent.
After hearing the report of the lawyer Pawlek[?] it was resolved: 1) working time in the mines must last no more than 8 hours; 2) the workers must receive ready-prepared lamps for work; 3) to raise the coal allowance (deputat); 4) to pay holiday time according to the normal wage; and 5) the agreement shall apply to all industrial enterprises.
City council sessions postponed because of the eve of the holiday

[Sosnowiec (?) — City council.] Yesterday and today, Friday, sessions of the local city council were to have taken place. The Jewish councillors therefore applied to the chairman of the city council asking that, because of the days before the holiday, the sessions be postponed. The request was taken into account, and the sessions will take place on the 27th and 28th of this month.
—o—
Vilna Troupe performs on Chol Hamoed Pesach in Sosnowiec.
[Sosnowiec — Theatre.] On Monday of Chol Hamoed Pesach the Vilna Ensemble [Vilna Troupe], headed by the artists Nechama, Karish, Kash, Shriftzetser, Malvina[?] Rafael, Litvina[?], Gradner and others, will give only 1 guest performance at the Sosnowiec Municipal Theatre, in Leo Fall's great musical operetta "The Rose of Stambul". The troupe has already proven itself here in its brilliant production of "The Golem", and there is no doubt whatsoever that we are dealing with a first-class theatre in the full sense of the word. The troupe has decided to present itself in our region with its excellent operetta forces in one of the richest European musical creations by the German composer Leo Fall.
—o—
Hersh Lipshitz, of blessed memory.
[Sosnowiec — Obituary.] On Wednesday the news caused mourning in the town that one of the town's notables, the long-time resident and grain merchant Hersh Lipshitz, had died suddenly. In the course of his life the deceased earned the greatest sympathy among all the inhabitants of the town, without distinction of nationality. When the Polish courts were established he was elected the first justice of the peace in Sosnowiec. The deceased was also a charitable man and took part in all public campaigns.
—o—
He "inspected" the letters to military men.
[Sosnowiec — Post office; crime.] The official at the Sosnowiec post office, Wojciechowski, who was employed sorting letters, had for a long time been "inspecting" the registered-value letters.
During the search of Wojciechowski's flat dozens of letters were found, as well as many postage stamps the official had removed from letters.
He committed the largest number of thefts on value letters sent to military men.
The official has been handed over to the investigation office.
—o—
Soap and oil merchants will have to take an exam.
[Poland — Trade; regulations.] An ordinance is soon to be issued under which all those who trade, wholesale or retail, in oil [petroleum], soap, paints and all kinds of chemical products will have to take professional examinations.
The examinations will take place in 3 series in the presence of representatives of the authorities, the chambers of commerce and delegates of the organisations concerned,

People's or Private Institutions?

[Economy — Jewish banks; opinion piece.]
(What is the purpose of the cooperative [„געז.“, probably “social/cooperative”] people's banks? Do they really fulfil their tasks towards the people?)
A Jew complains [?] to me: You keep writing that we. The public has no sense of responsibility towards the masses, that we — you say, [unclear word] — do not care that [—] social institutions be set up at the proper level, that everyone should benefit from them, that those who need support should be supported; and truly we understand that you are right, when you point out to us that as soon as we understand the responsibility of society and for society. We know — says the Jew — that every healthy people must know the necessity of its social institutions.
Unfortunately this is not understood among us; unfortunately people do not know how properly to socialise the institutions that are created among us on social foundations. True, people do not know how to set them up properly, and what is more, they also do not know how to maintain them. So this is how it is: neither does the public support them, nor do the leaders, those at the helm, make them such that they bring benefit to the community, that they really be institutions exclusively for the whole of the population.
So the one depends on the other: neither does the public see to it that we should first of all have rock-solid institutions which we could be proud of, that we possess such and could boast of them; and on the other hand, when we already do have such, the leaders of the institutions unfortunately do not show proper understanding of the matter.
True, first of all one must have well-established social institutions, and only then can one see whether they serve the benefit of the general mass of the population.
It goes without saying that we need first and foremost healthy and well-established institutions, but one cannot agree that we have none at all. We do have such, and if they are well established and do not bring the proper benefit, this proves that their leaders do not fulfil their tasks properly.
We have at least one single corner of Jewish life where the institutions prosper well — we mean our banks. We have several Jewish banks in every town and all of them develop well, all of them stand at the proper material level, and I do not at all agree with my fellow writers who have more than once stated in this very place that it is becoming dangerous when too many banks are founded, when these banks begin to be turned into little shops. No, on the contrary, let them become popular, let them penetrate every stratum of the population and let them learn the trade; the more they try, the more they will learn.
And therefore we must welcome the newly founded bank, and we need only wish that it understand, in the full sense of the word, its tasks, its obligations towards the community.
Until now, unfortunately, the leaders of our financial institutions do not understand this, for although we have well-established banks, they do not serve all strata of the population exclusively.
People here tell, after all, that while various members cannot get their customers' bills discounted for a few hundred złoty, others come in their place and get heavy thousands discounted.
So there are privileged persons whom the institutions serve and who make use of them properly, even beyond their means, while others cannot get even their minimal number of bills discounted.
One must not forget that those who get the larger sums in the Jewish banks have access everywhere and can arrange their position [?] so that even if they [?] are discounted only a half or a quarter [?], it is no harm either, because they have access everywhere and do not depend on this or that bank; whereas when the small man is not given his few hundred złoty, he is crushed, he cannot turn to others, and when "his" bank throws his few bills back at him, he is left hanging in the air and does not know what world he is in.
So the protection [favouritism] system exists in our banking institutions in its full size and breadth. One has to know how to talk to the director of this or that bank, one has to know how to get on with the council and with the board, and then one can attain the level of unlimited credit.
Can we call these institutions social? Are these banks for the community, for society, for the people? At best one can call them protection banks for a select few, for certain categories of people, at whose service they stand at any time and for whom [?] huge operations are made, while the average man of the people has almost no access there; for the fact that one grants [unclear words: "berlen or shterlen"] a hundred-złoty note now and then for form's sake, to show that the door is not shut to them, does not yet mean that the bank serves their interests, that it fulfils its needs.
Our banks are created and maintained by all strata of the population, and therefore they must serve the population exclusively, and all sorts of protection systems and various side considerations must be removed there. That is what does not stand on a healthy basis, that is what cannot be called honest conduct.
If we want our financial institutions to be called people's banks in the true sense — of the people — and really to be such, then first of all the protection system must be removed, which unfortunately has forced its way without exception into all our banking institutions.
That is what one must remember and guard well on every occasion.
Dr. Papuri [?].
The First Days of Passover

[Będzin — Passover in town; local feuilleton.] The days of the first days of Passover were cold, both outside and indoors. The cold began right from the eve of Passover, when the blood of the poor froze as they paid — thanks to the prohibitions — 1 gulden and 80 groszy for a kilo of "pletslekh" [flat cakes; apparently matzah]. The gentlemen meat suppliers, too, added 20 gr. to a kilo of meat. The surcharge — so people say — was made in honour of the holiday, but connoisseurs, the fine noses, interpret it thus: that the 20 groszy [?] were taken because certain butchers had paid a sum of 200 zł. so that they would be permitted to bring meat from Mysłowice.
———
Warmth [?] and a festive mood prevailed at the Seders in the orphans' shelter ("ochronka"); there, on the third floor of Zmigród's house, 40 boys celebrated the Seders like true "princes".
Year in, year out, the board of "Dobroczynność" [?], having no means to provide for the unfortunate children, distributed them among benefactors in town. This year, on the initiative of the "orphans' mother", Mrs. Cesia [Tsisha] Szajn, the "traditional shame" was lifted from the children — or rather only from the boys, since the orphan girls spent the holiday among strangers...
The tables laid with every good thing received the children in their holiday clothes, who recited the Haggadah with great "enthusiasm" and supported the Shulchan Aruch [the "set table"] even more.
The children allowed themselves extra cups, and at every cup wished each other that next year, as free men, they would already be freed from the cramped quarters on the third floor and find themselves in the new building that is being built for them...
———
In the cultural field there was a truly terrible crisis. Dr. Kruk's lecture "The Crisis in European Culture" had a "bombastic" [?] effect on the listeners, and a "crisis" began to reign in the hall. Especially in the gallery, which brought it about that the lecture was interrupted for a while..;
———
The "Muze", which has lately become so popular thanks to "At Night in the Old Marketplace", wanted to honour the poet Yitskhok Leybush Peretz and in honour of his 14th yahrzeit arranged an "academy" [commemorative evening].
The organizers, wanting [?] it to be "round and pointed", also arranged a dance evening as a "dessert". It is really a blockhead's question: what connection does honouring Peretz have with the Charleston?
— The result: the academy and the "kosher" [?] ball turned into a dance of the dead...

The Cup-Gift for the Jewish Teams in Zagłębie. First Conference of "Hakoah"—"Maccabi"—"Kraft"

[Zagłębie — sport; the paper's initiative.] On Sunday, in the apartment of the editor Mr. Szpigelman, the first conference took place on how to organize the so-called "puchar" [cup], which the editorial board of the "Zaglembier Tsaytung" has decided to give to the best Jewish team ("drużyna") in Zagłębie.
Taking part in the conference were the representatives P. Barenblat and M. Felsner ("Hakoah"), M. Lancman [?] and Szywek [?] ("Maccabi"), and Sh. Rozenblum ("Kraft" Będzin).
To the question of several delegates, for what purpose the editorial board had taken the initiative upon itself, Mr. Lewkowicz explained on behalf of the editorial board that, in deciding to give a gift to a Jewish team, the editorial board had not the slightest intention [?] of bringing itself or the paper any material benefit whatsoever; the initiative was taken solely in order to abolish the feelings of enmity and to uproot the prevailing antagonism that has taken root in the ranks of the Jewish teams in Zagłębie, and in particular between the teams "Maccabi"—"Hakoah".
The explanation was received by the delegates with great satisfaction, and they welcomed the initiative of the "Zaglembier Tsaytung", which strives to unite the Jewish teams into one great force that will represent them to the outside world.
After a short debate concerning the regulations, the proposal of Mr. Szymek was adopted that, since an error in the date had occurred in the first invitations, a second conference be called. For Sunday, 5 May, to which all the other teams in Zagłębie are also to be invited.
The conference will take place at 6 in the afternoon, and we ask all teams that receive invitations to delegate their representatives, who are to take part in the final decisions.
From Sport

[Sosnowiec and Dąbrowa — sport; football.] "Hakoah" 1—"Maccabi" 1 3:0 (1:0).
Maccabi won an undeserved victory over the technically better Hakoah in the friendly match played on Thursday, the 1st day of Passover, on the "Ruch" ground in Sosnowiec. The course of the game was even; though at moments "Hakoah" had the upper hand, "Hakoah" nevertheless did not manage to exploit very fine moments.
Already in the 3rd minute "Maccabi" (Lefik) shoots the first goal. The "Hakoah" attack begins, but without success. And the first half ends 1:0 for Maccabi.
In the second half Hakoah has more of the play and attacks the Maccabi goal continuously. But the "Pomac" [nickname, apparently the goalkeeper] and the Maccabi defence answer, beating off every ball. Still Maccabi manages in the 31st minute to shoot the second goal and immediately afterwards the 3rd goal. The rest of the time belongs entirely to Hakoah, but when Hakoah's attack comes up to the opponents' goal they cannot find their bearings, and so the result remains unchanged until the end of the game.

A victim of the excessive tax assessment.
The latest assessment of the turnover tax has put the local Jewish merchants in a desperate position. Turnover was raised by 40, 50 and in individual cases even by 600 per cent compared with last year. The tragic case of the manager and co-owner of the firm „J. Glikstein & Co.“ — Joel Glikstein — can serve as an illustration. For the year 1927 the said firm was assessed at 150 thousand zł., and for the year 1928[?] at two million zł., i.e. to pay 55 thousand zł. Mr Glikstein was hoping that the Main Commission would reduce the tax for him, but how astonished he was when on Tuesday, 23 April, right after receiving the „nakaz płatniczy“ [payment order], the Będzin[?] tax office sent out a bailiff, who placed a distraint on all the merchandise, giving as the reason „so that the firm should not liquidate the business and evade paying the tax“... While the merchandise was being distrained Mr Glikstein suffered a heart attack, and two days later he died.
The deceased was torn from the world in the bloom of life, at the age of 32, and leaves a wife and four children. The entire Jewish population, among whom the deceased was much beloved, took part in the funeral.
D. R—c.

[Zagłębie — opinion piece; matzah prices, the rabbinate and the kehilla.] (Why is the poor man's matzah so expensive? Who is to blame, and could it have been prevented?)
Something is quite different today from what it once was; today one no longer knows any limit or any distinction — things go as they go, and nobody tries to find out whether they must and can be otherwise, or whether they have to be done this way or that.
Nowadays lawlessness [hefkeyres] reigns in every sphere [?] of our life; wherever you go and wherever [?] you stand there is no responsibility, everyone keeps a free hand and can do whatever and however he pleases; nobody knows how to take the other into account, nobody wants to have pity on the other, and nobody wants to feel for him at all.
In connection with what has this come up? Precisely in connection with this year's Passover. As is known, the most important question for a Jew is the piece of matzah that he has to bring into his home, and which comes to him with so many difficulties.
A Jew comes into the editorial office and asks to be heard. He knows, he says, that the newspaper is not made to concern itself with matters of kashrut, and he does not mean to demand that of us either — yet precisely for that reason he asks us to hear him out.
The Jew relates: I myself am a grain merchant; this year I brought in holiday flour and, as usual, I paid the rabbinate the proper fee [„taxe“] for certifying the flour „kosher for Passover“; I even had to pay for the droshky, and after all that I sold the flour below 75 groszy a kilo — I made no profit at all; and yet the bakers received the flour at the above-mentioned price. It is impossible to understand how the rabbinate and the Jewish kehilla administration allowed a kilo of matzah to cost 170—180 zł. [so printed; presumably groszy, i.e. 1.70—1.80 złoty] — so the baking cost more than the flour. Has anyone ever heard of exploiting the population like this? Is that why it is „bread of affliction“?
Was kashrut really guarded so carefully that a kilo of matzah should go up so much after the flour was certified? After all, one knows that the shmura was not what it used to be in the old days; so the question arises: why did such extraordinarily high prices have to go onto a kilo of matzah?
But what then — the bakers know how to get their way [?]: first of all they took advantage of the rabbinate's forbidding outside matzah, so that nobody would encroach on their territory, and then they would be sole rulers and do as would be most convenient for them and most profitable for their pockets.
Matzah for Passover is, after all, an article of first necessity that even the poorest man must have; so why did a rabbinate together with a Jewish kehilla administration not want to see to it that here not everything could be done as each baker pleases? And if the rabbinate is already being paid for certifying the oven with matzah, with other supervisors [„makhshirim“], must everything therefore be ownerless? Should the bakers then be able to charge any price they please? We get nothing at all from our kehilla administration — at least in return for the taxes we bring it, it could have taken care that we should have cheap matzah for Passover. And if it did not want to deal with the matter itself, it should at any rate have acted so that the rabbinate would concern itself with it. Issuing the ban on outside products so that the local ones can make capital out of it is surely not everything.
We live, after all, at the present time in hard enough conditions; the earned grosz of the average Jewish merchant has been cut down [?] to a minimum — to say nothing of the small trader and the artisan. This element ought to have been kept well in mind — so why should the bakers have been given a free hand to charge for an article of first necessity as much as their hearts desire?
Fish and other products, too, have gone up „in honour of Passover“ in an unheard-of way; and had we had a healthy economic society that understood the necessity of leading a normal, healthy life, all this would not have remained so lawless as we see it today.
It is hard enough for a Jew, as it always has been, to bring Passover into his home; one should have taken care to ease the difficult situation for him — meanwhile we unfortunately see the opposite: everyone looks out for himself and does as he likes and as suits him best, and there is no economic leadership that would come and cry out: Enough! One must not exploit the population just because it wants to have Passover matzah and holiday products.
From a practical and purely Jewish standpoint the rabbinate should have been interested in the Jew not having to overpay so much for his products merely because they bear the hechsher of the local rabbinate.
It must not be allowed that in the name of „kashrut“ so much lawlessness and boundless appetite to fill pockets should reign — and that at the expense of the broad strata of the Jewish population.
It is unheard of that such deeds should be permitted by people with sound notions and with concepts of truth and honesty.
R. Les.
Too Late for Happiness

[Story — a Chol HaMoed tale.] (A little Chol HaMoed tale).
Miss Bronia fell in love with a young man, a modest bookkeeper, Zygmunt. She was not bold enough to tell him so, and he her — even less so, because Miss Bronia is an only daughter and has a large dowry. Zygmunt was an excellent expert in bookkeeping ledgers, but the book of life he did not know.
So he did not know that if a young man wants to please a young lady he must dress elegantly; besides, Zygmunt also [printed „ikh“, “I”] saved on food and therefore acquired a pale look. More than once he wanted to ask for her hand, but it did not come easily to him to make up his mind, because if one goes, one must put on a fine suit, new shoes, and why not also eat properly beforehand, so that at the table one should not notice that he is so hungry. He therefore arranged things like this: one week he ate lunches, and the second week he bought himself “elegance” with the lunch money. Thus nearly two years went by. Miss Bronia grew richer by a few more years, and Zygmunt by a few clothes and even a little money.
And at last he made up his mind [printed „retsidirt“].
It was the first day of Chol HaMoed Passover. He put on the few new garments he had acquired over long months, the new necktie, a refreshed hat, and went off to his heart's beloved Bronia.
He rings — not, as before, barely, barely, but boldly and loudly. The door is opened for him, he bursts into her room; she sits on the sofa, smiling, happy — but next to her sits somebody else.
Miss Bronia greets him and introduces the new guest in the house:
— Mr. Zygmunt, my fiancé.
— — — — —
Ah, how many sleepless nights had Mr. Zygmunt spent dreaming of hearing such words from his beloved. But how differently they sound: the sentence rings in two parts: “Mr. Zygmunt — my fiancé.” Who, then, is the fiancé?
But he sees that it is not he who is meant.
Zygmunt lost his balance, and when the strange young man held out his hand to him, he cried out with all his strength:
— Robber! Why are you robbing me?
Bronia burst out laughing, the young man even louder; things began to swim before Zygmunt's eyes, he fainted, and when they revived him he kept talking as if in his sleep:
— So many years... hundreds of lunches saved... now he comes, a stranger... by what right?
Miss Bronia had wanted to write the tenoim [engagement contract] during Chol HaMoed, but because of the incident with Zygmunt it was postponed.
Pik.
The Chol-Hamoed Guests

[Humour — feuilleton.] (Monologue of a Jew with a big family) — by Y. Aberzhanek[?].
What do you say to my burnt troubles? What do you say to this plague? I'll do something to myself, I'll run away to where the black pepper grows!
I beg you, tell me, where in the world has such a thing been heard of — that one should take a whole, healthy, living person and want, of all things, to bury him alive? Robbers, bandits, man-eaters, Hottentots, why have you set upon my young years? Why have you ruined my holiday?
At whom am I so angry, you ask? And because of whom do I want to run away to where the black pepper grows? You really don't know because of whom? — Because of my wife's family — the Chol-Hamoed guests!
Chol-Hamoed guests are never anything new for me. Ever since my wedding, ever since I set up a household of my own, I have had Chol-Hamoed guests every Chol Hamoed: sometimes an uncle with an aunt, an aunt with an uncle, sometimes two aunts, two uncles, sometimes a cousin "from the seventh floor", sometimes a cousin many times removed, a groom with a bride, in-laws, in-laws' wives and just plain guests.
I am already used to all these Chol-Hamoed guests. Every evening after the first festival days I already expected several guests from the provinces, for whom one indeed always prepared[?] a little liquor, fruit, snacks and sweets — and why not? How do you say? "A pinch on the cheek, so the colour holds." So I really pinched myself every Chol Hamoed, and if by chance I didn't pinch myself, my missus pinched me, and the colour held somehow...
As you see, I am already, thank God, used to the trouble called "Chol-Hamoed guests". But such a defeat, such a "zjazd" [convention] of Chol-Hamoed guests as this year I have never had.
Right on the first day of Chol Hamoed, at the very crack of dawn, I am still lying in bed when I hear a "call" in the other room — kissing and well-wishing — and before I can make out what all this kissing and wishing is, the guests are already beside my bed: Uncle Hersh Ber with Aunt Dvoyre Yachet from Żarki. God guard and shield you from the kissers of Żarki, and even more from the kisseresses of Żarki. If a Żarki kisseress attacks you, you are lost to all the worlds; she sticks to you like a fly to flypaper — impossible to tear off. On the right cheek, on the left cheek, and again on the right cheek, and back on the left cheek. And as if to spite you[?], the kisseresses are old women with lemon-yellow faces, with red, bleary[?] eyes and one tooth in the mouth. Well, I ask you: wouldn't my heart have gone soft if you had to, on an empty stomach, submit to smooching with such a "grogresin"[?]?
We had hardly finished rejoicing over Aunt Dvoyre Yachet and Uncle Hersh Ber — a new round of kissing... What now? New guests: Keyle Beyle Luzer Wolf's from Olkusz, my wife's cousin. And maybe you think Keyle Beyle Luzer Wolf's came alone? You are mistaken — with a daughter; and maybe you think the daughter is alone? Wrong again — Keyle Beyle's daughter has a fiancé with her, a young fellow with an earring[?], tall and fat as a telephone pole, a pair of red, overfed cheeks, a shaven mug, a wide raincoat, shiny patent-leather boots and a maciejówka cap with a shiny visor.
When I took a look at this "groom-lad" and remembered that this "young-man-chik" had come to me for "board", I went cold and hot. Why, he could swallow me like a sprat after a swig of vodka...
A minute later they were all — Uncle Hersh Ber, Aunt Dvoyre Yachet, Keyle Beyle Lazer Wolf's, her daughter with the groom ["bachir", sic] — sitting around the table. My wife bustled about; she had a whole import and export: my wife "imported" the bit of liqueur, wine and fruit from the cupboard to the table, and my guests "exported" part of it into their mouths, and what the mouths didn't swallow, the pockets took... Excelling at the gobbling business was, naturally, Feygl Leah Zerach Freydin's youngest little son, Keyle Beyle's daughter's fiancé: everything burned up under his hands; after every macaroon[?] he downed a glass; with every glass he rubbed a festive "l'chaim" into me with his lad's "little hand", and at every handshake of his "hand" I saw all my great-grandmothers, who already rest in bright Paradise... After every squeeze sparks flew before my eyes. The whole time, seeing strangers gorge and guzzle, vying[?] at my expense, I gnashed my teeth, and my wife kept pleading with the guests: why are you sitting idle? Why aren't you drinking? Don't wait to be begged! Have a piece of babka, it's homemade; Aunt Dvoyre Yachet, peel yourself an apple; young man (by this she means Feygl Leah Zerach Freydin's son), pour yourself a glass.
So my wife goes round the table begging the Chol-Hamoed guests for mercy to eat and drink, and my heart drips [blood] as I watch fresh bowls[?] of apples and nuts being poured out non-stop, and the little bottles of liqueur and wiśniak [cherry brandy] drying up under their hands.
But even here the troubles don't end yet. Our family is, no evil eye, a large one. Right in the middle of it, as the guests were in the midst of making merry, Chol-Hamoed guests and plain guests began pouring in from all sides, men with wives, one "parka" [couple] after another, each couple with a few little children by the hand. At the table it gets cosier. Empty bottles are taken off and full bottles put on; people eat and drink till the smoke rises.
When the sideboard had been emptied, Aunt Dvoyre Yachet says: Well, now we'll go for a little "stroll". And when Aunt Dvoyre Yachet goes, Uncle Hersh Ber goes too, of course; my wife also dressed up festively, and all together we set off for a stroll through the town.
Here, on the stroll, I cursed my years: at every silly thing they stopped, and I had to explain to them what it is and what it is for.
But not with everything were they satisfied. What kind of "porządek" [order] is this — a "kolej" [railway, i.e. the tram] in the middle of the street!... In Żarki at least one can cross the street without trembling before a "kolej", lest one lose[?] hands and feet. And what, Keyle Beyle marvels, are those poles on the roofs with wires? That must be, answers the groom-lad, for chasing pigeons.
And I walk on, my heart heavy, my head spinning. I have to answer all the questions. I feel I'm falling off my feet; another minute and I'll faint away.
Coming to the corner of Potocki [Street?], the couple, the groom with the bride, took their leave, and Aunt Dvoyre Yachet and Uncle Hersh Ber I took into the "Nowości" [probably a cinema] and so, barely and with great trouble, got rid of the calamity.
Having come home, I finally breathed more easily and lay down to rest a little; I was just about to catch a nap when, right in the middle: "Vayavo" [and lo, he came]! The calamity is here! Aunt Dvoyre Yachet and Uncle Hersh Ber — sulking. What's the matter? They didn't like it; for nothing, says Aunt Dvoyre Yachet, they spent money.
What did they show? I ask them.
Go on, go on, Aunt Dvoyre Yachet fumes. For that one should pay money? They didn't show anything for the money! For sitting in an empty hall one should pay money?
But what did they show on the sheet [screen]? — I ask them.
In short, as it turned out, they had sat the whole time in the "poczekalnia" [waiting room] of the "Nowości", and after sitting there two hours they went home angry.
Later Keyle Beyle, the daughter and the groom came back too. My wife set about making up beds, arranged pairs: two women in this bed, two men in the other bed, the bride on the sofa. And I myself? I made up a bed for myself on a table and tossed the whole night as if in a fever, and when in the morning I got down from the table I hadn't a whole limb left in me, and now I've just come from the feldsher — a whole 60 cupping glasses he slapped on me. A trifle, after such a night!...
God guard and shield you from a big family, from a wife who is hospitable, and from Chol-Hamoed guests who eat you down to the bones, and because of whom you have to have cupping glasses put on.
Oh, what a Chol Hamoed I had this year with the Chol-Hamoed guests!...
The Seduced Girl.

[Literature — serial novel; instalment 2.]
Dr. A. Weissman [Wajsman].
(A novel of Jewish life in the Old World, based on historical facts.)

When the news reached the shtetl there was an uproar. Hanna, the mother of the vanished daughter, tore the hair from her head and screamed at her husband to run as fast as he could and chase after Mania. Perhaps they might still manage to rescue their daughter from the great misfortune and the great disgrace.
— They will stone us. What do you mean, ride on Yom Kippur? Unless the rabbis order it.
— I'll go myself! — Hanna screamed in a voice not her own — I won't leave my child in gentile hands.
Suddenly a deathly silence fell.
— They're coming! They're coming! — people whispered — Shh, here they come!
In the great silence the old rabbi appeared from the great beis-midrash, a silver skullcap on his head and a white kittel. Behind him came all three dayanim [rabbinical judges] of K.[?]. A great sorrow covered the rabbi's wrinkled face. His long, snow-white beard trembled, tears appeared in his eyes, and in a heart-rending voice he called for Zelig and his wife.
— Where is Reb Zelig with his wife? Let them come closer to me!
Reb Zelig and his wife, like guilty people, heads bowed, slowly approached the place where the rabbi and the dayanim stood.
— Reb Zelig, you may travel with your wife. The Holy One, blessed be He, and all Israel will forgive you; may God help you rescue your child from gentile hands. It is a great mitzvah. Lose no time. Go as quickly as you can, and may you succeed on your way!
The crowd shuddered on hearing the rabbi tell them to travel on Yom Kippur.
As if it had sprung up from under the ground, a wagon with two horses appeared.
Weeping terribly, Reb Zelig took off the white kittel and, together with his wife, climbed into the wagon. When the wagon moved off, the whole crowd burst into terrible weeping.
— On Yom Kippur! On Yom Kippur! Such a misfortune, such a decree[?] has poured down!
The air in the shtetl shook with the enormous weeping, and that Yom Kippur the cantors and the worshippers pleaded piteously with the Creator of the world to forgive the great sin of profaning and desecrating Yom Kippur, which falls upon the whole town like a great punishment.

Chapter Three.

In the shtetl every Jew felt a deep pain, a terrible grief. Something tore and plucked at everyone's heart with pain — as though each and every one had had a child of his own run away on this Yom Kippur.
Mania, Maniechka! Who didn't know her, who didn't love her! There was something in her of the "seventh charm" [an extraordinary grace]. Not tall, yet her figure was slender, well-grown, as if turned by a great artist. Coal-black curls floated wildly on her beautiful head and would not stay in place. At her every slightest movement her hair curled each time into a different lovely shape, which each time lent her a new charm, a new grace. While talking, her pretty, small, white hands would rise to her head every minute to smooth her hair, so that it would lie in place and not fall over her face and cover, as with a thin, black, silk tulle or voile, her black, lively eyes; but her curls would never obey, and always played and danced over her clear, white face.
Despite her twenty years, her face always sparkled with childlike charm. Her little mouth, the two even rows of teeth, the dimples, together with her curls, recalled the faces of beautiful child-angels, who attract, gladden and revive every heart, old and young.
If one were to weave[?] little silver wings onto Mania's shoulders, one could paint from her the little angels — the beautiful, good, merry and sweet ones — that one sees painted in pictures, flying among the clouds, from where they look down at you with big, round, childlike eyes.
Everyone loved Mania as a beautiful, good child; everyone pitied her in that misfortune. Everyone's heart bled for the great misfortune that had befallen her parents. Only two persons there were who secretly, deep in their hearts, rejoiced at Mania's misfortune.
These were Madame Szerman and her little daughter Klara.
At the first "break"[?], when the women came out of the synagogue and the houses of study to rest a little in the street and wait for Musaf, Madame Szerman and her daughter were also among the women, who did not stop talking about Maniechka and her unhappy parents.
Madame Szerman, as the richest lady of the shtetl, was surrounded by women waiting to hear what she would say about it. Madame Szerman, after all, is no Jewess "from behind the stove" [i.e. no simple, ignorant woman]. Madame Szerman is the only one in the shtetl who travels abroad every year and sees a whole world of people.
Madame Szerman, a tall, stout Jewess of fifty, stood among the women and spoke with a put-on look of pity:
— May no Jewish home meet such a misfortune! A great pity on the parents, decent people. Their precious little daughter deserves the stick, and to tell the truth, I have no pity for her at all — she was already an apostate in her mother's womb. She had no idea what to do with her pretty little mug (face). Pushed herself into everyone's eyes. And if you really want to know, the parents are to blame too. What business has the daughter of such a pauper crawling into Christian society? Here stands my Klara — imagine — and she knows better how to behave in society. How many times she has already been abroad with me — imagine, there you find a rather more respectable society. Counts and princes come to Karlsbad, and my Klara has been everywhere, and, praise God, I have never had anything to be ashamed of with her. My daughter and I once met the Austrian emperor Franz Joseph out for a stroll in Karlsbad, and many more princes and princesses; after all, people come there from all corners of the world — even the English king walks about there dressed as plainly as we are — and it's nothing!
Hearing such famous, great names, the women held their breath from great curiosity and sheer wonder.
— Imagine — Madame Szerman went on — my daughter has already been among people and knows how to behave among people. What value, imagine, does a feldsher, a pharmacist or even a doctor have for her, and all the others of whom our aristocracy consists? No more than that — after all, one is only human. In the long winter nights here in the shtetl one could — may it befall my enemies — go mad from boredom, especially such a child as my Klara. She does come into their company sometimes too, but to push herself into people's eyes like her? — May God protect all our dear ones!
— They're starting to pray Musaf! — a voice was heard. The crowd standing outside began to hurry into the synagogue.
While the crowd was pushing in the doorway, a voice suddenly rang out:
— Water, water! Someone's fainting!
(To be continued.)
Greetings from Home Folk in Eretz Israel

[Eretz Israel — travel impressions and greetings from Zagłębie people in the country.]
(From our special correspondent).
Today I visited the great Rutenberg enterprise, which will electrify the whole of Eretz Israel with the power of the Yarmuk river and the Jordan. The exploitation of the Jordan, where 500 workers are employed, is of enormous importance for the development of manufacturing and industry in the country.
This very year the government is setting about exploiting the second sea of Eretz Israel, the Mediterranean, for a port in Haifa, which will make possible the development of trade with the East and with Europe in particular.
In general, the Jewish Yishuv here stands before a new era in the history of the colonisation of Eretz Israel, in which Haifa, the „city of the future“, occupies a place of honour. As I wrote recently, the severe 5-year crisis in Eretz Israel has been mastered and completely liquidated, and the many thousands of unemployed, as well as the 600 pioneers (halutzim) of the 5th aliyah who arrived a few months ago, have found employment — so much so that lately there is even a shortage of working hands. The General Jewish Workers' Organisation [the Histadrut] has called on the Zionist Executive to apply to the mandatory power for fresh certificates for halutzim and halutzot, who can be settled in the colonies and in the „women workers' farms“ (meshkei ha-poalot).
The fifth aliyah, whose swallows have only just appeared, has brought with it, besides the halutzim, also many rich people, capitalists, who buy land here and plant orange groves (pardesim). Today's capitalists, seeing the mistakes of the earlier, hasty aliyah, put their capital into the most secure business — into orange groves, whose oranges have won great renown on the world market.
This private purchase of land will, of course, with one-hundred-percent „Hebrew labour“ (Jewish labour), open the gates to a new, large, organised and planned emigration to Eretz Israel. Unfortunately, very many grove owners, and in particular those of Petah Tikva, show little understanding for Hebrew labour and employ thousands of Arabs, which causes frequent conflicts and quarrels between the workers and the employers. Even during the Purim carnival, when the public was in a festive mood, the following incident occurred: Petah Tikva, as it is called — the „mother of the colonies“ — displayed its products on several motor cars and lorries, e.g. oranges, lemons, bananas and other fruit. A large [group of] halutzim fell upon the vehicles and forced the drivers to „take themselves off“ from the carnival procession, arguing — and rightly so — that Petah Tikva, with its Arab, non-Jewish labour, has no right to rejoice in a Jewish folk festival.
On the way to Haifa I visited Hadera and the kvutza „Gan Shmuel“, where I met the Będzin halutza Sara Szapiro (Shapira), who as a student abandoned the university and her studies and went to Eretz Israel. Coming into the kvutza, picturesque by nature, which no longer draws on the Keren Hayesod budget and which, by the way, makes a profit every year, I found Miss Shapira picking oranges. To my questions she answers in a vigorous Hebrew that she wants to know nothing more of the parasitic life of the Diaspora, and that it is in general hard for her to tear herself away from collectivism, to which she is strongly attached.
In Haifa I lodged on Mount Carmel with former pupils of „Yavneh“ and present students of the local Technion (Polytechnic), Zeev and Abraham Ehrlich. Zeev Ehrlich, a fourth-year student of architecture, sits this year for the examinations to obtain the title of architect. The younger, Abraham, from the third year of „Handasa“ (engineering) — again the second year.
Accompanied by the young people from Będzin I became better acquainted with the city of Haifa, with Acre, the Technion, the „heavy-industry factories“ Shemen and Nesher, and Rothschild's matzah mills; and on the strength of these observations one has to agree with the slogan preached by Haifa's local patriots: „Jerusalem, city of the past; Tel Aviv, city of the present; and Haifa, city of the future“!
———
I pass on the following greetings from the Jews of Zagłębie: Mr Natan Sternfeld, a former „Agudah man“, came to love the country greatly on arriving in Eretz Israel, and despite all difficulties he did not leave it, but with much patience waited out the bad times and settled down. He has a „malon“, a hotel, which serves at the same time as a meeting point for the Zagłębie people, who recall the old times and read the „Haynt“ and especially the „Zaglembier Tsaytung“, which brings them news from their former home.
Mr Szlama (Shlomo) Kokoszek [?], a Sosnowiec merchant, has taken up a productive life in Eretz Israel and is today an excellent „banai“ (bricklayer). Mr K. has work, and for some months now he has been employed on the construction of „Beit ha-Briut“, the sanatorium named after the American Jewish philanthropist Mr Nathan Straus. It is interesting to see a former draper standing on scaffolding, building a Jewish land with mortar and bricks. His two elder daughters also earn their living, working in stocking and cardboard-box factories.
Travelling to Haifa I visited the colony of Hadera, where the first Polish halutzim to arrive, from the kibbutzim „Shacharia“ and „Hashomer Hatzair“, have been settled. The new halutzim — among them the leader of the Polish „Hashomer“, Mr Y. Riftin, and the Zagłębie halutz Abraham Reigherc from Zawiercie — have work, which is also provided for the coming months.
From Hadera we set out — I and the Sosnowiec halutz Moshe Abramowicz from Binyamina — riding on donkeys, on a hot summer day, to the old historic city of Caesarea (printed „Laesarea“), where I viewed the walls, caves and ruins which have remained to this day and which bear witness to the Jewish independence of old.
From Binyamina I travel to Atlit, where at the station a large inscription strikes the eye: „Atlit, fortresses of the Crusaders“ — the fortress of the Crusades, who in their „holy wars“ shed rivers of Jewish blood. A narrow path leads to the ruins of the former „holy“ fortresses, and the area is overgrown with ripe ears of grain, which sway in the quiet wind against the burning sun.
On Hadar Hacarmel I visited the first Będzin halutz, of 18 years ago, Mr Yehuda Schneor, who after various vicissitudes has risen to the rank of „Rosh ha-Moatza“, mayor of Hadar Hacarmel. Mr S. sends greetings through this paper to the editor Mr Szpigelman, to Nute [?] Landner, Eng. Szmudzki and all his old friends.
From Mount Carmel I go down to Bat Galim, where Mr Mendel Birencwajg (Birnzweig) of Będzin lives.
The shore of the Mediterranean, which the inhabitants have named „Bat Galim“, meaning „daughter of the waves“, is splendid and charming. The blue of the sky, the gleam of the calm sea, the illuminated Carmel, the fragrant scent and the golden rays of the setting sun enchant and intoxicate.
Over a glass of Arab coffee a long conversation develops between Mr Birnzweig and me about his life in Eretz Israel. Mr B. is on the whole satisfied with his situation; his two sons, Iziek and Maniek, earn very well. Mr Maniek Birnzweig, whom the football fans in Będzin still remember as an outstanding „back“ of „Hakoah“, now plays for Haifa „Hapoel“ and is the favourite of the Eretz Israel football public.
From Haifa I travel to Acre, which also holds memorials of former times. I visit the museum, Napoleon's fortress of the year 1799, the Arab house of prayer (mosque) named after Jazzar Pasha, and the well-known prison in which Mr Vladimir Jabotinsky, founder of the Jewish Legion, was held under arrest during the Arab riots of the year [19]20, and for this reason he is known by the name „the Hero of Acre“ (ha-gibor me-Akko).
M. Hampel.

Będzin
Annual General Meeting of the „Credit Bank“.
The Bank Has Received an Addition to Its Name.
On Sunday the annual general meeting of the Credit Bank took place. It had been announced that the meeting would be held in the hall on „Góra Zamkowa“ [Castle Hill], where masses of members streamed, but at the last minute the bank's management learned that the „holy hall“ was occupied by an academy of priests, and it held the meeting in the premises of the Merchants' Association, where about 170 members assembled.
The bank manager, Mr. M. Tenenbaum, opens the meeting and greets the delegate of the head office in Warsaw, Eng. Szaszkes. The delegate's coming here proves — says Mr. Tenenbaum — that the head office has finally changed its hitherto stepmotherly attitude towards the banks in the provinces. He also greets the representatives of the „sister“ institutions, Messrs. Gastan[?] Abramczyk and J. M. Wajgryb (of the Bank Kupiecki [Merchants' Bank] in Sosnowiec), Mr. Biksbaum (of the Bank for Small Traders and Artisans in Sosnowiec), and simply guests, non-members, who are present.
The chair is handed to Eng. Gustaw Weinzieher; he invites as assessors Messrs. Elimelech Ratner and Michał Lewin, and as secretary — Lucjan Rechtman.
Owing to the absence of the president, Mr. Rubinlicht, the activity report is delivered by Mr. Marek[?] Szejn, who presents some characteristic features of the colossal development of the bank. The net profit for the year 1928 amounts to 39,400 zł.; deposits 320,000 zł.
The report is accepted with satisfaction, and the members express their thanks to the board and council, and also to the manager, Mr. Tenenbaum, for their thank-worthy activity.
On the item of distributing the profits a discussion develops, and the proposal of the supervisory board is adopted that, so that depositors may be calm and not take fright at every political wobble, the profit shall remain as reserve capital.
In accordance with the ordinance of the Minister of Finance the name is changed, and the bank will be called „Spółdzielczy Bank Kredytowy“ [Cooperative Credit Bank].
The credit for a member is raised to 20 thousand zł.
Loans that the bank takes for itself may amount to up to 1½ million zł.
Then Mr. Szaszkes spoke about the growth of the cooperative banks in Poland and stressed that he admires how well the bank has developed.
The elections bring no change at all. Only Mr. Tenenbaum was also elected to the board.
Mr. Ben-Zvi in Będzin

On 17 May the leader of the Jewish workers of the Land of Israel, member of the presidium of the Va'ad Leumi and member of the Zionist Actions Committee, Mr. [Yitzhak] Ben-Zvi, is coming to Będzin.
Together with the late Ber Borochov, Mr. Ben-Zvi was a founder of the Poale Zion movement. 29[?] years ago he came to the Land of Israel and at once took his place as a leader, where he stands to this day. During the War he was expelled from the Land of Israel by the Turkish authorities, and he then came to America, where he threw himself with all his fervour into organising the Jewish workers for the Land of Israel.
After the Jewish Legion was formed he joined it, and together with it he came to the Land of Israel. He immediately resumed the leadership, and to him are owed in large part all the international connections and the successes that Zionist work has recently had.
Mr. Ben-Zvi is also known as a scholar; he is especially known for the book on the Land of Israel which he published together with Ben-Gurion. As a leader of the Va'ad Leumi he works tirelessly at the organisation of Knesset Israel. He courageously defends our rights in the Jerusalem city council, of which he is a member.
In Warsaw Mr. Ben-Zvi was received with great satisfaction and interest.
He received the Jewish daily press at a press conference, where Mr. Ben-Zvi described the present situation in the Land of Israel. Detailed reports of this press conference appeared in the newspapers.
It is characteristic that the editors of the PPS organ "Robotnik" approached him to write a treatise on the situation in the Land of Israel.
And indeed, for the first time a larger article on our situation in the country, written by Mr. Ben-Zvi, appeared in that organ.
Mr. Ben-Zvi is coming to Będzin in the interests of working Eretz Israel. His visit has aroused great interest in Zionist circles as well as among the Jewish workers.

At the last board meeting of the Tenants' Association the desperate situation of the evicted Salewicz[?] family was discussed. It was decided to open a "ring"[?] (collection) in the "Zaglembier Cajtung" for the benefit of the family.

At the same Court of Appeal 10 trainees from the Sosnowiec District Court passed the judicial examinations, among them 4 Jews: Mgr. Lejbowicz (Sosnowiec), Dr. Rechtman (Będzin), Gawak[?] (Częstochowa) and Brauman (Katowice).
Sosnowiec. General meeting of the Bank Kupiecki

On Sunday the annual general meeting of the "Bank Kupiecki" (Merchants' Bank) took place in the "Hotel Polski". This time the meeting did not proceed as last year; rather, the reports were heard quietly and modestly. The board, which received the absolutorium (discharge), is proceeding with renewed strength to enlarge the bank's premises and will care in future for the benefit of the members.
With some 200 members present, the chairman of the supervisory board, Mr. D. Dudkiewicz, opened the meeting, greeted the guest Igosz[?] Szoszkes and proposed Mr. B. Rozman as chairman. The latter took the chair and invited as assessors Messrs. Ch. Kuperminc and J. Grachowina[?], and as secretary J. Kra[—]lawski.
Before proceeding to the agenda, the deceased member H. Lejchter was honoured by rising.
The activity report was given by Mr. G. Abramczyk. The turnover for 1928 amounts to 12,678,119.46 zł. The bank has 434 members; the net profit is 21 thousand zł.
The report was adopted unanimously; also adopted was the budget for 1929, which provides for an expenditure of 7 thousand zł. a month, with the board entitled to raise it by 10–15 per cent.
After the address of Mr. Szoszkes, who declared at the same time that the bank is being run properly, the members retiring by lot were elected by acclamation.
At the end, thanks were expressed to the office manager Mr. Jakub Gelbhaar and to the whole staff for their exemplary order.
550 families received kimcha
The kimcha [Passover flour relief] campaign, which this year was carried out by the community (gmina), brought in 10 thousand zł. The sum was distributed among 550 families, 10 to 50 zł. per family.
'What does Pogoń care if Sosnowiec is angry'..

There is in Pogoń a "free-loan fund" (gmilas khesed kase) which has a tradition of organising flower days in the name of the local free-loan fund.
Last year this was done by stealth: on the tags the word "Sosnowiec" was printed in Rashi letters. This year, however, the initiators were no longer afraid that Sosnowiec would be angry, and they went out into the streets with tags "for the benefit of the free-loan fund in Sosnowiec".
When the board of the local fund learned of this scandal, they tried to intervene with the police, but there they were told that the organisers have a permit for it.
'The deeds of the sons the fathers inherit'...

A few months ago the house-painter K. abandoned his wife, with whom he had lived for 12 years, and married the daughter of his neighbour.
The desperate wife tried to use various means against her base husband, but he laughs at everything.
This Passover the first wife decided to take revenge on the girl's father; to that end she went into the beys-medresh, where she made the old man a "mi-sheberakh" [i.e. publicly shamed him].
Soon sides were formed and a brawl broke out.
—o—
Knurów.
Defeat of the "Do Czynu" editor.
Last week the editors of the well-known Jew-baiting gutter sheet "Do Czynu" organised a meeting. The speaker was the editor of the sheet. But hardly had he begun to speak when the assembled public, which consisted of workers' elements, gave him a "festive reception"...
Seeing that he had come off very[?] badly, he quickly took himself off and fled "to where the pepper grows"...

When Spring Comes.

When spring comes the forest sings, the birds sing, man sings. Everything and everyone rejoices in the wonderfully beautiful month of May. So people used to sing and say once. Today that too has stopped. Something has changed in the order of Creation, something has turned completely over and upside down. Long did we wait for spring. Long did the frost torment us and refuse to let go, long did we have to hide in our houses, afraid to stick our noses out. In the street the fierce cold reigned, at heart it was gloomy and sad, but the fierce cold also penetrated the house, and only the hope for the whole summer still gave a little comfort. At last we lived to see it. Spring has come in all its splendour and brilliance. But somehow one does not feel like singing, the sun does not warm, and in the home a fierce cold is felt.
Spring has come; its signs show themselves only in that one has to think about a new garment, about new expenses, about the due dates of taxes that must be paid. No joy, no relief has it brought us.
In the Jewish street a cold wind is blowing. A terrible despair has gripped Jewish society[?]. Wherever one goes, wherever one stands, one hears only sighing and groaning. In the big city one hears it far more often and far more clearly than in the provinces. The foundation on which our economy stood has somehow shifted from its place, and the whole building is cracking. Everyone feels this today, but not everyone sees and understands what has happened here.
Our economy is on the whole still quite primitive; we still stand on the first rung of the economic ladder. We work with primitive methods: the peasant tills his field with the old plough harnessed to a pair of oxen, the smith hammers on the anvil, the tailor goes with the needle, and the shopkeeper sells his goods for the gulden and the grosz exactly as our great-grandfathers used to do.
Into this primitive state the new age suddenly burst in with all its modern demands. We introduced the most modern social laws. In many details we have already surpassed the Western European countries; we introduced state and communal taxes, making use of every system of taxation that exists in the world. We are like that poor man who inherited from a rich uncle a treasure of clothes and put them all on at once. He went out into the street in three pairs of trousers, half a dozen coats and some three fur coats. He did not know that every garment has its season and that one cannot wear all the garments together.
Our situation is best characterised by that verse: "There is no straw given unto thy servants, and they say unto them, Make brick" — no straw is given, yet bricks must be made. We have no raw material, we do not have the straw from which and on which one can knead, and we are required to deliver goods, to deliver money, and precisely in cash. At a time when everything revolves around bills of exchange, when nobody sees a cash grosz before his eyes, it is demanded that we pay precisely in cash, and on top of that the taxes amount to almost three times as much as the cash money circulating in the country!
When spring comes the forest sings, the birds sing, man sings — so it used to be said. Today it seems that the order of Creation has changed. Whether the forest and the birds sing, I do not know. But people certainly do not sing. Above all, no spring is felt in the Jewish street. A deep melancholy has been poured out over everyone; we feel that it cannot go on like this. Something must happen, something must be done to avert the catastrophe.
Sz. I. Stupnicki.

A Cup, the Gift of the Editors of the "Zaglembier Tsaytung", for the Strongest Jewish "Club" in Zagłębie.
Conference of 8 Jewish "Clubs".

Last Sunday, under the chairmanship of Mr. Lewkowicz, the second conference of the Jewish sports clubs in Zagłębie took place, to consider how to organise the matches for the "cup" (puchar) donated by the editors of the "Zaglembier Tsaytung".
Taking part in the conference were: for "Hakoah" — Z. Lichtensztajn; "Kraft" Będzin — Sz. Rozenblum; "Maccabi" — Lancman, Szywek; "Shtern" Będzin — Jehuda Rotenberg and Melcer; "Arye" Sosnowiec — Rozencwajg and Moszkowicz; "Shtern" Sosnowiec — Pomeranc and Blumensztok; "Kraft" Dąbrowa — Mr. Zygrajch; "Morgnshtern" Będzin — Jakubowicz and Fruchtcwajg.
After going over the report of the first conference, the position of Mr. Szywek is accepted, that with the "cup" the editors aim to raise the physical development of Jewish youth.
After electing a rules (regulamin) commission of Messrs. Lancman, Melcer and Rotenberg, the agenda was dealt with, comprising the following points: 1) propaganda, 2) where the matches should take place, and 3) the financial question.
After a short discussion it is resolved: 1) the editors of the "Zaglembier Tsaytung" shall give space to educational articles, 2) the matches shall take place in the towns of Będzin, Sosnowiec and Dąbrowa, and 3) 25 per cent of the net proceeds shall be placed at the disposal of the editors, who shall allocate the sum at their discretion.
Next Sunday at 6 p.m. a conference meets again to elect a committee.
Sport.

„Ruch" 1 — „Maccabi" 1 0:1 (0:1).
On Sunday the 5th of this month a championship match of Class "A" between "Ruch" and "Maccabi" took place on the "Ruch" ground.
In the first minutes "Ruch" managed[?] to exploit a confusion in front of the "Maccabi" goal and in the 10th minute scored the only goal.
"Maccabi" does not stay behind and begins to attack the opponents' goal, but without success[?]. In the second half the play becomes sharper on both sides. "Ruch" keeps passing the ball back to the goalkeeper. But "Maccabi" attacks the opponents' goal sharply. "Ruch" answers this with very brutal play, and the referee does not react to it. This gives the "Ruch" players more courage, as a result of which "Maccabi" has to give up the match as lost.
The other matches held that day in Class "A" brought the following result:
"Sosnowiec" — "Zagłębie" 1:3.

On Sunday a protest meeting against the proposed law to raise rents took place at the Artisans' Association in Olkusz, chaired by the president, A. Glikstein. The participants adopted a protest resolution and decided, following the instruction of the artisans' central office, to send the resolutions to the organs of government.

General Meeting of the Bakers' Guild
In connection with the voivode's approval of the bakers' guild of the local powiat (county), a general meeting of all master bakers of the local powiat, Jews and Christians, took place on Sunday in the representatives' hall of the town council, with the aim of electing a representation.
In the presence of 50 members, the meeting was opened by its initiator, the ławnik (alderman) A. Blum, who greeted those assembled in the name of the magistrate (municipality) and wished them success in their further activity. Mr. L. Jakubowicz (Wolbrom) was unanimously elected chairman, with Cichoń [?] and Zadeński as assessors. When it came to the elections, a long and passionate discussion developed about the method and about the persons who should be elected; thanks to the chairman's energy all disputes were settled and the following representation was elected by acclamation:
As elder (starszy) Mr. Cichoń (Olkusz); as deputy elders (podstarsi) L. Jakubowicz (Wolbrom), J. Safirsztejn (Olkusz). On the board: Abramcze Sztark, Jankiel Waltman (Olkusz), T. Zadeński (Skała), D. Rozenberg (Żarnowiec), S. Magowicz [?] (Pilica), J. Manowicz [?] (Wolbrom). Deputies: Finkel, Manesa, Zylbermincz, Bogdalin, Szpigler and Szwarc.
