Bankruptcies and Lawlessness (On the Founding of the Committee to Fight Malicious Bankruptcies)

[Będzin — economy and trade; opinion.] However good things may be in Poland, however fine the situation may look, however excellent the economic conditions may be — for whomever they are so, it is only for a certain contingent and by no means for the community as a whole, for the broad masses of the population. And if there are people of the middle class, of those whom we consider well-off, the conditions in which they live are very, very hard, so that more than one firm, when we [sic], of the better-situated, go under as soon as they are taxed more heavily for one year or have greater obligations than they could afford.
This in itself shows how "strong" our better-situated element is, the one that more than one person envies seven times a day — to say nothing of the not-well-situated, of the second category.
After all, we live today in enormously hard conditions; after all, the incomes [sic; perhaps "expenses" was meant] are so great and the obligations so heavy that one false step and one position that did not work out [?] can throw one off balance, and one can only rarely climb back up to the former level.
So easy is it in our times to slip and no longer be able to catch one's breath again.
After all, we no longer live in the old days, when every penny's expense was precisely weighed and measured; today one must know how to arrange one's life, how to make one's combinations, so that one can live and exist, remain standing on one's feet. To live in today's conditions means to study life, to acquire experience, to be shrewd and to know the tasks and the meaning of existence.
Be that as it may, we have great worries about tomorrow and grave cares about how to get through today. The steep decline, the heavy burdens that lie on almost every citizen, often make it impossible to secure one's existence for the future.
And when we hear today how big firms suspend payments, it is a self-evident thing; nobody is surprised, people know that everyone has great obligations, taxes, debts and unforeseen expenses, so that he could not, as the saying goes, get over — so he had to go under.
To go bankrupt is today one of the easiest things; it is also understandable, because if firm X or Y received protested bills of exchange instead of cover, it was swept along against its will by the current [printed: "geviser"], and the catastrophe happened.
Such bankruptcies are excusable, because one understands that they could happen and are quite often unavoidable.
But there is also a second kind of bankruptcy, a bankruptcy for which one prepares slowly, step by step, consciously; one takes up such a matter with deliberation and studies it closely, so that the business should run as well as possible and the combinations should succeed on as broad a scale as possible.
These reckless, speculative deeds too are called by no other name than bankruptcies.
We know that people go bankrupt, or better said take money, not because they were not paid, but because they want to get rich all at once; the business pays off for them, whatever may come of it and whatever may happen.
More than once one hears that Shmerl or Berl took goods on credit for so-and-so much, took them for himself and vanished to where the pepper grows; a second sent false bills of exchange out into the street to be discounted; a third went into a business with his bare thumb [i.e. empty-handed], risked nothing in cash — and what the end of such combinations is, is self-evident. One sees afterwards that no foundation for existing was ever laid in the first place; nobody reckoned on going a straight, normal way; nobody was after anything but taking and taking for as long as it would go.
One understands that a person can go bankrupt; one understands that a misfortune happens and the merchant gets caught with people [i.e. loses his money with debtors] or fails with a business and falls — these are understandable things, and to such people one must extend a hand and help them up.
But by no means may one compare those who come consciously and maliciously to take money and people's toil with those who go bankrupt out of need, because they, let us say, failed in one season.
And therefore the founding of the committee that has been formed at the Będzin "Merchants' Association" (Sokhrim-Fareyn) is to be welcomed; its task is not to allow the dangerous microbe to spread. The committee has taken upon itself the task of fighting malicious bankruptcies.
Certainly such recklessness must not be allowed in the Jewish street; certainly unheard-of swindles must not be allowed, swindles to which the reckless people have already grown accustomed as to perfectly kosher means; certainly one must fight against the unheard-of deeds that constantly poison the air in the Jewish street.
There must be a fight on the right and on the left to uproot the dangerous microbe that has only just burst into the world of commerce.
The investigation must be properly carried out in every case, so that not only the one who grabbed should be punished but even the one who gave, if it turns out that the latter gave only because someone came to take...
One struggles for existence, one struggles to be able to trade honestly, to earn and to remain standing on one's feet — and at such a moment simple speculators sneak in and want to get lucky all at once from other people's labour; to this one must respond with due severity.
One must help the honest merchant to remain standing on his feet in case of a catastrophe, and take revenge on those who come consciously to snatch other people's hard toil.
R. Les.
Deeds Worthy of Gratitude

(A visit to the girls' "ochronka" [children's home].)
By Ben Amotz.
...We children of the Jewish people are poor [? two unclear Hebrew words, "betsikhes uvikhsos"]. Only in one field are we "rich" — in the field of societies. There is no other people on the whole globe that possesses such a "wealth" of philanthropic institutions as we Jews.
We do not puzzle over which institution is more useful, deserves more sympathy and support. No, that is nobody's concern. The motto "Whoever stretches out a hand is given" we uphold firmly. Thanks to this, public-workers grow like mushrooms after rain; no sooner do a few "personages" get together for the public good, people who possess a certain measure of audacity, than they immediately found a society. Where the income will come from does not worry them; all one needs — they say — is donors, and donors, thank God, will not be lacking...
And societies are created, collectors come and the public pays... Not only the monthly dues, but every few weeks a fresh outcry [? "vayitsaki"]: Jews, to the rescue, the society is in danger...
From such squealing something does come into the till. In truth the society does need money, and a great deal of money, so that it suffices for collectors, for publishing newspapers — and what about [?] other expenses? Such as photographs, banquets, mi-sheberakh money and the like...
An exception in this field are the "orphan homes", the so-called "ochronkas". These modest institutions were created and exist to this day thanks to the Jewish intelligentsia, which took upon itself the task, like the assimilationists of former days, of creating productive [people] for the Jewish masses.
The "ochronkas" are run to this day by people who strive to create "something out of nothing", to bring the poorest, most neglected children up to the level of useful, accomplished people in society; and in the managements of the "orphan homes" we do not find the types of today's public-workers, so to speak [?], who push their way onto the "benches" for the sake of publicity, and a large part [of them] for their own benefit... but people who do not trumpet every Monday and Thursday, who work quietly and achieve a very great deal...
———
On the ground floor of the house at Kołłątaja 55 is the "ochronka" for girls. We paid our visit on the Sabbath, while the children were eating the Sabbath meal.
Scarcely have you crossed the threshold of the bright rooms of the ochronka, being greeted with a broad "Gut Shabbes", than you are already bound by a special affection to the institution.
In the first room, which serves as kitchen and dining room, about ten girls sit around a long table, many of them already on the way to a "goal": they have already gone through all the grades of the elementary school, learned a trade and become self-supporting...
In the second room — younger children, dressed in their Sabbath clothes, are eating lunch. Their outward appearance and physical development bear witness that the children, thank God, have an appetite, and nevertheless there are leftovers [?] too. On the table lie, "abashed", whole "untouched" challahs; apparently this "luxury" is no "novelty" for them...
After lunch. The children are sated; it becomes very joyful; one sings, the second recites, and the "programme" is concluded with "Zug o Prat" [Even or Odd], recited by a pupil of the "Yavne" school; she is not the one and only one at "Yavne". The very gifted girls of the "ochronka" study at "Yavne", where they make good progress in their studies.
Twelve-year-old Gutshe [?], a pupil in the first class at "Yavne", curtsies politely and tells you about the moment when Joseph's brothers came to Egypt and did not recognize their brother Joseph, who was by then already second to the king...
While the dark, charming [?] little girl from the "ochronka" tells the story, I think to myself that the same story is topical today too: if the rich ladies [?] of Będzin had known the abject state of these same 48 children back then, when they were taken into the institution, and came in today and saw how the once stunted children, candidates for parasites and tramps, have grown up on a par with decent people, brought up (let it stay between us — perhaps even better) like children of educated homes, they, like Joseph's brothers, would not recognize them...
Like a splendid thread runs the short report given by the faithful, devoted educator Miss [Frl.] Szarf, and once again the same truth is confirmed: talented children are to be sought only in the low alleys, among the poorest strata of the people.
Yes, one has to see it: it is very interesting to leaf through the school exercise books and see the children's abilities, to look at their own embroidery. "What more do you want?" — the educator says to me — "if some lady, of the intelligentsia of course, wants to decorate her salon with a magnificent piece of handwork, she orders it from the 'ochronka' girls..."
— Does anyone visit the institution?
— No, I get the answer; apart from the "opiekunki" [patronesses] of the "Dobroczynność" [charity society], nobody of the town's "notables" comes to us. Whom do such "trifles" interest — how orphan girls are brought up?...
— Truly so: who indeed bears such "trifles" in mind? Above all, they, our ladies, have no time to occupy themselves with such matters, for in winter it is cold, after all, and in summer one must enjoy the fresh air; and then, where are the toilettes, and other similarly important matters?...
— My thoughts are suddenly interrupted by a little girl with big, diamond-bright eyes, who asks me:
— "When will the building for the 'orphan house' be finished already? Oh, I so don't want to go home to sleep"...
— Don't worry, little lamb — I began to comfort the child — it won't take long now. The Jews of Będzin are blessed with a good trait: interest they have in nothing at all, but when someone cries out:
— Reb Yid, give money! — they don't think long and count it out...
— Good Shabbes, dear children! See you soon in the new building...
— Would that it were so! Would that it were so! — rang out the little children's voices...

The Misled Girl (4)

[Serialized novel — Jewish life, conversion; "The Misled Girl", installment 4.]
Dr. A. Weissman.

(A novel of Jewish life in the Old World, based on historical facts.)

"Mania is not guilty, Klara. Everyone accuses her, everyone curses her, because nobody knew her. She is not the only one who falls into such a misfortune. Hundreds of Jewish daughters fall into their hands, each for a different reason; very few are themselves to blame for their misfortune. But I will not rest until I have rescued her from their hands — if only I regain my strength. I will demand nothing of her; I only want to rescue her from their hands, into which she has fallen."

"Her parents have already gone to look for her; perhaps they will find her."

"Unhappy parents! What will they be able to do, even once they know where she is? It is hard to tear out of their hands the unhappy victims whom they rob from us with fine and pious little speeches!"

Wearily he let his head sink onto the back of his chair [?] and stopped talking.

Quietly, without words, the two of them sat on the veranda. Night began to fall. The last rays of the setting sun played on the leaves of the trees. The shadows grew and took up more and more space.

Little by little the women began to leave the synagogues; the men were already at the end of the evening prayer. Another minute or two, and the number of people coming out of the synagogues grew and grew. The men stopped by the synagogue and sanctified the new moon, which strolled proudly across the clear sky. It looked as if it had been waiting here by the synagogue a long time for the Jews to finish praying Maariv and come out to sanctify it.

Tired from fasting, the crowd walked slowly home from the synagogue through the shtetl and dispersed into various lanes. From some distant monastery, in the quiet, bright night, various tones of the monastery bells rang out over the shtetl; the crowd shuddered, remembering what they had lived through that day, having seen how Reb Zelig Sore's and his wife had driven off after their daughter to look for her.

Involuntarily the crowd looked toward the side from which the monastery ringing could be heard. Far away, somewhere out of a [?] village, they saw the spires, gleaming proudly golden in the bright night.

"Who knows, maybe Reb Zelig's daughter is in that monastery!" someone called out. "Maybe they are converting her right now.."

At that the crowd trembled with fear.

"Maybe the apostate herself is ringing the bells," an old Jewish woman called out, "because, as they say, it has been the custom for many years that when a Jewish child is converted, the apostate, man or woman, must first ring the bells of impurity for a whole month."

"Grandma, I'm afraid!" called out a small child who was walking with the old Jewish woman.

"Don't be afraid, my child! God will protect us."

"Grandma," the child asked, trembling, "is hell burning now?"

"For her, for the apostate, all the hells are burning now. Us, together with all Israel, God, blessed be He, will guard and save."

The child held on tighter to the grandmother, who was walking home together with the whole crowd.

The monastery bells did not stop ringing out in the air. From their echoes, on that night, a dread fell upon the whole shtetl. — — — —

Chapter Five.

In the night, when in the shtetl K. the Jews, after the great fast, sat in their houses at laid tables, eating and drinking and each telling in a different version about the terrible misfortune that had befallen Reb Zelig Sore's, who had driven off that day with his wife to rescue their child from conversion — on that same night, in the little village named after the local stream "Zastavke" [Zastawka?], where Reb Zelig Sore's family lives, the old Jewish woman Dvoyre, Reb Zelig's old mother, sat all alone at a laid table, looking at the "kapores" that had been prepared and cooked since yesterday:

The village of Zastavke lies only one mile from the shtetl K. — the same stream that runs through the village also runs by the shtetl.

"Zastavke" is a narrow stream that winds from somewhere far away. Here, by the village, it spreads out wider and digs deeper. At this spot stands an old water mill, which from many years back belonged to Reb Zelig Sore's father, Dvoyre's husband, Reb Yitskhok Hersh Sore's.

The mill is a small, old, [neglected?] building with a large wheel which the water drives slowly; before Passover, when the water rises, the wheel turns faster, more lively, and the whole old mill takes on a somewhat youthful look and fresh strength. Next to the mill, on a small hill, stands an old house with several small windows, where Reb Zelig has lived with his family for many years.

When everyone left yesterday for the shtetl to pray, they left behind Mania and the old gentile from the mill, whom they had told to keep an eye on the house.

Having learned of her misfortune later than everyone, Dvoyre drove home right after the fast, thinking that perhaps they, her son and daughter-in-law, had already arrived.

But she found no one except the old gentile from the mill, who, as on every night after Yom Kippur when his masters came home from synagogue, had taken out the cold kapores, set them down on the table and put up the samovar.

Old Dvoyre sat and looked sadly at the kapores.

Three white hens and one white rooster she had hatched herself and fed the whole summer. By day she fed them from her own hands, and every evening she let them into the chamber to sleep. The whitest and prettiest hen, without a single black feather, she picked out and said:

"This will be a kapore for Manyechke on the eve of Yom Kippur!"

And now the cooked kapores lie before her eyes on the table, and there is no one to eat them all day.

Dvoyre listened to every rustle, to every creak of the door — maybe someone is coming — but [printed "amer"] nobody came.

"If only Khayim would come! Why doesn't he come? Everyone, everyone has abandoned us!"

She could not sit still in the house. She went out in front of the house, sat down on a log and gazed into the distance; from all the roads and paths leading to the house it seemed to her that Manyechke was coming, Manyechke was speaking. There, she hears her sweet voice. But no. It is only the running stream speaking, quietly and sadly...

Suddenly her eyes stopped on a large house that stood on a hill on the far bank of the stream. The house now looked out from among the trees with lit-up windows.

"Surely guests have gathered there. Once again a birthday, a party, a celebration at their place," Dvoyre muttered. "Gentiles remain gentiles; what else should they do but rejoice and carouse? What do they lack in the world?"

Dvoyre sighed.

"They begrudged us such a precious diamond, and snatched her from us, tore her away. Woe, [?] woe!"

She could no longer look at the house from afar.

"Oh, if I were younger, if I could run, I would run, I would drive. I would turn the whole world upside down and rescue my child!"

Dvoyre went back into the house, but she could not sit still. Every moment it seemed to her that someone was driving up by the window. Several times she went out, but she saw no one.

Suddenly she heard the familiar heavy steps of the old gentile who works in the mill.

"What is it?" she asked. "Has someone arrived?"

"No, only a letter that someone gave me for you."

With trembling hands she tore open the letter and read the terrible words, in Yiddish, in [her?] own hand.

"My dear ones! Save me! I am in a locked room, but where — I don't know. I am a little to blame myself for my great misfortune, but save me. I ran away from you through the 'wild forest', through the shtetl Ts., and further on I don't know. Your Manyechke."

Good Day...

By B. Kovner.
It was, if I am not mistaken, the beginning of spring.
The grasses had already shown their young green heads, opened their mouths and swallowed sunshine and warm breezes.
They know what's good, the young little grasses...
The trees had sent out their buds to announce to the whole world the joyful tidings that soon, soon they would set to work. First they would begin to blossom, then they would roll up their sleeves and make apples and pears and plums and cherries — they would not stand with folded arms, they would earn their bit of bread.
And what, do you think, did the rivers do? They roared and burst into song on all their instruments and started running straight out into the world.
The forests go without saying: they began to put on their green leaf-dresses, embraced their dear guests, the birds, and the birds rebuilt their last-year's nests, put in new furniture and began to think about new loves and new songs.
In short, it was, if I am not mistaken, the beginning of spring. More or less Passover time, or a couple of weeks after Passover.
Since I became a married man I have lost my memory, but one thing I remember clearly:
When my neighbour came into my home, the morning was fine and clear, no later than half past six.
What the neighbour looked like that morning is not so important to know, for what will you get out of knowing that her name is Madame Plotke and that she had dishevelled hair and was unwashed and wore a dirty dress and shoes without laces and no stockings at all? Or what will you get out of knowing that her little tongue works at 60 miles a minute? That in five minutes she can talk over the whole street? Or what will you get out of knowing that she talks the whole time standing up, and that when you ask her to sit down she answers:
— Thank you, I'm in a hurry to go, I left my husband and my children just like that, my husband hasn't eaten yet and the children are still asleep, they have to go to school soon. It's already almost half past seven. Oh, how time flies"!
That is the kind of neighbour she is, Madame Plotke. Now that you already know who she is and what she looks like, we will come to the main point:
After she had already gossiped about every single person in the block, even those she does not know and has never spoken to, and after she had already let it be known 30 times that she must go, because she had dashed out of her house just like that, and every moment had taken the door handle into her hand — any minute now she's going home — only then did she remember what she had come to my wife for:
— Guess [?] what I came for, you'll never guess! Oh, is it hard for you to guess? I came to ask you a favour: I want you to lend me a head of garlic. I want to make chopped meat for dinner today; my husband is very much in love with chopped meat — for chopped meat he would give you away his wife and children. But he likes the chopped meat to be chopped or ground with garlic. Garlic, says my husband, adds the real taste and the proper flavour... And I don't have any garlic in the house, so I came to you... I know that your husband also likes chopped meat sometimes, and surely also like my husband, with garlic — all men are alike in these things. My brother eats garlic with bread: he takes a piece of dry bread, rubs garlic on it and eats.
That, he says, is much healthier than the most expensive roast; when he has bread with garlic it is a holiday for him, a Simchat Torah! So I came to ask you for a little head of garlic; when I'm out in town I'll buy you back another head... But I beg you, Madame, make it quicker, I have no time, my husband still has to eat breakfast and the children must go to school.
My wife hands her a head of garlic, Madame Plotke thanks her, makes for the door, is already holding the door handle in her hand, and just then she remembers some story:
— My dear Madame, have you already heard the news? No? How come? A wonder! The whole market is boiling with it!
— What news? — asks my wife.
I mean the news about Mrs. Grinberg — her husband walked out on her yesterday, of course! I would tell you the whole story, why and when [?], I know everything, only I have no time now, my husband hasn't eaten yet and the children have to go to school (she buzzes [?] a secret into my wife's ear), I know the whole story... I'll tell it to you later; now I must go, it's already late. Will you be at home later? Yes? Then I'll come over. Good day, thank you for the garlic... So you will, that is, be in in the house in the afternoon? Very good — a precious piece of goods, that Mrs. Grinberg! As my brother-in-law says: nobody throws things away for nothing. Good day!
— Good day! — answers my wife — you won't forget to come in later?
— I won't forget! When I say something, it's said, good day!
— Good day!
— Good day! Go in good health. Watch out, the stairs are winding, you'll fall down yet.
— Good day! Yes, I forgot to ask you: you're surely going to the butcher's soon; if so, I want to ask you a favour: ask him whether he has a sheep's head. If not a sheep's head, then ask him whether he has calf's liver. Yesterday I asked him whether he had liver, and he answered me that ever since he has had to deal with women like me, he has no liver left.. we get on his liver.. so I don't want to go in to him any more. Good day! Yes, if by chance you have yesterday's paper — I'm reading the novel in it! You'll look it out for me? Very good! Good day! Hush, before I go — you know Madame Fliame, don't you? The one with the freckles — she's already sucking lemons again.. I shouldn't sin with my words.., only six years after the wedding and already with the fourth, good day!
— Good day!
Dear readers! Perhaps you know of another flat? I can't stand it any longer. This Madame Plotke with her "good day" will drive me out of the world. Find me another flat!

The Shekel-Payer Has the Floor (A letter to the editors)

[Zionism — the shekel and the Congress; letter to the editors.] The Congress is approaching — the Jewish parliament, the highest authority of the Jewish people. Among all nations the eve of parliamentary elections brings feverish preparation. Every citizen checks carefully whether he will have the right to vote, so that as a free citizen he may express his will. The holders of power step down from their pedestals and come to the ordinary citizen, who decides how his country shall be governed. Everyone — Englishman, Frenchman, German, Pole or American — is proud that with his ballot he creates the new forms of his nation, culture and progress.
Therefore election day is for them a day of judgement. So it is understood among all nations, but among us Jews, unfortunately, it is not so. Our foolish "householder mentality", the dismissive twist of the thumb, turns the right to vote into nothing. Everyone tells himself: "Somebody else will vote." Mockery and belittling are also part of our tragedy. What for others is self-evident is for us, at best, something out of the question ("mehichei teisei").
But if for the Jews at large it is a matter of indifference, for us Zionists — the bearers of the culture of the Jewish people — it is simply a crime. In the last moments before the Congress, when the party struggle is at its hottest, people deeply regret that they did not provide themselves with the right to vote — with the shekel. But by then it is always too late. We must remove this fault now. The 16th Zionist Congress is approaching, which will no doubt be the most important since Herzl's death. Never before have we faced such problems as: the Agency, aliyah, political concessions, urban or rural colonisation, a majority in Eretz Israel or not. The delegates will decide these questions, but we Zionists, the great mass, must first of all be transformed, before the whole world, into a huge disciplined army. Polish Jewry, the reservoir of human material, must prove that we are vitally interested in sending a large number of delegates, because we still have to fight for the right to be treated in Eretz Israel as equal with others. We must see to it in good time that at the Congress Polish Jewry — both the halutzim and the middle class — is given its proper place. We must also remember that everyone is now watching us Zionists: the English government, the League of Nations, and our internal enemies and "friends" as well. The shekel is the legitimation of the state in the making [?]. The shekel will decide whether the whole world will reckon with us as a resolute camp that marches forward with iron steps, forging the future of the people of the prophets, or will regard us as Don Quixotes who, because of the small number of shekel-payers, deserve nothing but laughter. The number of shekels sold is the mobilisation of Zionist strength. We, the unknown builders of Eretz Israel, will now decide on the building of the Land by means of the shekel.
The slogan of Zionism now points in one direction: buy and spread the shekel of 5689! Provide yourselves with the right to vote for our parliament, for the Congress! The floor now belongs not only to the owner of a cheque-book.
The floor belongs to the shekel-payer.
David Hafer,
Chairman of the Shekel Committee.
Ten Years of Honour (On the 10th jubilee of "Dos naye lebn") —o— Excursions to the Poznań Exhibition —o— Keren Hayesod Conference in Katowice

[Press — a Białystok newspaper's jubilee.] Lying before our eyes is the 10th-anniversary jubilee issue of the Białystok daily newspaper "Dos naye lebn" (The New Life), which is incidentally the 1000th issue since the day the paper began to appear.
We also have the 5th-anniversary jubilee issue, but what a colossal difference there is between the first and the present five years! We see how the paper has grown, developed and risen to the level of a solid and clean newspaper that fully understands its tasks and duties.
One sees that the editor, Mr. Pesach Kapłan, and his collaborators know how to make a newspaper for the people that is at the same time a modern cultural organ and a guide.
Whatever issue of "Dos naye lebn" we take into our hands, we take pleasure in it, seeing how everything is polished, how everything there is crystallised. We feel that these people still possess loyalty [?] and reverence for the printed word, which today, unfortunately, has been so desecrated.
On the 10th jubilee we wish the editor Mr. Kapłan and his collaborators that their holy work be renewed with fresh courage and that their organ be the pride and honour of Jewish Białystok.
Y. S.

As we have already reported, a municipal committee has been formed at the Będzin magistrate, which has set itself the task of promoting the Poznań exhibition and organising excursions.
The committee consists of representatives of the magistrate and delegates of economic, cultural and sports institutions that have shown an interest in the exhibition.
The committee has already set to work. On Sunday, 2 June, the first one-day excursion to Poznań is being organised. The expenses are minimal, amounting to 25 zł (not including meals). Several two-day and one-day excursions are also planned, about which announcements will be made in the coming days.
The committee, which is in constant contact with Poznań through special envoys, will endeavour to enable the broad strata of the population to visit the exhibition by reducing the travel costs (which is possible only for a group trip) and by reducing the cost of the stay in Poznań to a minimum.
The committee will also gladly provide information to institutions wishing to arrange independent excursions.
Interested persons are received by the committee's secretariat, which works on the magistrate's premises every Monday, Wednesday and Thursday from 5 to 7 p.m., where information and guidance are given on all questions connected with visiting the exhibition.

[Upper Silesia — Keren Hayesod.] Keren Hayesod Conference in Katowice
On Sunday a conference of Keren Hayesod delegates from a number of countries [?] took place in the hall of the Jewish community in Katowice.
With 66 delegates present, Mr. Miller opens the conference and gives the floor to the delegate from Brno, Dr. Hugo Bermann [?], who delivers a very fine lecture on the task of the Keren Hayesod and appeals to the Upper Silesian population to take part and help the Keren Hayesod.
The floor is taken by the director of the Upper Silesian Keren Hayesod, Mr. Finkelstein. He reports on the activity so far and on the task still before it, and appeals to the Jews of Upper Silesia to work with more energy, since there are still enough Jews in Upper Silesia who can pay and do not pay for the Keren Hayesod.
Then the delegates from Skoczów, Królewska Huta, Bielsko and Katowice give their reports.
In the middle of the conference Dr. Schwarzbard enters and explains that he was late because he had been at a conference in Królewska Huta. The guest is given a warm ovation.
Dr. Grünstein (Bielsko) closes the conference with the remark that at the next conference there should be a more festive, Sabbath-like mood.
Director Finkelstein asks us to convey through the paper a hearty greeting to the comrades in Zagłębie.
G.

The Municipal Budget for 1929/30 before the Plenum of the City Council.

[Będzin — municipality, budget.] On Monday the City Council held a session; among the items on the agenda was also the important point: approval of the budget for the year 1929/30. Although the budget (together with the extraordinary one) amounts to no less than four and a half million zł., the Jewish councillors, among them also merchants, came to the session like "greenhorns"; the Jewish councillors held no meetings at all to consider how to act during the budget debates.
As an illustration may serve the fact that during the third reading at the session — of the statute of the tax on railway freight — an amendment was introduced that the levy on timber be reduced from 80 to 20 gr. a ton. The amendment was not supported by the merchants' representatives, and naturally the amendment was rejected.
In general a disharmony reigns among the councillors; one seeks only personal scores, which bring no honour to the Jewish population...
———
The chairman, Mr. S. Fürstenberg, opens the session and proposes that the City Council protest against the brutal attacks on the Polish artists in Opole. The protest is adopted.
Before proceeding to the agenda, 4 urgent motions are dealt with, among them one by Councillor Mrs. Ratner concerning the fact that on the Third of May Square the pumps are not working and the residents there are almost without water.
To this motion the vice-chairman Mr. Rubinlicht replies that the Magistrate is acting and will see to it that there shall be no lack of water at that place (right after the promise the pumps broke down...).
A lively discussion, which for a moment led to personal attacks, was provoked by the urgent motion of Dr. Rechtman that the City Council amend the 17th point of the statute concerning the pensions of municipal officials.
That point, which provides an entitlement to a retirement pension for the presidium of the city administration, heated tempers, and a sharp exchange took place between the mover and the vice-president.
The motion is referred to the committee for general affairs.
After that Mrs. Ratner reads a declaration in the name of the Jewish National Bloc, and Jakub Erlich reads a declaration in the name of the Right Poale Zion.
While Erlich stresses in his declaration the demand that the Magistrate open Jewish public schools in which teaching would be in the Yiddish language, a shout is heard from the Endeks [Polish National Democrats]: "We will not allow it!"
After the tax statute on railway freight is settled in third reading, the second reading of the municipal budget is taken up.
Before the budget discussion President Michał [?] delivers an exposé, in which he points to the rational composition of this year's budget. Referring to revenues, the president explains that although the population pays 300 thousand zł. a year less for electric light, the Magistrate still has a revenue of 180 thousand zł. a year from the power station.
The budget committee — says the president — relying on taxes and other revenues, has enlarged the tax statutes, which provide for an increase and [sic; read: of] 138 thousand zł. a year...
In conclusion the rapporteur appeals to the City Council to approve the budget.
Then Dr. Rechtman takes the floor, dwelling precisely on all items of the expenditure and revenue of the budget.
Dr. Rechtman sharply criticises the composition of the budget. We are — he says — like a puppet in the hands of the city administration, which comes to the City Council with ready-made budgets. But about the whole economy no advice is asked of the City Council, and the latter has no notion at all of what the city administration is doing.
The rapporteur of the budget committee, Mr. Jakub Erlich, defends the budget, which is then adopted in second reading.
The ordinary budget amounts to 1.889,565 zł.
At the session Councillor Kleinman raised an interpellation concerning the abolition of the tram stops at the Magistrate and at the new station.
The president promised to give an answer on this at the next session.
—o—
Heavy Penalties for Trading on Sunday.
On the 10th of this month the voivode issued strict penal regulations for trading on Sunday. The penalty provides for up to 2 thousand zł. or 6 weeks' arrest.
Work at the Railway Station Halted.

[Będzin — railway, construction.] By order of the railway authority the construction work at the old station has been halted. The reason is that the fund for investment purposes has been withheld by the government.
Tactless Conduct of a Tram Conductor

[Będzin — transport.] On tram number 1 a fairly large number of Jewish passengers rode to the cemetery on the road to Czeladź.
The conductor took payment from the passengers as far as the said stop, but out of spite gave no signal to stop, and the tram carried them almost to Czeladź.
The passengers consequently had to hire a cart and ride back.
Woe to the Wicked and Woe to His Neighbour...

[Będzin — police; communists.] On Saturday night at 11 o'clock in the evening a communist youth demonstrated in Kołłątaja Street.
When police appeared, the demonstrators scattered. Many of the demonstrators went off to the "Górka", where several policemen later arrived, and all the visitors on the "Górka" were taken to the police station, where everyone's identity was checked, and those, 26 young men and girls in number, who did not have the proper identity papers on them, were sent the next day to Sosnowiec to the investigating judge, who released them only on Monday at midday.
Where Is the Cat and Where Is the Butter?...

[Będzin — banking; "Agudah".] Last Sunday the general meeting of the "Agudah" bank took place. A larger number of members came to the meeting, not like "other sheep", but they had a "tongue" and told not at all pretty little stories about the bank's managers; among other things Mr. N. related that when he came into the bank to discount a bill of exchange, a member of the board nudged him with his foot as a sign that he himself would discount the bill for him..
Interesting was the question of the opposition, which asked the blunt question: how is it possible that with such huge turnovers the bank has not a penny more [printed: "kher"] profit than the "Bank Kredytowy"?..
Tram Service to Czeladź Increased
[Będzin — transport.] From Sunday the tram service to Czeladź has been increased. Instead of every 40 minutes, the tram now leaves for Czeladź every 20 minutes.
Tenants, Come to the General Meeting on Monday the 20th of This Month.

[Będzin — housing; tenants' association.] Last Sunday the annual general meeting of the Tenants' Association was to take place; owing to unforeseen and technical reasons only a small number of members came to the meeting, so the board decided that the meeting will take place on Monday the 20th of this month in its own premises at 5 o'clock in the afternoon.
At the present moment the Tenants' Association is very useful for the large number of tenants, against whom various factors lie in wait to make their situation harder, and at every attack the local Tenants' Association is the first to put up vigorous resistance.
Therefore it is the duty of every tenant to show interest in the association and to come to the general meeting, at which very important points are to be dealt with.
A Meeting (Pgisha).

[Będzin–Sosnowiec–Zawiercie — Zionism, youth.] Next Monday the Będzin, Sosnowiec and Zawiercie branches of the „Histadrut ha-No'ar ha-Tsiyoni named after Theodor Herzl in Poland“ (Zionist Youth Organization) are organizing a get-together (pgisha) in Buczyna near Ząbkowice. The agenda consists of assemblies, entertainments[?] and a „Herzl Academy“ in honour of the birthday of the great Zionist leader.
The academy will be opened by the curator of the Będzin branch, town councillor Mrs. Necha Ratner.
Sosnowiec — Boys and Girls Will Not Learn Together in the „Powszechne“ Schools.

[Sosnowiec — education.] On Monday a meeting of the county (powiat) school board took place in the hall at Małachowskiego 42.
Apart from the various items on the agenda, the priest who was present proposed that, for the sake of morality, the system hitherto in force in the „powszechne“ (public elementary) schools be abolished, and that boys and girls should not learn together.
The same priest also proposed that the school board give material help to those teachers who, because of their material situation, are unable to bring their wives here.
In the name of the Rabbi of Będzin (who was also present) Mr. Wolwele Erlich took the floor and declared that the Rabbi had already intervened so that boys and girls should not learn together, and that he supports the proposal.
The proposal was adopted by a majority of votes.
Then a second proposal was adopted, which deserves great attention.. The proposal says that the number of women teachers must be as large as the number of men teachers, in any case not more than 50 per cent of either sex..
The Catastrophic Situation of the „Talmud Torah“. Classes Are Not Being Held.

[Sosnowiec — education, community.] In the local „Talmud Torah“ classes have still not been resumed since before Passover. The reason is that the deficit is a large one, the melamdim (teachers) are not receiving their wages, and the committee is looking for a way to bring the institution to a state in which it can exist.
There is a plan that in the Talmud Torah no Gemara should be taught at all, only up to Chumash with Rashi. For this purpose half of the melamdim are to be cut, and as a result the deficit will grow no further.
The Synagogue in Old Sosnowiec Sealed.

[Sosnowiec — community, municipality.] For several months now the local magistrate (town council) has been demanding of the Jewish community (gmina) that the exit of the women's section („vayber-shul“) of the synagogue in Old Sosnowiec be made of stone and not of wood.
The community did not carry out the magistrate's order, and the result was that last Sabbath the synagogue was sealed by the magistrate.
To Exist or to Liquidate...

[Sosnowiec — commerce, associations.] The „Merchants' Association“ (Piłsudskiego 12) is going through a severe crisis: there is no board, the members take no interest, and consequently the deficit grows...
The commission, Messrs. Y. M. Wajgryb[?], Sz. Warman and M. Merin, has already called meetings several times, but without success.
Because of this the commission has decided to put the question on a knife's edge. Next Sunday a general meeting is being called, which must decide whether the association can exist or must be liquidated.
So then, the Sosnowiec merchants now have the floor...
—o—
„A Grab-and-Run Business“...
A certain B. came in to Mr. M. W. Łęczycki and introduced himself as having a business in Wodzisław (Upper Silesia) and wanting to buy bags against bills of exchange. As a reference that „he is good for it“ the buyer pointed to Mr. Rybnicki, where Łęczycki did indeed receive good information.
The buyer took goods for 600 zł. and travelled to Będzin, where he sold the goods for half nothing...
—o—
Reb Yankev Pays...
In a conversation between the gmina (community) secretary, Mr. Lewenhof, and the starosta, the latter declared that if the kehilla leaders do not pay the first fine of 100 zł. in the coming days, the sums will be collected by the magistrate.
A Statement.

[Będzin — press, polemic.] In connection with the fact that „Unzer Tog“ (Our Day) has come out with a brand-new „sensation“, namely that the editors of the „Zaglembier Tsaytung“ have taken a novel by Spektor and are printing it under the name of Dr. Weissman, I consider it my duty to make the following statement:
A few weeks ago a young man turned to me, as librarian of the „Hazamir“ library in Będzin, and told me that the novel being printed in the „Zaglembier Tsaytung“ is Spektor's.
I reported this to the editor, Mr. Szpigelman, who thanked me for the remark and explained to me that the matter was news to the editors, because the editors possess the novel [as one whose] author is Dr. Weissman, and the editors would react to it as is proper.
Moshe Milsztajn.
(Editorial note): Mr. Milsztajn's short statement is already striking proof that the base incitement of the sadly notorious „Tog“ swings beyond all limits of decency. From the moment Mr. Milsztajn drew our attention to the fact that Dr. Weissman is not the author of the novel, we — despite the fact that the whole novel which we possess was printed in one of the largest and most popular Yiddish newspapers in New York — understood it as our moral duty to turn to our highest authority, the „Association of Jewish Writers and Journalists in Warsaw“, to whom we handed over the whole matter.
Two weeks ago we received a reply that the Journalists' Association is in the same doubt, and has therefore turned to its colleagues in New York, asking them to make known who the author of the novel is: Spektor or Dr. Weissman?
As for the vulgar insults from those who busy themselves with that thing which they call, so to speak, „Tog“ — it is beneath our dignity to polemicize with such people.

First excursion to Poznań — postponed.

The Będzin magistrate (municipality) has begun organising excursions to Poznań, to the national exhibition being held there. The first excursion was to have taken place on 2 June (czerwiec), but because it was to be a one-day excursion there were few people interested in it.
For this reason the magistrate has decided to organise 3-day excursions, which will begin on 22 June.
—o—
1,500 bills of exchange to the notary in one day.
Last Tuesday 1500 bills of exchange were sent from the Jewish banks of Będzin to the notary (rejent, i.e. for protest). Besides this, the number of bills was increased by those from the post office and the Agrarian Bank.
— A sign of the present times...
—o—
In August we shall drink good water.
This Wednesday a delegation of engineers, experts on water supply, stayed in Zagłębie and inspected the filters built for the water-supply system.
The builders of the filters promise that in the month of August (sierpień) of this year the water supply will be in operation.
The Będzin magistrate, too, has already contracted an entrepreneur to lay the water pipes throughout the town.
—o—
„Revenge“ on a shammes.
The shammes (beadle) of the „Nosei“ society (bier-bearers), Szymon Zendrin[?], informs us that on the night from Sunday to Monday he was taken to the police commissariat, where he was told that he was being arrested for having stolen the holy vessels of the „Nosei“ society.
The next morning the shammes was taken to the examining magistrate in Sosnowiec, and the judge, having acquainted himself with the charge, released the shammes.
Mr. Szymon Zendrin[?] declares that the gabbaim of the society „staged“ this because he had sued them in court over a debt of two hundred złoty.
—o—
A shekel meeting.
Tomorrow at 3 o'clock in the afternoon a shekel meeting of all factions will take place at the premises of the Zionist Organisation in Będzin.
—o—
Meeting of „Hachnasat Kallah“.
Next Thursday a general meeting of the „Hachnasat Kallah“ (dowering poor brides) society will take place at the premises of the Będzin „Artisans' Association“.
The society has for many years carried on important work, and it is desirable to support the institution.
—o—
Board of the municipal power station.
On Wednesday two representatives of the Będzin town council were elected to the board of the municipal power station (elektrownia). Elected were Messrs. Jakób[?] Erlich and Director Błażejewicz. As chairman of the supervisory board — Vice-President Mr. Rubinlicht.
—o—
Tonight — a performance by the Vilna Troupe.
The Vilna Troupe, which has again made a name for itself here with its production of „Kiddush Hashem“, will tonight, Friday, again delight the Jewish theatre public with a play not yet performed.
„Underworld“ (Unterwelt), a drama in 4 acts and 14 scenes by František Langer, will be staged. The entire ensemble takes part.
—o—
The „Orphans' Week“ begins today.
As in all the larger towns in Poland, the Sosnowiec „Dobroczynność“ (charity society) is also organising an „Orphans' Week“. For this important purpose various events will take place, such as cinema, sale of badges and (sports) matches.
The proceeds are for destitute orphans. Let everyone help, so that the campaign is a great success.
—o—
Summer camps for older children.
The Sosnowiec „Dobroczynność“ together with the board of „TOZ“ (Society for the Protection of the Health of Jews) are organising to send a larger number of children aged up to 16 to summer camps.
4 weeks at the camp will cost one hundred złoty.
Exact details are given by the secretariat, Piłsudskiego 12, from 7 to 8 in the evening.

"Tsaar Baalei Chayim" (Cruelty to Animals)

[Article — shechita and the prevention of cruelty to animals.]
A conference of the societies for "Tsaar Baalei Chayim" [prevention of cruelty to animals] is now taking place in Vienna, and already in the first days they adopted a resolution to demand that Jewish ritual slaughter (shechita) be banned. The demand was supported by scientific papers and films, through which the "cruelty" inherent in the Jewish form of slaughter was demonstrated and explained. With great effort the Jewish members of the congress managed to halt the attacks and calm the tempers. But they did not manage to shout down the resolution, and it was indeed adopted. Now all the enemies of Israel will have something to lean on, and an agitation will begin against the Jewish form of slaughter.
Tsaar baalei chayim — certainly it is a great matter. "And His mercies are over all His works." The Creator is called [merciful] because His compassion extends over all creatures. In the Torah there are plenty of laws, such as the prohibition of a limb torn from a living animal, "Thou shalt not muzzle the ox when he treadeth out the corn" — one must not close the ox's mouth while it works at the grain, i.e. so that it can snatch something into its mouth and enjoy the fruit of its labour, and the like. Even regarding eating meat, which was considered a luxury, it was said that only when things are going quite[?] well for you and you want to eat meat, you must first slaughter it, let out the blood; that is, shechita was regarded as a humane form of killing a living creature, and as such it is not questioned to this day. The society people argue only that today there are other methods, above all stunning the animal before slaughter by electricity, which makes it feel no pain at all.
As we see, the matter of tsaar baalei chayim is not at all foreign to us Jews; we were already commanded it in the Torah, we have it in life. On the other hand, eating meat is for us no commandment at all; one can do without it as well. But how much hypocrisy, how much falsehood it takes for people nowadays to gather in Vienna and think out of compassion about animals. How far is Vienna from Geneva? There, for the umpteenth time, representatives of the whole world are sitting and considering[?] a proposal on reducing armaments. One would think: what could be a greater cruelty to living creatures than these weapons of destruction being prepared against human beings — the various kinds of flamethrowers, poison gases, ultra-violet or ultra-red [rays], which are capable of burning, poisoning and blinding thousands of people with a single ray. All these preparations for the future slaughter of human beings are in order; there all the tsaar-baalei-chayim people have nothing to say; there diplomats and generals sit and consider the matter from the standpoint of whether it pays, whether it calculates, and whether it will not harm political or economic competition. Only here, when it concerns oxen, here they are all present with their soft hearts that cannot bear to watch the suffering.
Tsaar baalei chayim! Certainly it is a great matter, but the only one you can catch by the hand is the Jew, because only Jews need to make the great preparations when they want to eat a piece of meat. Only Jews must have a special shochet with a special knife (chalaf). Only they do it in such a way that everyone knows where and when slaughtering takes place, and there can be supervision. Among other people, where everyone slaughters, where everyone knows the craft, where it can be done whenever one wants and however one wants, where no supervision at all is possible — there truly terrible cruelty is committed. Have you ever seen and heard the cries when a pig ["the other thing"] is stabbed and they want, God forbid, that not a drop of the blood should go to waste? Have you ever seen how crayfish are boiled alive and they writhe in the pot?
Over this cruelty there is no supervision and nobody speaks of it; only Jewish shechita is the one, last cruelty that need only be removed from the world and everything will be in order. Over such people the prophet already lamented: "They that sacrifice men kiss the calves" — those who slaughter human beings and kiss calves...
S. J. Stupnicki.
Sport / A Sports Ground Opened in Modrzejów / Zawiercie: A Flood

[Sosnowiec — sport; followed by: Modrzejów — sport; Zawiercie — flood.]
Last week the Sosnowiec "Maccabi" was invited to Kielce to play a series of friendly matches with the local clubs. "Maccabi" played 3 matches in a row and came out of all of them victorious. This made a very good impression on the inhabitants of Kielce, who in gratitude gave stormy ovations to the "Maccabi" players, and out of enthusiasm the crowd sang "Hatikvah" on the field.
The first match took place between
"Maccabi"—"Sokół" 0:1 (0:1).
On Saturday, 18 May, in very bad weather, so that it was impossible to play, the only goal was scored by Lemik.
The next day, Sunday, the second match took place between
"Maccabi"—"Maccabi" (Kielce) 0:3 (0:2).
"Maccabi" fielded here 3 reserves that it had brought along and won[?] the match very easily 0:3.
The return[?] match took place only[?] on Monday, 20 May, between
"Maccabi"—"Sokół" 1:5 (1:4).
"Sokół" had challenged "Maccabi" to a revenge match. "Maccabi" played very nicely and simply showed a fine combination game. Already in the first minutes "Maccabi" (Lemik) scored the first goal. In the 10th minute the second goal (Piekarski); afterwards "Sokół" scored its only goal from an "own goal". Teitelbaum[?] shoots the third goal and Lemik the 4th; the first half ends 1:4 for "Maccabi".
In the second half, however, "Maccabi" gives[?] the spectator a lesson in technical play and scores only one goal (Lemik). The final result remains 1:5 in favour of "Maccabi". Amid very stormy ovations and singing "Maccabi" leaves the field.
Next Sunday "Maccabi" will play a championship match in Class "A" against the ex-champion of Zagłębie — "Victoria". After the victory Maccabi achieved in Kielce, the match promises to be interesting.
Ch. P—r.
—o—
A Sports Ground Opened in Modrzejów
The opening of the own sports ground of "Shimshon" in Modrzejów attracted several hundred spectators. The opponent was a team (drużyna) from Upper Silesia. The result: 2:1 in favour of "Shimshon". Although the Gruzinki[?] side are a physically stronger team, "Shimshon" had better technique[?] and the upper hand the whole time. The goals were shot by Brenner 1, the second through a beautiful shot by Frischer. Particularly distinguished were the brothers Begrzyński[?], Brenner and Steinhaus. The Modrzejów team promises to be a good Jewish team, and it is to be expected that it will have to be reckoned with.
—o—
Zawiercie: A Flood
On Saturday there was a heavy downpour here for several hours on end. On Małe Zawiercie [Little Zawiercie] and Porębska Street the water got into several houses. The road to the railway bridge was completely flooded.
In the village of Żerkowice[?] a 20-year-old Christian woman was swept away by the current of water and drowned.
The same tragic fate befell a 3-year-old child from the village of Rokitno.

A stormy meeting
On Sunday a general meeting of the members of the "Bank Ludowy" [People's Bank] took place [in Dąbrowa Górnicza]. The agenda was: election of a board and a council, and free motions.
The so-called opposition demanded that the free motions be considered before the elections. Because of this a stormy discussion broke out, which led to personal insults. As a result the meeting was broken off, and the elections will take place in two weeks' time.

At the last board meeting of the "Merchants' Association" (Sokhrim-Farayn) the resignation of its present president, Mr. B. Rechnic, was dealt with.
Having heard Mr. B. Rechnic's statement that he is no longer able to run the institution, the board resolved not to accept the resignation, but to elect two vice-presidents.
The board also resolved to name Mr. B. Rechnic honorary president for his tireless work up to now.

On Sunday the third annual general meeting of the free-loan fund took place in the beit midrash. In the presence of a few hundred members and non-members, the president Avremele Faluch [?] opened the meeting. Reuven Dafner was elected chairman. As assessors: A. Parasol [?] and M. Żarki [?].
A strike of shoe-upper stitchers (Stepper).
It is almost a year now since a trade union of needle workers ("Nadl-Farayn") was founded in our town. During the time of its short existence the board has made every effort to improve the situation of the workers, and in particular of the stitchers. To this end the master craftsmen were called to a conference, at which the situation was discussed.
The strike, which lasted 10 days, took on a very serious character but nevertheless led to a victory. The strike was ended with a 40 per cent rise and a 9-hour working day.
—o—
A tragic death.
On Thursday morning the Jewish carter Yisroel Dovid Richtiger drove with merchants to the market in Koziegłowy. After driving a few kilometres he met a loaded Christian cart travelling on the left-hand side. Wanting to avoid the Christian, he swerved to one side, but at that moment the 2 carts collided, and the loaded cart ran over a Christian woman who was standing at the side. The Christian woman was killed on the spot. The carter has been arrested.
Sh. H.

Theatre Notes

[Będzin — theatre review; radio.]
(On the performance of "Kiddush Hashem" on Friday the 17th of this month in the "Corso" theatre, Będzin.)
The Yiddish theatre is going through a hard time. Since the great success of "The Dybbuk", no play of the "Vilner" [the Vilna Troupe] apart from "Kiddush Hashem" has aroused any strong interest.
At last we have lived to see this production here in Będzin, and I take the liberty of not agreeing entirely with the general conception of the staging, because the "Vilner" show us the Jew as he is, his old physiognomy and not the new physiognomy that is being forged in the boiling cauldron of new ideals; they show us "Kiddush Hashem" as passion [passive suffering], which no longer interests us, for we long for an active "Kiddush Hashem" with a strong ideological pathos, with an idealistic world-view.
How was the play performed? And here we must say that the Vilner gave us the maximum. In the first place stand Kamień, Wajslic and Orleska. The first with his extraordinary, singular [?] power. In one row with them — what a wonderful young talent is Hirszfeld, who is unquestionably shaping up into a great actor. The spectator cannot tear his eyes away from Wajslic and Kamień; they have to act with a great deal of mimicry; Kamień is an actor of wondrous power. The tension and the pain when the prince comes in the middle of the candle-lighting to buy brandy! Splendid is Jakob Wajslic in the role of the holy little tailor; heartfelt and Jewish are his melodies. Mrs. Orleska played Devorele with much grace and understanding. Very good was the young Magsdorf [?] as the parnas. Of course, at times, in particular moments, one feels that the inspiring breath of the Vilner of old is missing. Extraordinarily strong was the "bear-dance" scene, which shook the whole theatre audience. One more thing: the performance suffered a great deal because there were no proper sets, and from the poverty of our provincial theatre stages in general. One thing must be granted to the "Vilner": the obstinacy with which the Vilner constantly try anew to break through a wall in the tradition of the old Yiddish theatre — is one of their interesting traits and a great merit for the development of Yiddish stage art.
Herman Lewensztajn.
