Our "City Fathers"

(The situation in our self-government. What is done there? How was it once? What way out is there?)
When one goes home from a Będzin city-council session, one laughs on the way; one is ironical and amuses oneself [?] at the expense of our "city fathers".
In truth, however, there is nothing to laugh about and nothing to be ironical about. When we, simple people, not representatives, consider the situation of our municipal economy, it is no laughing matter at all; when we begin to discuss the municipal position seriously and with plain common sense, one must come to the conclusion that the citizenry of the town will suffer very, very much here under the present state of affairs.
A budget is being considered. A budget not of some middling sum, but of several million złoty. And in this very deliberation one ought, it would seem, to have been serious and sincere, conscientious and honest — meanwhile we unfortunately see envy, hatred, feelings of revenge, backstage politics, and people tripping one another up.
The main thing, the essence of the matter, the crux, is thus to play the comedy, and our representatives really do take pains that the comedy should come out in all its splendour and grandeur, to the point of disgust, to the point of losing one's patience — and incidentally, precisely during the "entr'actes", the million-strong budget, which is set at 4 and a half million złoty, will be smuggled through from the side.
One can therefore already form an idea of what such an economy may look like; it gives the impression that one is playing the lottery, and we are subject to fate and do not know how we will come out of it...
After the city-council elections were held, there was triumph among us over the enormous victory we had won, obtaining 16 Jewish seats, and the victory is indeed a great one; but how do we look with the "great victory"? They are fragmented, and how little understanding do they have for common, fruitful work? For running a sound economic household?
The people lose their equilibrium; they altogether do not know where in the world they are. They take no account of their Christian colleagues, not a few of whom take delight in these spectacles; nor does one take account of the onlookers, of the gallery, of the voters who sent them into the city council — it would seem — not to conduct politics and not to stir up agitation, but plainly and simply to run the municipal self-government, to defend just demands and to protect class interests.
But who has in mind defending interests, protecting civic rights, as soon as people forget where in the world they are.
As a characteristic, a small example: before setting about the normal [?] work, nearly all the factions read declarations, and in the declarations, as is well known, there are demands; these magnanimously promised to demand this and that from the self-government. Others planned to demand something else — only one single class read no declaration and consequently had no demands at all, and that is none other than the merchants.
You understand: Będzin is, after all, it would seem, a town of merchants, whose representatives would surely have had something to demand and to say to the city council. During the elections worlds were moved; the merchants played first fiddle, they formed a bloc and indeed got representatives elected — and now there is nothing, as if nobody sat there and as if they had no demands. And that the merchants have no representative there one sees from the fact that when the matter of reducing the excessive tax on goods sent by rail came up, there was nobody to support the improvement, and so, of course, it was rejected.
That is what the merchants' representation in our city council looks like.
Horror seizes one when watching how our representatives manage the municipal interests; it makes one's heart ache to see how such work is being banalised — work that formerly took up so much consciousness [?] and was bound up with many fine ideas and honest ideals. When there were intelligent Jews in the city council, they were a stumbling block for the small-minded [?]; people made up about them — for all their purity and honesty — whatever was in the cards, and tried to drive them out. And now that the "stumbling blocks" have been removed and there is no longer anyone to disturb them, things are done openly and freely, just as anyone pleases — and here we have a picture of what the activity of — no evil eye — 16, read: sixteen, councilmen looks like.
We lack intelligent, schooled and experienced public representatives who would not permit the chaos that has now been brought about. We lack the personalities who would have the courage to bang mightily on the table and say: Enough!
You have been loose enough until now; it must not go on any further; we must no longer permit such deeds, so that Jewish honour is not degraded [?].
But unfortunately we do not now have the strong personalities who would understand that public activity must be guarded like the apple of one's eye, and that as soon as it is neglected, it becomes a matter nobody looks after.
And yet even in the present sad situation one cannot permit that, apart from degrading Jewish honour, nothing else should be done. One must surely understand at last that one finds oneself in a place where one may not let oneself be made a laughing-stock before people.
The representatives must surely understand what their voters sent them into the city council for, and what tasks they have in order to run the local self-government.
Our councilmen must surely, in the end, concentrate and create a unity that will permit neither doing nothing for the good of the town nor, at the same time, suppressing Jewish prestige.
A Jewish club [caucus] must surely be created once and for all, where people may even quarrel, but into the city council one should come as courageous people and as Jews.
Let the Jewish club that must be created be the kitchen where the dishes are to be made, which give off their aroma only when they are served at the table...
Under other circumstances we see no possibility of continuing the work for the good of the town and for the good of Jewish Będzin.
R. Let [?].
Our Share Capital

[Article — economy; the Jewish banks.] The deep upheaval that has come into our lives over the last 10 years can be seen most strikingly in banking.
At first glance one might think that in this respect we have won a great victory: we have quite a broad network of purely Jewish banks, which employ dozens of clerks and finance almost the whole of Jewish commerce and small industry.
In truth it is for us one of the sharpest signs of poverty.
Before the war the banks were mostly private, apart from the state [bank]. A financier or a group of financiers put in a large sum as share capital. On that basis one obtained credit at the State Bank. On the basis of these two sums the larger private banks then extended credits themselves, established relations with other cities and countries and carried out operations.
Today it is different. There is no money of their own [?]. All these so-called banks of ours, which play such a big role in our lives, were built from the outset on donations or charitable loans from our great foreign philanthropic institutions, chiefly from the "Joint"; other banks had in their statutes the magic word: cooperative.
In this very word lies the true secret of the existence and growth of the banks in recent years.
The few tens of thousands of dollars from the "Joint" together with the "ICA" would [?] certainly not have had the power to create the great miracle that has unfolded before our eyes.
Here, in the cooperative banks, the extract of Jewish combinatorial ability is concentrated. Here the Jew shows his wondrous power to create something out of nothing; here the secret of tzimtzum [contraction] is revealed. The loan of a few hundred złoty is turned over several times in trade, and the result is that it is more or less enough to pay taxes and repay the loan on time.
The whole currency is perhaps merely sorcery, hocus-pocus, an illusion. After all, one never actually sets eyes on it [?]. Something goes round — bills of exchange are rewritten, here prolonged, here discounted, here collected. Something — strange banking operations are carried out, bookkeeping current-account entries. Something has to be attended to here at the bank's management, here at the notary; the brain does not stop day and night combining, planning, and the bottom line is that day after day, week after week, month after month — one already has to draw up the balance sheet...
And since the whole economic essence of our life now consists only of combinations, it is no wonder that we now have such a large network of banks.
So we have a bank for merchants and craftsmen, besides that another, separate merchants' bank, and a loan fund for merchants, and a loan fund for small shopkeepers, and a gemilut-hasadim [free-loan] fund for petty little traders, and a bank for property owners. Another wonder is that we have no bank for tenants — they of all people need a real bank to pay the rent...
The banks are all communal, because the community, the cooperative — that is their entire share capital.
And therefore — before the war, when a bank used to be founded on real share capital, great care was taken that this capital should not be fictitious, but should really be in the bank. Today's share capital, as said, is the communal character. No wonder, then, that we demand of the banks a firm communal foundation, not a fiction of democratism.
For that bit of democracy is, after all, the whole "something" that we have invested in the banks...
P. K.
In the Air

By M. Lipson.
The great Zeppelin, which flies from Germany to America in eighty hours, is already a "crawler".
It is already too small for us, the flight — too slow, too little angelic.
The "Goodyear Company" [?] is setting about building such angelic Zeppelins as will be even larger and will fly even higher.
In a single day and night hundreds of people will fly over from here to America and from America to here.
It may be that a person will work in Berlin, live in Paris, and travel in the morning and in the evening to work and from work.
The whole world will become one, one piece of air.
Within the cities themselves people will surely fly through the air: some on an air-"horse", and some in an air-"taxi".
And perhaps we will abandon the earth altogether, the sinful earth, as it is called — and live in the air, dwell in air-houses, in air-cities, work in air-businesses, stroll in air-streets and air-parks.
We will become airy, angelic.
[?] We are already not far from that.
We are already becoming air-people now, more air than people...
Our whole life is airy, hanging in the balance, without a foundation.
The old generations were rooted, they were earth-people, even when they occupied themselves with trade, with crafts.
With them everything was substantial, grounded on a foundation.
When one built a house — it was for years, for generations, for children and children's children.
When one set up a business — it had a foundation, so that it should endure.
When someone was blessed with a talent — he created substantial things. He worked on his works, learned and created, learned while creating and created while learning, filed, polished, erased, wrote, until great works came out.
And that is why in former generations great things were created, poems a thousand lines long, novels in many volumes. People created with breadth, with ambition, and that is why what they created endured.
Children stayed around their parents, did not fly about in the air and did not fly away.
When a child grew up, the parents began thinking about a purpose for it, thought it over calmly, down to earth, took counsel, searched, inquired — and took pleasure in the searching and the inquiring.
Then the destined one came and a celebration was held, a wedding — and it was solid, substantial. People caroused for days and weeks, played music, danced, rejoiced themselves and others — and felt the ground under their feet.
They held the cup of life with both hands and drank from it as practised drinkers drink wine; slowly, drop by drop, to taste the flavour more, to prolong the pleasure.
Today's generations are airy, superficial [?], feather-light.
We do not walk, we only run, we fly, we are borne along in the air.
We take life lightly, and life takes us — even more lightly.
If we set up businesses, trades, they are light, airy, and a wind carries them off quite quickly. Today there is a furniture shop across from you, tomorrow a draper's, the day after a restaurant, and a day later a soda-water stall...
Today's children fly away from their parents before they have even grown wings; they just fly about in the air.
Children today do not rely on father and mother to provide for them with a purpose; they provide for themselves, easily, airily, light-footed and light-minded. They meet at a ball, at the theatre, they "go out" and they "go in" — and they go to the wedding canopy.
And the wedding with the supper, with the whole ceremony, is also light, airy; bride and groom air out their borrowed wedding clothes and the couple is already flying off on the honeymoon.
And soon one will see a note stuck up on a shop in which the proprietor announces:
I'm going to get married, I'll be back in an hour.
Our writers and artists, too, create lightly, airily, create half-things, trifles. There is no foundation for great breadth, for great ambition.
And even the half-things, the trifles, hang in the balance, not fully said and not fully written, more blank page than script — that is how modern it is.
And the more modern a writer is, the airier he writes, ever fewer lines and ever fewer words. One word — one thing, one thing — one line, one line — one page.
Among the ultra-moderns, the "Inzikhists" [the Yiddish "In zikh" introspectivist poets] and the "Farzikhists" ["for-themselves-ists", a pun], one needs no words at all. Only void, only blank page. With a single "meow" set out in short lines one gets away with a whole poem in blank verse. Words are too substantial, too coarse.
We are a generation of air. We are airy both in literature and in life.
And that is why we never have any time. We keep running, keep flying, we do not stop even for a minute, because there is nowhere to set one's foot down...
We have no time to eat, to sleep, to live.
We drink from the cup of life like a glutton and a drunkard, snatched, hurried. So we both have no pleasure and we drink it up quickly.
At forty, when the older generations still had full cups, we are already old men and are already at the last drops...
They had time and strength to set out on the road for weeks and months, to make long stops, to halt at inns, in towns, to eat their fill, sleep their fill and talk their fill.
And when the railway came, they asked:
Look, I beg you, what is all this rush?...
Among us no one asks such an innocent question. With us it is already all rush; for us it is already too little to travel from Europe to America in five days, we must fly to America in a day and a night, in a couple of hours.
For anything longer we have neither time nor strength.
We are an airy generation.
We live in the air, even when we still walk on the earth.
The Sad Situation of the Talmud Torah

[Sosnowiec — education; opinion article.]
(The question of education among others and among us. — Can the indifference be changed?)
It is no longer news that the question of education is one of the noblest problems in the modern world-view. It is known that education demands the greatest competence, which should study how to develop the idea of the matter ever more beautifully and better. Among modern nations the world of children occupies the highest place. Who is not engaged[?] in the education of children? The finest, the best, the noblest and dearest — whoever has any understanding of the idea — occupies himself with the delicate matter called the education of children.
And who are the educators, the teachers, the guides? It goes without saying that they are people who have embodied themselves, body and soul, in the children's world, who study the children's physiognomy and penetrate deep, deep into the little souls of the children. The higher a nation stands, the more culturally developed a nation is, the better and better the people chosen to educate the future.
The children, the school, the teachers — among the nations of the world this is, after all, an entirely separate world; this little world strives by every means to be isolated from the great wide world. The teachers have their own world-view, their own special and peculiar customs and regulations. There is therefore no doubt that, first and foremost, only well-educated people with proper qualifications may be granted access to enter the little world of children.
When we begin for a moment to compare ourselves with the great modernised nations, we then see in what poverty, in what sad spiritual state we find ourselves. Who among us takes an interest in the education of children, and who are the educators? To which father or mother does it make any difference who the teachers are and in what way they deal with this delicate problem, which demands so much understanding, so much awareness?
The parents have done their duty before God and man once they have handed their children over here or there, to this school or that. The only thing that does interest them is that at the end of the school year they should not be held back in the same class.
But however little others may take an interest in the children of the secondary schools, it bears no comparison with the great interest the nation takes in the children of the elementary (people's) schools, where the strata of the population from the middling down to the very lowest are concentrated. The children are guarded like an inestimable treasure. Care is taken that the best educators should be found there, that they should have the finest opportunities to develop their talents, that they should have the most beautiful and comfortable premises.
And now it is interesting to cast a glance at how the children of the poorest class are brought up among us, and who their educators are.
Let us take, for example, our Talmud Torahs, where the very poorest children are supposed to be educated.
Who does not see in what condition our Sosnowiec Talmud Torah finds itself, and who its educators are? Can one at all speak of this institution as of an educational establishment? Every conscious — or, better said, somewhat modern, well-educated — person must surely blush with shame if he happens to speak of the Talmud Torah as of an educational establishment.
Besides, we see that there is nothing there — neither teachers nor melamdim; there is sheer chaos (tohu va-vohu), and the melamdim are not paid their pittance salaries, and it has been brought to the point of liquidation.
So the question arises: can Sosnowiec not maintain one single Talmud Torah? After all, we know that even in the smallest shtetl there are Talmud Torahs. The defect here, however, is that the Talmud Torah, which ought to be a municipal (communal) one, is not. Otherwise Sosnowiec could surely maintain such an institution and could afford a larger budget, so that the melamdim should not perish from hunger.
But everywhere partisanship and politics prevail, and one faction will not let the other in, so that the institution has in this way become a kind of private little shop, where one may not say a word of opinion to the other. That is why our institutions, which ought to occupy an honourable place, are brought to such a sad state.
One would think that with an educational establishment such as a Talmud Torah there was nothing to fear from people forcing their way in, and nevertheless the institution has been brought to such a terrible state that locks will have to be hung on the doors.
Can one imagine anything similar among other nations? Can other nations even conceive the notion of bringing a popular institution for children to this terrible state?
If people truly want to have such a Talmud Torah as a city like Sosnowiec ought to have, it can undoubtedly be created; but one must not tremble before the bright light and before the rising sun.
Let the institution be made public; let the task that such an establishment must fulfil towards the broad masses of the population be understood; let it be demanded that the whole city come to the aid of maintaining the institution; let a general meeting be convened, where everything will become clear and evident, and then the institution can be reorganised so that all strata of the population are concentrated in it.
It is a desecration of God's name (chillul ha-Shem) that in such a city as Sosnowiec the Talmud Torah should be in such a terrible state.
The Jews of Sosnowiec certainly, certainly want to give money and maintain a Talmud Torah, but they must have the guarantee that the institution is a municipal one and takes in all poor children. If it remains a private little shop, one cannot demand that it be maintained by the whole city.
The hitherto leaders of the Talmud Torah must therefore come before the city with clear words and say what they want of it and what they have to give it.
Dr. Papuri.
We Are Far-Sighted. (A Little Feuilleton).

[Będzin — short satirical feuilleton.] Yesterday I talked with an American, that is: a Będziner who has become an American and has now come here on a visit.
"You know," he says, "our Będzin is a far-sighted town."
"Where do you get that from?"
"From a lot of things."
"For example?"
"For example, the buses."
"The buses?"
"Yes. You here marvel at the electric tram. But with us in America the electric tram is already a beaten-out hoshana [a worn-out, obsolete thing]; it looks like Mendele's nag [Mendele Mocher Sforim's 'Di Klyatshe']. The main thing there is the bus."
"Very nice. Well, and another example?"
"Another example? The sewerage."
"But we have no sewerage at all."
"That is exactly what I mean. With us in America it is already going out of fashion. With us the plan is being seriously considered to spare letting out all sorts of dung and filth — to burn them on the spot. So why go to great expense on sewerage and drag the town into debt, when soon, in our days, that reform will come, which will cost a trifle: just buy a powder [proszek] and you are done."
I did not ask our American guest for any more examples. I understood the rest by myself.
I understood why my daughter's fiancé keeps putting off the wedding day. Until now I thought he was waiting until I get the two thousand dollars from America to cash. Only now is it clear to me: he is waiting until the fashion of free love is introduced — then they will spare themselves the wedding altogether...
I now also understand why our democratic associations will by no means let themselves be reformed. Indeed, why repair what is old and worn out? They will simply wait until the dictatorship comes. Whether from the right or from the left — it is all the same; something new has to come after all. So it is a pity to bother now...
I have also understood why my missus is not having a summer dress made now. I kept thinking she was waiting for a little promissory note [weksel] of mine. Not at all! She is waiting until it becomes the fashion to go about entirely in Eve's costume..
In short, a great many things have become clear to me: we are indeed very far-sighted.
Argus.
Greetings from Home, from Eretz Israel. (From Our Special Correspondent).

[Palestine — letter; Zagłębie natives.] During my excursion in the Jerusalem area I did not forget the Zagłębie Jews who live in Jerusalem either, and I devoted almost a whole day to them, solely for visits and receptions; at the same time I was received by the well-known Jewish poet and president of the "Keren Hayesod", Mr. Leib Jaffe, as correspondent of the "Zaglembier Tsaytung".
Mr. Leib Jaffe, who is no new face to Zagłębie Jewry, has just returned from his tour of Poland, where he conducted the "Keren Hayesod" campaign with great success and made peace in Polish Zionism between the warring tendencies "Et Livnot" and "Al HaMishmar".
Mr. Jaffe receives me very cordially in his office, questioning me about the national work in Będzin, where he stayed a few months ago. In our lengthy conversation Mr. Jaffe again mentioned the satisfaction with the Keren Hayesod "Magbit" (appeal) in Zagłębie, which with its successful results beat the record of all the towns in Poland.
Mr. J. shows me around all the rooms, acquaints me with the work of the "World Office" of the Keren Hayesod and introduces me to his staff — among whom works Miss Fruma Blumenfeld of Modrzejów (near Sosnowiec) — as a young Zionist activist from the "famous" and "popular" town of Będzin.
Mr. Jaffe asked me to convey his warmest greetings to the Zagłębie Jews he had met, and in particular he sends greetings to the chairman of the Będzin Keren Hayesod committee, Mr. Fürstenberg, to the honorary chairman Mr. Schein, to the chairman of the Zionist Organization Mr. Hampel, to Mr. Buchowicz of "Mizrachi", to Mrs. Necha Ratner of "WIZO", and to many other activists who distinguished themselves in the campaign for the "Geulat HaAretz" fund.
From Mr. Jaffe I went on to the second national institution, the "Head Office of the JNF" [Keren Kayemet], where Miss Scharf of Będzin works. Miss S. too acquaints me with the work of the beloved people's fund, shows me the "Golden Books" and introduces me to her female co-workers. Miss S. is getting leave these days, which she is using for a pleasure trip to Będzin. Since the Scharf family will soon be rejoicing in her, it is superfluous to report about her in the columns of the newspaper.
In the national bureau of the Keren Hayesod, the well-known, devoted Sosnowiec Zionist Mr. Shabtai Weiss works as bookkeeper; I found him in the office at work, diligently absorbed in the books. Mr. Weiss, as a regular reader of the "Z. Ts.", is thoroughly acquainted with all the details of Sosnowiec Jewish life and expresses his regret that the Sosnowiec Zionists show far less activity in the Zionist field than their neighbouring Będzin comrades. At the same time, however, Mr. W. tries to defend them on account of the death of his long-time comrade and friend Dr. Abraham Perlman, of blessed memory, whose loss Sosnowiec Zionism feels and at whose head the deceased stood tirelessly for so many years. Mr. W. is especially pleased with the successful "Keren Hayesod" campaign in Zagłębie, which was a model for all of Polish Jewry and about which the Warsaw Jewish newspapers wrote with such great praise. The success even reached Eretz Israel, to the point that the entire local Hebrew press — "HaDavar" [=Davar], "Haaretz"[?] and "Doar HaYom" — carried special dispatches spreading the good news of the self-sacrifice of Zagłębie's Jews for the building of the Jewish homeland.
Having only a little time before my car left for the Dead Sea, I could unfortunately not talk at greater length with the amiable Mr. Weiss, and only asked him in passing ("on one foot") about his situation, with which he is very satisfied. On parting Mr. Weiss asks me to give his regards to all his friends, especially Messrs. Dr. Melodysta and Y. M. Weinreb.
Mr. David Patak of Będzin, on learning of the arrival of a "landsman" in Jerusalem, visited me at the "Hotel Tel Aviv", where he talked with me for hours and consulted me on various questions. Mr. P. is a good joiner [stolarz], a skilled craftsman, and from his work he has saved a nice sum. Mr. P. complains to me that precisely now, when he has settled in well, his mother, a widow, demands that he leave Eretz Israel and come home to Będzin. Mr. Patak asks me to use my influence with his mother and brother so that they do not pull him home, and he believes that within a short time he will be able to settle his mother in Eretz Israel. I fulfil his request and turn to the P. family: leave your son and brother in Eretz Israel!
I visited Mr. Berl Halter, who came to Eretz Israel a few years ago and settled in Tel Aviv, taking up a "mis'ada" (restaurant), which was the easiest little business in the spirit of the Fourth Aliyah. With the outbreak of the severe economic crisis the restaurant owners were the very first to fall victim, and Mr. Halter wound up his "business" and went to Jerusalem, where he finally managed to get settled. He holds an agency for butter from an Australian firm, and every morning early his son, riding a bicycle [rower], delivers the goods to the customers in the city and surroundings.
In Jerusalem I also meet Mr. Leibek Apelbaum of Modrzejów. Coming to Eretz Israel 5 years ago, he joined the "Labour Battalion named after Yosef Trumpeldor" and worked for a long time at Kfar Giladi, which lies in the Upper Galilee; after the split that occurred in the "Gdud" for ideological reasons he left his first place, finding work in Jerusalem as a "banai" (bricklayer). Mr. A., as well as Mr. Yehoshua Kamerad of Będzin, who works as a "haklai" (farmer) in the colony of Hadera, I later saw on the 1st of May in Tel Aviv, taking part in the ridiculous street demonstration of the "r-r-r-revolutionary" split-off Left "Poalei Zion", who mobilised all their forces from the whole country and demonstrated — as "Davar" reports — with 100 (read: one hundred) persons. As is known, the organised thirty thousand Jewish workers do not demonstrate on the 1st of May in Eretz Israel, fearing bloodshed and disturbances, which the workers' Yishuv still remembers from the bloody year 1921, during which the interesting writer Y. H. Brenner was murdered by Arab hands.
Further greetings in the next letters.
M. Hampel.
Tel Aviv, 9th May 1929.

The Misled Girl (5)

[Serialized novel — "Di farfirte" (The Misled Girl) by Dr. A. Weissman; installment 5, chapter six.]
Dr. A. Weissman.
(A novel of Jewish life in the Old World, based on historical facts).
5.

Old Dvora could barely stand on her feet. In a trembling voice she asked the old gentile:
— Tell me, Żybek [?], who gave you the letter?
— A passer-by, a peasant.
— Where is he?
— God knows. He left right away.
— Do you know him?
— No, a stranger.
— Can't you tell me what he looked like?
— The devil knows. I had no time to look.
— Perhaps you can find him? Come with me to look for him.
— What, who, when? It's nearly an hour already since he left.
— Come, let's go, perhaps we'll still find him somewhere, perhaps he stayed here in the village for the night.
And both old people set off through the village. — — —

Chapter Six.
The house that Dvora had seen from afar, from the other side of the river, so splendidly lit up, was called in the village the "White House", because it was always whitewashed with lime, and its whiteness caught everyone's eye beside the other little village houses, which were dark, dirty, and had taken on strange colours from the rain.
In the White House, which consisted of many rooms, lived the estate steward Siwiański with his large family, made up almost entirely of women: his wife, Madame Siwiańska; their six daughters, the youngest of whom was about twenty-five; the steward's old mother; the wife's grandmother; three fifty-year-old spinster nieces; and a couple more aunts whose husbands had died young: one was shot by mistake by a friend when they went out hunting wild ducks, and the other died of consumption. Having sought suitable matches in their younger years and found none, in their old age they settled with their nephew Siwiański, who was a good family man and an honest person.
Despite the small salary he used to receive, he nonetheless lived quite lavishly; quite often "soirées" were held here in the "White House", and guests often drove in from all sides. For besides the holidays of the year, when in the quiet, boring life of the provinces people like to pay visits, the White House often celebrated the birthdays of the six daughters, the birthdays of the three spinster "panny", of the two aunts, of the steward's mother, of his wife's grandmother, and of course the birthday of the master and mistress of the house themselves.
All their acquaintances had the dates of the birthdays precisely written down, as pious Jews have — to make the distinction — the yahrzeits of their parents, and so guests often drove over to the steward's and the White House was very often lit up.
Even though the steward held a small, insignificant post on the estate of Pan Wabowski [?], a Polish magnate and owner of several villages in that district, his house was visited not only by his colleagues, stewards and servants of the rich squire and of other whole estates, but also by priests, doctors, fervent Catholics and the rest of the provincial nobility, because the Siwiańskis were regarded as people of lineage, as nobility. Their house was a kind of centre of Catholicism, where councils were constantly held on how to strengthen "the faith", how to spread Catholicism and make it a ruling power economically and politically, so that the whole world should bow and kneel before it — above all, how to convert the Jews to it.
Among their relatives were several monks and nuns who held various posts, great and small, in the monasteries of Poland and Galicia, and, as people tell, a few of them are in Italy, in the monasteries of Palermo and Naples, and some even in the monasteries of Mexico and America.
As is well known, Catholicism is a power that has spread its net over the whole world. It is a power united and centralised in secret, far more widely across the whole world than people know or imagine, and a secret union prevails among all the Catholic forces, agents, cardinals, monasteries, priests, monks and nuns everywhere.
It is said that when Catholicism in Mexico recently ran riot and rolled up its sleeves to extend its rule over the whole country, politically and economically, before President Calles took them on, the Catholics, and clipped their wings — in that whole stew in Mexico Siwiański's house also took a large part, in that money was quietly collected in this house and sent to the ringleaders of the Catholic uprising against the Mexican Republic.
One must not forget that Pan Siwiański's house and family counted among the very most important and distinguished families among the squires and loyal Catholics, regardless of their poverty. It is also told that Siwiański's great-grandfather had in his time been a "pułkownik" [colonel] in the army of Napoleon III and fought against the French Republic, which the family recounts on every birthday with special pride.
No wonder, then, that precisely in this house all the secret forces of the Catholic world gathered and worked in secret to support Catholicism and to help it with strength, effort and money, as much as was needed.
The father of the large family, the steward Siwiański, was after all, as they say, an "adon befikdekha" [?], that is, a poor, hard-working labourer; he was always worn out, overworked; all day long he went about among the fields and forests of his squire, drove around the estates, sometimes drove into town, and was altogether a harried, overworked man, carrying on his shoulders such a large, enormous family — a family of fourteen women...
The salary was very small. But the fact that he had, free of charge, such a large dwelling and a few morgs of land where he grew various vegetables and fruit, plus half a dozen head of cattle, geese and hens, which cost him no money — all this gave him the means to keep a squire's house and maintain the honour of his old family lineage.
All day long Siwiański was not at home. Therefore all fourteen women in the house had plenty of time to idle about, gossip about every acquaintance, pray, drive to the convent, spread tittle-tattle and chase after Catholic "mitzvot".
The three "panny", the two nieces [sic] and one of the steward's daughters always went about dressed in black, even at the soirées when guests came.
It was precisely the black clothes that showed they had already given up for good on getting married. The other five daughters still went about in light-coloured clothes, a sign that they were still counting on chances of making good matches.
Besides gossiping, those who went about dressed in black loved to busy themselves with Catholic good deeds. It goes without saying that the greatest good deed in their eyes was when they succeeded in "saving" and "purifying the souls" of Jewish children.
Such good fortune befell them more than once in their long lives, thanks to their being members of the Siwiański family, which had taken upon itself the task of enlarging the Catholic "hosts" in the world. All their acquaintances envied them for it. They received many letters of thanks from monasteries for their great work, and were promised the world to come.

Our Panorama

[Towns of the region — feuilleton.]
(In the provinces worlds are turned upside down. — Former strongmen risen in "resurrection of the dead". — A holy war against a rabbi. — Defiling the rabbi's seat. — Questions before the Seder. — A silver candelabrum evicted. — Building materials turned into Łódź "parcels". — Living in "darkness". — Youth without a "grandfather".)
The good-hearted provinces make themselves heard. There — so it seems — the everyday worries are not as heavy as in the bigger cities. There worlds are turned upside down as once, in the good old days, when "strongmen" (takifim) lorded it over the holy flock; there the old tactics of war are still used against enemies, against the weak, and the latter have only one recourse — to write to the newspapers, as if to say "let the public see and judge" [?], so that the world may "hear of" the injustices and judge the guilty...
We have received such letters of complaint from several small towns connected with us, i.e. from our "allies" in our voivodeship...
Every town has its own "Yente", only in each place she is "veiled" differently; but the last outcry of each one ends with:
— Have pity! Write! We have no more strength!
———
We shall begin with Pilica. Firstly, the town is geographically closer to us, and secondly, it is a place where once stood the cradle of "Torah and greatness in one place". It had the finest rabbis, good Jews, famed across half the world, and around the rabbis gathered fine Jews, men of Torah with good qualities, great givers of charity.
Today too the rabbinical seat [printed "pisa" for "kisse"] of Pilica is held by a rabbi with every virtue, a great Torah scholar, versed in worldly matters, a man able to fill the rabbinical seat of a large community; but he has two "flaws" which "prevent" him from living in peace...
The "flaws" are: 1) he is not harnessed to the chariot of the "holy" Agudah, and this is the main thing — instead of travelling to Ger he travels to Aleksander...
The war against the Pilica rabbi is waged systematically. All the Ger Hasidim have been mobilised for the "holy struggle", even old men with their righteous wives; also helping are R' Meshulam's organ, "the holy Jew", and those who can be used for a handout... namely: to give the rabbi a shove when he enters the beit midrash, to smash the window-panes of the rabbi's flat, and to tear the "rabbi's seat" off the eastern wall and throw it into...
In general the local "Agudah" and its hangers-on decided to spite the rabbi and to behave like "Moyshe Kapoyer" (Moses Upside-down), doing everything backwards. When the rabbi proclaimed that outside matzot were forbidden, the Agudah men made a point of buying the forbidden matzot and "chewing with both cheeks"...
The "revenge" applies not only to matzot; it takes on more serious forms, and there is a danger that if the war in Pilica is not liquidated soon, many living agunot (deserted wives) will be left there...
Here is a young married man, a Ger Hasid, who came home from prayers on the eve of Passover at night, and before he began conducting the Seder, before he had even drunk the first cup, he turned to his "queen" with a brand-new question:
— Tell me then, wifey, whose side are you on? The rabbi's, or our dayan's?..
— What kind of question is that in the middle of the night? — answered the naive little wife — Whose side am I on? I hold as He in heaven commanded...
— What do you mean, "I"? — the "sharp" young man began to thunder — You, you, you too are on the rabbi's side? On the side of our "enemy"?..
— Mordechai, take! — our young man commanded... You surely think he told Mordechai to take the Seder plate and say "Ha lachma"? — You are mistaken. On the eve of Passover at night, after coming home from prayers, when a "king" cries out "Take!", it means one should take the few belongings and, on the other side of the door, say to the wife "Pour out thy wrath"...
Our "hero" did just that, "asked" the little wife — who, without any ill intent, God forbid, had said she would hold as "God commanded" — and she got more than the ten plagues of the Haggadah...
———
The Jews of Wodzisław suffer from a "candelabrum" disease. In Wodzisław there are two brothers (shnei achim), Hasidic Jews and rich besides, but "something" is missing in their souls. You can guess yourselves what the "something" is — apparently they are not "Agudah" members...
The two brothers placed in the beit midrash a silver menorah with six branches, six arms, in memory of their late mother.
The beit midrash became bright in every corner, the Jews were delighted, had no need of spectacles, and the donors received countless blessings for the gift.
But the joy of the Wodzisław Jews, of the worshippers in the beit midrash, was soon disrupted. "A black cat ran across" and informed the mara de-atra (the town rabbi) and one of the dozors (community board members) that the donors' wives had quarrelled before Passover with the dozor's wife..
Well, can one allow a menorah to shine in the beit midrash from such people whose wives do not live in peace with the dozors' wives?..
So it was. A meeting was held and it was done and settled: it was ruled that the candelabrum be sent away from the beit midrash [misprinted].
— "A kapore the little hat with the little horse" (who cares).
When the donors learned of the decided eviction, they did not wait until the verdict was carried out, but took the menorah back from the beit midrash and set it up in the Trisk shtibl where they pray.
On the eve of Passover the congregation comes to pray — what happened? Where is the menorah?...
Well, there was no lack of questions; above all the congregation turned to the "Four Sons", to the dozors, and asked them:
— Mah nishtanah? Why have you disgraced the beit midrash?
All these questions — as our correspondent reports — remained with the old answer, "Avadim hayinu": the heads of the community do whatever they please; shout as much as you like — the heads of the community argue — we have achieved our aim.
— The candelabrum has been evicted from the beit midrash...
———
In the same voivodeship there is another little town that possesses such specimens. The town of Koszyce too groans under the high-handed rule of its dozor.
There is in Koszyce a dozor who rules like Mussolini, does whatever his heart desires, and if you don't like it — "call me nutcracker" (i.e. I don't care).
As an illustration of this cobbler's dictatorship we cite the following fact:
And it came to pass at midnight that a fire broke out in the beit midrash in Koszyce and the holy place went up in flames. Since this is no poor community, a meeting was called on how to rebuild a beit midrash.
Of course nobody refused the mitzvah; people gave as much as possible, confident they would soon see the new building.
And the community did indeed live to see — not the building [printed "reb binyen"], but the "fine" deeds of the Koszyce Mussolini, who sold the building materials, and his cronies took the money to Łódź...
Teeth gnash, fists are raised, but the Koszyce dozor laughs it off, strolls about the market square, hands in his trouser pockets, and revels in the fact that the Koszyce Jews are angry...
The Koszyce youth already lives in better conditions. In the town the lamps of today's "civilisation" do not yet shine, and the youth lives comfortably "in the darkness"... Nor do they bother with such "nonsense" as Zhargon (Yiddish) [printed "vsharg'on"].
And when now and then a young man from Zagłębie comes to the town and asks the youth of the fair sex who is the grandfather of Yiddish literature, they laugh at the "foolish" question and answer: "We don't need any grandfathers in the darkness"...
— Quite right, rejoice, young man...
Ben Amotz.

Lag BaOmer in Meron.

[Land of Israel — Meron; Lag BaOmer.] The great bonfire on the grave of R' Shimon bar Yochai at the hadlakah (lighting).
In Meron people gather by the thousands: old, young, pious, free-thinking, rich, poor, Hasidim, halutzim (pioneers). Everyone brings bundles, pillows, food, water.
At four o'clock the procession arrives with the Torah scroll. The Torah scroll is an old one and is always kept in Safed with a Jew who holds a hazakah (hereditary right) to it, and every year people come to his house to take the Torah. The mayor of the town, the head of the police and the head of the municipality, and H. N. Bialik and a few other people have the honour of carrying the Torah scroll out a certain distance up to the automobile, and at a mile from the building where the grave is. In front walks a group of Sephardi Jews carrying two flags, a white one and a red-coloured one. After them many[?] people dance, sing and clap their hands, and after that come the bearers of the Torah scroll, up to the graves of R' Shimon bar Yochai and his son R' Eliezer ben Shimon. The graves are in a synagogue, or more correctly, the synagogue was built around over the graves. One enters first through a gate, then into a large room without a roof. On both sides there are stairs leading to a gallery with iron railings all around, up to the roof of the synagogue, which is higher than the front room. In the middle of the front room stands a solitary tree; next to the tree a large pillar, on which hangs a large lamp. The roof of the rooms is a gallery. The wall opposite the entrance separates off the room of the synagogue in which the graves are. The wall is made with windows, and when you enter the first room you see through the windows the graves with the hundreds of little candles burning on them. But it is easy to talk — you go in! It is impossible to push your way through. In the side rooms sit women with children and their whole household. These are among those who do not come to look, but who believe that the longer they stay there, the more they will be helped in what they lack: health or livelihood, or other things. Little candles are sold for lighting on the graves, but it is impossible to get to the grave, because around the graves lie hundreds of women with children stretched out. They do not care at all what goes on around them. Others sit and say tkhines (women's prayers). Men say Psalms, others say the "Zohar", which was composed by bar Yochai at the time he was hidden in a cave for many years. There is nowhere to set a foot; people sit on the ground and pray. Others, luckier ones, have little benches.
In the front room of the grave, by the tree, there is dancing and singing. The music is two clarinets and a drum, and the dancers are all kinds of Jews: Sephardim, Yemenites, Ashkenazi Jews in shtreimels, Jews with wide and narrow belts, Jews in skullcaps, Jews in European dress, halutzim, etc. They dance in several groups with great fire and heat, like practised dancers, keeping time, and sing songs that end with "bar Yochai! bar Yochai!" An old man with a white beard, in a long kapote, with a skullcap on his head and a white kerchief round his neck, holds a little stick in his hand and dances in the middle of the circle (krahod), dances like an artist and sings a song, and after him the whole crowd answers: "Blessed is he from the mouth of the Most High, holy is he mehariyon, me'or Galil ha-elyon, our master bar Yochai, bar Yochai, bar Yochai"! The further it goes, the greater the ecstasy; people rest a while, drink beer and start again with greater fervour, and people push one onto another to see it.
At seven o'clock a call is heard: the Rebbe is being led to the "hadlakah"! At once one sees the Rebbe accompanied by the Hasidim, with police in front and on all sides, because the whole crowd has rushed to see the Rebbe; everyone wants to be close and see how the Rebbe will perform the lighting, and at the entrance life is in danger. The police work hard until they manage to stop the stream of people. Soon one sees two great bonfires, and the Rebbe with the Hasidim and other Jews dance around the fires. The fires burn until morning; every so often fresh olive oil is poured on and various things are thrown into the fire. Many tear their garments off themselves and throw them into the fire, women throw valuables, people write notes to Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai and throw them into the fire, and the oil that is spilled the women take and rub on as medicine[?] for their illnesses. All night the fires burn and the dancing and singing do not stop.
At the very break of dawn the women begin to cut the children's hair. This too is one of the customs at the hadlakah at Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai's grave. One waits with cutting the child's hair until Lag BaOmer.
When It's Spring...

[Feuilleton — spring in the "Górka" park; antisemitic harassment.] (A "Górka" sketch).
These are the generations of spring: — thus[?] spring is born: the snows melt, little streams run in the whitewashed gutters, God, blessed be He, lets the sun out of her fur-case, where she lay all winter packed in cotton wool, so that, God forbid, she should not freeze...
In the first few days she works only hours[?]: shines a little in the morning, a little in the afternoon, and goes to sleep with the chickens, right away. Well, one can't demand of a young sun that she work a full eight hours... And the further it goes, the more she bestirs herself[?], the sun, takes herself in hand and becomes ever more human, and already crawls over the roofs, plays pranks[?] around the attic rooms, drives the melancholy out of hearts; humanity revives, the blood runs in the bodies, the blood heats up, the blood gets excited — it's spring in God's world!
The "Górka" is opened: "let all who are hungry come" — whoever wants to catch a bit of air must pay 15 groszy — it's spring in the world...
All the benches are occupied. Older women sit half reclining and chat among themselves sedately and graciously (statecznie i łaskawie), the plump-bodied hens that turn about in small-town yards and peck calmly and pleasantly. Older gentlemen, worn out from their young years, who have already married off their children with nakhes and joy, sit and read a sheet of newspaper and argue whether foreign passports will get cheaper... Youth circulates in the avenues, snatches a flirt, a glance, a wink of an eye, and couples stroll in the side avenues and delight in the spring.
And when one gets tired of strolling, one rushes up stormily and grabs a bench somewhere, sits sprawled on the benches, scribbles in the sand with little sticks and accosts girls passing by:
— Panna Salcia, perhaps you'll sit down?
— Co za śmiałość! [What impudence!]
— Perhaps after all?
— Gałgan! [Rascal!]
A rascal is a rascal. One goes on sitting and goes on waiting for some stray young lady, from whom one will again catch a rebuff.
Schoolboys also have their spring. All day long one sits in school, racks one's brains over 4 times 16, catches "pałki" (bad marks) for everything under the sun, the teacher swears with "cham" (boor) and "osioł" (donkey), and so much bad blood builds up — so where does one unload it? It's spring after all, so one goes to the "Górka", and when one gets there the bad blood gets even worse:
— Psiakrew. Tyle Żydów [Damn it. So many Jews], all the benches taken, Jews everywhere, the whole "Górka" even stinks of onions...
So one talks, at first among oneselves, slowly and openly, like the sun — the whole cause of spring, the whole cause of the excited bloods — and one escalates: the words get ever louder, and the more the tongue rises, the less the hands can rest, the more they start itching and one feels like doing something with them... But one is, after all, a gymnasium pupil, and one is a little afraid of being informed on to the teacher, who could next day give two "pałki"; so one gets hold of an "andrus" (street hooligan), one of the "andruses" who hang about with patched knees in their trousers and open collars, of the "andruses" who say a word and spit a little sideways; one takes such an "andrus" and sets him on:
— Huzia na Żydów! [Sic 'em, at the Jews!]
The "andrus" goes up to a bench occupied by Jewish-looking young men, gives a "szpak"-look[?] from under his big cap-peak (daszek), spits sideways and gives an order:
— This bench is to be vacated at once, because our own lads (swojskie chłopcy) are coming here... And if the oral intervention doesn't help, and the little spit to the side doesn't either, the "andrus" rolls up his sleeves, plants his fist in the heart, and the one who resists the order falls backwards, and after that the work is already easier; once there is a bit of commotion, one can already from behind[?] land a blow with a stick, tear off a coat-flap, etc.
When it's spring in the world, and so much bad blood!..
Y. Sarahles[?].

Second Reading of the Municipal Budget

What's new in Zagłębie? (date boxes: Friday, 14 Iyar 5689 — Piątek 24 maja 1929.)
Będzin
Our City Council is debating the municipal budget in second reading. The sessions are boring; were it not for Councillor Narczarczyk [?], who provides merriment with his sermons, most of the councillors, poring over the million-złoty budget, would have fallen asleep...
At Thursday's session, while the per-diem allowances (diety) of the aldermen (ławnicy) were being considered, Dr. Rechtman proposed abolishing the fee of 15 zł. that an alderman takes for each session.
The aldermen left the session in protest. The motion was rejected.
At the same session, the motion of the Deputy Chairman of the City Council, Mr. Jakub Erlich, that the Magistrate's notices also be issued in Yiddish, was adopted in second reading.
———
At Monday's session, which lasted almost 4 hours, there was a debate on the item for schools and culture, for which a sum of 280 thousand zł. is provided.
Councillor Mrs. Ratner demands that a sum of 3 thousand zł., listed for hygiene and sport in the schools, be struck from the budget expenditure.
Under the paragraph of subsidies for private schools, Councillor Herszel Erlich proposes that the subsidy of 2,800 zł. for the schools "Sorchi" [?], "Yesodei ha-Torah", "Talmud Torah" and "Beis Yaakov" be raised to 6 thousand zł.
The motion is duly supported by Councillors G. Rechnic and Mrs. Ratner. The latter proposes that the 3 thousand zł. she had proposed to strike be allotted to the 4 Jewish schools.
The motion is adopted.
Also adopted is the motion of Alderman Żebrowski that Mrs. Bojarska's [?] school receive a subsidy of 2 thousand zł. and the Replińska school — 3 thousand zł.
Under the item of the "powszechne" (public elementary) schools, Councillor Fajner proposes that in the evening courses for adults the subjects of music and chemistry be taught in Yiddish.
The motion is referred to the school supervisory authority.
An interesting discussion is provoked by Mrs. Ratner's motion that out of the 40 thousand zł. subsidy for the local Real School, 5 thousand zł. be taken off for the "Orphans' Home" now being built (a subsidy of 30 thousand zł. is allotted for the "Orphans' Home").
Taking part in the discussion are Director Błażejewicz [?], Dr. Rechtman and M. Lewin, who are in favour of not reducing the subsidy for the school.
After the president's assurance that care will be taken to increase the subsidy for the "Orphans' Home", the proposer withdraws her motion.
General Meeting of Tenants

On Sunday, in the association's own premises, the annual general meeting of the "Tenants' Association" took place under the chairmanship of Mr. M. Lewin.
After the report on the activities given by the secretary Kozłowski, thanks were expressed to the old board.
The budget, in the sum of 3,000 zł. a year, is adopted after a short discussion.
Under the item "elections" a motion was put forward that the present board be re-elected by acclamation; on the other hand, Mr. Eliezer Bożykowski [?] is expelled from the board and also as a member — he, in order to grab a "seat" on the City Council, put up a list of his own, which also suffered a defeat.
Messrs. Blachman and Woźniak are also expelled from the board for not attending board meetings.
Caught Red-Handed...

Thieves got into the local vodka bottling plant [?] and made themselves at home. The caretaker, who saw it, notified the police, who turned up just as the thieves were carrying out a fair number of bottles of vodka.
At the police station the thieves explained that they had been getting ready to throw a "bibka" (a drinking party) and already had meat; all they were missing was a bit of the "bitter drop"...
She Grew Weary of Life...

Suicide of a Jewish girl.
On Sunday morning, 24-year-old Laja Walgerman threw herself from the second floor of the house at Małachowskiego 44.
The suicide was killed on the spot.
The cause of the tragic suicide is a chronic illness from which the girl had suffered for a long time; seeing no hope before her, she put an end to her life.
When the Tax Is Paid, You Must Pay for the Cart...

The following tax episode happened to Mr. Nachum Merin last Wednesday.
The "wagon" of the "Urząd" (the tax office) stopped in front of Mr. Merin's shop, and a bailiff stepped up to carry out a distraint for 263 zł. which Mr. M. owes in property tax.
Mr. M. had already paid the tax back in winter, and he proves it with a receipt.
But the bailiff, seeing such a "sanction" before him, demanded at least that Mr. M. pay him two zł., which the cart costs.
Because of this a sharp dispute broke out; the bailiff called a policeman, who naturally agreed with the bailiff's demand, and Mr. M. paid for the "wagon".
Festive Herzl Academy / Aleksandrów Hasidim Found a Yeshiva

Because of the bad weather, the gathering of the "Histadrut ha-No'ar ha-Tsiyoni" (Zionist Youth Organisation) in the name of Theodor Herzl took place not in Ząbkowice but in the premises of the local Zionist Organisation. With a crowd of young people, invited guests, and also in the presence of the curator Mrs. Necha Ratner and the Central Committee member T. Barensztajn, A. Frenkel opens the festive "Herzl Academy". After the singing of "Hatikvah", Mrs. Ratner speaks on topical matters (in Hebrew); further speakers on Herzl, his life, work and significance are several members of "Herzliya" in Będzin; Miss Steinberg (in Hebrew): on the importance of the Hebrew language; and T. Barensztajn, who makes a strong impression on the audience with his lecture on "The Ideological Foundations and Development of Our Organisation". The official part of the academy ends with singing and hora dances.
The continuation of the festivities took place later in the organisation's own premises, where the Będzin branch arranged a banquet for the guests.
—o—
Aleksandrów Hasidim Found a Yeshiva.
The local Aleksandrów Hasidim have founded a yeshiva named after the "Yismach Yisroel", the late Rebbe of Aleksandrów. The well-known gaon Rabbi Shmuel Zylbersztajn of Łódź has been engaged as head of the yeshiva.
The Public Must Spare the Grass

The Tramway Directorate asks us to announce that, under the agreements with the local governments of Sosnowiec, Będzin and Dąbrowa, the places where grass grows on several streets in the towns must not be disturbed.
The Tramway Directorate therefore asks people not to destroy the grass and not to step on the fenced-off plots.
Hit by a Tram and Escaped Unharmed / Małachowskiego Street and 3 May Square Will Be Brighter / A Lecture / A Hebrew Lecture

On Sunday, on Małachowskiego Street, the tram struck a Jewish passer-by. From the blow the Jew fell several times, but he escaped unharmed.
—o—
Małachowskiego Street and 3 May Square will be brighter.
The municipal administration has decided to put up another 10 electric lamps on Małachowskiego Street and 3 May Square.
—o—
A Lecture.
This Sabbath, at the "Korso" [?] theatre, the feuilletonist of the "N. Folkstsaytung" and Sejm correspondent Mr. B. Shefner ("Beys-Shin") will give a lecture on "Sketches and Characters of the Old and the Present Sejm".
—o—
A Hebrew Lecture.
In connection with the founding of a Hebrew elementary school in Będzin, the General Secretary of the Central Committee of "Tarbut" in Poland, Mr. Moshe Gordon, is coming here on Sunday and will give a Hebrew lecture on "People and Language".
The Hitherto President Mr. Moszkowski Expelled from the Small Traders' Union. A Stormy General Meeting / Jewish Parents Declare for Coeducation

[Sosnowiec — small traders' union; followed by an item: parents for coeducation.]
Sosnowiec
The hitherto president Mr. Moszkowski expelled from the Small Traders' Union.
A stormy general meeting.
Last Sunday, in the hall of the „Hotel Polski“, an extraordinary general meeting of the local small traders took place under the chairmanship of Mr. Aliner.
The report on the activity to date is given by the secretary Mr. Gancwajch, who points to the irregularities that have prevailed in the union of late: there were many „bosses“ for their own pockets... Above all, those who had taken it upon themselves to rescue the situation of the peddlers „cashed in“, and made a business of it for their own earnings...
Among the persons whom Mr. Gancwajch lists as having „pocketed“ there also figures a staff member of the well-known local blackmailing coal paper...
In the discussion on the report Messrs. Gelbard, Gutfeld, Fiszel, Skowron and Żelanka take part. The last-named describes the intolerable wrongs that the board committed against the peddlers and against the members in general. The speaker also criticises the director Burka, who came here supposedly in the interest of the small traders, and having come here busied himself with making „policies“...
Mr. Wiss proposes that those guilty of the abuses be brought before a public trial.
After the discussions resolutions are adopted: 1) to express thanks to Deputy Dr. Thon for his successful intervention on behalf of the traders in Upper Silesia; 2) to expel the hitherto president Mr. Moszkowski from the Small Traders' Union.
Then secret elections take place, which gave the following result:
To the board: H. Aliner, W. Gancwajch, R. Żelanka, Peres, Skowron, Weiss, Dafner, Dwigski [?], Apetowski, Berkower and Brandes. Deputies: Wortsman, Rozenfeld and Szlezinger.
—o—
Jewish parents declare for coeducation.
In the folk school under the direction of Mr. Majerczyk a meeting of parents took place, which dealt with the decision of the district school council to abolish the coeducation system in the public (powszechne) schools. All those assembled, numbering 300 persons, declared themselves for coeducation; 5 were against..

General Meeting of the „Merchants' Union“ / Monday — Session of the Chamber of Commerce / Drama Studio / Conference of Chamber-of-Commerce Councillors / Trial at the Labour Court / Turnover Tax / Burglary at the Czech Consulate in Katowice

[Sosnowiec — merchants' union; followed by six short items: Chamber of Commerce, drama studio, councillors' conference, labour court, turnover tax, Katowice.]
General meeting of the „Merchants' Union“.
In connection with the catastrophic situation of the „Merchants' Union“ (Piłsudskiego St.), the third general meeting took place last Sunday.
To the meeting, which was to decide the painful question of the existence of the institution or its liquidation, there came, as always, a small number of merchants — only those who have an interest in the organisation.
Mr. Weinreb opens the meeting and invites to the presidium the members of the organising committee, Messrs. S. Warman and M. Merin.
Mr. Merin points to the weak interest the merchants show in the „Merchants' Union“, which has existed for eleven years already and is an important factor for the merchant community. „My opinion is — says Mr. Merin — that since, despite the committee having applied all means to keep the union alive, the members have no interest whatsoever, the union should be liquidated.“
Then part of those assembled declare that the union should go on existing, and the following board is elected: Y. M. Weinreb, S. Warman, M. Merin, B. Żepkowicz, D. Dudkiewicz, R. Czapnik, S. Haginman [?], K. Fiszel, S. Dalesman, B. Zelinger [?] and M. Rozenman.
Deputies: Y. Gliksman, A. Czarnocha, Y. Grochowina, Y. Jungster and B S. Beser.
The first constituent session takes place next Sunday.
—o—
Monday — session of the Chamber of Commerce.
Next Monday a session of the Chamber of Commerce for Zagłębie will take place. On the agenda: the election of a presidium and other questions.
—o—
Drama studio.
At the society „Art Courses“, Kołłątaja 3, a drama studio has been set up under the direction of the actor S. Fir—Szapiro.
In the coming days the lessons in music, diction and rhythm will begin.
—o—
Conference of Chamber-of-Commerce councillors.
Next Sunday a conference of the councillors in the Chamber of Commerce from the whole Kielce voivodeship will take place here.
The conference is to decide the position of the Jewish councillors regarding the election of a presidium in the Chamber of Commerce.
—o—
Trial at the labour court.
Next Wednesday the trial against the editorial office of „Unzer Tog“ will come before the local labour court; it has been sued by the typesetters Moshe Dawid Arlerfligel [?], Salomon Fridman and Salomon Lancman, who are owed a debt of several hundred złoty...
—o—
Turnover tax.
As is known, on 15 May the deadline for paying half of the turnover tax for the year 1928 expired. The tax offices have already received instructions to carry out distraints for unpaid turnover tax. Notwithstanding this, taxpayers may still submit requests to have the turnover tax split into instalments.
—o—
Burglary at the Czech consulate in Katowice.
Unidentified safe-breakers got into the office of the Czechoslovak consulate, broke open the safe and stole 5 thousand crowns.

Joseph the Righteous's Advice Did Not Help

[Article — economy; grain reserves.] Who does not remember the fanfare (the "parade") that was made around the government's project to store grain in magazines, to build large granaries, to buy rye for millions of złoty and put it away for safekeeping, in order to ensure that, God forbid, there should be no dearth and that prices could not be screwed up, etc.
We allowed ourselves at the time to mock the freshly-baked economists who want to imitate Joseph the Righteous and store up grain; we pointed out the difference between our time and the time four thousand years ago: that today the price is calculated according to the world market, that today one cannot know at all what the grain situation will look like half a year from now; we pointed to the risk inherent in such an undertaking, which is only capable of tearing a branch of livelihood away from the Jews, yet will bring no benefit either. But all these arguments did not help, and now Warsaw faces a loss of heavy tens of millions.
How did this happen? Simply because we rush with progress; we want by force to overtake Europe at a time when we are not properly prepared for it. In Europe it is indeed the custom that when the grain is taken off the field, an account is made and one knows at once how much there is to eat and how much there is to export, or how much must be bought in, because it was a [rough reckoning?]. There it is possible, because neither the peasant nor the landowner has any reason to give false information. They state correctly the quantity they have taken from the field. With us the producer has reason to be afraid to declare the correct quantity. He is simply afraid of the taxes.
So it happened that after the harvest we received statistical information that grain would be scarce. Exports were therefore prohibited, and the large cities gathered reserves, for which they paid high prices. Now, when the new harvest is approaching, the landowners have thrown onto the market the grain stocks they had kept hidden, and there is therefore an enormous surplus with simply nowhere to put it.
It would even have been possible to export abroad, where good prices can still be had; but we are waging a tariff war with the German, and he makes difficulties for the import of grain from Poland.
Thus the remarkable situation has arisen that precisely before the harvest of new grain prices are falling, and the cities that laid in reserves are simply being impoverished, losing hundreds of millions.
S. J. Stopnicki.
Esperanto, the World Language (Dedicated to the Esperantists' Rally in Będzin on Sunday, 2 June)

[Będzin — Esperanto; article.] Today, in the age of radio and Zeppelins, when within a few dozen hours we reach other parts of the world, when within 10 minutes we can, while in Warsaw, hear what is going on in Berlin, London, Paris, etc., the question of an international language becomes in this respect an ever more important problem.
The question then arises: can Esperanto be the language of the nations? The answer of us Esperantists is: yes.
First: because the Esperanto language is very easy to learn; second, the whole Esperanto grammar consists of only 16 grammatical rules and does not have the complexity of other languages, so that the Esperanto language can be learned within 3 to 5 months.
On the importance of an international language such minds as Leibniz, Kant, Voltaire and Tolstoy have spoken out (the last-named learned Esperanto within 8 days).
The problem was "read" [so printed; probably for "solved"] by the well-known Warsaw Jewish doctor Ludwik Zamenhof, born to Jewish parents, who already in his earliest childhood years felt the heavy burden of multilingualism and its consequences. Being gifted, he displays special talents for languages, and dreams of creating a universal language for all nations and countries. And in this he succeeds. In 1878, already a pupil in the 8th class, he celebrates with a circle of friends the birth of Esperanto. In 1885 he graduates from the medical college in Moscow and specialises as an eye doctor. At that time he looks for a publisher to bring out his first work, but in vain. In 1887, thanks to his fiancée and the assistance of her wealthy father, the first Esperanto work appears under the title Lingwo internacia by Dr. Zamenhof.
Today there are Esperantists all over the world, mainly in the Western European countries and in the Far East (Japan, China); many trading and export houses abroad have already introduced Esperanto as an international correspondence language, e.g. the Leipzig Fair and other institutions.
From year to year international congresses of Esperantists take place; the next World Congress of Esperantists takes place in August this year in Budapest. At such congresses various peoples gather, such as Japanese, Chinese, Australians, Europeans, and discuss various problems in Esperanto.
Esperanto makes great strides forward from year to year, and near is the time of its victory.
M. Rozen.

Olkusz: Bandit Attack on a Train — Jewish Merchant from Radom Killed

[Olkusz — crime.] On Tuesday at 11 o'clock at night, between Bukowno and Olkusz, a masked bandit entered a compartment of a 3rd-class carriage in which only Jewish passengers were travelling, and demanded money from the passengers, threatening to shoot them if they refused. A few Jews handed over their money at once, but one put up resistance and would not give. The bandit immediately fired several shots at him, whereupon the victim fell into a pool of blood, severely wounded in the chest; after that the bandit vanished.
At the alarm the train stopped. As far as the railway station in Olkusz the man who had been shot still showed signs of life, and while he was being carried into the municipal hospital he died. The entire police force was put on its feet. At the hospital the doctors certified death. In the middle of the night the news spread through the whole town and made a terrible impression. According to the passport found on the murdered man, his name is Natan [printed "Gtan"] Zygman, 42 years old, a butter and cloth merchant from Radom; 700 zł in cash were also found on him.
A. B.

I.
Honoured Mr. Editor!
Allow us to publish in your esteemed newspaper the following open letter:
Reading in the Dąbrowa [Dąbrowa Górnicza] chronicle in the last issue of your esteemed newspaper a report under the title "A stormy meeting" — we, members of the "Bank Ludowy" [People's Bank], find it necessary to draw your attention, very honoured Mr. Editor, to the fact that you were falsely informed about the course of the last general meeting of the "Bank Ludowy".
This is what happened: on the agenda were the election of a board, a council, and free motions. We state that the motion of the "so-called opposition" to change the agenda did not lead to any personal insults; on the other hand, regrettably, the following happened: when the "so-called opposition" — which, incidentally, had a considerable majority at the meeting — put several clear questions, such as whether it is true that the manager of the bank, Mr. B. Rechnic, and several persons who stand at the head of the bank are founding a so-called cooperative bank of their own; whether it is true that in the year 1928 no board existed at the bank; and other questions about the order in the bank — Mr. B. Rechnic answered with such epithets as: "you won't live to see it", gentlemen of the opposition; "that's how I wanted it"; "whip me with a riding crop", etc. That was the factual and clear answer, [mildly (?)] speaking; and a council member, Mr. Y. Mincz, supplemented it with a blessing: "[?] eighty thousand black years". At these "pearly" words those assembled became very agitated, and in protest several members left the meeting, headed by the well-known local public figure, founder and former bank president, Mr. N. A. Gutman.
The "cultured" and "intelligent" public functionaries, seeing that their defeat was unavoidable, staged a personal attack on one of the members, the epilogue of which will end in court. As a result the policeman present dissolved the meeting.
Because of such unheard-of treatment of members of a public institution, we express our sharpest protest and declare categorically that in future we will not tolerate such base conduct.
(10 signatures follow).
II.
Esteemed Mr. Editor!
Give me space to print in your esteemed newspaper the following letter to the board of the "Linat ha-Cholim" in Sosnowiec.
Last week I turned to the board of the above-mentioned institution with the request to lend me a "vange" [probably wanna — a bathtub (?)] for my sick wife. As a pledge I offered 2 silver goblets, but the "compassionate" vice-president, Mr. Lejbisz Sznajman, refused to lend me the "vange" because I am not a member. My pleas did not help — that I, as a poor porter who barely earns a dry piece of bread, am not able to pay for the "Linat ha-Cholim" — I did not get the "vange".
I therefore have the honour to publish through your esteemed newspaper the scandalous fact that the "Linat ha-Cholim", the institution subsidised by the kehilla and supported by the city, should not come to the help of a sick Jewish family.
Respectfully,
Icchak Jakub Szajewicz.

"Makabi" — "Victoria" 1:1 (0:0).
On Sunday a championship match was held on the "Victoria" ground between "Makabi" and the ex-champion of Zagłębie, "Victoria". The match took place before some 1000 spectators and was very interesting; only the referee was somewhat irritating — he is unfortunately not qualified for "A"-class teams.
At first the play is open, but later "Victoria" gains a slight superiority and has very favourable moments, which it does not exploit. "Makabi" also gets its say, but the wings of "Makabi" do not keep up with the tempo of the half-back line ("pomoc"), so that the centre attack of "Makabi" finds it very hard to get a shot at goal.
In the second half "Victoria" begins to play very brutally, to which the referee did not react, and instead of sending off the player Gagel of "Victoria" he actually sends off the player Fiszel of "Makabi". This arouses bitterness among the Jewish spectators, but "Makabi", disregarding the fact that it is playing with 10 men, bombards the opposing goal, and in the 30th minute the referee awards an 11-metre kick to "Makabi", and Szmidt converts it into a goal. Immediately afterwards the referee awards an 11-metre kick to "Victoria", and they equalise, and the final result remains 1:1. Best on the pitch for "Makabi": Szlezinger, Szmidt, Bałagzka [?]. Referee Mr. Śliwa — not decisive.
