The Fruit of the Times (Trade Then and Now. Why Does No One React to the High Prices?)

[Economy — opinion.] The economic conditions in Poland are anything but cheerful. Witness the waves [?] of protested bills of exchange and the great number of bankruptcies, which have become a quite ordinary phenomenon, a normal occurrence.
We live under hard conditions of existence; expenses nowadays are so great — the tax burdens, the housing question, the various outlays we have — that they oppress and stifle the small and average citizen.
At the same time, however, it is characteristic that, for all that, business is still not conducted on a normal basis to this day. Nowadays one must, after all, be careful in giving goods [on credit] on the one hand, and on the other hand earnings must be calculated so that one can both be competitive and still earn after deducting the enormous administrative expenses.
But what do we see? We see neither the one nor the other: people neither try to be competitive nor earn properly according to a normal calculation. Instead [?] — either one trades without profit, after the Jewish formula "what do I lose on it," or one tears off a price that follows no calculation or costing whatsoever.
The war years caused disillusionment and demoralization in every field of our life; in every corner one senses something puzzling, astray. The war threw mankind off the bridle — the wheels have left the rails; they cannot keep to the prescribed road, where they feel too cramped, too fettered.
And that is why, to this very day, such a terrible chaos (tohu va-vohu) reigns, to the point of losing all balance.
We see how people trade and deal, do business and turn the world upside down, at a time when we know positively that they have not put even a worn coin into the business; moreover one earns almost nothing on the goods, and truly honest merchants stand pondering how such a "Sperl" [?] can keep dumping goods without end — and the end is that such a one [?] goes bankrupt, pockets the goods together with the money and takes nothing and nobody into account... And indeed such people have no respect for anyone, no fear and no sense of responsibility; they play the lottery and do not in the least reckon how it will all play out later.
The question arises: can an honest firm match the conditions and prices offered by such a newly risen "star"? Can it compete with those who are themselves lawless and who also squander other people's property? Naturally, with this kind of trading the ground is cut from under the feet of the honest, decent firms, those that understand the idea of "live and let live."
And just as the reckless lottery players sweep solid and honest firms off the surface thanks to their swindling schemes, so it is also the other way round: there are swindlers who keep watch and wait for an opportune moment, and at such a moment they tear off a price beyond all reason.
Thus we know, for example, that for Passover the price of fish began to rise, up to 8 zł. a kilo, and there it stays. The question arises: what on earth has suddenly happened to cause such dearness of fish? What is it — are they getting lost in the waters, are they emigrating from Poland, or what? The answer, however, is that the fish are not getting lost in the waters, nor are they about to leave us. It is simply this: the fishmongers presumably joined hands for the holiday and set a price to make your mouth water. Well, it stands to reason that the lust for money is great and that raising a price is surely [?] easier than lowering it; hence it is self-evident that it is considerably more comfortable, both for the pocket and for one's health, to take as high a price as possible. And after them followed the butchers, the poultry dealers, and in the end our bakers — may they be healthy and strong — could [?] not stay behind either.
True, they have not raised prices; but the thing is that for some weeks flour has been falling steadily, and the baked goods still cost the same price as before.
As is known, rye flour has been falling for several weeks already, and the price of bread [sic] has been reduced by only a few groszy. The baked bread pretends to know nothing. On the other hand, they are very much aware when prices are about to rise. Should flour now rise, say, by 1 zł. a sack, our bakers would forget that they did not lower the bread price when flour fell, and they would instantly raise the price of bread on you.
Here one must not forget that in our municipal councils (magistrates) there are commissions whose task it is to fix prices of first-class foodstuffs; that is, they are supposed to keep watch so that the population is not exploited on articles of prime necessity.
So the question indeed arises: where are these established commissions, which are supposed to see to it that the population is not wronged when buying bread or other first-class foodstuffs?
These are unheard-of doings — and could anyone have imagined that at a time when flour keeps falling the bakers would have the nerve to pretend to have forgotten everything? And still more annoying is that the commissions existing alongside our municipal self-government bodies should also remain so indifferent to the unheard-of injustice that the population must overpay so much money for such a "luxury" as bread.
When one says that in our times lawlessness reigns in every field of our life, there is surely no arguing with it [?].
R. Let.
25th Jubilee of the Antwerp Diamond Bourse

[Abroad — Antwerp, Jews.] This month marks twenty-five years since the diamond bourse in Antwerp was founded. At the beginning of June the bourse will celebrate its jubilee with great pomp; many personalities from the city administration and the commercial world will take part in the celebration.
Since almost all members of the bourse are foreigners (Jews), the Belgian government will be represented by the Belgian Foreign Minister, who will deliver a special address of greeting and will point out [?] the great merit of the foreign diamond dealers, who have strengthened and consolidated the diamond trade and made it beyond competition from any other city in the world.
The president of the bourse, Mr. Sam Tolkowsky, will, on the eve of the celebration, deliver a major speech in French over the central radio station of Belgium on the development of the diamond trade and its prospects for the future. The speech will be broadcast all over the world.
Since up to 90 percent of the bourse's members are Jews, the food during the celebration and the special luncheon to be given will be strictly kosher. Thus this time the government representatives too will enjoy kosher food...
A Mentally Ill Jew Made “Rachel's Tomb” out of Human Bones...

[Będzin — burial society; a strange incident.] On Friday the Rabbi of Będzin sent for the gabbai of the Chevra Kadisha, Mr. Mendel Ferens, and told him that a woman had come to the rabbinate and related that her husband, Yekl Weissblatt, who lives on Kościelna Street, had taken bones out of a grave in the cemetery behind the “Górka” [the hill] and then buried them in a room.
Mr. Ferens took an interest in the matter and, together with Mr. Meir Berger [?], went to Mr. Weissblatt's dwelling.
At first Weissblatt denied it, saying he knew nothing, but when Mr. Ferens offered him 10 złoty to show where he kept the bones, he agreed and opened the room, where the following scene was seen: a patch of earth had been ploughed up [?]; on the earth stood a tree branch woven into a “Star of David”. Here — says Weissblatt — “is Mother Rachel's tomb”..
At the request of Mr. F., Weissblatt pointed out several pieces of human bone.
The bones were buried among the graves in the above-mentioned cemetery.
As we are informed, Weissblatt has not been in his right mind for several weeks, and for that reason he was also dismissed from his work at Fürstenberg's brickworks.

Theatre Notes.

[Będzin — theatre; review.] “Underworld” (Periferie) by František Langer, a drama in 4 acts and 14 scenes, staged by the Vilna Troupe on Friday the 24th of May this year. Director: Y. Valren [?]; sets: Fritz Kleinman.
The second performance of the Vilna Troupe was a new triumph for the Vilner. One must state that Będzin has not for a long time seen such theatre, to which the actors have so serious an attitude. Precisely with the Vilner one feels that stage acting is for them a religious service. Such a strain of the soul at the moment when the types they create are brought onto the stage — this almost religious absorption is a peculiar trait of the first Vilner and continues to this day.
“Underworld” was played to a packed hall. I am, however, doubtful whether the great material success can be a criterion of the play's worth. One thing, though, is certain: “Periferie” is theatrical — full of movement and gripping action. The simple man finds there what his heart desires. A man of the underworld who loves a prostitute. That “love” can be “weak as a helpless girl”. A degraded judge, a drunkard, who asks a crown for a piece of advice to a tormented soul; a man who lost his high office only because he preached that with no prisons and gallows can one cure the world of crime, but rather one must provide every criminal with every good thing, with suitable work, educate the children, let them study, because man is good by nature, and only the prescribed laws and order create criminals of all kinds.
For 30 years this judge waited for the “miracle” that would prove to the world that under a criminal's coat there also beats a human heart, ready to sacrifice itself for crimes over which the conscience torments it. After 30 years he lived to find the underworld type who would cry “I have killed, punish me”. Frank is the name of the man whom fate brings together with the judge, to whom he confesses that he killed a man by accident, and his conscience gives him no rest. At the police they do not believe that he murdered, because the traces did not prove that he was [?] the murderer. His assurance that he alone murdered does not help; they drive him out of the police station. The judge, in order to show the world the man of the underworld he had dreamed of, whom he had sought for 30 years and met by chance, advises him: you want to be believed — kill another man, so that you will be believed; the world will not come to an end if you do away with one more person. You, however, will be saved, and I will prove I was right. And Frank kills his own beloved, at the same time calling the police, to whom he cries: I have killed!
This play works very well thanks to its theatrical effects and the piquant moments in the action, and still more thanks to the good ensemble playing of the Vilner. Joseph Kamen as Frank is warm and vigorous; the intelligence of his acting bubbles out of every movement and gesture. Jacob Waislitz as the “Judge” created an unforgettable figure, perhaps the highest point of stage achievement; he simply bewitches you — and how easy it would have been to overplay this role, and how artistically Waislitz overcame this danger. Mrs. Orleska [?] is without any doubt an actress of great intelligence and, as always, was good in the role of “Anga” [?].
Barbarka (Magsdorf [?]) and Toni (Hirschfeld) played their episodic roles in broad lines, sharply underlining the characteristic traits of their figures.
The rest of the ensemble too commanded their roles as is proper.
It is characteristic of the Vilner that they never stop, even in the hardest time, enriching the plays they stage, beautifying them, festively adorning them; they do not stint on money for good sets, for which they deserve a quite special yasher-koyech.
Herman Löwenstein.
Social Obligation

[Sosnowiec — merchants; society, opinion piece.]
(How should the present interest in a professional association be understood?)
Time and again we come up against it; at every opportunity we see our brokenness, our nil understanding of our own interests, of our most painful questions.
We attended a general meeting of a "Merchants' Association" in Sosnowiec. One might have thought that important questions had been placed on the agenda, questions apt to improve the interests of the members. But who says so? Whom does it occur to that this is what a professional association is obliged to concern itself with? Indeed, the question placed on the agenda was whether the association should exist at all or whether it should be liquidated completely.
Do you grasp such a question? A "Merchants' Association" has nothing to do in the Jewish street; the people of merchants, of dealers and shopkeepers, is already so well off and comfortable that they need no professional association whatsoever, that the matter interests them not in the least, and it only has to be removed, cleared out of the way, because it is a nuisance; it is a superfluous object nobody looks at, and nobody needs to carry such a burden on his shoulders.
That is how we see our brokenness, our helplessness, our failure to understand for what aim and purpose professional institutions are created and what they are called upon to do.
It would seem that Sosnowiec has Jewish merchants, and not only does it have them — at first glance one thinks that one is dealing only with merchants, and the association belongs to the middling merchants, to the average Jew, to the people, to the one who at every step is most burdened [?], to the one who cannot help himself and who, as soon as anything happens, must have an adviser, a lawyer, someone to go and defend him, someone to speak on his behalf.
It is therefore impossible to understand where this category of people gets so much coldness, so large a dose of indifference, which causes so much trouble in the little world of the merchants.
How often we see these Jews going about as if stunned [?] after a tax has been assessed on them, complaining that they will be ruined if the decree stays on their heads as it was handed down "in the high windows". One would have thought that at such a moment one must come into the association and examine the situation, discuss the future of this or that merchant, of this or that burdened one [?], down to the point of ruin; and once such an institution is removed completely, to whom will the helpless Jews turn then — those who not only cannot defend themselves but cannot even bring out two words?
And if there is no "Merchants' Association", who will intervene for the merchants as a body when the need arises to speak in the name of the merchant class? How often do we come upon such encounters, such obstacles?
We know that, regrettably, we have very, very little benefit from our professional institutions and even less from the merchants' associations as such, and because of that the merchant concludes that he does not need the association, that it is superfluous to him — for if he has no benefit from it, what is it needed for?
No one tries to analyse the matter: that such an institution is as necessary to the merchant as life itself; no one tries to be willing to understand that if the association brings him no benefit, this is no proof at all that the institution is unnecessary, but on the contrary, that it must be brought to the level at which one does get the proper benefit from it. Do we ever stop to think what colossal benefit we could have from our professional institutions if they stood at the proper height? No, we never give ourselves such an account, otherwise we would make an effort to have good professional institutions, otherwise the question would never have come to mind — the simply ridiculous question — whether it should exist, or, better said, whether one should liquidate the institution that should have been the guide for every merchant, the ABC of the mercantile method.
Among us people do not want to understand that nothing comes of itself, that everything has to be created, that every thing must be built systematically, and that often years go by before fruits show themselves. Not to speak of the fact that socially we are so poor that not only is nothing substantial, real, done in this field, but people are not even interested in its being done at all.
With us it is quite simple, quite primitive: there is no benefit from this or that association, from this or that institution — let it be removed, let it be taken off the Jewish street.
That is how indifferently — we would say criminally — we treat public affairs, how banal we are when it comes to considering social deeds. Surely one must understand at long last that nothing comes of itself; with folded hands nothing can be created.
Why fool ourselves. Nobody makes the effort to raise the community to a better social level, and one cannot hold it against the simple Jew that he has no interest in his association. Nobody has taught him that he needs an association, and he does not know that such a body may one day be of use to him in life, because in the present situation he cannot imagine it.
At such a moment the better ones, the more understanding ones, ought to have come and said that we must root in the masses an interest in society; and if they do not do so, if their activity consists only in confirming that the masses have no understanding of the common good, that is truly sad and painful.
The better ones must come and educate their fellows and show them the great thing of concentration, of understanding social tasks — social obligation.
Selekt.
A Word in Season

[Będzin — charity and health; summer colonies for the sick.]
(On the "ring" for sending poor sick people to summer colonies)
For several years now the board of the Będzin "Dobroczynność" [the charity society] has taken upon itself the initiative of sending a few dozen poor sick people to a summer colony.
In dozens of cellars and attic rooms they lie, the sick, of various ages, breathing in stifling air and poisonous smells, waiting impatiently for the dear summer to come, when, with the help of philanthropy, they will be able to enjoy for a few weeks fresh, healthy air, to drink in fragrant flowers, to sate themselves on beautiful natural landscapes, on lush fields and pine trees.
Dozens of such requests reach the board of the "Dobroczynność" every day, and it gives each one fine promises, gives hope — "you will go"...
For this campaign money is needed, and everyone must give, above all those who have the means to spend every summer at health resorts; that element must take upon itself the duty not to forget its sick brothers and sisters.
Today the "cure ring" [donation chain for health cures] begins. The first donation, of 100 zł., is given by the family of Y. Szajn. Let the beginning then be "schejn un gut" ["fine and good" — a pun on the family name], so that the dozens of sick people are not left abandoned.
Sh. L.

Every Jew with His Bundle

[Feuilleton — humour; Jewish types.] Every Jew has a yoke; every Jew carries a yoke on his head. A Jew who has no yoke is no Jew at all.
Pious Jews have a yoke, the yoke of the Kingdom of Heaven. A pious man bears the yoke of the Torah, the yoke of the commandments; that is the old Jewish yoke, the yoke the Jews took upon themselves at Mount Sinai.
A Jew who does not keep the commandments of the Torah is called a "porek ol" [one who casts off the yoke] — one who throws off himself the "yoke of the Torah", the yoke of the commandments.
So people think that these Jews, these "porkei ol", have no yoke at all — but it is not true: they create another yoke for themselves, they carry another yoke.
And it is comical to see these Jews in their new yoke-harness, in the reins of the new yoke. It is ridiculous to see them, the supposedly free people who wanted to free themselves from one yoke, having taken upon themselves a new one, a much heavier one — and how they make themselves ridiculous.
I know a Jew who carries on himself the yoke of a world revolution. He eats with the world revolution, drinks with the world revolution and sleeps with it. In the middle of a meal you can hear him say:
— Ah, how much better the food would taste to me if it were already after the revolution! He says such a verse after a drink too, the way he once used to say a "Borei nefashot" [blessing after food]. And this verse he also mumbles in his sleep.
He lives with this yoke. When he reads a newspaper he looks only for the world revolution. "Has the world revolution come yet?" — he asks as he takes a newspaper in hand and rummages and searches. In every scrap of news about an uprising, a revolt, about unrest and even about a quite ordinary strike he sees the coming of the world revolution. To every question he has a ready answer — the world revolution.
The workers' question will surely be answered after the world revolution. The Jewish question — without a doubt; the women's question — certainly. Envy and hatred will be abolished from the world after the world revolution. A love tragedy? — after the world revolution. The only answer is the world revolution. — Just wait for the world revolution.
So he has a ready answer for everything.
He truly carries the yoke of the world revolution on his head.
And here is a second Jew, who carries the yoke of culture, of progress, of civilisation, of advancement and of going forward.
This Jew is even more unhappy than the first, and the yoke he carries is much bigger still.
This Jew makes sure that the world should be full of light and education, strive only forward, and that the last shadows of the Middle Ages should disappear.
And he is the ambassador, the envoy of this mission in the world.
That is how he feels.
He goes about, watching and guarding the world's property.
If someone gives a yawn that could be interpreted as a second's damage to his world-property, he becomes frightened; if someone else, on the other hand, gives a "gos"[?] that could be understood as a second's increase of his world-property, he becomes a happy man.
Recently I come upon him sitting, reading a newspaper and groaning.
I come closer and see that he is reading the news about the latest natural catastrophes.
— Well! What do you say to that? — I ask him.
— Oy vey! World culture, world culture!
I ask him:
— Is that all? And so many Jews suffered from it, there are so many dead and wounded, so much property destroyed!
— All that is rubbish [lit. mud] — he says to me — the main thing is world culture! World culture: the world has gone backwards, no small matter — the Middle Ages! Oy vey!
Again I know a Jew who carries the yoke of art, especially of Jewish art.
When this Jew meets me he laments and weeps:
Oy, woe is me, Jewish art, the Jewish one, oy, woe is me, the Vilna Troupe is suffering exile, the best actors have to do clownish tricks in an operetta, oy, woe is me — today so many young Jews who paint and draw and do sculpture work!
— Don't eat your heart out, I tell him, come, let's have a glass of tea.
— And how can I drink tea when Jakob Weislitz is a wanderer? How can I drink tea, how can I!
And here is another Jew, of a different sort already, who carries on himself the yoke of politics.
This Jew holds himself responsible for the whole of world politics; he carries a pain in his heart that he did not prevent the World War. But he also has a justification: he did not want it, and he used every means to avoid the war — but is it his fault that they would not listen to him?
And now he keeps an eye on politics; he watches every step of Voldemaras, of Dr. Stresemann, of Piłsudski and of Huber [Hoover?]. When it comes to some disputed question — as, for example, when there was the commotion over Vilna — he was all fire and flame; he watched over politics so that, God forbid, it should not come to a catastrophe.
And I may assure you that if we do not have a war now, we have him to thank for it — this Jew who keeps watch over politics; he has an eye on them.
He carries the yoke very heavily, but with pride...
So all Jews go about, each with a yoke.
There is no such thing as a Jew without a yoke. A Jew without a yoke would be like a Jew without a hump on his back.
And if a Jew has no yoke at all left to take upon himself, because all the yokes have already been snatched up by others, he takes upon himself the yoke of Yiddish or the yoke of Hebrew, the yoke of vegetarianism, the yoke of buying books, the yoke of fighting against modern marriage.
And the more idealists now join the Jewish street — and, as is well known, a couple of million idealists join every day — the more the yoke-bearers, the "bearers of the yoke", multiply, so that soon there is no yoke left.
Bearers there are, shoulders stand ready, heads are bowed — but there is nothing to carry.
The yokes, the better ones, have already been snapped up.
For here too there is competition.
There are already people, small people, who invent new yokes.
Everyone comes and brings his own bundle; everyone has his yoke.
And how many Jews have other yokes; how many Jews have, for example, a yoke of cooperative houses, of turning Jewish children into goyim, and still others.
When I tell you there is no Jew who has no yoke — you may believe me!
Gamliel.
The Seduced Girl (6)

[Serialized novel — "The Seduced Girl", a novel of Jewish life in the old world; installment 6.]
Dr. A. Weissman.
(A novel of Jewish life in the Old World, based on historical facts.)

But they strove [?] above all to convert Jewish daughters rather than Jewish sons.
— Jewish daughters are good and pious. It is a real sin that they marry Jews; then they multiply the same ugly, depraved creatures as their husbands and fill a new [printed "gayye" = "naye"] world with Jews!
— Jewish girls, as long as they are not yet married, can be persuaded of everything and made into good people and good Christians.
Such conversations the fourteen women often held among themselves, especially those of them who were dressed in black. Such conversations were often held, too, by the guests who frequently came to them. They constantly talked and planned how to convert all of Israel in one day, in order to multiply and enlarge Catholicism and make "it" a world power. Or they talked about the great future awaiting Catholicism in America, and especially in Mexico, or they talked about converting the Jews right here on the spot, at any price!
— I ask too, — the two aunts, the "ferupsene" [?] aunts, argued [?] at the gatherings, — why do we keep silent and do nothing to convert the Jewish daughters of our neighbours? Look, how does the Jew Zelig come to have a daughter like Mania? She looks like a count's child; even in her speech and in all her manners she does not look like a Jewish child; she is so good, so decent — why do we keep silent?
All the residents and all the guests of the "White House" loved Mania very much; they would keep her with them for hours whenever they managed to get hold of her.
— It gladdens the soul, — the women would say to one another, — when you look at this pretty, innocent child, who, poor thing, was so unfortunately born a Jewish child... It becomes bright in every corner when she comes in to us.
— And the 14 old women would look enviously from the "White House" at the little hill where stood the little house of Reb Zelig Sarah's ["Zelig Sores"], which lay opposite, across the running river.
There, in the little house, reigned young life and the bright world, and here, in the "White House", reigned old age, weakness, death and the Christian "world to come", with graveyard leaflets.

Chapter Seven.

This evening it was especially merry at the Siwiańskis' [?] house. Usually, when they gathered, they would talk about the weather and chew over for the hundredth time all the gossip and tittle-tattle [?], because dull village life provided no better material for conversation. Sometimes someone told some news from the papers, [and then] there was nothing to say concerning Catholicism; or, when the material ran out, they would ask one another how they were feeling in health, and so that the material for talk should not run out, even the perfectly healthy would complain that they felt ill, for if someone were to answer "I cannot complain about my health", then the material for talk runs out. But if one complains about one's health, people will start giving you remedies from all sides and telling packs of stories about how so-and-so got well from such a remedy, and meanwhile there is material for talk until the food is served.
Once the food had been served, the topic was soon switched to "the laws of eating and drinking" — gorging and guzzling.
The men outdid one another in the number of glasses and little glasses of vodka, liqueur and wine they had poured down [?]. The women were more occupied with sweets.
This evening, apart from the gorging and guzzling, all conversations were put aside, and the topic of the evening was Mania, or Manieczka, as the Siwiański family used to call her.
All eyes now looked at Ludwig, whom people had always barely looked at; everyone now looked at him as at "the hero of the day".
Because of his family, which came from simple peasants, and also because his father held such a small post as a feldsher [village medic] in the village, Ludwig had no great place in the pedigreed house of the Siwiańskis. He was always among the invited guests only because, firstly, he had finished a four-class school and was no longer a simple peasant, and secondly simply because he was a young man in the Siwiańskis' house, where there were six young ladies, besides nieces and aunts, and on such evenings educated cavaliers were badly needed. And although in the Siwiańskis' house they looked down on him, they still invited him to such evenings, and whenever he did not come he was sorely missed in the women's company.
This evening Ludwig was "the hero of the day"; all at once he had grown several heads taller than the empty pedigreed folk.
Above all, the two aunts, who kept whispering secrets with him, did not leave his side.
But everyone noticed that Ludwig was in a very bad mood today and did not answer willingly.
— What is the matter with you, Ludwig? — one of the aunts, whom they called "Panna Fanfi", asked him — you ought to feel today the happiest man in the world! You have done such a great and holy thing, which the greatest people live out their lives without attaining. Everything in life is nothing at all compared with what you have done. I now count you the happiest man, whom everyone should envy.
But Ludwig kept silent; tears stood in his eyes; it was hard for him to utter a word.
Both [printed "bey'e"] aunts and the nieces, the old maids, still did not leave his side.
— You ought to feel the happiest man in the world! — Panna Fanfi went on snuffling, for she spoke somewhat through her nose — the beautiful Mania will be your wife, and she will be a very good Christian; God and people will envy you! Ludwig, Ludwig!
— There is nothing to envy. She is a Jewess after all; a Jewess remains a Jewess! — Ludwig grumbled — Ah, if she were not so charming I would not have wanted to look at her and to live through what I lived through in [printed twice "in in"] that cursed night.
— That means you are doing it only for the sake of your sinful passion, because she is beautiful? — Aunt Fanfi reproached him and exchanged a glance with the other aunt, as if to say: "What comes out of a cat says 'meow' — a peasant remains a peasant."
— Sinner! — Panna Fanfi continued — you do not even know what you are saying. Ah, if you could understand how great is the thing that has fallen to your lot to do, you would feel differently and speak differently!
— Believe me, good Fanfi, if she had not been so charmingly beautiful that night, I would have torn her to pieces and thrown her to the dogs.
Both aunts and the three old-maid nieces, who had heard Ludwig's words, positively jumped back from him.
(To be continued.)
Everything in the World Speaks

[Feuilleton — parable and essay.]
In my cheder years I greatly envied King Solomon on account of one thing. I begrudged him neither his kingdom, nor his wondrously beautiful palace, nor all the costly foods and drinks he ate and drank, nor — to make the distinction — the thousand wives he possessed.
My envy concerned only his knowledge of many languages. I longed to know thoroughly, as he did, the language of birds, the language of leaves, the wooden and stone languages, the tongues of fire and water, of mites, of ants and of all other kinds of little creeping things.
I began my first studies with stones. In our shtetl there were very many of them, and they were very conspicuous — and they landed on the heads of the shtetl Jews... Gentiles they did not love: when a Jew would sometimes throw a stone at an enemy of Israel, the stone would bounce away a verst from its target... But every time a gentile threw a stone at a Jew, even offhandedly, that hard "inanimate object" would hit precisely and split his skull. Such lovers of Israel were the stones of our shtetl...
So I took a stone that was stained with Jewish blood and argued it out with it: "Just tell me, you hard murderer," I asked it in a stern tone, "why does your kind bear such hatred for us Jews? By rights, it seems, you ought to have stood by the 'children of Israel' as firm as steel and iron, since the Torah did take pity on you and forbade lifting a hammer or a sword upon you when building an altar"?
The stone did not reflect for a minute and at once gave me the following answer:
— Your question, son of man, is a foolish one. You suspect the innocent when you think that we stones have something against Jews in our hearts. Stones have no heart at all, the way you humans do, and therefore they are not capable of "pleasure" [?] or hatred... We are nothing more than blind messengers of nature, and nature evidently willed it so: that wherever a stone is thrown, it should fall on Jews...
My naive childish reason told me then that I was already done with the stones, that I already understood their language and knew their nature, and I set about the plant world. I took my life in my hands and stole into the garden of a poor peasant. There grew various kinds of flowers whose names I had not the faintest idea of. But they were all so charming, so enchantingly beautiful — yet they paid me no attention at all. They were amusing themselves [?] with the golden sunbeams that caressed them, and probably paying them sweet compliments...
I went up to a young blossom that was still lying in its bud-cradles and greeted it tenderly. But — not a sound, not a response; it does not answer. I go on, and see: on an old, aged flower, already wilted in places, there stands a big bee, buzzing murderously and sucking its flower-blood. I grab and chase away the bloodsucker and rescue the innocent one from its poison. Then I heard a voice, a voice of fragrance, a rarely delicious voice of aromas that resounded into my nostrils... and the voice was accompanied by the following words: "First of all I thank you, unknown but noble son of man, for saving me from certain death. Although, to tell the truth, we flowers don't much care about living anyway [?]: death always hovers over our heads, every minute we expect to be plucked, and that is a terrible feeling. The constant fear of death is worse than death itself. Our misfortune lies in being too delicate and too beautiful. Your humans are in love with us, and so they tear us out before our time. A strange love your two-legged ones have: it uproots its beloved... Yes, a great part of your kind are vile hypocrites: they do us all sorts of wickedness and still consider themselves friends of humanity."
I lowered my head in shame and quietly slipped out of the garden. I did not want to hear any more of the disgrace of my kind, and I already regretted the whole business. I will gain no honour [?], I thought, from holding conversations with the creatures of the non-human worlds. And from then on I stopped envying King Solomon.
Years went by. All that time I was a prosaic, practical man, who hated every form of mysticism — only the "revealed"; only things that were open and manifest to all interested me. But lately the old inclination toward the "hidden" has awakened in me, because the present-day "revealed" is not at all pleasant [?]; one can do nothing with it. Here we had thought, for example, that we Jews could, in today's modern times, make do with natural means to bring about our redemption — yet it begins to look as though without miracles altogether it really will not work... For we cannot build on the justice of man and on the liberalism of nations. I began to believe that there is more justice and also more intelligence in stones, in plants and in every living creature than in the one who proclaimed himself the topmost rung [?] of creation.
So once I was sitting by the seashore, sunk in a dreadful melancholy, gazing with mute looks at the mighty king of waters. Right up to my feet swam a little wave, and it spoke to me thus:
"You wonder why we, the waters, do not speak to you humans. If so, you are mistaken. We speak to you constantly. But you are never quiet enough to be able to hear our words. Not only we, but everything there is in the world has a language and speaks. There are only individuals, a chosen few of your kind, who understand the rustling of the wind, the notes of birdsong, the voice of water, the script of the clouds and the colour-ideas of flowers.
"Perhaps you wonder why you cannot grasp and attain the conversation of birds as the heroes of the legend did, and perhaps you doubt altogether whether in the crow of a rooster, in the miaowing of a cat and in the bellowing of an ox there is any sense and content. All this comes from your not grasping how far up or how far down ideas can reach. There are, for example, some sounds that are too high and some that are too low for the human ear to be able to catch them.
"There are also many colours besides white and black and green and yellow, etc., that are too delicate for the human eye, and it cannot distinguish them. It is the same with thoughts, or with the perceptions of the soul. There are great worlds of ideas that are too simple for you to catch, and there are other, infinitely great worlds of ideas that are too lofty for you to comprehend.
"And not only are the lofty ideas of the upper worlds higher than your highest ideas, but many ideas of the lowest worlds, too, are weightier and contain more meaning than the highest thoughts you boast of so much.
"Bow your head, O man, before all the beings and creatures found on our planet! You understand no more than we do, and you are no greater favourite of Divine Providence, for we do not go against her will. We do not stray from the direction she marked out for us from the six days of Creation on, whereas you rebel against her — she gave you [?] the way of humans, and you walk in the way of beasts."
Such a lofty sermon the little wave delivered to me in a single breath — and then it melted away into the water...
Ploni ve-Kohen.
In what light Zagłębie is seen through the eyes of foreign visitors

I.
The editor of the "Lodzer Togblat", Mr. Israel Kahan, who a few weeks ago paid a visit to Zagłębie and Upper Silesia, conveys the following impressions, which we consider it important to acquaint our readers with, although in certain details they are painted with a great deal of light and and also shadow... Ed.
Smelters and pits.. chimneys and smoke..
Kilometres long they stretch here, the mighty workshops below and above the earth. The scrawny, sooty factory chimneys rise up uncannily and spread [?] over God's little world, spitting black smoke upon people and land, which veils the bright radiance and gives the whole region such a strange colouring...
That is the first impression of Zagłębie and Upper Silesia — the most important industrial district of Poland, one of the most splendid and richest industrial districts in the world.
The coal and iron basin is a kingdom unto itself, a kingdom of feverish labour, an underground one, hidden from the stranger's eye. Hundreds of thousands of human lives are risked here every moment in extracting nature's inexhaustible treasures from the bowels of Mother Earth.
At every step one runs into problems here — underground and above ground; questions of a social character and of the forces of nature become entangled with the burning issues of economic life and the struggle of nationalities, and everything flows together and carries the observer off into a new, unknown sphere, shaken by foreseen and unforeseen explosions, underground floods, catastrophes.
It is a world unto itself. A restless, feverishly working, fascinating world.
But for the time being this underground world does not interest me. I want to become acquainted with what goes on above these hidden hells — with the creating and doing, with the trade and traffic, with the hubbub and commotion around the coal pits, the iron and zinc smelters with their choking smoke and poisonous gas, which has become the most delicious perfume, luring, tempting and drawing hither the unfortunate, livelihood-less Polish Jew...
———
My first visit was to Będzin. An old town of lineage, with a past that reaches back a full thousand years.
One cannot say that the people of Będzin pride themselves on this lineage. It is true that a great many Będzin inhabitants [printed "Bendiger"] do not even know of their honourable past. This is, as they say, "a little America", and apparently one values personal merit more than ancestry.
I took a walk to the greatest sight of old Będzin, to the ruins of the historic royal castle on the hill beside the river "Czarna Przemsza". A castle and remnants of a very old fortress, said to date back to the years 1001—1020. My companion was a local journalist. But however hard I tried to find things out, he was extremely sparing in his explanations.
I also spoke with several Będzin "obywatele" [citizens], one-hundred-percent Poles. They too were scarcely informed about Będzin's pedigree. Only at the Jewish vice-president of the town were some riddles solved for me.
It is astonishing how little understanding there is in Poland for antiquities. In another country such a historic corner as the castle ruin with its fortress ramparts, which are still living witnesses of the Swedish invasion in the 12th century [sic] and of the uprising battles of 1863, would have been guarded like a relic. With us, however, it was forgotten and neglected, and only the "Jewish magistrate" took care to lay out a decent "square" there. It preserved the ruins and saved the stone remnants of the castle from complete disintegration.
———
Będzin, with its old lineage, which bears the name of the armour-bearer of the Polish king Bolesław Chrobry (Będa), has a glorious, stormy past behind it. Many historic battles were fought out here; here the Polish king Jan Sobieski III had his headquarters, and here the attacks of the "Ślązaks" [Silesians] with their predatory ambitions were repulsed.
But later Będzin became a forsaken backwater [?]. Only the influx [?] (the enemies of Israel call it an "invasion") of the Jews pulled the town, richly blessed by nature, out of the "higer-plet" [?], raised it to a new life and made it the liveliest commercial centre of the whole region. Today Będzin is the most Jewish town of Zagłębie. One can say — a Jewish town, Jewish through and through. Up to 75 percent of the population (about 70 thousand) are Jews. Commerce and manufacturing are mainly Jewish, the chairman of the town council is a Jew (the great industrialist Mr. S. Fürstenberg), and a president the Jews of Będzin also have who is Jewish — that is the vice-president of the town, Mr. L. Rubinlicht; even the only newspaper (a weekly) appearing in Będzin is a Jewish one.
I spent more than an hour in the office of the Jewish vice-president of Będzin. Various senior officials of the magistrate came in during our conversation to settle current matters, and all of them addressed Mr. Rubinlicht as "Panie Prezydencie" [Mr. President]. Respect and esteem could be felt in that attitude. He has considerable merits for the town and truly deserves this regard. For 12 years Vice-President Rubinlicht, a merchant by profession and a Zionist by conviction, has been active in the field of municipal self-government. Formerly he was chairman of the town council; now he is vice-president, already in his second term.
The municipal economy has risen greatly during the period of his rule, and the public-utility institutions have grown to such a degree that they also bring the town a great deal of income.
Because of his high office President Rubinlicht has greatly neglected his private business. But he has the satisfaction that the Jewish population is now treated by the magistrate as an element with equal rights. The Będzin Jewish gymnasium "Yavne" enjoys an annual municipal subsidy amounting to 5000 zł.; the Jewish orphanages are fully maintained by the town (last year the subsidy reached 30 thousand zł.); the same goes for the old-age home, the Jewish maternity clinic, the free-loan (gmilus-khesed) fund, etc. Even the "Yiddish Scientific Institute" [YIVO] in Vilna receives support from the Będzin magistrate. True, not a large one — altogether a few hundred zł. — but it was a matter of principle. And when the local magistrate arranged two [summer] colonies for needy schoolchildren, 50 thousand zł. were earmarked specifically for a colony for Jewish children with a kosher kitchen.
With us in Poland all these are exceptions, gratifying exceptions. Especially the subsidy for the Jewish gymnasium — let it be recorded.
* * *
Nevertheless it had to take more than ten years, even in this "Jewish town", before the municipal parliament dared to bring itself to a resolution that all official announcements which the magistrate issues to the population should appear, besides in Polish, also in Yiddish...
When I was in Będzin a real war was going on over this. The Endeks and the "Sanacja" made every effort so that it should not come to such a "desecration of Polishness" — the Sanacja had its own motives in this, since the Jews had not formed a bloc with it during the town-council elections — but this opposition was powerless. The resolution later went through by a majority of votes... After all — a Jewish town!

What's Happening in Zagłębie? — Będzin: Stormy debate at the 2nd reading of the budget. "Jews are spies!" shouts a councillor of the "BB"

[—] Thursday[?], and this Tuesday and Wednesday, the town council of Będzin, chaired by Mr. Fürstenberg, considered in the second reading the important budget expenditures for the year 1929/30.
Interesting and amusing was Thursday's session; the councillors did not stint on humorous material for the gallery. Hardly had one councillor come out with some proposal than others did the same, which led[?] to many moments of self-[—].
Under the item scholarships for students, a proposal by Dr. Rechtman is adopted that the sum be raised to 2 thousand zł., to be divided as follows: a thousand zł. for Jewish students and a thousand for the non-Jewish[?] "Koło" [student association] in Zagłębie.
Under the item culture and art, councillor Kleinman puts[?] a proposal to allot a sum of 1500 zł. to the People's University at the Artisans' Association.
Immediately afterwards alderman (ławnik) Żebrowski proposes that such a subsidy also be allotted to the Christian artisans.
Almost all the clubs [council factions] do the same, demanding subsidies for their libraries (even ones that do not exist)...
———
At Monday's session the first item was: care for school children[?]. Dr. Rechtman protests against the budget committee, which struck out the sum of 2,70[—] zł. for a dental clinic, and he demands that the sum be increased to 6 thousand zł., so that school youth may have the possibility of receiving dental care.
After a short discussion the proposal is adopted.
Councillor Mrs. Ratner proposes that the item for supporting poor women in childbirth be raised by 3 thousand zł., so that the new mothers can stay in the hospitals at least 10 days.
The proposal is adopted.
The item for feeding school children is raised, on Dr. Rechtman's proposal, to 11 thousand zł.
Before considering the item social welfare, President [mayor] Michał[?] gives a short exposé, in which he points out that a sum of 411 thousand zł. has been provisionally set in the budget for social welfare.
At the item sending children to summer camps, councillor Feiner draws attention that this year the system of favouritism must not be repeated, and that the children who need it should be sent to the summer camps.
A surprise for the "Agudah" councillors was the proposal of Mrs. Ratner that for the Jewish children sent by the municipality (Magistrat) to Busko for a cure, care be taken that they have kosher food, because every year the children eat treyf food..
To this the municipal administration declared that on this question they must come to an understanding with the municipalities of other towns in order to obtain together a ritual (kosher) kitchen...
With this the session ended at half past twelve at night.
———
Wednesday's session was a stormy one. Here once again the axiom was confirmed that when it concerns a matter connected with Jews, they come out against them from the extreme left to the extreme right. The antisemitic agitation was caused by the innocent and just proposal of Mrs. Ratner, who demanded that the Jewish orphans supported by the municipality be subsidised with equal rights[?], i.e. that for the Jewish orphans too the municipality pay 70 zł. a month instead of 30..
The first to come out in the "agitation" with antisemitic "flowerlets" was alderman Hetmańczyk, the "comrade" of the right P.Z.[?]. But the antisemitic "record" was beaten by councillor Gac[?], of "Eig-sl"[?]; he used such arguments as that the Jews have no merits toward Poland, but are only spies..
At these words a great uproar arose among the Jewish councillors, and after the sharp protests of Dr. Rechtman, who demanded that Gac be excluded for 3 sessions, of Mrs. Ratner and of M. Lewin, the Jewish councillors (except the Left P.Z.) left the session in protest.
Unheard-of scandal at the "Hanukkat ha-Bayit" celebration of "Ahavat Chesed". Cantor Żupowicz insulted in a base manner

[—] On Sunday evening there took place a 16th-anniversary jubilee celebration and at the same time a "Hanukkat ha-Bayit" (house-warming) of the premises of the "Neu"[?], "Ahavat Chesed".
At this celebration the town cantor, Mr. Żupowicz[?], who had been invited by the institution's board to lead the evening (Maariv) prayer, was insulted in a disgraceful manner.
The scandal was caused by the following reasons:
At the head of the institution stands the well-known "town president", who wants on every occasion to display his rule... When the board of "Ahavat Chesed" decided to invite cantor Żupowicz, the president, who is [—] a member of the kehilla board[?], took upon himself the mission [of seeing that] the gmina [community] should commission[?] the cantor to pray on Sabbath at "Ahavat Chesed".
The cantor fulfilled his mission and [—][?] was there on Sabbath and prayed Musaf at "Ahavat Chesed". The official celebration took place on Sunday, and in order that the celebration be an elevated one, the board of "Ahavat Chesed" decided that the cantor should pray Maariv with the synagogue choir.
The above-mentioned president, knowing that he himself had also agreed to dismiss Mr. Kalmus as choir conductor, worked hard throughout Sunday so that the choir would sing along as well. To this end he intervened several times with the kehilla president, and also sent messengers to the cantor [saying] that "he takes the responsibility upon himself", as long as the cantor would pray together with the choir.
But the cantor declared categorically that as long as he did not have the consent of the kehilla president, Mr. Prawer, he would not pray.
The "pisiner"[?] president, however, wishing to show his authority, casually engaged the conductor with the choir, and informed the cantor that "the choir will not be there".
When the cantor came up on Sunday evening for Maariv and found the conductor with the choir, he again declared that he would not pray with the choir, because so the president of the kehilla instructs him.
Then the president turned to the conductor and choir that they should leave the premises, and the cantor began to prepare for the prayer.
But just as he wanted to begin, the president's "Walanens"[?], the she-eino-yodea ("one who does not know") type, Jaskierowicz, sprang at him and showered the cantor with the most disgraceful insults.
As a result of the disgraceful abuse Mr. Żupowicz turned to the president asking what he should do, and received the answer: go home...
The cantor took off his tallit and left in great humiliation..
Maariv was then prayed immediately afterwards by the conductor with the choir...
———
From a "neutral" source we are informed as follows:
The hatred toward the cantor began as soon as a delegation of "Ahavat Chesed" approached him and invited him to pray on Sabbath and on Sunday — Maariv.
The delegation left dissatisfied, because the cantor's wife set such conditions as could not be accepted, and in general the delegation was not received properly. The cantor also performed the Sabbath prayers hastily... and because of this the board of "Ahavat Chesed" decided that, so that the celebration should be complete, the cantor should pray with the choir.
— We refrain for the time being from expressing our position on the substance of the matter, but the attack on a prayer leader (shaliach tzibbur) in public we brand as a base deed.
Killed by lightning

On Saturday afternoon, for a short hour, a torrential downpour fell, accompanied by strong lightning and thunder. One bolt of lightning struck a 54-year-old Christian woman who was grazing goats in Gzichów, and killed her.
“Don’t Climb Where You Needn’t”..

On Sunday two young Christians made a bet that whoever climbed up onto the “szczyt” [top] of the castle on the “Góra Zamkowa” [Castle Hill] would get a present and a bottle of brandy.
One of them decided to take the step and began to climb, but when already near the “szczyt” he fell down and broke both his legs.
In a very grave condition he was taken to the municipal hospital.
The Water-Mains Work Begins on Monday.

On Tuesday the water-mains committee held a meeting at which the tenders for awarding the water-mains work were considered.
The committee decided to accept the tender submitted by Eng. G. Weinzieher.
The work begins next Monday. The work will start on Modrzejowska Street.
An Important Circular Concerning Closed Bakeries.

The local bakers’ guild (cech) has received a circular (okólnik) from the starosta, informing the bakers whose bakeries were closed on sanitary grounds that the bakeries may be reopened once the bakery meets the sanitary regulations.
Whoever wants such a commission [inspection] must pay 50 zł. at the starostwo.
Mr. Shefner’s Lecture

which took place last Sabbath gave the listeners an intellectual treat. The lecturer brilliantly portrayed the roles and types of the former and present Sejm deputies.
In a fine Yiddish and in a successful satirical tone Mr. Shefner gave us a gallery of types that splendidly illustrated the “activity” of the deputies in the Sejm, so that the audience gained an idea of the former and the present parliament.
A Concert of the Living Word.
The artists of the Vilna Troupe, Messrs. Weislitz, Kamen and Orleska, will present this Sabbath, 1 June, at 2 p.m., at the “Corso” theatre, sketches and recitations from the best Yiddish classics.
Sosnowiec — The First Plenary Meeting of the Local Chamber of Commerce.

A request to the government to abolish the turnover tax.
On Monday the Chamber of Commerce, by order of the Minister of Commerce, held a meeting. The meeting took place at the “Club” of the industrialists in Dąbrowa.
Instead of at 11 a.m., the meeting began at 2 p.m. In the meantime consultations took place about the election of the president and vice-presidents, and above all the commerce councillors were very “active” at the free buffet...
Jewish councillors were present not only from Zagłębie but also from Zawiercie, Częstochowa, Kielce and Radom.
The meeting is opened by the election commissioner Salaszyński [?], who greets the councillors in the name of the government and invites the oldest councillor, Senator Hempel, to take the chair.
Then a president, six vice-presidents and a board are elected. As one of the vice-presidents councillor Mr. M. Geifeld [?] (Częstochowa) was elected, and as a member of the board Vice-President Mr. Rubinlicht was elected.
After adopting several formal points, among them the budget, it is decided to send telegrams of greeting to the President of the State, Marshal Piłsudski and Minister of Commerce Kwiatkowski.
Then a motion is adopted to intervene with the government so that the turnover tax, which undermines the existence of the Polish merchant class, be abolished.
—o—
“All May Slaughter” — but only whoever has a slip from the gmina.
Lately a measure of lawlessness has arisen in the local slaughtering question: the shochtim slaughtered for Modrzejów butchers against slips from those who represent the community there, and thereby the local gmina treasury suffered loss.
Because of this a meeting was held at the gmina with the participation of members of the rabbinate, who decided to instruct the shochtim not to slaughter except for those who bring slaughter slips from the gmina.
—o—
The Synagogue Is Being Repaired
At last the community board has realised that the synagogue cannot remain in such a low state, and is proceeding to repair it. Meanwhile the roof is being repaired — it is summertime, after all — so that the worshippers in the synagogue should not suffer from the rains...
—o—
From the Labour Court.
On Wednesday the labour court was to hear the case against the publishers of “Unzer Tog”, whom the typesetters Adlerfligel, Friedman and Lantsman have sued because they are owed a debt of about a thousand zł.
Because an important witness was missing, the case was adjourned.
—o—
Political Arrests.
The local police have arrested for anti-state activity Messrs. B. Reizman, M. Singer, Ch. Poltorak, Y. Spitzberg, Dora Kaiser, Sala Warszawska, L. Rabak and Goldshlak. The last-named came here from Chmielnik only last Friday, and the next day, Saturday, he was arrested as a participant in a demonstration.
—o—
A Bicycle Injures a Jewish Girl.
Miss Gimliakewicz, while walking in the street in Modrzejów, was run into by a bicycle, which injured her hands and feet.
—o—
From the “Merchants’ Association”.
On Sunday the new board of the “Merchants’ Association” (Piłsudskiego 12) held its constituent meeting, at which a presidium of the following persons was elected:
President — Mr. Y. M. Weinreb; vice — Sh. Warman; treasurer — R. Czapnik; and house manager — B. Zelinger.
—o—
For Illegal Trading in Cigarettes
the local district court sentenced Mrs. Sarah Mentlik to pay 385 zł. or 19 days’ arrest.
The cigarettes and tobacco found during the search were confiscated.

What, Don’t They Have Time?

[Zagłębie — opinion; traffic and road safety.] You have surely heard the story told of the old Kotzker [Rabbi Menachem Mendel of Kotzk]: how Hasidim once came to him and told him that a railway was being built on which one would travel in 6 hours instead of the 3 days one spends dragging along in the covered wagon. The Rebbe heard out the news, thought it over and finally asked:
“But what — don’t they have time?”
This question of the old Kotzker always comes to my mind whenever I hear of catastrophes that happen with automobiles, trams, motorcycles and other instruments of destruction of our time. What, don’t they have time? — I ask. People already drive twenty kilometres an hour, twenty-five, thirty, forty, up to eighty kilometres, and it is still too little; they insist on having “kefitsat ha-derekh” [miraculous shortening of the road], they insist on being at the destination before they have even moved from the spot.
I am not so naive as not to understand that time is money. I understand that rapid transport, the possibility of going to Warsaw and back in one day, is today a necessity and one simply cannot do without it. But everything must have a limit! One must, after all, also take the other person into account and not put his life in danger merely because I think that I have no time!
Here before me lies a letter from a father who begs for mercy, that something be done to save the children who play in the street in summer and are run over like chicks by the racing automobiles. The father believes that this is more than carelessness on the part of the chauffeurs, that there is recklessness here and perhaps something more. The cars, driven by irresponsible people, run children down, and nobody cares in the least about it.
The complaint seems a little old-fashioned. The automobile must hurry, must race, because the faster it goes the better for it; the more it earns. But the question arises: is the public there for it, or is it there for the public?
And as for the complaint being old-fashioned — even that is not so bad. In Switzerland, which lives off foreign tourist traffic, there is a canton — Graubünden is its name — in which it was simply forbidden to drive an automobile. The peasants did not want these destroyers among them, of which the horses are frightened, and a ban was imposed on this devil. And the rich tourists who roam across Switzerland in their elegant cars had to turn back at the border of the canton, or leave the car standing and go on by horse. Whether the ban is still in force today I do not know, but in my time it was in force. And if Switzerland could allow itself such a thing, we may surely at least allow ourselves to prevent the wild chase of cars through the town.
The question does not concern Zagłębie alone. Elsewhere, too, people cry out against the bloody orgies that the destroyers perpetrate. Elsewhere, too, measures are taken against the racing. But if elsewhere it is only a question of public safety, with us it is a question of life and death for hundreds of innocent children, whom one cannot — and is not obliged to — keep locked up at home. The children must be let out into the so-called[?] fresh air. Our magistrate [town council] has not yet managed to provide the population with a little garden where the children could catch a bit of air. Our children have to knock about in the streets, and there they are trampled by the automobiles that run like demons and kill old people and children...
Death will come to them anyway — so what, don’t they have time?
Ch. Landau.

“Sosnowiec”—“Maccabi” 1:1 (0:1).
The above match was supposed to be a championship match, but because the referee did not turn up at the ground, a friendly match was played.
“Sosnowiec” took the field with the best forces at its disposal. “Maccabi”, on the other hand, was weakened by several reserve players.

Letters to the Editor

I.
In issue No. 22 of your esteemed paper a would-be protest was printed against us because we used "uncultured expressions" with regard to the meeting. In that protest the "majority" spoke groundlessly and did not have the courage to publish their names — proof that they were afraid the disgrace before the outside world would be too great. Heaven forbid the Jewish street should find out who the poor protesters are, and who takes the floor on the laws of parliamentarism and intellectuality... As to the matter itself, the situation would have brought much benefit: first, one would have seen "who are they that go" [Exodus 10:8], and second, we would have been spared polemicising with such people. But because the "pipige" [?] protesters did it anonymously and were ashamed of their "firms", we are compelled to explain the following:
At the last general meeting of the "Bank Ludowy" [People's Bank] a handful of people from the so-called opposition gathered, forming a "majority" of 10 (read: ten), and incessantly used a "something" language, i.e. the whole time they made a racket that "something is being said", "something is being told", "something is going on" and "something has flown". Naturally, as long-serving, untiring bank manager, who has stood like a faithful soldier at his post for several years, and as devoted members of the board, we demanded open criticism, the truth in its full breadth. If — we declared — we are no good, then take over the bank yourselves; you are, after all, "cultured", "intelligent", so with you the bank will only now be truly raised up...
Naturally, had the "majority" not had provocative intentions, they would have accepted our proposals with open arms. But the gentlemen "intellectuals" do not want to take over the bank at all; they just went on talking about "something". Then we forgot the principle "Answer not a fool according to his folly" [Prov. 26:4; misquoted in print] and in great agitation we threw out the words: "You will not have the privilege of discovering any malversation [embezzlement] with us, and such destroyers and wreckers should go to the eighty winds"...
Yes, gentlemen of the "majority"! It may be that in the "cultural sense" you stand much higher than we do, but the institution we have built, and for which we went through the seven chambers of hell, we will not hand over to such hands as yours; and in general we promise you that we will no longer polemicise with you, for you yourselves will admit that it is beneath our dignity.
Respectfully,
B. Rechnic, Y. Mintz.
II.
Most honoured, esteemed Editor!
Having read last Friday in your esteemed paper about the great humiliations and bloodshed inflicted on me last Sunday at "Ahavat Hesed" at the dedication of the house, I ask you, esteemed Editor, to publish the following:
As for the insolent and vile act that the "well-known" Jaskierowicz committed against me in public, I do not see fit to speak of it now, for it is beneath my dignity — let the public see and judge. But regarding what you wrote from the "neutral" source, I declare categorically that when the delegation of "Ahavat Hesed" came to negotiate with me, neither I nor my wife set any difficult conditions whatsoever, and we received the delegation with the greatest respect; Mr. Meir Leml Sendyszew, who was in the delegation together with Jaskierowicz, can bear witness to this. In general, whoever comes to me I receive with the utmost honour.
With feelings of respect,
Ozer Menachem Żupowicz

Great Success of the Polish Rubber Industry Abroad

In 1924 a rubber enterprise came into being in Łódź, founded by an English-Swiss-Polish rubber-industry joint-stock company "Gentleman", which at the exhibition in Nice gave proof that Polish products in this field can compete with foreign articles.
The exhibits of the "Gentleman" firm, which were examined at the exhibition in Nice by qualified experts, were awarded the highest distinction, a large gold medal.
The high recognition by the administration of the exhibition in Nice confirms that a brilliant future awaits the rubber industry, young in this respect, and only when one can compete with abroad with our products — and not only satisfy our domestic consumption, but also export and acquaint foreign countries with a new branch of our industry.
The success in Nice of the "Gentleman" firm should be a source of pride for every Polish citizen, because it confirms that our industry stands at its proper height.

Olkusz — The murderers of the murdered Natan Dawid Zygman caught
Soon after the attack on the train in which the Radom chairman of the merchants' association, Natan Dawid Zygman, fell victim, the police began an energetic investigation and discovered the murderers. Their names are: Julian Żuryła [?], 23 years old, and Jan Cembruszyński [?], 21 years old, both from Olkusz. They have confessed to the attack. The report in the Warsaw press that tens of thousands of złoty were robbed from those attacked does not correspond to reality. In total the following was robbed: from Avromele Żargowicki 10 zł., from Alter Szapir 18 zł., from a Jew from Łagów [?] 8 zł., and from Dawid Zeliger 50 gr. Nor is it true that the slain man tried to tear the revolver from the bandit and resisted; he merely rose from his seat out of surprise, for which the bandit shot him. The same bandits also carried out, on the second day, the attack on the train to Ząbkowice.
A. B.
