Wolbrom — On the Interest-Free Loan Fund

[Wolbrom — welfare; free-loan fund.] Here in Wolbrom a gmilus-khesed (interest-free loan) fund has already existed for 6 months, and it has already issued 170 loans to small traders and craftsmen. The local Jewish community has given us an annual subsidy of 750 zł., and the "Urząd Gminy" [printed "Ushand gmine" — the municipal office] has also approved 200 zł. for us. Last Sabbath the chairman invited the visiting chief cantor (Ober-Kantor) Mr. Baruch Grajs of Drohobycz to give a concert for the benefit of the free-loan fund, which truly turned out very well.
Aszlg.
Our Popular Interests (The Downfall of the Sosnowiec „Small Traders’ Association“ and Its New Birth)

To what extent everything [?] among us is ownerless, to what extent we treat everything with criminal indifference and banality, can be illustrated by the sad affair of the Sosnowiec „Small Traders’ Association“ (Kleinhendler-Fareyn).
The abuses that took place there, the unheard-of, impermissible deeds that were smuggled in there — so that it came to the point that the association was broken through and through, that the institution was rotted and destroyed through and through.
This is simply unheard of, that an institution counting nearly a thousand members could collapse in the blink of an eye; and after all, we measure the usefulness of an institution by the size of its membership: the more members an association has, the more justified it is, the more chances it has to take a place at the top and to play a social role in our life.
That is how it always [?] is with us: as soon as an institution attains a right to exist, as soon as it turns out that it must occupy a place in our social life [?], a sudden storm wind comes and wipes everything out. And it is no small thing, how necessary an institution is once it reaches a membership of a thousand.
Since our economic interests are at such a low level, the Jew who is a member of a „Small Traders’ Association“ needs so much social support, so much enlightenment in the social sense, that hardly has he become a member there and received some support from the institution — and hardly has it collapsed — it is truly a catastrophe for him. After all, we know well that an association must be for its member a guide, a „moreh derekh“, that must show him along which line to continue his life’s path and how to fight on his hard road of life.
After all, we constantly agitate among the popular masses that they must be united in a social institution, that they must have the body that will care for their tormented today, and that they should have the possibility of reaching a better tomorrow.
After all, we feel at every step how hard life is becoming for these people; on the shoulders of the broad popular masses lies the difficulty of continuing their poor existence, since one wants to fence off the road on which they walk and block the small path they have found for themselves and from which they draw their poor livelihood.
And people like these start being persecuted, they start being chased away: here they may not stand, and there they must not sit; and on top of that they are wronged by the tax authority, and it reaches the point that even if they were already to sell their bit of poor merchandise, they still would not have enough to pay what is demanded of him.
After all, we know how helpless a Jew remains when he reaches this stage. And here the question arises: who is to speak for him at such a terrible moment? Who can fight for him and get it done that he is not broken? After all, we know that such a Jew is in no way able to act for himself. Neither can he, nor does he know, in such brokenness, what to do and how to speak, nor will anyone listen to him. Besides, we know from practice that as long as everyone goes on his own, nobody achieves anything. But one cannot compare the great benefit that social concentration has at such a serious moment. After all, we understand the importance of an institution when it goes to intervene for its members. And an institution — the greater the number of members it counts, the stronger the power it has to demand justice, the more courage it has to claim what is due to it.
Can we then estimate the great value an institution has when it counts nearly a thousand members? We cannot even imagine the strength and the power such an institution possesses for the community. Such an institution must be reckoned with everywhere: the authorities, the headquarters in Warsaw and the whole community alike look upon such a united body as upon a giant that must be reckoned with, willy-nilly.
And when such an institution collapses, when abuses are committed in such an institution, one must react properly to such unheard-of deeds, which degrade the Jewish community; and meanwhile the small trader is orphaned: he has no one to speak in his name, no one to defend him.
And therefore the fact is to be welcomed that the institution has now been reorganized and a fresh stream of life has been poured into it. It is to be welcomed that the accused have been removed and in their place people have come in who have taken upon themselves the power of work, the power of initiative, the power of the will to achieve for the broad strata of the Jewish popular masses.
Let these people see to it that the institution is properly reorganized, for there is a broad field here, and it stands and begs to be reaped; there are members who stand ready to support such an institution, provided only that it defends their honour at the time when it [sic; probably: they] needs it.
Let our „Small Traders’ Association“ show from now on signs of life, signs of activity, signs of awakening — and that will then give it the proper satisfaction.
Let the new board prove to us that it understands how to run such an apparatus, which is so necessary to us in our life, both in the economic and in the general social sphere.
The institution has the possibility of bringing its members to a higher level, both in the economic field and in the social sense.
We therefore wish to place great hopes in the new board, which must understand its important tasks on the new road of life.
Selekt.
The Law on Holidays for Workers and Employees

[Poland — labour law; holidays.] On the occasion of the start of the holiday season we wish to inform our readers about the exact[?] regulations concerning holidays.
First of all it must be noted that the right to a holiday belongs to workers employed in industry, mining, trade, office work, transport, hospital service, institutions of public welfare and other workplaces, even if they make no profit, and regardless of whether these workplaces are private property, state-owned or a body of local self-government. An exception are workers in seasonal enterprises in which work lasts less than 10 months a year. All workers employed in the enterprises mentioned have the right to enjoy an 8-day holiday — [for] workers who have been employed for a year in an enterprise — and 15 days when he has been employed for 3 years in an enterprise. Workers younger than 18 have the right to a 14-day holiday after a year of work. And although the industrial and craft establishments [in question] are not subject to the holiday law, the pupils and apprentices ("terminators") in those establishments nevertheless also have the right to enjoy a holiday, just like the juvenile workers.
Mental (white-collar) workers employed in office work in commercial and industrial enterprises have the right, after half a year of work, to enjoy a 14-day holiday, and after a year, a paid holiday of one month.
It must be noted that the holiday period, i.e. 14 and 15 days, is counted by the calendar, so that Sundays and holidays are also included in the holiday. If the worker in the establishment concerned interrupted his work through illness, an accident, or because he was called up for military service, this is not regarded as an interruption of work.
If a worker breaks his work contract without prior notice, to which the employer was entitled, that worker loses the right to a holiday. The holiday period must also be paid. But if a worker works during the holiday in another enterprise, he loses the right to claim wages during his holiday. If the work is contracted on piece-rate ("akord") or by the piece, the holiday pay is then calculated on the basis of the average earnings in the previous 3 months before the holiday. Apprentices ("terminators") and learner-boys may not receive for the holiday period a lower wage than the sum[?] on which they must be insured in the sickness fund.
If the worker has fallen ill and cannot enjoy his holiday, the holiday must, at his request, be postponed to one of the following 3 months. If the worker broke off relations with the enterprise and resumed them no later than within 3 months, his previous working time must be credited to him for the purpose of the holiday. If there are several workers in an enterprise, they can agree among themselves on the order of the holidays and arrange it with the management, but in such a way that in the period from 1 May to 30 September at least [—] of the workers employed in the enterprise concerned enjoy their holiday.
If in a craft enterprise more than 4 workers have worked for a period of more than 6 months, the workers there have a right to a holiday. If a partial or complete change of the owners of the enterprise occurs, the workers do not lose the right to a holiday. If the worker does not take his holiday at the time set for him, he loses the right to his holiday and has no right to claim compensation. In his work contract he cannot renounce his holiday, nor restrict it. The employer may count the holiday period as a notice period. The beginning of the working period is reckoned as the day on which one reports for work, even if through the employer's fault he has not started his work.
As "workers", regardless of their age, the holiday law regards the following employees: [those] performing administrative and supervisory activity and not performers of physical labour, such as managers, stewards (intendants), operational staff such as engineers, technicians, foremen, warehouse managers, forwarding clerks, office and chancellery work, accountants, draughtsmen, cost calculators; those performing commercial activities, such as shop and bookshop assistants ("subiekci") who have completed a vocational or secondary school and have done a practical training; [those] in drugstores, pharmacy, cashiers, dispatchers, agents or canvassers, artists, musicians, artist painters and draughtsmen, and those employed as staff at a doctor's.
The wages for the holiday period are paid later. If there was no other agreement, the normal wage during the holiday is calculated according to [how] the worker is paid — by the day or by the hour. If a worker works in an enterprise fewer than 6 days a week, the holiday pay is calculated proportionally, as if the worker had worked the whole month.
Time Is Air

L. Kosman
One needs to take a holiday now and then, not so much to rest one's own spirit as to discover things you do not notice at all in the daily hubbub of big-city life.
Thus on my present holiday I discovered that time is a curious thing; it has properties you can see better from afar than from near, and it is altogether more play, more imagination than reality.
In the city, when you are busy, you have no time to think about time; you do not notice it at all — it simply slips away from under your hands. Part of your time goes in trains and trams, where it seems to you that every sense of time and space vanishes. The regular hours you work are not time to contemplate either. And the time left over besides work, sleep and eating can hardly be considered time that can be noticed and reckoned.
Only when you are on holiday, far from the city and the bustle, between sky, mountain and valley, where time lies shaped[?] together with nature and plays along with nature's play — when sunshine is time and rain is time, and you notice the difference — only then do you see what perspective time has and what a curious play it is in our life.
And so freely does time lie among mountains and valleys that you begin to measure it in decades, whereas in the city you lack even the measure of a day, because it is not yours.
The measure of week and month is handed to you in the calendars that are sent to you.
And having time to think about time, you discover that time is a precious article whose value you know only when it is entirely yours. The trouble with time in the city is that it is bought from you, and then it loses its true value.
And one more thing I discovered in the lap of nature: that one could do far more with time than city civilisation allows it. The only trouble is that few people know the secret; when more come to know of it, a nature-revolution against civilisation will yet break out.
And perhaps such a revolution will never come, because people by nature like to be forged into steel and stone.
People think of a social revolution, of making man equal to man. That can never be, as long as some people will forever sit between sky, mountain and valley, and some within great walls, in steel fortresses.
Inequality does not begin with the "tempele"[?] money, but with the little bit of air we breathe into our lungs.
As long as all people do not breathe one and the same air, no social revolution will be possible.
Let the barrels of money be divided into big bowls — it will not help. One must begin with the division of air, and the money will melt away of itself.
It is the breath that distinguishes one man from another, not money. The latter is an addition, not the beginning of inequality.
And so, walking between mountain and valley under a clear sky (even the overcast one is [dear?] to the heart), I cried out: give everyone equally to breathe this air, and you will have social equality.
The communist friends at my side at first wanted to raise a protest. They do indeed think highly of fresh air — the proof being that they came out to draw it in — but somehow they are used to hearing of other differences in social inequality, and my remark sounded too "pure-airy".
Long debates were not needed. Here, in the lap of nature, on whom the sky smiled equally, the mountains beckoned equally and the air streamed equally into our nostrils, we quickly came to agree on the airy part of social equality.
And then I saw the significance of air. Let it only stream equally into everyone's nostrils, and the social question is solved. Here, at the health resort of the air-drinking guests, the question was already a solved one.
The only trouble is that too many remain in the city, in the steel fortress, and are unable to grasp our great truth.
And as regards time, I became convinced that for it too there is a remedy on the other side, far from the steel fortress.
But the fortress calls me back, and I fear that here I shall forget both the remedy for time and the blessing of the air.
Only the awareness that somewhere there are sky, mountain and valley, where time has value and air is apportioned[?] to all equally, will stand by me.
Antisemitic little flowers... — (When you demand justice, you get spat upon with insults)

(When you demand justice, you get spat upon with insults.)
And once again the old, familiar antisemitic ditties have been heard — the ditties we thought already belonged to the past, that would at long last find their place in the historical archive.
So it quite often seemed to us, and so we had a right to think and to be sure, to feel and to understand. Quite often we believed that our former accusers felt that they had sinned against the Jews in Poland; we were sure that they instinctively feel this and see it at every step along their path of life. And we also had grounds to think so, because, working together in the public field, sitting under one roof and running the local self-government, the municipal economy, people had the opportunity to confirm that Jews are not only honest and loyal citizens, that they do not merely carry the citizen's burden on their shoulders, but that we are burdened beyond our strength, that we strive beyond what is possible to bring everything together in brotherhood and unity, if only the country may flourish, if only the state may find itself in a better condition and on a higher level.
Many times we thought that people see it, that they feel it, how[?] they had sinned against us when they accused us of dishonest intentions and exaggerated deeds. And not once were these people honest and sincere and admitted to us that they had been mistaken and had greatly exaggerated at our expense; they were not ashamed to tell us so openly at a moment when they had succeeded in carrying out, in the city council or elsewhere, a common, brotherly public activity with which they remained satisfied.
And that too is quite understandable, for who knows better than we do that one can get along with us, that we always stretch out our hand in peace, not even reckoning with the dreadful thought that the outstretched hand might be left hanging in the air, that it might be insulted. And how many times has that actually happened? How many times have our Christian councillors in the city council repaid us with evil instead of the good, the glory and the honour we gave them?
And nevertheless we pretended to have forgotten everything, we did not want to make a fuss about it — and who knows, perhaps precisely for that reason they found the courage to insult us at every step and on every occasion to throw shame and disgust in our faces.
And here these fine, "pearly" insults have once again been hurled from the public tribune of the Będzin city council. Our antisemites, who, it seemed, had already got used to living with us, have once again displayed their "cultured" nakedness and shouted that we Jews are the traitors of Poland, that we have shed no blood for the country, that we pay no taxes, that we are this and that, such-and-such..
And what was it all about, what were these shameful insults over? It is a disgrace to say, a shame to utter it. It was, all in all, about nothing more and nothing less than subsidies for innocent orphans.
After all, the civilised world does not know how to distinguish between a Jewish and a Christian orphan; an unfortunate, forlorn child is equally unfortunate, whatever nationality or country it may belong to.
And when Councillor Mrs. Ratner came and spoke to hearts, to human hearts, and showed that the Jewish orphan must not be wronged as against his Christian companion; when she said that the unfortunate children are all equally unfortunate and demanded equal rights for them — there arose the terrible scandal that we are rich and need to be given nothing at all.
And it is characteristic how far the egoism of our antisemites reaches. They cannot bear to "give" us such a subsidy for our orphans as the Christian orphans receive. And it is interesting that when it comes to granting subsidies, people forget — or perhaps they pretend to forget — that it is we who are the givers and, heaven forbid, not the takers, for it is very well known who is burdened with taxes in a Będzin like this.
And what did Councillor Ratner say? That the Jewish orphan should be subsidised with the same 70 zł. a month as the Christian one, whereas for the Jewish orphan only 30 zł. comes out. So this is a wrong — to allow oneself to demand such a thing[?], i.e. to compare Jewish children with Christian ones. That the money comes from Jewish pockets, and that despite all this the Jewish child is nevertheless wronged — that does not matter, that is nonsense..
It truly cries out to heaven; it is unheard of to allow oneself so much oppressing and insulting and reviling and disgracing, and all this only because a councillor has the courage to demand what is due to him, what common sense dictates — that his rights must be recognised.
The only thing to regret is that the chairman of the city council did not react as he should have to these unheard-of deeds, which he ought not to have permitted, for it is high time not to let ourselves be whipped over the head for nothing and once again for nothing.
Perhaps the lesson would have taught our councillors something for the future? Perhaps we too would have learned to answer the way one is greeted? For we must prove once and for all that one has to reckon with those who carry all the civic duties on their exhausted shoulders, and that they do not deserve, in return, to be insulted in hooligan ways and to have people incited against them for all the world is worth.
R. Let.
A Little Feuilleton. The Hatless Intellectual...

[Feuilleton — humour.] Pan [Mr.] Feliks Kracbarszt, a modern young man and, frankly, a "pierwszorzędny" [first-rate; reading uncertain, see note], has been pestering me for weeks now, ever since summer began: why don't I follow the fashion, and why do I wear a hat in the street?
— What do you need a hat on your head for? [?] — he wonders at me. — Why, that's szaleństwo, zacofaństwo [madness, backwardness]! And who? You! A man with wykształcenie [education], with intelligence, a man w ogóle [altogether] modern! Jak panu nie wstyd? [Aren't you ashamed, sir?]
— Przecież [surely] a person, i w szczególności [and in particular] an intelligent person — my young man goes on — must distinguish himself (wyróżnić się) somehow from the rabble (hołota); a na przykład [for example], just as he once distinguished himself by his hat when the rabble wore little hats of every shape; a jeżeli [and if] fashion orders the hat thrown away and put in mothballs for good, then it is bardzo naturalne [very natural] that we, the intelligentsia, must follow the fashion. Czy nie mam racji? [Am I not right?]
— Doskonale rozumiem [I understand perfectly] — my young man develops his theory of hatlessness further — that a nowoczesny [modern] intellectual must distinguish himself from his otoczenie [surroundings] not only by his bare head. An intellectual, a prawdziwy [true] intellectual must be nicely combed, must always have a fresh crease in his trousers, must wear elegant "lamshn" [? shoes] and jedwabne skarpety [silk socks], must wear an intelligent tie, i tak dalej [and so on], ale to co jest najważniejsze [but what is most important] is to go about the street without a hat, nawet [even; printed "gavet"] in the greatest heat, in the thickest dust (kurz) and in the worst weathers (pogody).
— Co prawda [true enough] — my young man continues in one breath — going about bare-headed has become so rozpowszechnione [widespread; misprinted] nowadays that byle kto, a lada stary kamasz, przepraszam za wyrażenie [any nobody, any old boot, pardon the expression], who has never held a comb in his hand, stawia się [shows off] today with his bare head, whereas dotychczas [until now] it was only for the wybrańcy [chosen few], for the śmietanka społeczeństwa [cream of society], and only a director, a doctor, a hairdresser, a dancing master used to go hatless, ale to się nie liczy [but that doesn't count], because, as the przysłowie [proverb] says, "Poznać pana po cholewach" [you know a gentleman by his boot-tops], and an intellectual wants, jednak [after all], to distinguish himself from others. Czy nie tak? [Isn't that so?]
— I wie pan [And do you know, sir] — my young man urges me with ever-growing pathos — that going bare-headed is, oprócz wszystkiego [besides everything else], simply a brilliant [?] and practical wynalazek [invention]. Po pierwsze [firstly], you save a hat for the time being, which nowadays też coś warto [is also worth something]. Po wtóre [secondly], you save the bowing with your hat, and with one "Moje uszanowanie" [my respects] you're done; you also save a... jednym słowem [in a word], it's good, it's nice and praktyczne [practical]. Po co tu dużo gadać? [Why say much more?] — Dlatego właśnie [that's exactly why] — my young man won't let go of me — as a prawdziwy przyjaciel [true friend] of the whole intelligentsia, radzę [I advise] you zarzucić [to throw off] the hat and go only bare-headed, just like me and the whole nowoczesna [modern] intelligentsia, and jak Boga kocham [as God is my witness], you will always be wdzięczny [grateful] to me. Zobaczy pan! [You'll see, sir!]
I had to promise my przyjaciel [friend], Pan Feliks Kracbarszt, to follow his advice, and only that way did I barely, with great trouble, get rid of him.
M. Mandlzon.
Greetings from Home, from Eretz Israel.

[Eretz Israel — letter; Zagłębie people in Palestine.] (From our special correspondent).
In Tel Aviv the series of festivities, manifestations and demonstrations is already over, and Tel Aviv, drunk with joy and enthusiasm, is again getting down to "Bereshit" — to the daily cares of creation and work. The dozens of holidays, jubilees, receptions, balls, concerts and plain "neshafim" [soirées] are over; the press, which announced new "festivals" to the reader every day, has suddenly fallen silent, and the city kiosks, which hour by hour were plastered with huge, shrieking posters heralding new surprises, now stand poor [?] and bare.
Who is able to convey all the festivities we had here from Purim until after Passover? Do not all the reports and letters about the Purim carnival, the "Exhibition", the 20th jubilee of Tel Aviv, the 25th jubilee of the Second "Aliyah" and of the "Teachers' Federation", about the Maccabi "Kenes" (conference) and the house-warming of "Ohel Shem" of [?] the "Oneg Shabbat" come out pale and feeble next to the real thing?
But Tel Aviv can do more than dance and sing: it can also create productively and do physical work.
Go out in the morning into the streets of Będzin, Dąbrowa and Sosnowiec and see how many Jewish workers hurry to the coal pits, factories and workshops — couldn't you count them on your fingers? And in Tel Aviv at 6 in the morning the street swarms like a beehive with the workers running to work. Often I stand for hours watching the Jewish "Manchester" in miniature, and my heart swells with pride seeing workers in short knee-breeches, with rolled-up sleeves and bagel-rings in hand, running and riding to work — some on a bicycle, some on a bus and some by train. For a long time in the morning hours I wander through the workers' neighbourhoods, the workers' quarters, from which stream hundreds and thousands of women and men loaded with shovels, hoes and other work tools, and I cannot tear my gaze from those whose forefathers built Pithom and Raamses for foreign nations and whose grandchildren today build with blood and sweat a land of their own for their own people.
Blessed are you, Jewish people, when you hear again the beat of the hammer in the Jewish smithy, the noise of the machines in the factories and the work song "Labour is our whole life" of the halutz who cuts the ripe ears in the Jewish fields!
———
I met the sons of the Będzin rabbinical decisor (moreh hora'ah) R' Hanokh David Fridberg — Shlomo Yoel, Chaim and Menachem — who work in the colony of Petah Tikva. Shlomo Yoel has a post in the "Labour Exchange" of "Hapoel Hamizrachi", Menachem is a locksmith, and Chaim has no fixed, definite job.
With Shlomo Yoel, who was an active worker in the Będzin "Tzeirei Mizrachi", I had a long talk about his situation, of which he does not complain. True, he had bad times, he was ill, but he accepted everything with love, because the work of building Eretz Israel, a difficult task, demands much perseverance, strength, love and attachment to the land.
Mr. Meir Gożelany [?] of Będzin has a good post with a nice salary as a bookkeeper in an English-Jewish firm in Jaffa.
Miss Chana Szental of Będzin has a post in the "Culture Committee" in the cultural department of the General Federation of Jewish Labour. Miss Sh., whom the Będzin theatre public still remembers as a talented actress of the local "Mu'a" [?], plays in the local dramatic section "Ha'Ohel", directed by the talented "Habima" actor Mr. Moshe Halevi. In all the "productions" (performances) the "Ohel" has given so far — "The Fishermen", "Jacob and Rachel" and Peretz's staged [...] [?] — Miss Sh. too appeared in responsible roles and was received, like the whole splendid ensemble, with great success. The "Ohel" is now preparing to bring to the stage the drama "Jeremiah" by the German-Jewish writer Stefan Zweig, who is coming to Eretz Israel especially to attend the premiere.
In Nes Ziona, which lies between Rishon LeZion and Rehovot, I visited Mr. Alter Erlich of Sosnowiec. Mr. E. is a teacher in Nes Ziona and at the same time a bearer of culture, a lecturer for the "Culture Committee". Mr. E. gives lectures on subjects from world literature, such as Romain Rolland and Rabindranath Tagore. Mr. E. is an active labour activist in his colony, a member of the "Nes Ziona Workers' Council" and head of the local branch of "Hapoel Hatzair".
Mr. Yosef Abba Szlezynger, who came to the country with the Fourth Aliyah without any definite plan made in advance and without vocational training, has structurally "revolutionised" himself together with his children and turned from a scrap-iron dealer into a "nagar" (carpenter). In the first period after his arrival in Eretz Israel, when there was as yet no room for small iron dealers, Mr. Sh. abandoned his trade and worked on road building. During the crisis, from which Mr. Sh. also suffered, he learned carpentry; today he works in this trade and makes a not-bad living.
His eldest daughter is a dental technician and works in the dental factory of Mr. Blum, who in recent weeks became well known in Eretz Israel by putting up a fine, specially built house (it cost him 25 thousand dollars). The middle daughter works in Jaffa in a large underwear [soft linen] factory. Mr. Sh. owns a little house of his own and is spared rent, which is many times dearer than in Poland.
Further greetings and answers to letters — to follow.
M. Hampel.

The Misled Girl (7)

[Literature — serialized novel; installment 7, including the start of "Chapter Eight".]
Dr. A. Weisman.
(A novel of Jewish life in the old world, based on historical facts.)

"God, what has happened here, something so terrible? How dare you speak like that about Mania? She is a brilliant child! You yourself and all of us always adored her — something terrible must have happened."
"Something terrible really has happened," Ludwig answered with a deep sigh, and a terrible sorrow covered his face.
Everyone was frightened by his appearance.
"Who knows what has gone on here?" they all exclaimed in fright, exchanging glances with one another.
"Go on[?], Ludwig, you must tell us; after all, you are not the only one mixed up in this. You must — we are telling you."
Open-mouthed, they all waited for Ludwig to calm down a little and begin his story.
"I can't tell you anything today. Leave me in peace today. You will know everything, but not today. If I weren't in such company right now, I would have walked out. Leave me in peace, we'll put it off until tomorrow. Let us talk today about whatever you like — only not about Mania."
"But where is Mania now? That much you must tell us."
"Where else would she be now? With Sister Irina."
Everyone sighed with relief[?].
"If so, she is in good hands," Aunt Fanny spoke up. "Mania will be ours yet; no one has ever got out of her hands."
"You are mistaken. Sister Irina is indeed clever, pious, good and learned, but none of you knows Mania. Mania regrets the whole affair. Do you hear? Mania regrets it."
The word "regret" struck them all like thunder. They all clapped their hands together and almost screamed:
"If she manages to escape from there, then we are all ruined!"
"Ruined!" — the second aunt did not stop wringing her hands.
"Calm yourselves," said Aunt Fanny. "No one has ever run away from Sister Irina yet. I have always believed in her 'bryhshaft'[?] [prob.: skill / resourcefulness]; this very week I will go down to the convent especially. I must know everything."
"Will you see Mania?" they all asked.
"I don't know; I'll see there how things stand. I would never have believed it," she said, fanning herself with her 'gauze'[?] [perhaps a gauze scarf / a fan]. "Mania was so well prepared already, she was burning to escape as fast as possible from the accursed Jews. I don't believe it, I don't believe it, it is impossible!"
"So — you don't believe it? You can ask Jan: he disguised himself as a coachman and drove the horses when we ran away."
Jan was the younger brother of the ekonom [the estate steward], a shaygets, a 'piper' [whistler, ne'er-do-well], a 'marim'[?] at murder, a fanatical Catholic and a hater of Israel. He too served at the same estate-owner's manor, and he too was present that evening.
The nieces, the old maids who used to hang about him and had more than once tried to match themselves to him, sought him out and brought him to the company of conspirators, so that he would testify that Mania had come to regret it.
"Is it possible?" they asked him.
"Let Ludwig tell you himself."
"He has already told us."
"So what do you want from me?"
"We want you to confirm it too, because we don't believe such a thing."
"Why won't you believe it? Besides the fact that she regretted it, Ludwig also got a big, fiery slap in the mug from Mania's pretty little hand."
Ludwig jumped up and threw himself at Jan, but the women intervened. The rest of the company present that evening came running; everyone wanted to know what was going on, but the women hushed the story up.
"I will go to the convent 'mun haytige'[?] [prob.: this very] week," said Aunt Fanny. "From them, from the two young men, we will learn nothing."
The company had already sat down to supper. There was a clatter of knives and forks, and they ate of everything the world rests on with great appetite and gusto. They clinked glasses and goblets one with another, and showed 'bryhshaft'[?] and prowess in drinking and in emptying the bottles of brandy.
That evening Ludwig drank more than ever and got as drunk as Lot. All the guests praised him for entertaining the company.
Those who knew Ludwig more closely wondered why he had suddenly begun to drink so much. He was drinking truly like a goy.
Jan looked at Ludwig with disgust for his heavy drinking. Ludwig kept shouting aloud that he would kill Jan.
Everyone laughed at how Ludwig was talking out of drunkenness.
It goes without saying that the whole crowd drank, guzzled and boozed, and soon began to blame the Jews for Mania's change of heart; to vilify the Jews and throw mud at them for — — for being Jews.
"Certainly the Jews won't keep quiet. Zelig and his wife set off this very day to look for Mania. We thought Yom Kippur was the safest day — nobody would chase after them; but in the end, nothing at all is holy to the Jews, and they went after her on Yom Kippur."
"They say their rabbi ordered them to travel on Yom Kippur!"
"There you have an accursed people, to whom nothing is holy!"
"Mania is too close," one woman called out, "and that is very dangerous."
"The convent is too close; Mania will have to be taken a little farther away!"
"That's right," all the drunken men and women agreed. "It must be done as quickly as possible, or else a disaster may still come of it for us!"
"We must go tomorrow already."
"That is still too early. They may still notice and follow us. Old Dvoyre already suspects us now of being to blame for her granddaughter's flight."
"But it can't be put off. It may still become too late. We must go to the convent tomorrow already. We must consult with Sister Irina, so that she sends Mania farther away."

Chapter Eight.
When you ride a few miles out of the shtetl Z., you see from a distance the golden[?] spire of a cloister. It seems as if the spire reaches right up into the clouds. But the farther you ride, you notice how the gilded spire separates from the clouds, and before your eyes you see a great hill. On the hill stands a large old building, surrounded all around by a walled park.
It is quiet all around. Only the ringing of the bells disturbs the silence from time to time. The sound of the bells carries far, far away and so reminds the shtetls that in the walled parks there are living people who lead a separate life — a closed-off, secluded world.
This is the Catholic convent, and it reminds us of the closed monasteries of Spain, where the terrible victims of the Spanish Inquisition were locked away. There, between the stone walls of the Catholic 'murte'[?] monastery, languished the unfortunate Jewish souls who had the misfortune to fall into the claws of the Jesuit band of soul-snatchers. There they were tortured for long years until they gave themselves over to apostasy; or — when they stood firm and withstood the trial to the end, refusing to exchange the Jewish 'rendl' [gold coin, i.e. their Jewishness], and laughing at all manner of harsh tortures and bodily torments, just so as not to deny, God forbid, the living God and to remain faithful to the belief in the oneness of the Creator — they were burned alive on the pyre[?], at an auto-da-fé, with the Jewish "Shema Yisrael" on their lips.

Letters from Home.

[Będzin — satirical feuilleton, letter to a friend.]
B.H., week of the portion “Number the sons of Levi” [Bamidbar]...
My friend Reb Shlomo, may his light shine.
After my greetings: I ask you not to bear me any grudge for not writing you an answer immediately[?]; the reason is precisely today's Torah portion. — You will surely wonder: “what has the Sabbatical year to do with Mount Sinai” — what connection does my answer have with today's portion? So I ask you, Reb Shlomo, to look into the Midrash on today's portion, and only then will you understand that the two things, my answer and the portion, are connected with one another.
The Midrash on today's portion brings a question about an infant born at six[?] months on the Sabbath: may one desecrate the Sabbath for its sake? The question was put to Rabbi Abbahu, and he answered: ZYT“A[?] IPT“A UT“H ARNU“N.
The very same question is today very topical among merchants. All of a sudden that kind of money has vanished from our globe, and there exists a new “currency”: an oblong piece of paper ruled with black lines, with only a little space on the back for signatures...
Well, when one goes today to any merchant to buy goods, he faces a hard question: “whence do we know that one born at seven months is viable” — will he still pay the bill of exchange? And the answer is:
— “ZYT“A APT“A UT“A ARNU“N”...
That is: he has been, and will be, bankrupt...
Yes, today is “the season of our bankruptcy” [a pun on the festival formula “the season of our freedom”; pleyte = bankruptcy]. Once, when mankind was not as “cultured” as today, when impudence did not have such great power, a bankrupt of this sort had to flee the country, go off to distant lands, leaving a stain of shame, a yellow patch, on his whole family; it was hard to make a match when the family contained an “ansetser” [a defaulter]...
But today, when the fashion of nakedness is at its height, when in the name of honesty and justice all sorts of deceptive deeds are performed, “there is not a house where there is not one dead” — there is no merchant who is not already up to the second verse of the “Song of Songs” [“bay'm bay'm” thus doubled in print]; it has come to such a pass that when two merchants meet in the street, the first greeting is:
— Where are you at?
— Me? Already past the “regulation” [composition with creditors].
And do not think, Reb Shlomo, that after the regulation anything is left in the pocket — God forbid! The merchant does not go bankrupt for profit. His whole “work” is only so that the bailiff should not take away his last belongings...
That is how our economic situation stands. On the political field, on the other hand, we have stayed behind... we are going backwards.. All fashions lose their value, their gloss, and our eyes and senses yearn once more to live in the old world..
Some two or three years ago we lived in a “political” world: everything, deed or thought, and in general anything that happened at all, had a political basis; even such an innocent matter as breaking up the yeshiva in the Będzin beth midrash, or celebrating a siyum of a Talmud tractate, had political significance. Yes, that was once, but today “it has grown darker on the political horizon”, and instead of going forward we go back, back to the old system[?], to the old way, as our “fanatical” forefathers used to do...
The “greatest grief” has been caused us by the Radomsko and Aleksandrów Hasidim, who took upon themselves the mission of spreading Torah, and for that purpose opened yeshivas[?] where they study exactly as in “the old days”.. not even one day a week do they study “Daf Yomi”..
I even turned to one of the “Agudah” leaders, before whom I poured out my “bitter heart” over the “audacity” of the non-partisan Hasidim; the “Agudah” leader calmed me and gave me to understand that I need not worry — the yeshivas, he assured me, will not exist anyway; they, the non-partisans, “have no money”...
In the field of kashrut, too, a broad “change” has come about: all of Zagłębie is steeped in a sea of prohibitions. From the border shtetl of Modrzejów to Dąbrowa there stretches a chain of prohibitions and bans; wherever you go and stand you hear of new prohibitions issued by this or that rabbi. It has gone so far that even in our town council the kashrut question became topical; the only difference is that from the prohibitions issued by the clergy, złotys “wink” out..
In the town council, on the other hand, they are concerned with “abolishing” prohibitions, that is: that Jewish children whom the Magistrate sends to Busko for a cure[?] should not, as until now, eat treyf...
The one who laid the treyf dishes “on the plate” was, God forbid, not some “Agudah” councillor, who went into the town council to “defend the Jewish religion”, but in fact a Zionist — better said, a Zionist activist, Mrs. Ratner, who came out against the great injustice done to Jewish children who must eat “kosher-kvitsh”[?] during their cure..
Naturally, none of the Jewish councillors supported the motion — whose business is it? And the whole question depends on the grace of the President, who promised that “it will be done”... But be that as it may, the Zionists are very pleased that their councillor defends kashrut matters, and, as people say, the board of the Zionist Organisation has decided that when the appointment of a fourth moreh hora'ah [rabbinical decisor] becomes topical, the Zionists will put forward the candidacy of Mrs. Ratner..
And believe me, Reb Shlomo (let it stay between us), if this resolution were carried out, kashrut matters in our town would stand on a higher level than today.. and in the synagogue the shammes would not be announcing that the sausage at So-and-so son of So-and-so is nevelah and treyfah...
As for your questions, such as: has the spiritual chaos in the synagogue stopped yet? how much longer will the present dozors [members of the kehilla board] stay in power? and about the scandal that happened at “Ahavat Chesed” — I shall not write this time, because I am hurrying to the lecture of a certain Dr. Szalman, who “knows” the secret of “how to become rich”. I have a great desire for that — not for the lecture, but to become rich. A fine[?] thing is the little coin: for a little coin you have the world, and never mind after a hundred and twenty years — surely, surely: eulogies pour from every corner, the “Talmud Torah” children cry “Righteousness shall go before him”, and thousands of people whisper with their lips: “May good angels come to meet him”...
So have a good Sabbath, wishes you — your
Ben Amotz.
The main thing I forgot! I have just read in the newspapers that the mysterious poison casket of the terrible and beautiful Lucrezia Borgia is being put up at a public auction in Berlin; do take the trouble and buy it for me. Oh, how useful such a little box would be for cleaning out our “domestic mouse-plague”... The above.

In What Light Zagłębie Is Seen in the Eyes of Foreign Visitors

[Zagłębie — impressions/essay; series, part II.]
II.
And yet Będzin has no great joy from its Jewishness. One could say — quite the contrary. Because of it, it has plenty to sing and tell about [i.e. it suffers for it]. Here in Poland we have not yet reached the point of judging social phenomena objectively. People do not want to know that one yardstick can apply in municipal and economic life — achievement.
The favour of the deciding circles has turned away from Jewish Będzin. Goodwill is being transferred more and more to its neighbour S o s n o w i e c. Some 50 years ago this place was a village, known for its large, beautiful pine forest, and nothing more. From that very word — "sosna" [pine] — the name of the town is also said to derive. The "witz" [pun: Yiddish "vitz" = joke, and the town's ending -wiec] comes only now...
Sosnowiec — where Jews make up altogether about 15 percent — is now consistently favoured at the expense of Będzin. A chamber of commerce for Zagłębie is created — its seat is not Będzin but Sosnowiec; the district court and the labour court have been placed in Sosnowiec. The big Polish joint-stock companies establish their branches there. In short — Sosnowiec becomes the "metropolis", the one that sets the tone. Będzin stays behind. It is being reduced to a second-rate town.
It is a system. It is a tendency, although it has no great practical significance.
Zagłębie has grown greatly in the last ten years and climbs ever higher on the ladder of industrial and commercial development. The borders between one town and the next are steadily being levelled. D ą b r o w a–B ę d z i n–S o s n o w i e c is today in fact one large centre: one power station supplies current and light to all three towns, one telephone exchange serves all three places, and one electric tramway — which, incidentally, has been running for only 1 year — connects them.
When one travels from one town to the other, whether by tram or by train, one must be an excellent connoisseur of local conditions to be able to establish where Dąbrowa ends and Będzin begins, and where the Będzin–Sosnowiec border lies. Along the whole line — one long row of industrial establishments, one dense net of chimneys.
Still, there is a difference. Dąbrowa and Sosnowiec are mainly industrial centres; Będzin, on the other hand, concentrates the nerve of trade for all of Zagłębie. A trade that blooms and grows, where Jewish agility, Jewish initiative and enterprising spirit work wonders.
Zagłębie is today the liveliest, most bustling trading place in Poland. It is the bridge that links the crisis-stricken, bankruptcy-ridden [?] Łódź textile region with rich industrial Upper Silesia. A mighty crank [?] turns from the impoverished towns of "Congress Poland" to Katowice, Königshütte, far out to the German border, and keeps alive [?] in the present bitter-hard time tens of thousands of livelihoods that the economic crisis has crushed.
A tumult, a fair, as far as the eye can reach; a swarm of people; the pavements, the roadway — one tangle, colourful, noisy, mobile; merchants and shop assistants pull [passers-by] by the coat-tails, the passers-by are dragged into the shops, one is offered even bird's milk. Commerce is in full blaze...
I am on the "famous" Modrzejowska Street in Sosnowiec — the "Nalewki", the "Nowomiejska" of Zagłębie.
It is a remarkable picture that catches the eye. The crowd that fills the street so densely is a strange, unusual one. Young and old, men and women, more women than men, all in shabby clothes, neither townish nor rustic — it is something peculiar, special.
These are the "Ślązaks" [Silesians].
One recognises them at once. This is not the human material of core [?] Poland, of "our" Poland. Here there is none of the costumed wealth of colour of the Łowicz peasant dress, there is none of the pleasant primitiveness of the "Krakowiaks", nor is the slovenly finery of the "Congress-Pole" to be seen. The people and the clothing — grey, monotonous, exactly like the industrial region they come from, like the coal pits and smelters that have just spat out most of them, or their men, and that will soon swallow them again for long, long hours...
And this crowd, so foreign and strange to our eye [?], speaking the typical "Wasserpolnisch" and itself flowing like water, fills the town, draws in long, almost closed rows from the railway station to "Modrzejowska" Street and back to the station...
The essence of the story:
Once, in very ancient times, the local chronicles relate, Zagłębie was the point at which the attacks of the "Ślązaks" were aimed. They came running here armed, eager for war, to rule this neglected but blessed province, which had the misfortune to lie right by the Prussian border..
Today they come here again in their thousands, whole camps — it is a new kind of "invasion", a good one, a dear one, a welcome one: day in, day out they stream to the shops, empty the shelves of goods, but on leaving they leave the shopkeepers full drawers of takings. It is a rush that brings an abundance of livelihood, a golden (now only a "silver") rain of luck and blessing.
Appeal!

[Zionism — Congress elections.] We have been asked by the Central Bureau of "Et Livnot" in Poland to print the following appeal:
Fellow Zionists!
We are entering the election campaign for the 16th Congress. The time has come for soul-searching for every Zionist, who must think over the achievements of the movement and the great tasks it has to fulfil in the near future.
This year's Congress is, more than all previous ones, a Congress of decisions for Zionism. Not for mandates, not for personal honours, but for correct ideas, for the right path in today's work of building up — that is what this struggle must be about. And not phrases and polemical passion, but life and the experience of recent years shall decide which ideas are the correct ones and who has shown the right path.
1) We, the "Et Livnot" group, were the pioneers of the idea of the enlarged "Jewish Agency" back when a large part of the Zionist movement set itself against this plan, when others wavered, and still others supported the plan half-heartedly; when [printed "ווי"], out of necessity, we of "Et Livnot" saw in the realisation of the "enlarged Jewish Agency" the beginning of a new era for the building-up work in Eretz Israel.
6 years have passed since the struggle over the Agency began, and today the overwhelming majority of the Zionist movement awaits with faith and joy the historic turning point, when all the creative forces of our people will take upon themselves, together with us, the sacred right and the heavy burden bound up with the establishment of our national home.
2) Years ago we put forward the slogans of intensive upbuilding of Eretz Israel with all forces and through all forces of the Jewish people. At a time when the upbuilding of Eretz Israel had become one-sided, when colonisation rested on individual strata of the people and towards the others an attitude of disbelief and distrust had developed, we promoted faith in the creative Jewish hands and minds, without distinction of strata and classes. We argued that all strata must be treated equally by the Zionist movement, because they all hold within them great creative forces which sooner or later will develop for the good of the Jewish land and for the strengthening of the Jewish nation.
We were alone in defending this slogan. 6 years have passed, and the ranks of those who have understood the correctness of this slogan have grown enormously. The majority of the General Zionists in various countries, the Revisionists, a large part of "Mizrachi" and, to a wider extent, also the workers' parties today recognise the creative significance of the Fourth Aliyah, which developed and raised the percentage of the Jewish population in the country (from 11 per cent in 1922 to 19 per cent in 1928) [and not] only [printed "נור אויך"] also the number of industrial enterprises, artisans' workshops, plantations, business connections with abroad and with the neighbouring countries, investments of large private capital, which is now flowing to Eretz Israel in a rising trend, creating more and more possibilities for a larger immigration.
Today it is clear to every seriously thinking Zionist that the success of our colonisation depends on correct economic methods, that the creation of new employment opportunities and the enlargement of the aliyah are closely bound up with the development of private initiative and — apart from the national funds — with the influx of private capital into Eretz Israel.
3) With complete devotion and enthusiasm for the pure Herzlian idea we go to the elections for the 16th Zionist Congress.
For years, "statist" propaganda and genuine statist concepts have contended within the Zionist movement. While part of the movement played at statist fictions (government and opposition, etc.), we, the "Et Livnot" group, demanded rational administrative methods in the conduct of our work in Eretz Israel. For years we fought for a strong and purposeful leadership in Eretz Israel, which should not be a plaything in the hands of political passions, but should carry out unswervingly the programme of the building-up work as it is adopted by the Congress.
After long years of debates and differences of opinion, the Fifteenth Congress carried out our idea and elected an Executive for Eretz Israel. The objective observer will admit that this very Executive, despite all the difficult conditions, for the first time mastered the situation in Eretz Israel and became the leading factor in our building-up work.
4) For six years a debate has been going on in the Zionist ranks about the Zionist Organisation. The opposition groups swear their loyalty to the idea of the Organisation and at the same time they fragment the forces of the Organisation through internal struggles and exaggerated factionalism. We, the "Et Livnot" group, declared from the beginning that the Zionist Organisation must remain the decisive factor of ideas and that within the framework of the Jewish Agency it must play the leading role and provide the spiritual leadership. That is why we were against fragmentation, against the development of the process of splitting into factions and against any struggle for power within the Zionist Organisation. Precisely in order to strengthen the Zionist Organisation and to secure for it its natural leading role we strove for consolidation in the world movement and for peace and unification in the Zionist ranks in Poland.
These moods of consolidation and peace have now become universally popular; let it therefore be recalled here too that the first word against internal fragmentation and Zionist fratricidal struggles was spoken by our group.
This is the historical sum total of our course of ideas. The 16th Congress has to carry through the work that was begun and to carry out to the end the tasks that were outlined. The Jewish Agency must be realised. The further building-up work in Eretz Israel must rest on all strata of the people and take into account sound economic methods. The leadership must be strong and purposeful, the Organisation must be united and closed in its ranks.
For this we have fought for years in the ranks of the Zionist Organisation. For this the struggle must still be waged during the elections to the forthcoming Zionist Congress.
The formulation of these guidelines, as well as the exact setting of the tasks our delegates will have at the Congress, will be determined by the conference of "Et Livnot", which will convene on 9 June in Warsaw.
On the eve of the final victory of the ideas for which we have fought, confident of the trust of the broad Zionist circles in Poland, we call upon our members and sympathisers and urge them to strengthen our ranks and to continue with all their energy the work of enlightenment in all Zionist circles and groups.
Our way leads through today's Eretz Israel to the redeemed Jewish people, and through today's Jewish masses to a built-up, free Eretz Israel!

Będzin — Municipal budget before the plenum of the city council.

Tuesday's session of the city council was chaired by the vice-chairman Mr. Yaakov Erlich. Before the agenda, 3 urgent motions and one interpellation were considered. An urgent motion by Dr. Rechtman that the city administration should deepen the river in Małobądz in order to protect the neighbouring streets from flooding during a downpour. The interpellation, also by Dr. Rechtman, was addressed to the presidium of the city council concerning the repressions against the traders of the Old Market. The urgent motion is adopted, and regarding the interpellation the chairman declares that an answer will be given at the next session.
On the agenda: second reading of the budget. At the item "healing the sick", councillor Feiner proposes that a sum of 10 thousand zł. be set aside for sending sick people to various health resorts. Councillors Kleinman and Mrs. Ratner speak on the question, and Dr. Rechtman's amendment was adopted, that the item should also apply to support for those who are[?] undergoing a cure outside the city.
At the item "pension for the veterinary doctor", Mrs. Ratner and Dr. Rechtman speak, pointing out that the veterinarian, who is employed barely 3 hours a day, earns no less than about 18 thousand zł. a year...
None of the councillors from the other clubs reacted to this argument, and the question of reducing the pension is taken off the agenda.
The continuation of the second reading will take place next Tuesday.
School commission cleansed of Jews...

A few days ago a plenary session of the school commission (Dozór Szkolny) took place in the local magistrate under the chairmanship of President Michał, at which 2 representatives of the school system were to be elected. For years, 1 Christian and 1 Jew had always been elected without discussion, but at the last session the mood changed. No Jewish representative of the public (powszechne) schools was elected any more.
The Jewish candidate Mr. Rapaport received 1 vote...
“Der Iker” (“The Main Thing”) is playing today with the Vilna troupe.

The Vilna Troupe, which consists of first-class stage talents, made itself an excellent[?] name among the local theatre public with its staging of “Kiddush Hashem” and “Unterwelt” (“Underworld”). Today they are giving the not-yet-performed, rich-in-content play “Der Iker” (“The Main Thing”), a drama in 4 acts.
It is to be expected that this time too the Jewish theatre public will receive the artists as they deserve.
Magistrate bought a plot.

On Wednesday the presidium of the city administration signed the purchase agreement for the plot where the cattle market is located. The plot was bought from the French-Italian company for 236 thousand zł.
Laid down his mandate as councillor.
Mr. Lidobarski, who had entered the city council as representative of the small traders, has resigned as councillor. In his place Mr. Dawid Gitler enters.
Esperantists' convention in Będzin.

In the hall on “Góra Zamkowa” a convention of the Esperantist associations in Zagłębie took place on Sunday.
The participants in the convention were almost exclusively from among our Jewish brethren, mostly minors, who are, as always, the first bearers of culture...
The convention is opened (in Polish) by Dr. Jungster of Sosnowiec, who invites the leaders of the Esperanto language in Zagłębie to the presidium, reads the greetings of the organisations that did not come to the convention, greets the representatives of the city council, the city administration and the school authorities, and proceeds to the agenda with a lecture on the significance of Esperanto as an international language.
After the lecture the Esperanto hymn is sung and greetings follow.
On behalf of the Będzin city council the chairman Mr. Fürstenberg greets, on behalf of the city administration — ławnik Żebrowski, on behalf of “Frayhayt” (“Freedom”) — Mr. Weissalz (in Esperanto), and others.
Then the Esperanto hymn is sung and Mr. Wojciechowski gives a lecture on the development of the language. The speaker stresses that through the language the Esperantist becomes a citizen of the world, who unites all mankind into one culture.
As a demonstration, the Misses Gleitzer and Rozen recite very beautifully (in Esperanto). With this the morning session ends.
At the afternoon session the question of propaganda was discussed. A resolution was adopted to intervene with the school authorities so that Esperanto be taught in the public (powszechne) schools.
In the evening an entertainment took place, where the youth amused themselves “in the Esperanto manner”...
Subsidy for the “Orphans' Home” raised.
At the last city council session councillor Mrs. Ratner moved that the subsidy for the “Orphans' Home” be raised from 30 to 35 thousand zł. After the factual justification the motion was adopted.
Schoolgirls' excursion to Poznań.
Yesterday evening 48 schoolgirls of public school No. 4 left for Poznań and Danzig.
A Jewish Little Girl Falls into a Latrine Pit and Is Rescued

[Będzin — accidents.] In the house of Mr. Gisler on Modrzejowska Street a Jewish little girl fell into a latrine pit. At the girl's cries people came running, and with the help of a rope they pulled the child out of the pit alive.
Because of a "Mistake" They Committed a Burglary...!

[Będzin — crime.] On the night from Monday to Tuesday thieves broke into the electrical-supplies shop of Mr. Goldfeld, from which they stole goods worth a few thousand zł.
The thieves worked hard until they broke open the safe, where they found no more than 2 zł.
The next morning one of the thieves was arrested. Under interrogation the thief declared that they had carried out the burglary "by mistake" (al pi ta'ut), because they had had quite different plans..
The Summer Colonies Will Be Better Arranged This Year

[Będzin — welfare.] This week the Commission for Social Welfare held a meeting, at which it was decided that comfortable places for the children to sleep are to be arranged at the summer colonies in Sławków.
Academy in Honour of the Co-operative Holiday

[Będzin — economy.] In the "Korso" hall the management of the Co-operative Bank in Będzin held on Sunday morning an academy (festive assembly) dedicated to Co-operative Day, which was celebrated throughout the world.
The academy was opened and chaired by the vice-chairman of the bank's board, Mr. L. Bauszykowski [?], who invited to the presidium representatives of neighbouring co-operative banks and other communal workers, and gave the first word to the bank manager, Mr. Goldsztajn, who spoke on the significance of co-operation and its great benefit.
Messrs. Pesachson and the representative of the Credit Bank, Mr. Tenenbaum, also spoke on the subject.
In conclusion the bank's chairman, Mr. Fürstenberg, took the floor and said a few true words: that at the present time, when the Jewish masses are living through such a crisis, he very much doubts whether any family can save anything...
Sosnowiec — Plenary Session of the City Council

[Sosnowiec — city council.] (Sh.) After a rather long break, the 10th plenary session of the city council was convened on Tuesday; this time it was distinguished by its quick pace and by the adoption of all the magistrate's proposals almost unanimously.
———
With an hour's delay Chairman Dr. Pawełek opens the session. After the report of Dr. Rządkiewicz [?] the following resolutions are adopted unanimously: 1) to confirm the conditions of the Bank Gosp. Kraj. [Bank Gospodarstwa Krajowego] regarding the loan of 150 thousand dollars (the loan project had already been adopted at the last session on the 27th of last month), 2) to take a loan of 100 thousand zł. to complete the building of the school on Okrzei Street. The 3rd item on the agenda — the election of a member of the Voivodeship Council — is also dealt with quickly, and with 18 votes Dep. Bień is elected. Further, Dr. Burzyński [?] is elected as a member of the commission of the "Hungarian" [?] hospital in Będzin, and at about 9 in the evening the chairman closes the session.
On the Day of Their Father's Yahrzeit They Lost Their Mother — Tragic Death of a Jewish Woman

[Sosnowiec — accidents.] A tragic accident happened last Friday afternoon on 3 Maja Street.
Walking along the street was the 52-year-old Rykla Sztajnic, owner of a fruit shop on Warszawska Street. When she was not far from the "Cukiernia Warszawska" (confectionery), the passenger bus of the Tabiasz firm arrived. In the same direction, from the other side, a droshky was also driving, and the driver, wishing to avoid a collision with the droshky, hastily turned the bus back. At that moment Mrs. Sztajnic was close to the bus, and from the strong blow she was thrown against a tree, and from the impact against the tree she suffered a concussion. On the way to the hospital the unfortunate woman died.
The funeral of the tragically killed woman took place on Sunday. The wailing reached the heart of heaven. The coffin was carried along Modrzejowska Street and stopped at the house of Mr. Tabiasz as a sign of protest.
On the same day as the funeral a circumcision (brit milah) was to take place at Mr. Tabiasz's, which had already been postponed twice, and this time too the brit was postponed because of the tragic incident.
The killed woman left several unmarried children. On the very same day on which they lost their mother, their father had died a year ago.
The Trial of the Jewish Merchants — Adjourned

[Sosnowiec — courts.] Great interest was aroused by the trial which was to take place in the local district court against the merchants Dawid Fiura, Bernard Grajcer, Eli' Fiura, Wacław Mediński, Tomasz Banach, Józef Klimas, Josef Urbach, Szymon Ehrenstein and L. Gotrajch, who were accused of bringing goods from abroad in an illegal manner.
Also sitting in the dock were several officials of the customs office who had a connection to the affair.
138 witnesses were summoned to the sensational trial. The defence consisted of six of the best lawyers from Warsaw and three from Sosnowiec.
Because a few principal witnesses were missing, the court agreed to the defenders' proposal to adjourn the trial to an unspecified date.
The defenders also wished to release from prison the merchants Dawid Fiura and Jekl Grajcer against 10 thousand zł. and Eliasz Fiura against 20 thousand zł. bail.
—o—
Died at Her Son's Bedside.
[Sosnowiec — deaths.] At the age of 80 the esteemed lady Taubele Neufeld died in recent days. She died suddenly while visiting her sick son Heniek.
—o—
The Present Board Throws Off the Old Sins..
[Sosnowiec — organisations.] On Sunday the new board of the Merchants' Association (Piłsudskiego 12) held a meeting, at which the question was discussed of why the association has no representative in the Chamber of Commerce.
It was decided to issue a communiqué that the blame for this lies with the previous board.
—o—
A Bloody Fight over the Evening Prayer...
[Sosnowiec — community.] With a bandaged head Mr. Efraim Galenzer came to us at the editorial office and told the following:
Last Sunday G. was standing at the prayer stand (amud) in the beit midrash to lead the evening prayer (maariv). At that moment Mr. Jechiel Fajger came up and demanded that Galenzer let him take the amud, and when Mr. G. refused the demand, Fajger threw off his coat and threw himself on Galenzer, inflicting on him with an iron door handle several deep wounds in the head.
First aid in the beit midrash was given by Dr. Zalk, who with great effort stopped the bleeding and bandaged the wounds.
—o—
Guest Performances of "Ararat" in Zagłębie.
[Zagłębie — theatre.] The first Jewish chamber theatre "Ararat" of Łódź, under the direction of the poet Moshe Broderzon, has come to Zagłębie for a number of guest performances. On Wednesday and Thursday "Ararat" played in Będzin and had an enormous success.
Tonight a performance in the local "City Theatre". The programme: "Shoshanat Yaakov" and "Everything Dances".
On Saturday afternoon in "Nadaszczy" [?], Będzin, 2 programmes will be given together.
—o—
Town Administration in Czeladź — Resigned.
[Czeladź — municipality.] This week the town council in Czeladź held a meeting. At the meeting the mayor and deputy mayor made declarations that, because the government categorically refused to grant a loan, the town administration cannot run the town's economy, and they are laying down their mandates.

— Mr. Hilel Bolimowski [?] donates 5 zł. to "Malbish Arumim" (Clothing the Naked) in Będzin.

The Small Trader

[Article — small trade and taxes.] What does the small trader want? What does he demand? It is hard to formulate, to express in a few words what this kind of person demands, what hurts him and what he asks for. Whichever way you turn, it is all troubles; when there is no sound limb, how can one point to one particular point, to one fact? It seems to me, therefore, that the situation can be characterised by the fact that the small trader is fighting to be recognised as what he is: that it should be established once and for all and recognised by law that there exists in the world such a kind of person, such a kind of merchant, belonging to the category [printed "k tegoria"] which in economic language is called "small trader" — and that he should be treated accordingly.
On the ladder of economic life there are, after all, various strata. The government has, for example, recognised that there is the peasant, an ordinary farmer, and there is the squire, the owner of a large estate. Among landowners there are certain categories as regards paying tax. Thus we know, for example, that a peasant who owns 15 morgs of land counts as a poor man and is entirely exempt from tax. Yet this poor man is, even by our standards, a rich man, since he owns property worth 50 thousand złoty; but in agriculture it is held that his income is minimal and that he cannot pay any taxes.
In the urban economy there is hardly any minimum income at all for which one is exempted from tax. At most there is such a minimum for the worker, but that too is so small that only someone who is actually dying of hunger [printed "higiner"] is exempt from tax. Worst of all is the lot of the so-called "merchant". For him there is no consideration at all. He is measured straight away at full size. Here lies the misfortune of the small trader: it is a misfortune when someone is made into a rich man so that afterwards he can be turned into a pauper.
Does one need to give examples of this? Go into the small traders' association of whatever town you like, and listen to what people tell about the assessments of turnover tax for the last year, and you will be convinced that there is a forcible drive to make people into rich men, into big merchants with enormous turnovers. From almost everyone you will hear that his turnover has been reckoned at two or three times as much as a year earlier. Here, a grocery shop was assessed a year ago at 18 thousand zł., and this year already at 36 thousand zł. A second grocery shop was assessed a year ago at 25 thousand, and this year at a full 60 thousand. For one butcher the turnover was raised from 50 thousand to 135 thousand zł.
Such examples can be given without end. One sees that a tendency prevails to do away with the small trader as a type, to make everyone into big merchants. That would be very good and one could welcome it if one really saw [printed "geven"] the turnover, and hence the profit, grow. By putting a large turnover on paper one at most makes that man into a big pauper, but not into a big merchant!
And the whole [unclear word, printed "firenyit" — apparently "wrath/burden"] is poured out only on the small dealer, shopkeeper and merchant, because the big one keeps books — him one cannot assess just out of thin air, him one cannot estimate, and so all the anger is vented on the small trader who keeps no books and cannot defend himself at all. But the question arises: where is justice? Has anyone ever [?] seen many merchants who keep books whose turnover grew two-fold or even six-fold in the course of a year? If it does not happen there, one must understand that with the shopkeeper and dealer — a branch that suffers terribly from competition — it is surely impossible for the turnover to grow so much!
The small trader therefore fights for his recognition. He demands that a minimum for trade be fixed once and for all, just as it exists in agriculture, and that the minimum be stable, that it not depend on the good or bad will of an "inspector" or official; that it be known that the fourth category pays at most so much, the third so much, and so on. Let the assessments and the surprises come to an end.
That is how we understand the demands of the small trader, and we hold that the decisive factors must listen to the demands, for surely nobody wants to ruin a large stratum of the population!
S. J. Stupnicki.
Sport

[Sport — football.]
1. F.C. "Kattowitz" — "Hakoach" 3:4.
Had "Hakoach" come out for this match in a better line-up and not underrated the opponent, it would certainly have won the match. The best proof is the score up to half-time, 3:2 in "Hakoach"'s favour. In the second half the young players of "Hakoach" run out of strength, cannot keep up the strong pace, and lose the match. The goals were scored by Richter, Goldsztajn [printed "Noldshteyn"] and Lask. Weigberg distinguished himself in the "Hakoach" goal.
D.F.C. "Sturm" (Bielitz) — "Hakoach" 2:2.
The guests from Bielitz [Bielsko] showed fine football, playing technically and at a fast pace; above all the good positional play caught the eye — wherever the ball fell, a "Sturm" player was already waiting there. In the first half "Hakoach" plays very weakly, chaotically, without ambition; in the second half "Hakoach" shows play that is truly a pleasure to watch. The 2 players Rotenberg and Jankielewicz 2 stood out in particular.
In the first half "Sturm" scores 2 goals. 5 minutes before half-time Richter manages to score the first goal for "Hakoach" with a sharp shot from about 30 metres. In the second half "Hakoach" equalises from an eleven-metre kick [penalty] through Rotenberg. Although "Hakoach" now has great superiority, it does not manage to achieve the deserved [printed "ferdigisn"] victory, thanks to the ambitious defence of the guests. It is also worth singling out the young players Jankielewicz 3 and Nugberg, who stood in very well for their older comrades. Referee Mr. Jarza — good.
"Kraft" — "Shtern" 0:4.
The match between the above-mentioned workers' clubs ended in a deserved victory for "Kraft", which had a slight superiority over "Shtern" the whole time and scored 2 goals in the first half and another 2 goals in the second half.

To You, Comrades — Matriculants!

[Keren Kayemet — appeal of the gymnasium graduates; a "Ring".] The day on which we receive the matriculation certificate brings a colossal change into our way of life. We leave the school benches and hurry to the higher schools, universities, polytechnics etc., in order to prepare ourselves to take a suitable place in social life. In this joyful moment, however, we must not forget the duty which rests upon us as members of Jewish society. We must not forget that we must come to the aid of our scattered and dispersed brethren. We, as young people, understand best and feel most strongly the injustice which is done to us at every step, and therefore it is our duty to join the ranks of the builders of our old-new land, in the land of our fathers; with our sweat and toil we shall carry the bricks for the great building of our beautiful future, which awaits us only in Eretz Israel. We therefore consider it our duty at the present moment to help the upbuilding of Eretz Israel. To this end we are organising in the columns of the "Zaglembier Tsaytung" a "Ring" for the Keren Kayemet LeIsrael, whose task is to buy back the land of Eretz Israel from foreign hands. The land is [printed "in"] the foundation of every people, and therefore the KKL devotes its entire activity solely to the redemption of the land of Eretz Israel.
We hope that the action [—] which we are organising in the col[umns of the] "Zaglembier Tsaytung" will [—] with the greatest success. [—] [—]

From the Chess Tournament in Zagłębie

[Zagłębie — chess.]
The chess tournament, which began two weeks ago for promotion to the extra class, is already at the end of the first round. The 8 players taking part show equal strength, and no decisive superiority of any single player can be noticed, so that there is not a single player who is undefeated. The present standing is as follows: first place is held for the time being by Yechiel Kimelman (4 points) plus one adjourned game against Schweitzer (Będzin); Zucker and Merin (senior) 3 points each; Schweitzer (Będzin) 2½ points; Dr. Grodziński 2 points; Silberberg, Redlik (Będzin) and Feiner 1 point each — of these, Silberberg has played no more than 2 games, of which he won one against Feiner and lost one.
Most interesting will be the second round, which will decide which players are eliminated from the tournament, since only 5 of the above-mentioned 8 players will be admitted to the tournament for the voivodeship championship. The further contests will take place on Saturday at half past eight in the evening and on Sunday from 11 to 2 at midday and from 4 to 7 in the evening, in the premises of the Sosnowiec chess club.

I.
Esteemed Mr. Editor!
Allow me to publish in your esteemed newspaper the following lines, for which I thank you in advance. It arouses our greatest astonishment that you, Mr. Editor, print in your newspaper "information" from such persons whose only aim is to mislead public opinion. An example of this is also the latest "report" from the Dąbrowa city council, which simply outraged the Jewish population of Dąbrowa and therefore now compels us to give the following statement: 1) We declare that our policy is in full accord with the interests of the Jewish population of Dąbrowa, and so there can be no talk, as your informant writes, of our having sold the "birthright" for a "little smile", etc. 2) Regarding the 1500 zł for the cheders struck out at the second reading of the budget, we did indeed succeed at the Saturday session in getting this sum restored. 3) Regarding the supposed insult to the honour of the Jewish population of Dąbrowa, we state: Councillor Kicki (Sanacja), answering Councillor Czeplak, let slip a remark that the firm "Olen" is not a "smarkaty Żydek" ("snot-nosed little Jew"); the writer of these lines reacted to this immediately, and when Councillor Kicki wanted to apologise to the Jewish councillors' club, we told him that he must apologise from the rostrum — and so it was: Mr. Kicki apologised from the rostrum and expressed his regret for the words that had slipped out. 4) As to what your correspondent writes, that "the conduct of the deaf-and-dumb Jewish councillors has aroused bitterness among the Jewish population", we would like to draw your attention, Mr. Editor: perhaps you would really attend a few sessions of the local city council and see whether our policy is consistent, and whether we are in a position (3 Jews against 28 Christians) to do more than until now.
On behalf of the Jewish Councillors' Club
B. Rechnic.
