Conscious Calculation

[Zagłębie — economy; winter coal stocks.]
(The hard reckoning, and laying in coal stocks now for the winter.)
Economic conditions, the system of saving, prudent reckoning and calculation occupy no place whatsoever among us in the social sense. We do not have the authority (instance) that would point us to the proper steps to be taken in a given case.
To this very day, unfortunately, the greatest number of citizens are still under the psychosis of the war and of the "haste"[?] times — when money turned to ash, and "yesterday", however terrible and frightening it was, vanished into deep eternity to the point of oblivion. People do not adapt and do not want[?] to remember that we have long been living in different times, and that therefore life, the whole system and way of living must be arranged in a different manner.
We were, unfortunately, brought up in the war, when no one at all concerned themselves with a system of saving or with economy, and after the war too no one tried to take up the matter, so that none of us went through either the routine or such a school; and therefore it is no wonder that we have remained like this — neither on this side of the street nor on the other side of the street.
On top of that, ever worse and harder times came upon us Jews, so that we became helpless; one could not reckon and did not know how to calculate. The longer view vanished and was lost entirely, and people began to live without any system whatsoever and without any conscious reckoning. On top of that came piled-up tax obligations, which put quite respectable houses (firms) into the most catastrophic situation; losing their balance, they went down from the arena and lost contact with economic existence.
Of course, had we carried out an economic study that would have given us the proper guidance in case of a catastrophe, we would not have slipped. In such a case one would have reacted properly right from the start, and the dangerous situation would have been rescued on the spot.
But now the time has come when things cannot go on like this any more, and one must begin to arrange life differently. One must, in short, begin to live with reckoning; one must be economically conscious and get one's bearings on the spot.
In government circles too people are beginning to regard economic reckoning as a matter of the first importance. Not long ago we received a circular from the Kielce Voivode, who turns to us with the request that we devote several articles to the question of the necessity of laying in coal for the winter during the summer months.
At first glance one might think that writing that we, the inhabitants of Zagłębie, should lay in coal now for the winter would amount to talking into thin air; for why — many[?] would say — should we lay in coal, when we tread on it all year round? And indeed at first one may think so. But when we look deeper into the matter and begin to consider the question more seriously, we see that this is far from the case, and then we come to the conclusion that we too must provide ourselves with coal for the winter in the present months.
One need not go far: last winter we had a frost, and at that time, when people came to us for coal from every corner of Poland, merchants paid for coal whatever was asked and received coal by the wagonload, whereas we here in Zagłębie could not get a single cartload ("furl") of coal, because it suited the coal dealer better to sell his cartload of coal to the merchant who had travelled in than to bring such into the town; and at that moment one could not get even a little coal at any price — notwithstanding that we are immersed in this commodity on all sides.
This fact shows us how far even we here in Zagłębie need to provide ourselves with coal for the winter in the present months.
Of course we know very well that it is not easy to say that one should make coal stocks in summer for the winter, when it is hard to get through today, when one cannot cover [one's needs] with today's income. Of course in that case things are very, very bad, but this is surely not said of the public at large. There are still people who, with good reckoning and exact calculation, can save up and prepare coal stocks now for the winter, and these people should do so by every possible means, for this would benefit both those who will be provided with the stock — since they would thus have the purchased goods at cheaper prices — and later also even those who did not have the means to lay in a stock in summer, because in the great frosts there would be few private buyers (applicants) among us, so that the small[?] consumer would then have a better chance of getting a cartload of coal bought at a bargain.
We must now begin to live with reckoning; one must strive to be able to calculate well, both in business and in private family consumption. And therefore now is the right time to see to laying in coal stocks for the winter. As far as one is able, one must see to providing oneself with the necessary article, so that one will not have to freeze with one's family in case of great unforeseen frosts, and so that things will not thereby come to a catastrophic situation.
Reckoning, economy and calculation must now occupy the most important position in our middle class.
R. Let.
Ignoramus, Carry Me!

[Będzin — opinion article, charity and society.] Będzin is a town with a good few thousand Jewish souls, and even today, when things are bad and bitter and Jews have nothing to eat, there are still hundreds of Jews who have, thank God, a livelihood, and a solid one at that — and before me lies the report of the "Beit Yetomim" (Orphanage), an institution we make such a fuss of, and yet barely a few dozen have understood that they should support it.
And who are these few dozen? The very same people whose names you find in the financial reports of other institutions, philanthropic as well as cultural — for "TOZ" [Society for the Protection of the Health of Jews] and for the "Talmud Torah" alike, for "Keren Hayesod" and for "Tarbut" alike. The others — and through the head of everyone who leafs through the said report runs a fairly considerable number of names of those others, and they are people with purses, may it be said of all Jews — them you do not see here, not here and not there. They hide in their houses, sunk [?] in their fleshpots and in their heavy interest accounts, hunched [?] over their new portfolios of promissory notes, for still better days, for still more favourable [?] days for them, when one will amass still more money, when one will be still richer, and still stingier, and still more miserly — and still more money-greedy.
And remarkably — and let it be said openly here! — most of the names of these Jews, who consider themselves exempt from obligations towards Jewish society, belong almost all to one and the same stratum: to the so-called "fine Jews" ["sheyne yidn" — respectable, pious householders]. Grievances against the Jewish kehilla they have by the score, complaints — why so and why not otherwise — they will pour whole sacks of them over you; but when it comes to the purse, it's stop, it's: "Little bundle, don't budge!"
It can only be that we are dealing here with a specific psychology. The meaning of the hasid of old was first of all — humble. Today's hasid, into whom the Agudah party [Agudat Israel] systematically drills that everyone beside him is worth a garlic peel — "the peel of the garlic" — and only he, only he is "the top of the mortar" [the cream, the elite], and that thanks to him the world is not destroyed, God forbid — he sees himself [?] as great, he is a whole "ya tebe dam" [Russian "I'll show you!" — a swaggering big shot], a man of lineage, a man of the world. Not to mention when he also has a few groszy in his pocket, when it is warm for him under his pillow — then he surely looks down on the world from above. He does the Jewish people a favour with spirituality, and the others must rescue it with material means. He prays, and the others must... give money.
Yes, from their grievances, from their arrogance and from their locked purses one voice is heard:
— Ignoramus, carry me!
What I Heard, What I Saw

[Zagłębie — feuilleton: sketches from life.] Passed to the press by Ben Amotz.

Then and now.
Once, when the idea of assimilation was still in swaddling clothes, a fierce struggle was waged against it. The Jewish national fighters, with the help of the Jewish press, used their whole arsenal of ammunition against the well-known enemy, against assimilation. And it worked. The national idea prevailed, and the victors triumphed on the Jewish street that:
— Assimilation has gone bankrupt!...
A certain time has passed, new times have come, when the struggle against assimilation is no longer waged; on the contrary, people help indirectly to have the Jewish face covered with a foreign skin and to have other, non-Jewish forms quietly adopted.
In almost all Jewish institutions, especially in the banks, you can drop dead before the clerks do you the favour of saying a word to you in Yiddish... Even in the religious kehillas, where the whole working apparatus is run entirely within the bounds of mikvah and land[?] matters, the invitations to R' Todros or to R' Sperl to come to a meeting about the mikvah are not written in Yiddish.
Our Warsaw Jewish press, too, has lately introduced a [new] spirit: it has started to nurse and pamper the Sundays...
Once, when nationalism was not yet as "strong" as today, the Friday issue was full to overflowing; the best articles, the finest literary works were given in honour of the Sabbath as spiritual food for the Jewish reader.
But today, when assimilation is "bankrupt", the Sunday issues take the top place. In honour of Sunday the finest reading matter is given, in honour of Sunday the Jewish newspapers appear in large formats; several days in advance the glad tidings are announced that "the Sunday issue will have a rich content of feuilletons, articles, stories and the like". Even the "Holy Jew" has been "caught up in the business", and in honour of Sunday the "Tsating"[?] treats its readers to a "children's supplement"...
— You'll see — an acquaintance of mine, a nationalist, tells me — it won't be long before we also prepare fish and cholent in honour of Sunday...
— May he turn out a liar..

True words...
In the Katowice—Będzin train.
A Jewish young lady sitting in the same compartment is reading a newspaper, the well-known hate sheet "Do Czynu"[?]. She reads and laughs, even sarcastically, but it gives the impression that she "takes pleasure" in the pogrom articles.
And one passenger, a non-Jew of all people, was astonished at this and said to the reader:
— Why do you buy this sheet, whose aim is to incite and provoke pogroms against Jews?
— I buy it "dla ciekawości" [out of curiosity] — the young lady answers.
— Is that so? "Dla ciekawości"? You actually take an interest in the anti-Jewish incitement? You want to see how blood libels are spread against Jews? If you, proszę pani [madam], were not so curious, such a rag would not exist at all; the whole existence of this sheet is thanks only to the fact that you Jews are curious...
We, hearing the true words of the Christian, were ashamed; he is right, after all — how many antisemitic newspapers in Poland are kept up with our money; it is a bitter truth. There, where they spit in our face, we run gladly...
———
..Several pupils of Public School No. 4 who take part in the school orchestra come into the editorial office.
And they tell us:
Some of our musical instruments are broken and must be repaired, and we have no funds. That is why we have arranged a concert.
We have no complaints against the local Jewish public. Those whom we approached to buy tickets did not refuse, only at one Jewish firm, from which we had hoped to be properly supported, did we receive a great deal of "honour"..
? ?
Full of confidence, and paying no heed to the pouring rain, we spared no effort ["malaband"?] to go to the "butter kings".
— What do you want?
— We wanted to ask that the gentlemen buy a ticket to the concert we are arranging.
— Out! Get out! We'll find our own way to the theatre box office...

Harder than the parting of the Red Sea.
At the beginning of Magrushever [Modrzejowska?] Street in Sosnowiec, door by door, right next to each other, there are 2 shops of one and the same line of trade.
At each shop "grabbers" are mobilised, lying in wait on all four sides to grab a customer.
At the very entrance stand the shop owners too. Their task is also to help the "grabbers" pull the customer inside, into the shop.
In winning the "positions", it matters a great deal from which side the customer arrives.
— From the east, or from the west side...
And such a scene takes place: from the east side a "Ślązak" [a Silesian] appears; the "grabber" on the west runs ahead and offers him a "sholem aleichem". The "grabber" from the east does the same; both hold on to the "customer", and instead of praising their wares to him, one hears language like this:
"Don't buy there, they'll cheat you, there they draw Christian blood for matzot, the merchants are big thieves"...
This wild scene caused me much grief, and I recalled the words:
— "A man's livelihood is as hard as the parting of the Red Sea"...
———
Two brothers of one father and mother, born one like the other, both walked the straight path. Only in one detail did the two brothers differ.
One — a great rich man, the other — not. He was content with his lot and, as they say, drew his livelihood with honour.
They both died within the space of a month. Here the Angel of Death was "democratic":
— the rich man first and then the poorer one; more precisely, on the day of the shloshim [thirtieth day] the brother who was not rich died..
And what did we see?
At the rich man's funeral: thousands of people, a terrible crush, eulogies from above and below, countless praises, a commotion in town:
— The rich man has died!
And at the other brother's, who also had no lesser merits?
A small handful of good friends escorted him. To the question who had died, I got the answer:
— Some Jew, Cukierman was his name, has died...
In What Light Zagłębie Is Seen in the Eyes of Foreign Visitors

[Article — Upper Silesia and Katowice; economy and travel impressions; series, part VI.] By Israel Kahan.
VI.
Upper Silesia is an astonishingly interesting region. Its capital no less.
It is more than a województwo [province], more than a provincial district. It is Upper Silesia.
One may strongly doubt the claim of the "local patriots" that the "Ślązak" [Silesian] is a distinct "ethnic tribe". But unique he certainly is.
The local German is not quite German, the local Pole is not quite Pole, and the local "native" Jew, too, is kneaded from quite a different dough than the Jews in other communities.
More than anywhere else in Poland's western borderlands — in Poznań and Pomorze — anthropologically interesting types strike the eye here; the broad faces of the "Ślązaks" are strongly Slavic. The historical split [?] between German and Pole is a fact here, which even the most ardent German patriots — I mean the champions of the orientation towards the Reich — do not dispute.
During my visit to Upper Silesia there was still a commotion there over the arrest of the president of the "German Volksbund", Mr. Ulitz, who had been accused by the Polish authorities of high treason.
For all my wish to avoid the drastic political moments, I nevertheless happened to hear something from this side and that side, from these and those groupings. The conversations were restrained, cautious. The bitterness was still fresh, and every word was weighed...
But from the conversations I happened to have with the "extreme" German spokesmen, too, I could conclude that the alarm about a German "irredenta" in the Polish part of Upper Silesia is, even as regards the "theoretical" side, so to speak, mere noise-making with no real foundation. The furthest ideal reaches as far as territorial autonomy.
But this already touches on the complicated and tangled minority problem in Poland — a matter beyond the scope of my present articles.
* * *
The first thing that strikes the eye on coming to Katowice is the colossal traffic, the enormous movement in the streets.
A hodgepodge of languages rings out here. Day after day people gather here from all corners of Poland, and from abroad too: merchants, industrialists, factory directors, commission agents, collectors [? "kolektsyonern"], travellers of every kind and plain "riders" ["forers"]. Amid the Polish, German and English one can also hear, at every step, a pithy Yiddish.
Upper Silesia is the "Eldorado" of Poland in commercial terms. Here, in this wonderful corner rich in nature, one does not feel the countless dismal side-effects of the prevailing economic crisis. The cruel shortage of liquid money is not so acute here, nor does one know of the mysterious "paper bridge" — the bills of exchange — that makes trade in Poland shaky, uncertain, risky...
Other norms apply in trade here, and all doing and working is quite different here — somehow firmer, more secure.
There is something in the local life of the breadth with which Mother Earth has endowed this region — a region that possesses inestimable riches in mineral treasures, as rarely any other place on the globe. Upper Silesia is one of the few places in the world richest in minerals.
The coal mines here are intermingled with other underground treasures: lead, zinc and iron ore. All in enormous, grandiose quantities, and the shafts themselves are of very high quality and of a productivity rarely found elsewhere.
In this very place are found no less than 75 per cent of the whole Polish coal industry, two thirds of the iron industry, and the whole Polish zinc industry. Of the 36 mines that were working in Upper Silesia in the year 1920, before the partition took place, 50 mines with a workforce of 130,000 men fell to Poland's share [so printed: 50 out of 36].
Today the shafts and smelters [huty] work with great intensity, and the workforce employed in them amounts to more than a quarter of a million.
Katowice is the seat of this remarkable region, of the richest Polish province. And thousands, thousands upon thousands of broken and oppressed people in Poland stream here seeking fortune and recovery.
It is the last lifebelt for those who are drowning in the present bitterly serious economic situation in the country.
Katowice counts about 125 000 permanent inhabitants, and just as many visitors from outside are here on average every day. In reality, then, Katowice has a population of close to a quarter of a million. It is the city with the largest, relatively speaking, traffic of outsiders in Poland, and this circumstance naturally does not fail to leave its stamp on the physiognomy of Katowice.
In the numerous, well-kept, large and elegant cafés and restaurants it is hard to get a table; cabarets, variety shows and other night venues prosper here better than in all other Polish cities.
That is perhaps also the only trait that justifies the popular name "the Polish Paris".
* * *
The Upper Silesian województwo is not one of the largest in Poland. It has in all a population of about 1,130,000 souls, that is, much smaller than the Łódź one (2 252,769) and also than the Kielce, Lublin and most other województwa in Poland. But thanks to its flourishing large-scale industry, its inhabitants, as already said above, are economically much better off — firmer, stronger. Expectations of life are different here, the needs of the population — heightened. The poverty and stinginess — in earnings and in spending — that we are used to seeing in the other parts of our country are not noticeable here.
The worker's wage here is on average almost double that in our localities, and therefore the standard of living is broader, I would say — more humane. The worker, especially the urban one, and the middle-class man dress well, live [? "vigt"] decently; "nothing human is alien to him". He can and wants to allow himself it.
And hence — the vast consumption of goods in Upper Silesia, hence — the thriving trade, hence — the general prosperity.
Short Feuilleton.

[Short feuilleton — humour; the economic situation.] Diminuendo...
You surely don't know what kind of word diminuendo is, so I will tell you the plain truth: until yesterday I didn't know it myself either, and only by chance did it become clear to me.
This is how it happened:
Coming yesterday into a company of acquaintances, I ran into an old good friend of mine whom I had not seen for perhaps half a year. I was very glad to see him and naturally asked him at once how he was doing. He answers me briefly: diminuendo.
I was left in a sort of embarrassment: after all, he had answered me something, and what he said I did not understand; to ask again was not proper either — how can a modern person not know a word the other one answers with? So I pretended that I did indeed know what he had answered me, and I ask him further:
— How is your business going?
— Diminuendo — he answers me again.
It was not proper for me to go on asking what diminuendo is, and besides, I was simply afraid to risk repeating such an outlandish word, such a kind of "Targum language" [Aramaic]. So again I acted as if it were not meant for me, and asked another question:
— And how are things with you as to this year's going away somewhere for a rest?
— Diminuendo — again I heard as an answer.
It became very bitter for me that I did not understand "mai ka amri" [Aramaic: what they are saying]; perhaps it was merely a term of abuse... I tried to steer our conversation aside and asked him:
— You are a man of the world, after all, and you come to various firms — so how do things look among people?
— Diminuendo.
Master of the Universe, I thought to myself, You have already dragged me out of so much mud, so drag me out of this mud too.
It occurred to me to ask him what was new with him at the association ["fareyn"].
— Diminuendo.
My forehead was covered with a cold sweat, and the question was already on the tip of my tongue — what is this diminuendo?
God helped, and he asked me how I was doing. A happy thought occurred to me: come what may, I will answer him diminuendo too.
— Is that so? — he says — with you it's diminuendo too? And I thought it was diminuendo only with me.
But what good is that, I thought, when I still don't know what this diminuendo thing is; and I noticed that all the others who were sitting with us — not one of them knew what diminuendo is.
So I made up my mind: "let come on me what will" — lost anyway! If you can't get over, you must go under; if you don't know, you must ask. As it says there: "the bashful one does not learn" — he who is ashamed stays ignorant. And so I did ask him:
— Until yesterday — he says — I didn't know it either, but yesterday I heard how my music teacher explained it to my little daughter in this way:
— Among the low tones there are various degrees: for example, piano is low, pianissimo is lower still, and so it goes lower and lower, and the lowest tone, which the ear can barely still hear, which ends so low as if dying away — that one is called diminuendo.
— Is that so? — everyone exclaimed with one voice — then with all of us it's diminuendo..
Sar shel Esh.
Dr. A. Weissman — The Seduced Girl

[Literature — serial novel.]
Dr. A. Weissman.
(A novel of Jewish life in the Old World, based on historical facts.)
11.
Two older sisters, who already have husbands and little children, are there too; their husbands are still young fellows, very pale, weak, downtrodden, and their little children are sleeping or crying.
And Mania is seized with fright; she is afraid and thinks of the beautiful rich house with the cheerful, healthy people who are always merry there.
When Mania had grown up and begun to blossom, everyone noticed her beauty. The estate steward's (ekonom's) family grew fond of her, and the steward's daughter would often sit with her and pass the time with her. They also began to teach her to read and write.
And within a short time Mania became a real "panna" [a Polish young lady], so that no one could tell at all that she was a Jewish child.
Later still the steward's family took Mania into the rich house and would spend the evenings with her, and birthdays, together with all the guests, who would delight in Mania's beautiful looks, in her speech and in her manners.
And the squires of the surrounding villages, when they met Reb Leyzer Sore's, would say to him:
"Well, Leyzer, you have a daughter fit to hold her own in the greatest squire's mansion."
Reb Leyzer Sore's listened to these words with great pride and pleasure, and afterwards boasted to his acquaintances:
"My Maniechka is an accomplished [?] person; she can measure up [?] to the greatest squire."
In the room where Mania sat it had already begun to grow darker. She went over to the window and looked out into the garden. She tried to drive away the thoughts that had awakened her past, but she could not drive those thoughts away.
"Poor father!" she said with a sigh. "Once he was so proud of his Mania, and now he will have to be ashamed..."
And new thoughts now filled her mind: how would she be able to come back home tomorrow? For shame she would not be able to walk down the street.
"But let it be whatever has to be."
And again Mania thought about the next day, when she would at last be free. Suddenly the door opened and a woman came in with a lamp in her hand.
"You are sitting all alone in the dark," she said. "Do you know, a Jew and a Jewess have been here asking after you; they say they are your parents. It cannot be that such dirty people should be the parents of such divine beauty as you are."
Mania, trembling, jumped up from her seat.
———
Mania threw her arms around the woman and began to kiss her:
"Tell me, dear, you saw my parents? Where are they now? Let them in to me. I want to see them; come, let us go to them."
"God be with you, what has come into your head! I did not see them, I only heard. I beg you, don't tell anyone that I told you. I didn't know you wanted to see them; I was told that you ran away from them as from hell and came to us."
"Who told you such a thing? I love my parents like my own life, and tomorrow I am going home."
"Tomorrow you are already going home?" the woman asked, fixing a pair of frightened eyes on Mania.
"Of course tomorrow, what else? Am I to stay here?"
The woman began to kiss Mania's hands and begged her once more not to tell anyone that she had learned from her that her parents had been there.
The woman left the room, and Mania calmed down a little.
"Surely they will come tomorrow, and we shall go home together. It seems they received my note and found me. Oh, good, honest Jan! He really did hand them my note."
Sister Maria came in with a tray of good food and two glasses of tea.
"You are bored, my child; I have come to you so that you should not be alone."
Mania was glad of the "good" Sister and thought: perhaps she will tell her something about her parents. But the Sister invited her to sit at the table that stood by the window and offered her tea to drink.
The window was open, and a good, refreshing scent from the big garden drifted into the room.
"Just look what a beautiful night it is tonight," the Sister exclaimed, looking out of the window.

General Meeting of the House Owners.

[Będzin — Associations.] The annual general meeting of the House Owners' Association took place in the hall of the local City Council. 150 members took part.
The chair is handed to the president and vice-president Mr. Rubinlicht, who invites to the presidium Messrs. Rider and Piechowicz, Gołąb, Altman, and as secretary Mr. Rechtman.
Before the agenda is taken up, at the chairman's request, the deceased members Trener and Cukierman are honoured by rising.

Tragic Death of a Young Jewish Man.

[Czeladź — Accident.] On Friday towards evening a very tragic accident occurred in Czeladź, costing the life of the 20-year-old Hasidic young man Reuven Heide.
The victim had just been about to go to the mikveh when at that moment a Christian brought a raw hide to sell.
The victim's father wanted to carry the hide into the storeroom, but the son, out of honour for his father, did the work himself and went into the storeroom with the hide; in a corner there stood an empty basket, into which he threw the hide.
But as soon as he came near the basket he was electrocuted and, crying out "Tateshi!" [Daddy!], fell unconscious. A few minutes later the caretaker saw her landlord's son lying without signs of life and called for help, but it was already too late, and the doctor who was called established that Heide had been killed by electric current.
The terrible news spread through the town like lightning, and in every house there reigned a Tisha be-Av mood.
The whole Jewish population of Czeladź took part in the funeral of the tragically killed young man.
At the open grave eulogies were delivered by the local moreh tsedek [rabbinic judge] and a representative of the "Mesivta" in Warsaw, where the deceased had studied.

186 Jewish Boys Went to a Summer Colony.

[Będzin — Welfare and children.] On Tuesday, by the 5 o'clock afternoon train, the first group of Jewish children was sent off in specially prepared carriages to the summer colony "Zagłębianka" in Sławków. 186 children went, accompanied to the site by alderman (ławnik) Goldsztajn, councillor Klajnman and committee member Mr. Wajcenberg.
In the municipal budget a sum of 20,787 has been assigned for the summer colony for Jewish children, for boys and girls.
"Give Me Back My Son" — a Jewish Mother Cries to Zionist Activists.

[Będzin — Halutzim.] Last Saturday night several young people left here for Kielce, halutzim going to hakhsharah [pioneer training]. Among the young people was also a certain Landner, whose mother had tried to stop him from going. And when the mother found out that her son had already left for the train, she went to the station to hold him back from the "dangerous step"..
The other comrades, seeing a danger that comrade Landner might be "taken captive" by his mother, barricaded him in until the train left.
Then the mother turned to a policeman, asking him to telephone Dąbrowa so that her son would be detained there, "because he took money and belongings from her"...
The policeman was willing to do so only if she reported the theft at the police station (komisariat).
The next morning the mother turned to a number of Zionist activists and to the board of "Hashachar", demanding that they give her back her son.
As we are informed, the mother at least took her satisfaction by avenging herself on Moyshe Nadir: in her anger she burned two volumes of his writings...

Sosnowiec: “The Economic Crisis in Poland Is Already Over” — Plenary Session of the City Council

(Sh.[?]) Monday's session of the local city council in Sosnowiec was devoted specially to the general debate on the budget for the year 1929/30.
In the debate the PPS men [Polish Socialist Party] once again — as, incidentally, we have pointed out more than once in the columns of our paper — showed their antisemitic face at certain[?] moments, so that one might have thought that on the rostrum stood not an ally of the Left Poalei Zion but a very great antisemite. Incidentally, the PPS councillor Pal openly enough declared to the Left Poalei Zion that the PPS is not at all happy with the “match”, which in fact was never concluded at all...
———
An hour late, the chairman Pawlak[?] opens the session and announces that there are 2 points on the agenda: 1) election of delegates to the committee for the development of the city, and 2) debate on the budget. The city administration presents a list of the persons delegated to the said committee, among whom is also Mr. Maurycy Rajner as representative of the Jewish population. Councillor Dr. Malarista[?] takes the floor and protests most sharply that a representative of the Jewish population was designated to the said committee without agreement with the Jewish caucus. The President [mayor] replies that according to the law the associations send candidates, from whom the magistracy presents a list, and the city council may accept or reject the proposed candidates. Dr. Malarista takes the floor once more and says: The answer of Mr. President does not satisfy me at all. It is more necessary[?] to come to an understanding with the official representatives of the Jewish population than with lists from an association. I protest most sharply against such treatment of so important a matter.
After the list proposed by the magistracy is adopted by a majority of votes, the council proceeds to consider the budget. The rapporteur Dr. Radkiewicz, quoting official statistical data, stresses in his speech that the economic crisis in Poland is already over, and therefore there is nothing to fear regarding the budget's revenues. Because in previous years there was constantly a deficit, the finance committee could not increase many parts of the budget and had to remain at the “status quo”, i.e. almost as until now. The main income consists of taxes, municipal properties (majątki) etc. The rapporteur ends his report with thanks to the members of the finance committee, who treated the compiling of the budget seriously.
A co-report is delivered by Councillor Wolf (Endek [National Democrat]), who points out that the administration is too large; one sees no [effort] to reduce expenditure — rather it is constantly increased. It has already gone so far that the municipal tax is larger than the state tax.
Next in turn, the Poalei Zion councillor Hamburger delivers a longer speech, listing a number of sins at the address of the magistracy. “We want a secular Jewish school with Yiddish as the language of instruction!” exclaims Councillor H. (On the lips of his Polish colleagues “Iranian” [sic, for ironic] smiles appear.) The speaker announces a negative position on the budget.
In the name of the Jewish councillors' caucus, Dr. Malarista delivers a successful speech, saying: I cannot share the rapporteur's opinion on the present situation in Poland; one cannot rely on official statistical figures, for every statistic is far from the truth. It is nothing but a mistake that the economic situation is a good one. In the new budget there is no initiative whatsoever. The budget is the same as the previous one; neither the city administration nor the committee took the trouble to create anything new; the committee went along the same beaten path. It is a fact, however, that the budget has been increased. As a representative of the Jewish population I wish to point out that although the Jewish population bears a large part of the taxes, its demands have been satisfied in a minimal way. The reason for this is that here they still hold to “kramie jehrejfeh”[?] [phrase not deciphered]. Here “dem Bein”[?] [uncertain words, perhaps a councillor's name] interjects: “You must choose Palestine or Poland!”, to which Councillor Dr. M. replies that this is not the place to speak of it. Finally the speaker reads, in the name of the Jewish caucus, a declaration in the same spirit, which says that although the Jewish demands have not been fully satisfied, the Jewish caucus will vote for the budget.
On behalf of the PPS, Councillor Pal speaks; he declares himself for the budget, and “for that purpose”[?] [uncertain word] he considers it his sacred duty to settle accounts a little with the Jews.
“You Jews,” says the speaker, “demand special privileges, special schools, a special culture. Our club will not support the Jewish demands.”
Further speakers on[?] the budget are the Endeks Michel and President Marczyński, as well as the rapporteur, who answer all the reproaches that were made.
At about 1 a.m. the chairman closes the session.

A Sad Mistake
In Pogoń a policeman noticed at night a person hanging around near a shop and, suspecting that this was a thief, wanted to catch him. When the policeman approached the “thief”, the latter struck him. Then the policeman shot at him and seriously wounded him.
Later it turned out that the “thief” was in fact a madman...

Summer-house crisis.
This year there are very few summer visitors. This has forced the owners of summer houses to lower the rents of their flats, so that at "Czarna Nóra" [sic, for Czarna Góra] and at "Mazanik" [?] one can get lodgings for 100 and even for 50 zł. Prices of poultry and dairy products are also much cheaper compared with other years.
A tragic accident.
While the house of Gleitman—Rosenblum on the Market Square was being plastered, a mason touched an electric wire from which he could no longer tear himself away. Within a few seconds the wire killed him. Before this incident a similar accident befell 22-year-old Elchanan Apman, who was standing on a scaffold and, as he tried to move aside the electric wire hanging nearby, the wire caught his hand. Luckily a Christian saw it, grabbed him by his clothes, pulled him away and saved him from certain death.
A. B.

The Turnover Tax Should Be Levied as a Lump Sum (Ryczałt)

[Będzin — taxes; merchants.]
In government circles the question is very topical of changing the hitherto existing system of turnover tax, so that it should be levied „ryczałtowo“, i.e. as a fixed sum, and of abolishing the assessment commission.
On account of this matter the „Izba Skarbowa“ [Treasury Chamber] in Kielce has sent [?] inquiries to the leaders of the merchant circles, asking them to state their views on the question.
The same inquiries were also received by the district council of the Jewish merchants' associations in Zagłębie, which held a meeting yesterday evening in the premises of the Będzin „Merchants' Association“ and resolved that the hitherto existing turnover-tax system must unconditionally be abolished.
Farewell Performances of Dora Weisman and Anshel Schorr / For 8 Years He Fed on Dog Meat

[Będzin — Yiddish theatre; followed by a short item from Dąbrowa.]
Last Monday and Tuesday the Będzin Jewish theatre public saw Yiddish theatre played. The famous Jewish actress Dora Weisman and her husband Anshel Schorr, author of many theatre plays, created the most beautiful and splendid figures [?], and especially in the role in „Wife and Mistress“ („Vayb un gelibte“).
Dora Weisman is a great dramatic force. Every word, every expression that she brings out of her mouth creates an artistic delight.
Today, Friday evening, and on Saturday night (motzei Shabbat) the artists with their first-class ensemble give two last performances at the „Corso“ („Kor-so“). To be played: today „Stronger than Love“ („Shtarker fun libe“) and tomorrow evening: „Wife and Mistress“, and at the end a one-act play „The Drunken Woman“ („Di shikurte“).
—o—
For 8 Years He Fed on Dog Meat.
[Dąbrowa — crime.]
In Dąbrowa [Dąbrowa Górnicza] there were frequent cases of dogs simply [?] vanishing without any trace.
The police these days undertook a strict investigation, and succeeded in arresting two Christians, who confessed that they had sold the captured dogs to a Christian who lives in Zagórze.
The police went to the address given and found a great many dog skins. The Christian declared to the police that he used to sell the skins, and the meat he has been eating for 8 years already.

In the Light of Facts

[Dąbrowa — town council; article in an open discussion.] In Peretz there is a little tale of how a father, shortly before his death, calls his son to him and explains that he has buried a treasure in the garden, which the son must not take out unless he finds himself in great need. As a sign he laid a large stone there. The son, who lived well all his life and so had no need to touch the treasure, likewise, close to his own death and following his father's example, had his eldest son called to him and told him almost the same words as his late father. But to be surer that his son would find the place where the treasure was buried, he laid another stone there. One stone — he reasoned — might also be found somewhere else in the garden. This procedure of tradition from father to son went on for many generations, and each, wishing to be surer, added another stone on the spot of the treasure, so that in time the treasure was entirely forgotten and people devoted themselves wholly to the idea that one must lay a stone.
Why do I tell this? Because I had a similar impression reading, in the last issue of the "Zaglembier Tsaytung", a series of letters defending the Dąbrowa "Zionist" councillors. I must call out to the esteemed [?] authors of the letters: "Enough stones!" [printed "געגוג" for "גענוג"]. They also tell us something about a "treasure"; incidentally, the defenders even try to take Mr. B. R. under their protection, whereas Mr. L. P. [?] they leave outside. Then, a little material dependence... In political questions other factors decide.
I will put it briefly and clearly: is the conduct of the Dąbrowa Zionist councillors right? Have they fulfilled at least the minimum of their obligations towards their voters? And have they ever made their voice heard at all from the town-council rostrum?
I want to give an objective answer to this. The Zionist Organization in Dąbrowa decided at the time to go to the town-council elections independently. Owing to the intervention of some Zionist activists the decision was changed and a bloc was formed of Zionists, Mizrachi members and some non-party people, since a large part, perhaps the larger part, of the latter had voted for the Agudah list. The first candidate was put forward by the Mizrachi and the non-party people, and was incidentally a member of the Zionist committee. The second candidate was a pure Zionist, put forward by the Zionists. The first made a public declaration that he submits to all decisions of the Zionist committee, although he is the non-party candidate; he wishes, he declared at the time, to figure on a Zionist list.
The day after the election results it was seen that the Zionist councillors could be the "tongue of the scales", since by joining the "BB" club [BBWR, the pro-government Non-Party Bloc] they could create a stable absolute majority in the town council. Indeed the Zionist councillors were at once charged with negotiating with the "BB" club on the matter; but how great was the astonishment when one fine day one learned from the side, not directly from the Zionist councillors, that an agreement had been concluded under which the Zionist councillors undertake to vote for all proposals of the "BB", and as an equivalent the Zionist councillors receive a paper promise that the local Jewish population will be recognised as having equal rights...
And now comes the "activity" of these councillors. Under the agreement the Zionist councillors voted together with the "BB" club; thanks to this the whole town administration was elected from "BB" members, and the four-million budget drawn up by the club was adopted thanks to the Zionist councillors. The only, ridiculous sum of 1,500 zł. that had been provisionally allotted for Jewish needs was rejected in the plenum thanks to our "allies". Our councillors, paying no heed to the betrayal by "their allies", did not demonstratively leave the session, but stayed on in the hall and, like loyal, submissive slaves, went on voting for the proposals of the "BB". It is worth noting that in Olkusz, where there is by no means a larger Jewish population than in our town, the local town council decided to give, out of a budget of one and a half million, a sum of 9,300 zł. for Jewish needs.
The "BB" proposal to incorporate the surrounding villages into the town was adopted thanks to our councillors. What Lutosławski did not live to achieve in the Sejm, the "BB" carried through in Dąbrowa with Jewish votes.
At a town-council session a "BB" member insulted Jewish honour in an unheard-of manner; he came out against the Jewish people with vulgar, base insults, and the chairman of the town council, our [printed "אונזערט" [?]] "ally", did not find it necessary even to stop him. And here, where the voice of the Jewish councillor should have thundered and expressed from the rostrum the sharpest protest against the antisemitic councillor and also against the chairman, our councillors, in servile "ma-yafit" fashion, asked the said antisemitic councillor in the lobbies to withdraw his insults against the Jewish people.
The local tax, from which the old PPS town council had exempted the Zionist Organization, our present ally does not agree to [waive].
And in general we have not yet had the privilege of hearing the voice of the Jewish councillor from the town-council rostrum, whether on general municipal or on specifically Jewish matters. All wrongs done to Jews are passed over in silence, as if they had never happened. One's face simply turns red with shame when we try to analyse the activity of our councillors in the town council. On the contrary, let them show us what they have already accomplished for Jewish Dąbrowa. Have they intervened about a Jewish elementary school? Which Jewish institutions have been subsidised by the magistrate? On the contrary — show us, and we shall be satisfied. If not, you deserve the verdict: lay down your mandates!
Yechiel ben Menachem.

“The Growth of the Jewish Population in Poland”

[Poland — antisemitism; review of the Polish press.] (From the Polish press.)
One might have thought that the “Rozwój people” [members of the antisemitic Rozwój association], who once put much effort and work into making the Christian customer hold firmly to the principle of “swój do swego...” [“each to his own”], i.e. simply to boycott the Jewish merchant and craftsman — had calmed down somewhat. Unfortunately we were mistaken. Not only have they not calmed down, but they are active [?] in the press and in other ways, publicly calling for a boycott of the Jew. Supposedly this little bit of work is done on the pretext that there are too many Jews in Poland. But that is not all; they also know how to tell you [printed “אייך”], and with statistical figures at that, that the Jewish population keeps multiplying and is taking over ever more Christian shops and houses, which — because of bad business — must pass into Jewish hands.
Such a lament — and at the same time an incitement article — we find in No. 182 of “Kurjer Zachodni”.
“In Poland — writes the ‘K.Z.’ — a paradoxical situation is arising. In the whole country the population grows by about 500 thousand a year. Hundreds of thousands of Poles are constantly abroad as emigrants; besides that, great masses of Poles emigrate year after year, being unable to find any work at home. While in this way a fatal situation arises for the Polish population in Poland — we have on the other side a great influx of Jewry (?). There was a wish to organise for the Jews an emigration to Palestine, which (Palestine) was to be their national home [printed “הייס”, read “היים”], and in this way to reduce the number of Jews in Europe. Meanwhile very few Jews go to Palestine, but more come back from there, and they are well off in Poland; they find work and bread here.”
Having settled accounts with the 600 thousand “Litvaks” [Jews from Lithuania and Russia], who have received citizenship and stick [?] in their throat like a bone, the author turns to Jewish trade, which keeps spreading further and further. The “K.Z.” weeps crocodile tears that
“In a few years the streets that have a purely Polish population will look like the Nalewki [the Jewish street of Warsaw]. Trade is concentrated mainly in Jewish hands, but they are not content with that. They are not content with trade, industry and crafts. They even reach the so-called free professions. One finds them ever more in the bar and in medicine. It has already gone so far that some sickness funds in Greater Poland [Wielkopolska] bring in Jewish doctors from Lesser Poland [Małopolska], just as if we had no doctors of our own. In our universities the Jews make up 25 per cent of the students, i.e. one quarter of our future intelligentsia will thus be Jews; in former Congress Poland the theatre, literature and press are already full of them.”
The writer of the Jew-hating article proves in his further arguments how strong the Jewish press is. As “corpus delicti” he cites the recent events in Lwów, during which the Jewish press came out so sharply against Polish antisemitism, especially the foreign press, which carries large articles about the wrong being done to the Jews in Poland, and he arrives at the conclusion:
“To all this one must not close one's eyes; one must stand on guard and awaken society to the fact that in Poland there are newspapers that try to conceal the truth. These newspapers, although they are Polish and printed in Polish, work after all for Jewish interests.”
That is how they keep “standing on guard” and incite constantly, without a pause, against Jews. And this is done precisely by a newspaper in whose list of supporters, if one looked into it, one would surely find many, many Jewish names...
Sh. Sh—kh.
International Youth Rally in Vienna

[Youth movements — “Frayhayt”; Zagłębie.] Today, Friday, at 10 in the morning, the International Youth Rally opens in Vienna, where socialist youth from the whole world gather.
The rally has special significance for the Jewish socialist youth, because the world union “Frayhayt” [“Freedom”, the Poale Zion youth movement] will be represented there by about a thousand members from all the national unions, including from Eretz Israel.
The special train, starting from Warsaw, picked up the participants at all the larger railway stations.
Despite the great expense, 50 members of “Frayhayt” travelled from Zagłębie.

Hygiene and Local Self-Government.

(The terrible sanitary conditions in which we find ourselves. It is high time to improve them.)

At last summer has come too, at last it has also turned warm; but hardly had the sun appeared, hardly had the heat begun to burn, than we already bear the heavy burden on our conscience.

It has become hot in our sweltering Zagłębie, and with it diseases have already begun to spread, which bring very bad results. Contagious diseases are beginning to rage, and under the conditions in which we find ourselves there is great reason to fear serious and dangerous cases.

The doctors have indeed established that in Będzin, for example, there is harmful water in the largest houses, which stand in the centre of town; besides that, we know of many houses in which there is no water at all. Not because no water main has been installed, but because the landlord does not want to make the proper repair the house needs, or does not want at all to give the tenants the same conveniences they used to have. After all, he is not afraid that any of the tenants will move out...

Nor does the municipal sanitary service prosper as it should. It is still too little that some house-owner is fined for not keeping the courtyard clean, or that a policeman writes up a report when a little water is spilled from a balcony; all this is still nothing compared with the general grave hygienic-sanitary conditions in which we find ourselves.

A trifle: in towns that are compactly built, cramped at every step, the inhabitants cannot breathe a little free air, have no opportunity to stretch out and rest their exhausted bones. And the little children, the coming generation, whom we want to see healthy and strong, cannot play under the green little trees, to be breathed upon by the [?] of beautiful nature. Promenade gardens, open to everyone, we do not possess. We cannot even dream what the beauty of nature is, the comfort of resting among trees and grass and flowers and shade. We inhabitants of Zagłębie know nothing of all this, and when the great heat comes there is truly no place to be found where one can draw breath.

And how do our streets look? It goes without saying that one does not allow oneself to wet them; there is dust and more dust on them, and every time the tram runs a wave of dust rises, which settles on the passing population and also finds its way into the open shops and rooms. And the dust rises countless times, because the tram runs every few minutes, besides the motor and cart traffic, which do not clean the air either.

So is it any wonder that there is great fear of dangerous diseases, when dust and dirt reign in our most central streets and no one even tries to see to it that we should somehow be freed from the danger?

The police fine individual citizens for the smallest trifles — why do they not see to it that our self-governments, which have budgets of millions that must be covered by those same citizens, deal properly with this serious question? Why should our self-governments not lay out promenade gardens for their citizens? Why should the streets not be washed properly, so that there is never any dust? And when they do a "favour" once in a while and sprinkle the streets just for a taste, it is done as though one were administering a medicine [?]. Sprinkling, with us, takes on the face of the ridiculous.

With budgets of millions the towns ought to take on a different appearance; sanitary and hygienic conditions ought to take first place. It is therefore no wonder that, in such a sad state, things reach the level of disease.

A self-government must act so that citizens can live in the town, can drink the water, and above all have water at any time they need it, and live in modern hygienic-sanitary conditions.

It must not be allowed that a self-government should look on indifferently at municipal disorder.

It is a disgrace and a grief [?] and a crime when it is permitted to drink water in town that contains harmful microbes, or that while walking in the street one should suddenly be covered with dust. After all, one must not forget that we live in the twentieth century and that we are not in Asia but in the centre of Europe.

Our self-governments demand of the citizens that they conduct themselves according to the rules of hygiene; so let this institution show the citizens how it should look: let it come first and clean the streets and the courtyards for us, make drinking water available, and from this example the citizens will learn and do the same at home.

In any case, the self-governments ought to have more obligation toward the citizens than the other way round.

R. Let.
Must One Hate Jews?

[Article — antisemitism; the United States.]
A former antisemite tells how he became a friend of the Jews.
“Why should one hate the Jew?” — this question is asked by Elias Bens [?], a well-known American writer, a genuine Yankee by descent, a clergyman's son, who descends from no less than the pious “Puritans”.
He poses this question in an article of his [?]. One must admit that both the writer of the article and the magazine in which the article was printed show a good deal of courage in posing such a hard question now. In recent years the American press has avoided the question of antisemitism; it is, one may say, a kind of forbidden subject, which one does not consider possible to debate freely in public.
The writer confesses that for a certain time he strongly hated the Jew because of his specifically Jewish character traits. Like every antisemitically minded Christian, he saw in every Jew the embodiment of a particular type of person whom he hates. He saw in the Jew the repulsive, ugly sides and manners, and he hated him as much as possible.
Little by little, however, he began to think his way into the Jewish question. He began to examine his feelings and to strain them through the sieve of reason and clear understanding, and he arrived at unexpected conclusions. From an antisemite, a hater of Israel, he actually became a friend and defender of the Jews, and now he grounds his friendship for Jews in quite strong logical arguments.
When we see, he says, an Irish policeman who mistreats a citizen, we do not say: “That's how all the Irish behave. That's what they're all like”; but when we see a bad Jew, we think: “All Jews are like that.” This is the greatest injustice we commit. We hold a whole people responsible for one individual repulsive Jew.
Such a thought is no news for us Jews: we have been arguing it for hundreds of years at every opportunity. We have long been fighting, one may say, for the right to have our own outcasts. But it is interesting to hear such words from a Christian, a genuine Yankee, and a clergyman's son into the bargain.
Nor are his other thoughts about Jews very new. But they are interesting as the confession of a former antisemite. He beats his breast with an “al chet” for his former sins, and that is indeed something a little new.
He quotes the words of famous American personalities about Jews and shows that they too thought highly of the Jews as a people.
Thus, for example, George Washington once praised the Jews to the skies and wished them to feel at home in America. To the well-known Jewish editor Mordecai Noah [Mordecai Manuel Noah], John Adams and Thomas Jefferson once wrote very warm letters, in which they expressed a high opinion of the Jews and condemned antisemitism in sharp words.
The writer mentions various historical facts and moments when Jews proved themselves ardent patriots of America. He is convinced that Jews play a great and useful role in the intellectual life of the country. More than other peoples they help America to develop.
Jews, he says, support the most important institutions and enterprises (they even help to build Christian churches in America!..); they develop American dramatic literature, the American theatre and American art in general.
At the time of the Civil War the Jews showed much heroism and righteousness [?]. Many Jews were then raised to the high rank of generals and to other important military posts. The same happened in the last war. The Jews, who are no more than three percent of the general American population, provided more than four percent of the soldiers and officers in the American army in the last war. More than two hundred thousand Jews served in the army. Over three thousand Jews fell in the war. The heroic “Lost Battalion” consisted mostly of East Side Jews and was also commanded by Jews. These were the poor Jewish immigrants, the East Side shoemakers, tailors and peddlers, who displayed such remarkable heroism at that time.
The widespread opinion among Christians that a Jew is a coward is an old wives' tale. A Jew can fight for his ideals just as heroically as a Christian. The Jew, however, is more peaceably inclined and by his nature hates wars between peoples. Therefore Jews play an important role in the movement against militarism, against wars in general.
The fact that the Jew keeps himself apart from the Christian and is more or less nationalistically minded is explained by the writer by the Jews always having had to defend themselves against the [all? — printed “attte”] attacks and persecutions of their own enemies.
The writer regards Jewish lineage with great respect. He holds that we are of far nobler lineage than the highest aristocrats in the world;
We must judge every Jew separately according to his class, to which he belongs, and according to his own character, but not form an opinion about a whole people on the basis of a single Jew.
With this antisemitism one endangers American democracy and degrades [?] American society; [we] must free ourselves from such superstitions and from every sort of racial hatred.
On dilettantism in the Jewish press

In the last issue of our paper there was a notice devoted to the "true" reports that the Haynt brings from its so-called Zagłębie correspondent.
His latest "sensation" from Sosnowiec was, as our readers already know, convenient material for a provocation against the Jewish population of Zagłębie...
Until now we held the opinion of this "great man of the generation" that he possesses a little expertise in his trade — that as a modern melamed he has some knowledge, as they say, of the "small print"; but we were greatly mistaken: only now have we become convinced that the "gadol" is in truth also a great ignoramus.
The "secret" was revealed by Mr. H. Giebelski [?], secretary of the Jewish gymnasium in Kielce, who published the following article in the latest issue of the Radomer-Kielcer Lebn:
"For years now people here have been talking about the lawlessness on the part of certain writers and dilettante authors who have barged into every field of Jewish literature and, without any fear of authoritative control, write articles and treatises on subjects for which they are wholly unqualified. Unfortunately, however, dilettantism has lately become even more embarrassing, because it has penetrated widely into the press, and far more harmful, because the young and the ordinary Jew no longer draw their spiritual Jewish nourishment straight from the proper sources, as in former times, but solely from the Jewish press — and if they feed themselves on dilettante teachings, they remain mistaken for their whole lives..
Recently Haynt No. 124 came into my hands, in which was printed a report by the "special envoy" Ch. Klarman, whom the editors had sent to Kraków for the yahrzeit of the Rema, of blessed memory. The report says "that the Rema became famous through his 'Glosses' (Hagahot) to the Shulchan Aruch and through several of his scholarly books, such as: Yesodei Sifrei ha-Kabbalah, Shem ha-Gedolim (sic) and a commentary on the Zohar. These books — the correspondent says — are nowadays already 'rarities'."
Had such a special envoy, before carrying out his mission, taken at least the trouble to look up some biography or monograph about the Rema of blessed memory, he would surely have known that the Rema became famous not through the books Yesodei Sifrei ha-Kabbalah and the commentary on the Zohar, which were never printed and which the world has never seen, and certainly not through the book Shem ha-Gedolim, which was written a full 200 years later by the Sephardi gaon R' Chaim Yosef David Azulai — but precisely through the books of which the correspondent evidently, poor fellow, knows nothing at all, namely: Darkhei Moshe on the Tur, Torat ha-Olah, Torat Chatat, Mechir Yayin and the Responsa of the Rema; books which are not rarities at all, since they are quite widely popular among Jewish scholars and are reprinted quite often.
And in general, one would like to ask the correspondent how it ever entered his mind that books which became famous throughout the world could become rarities. Can one imagine, for example, that the books of Rashi, Maimonides, Ibn Ezra and the like should one day be missing from the book market and not get a new edition?
But just go and put questions to a dilettante...
It is only a wonder that the editors of Haynt, which regard themselves as such a serious organ, did not check the historical-scholarly assertions of the report, and so lightheartedly exposed the shallowness of their "special envoy"."
H. Giebelski.

How Jews Traded About a Thousand Years Ago

[Jewish history — the Jews and the Leipzig fair; article.]
(A page of Jewish history) by W. Haber. (Specially for the "Zaglembier Tsaytung".)

In the archives of the Leipzig fair there are documents and records that convey a piece of Jewish history over the last eight hundred to a thousand years. They are forgotten memoirs and descriptions which relate with great clarity how our brethren lived among themselves in those years, how they conducted their trade and how they lived with their non-Jewish neighbours.

The first descriptions come from the Jewish historian Abraham ben Jacob, who travelled through many countries and who tells us that already in those times — around the year one thousand by the present world reckoning — Jews lived in great numbers in Merseburg, not far from Leipzig; they traded in grain, flax and various products, which they made known throughout the whole region. Twice a year — after Passover and around Sukkot — they used to gather at the fair near Leipzig, where they would meet their brethren from the eastern lands. They, the eastern Jews, used to bring there not only various products of grain and food but also furs, hides and produce of the soil that could be brought over from those lands.

From that time we know that little by little the roads began to grow dangerous. It simply meant risking one's life as soon as one set out on so long a road, and one by one the Jews stopped coming to the fairs.

It is interesting that with the absence of the eastern Jews from the fairs in the Leipzig area, the Jewish community (the "kibbutz") in Merseburg and the surrounding places also gradually dissolved. The influence of the eastern Jews on their brethren in the West was missing, and little by little they emigrated from those places, little by little they gave up their Jewishness, and by the end of the 12th century not a single Jewish inhabitant is found there.

Only in the year 1268 do we find in the records the Jewish merchants coming to Leipzig for the fairs, and some of them also settled there and became commission agents, conducting the business of the Jewish sellers with the Jewish and non-Jewish merchants who used to come to Leipzig to buy and sell.

Since the roads were then still not safe from robbers, eastern Jewish merchants used to send their goods through trustworthy men to one of these commission agents, who would sell them at the best price. These commission agents appear here for the first time in the history of commerce in general. The chronicle of the Leipzig fair records with pride that in all that time not a single complaint was made about a dishonest commission agent.

Only at the beginning of the fifteenth century did Jews again begin to come to Leipzig with their goods themselves, although even then such a journey meant putting one's life at risk, and many merchants never came home from it. Robbers lay in wait above all for the merchants returning with the money they had taken in.

Nevertheless we find in the chronicle the names of great Jewish merchants from Poland and Russia, who used to come to Leipzig twice a year and were esteemed as the greatest traders. R' Moshe Libel and Aharon Berl of Mezrich brought thousands of furs and hides to Leipzig every year and paid weighing fees of about six hundred "Schock" of groschen a year. A Schock is sixty groschen; 21 groschen made one silver gulden.

It is also interesting which goods were brought to Leipzig from Poland and Russia. The records are quite exact; the following were brought: leather, furs, flax, oil, sugar, honey, almonds, raisins, pepper, cinnamon, cloves, spices, saffron, ginger, caraway, wine (especially Romanian). One sees from this that the Jews brought not only goods that grow in the eastern lands but also all kinds of goods which they had bought up in various regions. A large part of the Jews travelled for half a year at a stretch to various fairs in various countries, bought up all sorts of goods, and afterwards carried or sent them to Leipzig to be sold.

Only in the fifteenth century did the dangers almost cease, and then the stream of Jewish merchants to Leipzig began to grow and to increase from fair to fair.
Things That Happen — Married Life or a Get.

[Zawiercie–Częstochowa — family life; divorce.]
Last week a couple presented themselves at the office of the Częstochowa rabbi to carry out a divorce (get).

It was he who wanted the get — the husband, Szlama M., a young man from Zawiercie, who had brought along a mother and a brother and also, of course, the "woman of valour" herself. She, however, did not want any get until he provided her with a few guilders to live on.

From the talk of the husband, his brother and above all the mother-in-law, the following emerged:

Some 5 years ago the couple married in Sosnowiec. Before the wedding canopy they had not seen each other. Only while standing under the canopy did the pious bride raise her eyes and look at her destined one. And at that very moment the thought flashed through her mind: No! She would not live with him.

No sooner thought than done.

Right after the ceremony, when the couple was to be led to the "golden broth" [the wedding chicken soup], the bride vanished.

It goes without saying that the wedding feast never took place, and the in-laws went home with broken hearts and hungry stomachs.

A few weeks later the bride was found and brought, against her will, to her husband, who had wed her according to the law of Moses and Israel.

But she kept insisting that she would not live with him.

So a long time passed: she put on a wig, ran the household, but a wife to him she was not.

People intervened and tried to convince her that this is not how decent folk behave, that it is against the way of the world — but nothing helped. The young woman agreed to everything, only she could not be a wife to him...

Then her troubles began.

His whole family, the father-in-law and mother-in-law (who deal in greengrocery in Zawiercie), inflicted every misery in the world on the woman: they gave her nothing to eat, did not let her sleep in a bed, and so she lived on the scraps thrown out into the yard and slept in the attic.

Last week they came to the Częstochowa rabbinate (in Zawiercie one cannot give a get, because there is no river there) and all of them began to shout with one voice: A get! A get this minute, unless you want us to beat her to death, for we cannot bear to watch the suffering of the young man, who supposedly has a wife and yet no woman.

The poor young woman stands trembling all over, and before the dayan R' Yosele even had time to see about reconciling the couple, the three thugs fell upon the woman, tore the wig off her head, the coat, a shawl, threw her to the ground and tried to tear the stockings off her feet.

The woman wailed and screamed. The judges intervened, and the thugs ran off with the clothes in their hands, shouting that they would kill her if she would not accept a get.

The woman was left half-naked in the rabbi's office and poured out her bitter heart over her dark fate.

A while later a woman, apparently an acquaintance of the unfortunate wife, gave her money for a ticket, lent her a coat to cover her body and took her back to Zawiercie, to her husband, with whom she does not want to live as God commanded — and to go on suffering from her father-in-law, mother-in-law and brother-in-law and from all of them together.

N. L. P.
