The Faithful Wife

[Humorous feuilleton.] (Feuilleton). By M. Mandelzon.
God preserve and protect us, do you hear, from having a faithful wife — one who always looks you in the eyes, who watches over[?] you at every step and trembles over you as over a small child; such a wife, do you hear, is millions upon millions of times worse than a wife who doesn't love you, who isn't faithful to you and who, apart from your money, simply has no business with you at all. With such an unfaithful wife you are at least a free bird, because whether you have a wife or you don't, at least meanwhile you have a life to tell about. But with a faithful wife — what? Again "Puczikl" [a pet name], once more "Kotkele" ["kitten"], eat this, drink that, don't smoke[?], walk slowly, turn up your collar! And if you happen to be a bit worried, or you eat without appetite, right away: woe is me! You're ruined, poor thing! You need a doctor, as sure as you live! And at once she already has tears standing in her eyes.
And that is precisely the story with the doctor and with the dacha [summer cottage]! She, my faithful wife, insisted of all things that I go to the doctor, for the following reason: lately I somehow don't please her; somehow — she says — I am too pale, too weak. My eating isn't eating, my sleeping isn't sleeping, and altogether I'm somehow "run down", and she feels I am losing my strength. So of course I burst out laughing at my wife's idea, and I start proving to her that on the contrary, I'm perfectly healthy, and how healthy! A real hero — and the proof: I have the strength to endure such a long dead season without a groszy of takings, with so many different taxes and a great sea of protested bills. But my faithful wife won't be talked round, and she sticks to her own: I must absolutely[?] and without fail, this very minute, go to a doctor — which I had to promise her and carry out at once.
When I came into the doctor's, he told me, as is the custom, first to sit down, then to lie down, to undress, to breathe in, breathe out, to cough a little; he palpated me, tapped me, counted, measured and looked into my eyes, and finally he asks me: what is my occupation? I answer him that "by trade" I am a merchant, but lately, since trade lies deep in the ground, I occupy myself with writing and filing appeals, with knocking on the doors of various "urzędy" [government offices], with running around the banks about prolonging my promissory notes, about buying out little protested bills; I also run around after little interest-free loans [gmilus-khesed] — that, I tell him, has lately been my occupation.
The doctor hears it all out and asks me again: well, and do you have a wife? I answer him as truly as can be that, thank God, I have a wife, a faithful wife, who crawls right under my fingernails, who worries over me day and night, who doesn't let a speck of dust fall on me, and even caresses me, admonishes me and teaches me — truly like a real faithful wife. At this the doctor smiles, happy that he has caught the diagnosis, and says to me quite sternly: that I must "natychmiast" [Polish: immediately] go off to fresh air, that I must throw away all my commercial occupations, that I must leave the wife at home and that I absolutely must go away alone to a forest, to rest from my trading and from my wife, because things are in a bad way with my nerves; they have come badly undone, and if I don't calm them in time and don't tame them, it will go quite "schlimm" [badly] with me.
So I come home from the doctor and I tell my faithful wife that the doctor told me that I am very nervous[?], that there in my head the nerves have come unscrewed and are running riot, they are giving orders there like real hooligans[?], and that if I don't go "natychmiast" to a dacha, I'll go kaput with my whole bundle of bones and it will be lost for ever and ever.
When my faithful wife hears what a state her husband, poor thing, is in, she turns green and yellow, pale and deathly, tears start to pour from her as from a fountain, and she begs me for mercy: that I should have pity on myself, on her and on the whole family, that for God's sake I should obey the doctor and this very day go off to a summer residence; she will of course travel with me too, she will nurse me and look after my sick health. I answer her: all right, so be it — if I must go, I must; but the doctor expressly ordered that just as I leave all my business at home, so I must leave you too, my bright little dove, and that I must travel alone, precisely alone.
"What? Alone you want to go?" — my wife's faithfulness flares up — "May my enemies not live to see it! I'm to send you off alone and leave you, sick as you are, without me? Have you gone mad — may it befall my enemies — or what?"
"Whether I'm mad or not," I answer her calmly, "that I don't know; but that I'm already close to it, the doctor told me expressly, and that is exactly why he ordered me to be alone in a forest, without all the head-spinning troubles and without the faithfulness of a wife, because both things are harmful to my sick nerves."
Clear words, it would seem, which a not-faithful wife would have understood at once and agreed to at once; but my wife, may she live long, won't hear of any of it; she sticks to her own and keeps arguing that a husband, such a sick, ruined person as I am, must not be left alone; that without a faithful wife at his side my life isn't worth a groszy, and that if he goes, she must go along, and no other way.
So we have been wrangling for several weeks now. I argue mine and she argues hers; I hold with the doctor that a faithful wife is harmful to the nerves even in a forest, and she holds to hers: God forbid she should leave me, so nervous a man, alone without a faithful guardian such as she is to me. And meanwhile I have nearly become a ball of nerves already; I feel that any moment now I'll stop being a human being, any moment I'll go mad — and she still won't let me go alone.
And as you can indeed see, I still haven't gone to a dacha, though the heat burns and roasts, and whoever can, or must, is already lying in the lap of nature enjoying himself, while I and my faithful wife are still haggling, and God alone knows when we will come to terms. Only, dear people, if one of these days you meet me running around the streets in a very nervous state, you should know that it's all because of her — because of my faithful wife.
The Seduced Girl (11)

[Serialized novel — "The Seduced Girl", installment 11.]
Dr. A. Weissman.
(A novel of Jewish life in the Old World, based on historical facts.)

And it really was a beautiful, clear blue sky, and the moon, still young in the first days of the month, was strolling across it and seemed to be hurrying on an urgent errand.

— After tea we will walk a little in the garden, — said the sister. — There is nobody there now, and on such a night I always love to walk in the garden, when the trees whisper quietly to one another and praise God for His beautiful night, for the moon and the stars. Do you know, my child, that everything that lives in the world sings praise every morning and every evening before Him who lives forever? Even the trees and the grass and everything that grows.

— And even the river, — exclaims Mania, delighting in the beautiful night. — At home in our village there flows a little stream, and on the beautiful moonlit summer nights I used to love to come down from our hill and run there to the stream, where I would sit down on a stone on which the village women wash their laundry. It was quiet there; I would then hear the sweet voice of my father, who prayed the evening prayer [maariv] with a quiet tune, and it used to seem to me that the stream was also praying maariv together with my dad...

— My dear child, — the sister embraced her and gave her a kiss, — you have a rarely pure soul, which can reach with its prayers all the way to the heavens. True, rivers and seas pray and praise God.

For several minutes they sat quietly and did not say a single word to each other.

— On such nights our village is so beautiful, — Mania says suddenly. — Oh, how I would like now to sit by our stream, which surely speaks and prays on such a beautiful night. Tomorrow at this time I will surely already be there, yes, Sister Maria?

— Yes, my child; come, let us go for a walk in the garden.

— No, on such nights I love the stillness. It is so good here, so quiet; it is a pleasure to sit by the window and look outside.

In the great stillness there suddenly sounded a beautiful, heartfelt singing of prayer. — Oh, how beautiful! What a hymn of praise! The sweet melodies melt the heart, — Mania rejoiced.

— That is our sisters praying and praising the Name of Him who lives forever. And the sister knelt down, folded her hands and with glazed eyes began to whisper quiet words.

The singing was heard ever louder and louder and then lower, until it fell completely silent; then Sister Maria stood up and said:

— Now I have prayed for you, Mania, to Him who lives forever, that He forgive you all your sins, that He soften your heart, so that you may go on the good path.

— Am I then so sinful? — asked Mania.

— You are innocent, and therefore you do not understand your sins. If you understood, you would now be praying together with me to God to forgive you. This evening I did not go with all the sisters to the church, because I wanted to pray together with you to His dear Name; when I knelt, I did not see in you any need to kneel down too before Him who lives forever.

— Sister, what are you saying? I am a Jewish child, after all.

— You are a sinner, Mania.

At that moment the older woman came into the room and said:

— Our eldest sister asks you to come to her at once.

— Surely my parents are waiting for me there, — Mania said joyfully.

Sister Maria and the woman took fright, and all three went out of the room.

———

When Mania had been let into the room of the eldest sister, "Irina", Mania [sic; probably Maria is meant] went with the woman into a separate room.

— Well, did you tell her that her parents were here asking about her?

— Yes.

— What impression did it make on her?

— She was very glad and wanted to run to them; I asked her not to tell anyone that I had told her about her parents.

— And where are her parents now?

— They have gone back; they were assured that their daughter is not with us.

— And what if they do not believe it and come with the police?

— The police have not yet crossed the threshold of our monastery.

— In any case she will have to be taken away from here; there is danger here.

— Have no fear. If, God forbid, the danger comes near, we will hide her in our cellars, where the devil himself cannot get to. Be calm: such a dear child as our future sister Mania we will not let go.

— Well, we must go in to our elder sisters, to see what they are doing there, and you stay in your room; perhaps you will be needed.

In a large, richly decorated hall, with old paintings and many holy pictures on the walls, by an olive-oil lamp with flames of various colours, sat a woman of about sixty with grey, silvery hair, but thanks to her fresh-coloured face and straight figure she looked much younger than her years.

She sat and talked with Mania so sweetly and sugarily that Mania, who at first had not felt at home and could not find a place for herself, calmed down and answered all her questions calmly.

— Tell me, my child, do you at least know how fortunate you must count yourself to be here together with us under this roof, which protects us from all evil and from the sinful world? Many envy you; not everyone is worthy of it.

— You are still a pure, innocent little angel, and it would be a pity if you were to leave us. Just tell me, my child, what brought you to us?

— Ludwig seduced me, and how I came here I do not know myself.

— I know a little of the reason for your coming to us; I heard about you long ago. You say that Ludwig seduced you? But you are not a little child, to be taken by force. Ludwig only wanted to make you happy: what would have become of you if you had stayed with your poor parents, who would have married you off as unhappily as your unhappy elder sister?

— Who told you all this? — Mania asked in astonishment.

— And what did you think, foolish child, that anyone who wants can come in to us? There are princely children here, whom we do not accept so easily into our house of God. I must tell you that I have heard much good about you, and one such as you would have been the dearest sister to us; to my greatest sorrow I learned today that you want to go back home.

— Yes, — Mania brought out in a choked voice.

(To be continued.)
The Strict Father

[Short story — by Osip Dymov.]
Osip Dymov [printed "Osif Dimov"].
(A story).

David Shleyman was a hard man who never smiled; a very honest man, and an old-fashioned one too, living just as his father and his grandfather had lived: the same views, the same notions of life.

Besides his wife, his daughter Ida lived with him at home — a young, pretty girl with thick golden hair and a laugh that rang as if two wine glasses had been clinked together.

"What are you laughing so loudly about?" her father would ask her. "What has happened?"
"Nothing, I'm laughing."
"But there must be a reason."
"No reason. It's a beautiful day today, the sun is shining."

They could not understand each other — the strict, serious father of the old generation and the cheerful young daughter of today.

"What a strange father I have," she thought. "He doesn't see at all how lovely it is when the sun shines."

"What a strange daughter I have," he thought. "The sun shining is enough for her. She understands nothing."

And he went on being silent.
And she went on laughing.

The mother, of course, sided with the daughter, but was not against the father either [printed "negn", for "kegn"].

"Your father," she would say, "is a different kind of person, not like us; he has his worries."
"Why do you say 'us'? You too are serious and sad."

The good mother answered:
"I am sad because I know that I must leave you soon."
"Don't talk like that, dear, sweet Mother — you are young and strong."
"Young I am, but not strong; I feel that I have not much left to live. That is why I don't laugh the way you do. But I too laughed once, before I got married."
"Does that mean Father took your laughter away from you?"
"No, not Father — life. That is how life is, my child. Quite different [printed "nants", for "gants"] from what you think. But now you are young — laugh, smile, be happy."

The good mother fell ill. David Shleyman spared nothing to make her well again — the best doctors, the best nursing — but nothing helped, and she died.

"Be happy, my child," she said to Ida before she died. "Obey your father, he is a good man. But if your happiness should force you not to obey him, do as your heart tells you."

After his wife's death David became even sadder and more silent. Dark and heavy was the air in the house.

"The poor girl," people said, "now it will be very hard for her. Such a cheerful, such a merry little bird — to be kept in a cage. Her mother left her too early."

But a young heart forgets quickly.

And Ida began to laugh again as before — almost as before, a little differently and for a different reason [printed "agder", for "ander"].

She got up in the morning and it was a rainy day, yet Ida laughed all the same.

"What are you laughing about?" came her father's old question.

But now she could no longer answer as before:
"The sun is shining."
No, she said:
"Yesterday I met a young man."

Her father raised his heavy, silent [printed "shvaynndike", probably "shvaygndike"] eyes to her and asked:
"Well, so what?"
"Nothing."
"What about this young man? Is he so funny?"
"No, the opposite," Ida answered.
"I don't understand — then why are you laughing?"

Ida could hardly answer her father:
"I laugh because for me it is the same as the sunshine."

No, she could not say that; her father would certainly not have understood. And she herself, though she felt it so, only understood it later.

Yes, she understood it later. In the house it was dark, and the air in the room pressed down like a heavy stone. Her nature, her youth, her heart called her to joy, to life...

"What is the matter with you? The maid told me that you come home late," her father said to her.

Ida was surprised. She had thought her father would not be so calm when he learned of her coming home late. She had expected him to shout at her, to forbid her to come late, and she was ready to protest. But heavy, stone-heavy, were his words; he understood what it means when a young girl comes home late every evening, and her eyes shine, and she cannot fall asleep, and on getting up the next morning she laughs out loud, and even though it is raining and snowing she keeps thinking that the sun is shining and the blue sky hangs over the whole world?

So days, weeks, months went by. And indeed the sun — the true, the real, the white, the golden sun — began to shine in the blue sky that hung over the whole earth. Spring came, and...

And Ida stopped laughing.

So it sometimes happens with a girl left in the world too early without a mother: such a girl makes spring for herself too early — in winter.

Then the real spring is no longer spring for her. It is rather autumn ["asyen", from Polish jesień], fall — when the grain ripens, when the fruits grow heavy and hang down from the branches of the trees and are about to fall.

Ida changed, became serious, silent, quiet: now she resembled her father.

Dark, heavy, stone-heavy became the atmosphere in the house.

David Shleyman knew nothing, noticed nothing. He was busy with his business, withdrawing from life further and further.

One night he woke up in astonishment. He heard his daughter Ida crying in her room.

He went in to her and saw her wringing her lovely hands. She was not surprised that her father came to her in the middle of the night.

"Father!" she cried out, and her golden hair flared wildly around her tear-stained face.
"Father, kill me, do with me what you will, but I cannot keep silent any longer."
"What is it? What has happened to you?" he asked, and sat down beside her on the bed.
"You have always been strict with me, with my late mother, with the whole world. At home it was always sad and gloomy; you never understood me and you won't understand me now either."
"Perhaps I will after all. I don't know what you are talking about."
"I love someone, and I am soon to become a mother."
"How so? What are you saying — you're not even married?"
"No, but what am I to do, Father? I want to take my own life; better that you kill me."

And she lowered her pretty little head as if she really expected her father to kill her.

David Shleyman was silent for a long time; then he spoke in his heavy, cold voice:
"We will find a way, my daughter. The child can live quietly with us; if it has no father, it will have a mother and a grandfather."

And for the first time Ida saw a smile on his face.
"Der Kokh-Lefl" ["The Cooking Ladle"] — Lucky Me, a Summer Holidaymaker

[Humour — the "Der Kokh-Lefl" ("The Cooking Ladle") column, humour page; a satirical poem about summer holidaymakers.]
"Der Kokh-Lefl" ("The Cooking Ladle")
By Ben Amotz.
Dedicated to the dacha-ladies, the "straw widows" and the plush troubles.

Lucky me, a summer holidaymaker [letnik].

I'm a holidaymaker now, and lucky too,
From every side there wafts a smell —
I sit and "kheshe" [?] my sides
And catch some "fresh air".

That's taken care of by the nanny-goats [kozy],
The cattle and the goats;
The air presents me with "wild roses" [polne róże],
And in the hammock I sway.

What do I care for the bailiff [komornik]!
What are worries, woes and blows to me —
I leave them all for the thieves
In my flat — whole bundles of them..

Here I'm a real big shot,
Sitting "in the secret place" I sit
And make myself of everything
And of everyone a joke.

My wife writes: "Eighteen-thirteen" [?],
She opens her mouth wide..
So I say: "Go to the Finance Minister:
He says, after all — all is well."

And if the advice doesn't help,
I show her — the rain is falling,
"Neretegish" [unclear word] will surely come,
And all will be "all right" again...

"If only it would happen already,"
She says — "may it happen fast:
If instead of a holidaymaker [letnik]
I saw you as an aviator [lotnik]..."

I sit.. and sweat, lucky me,
Growing grey and old from woe,
And the rain is pelting down hard,
And I shiver — I'm cold!
Yankl ben Flekl.
Dacha Letters

[Humour — the "Der Kokh-Lefl" column; comic letters between a wife on holiday and her husband in town, in Yiddish larded with Polish.]
My radiant Itshe Ber!
I hasten to inform you [spieszę się donieść] that I and the little company have arrived happily [szczęśliwie] at the summer resort [letnisko]. The place [miejscowość] here is fabulous [bajeczna] — you should see it yourself — a forest [las] of nothing but conifers [igły]. The forest has just one drawback: it is a bit dark [ciemny], and since I am nervous [nerwowa], the forest ranger [gajowy] accompanies me with his rifle. Our Felia and Zoshka have also already found a well-matched company [dobrane towarzystwo], great lads [morowe chłopcy].
Yesterday I sunbathed in the sun [opaliłam się na słońcu]; I have become brown like a fried cutlet [brązowa jak smażony kotlet]. The landlady's son, a handsome [?] gentile lad, wants to teach me to swim; he says that within [w przeciągu] one lesson I will be able to do various water positions [wodne pozycje].
On Thursday night there was a strong thunderstorm here; a thunderbolt struck an old tree and smashed it to pieces. May I hear the same from you.
Your faithful wife
Sheyne Reyzl.

(From him to her).
To my wife, may she live long, Sheyne Reyze
(called Piękna Róża ["Beautiful Rose"]), may she live.
Your little letter gave me palpitations. Such an idiotic postman — why does he knock at the door, and I thought you had come. I tell you, we nearly gave up the ghost from fright..
Your news that you are sunbathing and that you look like a fried cutlet delighted me very much; only one thing I ask of you: that you should deal with decent men, who eat cutlets with a fork..
On the other hand, that the landlord's gentile lad is teaching you to swim causes me great distress — how can it be? How does a nervous Jewish woman go into the water, and with an uncircumcised man to boot? What will happen if you catch something in the water — God forbid, you could still get inflammation of the joints [zapalenie stawów]; these inflammations are very fashionable [modne] now.
And now, radiant Sheyne Reyzl — I mean Piękna Róża: forgive me for writing you little today; I wanted to write you a great deal, but ever since I read the well-known speech at the Czechowicz trial I have had, may it not happen to you, a dizzy spell. May I hear the same from you for ever and ever [immer und ewig].
From me, your contented husband, who hopes to see you like a fried cutlet,
Itshl Ber.
Passed on to the "Kokh-Lefl" by Honig-Foygl ["Honey-Bird"].
Advice for Zagłębie Textile Merchants

[Der Kokh-lefl — humour; Zagłębie — merchants; Będzin — town hall and kehilla.] Since the Zagłębie merchants have only air in their pockets these days and, on account of this, will not be able to go away this summer to dachas and spas, we offer here a series of instructions on how one can visit the world while sitting in Zagłębie.
For healthy merchants.
1) Do you want to travel to Eretz Israel to visit the Western Wall? Then go and try to collect a debt — and you will be told: "Talk to the wall."
2) Do you want to [?] travel to the Balkans? Tell a friend of yours to lend you an interest-free loan (gmiles-khesed) — he will surely answer: "Talk Greek to me" [i.e. I don't understand you].
For sick merchants.
1) Does one of you need a massage? Then turn to the Będzin city president...
2) Whoever needs a natural sweat should come to a session of the Będzin city council and hear an "Agudah" councillor speak Polish — it will drench you in sweat...
3) Do you suffer from nerves? Sit yourselves down in the Będzin municipal bath-house and wait for a bathtub.
4) Do you need injections (sprinklings)? Turn, in rainy weather, to the "Jaduszka" [?]...
5) Whoever suffers from insomnia should get himself a place to sleep in the Będzin gmina (community) offices.
A Packet of Tax Reliefs

[Der Kokh-lefl — humour; Będzin — town hall and taxes.] (Obtained by our councillors.)
Thanks to the fact that the Jewish councillors all unanimously approved the budget for this year, the magistrate has decided to grant the following tax reliefs to the taxpayers.
First of all, men up to 6 years of age and women up to 7 years will be entirely exempted from tax (also from the investment tax), without distinction of nationality.
Also exempted will be: all inmates of the madhouses and all landlords whose houses are on the plans.
Reliefs will be granted as follows:
Those who pay punctually will pay no interest.
At auctions (licytacje) neither the debtor himself nor cooking pots will be sold.
For the convenience of the taxpayers, the magistrate will make efforts so that they can ride by tram right up to the magistrate.

[Der Kokh-lefl — humour; Będzin — town hall, youth life.] In connection with the fact that the magistrate is putting up several more electric lamps on the Third of May Square [Plac 3 Maja], we have received the following protest from a group of young people, with the request to publish it.
We, the undersigned, protest most sharply against the Będzin magistrate, which with its reactionary reforms wants to disturb our freedom, our pleasure, our being together..
By increasing the number of lamps on the New Market our life is being darkened, and we will thereby be compelled to become wanderers [?] again on the Małobądz meadows.
Down with the electric lamps!

To the Dacha-Goers

[Der Kokh-lefl — humour; satirical poem, summer dachas.] (Prophetic.)
I am sent to you by God, —
He saw that you are "crazy",
He saw that you run and fly
To dachas with a light heart,
And do not reflect and do not consider
What the end of it will be, —
So He heard your pain,
And His pity awoke,
And He brought me to you,
He said to me: go and warn,
Let whoever can save himself,
And whoever does not obey is lost,
And you — you have done your duty: —
So know, unfortunate ones, know
What dacha life means! — —
For days and weeks you will run
Through forests looking for dachas,
And they will show you "villas" —
Pigsties and hen-coops (kotuchy),
And they will set you prices
Swollen like the Alpine mountains..
You will argue, protest,
You will weep — and you will pay!
Afterwards, when with luck
You have moved into your lodging,
You will little by little discover
All its fine virtues;
That at night a crawling [of vermin] runs about,
And the crickets sing hymns,
That the walls, of wooden boards,
Have frightful cracks,
That when the cold wind blows
A tekiah gedolah — it's unbearable;
That in the windows and in the floors
Big holes stand open, —
It is a wonder that the crickets
Have not yet run away...
You will jump and you will dance
To warm up a limb,
See [?] revenge on the bedbugs
Who freeze along with you!
Wrapped in six woollen shawls
You will tremble with cold,
The sun will go into mourning —
Be covered with black clouds,
But God's wrath is not yet
Appeased by this!
He will turn on the taps
Of the water-reservoirs above,
And a dreary cold rain
Will slap at your window-panes,
For days and weeks the rain will
Pour, splash as from barrels,
And the mud on the roads
Will grow deeper, bigger,
And the roof will start to weep
Over you and your bundle of money
That you have buried here
In a strange forest by mistake;
Laid up with colds, with wife and children
You will sneeze "by the minyan",
And look whether it isn't getting milder,
Whether it isn't stopping pouring,
You will stand pensive by the pane
And look silently into the murky void
And wait, like Noah's dove,
Whether the Flood is not yet dry.
And you will go to the neighbours
(A pinch in the cheek so the colour stays)
And tell them that you have
A villa — a gift from God,
With windows and with new stoves,
And it is warm — a delight,
And it is lovely and bright there —
But better that you keep quiet,
For no one believes your word,
And everyone knows that you are lying, —
With paralysed hearts you will
Return to your hut,
Where the oakum from the walls
Hangs like a matted (kołtun) beard,
And console yourselves, half-fainting,
That the walls at your neighbour's
Have even less substance,
And the roof is more broken...
You will want to make coffee —
The "Primus" will be broken;
You will go to light the lamp —
There will be no kerosene in it, —
Thus you will constantly
Bathe in this world —
But God's wrath is not yet
Appeased by this:
He will stop the rain
And seemingly show you the sun,
You will at once be enraptured
And go for a stroll in the forest —
Then He will lure you into the forest
And send mosquitoes upon you,
Like enraged wild beasts,
Whole peoples, whole swarms,
That will fall upon you
Like the wild cannibals,
And you will run away home
With hands and feet bitten thick.
And you will murmur "Ah, how lovely it is"
And — scratch, scratch yourselves in silence.
And on Friday evening you will sit
And remember those times
When you still had a home
And were still equal to other people
And ate hot lokshn
And browned [?] fat tsimmes,
And now you have cold coffee
In the hunchbacked "Primus",
You will curse your "villa"
And send God a fervent prayer:
"When You wished, You kept
Jonah from the whale's belly,
Daniel from the lions' den —
So help us too, dear God,
Help us out of the dacha-room"
But Heaven remains shut,
And the wall hears your prayer;
And Satan stands and laughs
And rubs his hands with joy:
Thousands you have paid,
Dachas you fancied!
So hold on now to the gift,
Freeze and sneeze till Rosh Hashanah!"
Ma Yafit.

[Będzin — local news; page heading "What is heard in Zagłębie?".]
On Tuesday afternoon, in Cukerman's house at Kołłątaja 24, the 73-year-old Azriel Pfeffer committed suicide by hanging himself in the attic.
The suicide — so we are told — had lately been in a bad state; apart from suffering from headaches, he was unhappy with the surroundings in which he lived. To have his sad situation eased, he applied to the heads of the "Moshav Zkenim" (old-age home) institution to be admitted there. But the efforts were of no use, and seeing no improvement in his situation he decided to commit suicide. To that end he went up to a small attic room, where he hanged himself with a wire.
The tragic event shocked everyone, because Mr. Pfeffer had worked hard all his life and earned his living honestly.
Seeing again in old age

[Będzin — local news, medicine.]
The 88-year-old Szymon Hirsz Fiszel came into our editorial office and told us the following interesting fact, which ought to serve as an example to the young Jewish doctors...
The old man happened to be at the local municipal outpatient clinic. There Mr. Sukiennik, assistant to the eye doctor Mr. Ul, noticed the blind Jew, took an interest in him and asked him how many years he had already been blind. On his own initiative and without any payment, Mr. Sukiennik examined the old man's eyes and found that if the eyes were operated on, the blind man would be able to see again... To that end Mr. S. prevailed upon the eye doctor Mr. Ul to examine him as well, and after the examination the old man was taken to the hospital in "Sheltse" [probably a misprint for Kielce], where he was operated on, and the 88-year-old saw the bright world again.
— Write about them, begs the man who can now see, my good messengers..
The budget found favour with the voivode

[Będzin — municipality, budget.]
Last Friday the municipal budget, the ordinary and the extraordinary, was sent to the Kielce voivode.
To defend the budgets, the vice-chairman of the city council Mr. Jakub Erlich, alderman Director Błażejewicz and, from the magistrate, Secretary Mr. Riedel travelled there.
The voivode approved the budgets with satisfaction and did not change a single item.
Kehilla representatives look after kashrut

[Będzin — kehilla, kashrut.]
For several years in a row now, the Jewish children sent by the magistrate to Busko have been eating non-kosher food there, and nobody reacted to it. A few weeks ago alderwoman Mrs. Ratner proposed at a city-council meeting that the city administration should see to it that the children sent to Busko receive kosher food.
The kehilla administration too began to take an interest in the matter and delegated alderman Mr. Gerszon Rechnic to Busko to acquaint himself with the situation — in what ways a kosher kitchen could be arranged for all the children who are in the institution there.
Mr. Rechnic, however, did not find the chief director in Busko and had to postpone the question to another time.
Don't leave a window open, because a "night guest" may slip in "to spend the night"...

[Będzin — crime.]
In the flat of Mr. Jehoszua Ratner on Czeladzka Street, a thief got in through an open window on the first floor and began pulling off the bedding.
The "experiment" woke Mr. Ratner, who caught the "guest".
At the police station the thief defended himself, saying that he had not intended to steal but "wanted to spend the night, because he is homeless"...
The Saturday storm and downpour in Zagłębie

[Zagłębie — storm and disasters.]
On Saturday night at 10 in the evening a terrible hurricane swept over Zagłębie, causing damage and also claiming human victims.
In Sosnowiec the storm wind blew down Barański's circus during the performance. A terrible panic broke out among the audience, everyone wanted to reach the exit; nevertheless nothing serious happened — only hats, shoes and the like were lost.
On Prosta and Wiejska streets electric wires were torn down, killing several horses, and the carter was injured.
On 3 Maja Street the tram mast began to break, and because of this tram service was interrupted for several hours.
In Strzemieszyce lightning struck a house on Długa Street, killing a Christian and injuring several people who were in the room.
The storm wind uprooted many trees.
A tragic accident happened on "Stara" Street: the wind tore the roof off a house, and in the process the electrical wiring was torn. A 4-year-old child stepped on the wires and was killed on the spot.
Poalei Agudat Israel conference

[Zagłębie — parties, Poalei Agudat Israel.]
On Sunday a conference of the Pa"i (Poalei Agudat Israel) groups in Zagłębie took place in Żarki, chaired by Mr. Snicer. The conference, attended by 175 members, was held in a hall because of the rain. The chairman of the district committee, A. Jedwabny, opens the conference, and after a presidium has been elected, greetings follow. Then Messrs. Snicer, Brezner and Jedwabny report on various questions, and a series of resolutions is adopted.
The Jewish Girls' Gymnasium Receives State Rights

[Sosnowiec — education.] On Sunday evening the general meeting of the parents of the Jewish girls' gymnasium was convened. All in all 6 (read: six) people came to the meeting, apart from the board. It pains the heart to see with what abstinence Jewish parents treat such an important Jewish institution, which, thanks to its high level, has already received — from the coming school year — state rights.
The meeting is opened by the president, Dr. Meladysta, who thanks the few persons who have come to the meeting, because a year ago not even such a number came and the meeting could not take place then. The board therefore had to go on conducting affairs without a general meeting.
Mr. Katz is elected chairman of the meeting; he invites Messrs. Gliksman and Binkowski as assessors, and as secretary Mr. Kromołowski. The minutes of the previous meeting are read out by Mr. Buksbaum, and the agenda is taken up; it consists altogether of 3 points: 1) reports 2) free motions and 3) elections.
For the general report the floor is given to the president, Dr. Meladysta. Before Dr. M. proceeds to the report proper, he devotes, with tears in his eyes, a few warm words to the memory of Dr. A. Perlman, of blessed memory, who until his last days helped and worked for the good of the Jewish gymnasium.
The speaker brings in a motion, later adopted unanimously, that, in order to honour the memory of the deceased properly, the school shall bear the name of Dr. A. Perlman, and also that the future board shall begin efforts to build its own building for the gymnasium. The whole memorial speech is heard by those present standing.
From the report given by Dr. M. we learn what a thorny road the Jewish gymnasium has gone through during the 7 years of its existence. When the school was taken over there was not even any furniture or school equipment; gradually, with slow but sure steps, the school, thanks to the board together with the headmastership, reached such a level that after the last inspection the Kraków Curatorium granted the gymnasium state rights. The speaker mentions with satisfaction that the rights were obtained not through submission or concessions at the expense of the Judaic programme, but because the gymnasium stands at the proper height. In conclusion Dr. Meladysta mentions with bitterness the abstinence on the part of Jewish society, among them also the parents whose children attend the school.
The cash report is given by Mrs. Jungster, who points out that the school has at present 150 pupils, of whom many do not pay the full monthly fee but enjoy reductions. It also turns out that despite the subvention from the kehilla the school has a deficit of about 15 thousand złoty.
On the cash report a discussion develops, in which Messrs. Warman, Buksbaum, Dr. Meladysta, Director Dr. Widerman, Dudkiewicz, Fürstenberg and Mrs. Jungster take part. After the discussion the general meeting grants the outgoing board a vote of discharge (absolutorium) and proceeds to the elections, which give the following result:
Dr. Meladysta, Fürstenberg, Reznik [?], Mrs. Jungster, Abramczyk, Buksbaum, Warman, Kromołowski, Mrs. Langer, Gliksman, Szpigelman and Advocate Dr. Proks.
At about 1 a.m. the chairman closes the meeting.
Protest against the Harriman Concession

[Sosnowiec — economy.] As we have already written, the government has granted a concession to the American Harriman company, which wants to electrify all of Poland and supply electric light at a cheap price.
The industrialists come out against the concession, pointing out that the concession will bring great harm to the economic situation in the country.
On Monday a special session of the local Chamber of Commerce took place, which adopted a resolution to protest against the concession project.
Municipal Budget Approved

[Sosnowiec — municipality.] The local city council has approved the budget in the third reading. On the motion of Dr. Melarysta [= Meladysta?], the "TOZ" receives a subsidy of 2,000 zł., "Maccabi" 2,000 zł. and "Malbish Arumim" 1,500 zł.
The dentist Rotsztajn demanded that Jewish newspapers and books should also be available in the municipal library.
To this the alderman (ławnik) Dąbrowalski [?] declared that if the Jewish readers demand it, the proposal will also be taken into consideration
The Yahrzeit of Dr. A. Perlman, of Blessed Memory

[Sosnowiec — community.] (Sh) This month falls the yahrzeit of our late kehilla president, Dr. Abraham Perlman, of blessed memory. In this connection memorial services will take place in the local schools. A solemn mourning academy will also be arranged.
On the day of the yahrzeit the unveiling of the tombstone will take place at the Sosnowiec cemetery
Concerning the drawing-up of the programme, a meeting will take place this Saturday night (motzei Shabbat) in the "Mizrachi" school.
To the Shomer Colony

[Sosnowiec — youth movements.] (Sh) On Sunday a group numbering 23 Shomrim [members of Hashomer Hatzair] left for the Shomer colony, which is located in Kauli [Kozy?] beyond Bystra. At the railway station a large number of parents, comrades and acquaintances gathered and saw the Shomrim off. The farewell took place with full pomp. Despite the heavy rain the whole group lined up in a row in front of the station, where the "commandant" Chlewicki received a "report" from the head of the group, Pergricht [?]. With cries of "Hazak ve-ematz" (Be strong and of good courage) the train with the cheerful young Shomrim departed.
—o—
The Performances
The performances of the well-known actress Dora Weissman and of Anshel Schorr with their ensemble have passed with great success.
Saturday afternoon and Sunday evening — farewell performances before their departure for America.
A Jewish Debate in the City Council

[Dąbrowa — municipality.] On Monday a session of the city council took place here. At the last point, interpellations, a very interesting "Jewish" discussion developed.
Councillor Bauszar [?] (PPS) interpellates: the Zionist Org. at the time applied to the magistrate with a request to assign a subsidy for its Hebrew-Yiddish people's library, and since the magistrate turned it down [?], the same organisation applied once more to the plenum of the city council, and notwithstanding that the letter was sent as early as 31 May, the chairman has to this day not allowed it to be read.
To this the chairman, Dr. Piwowar, gives the following answer: I have received the said letter and will by no means read it, because I hold that it is not desirable from our Polish state standpoint to support Jewish cultural institutions such as a library.. Councillor Janasa [?] (Endek): I do not understand at all what is going on here; the said letter is also signed by Councillor B. Rechnic, so why does he not interpellate, but only a representative of the PPS?!
Councillor Bauszar: as is known from the Jewish press, the Zionist Org. called upon its two councillors, and at the request of the Zionist Org. the PPS councillors' club interpellated.
Here one expected that a Jewish councillor would worthily take under his protection the honour of Jewish culture, and exactly the opposite happened. Councillor B. Rechnic takes the floor and declares that "the Zionist Org. stands on the Polish state standpoint, and the request letter was not read with my consent.
This exasperated the Jewish public in the gallery, which reacted against the conduct of the Jewish councillors.

Unknown thieves broke into the flour shop of Mr. S. Sztajer, from where they took out flour and other food articles worth 10 thousand zł.

It Would Be Laughable...

It would be laughable — if it were not so sad. We mean, of course, the stories one hears in the street about the various ways in which taxes are dunned from the public. We know stories from olden times, which grandfathers [?] tell their grandchildren — stories of lords who had to collect rent from their leaseholder, and of the tricks people used to devise in order to collect the rent. It will be very sad if from our times, too, similar stories remain that outdo even the inventions of the past.
A story is told that a bailiff (tax enforcement officer) came to a baker to demand overdue taxes. There were times when people had no bread, and then the bakers were rich. Today, when there is bread, the bakers are paupers. But the bailiff does not want to know about that; he demands what is written on the paper. But the baker still has nothing — so they take whatever is in the house. And when there is nothing at all in the house either, they take what is in the oven.
The bailiff came precisely at the moment when the bread had been put into the oven. Having come at the hot minute, he indeed did not let it get cold — or, more correctly said [?], did not let it get hot: he seized the dough together with the raw loaves that had only just been put into the oven. In vain did the baker beg him to let the bread finish baking and take it afterwards. The bailiff has no time; he must make use of the hot minute and take away the cold dough.
You will ask: what, for instance, does one do with raw dough? Who buys it, and whom can it serve?
A second story: a woman is dunned for a full thousand złoty of overdue taxes. They dun her, and there is nothing to take. But a bailiff finds a way. He lay in wait for so long that he caught the woman with five kilos of strawberries. It goes without saying that such a fortune, when caught on a woman who owes a thousand złoty, is confiscated. To establish the treasure, witnesses are brought, a protocol is drawn up, a droshky is brought, an auction is held — and for the goods one gets a full six złoty, but the expenses incurred came to nine złoty...
Such stories are told in the street in great number. One does not want to believe them; one wants to laugh. For how is it possible to take raw dough, do damage to someone else and get nothing out of it oneself? A squire of the old days could have done that — the kind for whom money played no role at all and who only wanted to carry out his whim; but how can a bailiff do it, who is collecting a debt and must bring in either goods or money? What kind of goods is it from which nothing at all can be got? Had the damage done to the baker been credited against the debt, it would still have been only half a misfortune. But the damage is not credited — so [?] what good is the harmful joke?
Or take the story of the strawberries: to whose account will the three złoty lost on the transaction be charged? Probably to the account of the state, since its people calculated badly. The question arises: why should the state, that is, all of us, suffer a loss only because the bailiff is a poor accountant?
Many such questions could be asked. But what is the use of asking? It would be laughable if it were not so sad. People are reduced to destitution, ruined for no reason — how can one laugh here?
Ch. Landau.
The Budget of the City of Sosnowiec

After a series of sessions, the Sosnowiec city council has adopted the budget for the year 1929/30.
In the new budget we find several items for Jewish institutions which, thanks to the intensive work of the Jewish "Koło" (council caucus), have been increased compared with the previous budgets. In the social welfare department there are the following subsidies: "Dobroczynność" (charity society) 11.800 zł., for the Jewish hospital 20 thousand zł., summer colonies for Jewish children 3,968 zł., half-colonies (day camps) 1,364 zł., and for "Malbish Arumim" (clothing the naked) 500 zł.
For the first time subsidies were granted to the society "SAZ" [?] in the amount of 2 thousand zł., to "Maccabi" — 500 zł., and to the society "Evening Courses" — 500 zł.
Comparing last year's budget, which was drawn up by the then-ruling socialist majority (P.P.S.), with this year's, we see that although the Jewish demands were perhaps not entirely satisfied, they have nevertheless been increased fourfold. Last year the total sum of Jewish subsidies amounted to 10 thousand zł., and in the current budget they amount to some 44 thousand zł.
Needless to say, much of the credit for the Jewish institutions being properly subsidized belongs to the Jewish ławnik (alderman), Adv. Dr. Fruks.
On this occasion we cannot pass over in silence the fact that the Endek "Kurier Zagłębia" came out, in connection with the Jewish items in the budget, with a leading article [?] pointing out that the greatest success in the current budget was achieved by the Jews. Under the title "What did the Jews get for granting support in forming the city administration," the "K. Z." writes, among other things, the following:
"We are fully aware that the best-situated materially in our city are the Jews. Among Jewish families there is surely no such poverty as prevails among Christian families. (!) Meanwhile, in the department of social welfare (in the budget) the Jews have been given proportionally more, and the same is the case in the department of public health protection. Why the separation? Why the privileges?"
The author quotes the budget items precisely, making a parallel comparison of the Jewish and the Christian subsidies, and concludes that
"summing all this up, one must state that, in return for granting help to the "B. B." club (Non-Partisan Bloc for Cooperation with the Government), the Jews made by no means bad use of their help in forming the ruling majority, to which the "B. B." club also agreed, to the express detriment of the Polish population."
It would already be high time for the people of the "Kurier Zagłębia" to come to terms with the idea that when a certain part of a city's inhabitants pays into the municipal treasury, over the course of a year, enormous, hard-earned sums of money, it deserves at least to have its just minimal demands satisfied.

A Clarification
Concerning the resolution of the Zionist Organisation in Dąbrowa to withdraw its councillors from the city council.
We ask you, Mr. Editor, to give us space in your esteemed newspaper, which is the generally recognised tribune for Jewish public problems here in Zagłębie, for the following question, which goes far beyond the bounds of a party. We do so with great eagerness — although Messrs. L. Puterka and B. Rechnic have not the slightest duty to consider the question and to argue about it — so that the Jewish public in Dąbrowa may become thoroughly acquainted with this important matter.
A week before the publication of the resolution of the general meeting of the Zionist Organisation in Dąbrowa calling on our councillors to lay down their mandates, there was printed in Zaglembier Tsaytung no. 25 a letter from the Jewish councillors, who relate that the reports in the Zaglembier Tsaytung simply agitated and aroused bitterness among the local Jewish population, how do they know that? Who expressed such things, when and where. And really, why do you deserve this? Is it because you admit that Mr. Kicki "blurted out" the words "smarkaty żydek" [snotty little Jew] at a plenary session of the city council? Is this how national Jews, Zionists, write? "Blurted out" — why the devil must you take under your protection the antisemite who always "blurts out", and whose Jew-devouring comparisons have long since become simply a byword — is this what Zionism teaches? Is this what we have learned from the struggle that modern national Jewry has had to wage for decades now from public tribunes, in order to preserve our national pride and to fight for rights for our own distinctive Jewish interests!
The councillors, Messrs. Puterka and Rechnic, apparently do not want to part with their "little seats", and to this end have mobilised around themselves individuals from a few minyanim, who figure as the so-called "public opinion".
The "Mizrachi", which signed a licorice-sweet, obsequious ("ma-yafit") "little letter to the editor", ought really to have been answered — but unfortunately we do not know their address. The "Mizrachi", which attached its signature, would after all have voted for Mr. Rechnic even if he had figured on a Bundist list (woe, woe to such a reputation!). The "Merchants' Association" is also a weapon with which one wants to armour oneself — on the contrary, why does Mr. Rechnic not give a report to the members of the "Merchants' Association"?
The upshot of the clarification is that our councillors are accused:
1) Of not wanting to come into contact with the board of the Zionist Organisation.
2) Of having sold themselves to the B.B. [the Non-Partisan Bloc for Cooperation with the Government, BBWR] without getting anything at all in return.
3) Of not having demanded any subsidy for the national Jewish institutions
4) Of not having reacted to grave insults from antisemitic councillors against Jewish honour.
5) Of not having found their bearings when voting on matters that may affect the Jewish population (enlarging the city, the telephone matter).
6) When some board members then tried to draw our councillors' attention to the letters that the Zionist Organisation sends via the city council secretariat concerning subsidies — Mr. Rechnic replied with the words: "Don't bother us with nonsense!"
Because of the deeds enumerated above — we, with the consent of the voters and in the name of the Zionist conscience, call for the second time on Messrs. Rechnic and Puterka to lay down their councillors' mandates.
The Board of the Zionist Organisation in Dąbrowa.

Responsibility toward the citizens.

(The crisis in the country and the increasing of the citizens' expenses.)
Everywhere and on every occasion, the leading circles take pains to show that all is well and fine with us, that we have ample room, and that nothing could be better.
Had these words been said just like that, they would have bothered no one; but when, on that account, people allow themselves to make larger expenditures, that is already dangerous — it begins to smell of mortal danger.
Whenever and wherever budgets are being drawn up, we are told that everything in the country is progressing, that business is flourishing, that the factories keep on developing, that the workers and artisans have work up to their ears, and therefore — therefore one may allow oneself anything in the world: one may make budgets of whatever kind one pleases, one may enlarge them as far as possible, and the population will pay it all with a light heart.
When the local self-government in Będzin was dealing with the budget, the Christian representatives said that the Jews in Będzin are well off and that they all have a lot of money, and therefore a large budget can be made.
Now that a budget of the Sosnowiec self-government has been drawn up in Sosnowiec, it was once again shown that everything is in the best order and that "the economic crisis in Poland is already over," and therefore one may allow oneself larger budgets and the citizens can pay them. And by the very same system other budgets are also being made, which increase the expenses of every citizen.
But one ought for once to do a little calculation with a clear head. Let people finally look around at where we stand in the world; let them consider honestly and sincerely whether one can afford to make, everywhere, so many heavy million-złoty budgets — can the population really pay all this? And is it indeed paid without compulsion, without resorting to distraints?
The economic situation in Poland is good — how does one know that? In what does this goodness express itself?
It is known that the situation in Poland is anything but rosy [?]; moreover, the crisis keeps growing and is taking on ever more serious forms. This is noticeable in the commercial world, in the credit institutions, to which, instead of bills of exchange that have been redeemed, protests come back; it is also noticeable among the artisans, who have no work; workers too are being laid off, and there is a large number of unemployed people without employment.
The truth must be told: Zagłębie and Upper Silesia are, in this respect, the most fortunate. Our corner is one of the richest and liveliest corners of Poland, so that here among us the crisis prevailing in Poland has until now been felt only very little. But now Zagłębie and Upper Silesia too are beginning to dance along with the Polish crisis. Now here too workers are beginning to be laid off, the artisans are ceasing to have employment, and the merchants cannot meet the obligations they took upon themselves.
We have grown used to seeing the small percentage of the well-to-do, those who occupy the top place in every field, and by that yardstick the general citizenry is measured here, and the conclusion is reached that everyone is well and fine, that all have work and employment.
One does not see, or pretends not to see, those who languish in darkness, those who do not stick their heads out, those who have no garment to put on, and those who go hungry in silence. The broad, wretched masses of people, who lack the courage to show their heads, do not catch the eye and are not seen in the country; they lie hidden away in cellars and attic corners; and the people of the middle class who have come down in the world do not show their faces in the bright light.
Let the people who imagine that everything with us is flourishing and developing so beautifully try to carry out a survey; let them study the situation of the general body of citizens, and then they will come to the conclusion that things are not at all as rosy as they superficially present them.
If there is in the country a certain number of well-to-do people, and even a certain number who have a livelihood, one still cannot ascribe this small percentage to the entire population.
Can [?] one get far by shutting one's eyes and saying: I see nothing, everything is fine and lovely and good? Whom can this system benefit?
We hold that the question is a serious one; it is in any case one of the most important current questions, which must be dealt with as quickly as possible; otherwise the consequences may be anything but favourable, for its aftermath [?] is often very, very dangerous.
After all, nothing good can in any way come of persuading oneself that all citizens are well off, and on that account burdening them with taxes beyond their strength.
One must, once and for all, render a clear account, so that the population should not reach the terrible point [?] of beginning to sink, which usually [?] leads to the abyss — and then there is no remedy any more, then one can no longer rise back to the former situation, to a situation of existence.
Let this question not be regarded as a trifle, let it not be taken lightly; let it be remembered that if one remains indifferent in this matter, the results for the country and for the citizens may be very, very serious — very, very grave in their responsibility.
R. Les.
Greetings from Home, from the Land of Israel

[Land of Israel — letter from Palestine; Będzin natives in the Land.]
(From our special correspondent).
I have only just returned from an excursion of several days through the most blooming and most fertile region in the Land of Israel, namely the "Jezreel Valley", which makes a great impression thanks to its beauty and natural riches.
The Jezreel Valley, which until not long ago was an area of pestilent swamps and fever (malaria), is today once again an area of blessing; the valley, which lay waste and desolate for two whole thousand years — is today once again covered with broad green fields and trees that stretch for miles and miles in length, so that today it is the pride and crown of the Land of Israel.
On the way to the Valley and Haifa I was awaited by a Będzin landsman, Mr. Avraham Szniaur [Shneur], who came to the Land of Israel with his mother, brothers and sisters a few years ago and settled in Haifa. Mr. Shneur commands the three languages of the country: Hebrew, English and Arabic, and works at the "Hadar HaCarmel Council[?]", in the municipal office on Hadar HaCarmel, where he holds a post as correspondence clerk.
In the workers' moshav Nahalal, whose principle rests on individualism, i.e. each family works the land on its own responsibility, but is at the same time obliged to "self-labour" (avoda atsmit) and to mutual aid (ezra hadadit) — I visit the settler Mr. Śliwka[?] from Dąbrowa [Dąbrowa Górnicza], and his wife Perl Tenenbaum, who worked for many years as a nurse at the Tel Aviv "Hadassah". Her post was taken by her younger sister Leah. During my visit to Nahalal I also met the former active co-worker of the one-time Będzin "HeHalutz", Miss/Mrs. Miriam Rotenberg, and her husband Mr. Yaakov Śliwka[?], who lives in Haifa.
From the conversation with my former landsmen I learned about the way of life in Nahalal and about their situation, with which they are very satisfied. Mr. Śliwka[?] works about a hundred dunams of land, which he received from the Keren Kayemet, and with funds from the Keren Hayesod he has set himself up with a farm of dead and live inventory [equipment and livestock].
In the large kvutza Ein Harod, whose name comes from the spring of water that bursts out of Mount Gilboa — I visit Mr. Moshe David Malec, who came from Będzin to the Land of Israel 9 years ago. 5 years ago Mr. M. joined kibbutz Ein Harod, whose principle is to engage in all branches of economic life (agriculture, industry) in order to satisfy all needs with its own production.
Ein Harod is rich in many waters, which were not exploited, and flowing freely they flooded the tracts of land, thus causing veritable[?] swamps and malaria, until a few years ago. When the Jewish workers went up onto the pestilent soil — they set about cultivating and draining the life-endangering "bitzot" (swamps), and they succeeded to such an extent that the spring in Ein Harod, which for thousands of years was a source of curse, is today a nest of life, fertile fields, woods and gardens. This was accomplished by the diligent Jewish hand, by sweat and sacrifices that were invested in this soil.
Mr. Malec, who grew from an "avreykh"[?] [young yeshiva scholar] into a manual worker and a "chaver"[?] [kibbutz member], works by day in the field and in the evenings on literary and scholarly articles, which he publishes from time to time in the literary supplement of the local workers' newspaper "Davar". Mr. M. is content with his collective life, but he is troubled by the fate of his brothers and sisters in the Diaspora. Learning from me that Będzin, his "native town", works diligently for Zionism and for the upbuilding of the Land of Israel, he rejoiced, believing that our work for the final goal of Zionism will at long last be crowned with success. Mr. Malec sends greetings to his parents, brothers and sisters, comrades and friends.
M. Hampel.
The Misled Girl (12)

[Literature — serialized novel; installment 12.]
Dr. A. Weisman.
(A novel of Jewish life in the old world, based on historical facts.)

"Yes, you say? But it is already too late."
"Too late —" Sania [sic; i.e. Mania] jumped up from her seat half-dead, and at once remained sitting as if in a faint.
"Don't be afraid, my dear [printed 'mayn nisht', a misprint], that we won't let you go; if you don't want to stay with us, we will not hold you. But it is our holy duty that whoever finds himself under our roof, we must protect him with all our strength from every misfortune that awaits him. And you, my child, are faced with the greatest misfortune if we let you go to your parents. Do you know, my child, what awaits you with them?"
"Love, the love of parents."
"You are greatly mistaken. Your parents will torture you, they will tear the beautiful hair from your beautiful head, they will burn out one of your eyes and burn your body with red-hot irons, because that is what the rabbi will order them to do."
Mania suddenly felt faint and fell off the chair; they began to revive her.
———
The next day Mania did not leave her room all day; she felt weak, and Sister Maria did not leave her side.
Only toward evening did they go walking in the garden again. For a long time the two of them walked that evening [printed 'ugt', a misprint for 'ovnt'], and the sister did not stop describing the terrible, cruel torments that awaited Mania from the Jews and her parents when she returned home.
"I don't believe," said Mania, "that they will do me harm at home. My return will surely [?] be a great disgrace for my parents, but they will not do me any harm."
But the sister told her about a Jewish girl who had also wanted to go back home, and afterwards came running back to the convent beaten and battered.
"Is she here?" Mania asked.
"Oh, no, she died long ago, and she lies in our cellars, among other graves of holy sisters."
Mania shuddered.
"There is a cemetery here?"
"For hundreds [?] of years. The holy graves protect our convent from evil and harm. You have not yet seen our convent. We will show it to you later. People come to us from distant regions, to the holy graves."
"And where are they?"
"Didn't I tell you — in the cellars —" and she pointed toward the side where Sania's [sic; Mania's] room was.
"Where? Here, under the building where my room is too?" Mania asked in terror. "There are graves under my room? I won't be able to sleep any more; I beg you, send me home," she pleaded with tears in her eyes.
"How can you travel? You are not well, and certainly at night we won't let you travel."
Footsteps were heard, and Sister "Maria" said to Mania:
"You see, here come our sisters." Sister "Irena" passed by, and after her several younger sisters with lanterns in their hands.
"See, Mania, they are going for your sake; they want to show you our convent — not everyone is granted such a privilege. It seems our elder sisters have taken a great liking to you."
And talking thus she took Mania by the hand and drew her along after the sisters with the lanterns.
Mania, out of fear and respect for the elder, followed unwillingly.
As they walked, the sisters whispered with their lips, as if saying prayers; by some buildings they stopped and crossed themselves.
But by one great wall, next to a large door forged with old, green-rusted irons, they all stopped and knelt.
Afterwards, when they had risen, one of them opened the lower door with a large bunch [?] of keys, and the company began to descend the stairs into darkness.
Two sisters held Mania by the arms and lit the unfamiliar stairs before her with a lantern.
Passing a few rooms with stone floors, Sister Irena called Mania to come closer to her — they would show her the most precious thing in the convent.
They all entered a large, long and wide cellar with many small windows; the whole stone floor was set out with large and small black coffins, some with gilded and silver ornaments.
"You see," said Sister Irena, "here in this coffin lie the dead bones of a saint who suffered for the Christian faith. Her holy bones were brought from Rome. Together with her they also brought the irons with which she was tortured.
In this coffin lies the skull of the first sister, who founded the convent; and the sisters who conduct themselves here well and piously may be granted the privilege that their bones lie together with the saints."
After this explanation they all went out of the cellar quietly, step by step.
When Mania came out of the cellar, she was told that someone from her village wished to see her.

From the Polish Health Resorts (Impressions of a Visit): Goczałkowice

[Goczałkowice — impressions of a spa visit; feuilleton.] By Ben Amotz.
There is a whole contingent of people — learned rabbis, "neogim" [sic; probably geonim, great scholars], etc. — who spend the course of their lives in small places, cut off from the noisy world where every minimum is blown up and advertised, and every good-for-nothing reaches power thanks to his noisiness, and a "world" talks about him and praises his deeds.
Places, too, share the same fate. Many natural treasures exist on the globe, and Poland too possesses beautiful natural regions which one speaks of quite rarely. The top place is taken by the places that have risen to the rank of first-class "firms" and have been crowned as the wondrous places where all kinds of ailments are cured...
Among the less popular health resorts in Poland is also the spa of Goczałkowice. This spa can compare in many qualities with other Polish health resorts such as Krynica, Szczawnica, Truskawiec and others. Goczałkowice is small in quantity, but in quality it possesses all the things a health resort needs: good air, a "park", beautiful promenade avenues, a dancing, a little wood — even a small one, but splendidly grown, and above all — dark, so that the little forest has many secrets to tell...
Nevertheless Goczałkowice has little luck: the number of guests is not large, and the main reason for this is, in my opinion, that the spa is close to Zagłębie, and the little wives who need a "cure" avoid the place, because for "living it up" Goczałkowice is not suitable: a small place, there are few guests, everyone knows what goes on at her neighbour's... and as soon as someone has the mere thought of sinning, it becomes known at once and the whole world is already ringing with it.
Here, for example, a year ago a young wife from Zagłębie took a fancy to "have some fun", and "all Będzin was in an uproar" [lit. "went on wheels"]. In the larger resorts, by contrast, where there are no such "terrible eyes", "life" goes on more normally: the wives are "faithful", and their husbands need only send money so that their "sick" wives may have the real "cure"...
Let us leave the "seer of hidden things" in peace for a while and devote a few lines to the spa establishment and its effects.
———
In 1856, at a depth of 700 metres, the "Solanka" spring [brine] was discovered, which contains 3 per cent salt and other healing substances such as iodine, bromine, lithium and radium.
The excavations were made for the purpose of opening a bath establishment here, and already in 1862 the first season was opened, and in that year 262 patients already came to take the cure.
Over time, thousands of patients suffering from podagra [gout], sciatica, fatty heart, chronic skin diseases, paralysis and women's diseases have been cured in the bath establishment — completely or to a certain degree.
The establishment is properly set up; care has been taken that the guests may enjoy a range of newspapers and periodical magazines in their free hours (except Jewish ones, naturally); in the park an orchestra plays twice a day — not a first-class one, everything suited to the park...
There are also several European-built pensions there, among them the Jewish pension of Mr. S. Goldwasser, which in the short time of its existence has made a name for itself not only among Jews but also among non-Jews; the latter, among whom are also known antisemites, are delighted with the tasty dishes in the "Żyrawskin" [sic; name of the pension?] pension.
In the Jewish pension there is also a dancing, which is active no more than every Sunday, when guests from the surrounding area come here on excursions and, in passing, snatch a little dance in the evening hours.
The dancing in miniature also cheers up the female sex; in the joy of the moment one is not particular about who the dancer is, as long as one dances, because the dancers reckon that what they enjoy on Sundays must last for a whole week; only if a "sick" dacznica [female summer guest] becomes "dancing" on an ordinary Wednesday, she has the option of dancing in the yard of the peasant cottage [chałupa].
The spa "distinguishes" itself by one more, very important detail. The "distinction" consists in the fact that "here no illnesses are common"...
A "proof" [?] of this is that in Goczałkowice, which is visited by about two thousand guests (over the whole season), there is no more than one doctor, whose task is to recommend to the guests which baths to take and what dose of "Solanka" to drink.
A pharmacy there is none at all... and when a case of illness occurs, first aid is given by the summer guests; if the patient does not get better, they bring him a "sister of mercy", who is very "knowledgeable" in all the evil illnesses. And when such a "professoress" finds in the patient something that has to do with medicine, she writes a prescription, a special messenger sets off to Dziedzice to fetch the medicine, and meanwhile, until the special messenger comes, the "sick" little wives, who are doing their exile here for the sake of a cure, fuss over the patient and give him "home remedies"...
A separate chapter in itself is the question of kosher food and how it is obtained — but about that another time.
