We Do Not Think About the Fate of Our Children (More on the Parents' Meeting at the Jewish Girls' Gymnasium in Sosnowiec)

[Sosnowiec — education; opinion piece.] The last general annual parents' meeting at the Jewish girls' school in Sosnowiec presented yet another sign of the apathy of the Jewish population in Sosnowiec. A special flavour was added to the matter by the opening speech of Dr. Melaristo [?], from which those assembled learned that at the penultimate general meeting, after the 1927/28 school year, only the board had turned up.. and the general meeting had then not taken place at all.
I knew that in Sosnowiec Jewish institutions do not stand high, but what happened at this meeting was dreadful. — The school counts one hundred and fifty pupils, and at the general meeting, together with the board, there were present a little more than a minyan of Jews...
Where are you, Jewish parents? The only thing you still have left is your children; in them, after all, lie your hope and your future... On them depends the future of the largest Jewish community in Europe. — You yourselves are responsible for their education and their future life! And just now, when thanks to the devotion of a few dedicated persons you have obtained a school of your own, you show such carelessness, such indifferentism, which is a crime towards your children and towards the future of our people.
It is true that you have become poor materially, but far more impoverished have you become — spiritually!
I cannot find words strong enough to censure your lack of any social sense, your lack of a feeling of responsibility for yourselves and your children — but a feeling of disgrace and shame must seize every thinking person, and fear every thinking Jew — for the future of a generation whose parents show so little interest in its education. — Woe to that generation, woe to its parents!
K—Y.
A Woman — a Devil

[Katowice — crime; fraud.] A story as if from a cinema film.

The Katowice prosecutor's office is now conducting an investigation against a certain Aniela Kamińska, the daughter of a minor railway official, who is accused of a series of swindles, blackmail and "fleecing" her admirers.
For 10 years Kamińska made a living by playing with the feelings of her rich admirers and drawing them into large sums of money under the cloak of love.
Her last years were one chain of swindles. Victims of her heart included lawyers, doctors, landowners, even an assistant prosecutor, a general and a police commissioner, all of whom she ruined financially, cheating them out of money, diamonds and jewellery against promissory notes. One of her victims, a certain engineer Bakiński of Lwów, committed suicide.
Besides that she drew in two counts, Count Lubieński from near Kraków and Count Szteński [?] of "Larz" [probably a misprint for Łódź]. From her "loves" she made such a fortune that she bought herself two houses in Katowice, a house in Bydgoszcz and an estate in "Rahne" [?]. In 1922 she presented herself as the widow of a Polish captain and obtained a concession for a railway buffet in Silesia. Recently she came to Poznań, became the bride of a rich industrialist, and on the wedding day stole the jewellery and all the clothes from him, ran off to "Rahne", and there illegally married a Pravoslav [Orthodox Christian], a certain Parsenik. Soon she ran away from him too, to Kowel, and with that her story ends.
The prosecutor's office has sent out a warrant for her, but it is still not known where she is, because she constantly changes her place of residence and alters her name.
Her officially registered "victims" number 20, apart from those who are ashamed to report their misfortune to the police.
And the Husband Went to His Wife.

[Summer feuilleton — story.] (A summer feuilleton) By Z. Lubin.

It is summer.
The wife is at the dacha [summer cottage]; the husband has stayed at home.
It is August time; the husband has come home from his daily occupation.
It was a hot, a very hot day. The husband is sweaty, harassed, tired, worn out, and as soon as he entered the house he threw off his clothes, his shoes and socks, and at once sat down by an open window.
It is quiet in the house, quiet and gloomy. No wife, no children, an empty house. And the husband feels so gloomy, and somehow it becomes hard for him to sit by the window.
It is still early, the sun has not yet set, and the husband thinks how to spend the evening.
And thinking so, a thought flashes through the husband's brain that wherever he goes he will be alone, all alone. And he begins to long for the company of a woman, and the husband thinks: "It would be more pleasant to spend this evening together with a 'woman'." And he thinks: "Who should the woman be?"
And the husband takes his address book out of his breast pocket and looks through various addresses, and here is Tania's address. —
Tania is a widow. Only about three months ago her husband died. He knows Tania very well; even before she married he was friendly with her, and she was close to him, very close. Tania married a man who was much older than she. She married such a man because she herself was no longer a young girl either, and there was no one else to marry.
For about five years Tania lived out her life with her old man. He used to drop in on Tania even after her wedding. But her husband was so jealous, he used to guard his wife so when a strange man came in, and a strange man did not feel particularly comfortable in Tania's house. [So] he stopped coming to her.
But now Tania's husband has died; she is alone again.
And the husband thinks: he will ring Tania, and if it works out he will come to her at once, to spend a while.
— Hallo! — he hears Tania's voice, and a warmth pours over his heart.
— Oh, look, just look who is calling — Tania speaks so sweetly on the telephone. And the husband feels good and goes on talking to Tania.
But one cannot say in the very first minute why he suddenly rang, so he asks how she is and how life goes. And Tania starts telling a tale of woe: next Sunday she must set the tombstone on her husband's grave, only she lacks money, and she goes about as if without a head.
And Tania's talk makes the husband feel bad at heart, because she is so preoccupied with setting up a tombstone on her husband's grave!... Somehow it doesn't fit... And on top of all her troubles Tania also complains that she is short of money.. She might yet ask for an interest-free loan — and how could he refuse.. And he cuts the conversation short.
— Good night, Tania!
Hastily and excitedly he searches his address book for a second address.
And here is Bliumke's address.
Who is Bliumke?
A girl, not young at all any more, but not ugly at all either, and with Bliumke it is so good, so good to spend time. She knows such hidden corners and paths, lonely avenues — and it is so good to be with Bliumke in a park, in a lonely avenue.. And the husband thinks: if only she is at home, she will surely agree to it, because Bliumke wants a man to put his arms around her; but there is another little trouble here: Bliumke's mother strongly dislikes it when a married man comes to visit her daughter. The mother would like men to go out with her daughter from whom a bridegroom might come. But what comes of a married man keeping company with the girl? — Nothing! It is still a leap to a match; because the mother [can] not stand it at all when he comes to Bliumke or even when he rings her, and when it happens that not Bliumke but the mother answers the telephone, it is very unpleasant for the husband... And now he also doesn't know who will come to the telephone — perhaps the mother? And that is so unpleasant for him..
But the husband's fantasy is already kindled with such a fire, which does not [go out] so quickly, so he goes and rings Bliumke's number.
And to the husband's bad luck it was not Bliumke who answered, but the mother herself.
And when the mother learned who was calling, she answered so coldly and so drily:
— My Bliumke is not in.
And as if wishing to make her protest even stronger, she asked:
— How are your children, your wife?
— They are at the dacha — the husband answered.
— Well, then one goes to one's wife — the mother's few words rang out so stingingly, so venomously.
The husband felt as if doused with cold water.
And the husband searched for no more addresses. And since he had been reminded of his wife, he had a thought: "Perhaps really just get up and go to the wife?"
And the husband began to reckon:
It is Thursday; he had in any case reckoned on going to his wife on Saturday, since on Saturday and Sunday he does not work. And almost every Saturday he goes to his wife, and today is Thursday, and if he leaves right away he will lose only one day of work, but it will surely not cost more than it would have cost if he "went out" with one of the two addresses... It will even cost much, much less.
And when the husband thought further, he realised that besides being cheaper it would also be much more comfortable. And the husband quickly packed the necessary things, ran out of the house, caught a droshky [cab], so as to get to the train as fast as possible, because time was short.
And the husband went to his wife.
The Last Session of the City Council before the Recess

Under the chairmanship of Council Chairman Mr. S. Fürstenberg, the last session of the local city council (Będzin) took place on Monday.
The P.P.S. [Polish Socialist Party] members, who have a "standing claim" on coming forward with "urgent" motions, did not stay behind at this session either and submitted an urgent motion, which is, incidentally, very characteristic.
The motion is that the city council should intervene with the building contractor Eng.[?] Mr. G. Weinzieher that he raise the wages of the workers.
Councillor Jakubowicz speaks against the motion, arguing that the city council has no competence to interfere in private matters.
On the motion of Vice-Chairman Mr. Erlich it is decided to pass the question on to the Magistrat (city executive).
Then the following questions are put to the Magistrat: 1) from Dr. Jarzębowski, whether it is true that construction of the post office is to be stopped, and 2) from Councillor Zemła[?], why the streets are not being sprinkled.
President (Mayor) Michel answers that he will intervene with the central authorities so that the construction work is not stopped; and as for sprinkling the streets — he says — whenever the "Jadźka" [nickname of the municipal watering cart] wants to go out over the town, it starts to rain...
The last answer provokes merriment in the hall.
For the work of the "Urząd Rozjemczy" [rent arbitration office] the following fees were fixed: from 1 to 2 rooms — 5 zł., 3 rooms — 10 zł., more — 30 zł., from shops — 15 złoty.
The claim of Mr. Eliezer Bożykowski[?], owner of the "Hotel Bristol", is considered; he suffered heavy damage during the war, when the military authorities requisitioned furniture and premises. The city council decided to grant him 2 thousand zł.
To the general assembly of the Union of Cities, which will take place in Poznań, the following were delegated: Messrs. Vice-President Rubinlicht, Vice-Chairman of the city council Erlich and Councillor Wasz[?].
After the agenda is completed, the chairman declares a recess until 15 September, wishing the councillors a pleasant holiday.
Labour Pains in Electing a Kehilla President

On Sunday an election for a kehilla (Jewish community) president was supposed to take place. Six board members came to the meeting and the meeting would have been valid, but suddenly Mr. Fajnski[?] left and there was no quorum left.
A Branch for Landkunde (Regional Studies)

Soon a branch of the Jewish Society for Landkunde (knowledge of the country) in Warsaw will be established in Zagłębie. Its task will be to awaken among the Jewish public in Zagłębie a love of nature and of knowing the country, by organising excursions to the nearer and more distant regions of Poland.
75 Jewish Families Threatened with Eviction

Mr. B. Pelc, who for many years has been dealing with the poor families supported with rent money by the local "Dobroczynność" (charity society), informs us that because of the institution's critical financial situation the rent campaign has been stopped, and as a result the 75 Jewish families — among them a large number of widows — are threatened with eviction from their flats.
Proletarian “Solidarity”

In Erlich's house on Kołłątaja Street a Jew was employed on building work. For this "insolence" several Christian workers wanted to beat him. At the Jew's cries some tenants of the house came out and rescued the Jew from the non-Jewish proletarians...
Meeting of the Cooperative Bank

Next Sunday the annual general meeting of the Cooperative Bank will take place in the hall of the "Craftsmen's Association". At the meeting important points for the members of this financial institution will be discussed.
From the “Merchants' Association” / A Theft Uncovered

We are asked once again to draw the attention of taxpayers that, when paying any tax whatsoever, they should demand that the receipts state for which tax the payment was made.
—o—
A Theft Uncovered.
A few weeks ago the shop of Mr. Goldfeld on Kołłątaja Street was broken into, and the thieves stole various installation materials from it.
The local police, who conducted an energetic investigation, succeeded in uncovering the thieves and also the receiver, Mr. Berman, at whose place 40 pairs of radio headphones, fans, etc. were found.
The thieves were put in chains and locked up in the local prison.
A “Polite” Answer

On Wednesday two uhlans (cavalrymen) came into the shop of S. Szydłowski in the Old Market to buy something.
While they were examining the goods they had asked for, they knocked Mr. Szydłowski's hat off and also dared to beat Mr. S. and his son.
Because of this Mr. S.'s son turned to a policeman and asked him to intervene quickly. To this the policeman declared: "They're not killing you yet"...
Nevertheless the policeman went into the shop, where he prevailed upon the military men to leave the shop.
The policeman refused to draw up a report.
Sosnowiec — Meeting of “Linat Hacholim”

[Sosnowiec — Charitable institutions.] After a break of two years, the president of the “Linat Hacholim” society [sick-care society] consented to call a general meeting of the institution.
The meeting, however, did not have the character of ordinary general meetings. It was merely a “report meeting”: a report on the activity was given and the board stayed in power, because the item “elections” was not on the agenda.
The president, Mr. Eliezer Grinciger, opens the meeting, complains about the fact that out of about 400 members barely two minyanim came, and he “nominates” Mr. Reuven Binensztok as chairman of the meeting.
Several of those present tried to protest against the nomination system, but nothing can be changed: if the president says so, so it must be...
The report on the two years of activity is delivered by Mr. Grinciger. It turns out that in the course of that time medical utensils were lent out to 1,370 sick people, medicines to 323 sick people, 899 sick people received 4.495 litres of milk, night watches at the sickbed — 316, visits by doctors and feldshers — 195. In the till there is 25 zł. 68 groszy in cash.
A discussion took place on the report, in which Messrs. Reuven Czapnik, Kalman Fuks, Shabtai Jungster and others took part, who levelled a series of accusations at the board, such as: that it did not want to lend medical utensils to sick people living in Old Sosnowiec; why the report was not signed by the audit committee; and that the administrative expenses of the minyan at “Linat Hacholim” are paid out of the monthly dues.
Original was the criticism of Mr. Fuks, who dwelt on the fact that there are 25 zł. in cash in the till at a time when all philanthropic institutions have deficits. This is the best proof — says Mr. Fuks — that the board is completely inactive and therefore has no expenses.
After the discussion the motion of Mr. Jungster was adopted, to express no confidence in the outgoing board.
The Jewish Girls’ Gymnasium Will Build Its Own School Building

[Sosnowiec — Education.] The fact that the Jewish gymnasium for girls in Sosnowiec has received state rights [public-school status] has aroused among the Jewish population of Zagłębie great satisfaction and interest in the institution, which only thanks to its diligent and systematic work has earned recognition from the school authorities.
As we learn, the attendance of pupils has grown considerably as a result.
The new school board has already begun its work; preparations are being made to set about building a building of its own, to be created by the whole Jewish public. The gymnasium will then bear the name of the unforgettable and prematurely deceased Jewish national activist Dr. Abraham Perlman.
A 10-Year-Old Boy Shoots a 9-Year-Old Girl

[Sosnowiec — Accidents.] On Sunday a tragic incident occurred in the flat of a policeman on Chemiczna[?] Street 2.
The policeman had gone out of his flat, leaving behind his 2 children, a boy of 10 and a girl of 6 years old. Together with the children a neighbour’s girl, 9 years old, was playing.
While playing, the policeman’s boy opened a cupboard, from which he took out a rifle, with which the boy threatened the other children.
The children, on seeing the rifle, started running out of the room. But at that moment the 10-year-old with the rifle shouted: “Stand still! Because I’ll shoot.” At that moment a shot was heard and the bullet hit the neighbour’s girl, who was taken to hospital in a hopeless condition.
A Fight Between a Flat Broker and a Tenant

[Sosnowiec — Housing.] On Tuesday morning things were “cosy” in front of the house at Mandushever[?] Street 26. The flat broker Mr. Kagszowski[?] and the tenant Mrs. Tajchner came to blows there.
The reason for the fight is the following.
The house belongs to Mr. B. Fiszel, who wants to build it up by one storey and already has a building plan for that purpose.
The building, however, cannot be started until the tenant Tajchner moves out of her flat. Because of this Mr. Fiszel has used various tricks, even tore down the roof of the flat, just to get rid of the tenant. The latter, who makes her living thanks to the fact that her flat is in the centre of Handlowa[?] Street, does not want to leave the flat until the landlord provides her with a flat where she can go on supporting herself and her children.
On this ground a fight broke out between the above-mentioned flat broker and the tenant, and the end of it is that the tenant’s “position” has been strengthened, because after the fight she is lying in bed..
For tearing down the roof, the trial took place on Tuesday in the local district court, which sentenced the landlord Mr. Fiszel to pay a fine of 500 zł. and to rebuild the roof within 8 days.
The Feet Discovered the Theft...

[Sosnowiec — Crime, court.] In the month of January a theft was carried out at the firm “Zelmetal”[?].
The police, who undertook a terribly thorough investigation, discovered no trace whatsoever of the theft. Then the police hit upon an idea and set out along a snowy path that bore marks of human footsteps.
This succeeded, and the thieves together with the loot were discovered.
This week the trial took place, and the burglars were sentenced to two years in prison.
A Belly with... Saccharin / Proceeds of a Badge Sale / From the Chess Tournament / It Didn’t Work Out for Him..

[Sosnowiec — Crime, smuggling.] The local police kept under observation a Jewish merchant who often came here, and at the railway station he was awaited by several people.
Because of the suspicion the passenger was taken to the police station, where it was established that he is Mosze Gast from Oświęcim and that he deals in trading foreign saccharin.
During the search 8 kilos of saccharin were found on him under his clothes.
On Monday Gast stood before the local district court, which sentenced him to pay 18 hundred [1,800] zł. or 80 days’ arrest.
—o—
[Sosnowiec — Culture, libraries.] Proceeds of a badge sale
On Wednesday a badge sale took place for the benefit of the library named after Dr. A. Perlman in Katrine[?]. Thanks to the energetic work of a few sympathisers, 561.41 zł. was collected.
—o—
[Sosnowiec — Chess.] From the chess tournament.
The chess tournament, which is to end next Sunday, stands as follows: Kimelman 7 points. Cukier 6½ pts. Redlich and Szwajcer (Będzin) 5½ points each, Fajner 5 points, Eng. Silips[?] 3½ pts. Merin and Zylberberg 3 points each, Dr. Gradziński 2 points.
From the result so far it turns out that Merin is already definitely dropping to class B, because he has already played all his games; unexpectedly Fajner reached “osh” [probably: also] 5 points! Dr. Gradziński has played very few games, so his last place is no proof; next Sunday will finally settle who the remaining 3 candidates for dropping to class B will be.
—o—
[Sosnowiec — Crime.] It didn’t work out for him..
The porter [woźny] of the “Sosnowiec Society” [Towarzystwo Sosnowieckie], while the cashier was away at lunch, managed to get to the till, from which he took out 1,500 zł.
Suspicion soon fell on the porter, who was handed over to the investigating judge.
Olkusz. — Sports. / A sports club “Maccabi” founded / A car kills a child

On Sunday a championship match took place between “Aryeh” Sosnowiec and T.S. “Westa” [?] Olkusz; the result was 0:1 in favour of “Aryeh”.
—o—
A sports club “Maccabi” founded
After great effort a sports club “Maccabi” has been founded. The organisers are: B. Weisselfisch, K. Weisselfisch, A. Parasol [?], H. Czarniecki, M. Patak, H. Legder [?], S. Legder [?], Ch. Gelbard and others. Mr. M. Lancman of Sosnowiec helped a great deal in founding the sports club. After the formalities were completed at the notary (rejent), the statutes were sent to the voivode for approval.
—o—
A car kills a child
On Tuesday, on the road from Sulisheva [Sułoszowa?] to Oytseva [Ojców?], a car ran over a 4-year-old Christian child, who was killed on the spot. The child's mother has lost her mind.

In Łódź a monthly for parents, "Ogniwa" ["The Link"], is published, from which we take the following interesting article, which is now, because of the school holidays, very topical. It is worthwhile that our mothers, to whom the content is mainly devoted, should read it attentively and also think for a while whether the sacred duty of keeping the young Jewish generation within Judaism really does not rest upon them.
Elen.

It is a disgrace that the Jewish father, who devotes so much time and energy to his daily work, does not remember, or neglects, his most important duty — to choose for his child a school in which it will receive a proper education;

The Jewish mother, thus[?] receiving the free possibility to decide on her child's education, does not base her decision on the pedagogical value of the school to which she wants to give her child, but on considerations of an entirely external nature.

Very often parents send their children to the kind of school that is "modern" at the moment, to which the manufacturer Mr. X sends his son and Mrs. Dr. Y her daughter, and to which "good form" requires one to conform...

It is a disgrace that there are many parents who send their children without consideration, and some even deliberately, to a school which in its spirit, its life, customs and ideals is entirely alien to Jewish society.

Very often Jewish children are sent to a school in which they are taught to regard their own society, and everything that is Jewish, with contempt.

It is a disgrace that falling away from the Jewish people is most widespread among us Jews in our diploma-holding intelligentsia. The Jewish lawyer, the doctor, the engineer, the bank director avoid everything that has any connection with Jewishness, afraid that it might harm their career. Their children they presumably send to any school, only not to a Jewish one — anything to be further from their own stock, from the cradle, from the past, anything to be closer[?]...

It is a disgrace that Jewish parents do not see and do not hear... They do not see the harmful influence to which their children are subjected in the alien environment: they do not hear the quiet sobbing of the child's soul, hurt by an offensive[?] word dropped unintentionally, by an ironic remark, or by a mocking nickname...

[It is a disgrace] that Jewish parents let themselves be dazzled by pretty phrases, by lofty expressions, by etiquette, by external glitter, behind which an empty superficiality hides.

It is a disgrace that Jewish parents absolutely want their children to be pale, colourless, without hues. About the colour of the face they worry — and how they worry! But the soul, the heart, the mind of the child — that may stay without homely virtues and Jewish colours, without feeling, without ideals, brrr.. That, after all, is "chauvinism": remaining what one is, and not being some kind of monkey. "Chauvinism" is what they call guarding one's own ideals and not chasing after what is foreign. "Chauvinism" — getting to know one's own people and culture. "Chauvinism" is having self-esteem, national pride, thinking of the past and longing for freedom, brrr... Away! Away with the "poisons".

It is a disgrace that for some Jewish parents it is enough[?] that the school does not hold lessons on the Sabbath. That alone is still not enough to understand and feel the Sabbath, the Jewish religion and culture, and to be a Jew..

There are parents who do not even care about the scrap that is called the lesson in "Mosaic religion". Incidentally, the Jewish parents are right. With that lesson (which, alas and alack, as it looks, is neither a lesson nor a religion..) or without it, it is all the same. What[?] good then is the whole comedy?

It is a disgrace that all this happens before our eyes, among us, and we all keep silent; nobody blushes for shame, nobody bursts out with truth and holy indignation, and nobody calls for a return from the false path.

It is terrible to think that it may soon be too late...

Look around you, Jewish parents — do you not see how your children are slipping out of your hands, how they turn away from you, and may perhaps one day become your enemies?...

A [woman] observer.
At the Shomer Colony.

The „Hashomer Hatzair“ in Sosnowiec has for the first time this year undertaken a campaign to organise Shomer colonies during the summer months. 80 shomrim are at the colonies. The older shomrim are in Brzozówka, beyond Wolbrom; the younger ones in Bujaków; and the last group, which is at the same time going through an instructors’ course, is in Przesiecz[?] (near Lamusze[?]).
In a splendid mountainous area, in the village of Bujaków, some 20 kilometres from Bielsko, is the first group, consisting of 32 young shomrim and shomrot, the so-called „kfirim“ (young lions). They have settled into two small village cottages. One cottage is assigned to the shomrim, and the second — a few steps further — is occupied by the shomrot. The Sabbath day that I spent with the young shomrim I shall never forget. Early in the morning, around 6 o’clock, the Shomer „kingdom“ becomes a bustle of running about and commotion. They are getting ready for the first morning assembly, at which the instructor of the colony, Zvi Pergericht[?], reads out the daily „report“ and divides the work among the „sadranim“ (orderlies) for the whole day. But this does not last long, and after singing the Shomer anthem we go off into the forest, where gymnastic exercises take place. It is simply a delight to watch how the tiny shomrim (barely 12—13 years old) perform gymnastic exercises that are quite hard for them, and one cannot deny it — the results show at once at breakfast... Between one course and the next they sing zmirot from the Shomer repertoire, the whole crowd joins in at once, and the soul is merry... I witnessed a very characteristic incident: when my companion, „commandant“ Chlewicki, and I were walking about the splendid „Beskids“, a shomer came up to us and addressed us with a question in Polish. Little Shoshana (a girl of 10) overheard this, and before we had even managed to turn around she jumped up and cried to her comrade: „Speak Hebrew! We are Hebrews!“ Only later did I learn that the everyday language at the colony is Hebrew, and those who do not master the Hebrew language well must use their free time to learn Hebrew.
After lunch the band of youngsters goes off to the nearby grove and, sitting down on the grass — in the Eretz-Israel manner — they turn to the traditional „Oneg Shabbat“, which consists of studying a chapter and lectures on various topics. I happened to hear a very interesting lecture about our great leader Dr. T. Herzl, whose 25th yahrzeit falls next Sunday. The very young listeners literally swallow every word of the speaker. Very interesting is the „discussion“: each one wants to outdo the other in telling who Dr. Herzl was and all that he did for the Jews.
But the little shomrim can also be quite merry even after such a serious „sicha“ (talk), and indeed right after the assembly they launch, shoulder to shoulder, into a jolly and cheerful „hora“, which the peasants of Bujaków watch with great curiosity.
The impression of this Shomer group, full of and bubbling with life, will stay long in my memory.
S. Strojch.

Once More: Bankrupts and Lawlessness

[Zagłębie — economy and trade; reply article.]
(A reply on the painful question to the Radom merchant Mr. M. B—r.)
In one of the earlier issues of our paper, in an article entitled “Bankrupts and Lawlessness”, we touched on the painful question of our economic interests and came to the conclusion that, if our merchants are suffering and tormenting themselves without end, at least a fence [a line of separation] should be drawn between those who must go under because they cannot get over [their difficulties] — that is, as soon as they have no way to stay on their feet they must go bankrupt — and those who do the same thing with a light conscience, for whom it is a premeditated act and to whom it comes as easily as crossing one leg over the other.
We argued then that one must not put on one and the same level the firms that go bankrupt because they have been broken — whether because of the enormous tax obligations with which they were burdened, or because they were caught out by their customers, who did not pay their bills of exchange — and those who cannot show what reasons forced them to go bankrupt; and we understood then that there are two kinds of bankrupts: forced ones and wilful ones.
Firms forced into bankruptcy, as we understood it, must be helped with every possible means in order to rescue them from the difficult situation into which the hard [economic] state of affairs drove them; the conscious bankrupts, on the other hand, we must avoid at every step, and if they cannot prove that understandable reasons led them to the catastrophe, then in that case they should be stamped on the black list as wilful bankrupts, as individuals who do not let others live and behave with total lawlessness. We therefore came to the conclusion that we must not tolerate these dangerous methods, and we proposed that a kind of committee be created whose task would be to fight wilful lawlessness.
And it is interesting: the question seems so painful that one could write and debate about it without end; unfortunately, however, none of our conscious, intelligent Zagłębie merchants said a word on the question; only a reader from Radom spoke up on it, and his article was printed in our “Zagl. Tsayt.” [Zaglembier Tsaytung] No. 26 under the title “That Is Not the Way Out”.
The author, a respected Radom merchant, M. B—r, does not agree with our opinion that such a committee could be created at all, whose judges would be clean and could decide on another person’s solidity and honesty; nor, in the author’s opinion, could such a committee establish who goes bankrupt wilfully and who does so because he has no other choice.
It is high time, the author says, to unmask ourselves and tell the pure truth, however sad it may be. So does the sad pure truth really lie in the fact that the judges themselves have also already gone astray? No, things have not yet gone that far, and precisely because we want the air not to be poisoned, so that a decent merchant can really remain orderly and honest — precisely for that reason one must [?] not close one’s eyes to reality, and must see to it that what is honest and clean is rescued, and fight against what is lawless and base, which unfortunately takes on ever more terrible forms — something that no decent merchant and human being may allow.
According to you it turns out that because times are bad an economic crash comes elementally, ruining the merchant class catastrophically, and protests [of bills], “klauzule” [enforcement orders] and distraints (“zajęcia”) begin to pour in. Of course in such a case the merchant is brought into the most terrible situation, and at such a moment he naturally remains helpless — so why do you call that a “wilful bankruptcy”?
Wilful bankrupts, in our usage, are those who take goods on credit as much as they can get and run off with them to where the pepper grows [to the ends of the earth], and afterwards one still has to go looking for them. We have been hearing of such things quite often lately. Of course, in this case those who give unlimited credit to these lawless people are no less guilty.
We also call wilful bankrupts those who throw goods around right and left at incomprehensible competitive prices, that is, cheaper than the original source gives them, and afterwards, after trading for a few years, they stage the big crash.
There are also various, various illegal combinations to which no decent firm can stoop — and the end is that a sound firm has to capitulate [?] because of the lawlessness of the wildly grown weeds, who bear no responsibility to anyone and reckon with nothing.
Of course, if the associations of our merchants and small traders stood at their proper height, the lawlessness would not have reached its present sad state, because at the given moment the member would have been obliged to explain to his association how he insists on selling below the price, or why he gives goods to irresponsible people.
But since for the time being we have no such bodies, such committees must be created, which will not allow goods to be thrown away to lawlessness so that the one who threw them can rob a hundredfold.
Incidentally, the question is topical and painful enough that it may well be debated, and it would be desirable that everyone who has something to say should let his true, sincere word be heard here.
The advice that the best and most radical means would be for us to fight for the removal of the “numerus clausus” in every field, for us to be admitted to government posts, and even for free emigration to come about, is certainly, certainly a good one. But there are, after all, many good things that cannot be realised at all, let alone when it is a matter of urgent, necessary help that must come as quickly as possible — at such a moment we certainly cannot let ourselves be drawn into fantasies and utopias.
R. Let.

"Friendship!" (A comprehensive [?] report on the Socialist Youth Rally in Vienna)

[Vienna — International Socialist Youth Rally; travel report.]
L. Szpigelman.

Whoever does not know the social order in modern Europe, whoever has not taken a close look at how things are under Vienna's Social Democratic government, could not imagine what Vienna is, and could have no notion of what the International Youth Rally in Vienna would look like.

But let us be honest and sincere and admit that even those who know Vienna, who know the strength and the friendship of the Viennese Social Democrats, could not imagine that the rally would turn out so imposing, so large and splendid as we saw it in reality. We had thought, after all, that the enthusiastic jubilant shouts, that the warm greetings of small and great, of young and old, were some kind of dream, a fantasy, a tale from the Thousand and One Nights.

For we saw how people from different parts of the world, people of different nations, meeting one another for the first time, are fused together into one great tool that we call "Man." We then formed the notion that this mass of people has one aim in life, one ideal — to beautify, ease and improve the conditions of human life.

Marching through the streets of Vienna, watching the heartfelt greetings of people who see each other for the first time in their lives, one had to come to the realisation that humanity is a kind of splendid work that can create the unbelievable, that can glorify the world into a beautiful and splendid edifice, where there will be room for all who are in the world and who want to forge through labour a beautiful future for mankind.

* * *

Splendid was the sight of the "red" train that set out from Warsaw to Vienna to take part in the International Socialist Youth Rally, carrying about 1,200 people, together with participants from Finland, Latvia, Estonia and East Prussia. From Poland there was the "TUR" (P.P.S.), and from the Jewish parties 180 from "Frayhayt" (Right Poale Zion) and 120 from "Tsukunft" (Bund). Each group with its own coloured blouses and red ties, in separate carriages. The authorities both in Poland and in Czechoslovakia treated us with respect, so that no one searched us or asked for any documents or tickets.

We were treated in an especially friendly way as soon as the train entered Austrian territory. There the peasants in the fields and the railway-line workers greeted the "red train" with the word "Fraynt-shaft!" ["Friendship!"]; many stations received the train with music and greeted it with red handkerchiefs and shouts of "Friendship," which lasted until the train pulled out of the station.

Before the train reaches Vienna, one passes many municipal houses decorated with red flags, with red flowers growing in the windows, and all this gives the city a festive mood. From the windows the "red train" is greeted with enthusiastic cries of "Friendship."

On Thursday before 5 p.m. the train arrives in Vienna at the Ostbahnhof, where it is received with music and with loud joyful greetings.

Thousands of people came to welcome the train; they lined up in two rows, and between them the arriving guests marched in good order and were greeted enthusiastically by the whole crowd.

On the large square in front of the station the guests stop, each group with its flags, and are greeted by the mayor and other personalities in German and Polish.

The greetings are answered by a representative of "TUR" in Polish, Mr. Szpizman of "Frayhayt" in Yiddish and Mr. Szafran of "Tsukunft" in German.

Afterwards buses came and took the guests' belongings, and the guests were taken by tram to their billets in large, spacious public halls in various parts of the city.

After the meal each guest receives a pass for free travel for three days on the trams and the underground railway.

On Friday at 10 in the morning all participants assemble before the great Rathaus square, from where the huge crowd marches off to the Heldenplatz, which lies in front of the Hofburg. There one saw a sea of tens of thousands of heads with countless flags of different countries and nations. Then came the opening, the speeches and greetings, and the concert part was also transmitted through the loudspeaker ["megaphone"].

On Saturday, in the course of the day, large meetings took place in various parts of Vienna, at which lectures were given by the most important Viennese socialists, such as Friedrich Adler, Otto Bauer, Karl Heigtz [sic; Karl Heinz] and others.

It was very beautiful when the "Internationale" was sung simultaneously in different languages.

Various kinds of sport were demonstrated, such as handball, football, athletics and various combat exercises.

In the evening came the most splendid thing, such as Vienna had never yet seen. On both sides of the Danube Canal, across the whole width of the streets, tens of thousands of demonstrators marched with torches in their hands, so that it looked as if broad bands of fire were marching, reflected in the river Danube.

The marching lasted on both sides from 8 to 11 in the evening, until the crowd reached the culminating point, i.e. the Rathaus, where the huge building was so artfully illuminated with thousands of electric lamps and floodlights that Vienna had seen it only for the second time.

The torchlight march to the Rathaus stretched several kilometres in length, and all the time they sang and shouted various slogans such as: "Down with fascism," "Down with war," "Long live Red Vienna," "Long live the International," "Long live the unity of the peoples."

During the whole march the windows were open and the streets were lit [sic; probably: filled] with people who greeted continuously and shouted enthusiastically "Friendship!"

On Sunday various ceremonies began again, among them the ceremony in the Vienna Woods and the mourning ceremony at the graves of the victims of the bloody Vienna events of 15 July 1927.

An incomparable picture was presented by the great gymnastics festival, where tens of thousands of young people performed gymnastics simultaneously, producing a mixture of many-coloured images, languages, song and costumes.

At the end the population showered the guests with flowers, chocolate and other sweets, and the greetings and shouts of joy were beyond measure.

It was interesting how exemplary the organisation was: Vienna had counted on 25 thousand guests, whereas there were twice as many, and in the end the number even reached 100 thousand — and yet everyone had a place to sleep and eat. Among the 100 thousand people, 18 nationalities were represented.

Besides Europe, there were guests from America and Palestine. The Jewish workers from Palestine attracted the Germans' attention because of the turbans on their heads, and they also demonstrated with the Hebrew language.

The new banner of the Będzin "Poale Zion" also fluttered over the streets of Vienna among other beautiful flags.

Viennese hospitality and their orderliness will never be forgotten among the participants, who saw before them a people of the highest culture, one that can impress every conscious citizen.
A Jewish Heart Has Stopped Beating... (On the first yahrzeit of Dr. Abraham Perlman, of blessed memory).

[Będzin — memorial; Zionism.] Perhaps it is only chance, and perhaps a caprice of history, that on the very same day on which, 24 years ago, the eyes of the greatest Jewish national leader of modern times, Dr. Theodor Herzl, closed — that on that very same day, a year ago, the good and great Jewish heart of the unforgettable comrade and public activist Dr. Abraham Perlman, of blessed memory, stopped beating.

For me the connection is no accidental one; it holds a deep symbolism that presses one towards thoughts and comparisons. There exist invisible threads that are sometimes woven between people with kindred souls — people who never knew or saw one another and yet always had the feeling that they were close, that they understood each other well, because the same feeling lived in their hearts, the same ideal, and in their minds the same formed [?] thought that calls to deeds and to self-sacrifice.

This is how one can explain why we Zionists, even when we do not yet know one another, are already acquainted and friends. The invisible thread of our great ideal binds us more strongly than anything. And fate willed that the kinship of souls between us and our dear departed comrade should remain strong and eternal, and it linked the memory of Dr. Perlman with the memory of our greatest leader — in this lies the deep symbol of the merits and spiritual worth of our comrade Dr. Perlman.

* * *

A year has passed since the sad news arrived and shook and shattered the whole Jewish public in Zagłębie, and we can boldly state that the place our late comrade occupied has not yet been filled; we still stand orphaned after his death and still mourn the terrible loss. We miss: the communal worker, the comrade, the man, the friend — Dr. Perlman. — With the whole strength of his energetic nature he stood in public work; with the gentleness of a good father and friend he treated the small, weak natures and always found a way out so that the cause itself should not suffer. Often a smile on his face, a glance from his deep eyes was enough for people to be hypnotised by his devotion, to go with him and let themselves be led by him. He stood on firm feet, on the ground of the sad Jewish reality of exile, but his clear gaze turned proudly and sincerely to our future in our Jewish land.

He understood, splendidly and as few did, the task of present-day work (Gegenwartsarbeit) and its connection with and significance for the awakening new [?] life in the Land of Israel. A disciplined Zionist, with a rare, exemplary obedience to all instructions, even when it was not so easy to carry out the instruction. "Our organisation," he used to say, "has no police and no bailiffs (sekwestratorzy) to compel us; we must find the strength within ourselves, in our ideal, and fulfil our duty without police and without bailiffs." And he fulfilled his duty, devoted his time, his energy and his strength, devoted [—] [family joys?] to his people, sacrificed everything his personality possessed, in order to move the Jewish public of Zagłębie to follow him.

And institutions arise, and societies and organisations develop which he created, so that everything still asleep in the Jewish soul should awaken. He roused people to hard work, showed a middle way, which nevertheless leads to a new life, to liberation.

At the centre of all his rich activity there always stood the Land of Israel, which he was still privileged to see being built.

The Land of Israel was his ideal, which awakened in him the irresistible wish to settle there, and it was this thought that did not leave him until his last breath.

And we all know that our comrade Dr. Perlman breathed out his soul with longing for the Land of Israel.

To everyone who stood close to him it was clear what a sum of energy and time he put into his devoted work for the Land of Israel — rarely does one find such understanding for our funds, chiefly for the "Keren Kayemet LeIsrael" (Jewish National Fund), as with the late Dr. Perlman. He devoted himself to this work body and soul, and often served [printed: "was devoted"] as a model for our young generation of how one can and must work for the Land of Israel. But that is not all; that alone would not give the proper picture of Dr. Perlman's work and of his renaissance conception for the Jewish people. The Hebrew language and Hebrew culture were, for him as a devoted and conscious Zionist, the main task of his work — tirelessly he stands guard over this postulate.

Already an older man, a few years ago he begins to study and to perfect his knowledge of the Hebrew language; everyone still clearly remembers his last appearance at the Hebrew recitation evening of Miss Bernstein-Cohen, which he himself arranged by his own efforts. "I won't do such things any more," he said to me bitterly after he had himself run around the town selling tickets and had met with crude incomprehension and ignorance (am-haaratzut) from more than one person; but how he beamed when the evening did succeed for him after all! When he had won a great moral victory for the Hebrew language, his face shone for the last time with the glow of the holy light of enthusiasm — that was his swan song.

To Dr. Perlman one may boldly apply the poet's saying: "Man and his personality grow with the higher tasks he sets himself." Dr. Perlman's personality grew into a leader of a great camp, thanks to the lofty ideal that brought him into the ranks of the fighters for a better tomorrow for [?] the Jewish people.

A year has passed since that terrible day, and we still stand, as on that day, orphaned and broken, and feel the grief. The place from which you were torn away from us is empty and bare, but your spirit fills us with holy faith and strength to stride on along the hard and dark road of struggle and labour, on which effects of light already show themselves, casting reflections on our future, on the awakening and self-building land —

Sleep peacefully, dear comrade! You have fulfilled your duty; you laid not just one stone in the great edifice of liberation. [—] Your bright spiritual eyes will always hover [?] [over] the splendid mountains of Zion, and they will bring you a greeting from a new generation that goes on building a people and a land.

Dr. T. Melodista.
The Tragedy

[Herzl — anniversary.] For the 25th yahrzeit (20 Tammuz). By Moshe Feinkind.
When Captain Dreyfus was degraded, Herzl was revealed...
Before his eyes the great tragedy of the Jewish people was then played out, and his Jewish soul was kindled within him, Jewish sorrow pressed upon his heart, and he came to his people.
He came from an alien milieu, assimilated, steeped in an alien culture, and he was a stranger to us too.
He began to feel the Jewish tragedy on his own skin, even in such a country where Mirabeau had preached „liberty, equality and fraternity“; he began to feel, to ache, to bleed, and, breaking with his past, he gave us the „Judenstaat“.
* * *
The idea was not new. The ordinary Jew had never stopped dreaming of it.
Long before him Jews and Christians dreamed of a Jewish „home“ in the Land of Israel or elsewhere.
This idea arose as early as Napoleon's times. Napoleon too in his time made the Jews a proposal about it; others did the same.
The Russian „Decembrists“, the Polish dreamers of freedom, Lelewel, Mickiewicz, etc., quite seriously occupied themselves with the problem, with the idea of the Land of Israel for the Jews.
Hess in his „Rome and Jerusalem“, Beaconsfield in his „Alroy“, Goldsmidt, and „Daniel Deronda“, Oliphant („Gilead“), Pinsker („Autoemancipation“), Rülf („Aruchas bas ami“), etc., etc. — all of them proclaimed the idea boldly and openly even before Herzl.
But with all of them it was only a pious wish; the people did not listen to their voice and the dream remained no more than a dream...
It was Herzl who first gave this dream a soul...
* * *
Herzl had a quite special fortune.
Diplomats and representatives of states, young and old, rich and poor, the learned as well as simple workers — all listened to his voice; he inspired them all with his appearance, with his „Judenstaat“; all looked upon his slender, aristocratic[?] figure and his patriarchal look as upon a Messiah, a prophet; all were enchanted, bewitched by him; all eyes were turned then to the modern „Zerubbabel“ on Türkengasse number nine, all, all...
The yellow badge of former times became the badge of honour of the „modern Jew“, of the one who wants to suffer, strive, fight and triumph together with his people. For those who fought he became a balm, for the despairing — hope, and for the deserters — a way back to Judaism, back to its values, back to its culture and its national life...
And the prophet of a new epoch becomes the creator[?] of a moral force, the leader of the Jews, the symbol of Jewish revival and renaissance.
But as quickly as he came to us, so quickly did he vanish from the Zionist horizon, from the Jewish sky covered with thick clouds. He has gone from us for ever; death robbed us of him; even today one wants to weep. But laments do not wake the dead, and the tragedy has its continuation...
The Seduced Girl (13)

[Literature — serialized novel; installment 13.]
Dr. A. Wajsman.
(A novel of Jewish life in the old world, based on historical facts.)

When Mania heard that a woman from her village wished to see her, she was very glad, thinking that her mother had come; but when they led her into the room, she saw the "aunt" from the family of the estate manager [ekonom] Siwiański.
At first Mania drew back, but seeing such a familiar person from her home, she was glad all the same.
"How do you come to be here, 'aunt'?"
"I have come to you; I wanted to see you and to know how you are getting on here. Are you content?"
"I want to go home; I will travel home together with you. What have I to do here?"
"Unhappy girl! How can such a thing enter your head? You will be the unhappiest woman in the world. Whereas when you marry Ludwig, you will be one of us and be happy all your life."
"Don't mention Ludwig's name to me. He led me astray; I believed him too much; I was mistaken in him, aunt. All of you took advantage of my youth; Ludwig and all of you are not worth my exchanging my parents and my faith for you. You took advantage of my bad situation, of my poor, miserable life at my parents'; you painted for me a sad, black life if I remained a Jewish daughter, but my heart does not feel that with you and in your circles one will find a better, brighter life."
"You shall not mention Ludwig's name to me any more; to me he is as good as dead. And I beg you: if you are my friend and want my happiness, take me home with you at once."
"Don't be so agitated, calm yourself, then we will be able to talk quietly."
Mania threw herself on the "aunt's" neck and with tears begged her to leave at once.
The "aunt", turning pale and frightened, with tears in her own eyes too, began to calm and console her.
"Calm yourself, Manieczka, it is already night now — where would we go?"
"No, at once, this minute. Yesterday too they put off my journey. I want to go this very minute, at once."
"Manieczka! Shouting is pointless here, this is not the village; no one here will hear your cries — the monastery walls are too thick for your voices to reach anywhere. If you speak calmly and quietly I can answer you; but if you shout, I will leave you and go away to Sister 'Irena'."
"I won't let you go; I will be calm, only let us leave now."
"One cannot at night."
"Then we will go on foot; I will not spend the night here."
"Until tomorrow it is no disaster. I still [printed 'gakh', a misprint for 'nokh'] have to see Sister 'Irena' — how can I just go away like that? Tomorrow we will travel."
"Let it be tomorrow, but I won't let go of you any more; wherever you go, I will go with you."
"But I have to go to Sister 'Irena'!"
"Then I will go with you too; I have already been to see her once."
"Already been! What an honour! You ought to count yourself lucky — no small thing! People wait for weeks until they can speak a couple of words with her, and you were invited to her — do you at least know what luck has befallen you?"
Mania, seeing how the aunt was beaming so with her good fortune, did not herself know what to answer, and began asking about her parents.
"How is Mother? Poor Mother, I can imagine how unhappy you [sic, second person in print] feel; I am afraid she will not survive it."
"Ha-ha-ha," the "aunt" burst out laughing, "what a child you still are. As soon as she learned that you had run away, she spat three times, gave you a good scolding — and that was all, everything as before. Your father travels about and works at his business, and your mother cooks dinner."
"And she doesn't mention me at all?"
"She has not mentioned your name even once. I was told that when some woman began talking about you, she did not want to hear about you. 'If Mania had died,' she said, 'I would speak of her — but not of the Mania who knew how to run away...'"
"It cannot be."
"You don't believe me? You can ask Jan [printed 'Yanen' (?), dative], who came here with me; he too is here in the monastery now."
"Jan, who saved me from Ludwig's hands, is here too? I want to see him and thank him."
The "aunt" was glad of these words, and new thoughts and new plans began to come into her head.

What's New in Zagłębie? — Będzin: Annual General Meeting of the „Cooperative Bank“

[Będzin — economy and institutions.]
Będzin
Last Sunday the annual general meeting of the Cooperative Bank of our town took place in the hall of the „Artisans' Association“.
The meeting aroused great interest. Despite the prevailing heat, over 400 members came, who listened attentively to the reports and in general treated the meeting very seriously, so that 270 members took part in the election of 2 board members and 2 [members] of the supervisory council.
As usual, the meeting was opened an entire hour late by the chairman of the board, Mr. Goldsztajn, who proposed Mr. Pesachzon as chairman [of the meeting], to which those assembled agreed. The chairman invites Messrs. Chaim Grajcer and Icek Fajgenblat to the presidium.
After the reading of the minutes of the last general meeting, the reports begin.
The report of the board and on the general activity in the year 1928 is given by Mr. Goldsztajn, who points out that the Cooperative Bank, as a social-cooperative institution, serves all strata of the local Jewish population. Thanks to this the institution is in a stage of the most flourishing development and has earned the greatest trust.
A striking proof are the figures: thus, for example, deposits [„wkłady“] grew in the first months of this year by 80 thousand zł. The total amount of savings comes to 298 thousand zł.
In the course of the year the bank issued loans totalling 120 thousand zł.; bills of exchange were discounted to the amount of over 1½ million zł.
The bank's management devoted special attention to the question of small and premium savings. From the penny [groszy] sums that artisans' children bring into the bank there is already a capital of 40 thousand zł.
This year the bank acquired a plot of land of 3,700 sq. metres, for which about 20 thousand zł. was paid and which is already worth 75 thousand zł.
The profit amounts to 13 thousand and 419 zł.
Then the report on the audit carried out by the auditor Mr. Szmojsz [?] is read; he confirms that the bank is in a satisfactory state and has prospects of a brilliant future.
The report of the supervisory council is given by Mr. S. Fürstenberg, who explains that the council held 72 sessions and inspected the cash and the general activity of the institution.
After the reports came the criticism. Mr. Moshe Hampel criticised the board for granting larger capital to the cooperatives being founded in our town, and also that the profit, relative to the large turnover, is very small.
Mr. Fajgenblat demands that the staff be enlarged, because the artisans who come to the bank lose a lot of time before their business is dealt with.
Mr. Fürstenberg replied, saying that the profit is — in his opinion — a large one too, because a bank for the broad Jewish masses need not chase after large profits; the main motto is that the rate of interest [„Zinsfuss“] should be lower.
As regards enlarging the staff — says Mr. F. — this cannot be carried out in the present small premises.
A discussion is aroused by the item: distribution of profits. It is resolved that 10 thousand zł. be placed in the bank as reserve capital and 3 thousand zł. be deposited in the interest-free loan fund at the „Artisans' Association“ in the name of Mr. Fürstenberg.
The budget in the amount of 76 thousand zł. is adopted.
The elections in place of those retiring by lot produced the following change:
On the board — Moshe Hampel, and on the council — Abraham Hirsz.

So That His Sister Gets a Husband, He Gives His Young Wife a Divorce

[Będzin — Human interest.] He is from Będzin, and the bride was from the shtetl of Neustadt. Some time after the engagement contract (tnoim), the groom's side demanded that a wedding date be set, but the bride's parents did not have the promised dowry and, with various excuses, wriggled out so that the wedding date would be put off until „he is helped“.
Time moved on, the bride's father had still not been helped, and the match between the Będzin groom and the Neustadt bride began to totter.
After long deliberations and consultations, the bride's father hit upon the following invention:
Instead of the dowry he offers a „current commodity“ — to make a match once more; that is, since the Będzin groom has a sister who is also ready for the wedding canopy, and he has a son who is looking for a bride, there will be another engagement contract, and the matter will be settled to the best advantage of both sides.
The ingenious plan was carried out and a second match was concluded: a Będzin girl with a young man from Neustadt.
When the dowry question had been liquidated, they began to prepare the wedding of a young man from Będzin with the bride from Neustadt.
Last Sunday the wedding was indeed celebrated.
How surprised all the in-laws were when they heard, the morning after the wedding, that the young wife regrets it and says no...
— Why? What has happened?
— It's nothing — she says — she doesn't want to..
The young wife's resistance aroused a lot of doubts, and „interested“ parties took the young fellow to doctors, who only „sharpened“ the situation further.
One doctor said that the bride's complaints were justified, whereas the second doctor said that she was simply a rebellious wife (moredet)...
But no interventions whatsoever helped; the young wife declared categorically that „she does not want such a husband“...
Meanwhile the wedding of the second couple was approaching — of the Będzin groom's sister with the young wife's brother from Neustadt.
And here the situation grew much worse, because the Neustadt in-law, the groom's father, declared categorically that if his daughter, the young wife, does not receive 3 thousand zł as „compensation for damages“, he will not give the groom...
The demand was settled after many entreaties and tears. The „revolutionary“ young wife received 2 thousand zł in cash with a get (divorce), and on the same day as the get her brother betrothed her former husband's sister..
Dispute Between the Magistrate and the Sejmik over the Municipal Hospital

[Będzin — Municipality.] A few weeks ago, as our readers know, the city council called on the Magistrate to take over the municipal hospital as its property.
On the basis of legal documents the Magistrate took the appropriate steps for the hospital to pass into its domain.
The local Sejmik (county council), which regards the hospital as its own property, comes out sharply against this and has turned with a complaint to the General Prokuratoria, asking it to state its decision on the matter.
The Prokuratoria has passed the matter on to the district court, and we shall soon have an interesting trial.

Sosnowiec: Revenge on the Gemilut Hesed Fund

[Sosnowiec — Free-loan fund.] The local Gemilut Hesed (free-loan) fund, which carries on intensive activity and is the only institution in our town that brings enormous benefit to the broadest strata of the Jewish population, has now met with resistance from a certain number of members — precisely of the well-to-do class — who refuse to pay the monthly contribution because the gmina (Jewish community) has burdened them with high etat (communal tax) sums.

The Będzin Magistrate Finds Itself Between “Hammer and Anvil”...

The serious danger to the market traders.
For quite a long time a fierce struggle has been waged over the old market. The owners of the Magistrate's market halls are bombarding the Magistrate [with demands] that the market be abolished and that all trade take place in the halls.
On the other side the market traders are waging a defence, since they foresee ruin for themselves if trade in the market is disrupted.
The hall-owners have also intervened with the starosta [district head], who declared that they should turn with the matter to the voivode [provincial governor].
The market traders are likewise sending their defenders to the Kielce voivodeship office, where the matter will be settled in the coming days.

The Olkusz Jewish Community Welcomes the President of the State.

On Wednesday at 4 o'clock in the afternoon the President of the State [Ignacy Mościcki] was scheduled to pass from Ojców through Olkusz to Rabsztyn for the ceremony of laying the foundation stone of the voivodeship sanatorium. The town administration made every effort to give the town a festive appearance. The streets 3 Maja, Kościuszki, Górnicza and Piłsudskiego were splendidly decorated in a sea of greenery, state flags and portraits of Polish heroes. Two splendid welcome gates were erected: one gate at the edge of town by the new power station, by the town administration, and a second gate by the “Westen Enamel Factory”, artistically constructed of all sorts of vessels of the “Westen Factory”. Delegations of all institutions and societies, among them the Jewish community with the Rabbi, may he live long, at its head, the “Craftsmen's Association”, “Postęp”, “Muza”, the “Gemilut Chesed [interest-free loan] Fund” and others, were lined up in the finest front. The whole road from Sieniczno to Rabsztyn was lined on both sides by tens of thousands of people. At exactly 6 in the evening, accompanied by his suite, there arrived

Fainted and died

Yesterday morning a Jewish carter in his forties fainted on Rybna[?] Street in Będzin.
The unconscious Jew lay without help, because „experts“ said that he was suffering from epilepsy — and the Jew actually died.
—o—
Zawiercie municipal administration and city council dissolved.
On the motion of the voivodeship, the Ministry of the Interior has ordered the dissolution of the municipal administration and the city council in Zawiercie.
The order was issued after an inspection (lustration) by a delegation of the voivodeship, which called the city's management into question.
The official Serugi[?] has been appointed commissioner until the new elections.
—o—
A murder at a wedding.
In a village near Olkusz a wedding took place at a local peasant's. When the in-laws were drunk, a brawl broke out among them, in which one man was killed.
This Wednesday 3 men accused of the murder stood before the Sosnowiec district court. After hearing a number of witnesses, who confirmed that the victim had started the brawl, the court sentenced the accused to 6 months in prison.
—o—

Persons whose turnover this year is much smaller than a year ago may apply in writing to the tax office (urząd) to have the instalments reduced in line with this year's reduced turnover.

A fire in a cinema.
On Wednesday at 11 in the evening the film being shown at the „Kometa“ cinema in Dąbrowa caught fire.
5 parts (reels) of the film were burnt.

The „Red Day“ was disrupted.
Yesterday, the 1st of this month, large police detachments were posted in the industrial localities and did not allow larger gatherings of the communist youth.
In the course of the week political arrests took place in Zagłębie.

Mr S. Zmigród went out to the Małobądz fields to get a little fresh air. There he was met by several hooligans, who terrorised him and took his pocket watch.

The Sixteenth Congress

[Zionism — the 16th Zionist Congress; article.]
In Zurich the Sixteenth Zionist Congress opened on Sunday [28 July 1929]. Why Zurich was chosen this time as the venue of the Congress, and not Basel, which already has a tradition of congresses, I do not know. Probably local reasons decided the matter, but it is truly a pity: the present Congress ought to have been held in Basel. The city on the Rhine, which received the First Congress after other cities had declined the honour, the city that saw so many stormy congresses, when the good burghers of Basel were disturbed in their sleep and stared in astonishment, not knowing what the Jews want and why they quarrel — it ought to have hosted the Sixteenth Congress too, which will be the Congress of Peace.
The Congress of Peace — that is probably what it will be called. There is hardly anyone to disturb its solemnity, no one to cause bad blood, no one to quarrel. The „Radicals“ came out of the elections battered („with tooth and eye“), defeated almost all over the world. The small group that will come to the Congress is in no position to achieve anything, and they have nothing to achieve either. Their opposition to the Agency [the Jewish Agency] is over; they have nothing new left to offer. Their dissatisfaction with the leader, too, makes them, after the Agency elections, simply ridiculous.
The Revisionists as well, who have a considerable group at the Congress with a strong leader, cannot accomplish much. In the better Zionist circles they are regarded as essentially an anti-Zionist force, and as such they are treated by the leadership. Only one way remains for them: to leave the Organization and „make their own Sabbath“ — to create their own Revisionist organization that would fight Zionism; but that would then be a fight from outside, the fight of an enemy, and not an internal fight among comrades. And indeed it is said that Jabotinsky intends to take this step. He counts on his guard going with him: Schechtman, Grossman, Tribus [Trivus?] and the „Brit Trumpeldor“. But he will think it over well before taking such a step; probably he will submit and stop the fight.
The Congress of Peace — that is probably what it will be called in history. It deserves the name even if frictions occur at it, even if claims and counterclaims are heard in Zurich; this will not spoil the general impression the world must gain of it. It is the Congress of Peace because at it the movement has reached the goal it set itself at the First Congress; then, thirty years ago, it was said in the programme that the movement embraces all Jews „who do not want to or cannot assimilate“. Many objections were raised against this formula, from the right and from the left. In time the formula was indeed changed, because the old wording made it look as if Zionism permitted and in a certain sense justified assimilation for those „who can and want to“...
Now it turns out that the old, original formula was the right one: there are no Jews who can and want to assimilate. The problem of assimilation has been taken off the agenda altogether. „Even the sinners of Israel are as full of commandments as a pomegranate“ — that is how it is now put, in the national sense. And precisely those who were formerly the last are now becoming the first; now one seeks out precisely those of whom it was formerly thought that they were the ones who can and want to assimilate — one seeks out precisely the non-Zionists on principle. For want of better, in Eretz Israel one had to make do with H. N. Bialik and other former cultural Zionists from Ahad Ha'am's cheder — „when there is no fish, a lox is a fish too“, one may say in this case...
The Congress of Peace — that is what it will be called. With it the series of party congresses closes and the era of all-Israel congresses begins. Now power and responsibility pass to the members of the Agency. Eretz Israel ceases to be the affair of a party; it becomes the affair of the whole Jewish people. Therein lies the significance of this Congress, on whose agenda there is no fuel for fire but only the power of light, and as the Congress of Peace we send it our greeting.
S. J. Stupnicki.
Olkusz: The Kehilla Budget Approved / A Festive Herzl Academy

[Olkusz — kehilla; followed by: Herzl memorial.]
The Jewish community [gmina] of Olkusz has received notice from the voivodeship that the kehilla budget for the year 1929 has been approved. At the same time the starost ordered a supplementary budget of 8 thousand złoty to be drawn up for renovating the kehilla buildings. Because of the critical situation of the Jewish population, the kehilla board decided, regardless of the consequences, not to draw up the supplementary budget for the time being.
—o—
A Festive Herzl Academy.
On Saturday and Sunday morning memorial services for Dr. Herzl were held in the synagogue. In the presence of all the Zionist groupings Mr. Warszawski conducted a solemn memorial service. In the evening an impressive Herzl academy took place in the blue-and-white decorated hall of „Tze'irei Mizrachi“. Miss Springer delivered a substantial speech about Herzl, depicting in fine strokes his life and his work for the Jewish renaissance. The festive academy ended with the singing of „Tehezaknah“ [?] and „Hatikvah“. On Monday a Keren Kayemet flower day was held, which brought in 105 zł., and the sale of Herzl badges 60 zł.
A. B.

In honour of the 25th yahrzeit of Dr. Theodor Herzl, memorial services were held everywhere, including in the towns and townlets of Zagłębie; they passed with great solemnity and made a good impression.
A painful incident occurred in the Będzin synagogue during the memorial service. When the guest from Eretz Israel, Mordechai Hampel, was given the floor, several youths, members of the Revisionist organization, made a scandal and prevented him from speaking by singing „Hatikvah“.
These irresponsible acts naturally aroused bitterness among the other Zionist groupings, and so a scuffle broke out, which caused the festive moment to be broken off, and the public left the synagogue with heavy hearts.
In the Będzin synagogue a varied public had gathered. After the appropriate prayers by the cantor Mr. Żupowicz [?], Mr. N. Landner [?] spoke on current affairs.
— In Dąbrowa a memorial service was held in the synagogue. Dr. Melodysta [?] spoke. The synagogue was packed full.
— In Katarzyna [?] the board of the Dr. Perlman library organized a memorial service with the participation of Dr. Melodysta.
Afterwards Mr. Karolnik appealed to those present to help by deeds to realize the ideals of Dr. Perlman.

The match between the above-mentioned group champions for the title of champion of the Kielce district [okręg] caused a great sensation in sporting circles and drew some 2,800 spectators.
In the first minutes "Hakoach" carries out a nicely combined attack, but the well-disciplined defence of "Sosnowiec" blocks every assault of "Hakoach".
"Sosnowiec" answers with a counter-attack. A very nice game develops. "Hakoach", however, cannot keep up at all with the strong and sharp tempo of "Sosnowiec", and in the 29th minute Jakubczyk scores the first goal from a corner kick [?].
"Hakoach" wants to equalise, but the result does not change.
In the second half "Hakoach" plays weaker than in the first half. "Sosnowiec" takes advantage of this. Already in the 2nd minute Czechan scores the 2nd goal from a breakthrough. "Hakoach" becomes a little livelier and stays [?] some 10 minutes in the "Sosnowiec" half. But "Hakoach"'s attack is not properly disciplined in front of the opponent's goal; they lack the boldness to shoot at the opponent's goal. In the 28th minute the referee awards a free kick against [lit. "to"] "Sosnowiec", and Gutman surely converts it into a goal. Most esteemed Editor!
In connection with the report on the annual general meeting of the Bank Spółdzielczy [Cooperative Bank], which was printed in the last number of your esteemed paper, where it is said that I criticised the board for granting larger capital to the cooperatives being set up in our town, I ask you to print the following lines in your paper:
I said that the bank must support the cooperatives being set up, but the board must take pains that the capital granted be covered back by the Bank dla Spółdzielni in Warsaw, so that the population should not be harmed [?]. These are the words I said, but I never said that one should not support the cooperatives being set up.
Regarding the bank's profit, I did not say that the profit is small because one charges low interest; I said that the declared profit is not the real one, because according to the turnover it ought to be larger.
I believe that you were misled by a tendentious reporter, who noted down in my name things I did not say.
In the hope that you will print the above lines, I sign with respect,

Esteemed Editors!
We ask you to print the following communiqué in your esteemed paper:
Taking into account that the activity of the Będzin Jewish kehilla in no way corresponds to the demands of the Jewish population, and that for a long time now all matters have been dealt with from tendentious motives — especially after the bloc concluded between the non-party Hasidim and the Agudah — the kehilla has been turned into a Kremlin [Kreml; also a pun on "kremer", shopkeeper] where purely personal interests find expression. The latest fact, which has only just occurred — the engagement of Mr. Yudel Kaminer as assistant secretary in the kehilla — confirms the rightness of our action; the fact shows clearly what was aimed at with the presidential election. Let the Jewish population properly assess this shopkeeper's dealing and understand what is being aimed at and what they want to make of the Jewish kehilla: a branch office [ekspozytura] of the "Agudah". Let the Jewish population react to the deeds that have been done.
