The Public Outlook. (Sosnowiec Jewish councillors — unity, responsibility, a moral lesson.)

[Sosnowiec — opinion; city council.]
Public [?] work, political activity, the interests of the community — all this must be weighed and measured, calculated down to a minimum. Every smallest mistake, the slightest false step causes troubles and misfortunes, pain and suffering, and brings misfortune into every corner of our poor life.
We have a gratifying phenomenon to note for our Sosnowiec public. However small and insignificant it may be, it is nonetheless a gratifying phenomenon, one that must be reckoned with and that truly deserves to be welcomed.
It concerns the Jewish representation in the local self-government [the municipality]. True, the number of Jews there is not large and they cannot achieve much; nevertheless we see, when we look at it all attentively, that this is in fact a great thing.
In the previous city administration, for example, we had a total of 2 Jewish representatives, who even with the best will could achieve nothing at all. Nobody listened to them, and because of that they also lost heart; they did not have the boldness to demand as a large group, a strong representation, must demand. People did not want to hear them out, and they had nobody to talk to.
Why was the situation so bad and sad? Because at the time of those city-council elections things were arranged so that Jewish votes would be disqualified, that many would not be on the [voters'] list at all, and on our side there was no proper reaction — we barely, by a miracle, obtained 2 representatives; and what role, what significance can a representation of two members have in the Sosnowiec city council?
At the last city-council elections the situation changed in our favour, and now, besides the two Left "Poale Zion" representatives, we have 5 representatives of the bourgeois elements; and a representation of 5 people must already be reckoned with, a group of 5 representatives must already be listened to — and that, we say, is a great gain.
Now the Jewish voice is heard more strongly in the city council; when [?] an injustice is done, one hears its bitter expression. It makes no difference whether our embittered words are heeded or not — what matters to us, with such a small representation, is that the opportunity is not missed, that what needs to be said is said.
And so we saw that last week the Jewish councillors organized a public report meeting, where we had the opportunity to hear what had been done in the city council through our representatives and what had not been done, what it had been possible to react to and what it had not. After the previous inferior representation [misprinted "migderwertige"], the present one has great importance for us, if only because the representatives reckon with their voters and find it necessary to get in touch with them and tell them what they are able to accomplish for Jewish Sosnowiec and what not.
It goes without saying that one must absolutely see to it that unity reigns among the few Jewish councillors, and that each supports the other at every opportunity; this is one of the most important conditions to which the councillors must submit, and with which they will thus be able to support much and quite often achieve [?]. Unity is a kind of secret force, so strong a power that it can never be fully assessed; only by chance do we get the opportunity to see the strength of a united power, and then we marvel at the useful results that arose, which look as though they came about entirely by chance. But when one thinks more deeply, looks at it with full seriousness and understanding, one sees that the gain arose thanks to unity and to a clear view of the present and the future.
In public activity every movement, every step plays a role; everything must be calculated and consciously goal-directed. Conversely, the smallest mistake, the slightest bad calculation brings enormous harm to the community for years to come. This is what must be reckoned with, and conscientious representatives must always remember it well.
More than once we have occasion to speak of public brokenness, of squabbling over nothing and again nothing, which brings so much bad blood into our life, poisons and pollutes the air, and reaches the point where one cannot breathe, cannot find a place of rest; and then, at such a moment, one becomes so dejected, so downcast, that one loses one's awareness, loses one's balance, at such a moment one stops believing in the power of the community; one then sees before oneself only loneliness and brokenness, apathy and pessimism beyond measure and beyond bounds. At such a moment one does not want to remember that not all is lost, that disunity does not reign everywhere, that bright horizons may still appear in our gloomy sky.
And now, when we see that our small representation strives in the self-government to bring common benefit to the citizens of the town and reckons with the demands and wishes of its voters, this must be welcomed.
May these deeds prove that the goodwill of public representatives is an important factor in real life and can achieve much for all strata of the population.
May the activity of the present councillors be a moral lesson for all those who want to work for the good of the community and its interests; let them remember that unity, energy and goodwill are the strongest driving force and can often achieve more than one even imagines.
True, sincere public workers must always keep this before their eyes.
Dr. Papuri.
The Unveiling of Dr. Perlman's Tombstone in Sosnowiec.

[Sosnowiec — Zionism; memorial.]
A crowd of several hundred relatives, friends and acquaintances gathered on Sunday at the Sosnowiec Jewish cemetery to take part in the memorial and the unveiling of the tombstone of Dr. Abraham Perlman of blessed memory.
Around the deceased's grave, which is full of wreaths, a cordon is held by members of a committee and of "Maccabi"; only the family, relatives and guests are admitted. The mood is solemn. The town cantor Mr. Icchak Lejchter with his choir, under the direction of conductor Mr. Szywek [?], sings a chapter of Psalms and "El Male Rachamim" in the name of the family, the Zionist Organization, "Mizrachi", the Jewish community (kehilla), "Keren Hayesod", "Keren Kayemet", "Maccabi", "Cheder Mizrachi", S.W.Z. [?] Halberstam and a large number of friends; each family pledged trees in the Herzl Forest, in the special grove named after Dr. Perlman. Together the pledges amount to about 150 trees.
After the memorial prayers Mr. Lewi Jungster speaks (in Hebrew), stressing that one should not be content with memorial prayers for the esteemed deceased, but calling on the living to prove by deeds that the ideals of the deceased will be realized.
A moving short speech is given by Dr. Meladiste [?], who dwells on the fact that on the day of the first yahrzeit the 16th Zionist Congress opens in Zurich, where the question of the Jewish "Agency" is being dealt with, in which Dr. Perlman took so much interest.
— Rest in peace, dear comrade, we shall never forget you — with these words Dr. S. ends his speech.
The cantor and choir sing "Hatikvah", and with that the memorial ends.
From the Polish Health Resorts

By Ben Amotz.
(Impressions of a visit)
Gotszalkowice [Goczałkowice-Zdrój].
II.
In the first article we dwelt on several qualities by which this health resort „distinguishes“ itself. But we forgot a very „current“ [i.e. popular] article for which Goczałkowice has won fame.
This current article is — gnats.. The first reception, pardon, I mean the reception of your feet, is given you by these pmes[?], these invisible little creepy-crawlies, thanks to which you instantly acquire an occupation:
— scratching yourself till you bleed...
The greatest „revenge“ they, the gnats, take on the fair sex that comes here for a cure, and at every step you meet elegant ladies with bandaged legs...
But that is not what we are after now. We only want to give what we promised earlier — a short characterisation of matters of eating in general and of kosher food in particular.
The question of kosher food concerns not only the resort of Goczałkowice but the whole[?] line on which the Upper Silesian spa and dacha resorts lie.
Our „dachnitsas“ (summer-holiday ladies) have cast disfavour on the dacha places of „Kongresówka“ [Congress Poland]. It has gone out of fashion for a woman who still talks of a „garsonówka“[?] to go for summer lodgings to the small surrounding towns or villages.
The dacha ladies know the truth: that the former dacha places are much better and more comfortable and, above all, much cheaper.
But what impression will it make when her „pszyjaciółki“ [przyjaciółki — girlfriends] hear that she spent her summer at, say, Olkusz, Kamieńsk, Złoty Potok? It is simply a „wstyd“ [shame] to spend the summer months on the beggars' line, where all the yentes go to graze...
It is more respectable and „intelligent“, after all, to boast: „I was in Szczyrk, Milówka, Bystra and the like.“ Oh, there is nothing to eat there? So what is the fuss? A little one doesn't eat one's fill, a little one brings over from home, a little one sins on top — and the dacha question is solved with all the pitshpeukes[?]...
Well, the grown-ups manage as best they can. Worse, however, is the eating question for the children, for whose sake one actually goes away, so that they may build themselves up a little.
— What does one do, then, when the little ones want a meat lunch and the railway-ticket cashier, who also has „ordination“ for slaughtering (because his great-grandfather, who descended from „Yordn“[?], was a shochet...), is not at home?
Then it matters a great deal what kind of mother the children have... If the mother's father is a sharp Hasid, the daughter rules on her own that at a dacha children may eat „bosor kvitsh“[?]. Quite indifferently the mother takes the little children under her arm and leads them into a Christian restaurant where (in her expert opinion) there are very „smaczne obiady“ [tasty lunches]... But when the mother is the daughter of a simple Jew, she has sorrow and sighing until she obtains something to eat for the little ones; she writes letters home asking them to send a few blueberry biscuits, a piece of sausage, and for Shabbat the „sick“ mother travels to a nearby shtetl, where she has a fowl slaughtered in honour of Shabbat and also in honour of her husband, the „straw widower“, who comes over for Shabbat — let him see what a respectable wife he has: even abroad she buys „bargains“...
Compared to other dacha resorts, Goczałkowice is an „exception“ in this field. The spa guests who come here from Zagłębie „labour“ in the sweat of their brow just to obtain kosher meat for Shabbat, I say[?] for Shabbat, because the whole week [printed „hokh“] one makes do with dairy „dishes“ — is there a choice? One is here, after all, on a „kuracja“ [cure]...
The shopping in honour of Shabbat is done with noise and uproar, so that the guests who live around and next to the Kurhaus are startled awake every Friday at 5 o'clock in the morning by the terrible voices and wild shouting.
There they run, the „sick“ women, baskets in hand, to Dziedzice, where they buy „bargains“ from the peasant women — various products and above all fowl, over which the Dziedzice shochet pronounces the blessing...
At 7 o'clock they come back with the dead stock, tired, with feeble hands and bandaged legs they drag themselves to their places of exile and set about the work..
The work is done collectively. Around the table standing in the yard of the peasant cottage the fowls are laid out and expert opinions are given as to which woman has bought a fat bargain.
More than once, however, the feminine idyll is suddenly broken by a woman crying out:
— Woe is me[?], a nail in the gizzard!..
— Heaven protect and defend me — cries a second — there you have perforated gizzards!
— Run to Dziedzice to ask a question [of ritual law].
— Yes, easy to say, run to Dziedzice on bandaged legs... I'll wait till my husband comes, let him go with the question...
And when the husband arrives, his woman of valour pours out her bitter heart to him, tells him about the perforated gizzard, and honours him with the trip to Dziedzice.
Well, does the straw widower have a choice? He takes the gizzard and off he goes to Dziedzice.
The local rabbinic judge examines the „antique“ and after brief deliberation says:
— „You must bring me the intestines as well“...
— Have pity, it is already Friday past midday, I myself am a [—][?] and I am in danger of coming back with my intestines...
— I told you, I must see the intestines.
And when the question-asker comes back, his „sick“ wife asks him curiously:
— Well, what's new?
— Give me the intestines here...

What Are They Sitting There For? (The Będzin heads of the kehilla. — Their rise and fall. — When do they intend to leave their seats?)

And we were[?] [—] so naive and believed that now [—] there would be an end to it; now — so it seemed to us — [—] the campaign is ending. For the time being it is all a "yesterday's day"[?] [i.e. a pipe dream]; only now do we see that not[?] only is it not over yet, [—] but they are only just beginning [—] to sit at the green table and to conduct [—] politics on which the world stands.
We thought that the moment the president of the Będzin Jewish Kehilla Board resigned from his office, there would be no more board, no more council, and the whole "cheder" would be dissolved.
For now it turns out that we are no good politicians, that we were too naive when we had the courage and the understanding to think so.
We simply could not imagine that, given the present sad state of affairs in the Kehilla Board, the events would not be an opportune moment to dissolve the institution, to put an end to the unheard-of deeds being done there.
We could not have reckoned that there would be people who would want precisely to fish in troubled waters.
We did not know that the Będzin Jewish Kehilla Board now needs a president in order to "save Jewishness"; otherwise people would not have moved heaven and earth, otherwise they would not have[?] brought the rabbi here all the way from Otwock and pushed through what they wanted, what the "Agudah" needed — they have got their own president, and their position is secured.
It goes without saying that against the person as a private individual one can have nothing; on the contrary — a very decent Jew, an honest man, a householder in the town. But one thing should have been understood: that the qualities listed above are still far too little even for a man to become a public emissary, to represent anyone at all, let alone when he becomes the representative of the entire Jewish kehilla, the president of the Jewish population of Będzin. And then, when this man begins to represent us and you, we and you have the right to demand of him that he be worthy of representing us and you, that he be capable of speaking in our name and in yours.
And let us be allowed to be frank and say that this man, with all his virtues, is not capable of speaking in our name or of doing anything whatever for our sake and for yours.
The man literally does not understand what such a thing as the public sphere is, public interest, public responsibility. He has never occupied himself with such matters. He is a simple Jew of the old generation, and he himself will quite honestly admit to you that he is not versed in "present-day matters".
It goes without saying that it is a piece of impudence on people's part to try to push this through, to talk such a Jew into believing that he would be fit to take over the responsible and high post which to this day, in all towns, is held by the most intelligent and most capable personalities. Previously, after all, this office was held among us by the former[?] Sejm deputy ("g. Sejm deputy") Dr. Weinzieher, and later by the president of the Polish zinc industry, Mr. Szymon Fürstenberg.
That is how we keep sinking, how we fall ever deeper and deeper — and yet nobody sees it, nobody feels it. Possibly some do see it, possibly many do understand and grasp how far we are going backwards — but they make nothing of it, they remain indifferent[?] and ice-cold to everything. Therein lies the real tragedy.
Incidentally, it is altogether incomprehensible what people are sitting there for, in the kehilla "shtibl", once it is turning into a real "shtibl of the dead".
Such an institution costs this town so much money — and who[?] gets anything out of it? If in former times the kehilla was a "shtibl of the dead", at least it cost almost nobody anything. But now, if it is also no more than a "shtibl of the dead", why does it drag so much money out of every single Jew? If people go on paying, then Jewish Będzin has the right to demand something of such an institution. So what do we get today from our Kehilla Board? For whom does it do anything, and what does it do?
But why repeat what has already been said so many times, what has already been written so many times.
Surely everyone knows that this institution costs the town a lot of money and that hardly anybody gets anything out of it. Surely it is known that none of the parnassim takes any further interest in running the institution, and that is precisely why the situation there grows ever worse and worse, uglier and uglier.
And therefore — what is the point of sitting there? Why burden the citizens with so many municipal taxes? The whole town without exception is incensed against the present communal leaders — so what do you achieve by it, when you are there and do nothing, since you are responsible for everything that is done there as long as you do not leave the kehilla seats.
It is high time you vacated your seats, if only because your term ended long ago. So what magnetic force holds you so tightly that you cannot free yourselves from it on your own? Is somebody forcing you to wait until the moment comes — and it is very near — when Jewish Będzin will unanimously begin to storm you and demand your resignation?
— So what are you sitting there for?
R. Let.
The Vienna Autumn Fair

It can be said with full justice that the expectations now placed on the Vienna Autumn Fair, which will take place from 1 to 8 September of this year, are very optimistic. The last spring fair, which was held under the worst weather conditions, nevertheless had a very good success. The heavy tourist traffic in summer and the great popularity of Vienna as an international travel destination give great and good hopes for the Vienna Autumn Fair.
In addition, the present autumn fair will feature various special events: the French and the Russian exhibitions, the fur-fashion salon, a textile-machinery fair, a radio exhibition, an exhibition of supplies for hotels, coffee houses and restaurants, an exhibition of fermentation products and luxury foods (Gärungs- und Genussmittel); further there will be an exhibition of technical novelties and inventions, a building fair and a road-building fair, [displays] of Austrian mining, of agriculture and forestry, of dairy and horticulture, an exhibition of livestock and fish, and the like — these will be attractions that will greatly enliven the picture of the fair.
The three fair buildings and the grounds around the technical fair are almost completely booked, because not only Austria's industry, crafts and agriculture are coming, but also exhibitors from 16 countries, who see in the Vienna Fair the best instrument for making connections with merchants from all over the world.
The fair management has obtained a whole series of facilities and reductions for the journey to the Vienna Fair. Whoever buys a fair pass (Messeausweis) from the honorary representative in his own country no longer needs an Austrian visa and also does not need a Czech transit visa; the German visa, too, is obtained free of charge. The Hungarian transit visa is obtained at half price.
With the fair pass one gets a 25 per cent reduction on the railways of: Bulgaria, Germany, the Saar Territory, Greece, Italy, Poland, Romania, Switzerland, Yugoslavia, Czechoslovakia and Turkey; the French railways have extended their return tickets until 12 September. On the Hungarian railways one has the right to buy a ticket for the lower class and travel in a higher class. Besides this, reductions on fares are given by the Danube Steamship Company and the Royal Hungarian Shipping Company, and many Yugoslav, Italian and Romanian shipping companies give reductions of 25 to 50 per cent. The large air-transport companies give reductions of ten to twenty per cent.
Revenge

[Literature — short story.] (A story) by Z. Szer.

Herman Lipshitz, a man in his forties, with a pair of blue, distant eyes, was sitting with friends at a table in a café; he was drinking black coffee, smoking a cigarette and slowly letting coils of smoke out of his mouth.

At the table a lively conversation was going on, but Lipshitz took no part in it. He sat lost in thought; a kind of quiet sadness lay on his face and on his soft eyes. He smoked cigarette after cigarette, sipped the strong coffee and kept silent.

Into the café came a middle-aged woman of some thirty-six to thirty-eight and a young girl of fifteen or sixteen. It looked as though they were here in the café for the first time, strangers, because the din of loud talk, the loud bursts of laughter and the thick smoke confused them so much that they remained standing in the middle of the café, until a waiter rescued them from their embarrassment and led them to a table.

In the café, where everyone knew everyone else, there was always a little stir whenever new, unfamiliar faces appeared, especially women's. At once people at every table would look at them. Because the woman and the girl who had come in were new faces in the café, and also because at first they had remained standing so bewildered in the middle of the café, they drew everyone's attention all the more, and everyone's eyes were fixed on them.

Lipshitz too craned his neck and raised his eyes to take a look at the woman and the girl; but as soon as he had looked, he seemed to shrink, sat back down, began to fidget restlessly on his chair, and with his fingers began nervously kneading a piece of soft bread.

"His Dora?... His former wife... What is she doing here?.. How does she come to be here? . And who is the girl? His daughter, surely!.. Can it be? Is it Ewcia?... Why yes, surely, it is she. How beautifully she has grown up!... But how do they come to be here?... Is it just a coincidence, or did they come in here on purpose?.." His heart began to pound, and his temples too, and the blood began rushing hastily to his head.

He looked once more at the woman and the girl. And the longer he looked at them, the harder it was for him to tear his eyes away, and the more restlessly and nervously he began to shift on his chair.

It was not long before Lipshitz rose from his chair, left his table and walked over to the woman and girl who had come in, followed by everyone's eyes...

* * *

Lipshitz's sudden approach so surprised and unsettled Dora that for several minutes she almost lost her breath. Different colours began to leap and change across her face. Her lips turned white as a corpse's, and her throat grew so tight that she had to fight for a little air.

Ewcia did not know Lipshitz, her father. She did not know who the man was. She could not understand what had suddenly happened to her mother, and with her innocent, curious eyes she looked restlessly and shyly from her mother to Lipshitz and from Lipshitz to her mother.

They had been separated for twelve years already. When he left her, Ewcia was a little over three years old, and Dora had suffered enough from it. She was left forlorn, unprotected and all alone, as if in the middle of the sea. How much she had suffered! What a bitter struggle she had waged to keep herself and the child alive! But it did not break her pride. She made him no scandals or hysterical scenes, nor did she come to him to beg. As soon as she saw that she was superfluous to him, she stepped out of his way and withdrew into her loneliness. She found a room with a poor family, where she could leave the child, and began looking for a means of living.

There were years upon years of torment. In summer she worked as a servant in a summer hotel, so that her child should have fresh air. Nothing was too hard for her, so long as her child lacked nothing. All those years she had one concern — to raise her Ewcia healthy and beautiful, to make a decent person of her.

To Ewcia she never spoke about her father; she never mentioned his name to her and never told her anything about him. When Ewcia was still a little child and began pestering her with questions about Papa — where is Papa — she would answer her: gone away, far, far away... She suffered a great deal from the child's questions. Her heart would pound and pinch [?], and more than once she had to run into another room to hide from the child and have a good cry. Later, when Ewcia grew older, and began herself to understand life a little and to learn of the troubles and tragedies of family life, she understood by herself, from her mother's silence and from her weary, dried-out eyes, her mother's misfortune, and she asked no more questions about her father.

Yet it always grieved and pained Dora that Lipshitz had so forgotten and renounced his child and never came to see her. "How can a father do it!" — she thought with stifled pain — "how can one tear one's own child out of one's heart like that!"... The one merit she found in him was this: that he, as she knew him, was a man without firm character, who was never master of himself, a slave to life and to his second wife, who held him firmly in her hands; but forgive him — that she could never do.

* * *

Lipshitz looked at Ewcia's pretty little face and his eyes shone with sudden joy. He could hardly believe that this tender, blossoming flower was his child.

Fatherly love now stormed up in him with such force. How he would love his daughter now! He is so hungry for the love of a child! He longs so for the caresses and tenderness of a child of his own — and she is, after all, his child...

"Dora," he said quietly to his former wife, "is this our Ewcia? How beautifully she has grown up!" — and he looked like a sinner at his wife and child.

All the hatred, resentment and bitterness that had gathered in her heart against Lipshitz through all the years in which he had left her alone with a small child now awoke in her. All the troubles and sufferings she had endured through all those years until she had raised Ewcia now rose in her memory, and she answered in an agitated voice full of bitterness:

"Yes, Mr. Lipshitz, this is my daughter" — and she looked at him with sharp, piercing glances.

So they sat for a while in painful silence. Then she suddenly stood up and said, with liveliness and boldness in her voice:

"Ewcia, my child, put on your coat. We are going."

* * *

In the street a fresh, cold stream of air swept over her like a wave. She filled her lungs with fresh air and breathed freely. Slipping Ewcia's hand under her arm, she pressed it more firmly to herself and walked with her with firm, quick steps.
Dr. A. Weissman — The Seduced Girl (a novel of Jewish life in the Old World, based on historical facts), instalment 14

[Literature — serial novel; "The Seduced Girl" by Dr. A. Weissman, instalment 14.]
(A novel of Jewish life in the Old World, based on historical facts.)

In the mind of the "aunt", Sichojańska [?], a new plan took shape:
Jan had rescued Mania from Ludwig; she is very grateful to him for not letting Ludwig harm her. They must be brought together, and it must be seen to that afterwards she marries him. Jan will grab at it with both hands; he is quietly in love with Mania to death, otherwise he would not have rescued her. He does not dare to tell her so, but if I step in here, a match will come of it.
And thinking thus, she said to Mania:
"Do you want to see Jan?"
"Yes, I want to thank him."
"Besides, you will be able to find out everything from him about your parents, because before our departure he saw your parents; from him you will learn everything."
"I will be very grateful to you if you call him in to us at once."
The "aunt" went out of the room to call Jan, who was waiting in the convent office.
The "aunt" asked Jan out into the garden and sat down with him on a bench.
"Tell me, Jan, do you want to see Mania?"
"I will consider myself fortunate if I can see her. After all, that is why I travelled with you."
"Only for that? And I did not know that it was only for Mania's sake... I thought you came because I asked you; knowing that, after Ludwig's bad behaviour towards Mania, she had become very kind to you, I asked you to travel with me."
"But I must confess, and here in the convent I will tell no lie: I have always loved Mania, only, seeing that she never so much as looked at me and was always friendly with Ludwig, I suffered a great deal in silence. But God sent me an opportunity in which I could show up Ludwig's bad behaviour and my love for her."
"I can only give you my blessing. Perhaps, thanks to you, she will go over to our faith. All of us and the whole convent will be grateful to you if you manage to persuade her to be baptised as soon as possible."
"That is my only wish. You know Mania, what a strong character she has. I will not use foul means like Ludwig; I esteem her too much, I love her."
"Perhaps it will go well. I will take you to her at once and leave you both alone, only be a man, don't be an old woman — you are a man, after all. If it goes well, so much the better; if not, you must use every means. You know that she must not be let go back to the Jews. If we let her go free, we could all come to grief. Just make up your mind firmly, stop at nothing, tell her that — that the way back to the Jews is cut off for her forever; tell her that when she comes home the Jews will torment her, and her parents will even help them, and that only with you will she be happy."
"Ah! How happy! I will work for her all my life, I will let no harm come to her, if only I may hear a kind word from her."
"You will be able to achieve everything, only be a man. Everything is in your hands, and the whole convent will help you too. Come, I will let you in to her."
They rose from the bench and set off along the long convent corridors, where the rooms of the "Sisters" are.
Even before Jan crossed the threshold of the room where Mania was, he already pictured her beauty, her eyes, her curls, her white, graceful [?] face.
"Here, go into this room," the "aunt" said quietly, "only remember, be a man! Later, still today, we shall see each other."
With trembling hands Jan knocked at the door, which Mania opened at once.
"Jan!" Mania cried out with joy. "I am glad to see you. I don't know at all how to thank you for rescuing me from vile Ludwig. I always took you for an honest man, but so much I did not expect even myself. You risked your life for me. Oh, my parents and I will never forget you. Like a good angel you always come in a time of trouble. You have already rescued me once, so rescue me now too, out of the convent, and take me to my parents. I believe in you; with you I will set out into the dark night, until we reach the first town and hire a cart there."
Jan could not utter a word.
"Well, why are you silent? Are you against me too?"
"Mania," Jan barely began, "you know that I am an honest, believing Christian. How can I commit such a sin as to take you away from the convent against the will of all the 'Sisters' and of the eldest 'Sister', Irena? I could lose both worlds, and no penance would help me afterwards. It would be the greatest sin for me if I committed such a transgression; I must not do it. If you told me to give up my whole life for you at once, I would do it with joy; but what you demand of me is not possible."
"What, then, good Jan, is left for me to do?"
"Be baptised, and then you will be free, then you will be happy. Why should you remain among Jews? And what kind of life awaits you among Jews?"
"And what awaits me here? My bones will lie, after a hundred and twenty years, in the cellars of the convent together with the bones of all the other 'Sisters' — no, no, I would rather live, and where my bones will lie after my death is all the same to me."
"Who will force you then to remain a nun? Once they have baptised you, you will be free and can live as you wish."
"They will not let me go; they need me here, I myself don't know for what black year."
"Just get baptised, and then I will see to it that you do not stay here."
"But my heart draws me to my parents; I want to be among my own."
"Then why did you run away with Ludwig?"
"Oh, it is a long story to tell you all of it now, but it will be enough if I tell you that I loved Ludwig with my whole life; only now Ludwig is completely dead to me. So what have I to do here?"
"Mania! If you really know what it means to love, you must stay here for the sake of another, who loves you with his whole life."
Mania drew away from Jan in fright.
"Who is it, then, who loves me so much that he demands my whole life as a sacrifice? Tell me, Jan, I know nothing at all."
Jan was silent...
Jan sat for some minutes with his head bowed. He felt that her heart was far from him, and with a pitiful face and a heavy voice he spoke the words:
"You ask who loves you so much that he demands your whole life as a sacrifice? I love you as my whole life; you are dearer to me than anything in the world, but I demand no sacrifices of you."
Jan himself was frightened by his words; he fell on his knees.
"I kneel before you as before a saint; I know that you do not love me, and perhaps you cannot love me, but I beg for pity."
Mania exclaimed angrily:
"Get up at once! I cannot watch a man on his knees begging for pity — it disgusts me.
A man must be strong and not beg. You know Chaim, who used to sit at our house; everyone knows that he wanted to be my bridegroom. He is a very decent and good fellow, and, if you want to know, a handsome young man as well, and yet I never liked him. And do you know why? Only because he is an old woman, too much of a goody-goody [?], with a pitiful face, weak, timid. Well, one can forgive that in Chaim — he is a Jew, a Jew cannot be otherwise. But if you, Jan, are like that too, that is beyond understanding. And it is just my misfortune that people with pitiful faces and weak characters fall in love with me."
"And Ludwig?"
"And Ludwig, you ask? He did not love me, he only deceived me, and you have seen it for yourself no less than I. If only he had been a little finer and more decent — how happy I would have counted myself if he had loved me."
"But I believe that nothing more can happen between you and Ludwig now."
"Certainly. He is dead to me, only my heart is wounded, broken."
"And what can you tell me — with what, Mania, can I go away from you [?]?"
Mania shrugged her shoulders.
"Do you at least know how much I love you?"
"I did not know about it before, but if you say so, I believe you."
"No, I did indeed notice that you were always kind to me: when as children we ran about the village together, you never hurt me like all the other village boys; we both loved to play together; then we grew up — what could I have noticed?"
"How blind you were! I was always together with Ludwig, who used to boast everywhere that you were in love with him; I too noticed that between you there was more than an ordinary friendly relationship. What more could I do than keep silent? For years I kept silent and suffered; there was no end to my suffering.
Like a shadow I would always follow you, and the fact that you never noticed me humiliated [?] me still more in my own eyes.
When it was decided at the Sichojańskis' that you and Ludwig would go away and that after the baptism you would both marry, I said that one could not rely on an ordinary carter, and I dressed in carter's clothes, and we travelled together."

Dachas.

[Feuilleton — summer; holiday dachas in Zagłębie.] (Feuilleton).
By J. G. Sztejnsapir.
With the coming of the dacha season a question lodged itself in my head and kept boring [?] into my brain without let-up: the situation in town is gloomy, the merchants are reduced to beggary on all sides, and nevertheless people here are going off to dachas this year not badly at all — where does it come from?
Just take a stroll through our homegrown "resorts" and you will see how stuffed they are with dacha folk.
About the surrounding villages there is certainly nothing to say: every village has become a health resort, and "from the whole town nations flock to it" — let a peasant merely announce that his "kurnik" [chicken coop] has become free, that he has slaughtered the rooster along with the hen, and in their place a "couple of people" will soon come running...
Where, then, does such a dacha epidemic come from? What drives our public so into the lap of nature — their lyrical souls, the "stuffed" pockets full of money, or something else?
I took such a strong interest in this matter and dissected it so thoroughly that I arrived at the meaning — there are no lyrical souls, there are no pockets full of money; the real reason is — the third version: the "something else".
And how does the "something else" express itself? Very simply: people run off to dachas not out of delight but out of grief [a pun: "viltog" — "veytog"].
History repeats itself, and we are now living through a time [?] again as in the era of "and it came to pass in the days of the German" [the German occupation in World War I]..
With only one difference: then people ran to seek the small-town cheapness — the cheap bread with the cheap potatoes; today they flee from big-city costliness — from the silk stockings with the modern little shoes and dresses.
A Jew, burdened with a wife and several daughters, who spins like a dreidel, signs ten-złoty promissory notes and has them protested, nevertheless allows himself to pay three hundred złoty for a dacha and sends his household off to sniff fresh air...
How can that be? The answer is: the Jew is no fool, he has done his reckoning in advance — he knows how much a week of little dresses, little shoes, stockings, cinema, theatre and what not costs him in town. And at the dacha, "in the lap of nature," one needs nothing at all, except the bit of food for the stomach, which costs money in town too — barefoot and naked is the height of fashion there, and baking all his daughters in the sun costs him far less in the village than baking his wife in town — at the baker's, on babka...
And this reckoning all Jews know, both those who have wives with daughters and those who have only wives. Since one talks [?] — for a nation of merchants it is simply out of the question.
Incidentally, besides the main reckoning there is an additional one: a dacha is an asset for credit, for matches, and above all — one is, after all, a bit of a human being oneself, one also wants to rest a little and stay in town without the family..
And the peasant in the village already knows the Jewish reckoning too — a Jew comes to him, he lets him his hut and climbs up to the attic himself, and when a second Jew comes he lets him the attic and climbs onto the chimney — in town, little Jew, you hang in the air, so let me have the same pleasure in the village...
So the Jew sits in the peasant's hut and draws village contentment in exchange for his town sorrow — here he is a "pan" [lord], for him the cows are milked, for him the hens lay — he is "doing dacha"..
And we are already feeling a shortage of dacha places; all the surrounding little towns and villages are flooded with dacha people, and it no longer has to be a forest with a river, just a bit of air to sniff and a bit of sun to bake in...
How then shall we quench this dacha-thirst in the near future?
There is a remedy: around Zagłębie we still have quite a few places where formerly one could not have a dacha because of the stench of the chimneys — now they can be turned into real resorts: the factories are closed, the chimneys do not smoke, and the Przemsza can replace the real mud baths...
Sooner or later this remedy, too, will have to be carried out, for poverty does not stand still among us — it grows, and together with it the "dachas" must grow too...
Ignoramuses and Boors (Amei-ha'aretz and Amei-ha'aratzot).

[Feuilleton — folklore and humour.] (Tales, anecdotes and folk sayings)
By Yosef Zelkowicz.
Already in the Talmud one finds all the contempt that the Jewish people felt for the amei-ha'aretz and amei-ha'aratzot [ignoramuses].
— At an am-ha'aretz's, according to the Talmud, one may not eat any bread unless one knows for certain that the grain from which the bread was baked has been tithed.
With an am-ha'aretz one may not set out alone on the road.
With an am-ha'aretz one may not associate, may not eat with him at one table, may not spend time in his company, etc., etc.
It is therefore no wonder that the ancient People of the Book — the people that has always responded to good and to bad with the Torah, and has always kept within the four cubits of halakha — that this very people never spared the am-ha'aretz, but took him apart and dissected him limb by limb with its sharp wit, with genuine Jewish mockery, and with its irony made him, as the saying goes, "like the dust of the earth" [ke'afra de'ar'a].
Hundreds and thousands of sayings, proverbs, tales and anecdotes the Jewish people can tell, mocking the amei-ha'aretz.
And some of them I want to pass on here to our readers.
— — —
An old Hebrew proverb says: "A mere questioner — an am-ha'aretz" — one who asks questions just like that, into thin air, shows that he is a coarse fellow. But in such a matter as ignoramuses the people does not content itself with a trifling [?] saying; on such a saying the people can tell dozens of tales about blockheaded questions that ignoramuses have posed, and how learned Jews answered them:
Esau Was a Dozor...
A dozor [kehilla board member], a coarse fellow who stands at the eastern wall next to the rabbi and listens as the rabbi says the Shema word by word while the congregation is silent, decides that after prayers he must shame the rabbi in front of the whole congregation with a question he will put to him, one the rabbi will not be able to answer.
After prayers. The rabbi stands with a few prominent men and tells them some more Torah. The dozor walks up:
— Good Shabbes, Rebbe, I have a question to ask you that nobody has yet answered for me.
— What is the question? Let's hear it!
— The question is: "Esau was a wicked man, wasn't he — so how does he get into the Shema? (Venatati esev besadecha — 'and I will give grass in thy fields')"..
To which the rabbi answered him on the spot:
Because Esau had a lot of money and became a dozor, they put him into the Shema...
Haman's Merit...
A coarse fellow once asks a scholar:
— What merit did Haman have, that a special portion was written about him — Parashat ha-Man, which Jews recite every day after prayers?
The scholar could see whom he was dealing with, and that if he explained that the portion doesn't mean Haman at all but the manna [man], and that the fellow simply knows no Hebrew, the coarse fellow would boil over and get angry — so he answered him with a little homily:
— Since Haman was hanged on the seventh day of Passover (according to the Talmud — on the second day of Passover), on the very same day that the Jews had to cross the sea, it follows that they could not at the same time be in Shushan, where Haman was hanged; therefore the Jews made a special portion that is recited every day after prayers, so that every day one recalls Haman's downfall — and so one naturally has a better appetite for breakfast...
— Then why don't we say "Haman" after prayers on Shabbes too?
— Because on Shabbes one has an appetite for eating anyway, since one makes Kiddush over brandy...
He Rattles Off the Holy Tongue Like Cupping-Glasses.
In a village there lived an arendar [leaseholder], a coarse soul, but for all that stuffed with money like Korah.
The arendar had three sons, like poles [?] and louts [?] like Esau.
When the sons grew up, the arendar took them to town to a melamed and said:
— Here, Rebbe, you have my "labour of my hands" — my bitter toil; take them and make people of them, as it is written in the holy Shulchan Aruch: "The Torah speaks of four sons" — lads, no evil eye, like bears...
The poor melamed tore his heart out, toiled [?] with them day and night and could not teach them even the shape of an aleph — such thick heads they had!
So the arendar thought it over, took them back to the village and brought a melamed down for them, a refined young man from the town.
The melamed spent three whole years at the arendar's, and in the end, when he saw he could achieve nothing with the "druvalyes" [lanky louts], he thought it over and ran away back to town at night.
Next morning, when the arendar woke up and noticed that the melamed had gone into "deep exile", he was no lazy fellow and ran after him.
In town he caught him, grabbed him by the collar and dragged him to the rabbi.
— "Good morning, holy tzaddik, with this Jew here I want a ben-Torah" [i.e. a din-Torah, a rabbinical lawsuit]...
— What do you want of this Jew? What din-Torah do you have with him?
So the arendar began to plead in these words:
— Holy Rebbe, I took on this Jew to study with my sons "ad shpistaav" ("ad sheyista'ev" — a beast, a firstling, may not be slaughtered until it has got a blemish) until the Torah comes crawling out of them over the top. On the contrary, let him say himself: "mazga" [sic] I kept him "three wives at my table" — for 3 years he gnawed my bones bare, "at the break of dawn", like a wild ox, and all of a sudden he makes a grab, "neither bears nor forest" — without a by-your-leave — and runs off! But I am no lazy fellow, and I did as it says in the holy Haggadah: "With my staff I crossed this Jordan" — I took my feet on my shoulders and ran after him! So I come up to the butchers' stalls and take a look — "and the child is not" — the lad is here!... So I grabbed him "by his bald head and his forehead" — by the collar and by the lapels, and gave a shout: "Ye shall cast it to the dogs" — in to the rabbi!
And here he is, holy Rebbe, and let him say "If I am not for myself, who is for me" — who is he and who am I! At my place, thank God, there is "darkness and gloom, chaos and void" — rye and wheat and barley and oats! But he?! He is "neither of thy sting nor of thy honey" — good neither for God nor for people!...
The rabbi heard out the claim and could by no means hold back his laughter, and asks him:
— Very good, you are quite right, but where did you learn to speak the Holy Tongue so finely?..
— I'll tell you, Rebbe, the arendar answered: the truth is that I really never studied; so you'll ask, Rebbe, "Wherefore should the nations say" — if one doesn't study, how does one know?! — Well, the answer is "avarim haygu" [sic, for avadim hayinu, "we were slaves"]: I have a neighbour, his name is Maciek; so once early in the morning I go out into the village like that, I meet Maciek and he asks me: "Nie widziałeś czasem, Jankiel, mojego psa?" [Haven't you seen my dog by any chance, Jankiel?] — that is, whether I, Yankl, hadn't happened to meet his dog?.. So I gave him an answer back, as it says in the verse: "Am I my brother's keeper?" — am I your dog's scapegoat?! And so, from then on, I let myself into the Holy Tongue, and that's how I rattle it off like cupping-glasses, holy Rebbe!...
A Jewish girl from a respectable home is ruined in Katowice

[Crime and incidents — Lwów, Przemyśl, Katowice; prostitution.] On Repisanga [?] Street in Lemberg [Lwów] a big brawl took place a few days ago. Around midnight, in the vicinity of the "Bagatela", a fight broke out between a drunken young Jewish prostitute and a pimp. The fight was a bloody one, so that the police had to intervene, and the prostitute was arrested.
It turned out that the arrested woman is called Rachel B., is twenty-some years old, very beautiful, truly "blood and milk", comes from a respectable middle-class home in Przemyśl, and fell victim to frivolity.
It began only a year and a half ago. The economic crisis took on ever wider forms. Merchants became impoverished, and the business of our Rachel's parents also began to go downhill.
Earlier her parents had been wealthy, so a handsome dowry had been saved up for her, but, as is usual with today's girls, she could not pick a bridegroom. Here the family pedigree did not suit her, there the groom was not elegant, handsome or educated enough; in another case the candidate for her husband was a small earner, and so on.
Times began to get worse and worse. Slowly the daughter's dowry was eaten up, and now the tragedy began:
She would have married by now and not looked at all the "shortcomings" she had previously taken into account in matches. But now only scarce takers could be found willing to take her without a dowry.
Seeing that things were not coming to a conclusion, her parents told the neighbours that they were giving their daughter a dowry of 5000 dollars; when it came to paying it out, it turned out that there was no dowry. Once it even went so far that the tnoyim [engagement contract] had been signed and the "breaking of the plate" held; when the groom found out that there was no dowry, the celebration was broken off and they parted.
This the girl could no longer bear, and having a little cash on her, she left. She travelled wherever her eyes carried her.
On the train she got acquainted with a person before whom the inexperienced girl poured out her bitter heart and told the whole story. This person took "pity" on her, introduced himself as a rich merchant and took her with him to Katowice. He lived with her for a short time, ruined her, and then threw her out.
Left as if adrift on the water, she began to fall from rung to rung; pimps and simply shady characters exploited the situation in which she finds herself, and she was hurled into the "abyss of life".
Finally she came to Lemberg. Here the well-known Lemberg pimps snatched her up and took from her every "earned" penny. It went so far that out of misery and hunger she began to drink.
Now she is once again sitting in prison for brawling.
Not like in the novel

[Feuilleton — humorous story; married life.] By B. Kovner.

Hershl comes home from work tired, angry, agitated, sweaty, famished; he throws off his hat and his jacket, goes over to the sink, washes his hands and face, remains standing and waits for someone to hand him a towel.
When he sees he is being left standing like that, he gets even more agitated.
"Give me a towel!" he shouts at his wife. "Why do you leave me standing like a golem with a wet face? Give me a towel?"
Hershl's wife is in no hurry; she is busy with the novel she is reading in a newspaper.
She likes the novel; she envies the heroine. The way she is loved by her beloved — nobody is loved like that! He kisses not only her cheeks, her eyes, her hair, her hands and lips, but even the hem of her dress.
Since she has been married to Hershl, he has never yet kissed the hem of her dress. Nor her hands, and certainly not her hair; lately he doesn't even want to kiss her lips, her Hershl... He says: "I hate kissing painted lips; it's simply unhealthy; doctors say to avoid painted lips" — while the hero of the novel doesn't stop to think. He kisses. When you have a husband like that, it's good; you know what life is; if she had a husband like the hero of the novel, she would become 15 years younger.
That is what she thinks, holding the newspaper in her hand, and she is in no hurry to give her Hershl a towel to wipe his face; for she doesn't love Hershl!
He shouts even louder:
"Why don't you give me a towel? With a proper housewife the towel is always ready."
"You know where the towels are — one takes it oneself!"
He takes a towel himself, wipes himself, throws it away, angry, grumbling, takes the comb out of his waistcoat pocket, combs his hair, and in doing so notices how his hair is falling out, and thinks: "My friends did tell me not to marry her; 'You'll regret it,' they said, 'you'll be chewing the earth because of her,' they warned him, and I didn't want to listen to them; now I have the misfortune in the house; that pretty little face of hers fooled me, her dimple is for me nothing but a grave... a grave where my youth is being buried..."
He looks around, sees no food on the table, the table isn't set at all, the stove is cold, nothing is being cooked.
What then is he going to eat? He is hungry, he feels faint; for breakfast he had a roll with butter and washed it down with a glass of cold milk. On meals like that you can't have any strength to work.
"Is there dinner?" asks Hershl, and his anger burns more fiercely.
"Go down to the tavern and eat something; I'm not hungry, I've just eaten, also at the tavern."
"Why don't you cook dinner like all decent women?"
"Because I am not a decent woman," she answers with a jab. "The very fact that I landed with a husband like you shows that I'm not decent."
"What kind of talk is that?"
"What kind of talk is yours? You may and I may not?"
"But [?] I want to eat!"
"I told you, go down to the tavern and eat!"
"I give you 100 zlotys a week, what do you do with the money?"
"I need a dress once in a while, a hat, a pair of shoes, underwear — I buy them for that money, and whatever is left over I have for food... but since nothing is left over, there's nothing for food..."
"So every week you spend the whole money on clothes?"
"Yes."
"It seems to me that when one looks at you, you aren't wearing any dress. It's something, but not a thing you could call a dress... It's merely a shadow of a dress, not even a shadow... In the old days you could barely have made a necktie out of one of today's dresses... not even a necktie... And nobody wears a hat any more, nor underwear, nor stockings — so what does so much money go on for clothes? Where are the clothes? Even the shoes aren't shoes... they look like slippers woven of straw, straw slippers — and for that one needs 100 zlotys a week? And you have no children either..."
He gets angry, grabs a plate that has been standing on the table since yesterday, hurls it to the ground, grabs his hat and jacket, runs out of the house, slams the door so hard it nearly shatters.
"Fall head first into the ground!" his wife's voice follows him. "May you not live to come back up!"
And she decides: if he does come up and makes scenes, she won't let him into the house at all; let him sleep at his mother's, the witch, at his sister's, the delicate one, at his good brothers' with whom he sits and plays cards.
She'll show him what it means to break plates, to insult her... Nowadays times are different...
And again the hero of the novel comes to her mind. Ah, what a gentleman he is! What a noble person! All heart, all soul, feeling... Rozalia, the heroine of the novel, really has it as good as can be; she really is happy!
What Is Heard in Zagłębie? — After the Lightning Comes the Thunder...

[Będzin — kehilla.] New kehilla president hires officials...
In the previous issue of our paper we carried a notice telling that the "Agudah" had won the portfolio of kehilla president in the person of Mr. Abraham Liwer.
The "power from above" also helped the Agudah to that position... from where a signal was given to the local rabbi, may he live long, that he should break off his cure in Otwock and travel to Będzin to help make R' Abraham Liwer president.
The whole fuss around the office was not clear to us — why push one's way into the dead gmina [kehilla]? Especially when its term is already nearly over.
But these days the matter has become clear — "surely the thing is known": the aim of the "Agudah" goes further and is not content with the president's chair. The aim is to fill the gmina with "Agudah" officials.
The first step has already been taken, and Mr. Yudl Kaminer has been engaged as an official (for what work?)...
When Liquidating a Business, One Must Notify the Starosta.
[Będzin — commerce.] The Merchants' Association asks us to inform merchants who are liquidating their businesses that they must report this to the starosta [district head].
A Hooligan Attack on a Young Jewish Man.

[Będzin — crime.] Mr. Yaakov D., bandaged, came into our editorial office and told us that on Sunday evening, while walking along Zamkowa Street, he was attacked by several young hooligans who inflicted several wounds on his head with sticks.
Covered in blood, the stranger [?] young man applied to the municipal hospital for first aid. At the hospital they refused to give him help until he had paid 5 zł...
Not Having Enjoyed the Ice Cream, He Vented His Anger on the Jewish Shopkeeper.

[Będzin — crime.] A certain Christian, Mr. B., bought ice cream from his neighbour Mendel Szwajcer, owner of a shop on Potocka Street. A few minutes later the customer burst into the shop in a murderous rage, threw himself on Mr. Szwajcer and his daughter, "treated" them to blows and also did considerable damage, overturning goods and utensils.
Before the police the "polite" customer declared that he had found a worm in the ice cream. Mr. Sz., however, proved that instead of a "worm" it was merely an elongated piece of vanilla.
The police drew up a report with Mr. Sz., and the latter has handed his claims over to a lawyer.
Landlords, Not Tenants, Must Do the Repairs.

[Będzin — housing.] In connection with the fact that business owners are being forced to smarten up the outward appearance of their shops, the board of the Tenants' Association has written to the starosta asking him to instruct the police that the landlords are obliged to carry out the repairs, since rent has already reached as much as 100 percent.
At the Slaughterhouse They Stab Each Other with Knives.
[Będzin — crime.] At the local slaughterhouse 2 Christian butcher-workers quarrelled, and one of them struck the other in the belly with a knife.
Collision Between a Tram and a Car.
[Czeladź — accidents.] On Będzińska Street in Czeladź a tram and a car collided. Fortunately none of the passengers was hurt. A report was drawn up against the motorman.
Slaughterhouse Passes to the Municipality.
[Będzin — municipality.] The local slaughterhouse, which for 25 years had been leased by Mr. G. Weinziher, passed yesterday into the hands of the magistrat [municipality].
A second group of Jewish children to a summer colony.
This coming Sunday the second group of Jewish children, 190 girls, will be sent at the Magistrate's [municipality's] expense to the summer colony "Zagłębianka" in Sławków.
Several hundred trees froze.

Owing to the severe frosts of last winter, several hundred trees froze in Zagłębie; they were damaged down to the roots.
The largest number of trees froze in Będzin.
Meeting of the kehilla council.

This week our kehilla [Jewish community] council held a meeting, at which it was resolved to buy a plot for the purpose of building a building of its own. For this purpose a fund-raising collection is to be carried out.
Back from the summer colonies

In recent days 50 "Tsofim" [scouts] have returned to Zagłębie from the summer colony (moshevet kayits) organised by the Będzin district committee of the Zionist pioneering youth organisation "Gordonia" in Piła, Augustów[?] Kamińsk.
At the same time 15 "Mitorerim" also returned from the colony in Głowno, near Łódź.
At the end of the week 10 "Magshimim"[?] left for the instructors' colony (moshevet menahalim) in Głowno.
Sosnowiec — Monday — a meeting of the trade section.

The premises for the local Chamber of Commerce are almost finished and will soon be at the institution's disposal.
Yesterday, Thursday, a meeting of the finance and tax commission took place, which dealt with the question of abolishing the present system of turnover tax.
On Monday the 5th of this month the first meeting of the trade section will take place. On the agenda: approving the regulations concerning food-product shops, how restaurants must be arranged, and other questions.
Tomorrow — judgement day for the city budget.

The municipal budget for 1829/30 [sic, read 1929/30] will be considered tomorrow, Saturday, at the Voivodeship. The budget will be defended in Kielce by President [Mayor] Marczyński, Vice-President Jarosz[?], bureau head Mroczkiewicz and Kierownik [department head] Olikowski.
Wanted to earn his bread and lost an eye.

At the Pogoń hospital the right eye of 16-year-old Moshe Wiger of Dąbrowa was operated on. In order to earn a living, the unfortunate young man had been working in the factory of the Klein brothers, and at work he lost his right eye.
Don't spit in the street, don't throw away scraps of paper — to avoid fines.

The local police authorities have received strict orders that the police are to see to it that the population does not spit in the streets or throw away butts[?] of smoked papirosy [cigarettes] and the like. For any infringement of this the police must punish with a fine.
A Christian Woman Lays a Wreath of Flowers on Dr. Perlman's Grave

[Sosnowiec — memorial.] Last Sunday, during the memorial ceremony at the grave of Dr. Perlman, an unknown Christian woman, the wife of a worker, pushed her way through the assembled crowd, ran up to the grave and laid down a modest wreath of flowers.
— "Oh, what an honest man he was" — she repeated several times.
After 7 Years the Murderers of a Jew Are Uncovered

[Upper Silesia — crime.] The Katowice newspapers report the following story:
In 1922 the dead body of an unknown Jew was found in a pit near Katuczna[?], in the Pszczyna district (powiat). At the time it proved impossible to find the murderer, and only now, after 7 years, has it by chance become possible to pick up the trail of the murderers, who at that time robbed the slain man of 29 thousand dollars.
The story was uncovered in the following way:
Last week a certain Chwałek, a re-emigrant from France, got mixed up in a brawl at a party. When the police arrived, Chwałek tried to escape; the commander of the police post, however, detained him personally, because he had noticed that the senior constable (starszy posterunkowy) showed no great desire to arrest him.
At the police post Chwałek was allegedly beaten, and he cried out in self-defence:
— I won't let myself be beaten by a murderer!
Chwałek was beaten during an interrogation and confessed that in 1922 the policeman Dara, together with the former commander of the police post Wiśniewski, had arrested and robbed a certain Jew near Katuczna. Chwałek is said to have been picking berries in the forest at the time and happened to witness the murder. The murderers then made Chwałek swear an oath that he would keep silent, gave him 7 thousand dollars and forced him to leave for France.
As we are informed, Dara is said to have tried to commit suicide, but he was arrested and, moreover, the police insignia were torn off his uniform.
As for the commander (przodownik) Wiśniewski, it is not yet known whether he has already been arrested, because for quite some time he has no longer been working in the secret police.
As it turns out, one must still wait for official confirmation of this report, since it is quite possible that the whole affair is nothing more than a bluff by Chwałek, out of personal revenge on the two police officials.
Guest Performances of a Jewish Operetta Troupe

[Sosnowiec and Będzin — theatre.] The troupe of Kamiński's Theatre in Warsaw has come to Zagłębie for a few guest performances. Among the artists we see famous and popular stars such as the American soubrette Betty König, S. Landau, Z. Katz, Ch. Sandler, Rotman, Lewina.
The repertoire is of the light genre, but the theatregoers are greatly amused thanks to the healthy humour and satire that bubble over from the artists.
Today, Friday evening, "Dos hundl" ("The Little Dog") will be performed in the Sosnowiec Municipal Theatre; tomorrow, Saturday afternoon, "Sibirer khasene" ("A Siberian Wedding").
On Saturday night in Będzin, for the last time, "Dos hundl" with Betty König in the leading role.
Unemployment Is Growing

[Zagłębie — labour.] In a number of factories in Zagłębie a larger number of workers have been laid off since the first of this month. Working hours have also been cut.
—o—
Sitniewski's Circus in Sosnowiec
[Sosnowiec — entertainment.] The well-known Sitniewski Circus, which a year ago enjoyed enormous success in Zagłębie, has come to Sosnowiec and opens today with a rich programme such as has never been seen before.
Saturday and Sunday — two performances.
—o—
Cheaper Flour and Bread
[Sosnowiec — prices.] At Tuesday's meeting of the price commission it was decided to lower the price of rye flour from 44 to 42 gr. per kilo, and of bread from 45 gr. to 43 gr. per kilo.
—o—
Two Weeks' Arrest for Stealing Postage Stamps
[Sosnowiec — court.] The local district court heard the case against an official of the local post office who was accused of tearing postage stamps off letters he was sorting.
The post official was sentenced to 2 weeks' arrest.
—o—
Because of an Insult He Committed Suicide
[Mysłowice — suicide.] The cashier of the German People's Bank (Volksbank) in Mysłowice committed suicide because the head of the bank had pointed out to him that a thousand zlotys were missing from the till.
—o—
Fraud in the Sick Fund Amounting to 40,000 Zlotys
[Sosnowiec — sick fund.] In the local sick fund (Kasa Chorych) a swindle has been uncovered, carried out by an official employed in purchasing medicines. The official wrote out payment orders (asygnaty) for 40,000 zł. and took the money for himself.
—o—
Mysterious Death of 3 People
[Czeladź — deaths.] On Będzińska Street in Czeladź a young Christian woman died suddenly on Tuesday. A few hours later her son, aged 29, died.
The police had not yet drawn up the report on the two deceased when a 48-year-old Christian man also died suddenly.
According to suppositions, they were poisoned by bad meat.
Dąbrowa

Dąbrowa
A municipal official must be only a kosher Pole...
The local magistrate runs a municipal children's library. For the post of librarian the magistrate has issued a competition notice, in which it is stated that the librarian must be of Polish nationality.
It is interesting to add that the city administration — only Sanacja members — was elected with the help of Jewish votes...

Almost a catastrophe

[Dąbrowa — Hasidim.] On Tuesday evening the Rebbe of Ger, may he live long, passed through. At the railway station in Dąbrowa a large crowd of Hasidim welcomed the Rebbe.
While the Hasidim were standing by the carriage and giving "shalom", a freight train unexpectedly arrived. The crowd still managed to run away and avoid a certain catastrophe.
—o—
Reducing the advance payments (zaliczki)
[Taxes — turnover tax.] Everywhere the appeals [?] against the assessed turnover tax are now being provisionally considered.
This is done by the assessment commissions or by the tax offices (urzędy).
If the commissions or offices recommend provisionally reducing the assessed turnover, the advance payments must at the same time be reduced as well.
The offices must notify the taxpayers of this.
In this matter a special ministerial circular (okólnik), no. L. D. v 8.518/1—29, was sent last week to all offices.
If someone has already paid the first advance according to the previous assessment, he may pay the second advance according to the provisional reduction and deduct the sum paid earlier.
—o—
The "Yavneh" gymnasium moves into the new building
[Education.] As we are informed, at the beginning of the new school year the "Yavneh" gymnasium will be installed in the new school building, which has been built with the finest splendour according to the newest school facilities.
The dedication (Hanukkat ha-bayit) will probably take place in mid-September.

A Jewish boy drowned

On Wednesday towards evening a 5-year-old boy of the Jura[?] family, of Zawadusze[?] Street, drowned on the „Szczybic meadows“ [Shtshibikhs lonkes][?] in Będzin.
The child had gone out for a walk with other children under the supervision of a governess, and while they were by the water on the meadow the child went closer and fell in.
It is said that a young Christian man wanted to jump into the water to save the child, but his „kochanka“ [girlfriend] stopped him from doing so, saying that it was a „żydowski“ [Jewish] child.
As we write these lines, the tragically drowned boy has still not been found.
—o—
Against the lump-sum turnover tax.
These days a meeting of the Chamber of Commerce in Sosnowiec took place, which passed a resolution opposing the introduction of a lump-sum (ryczałt) assessment of the turnover tax [podatek obrotowy] for small merchants and artisans.
The Chamber of Commerce is of the opinion that this is harmful, and will come forward with a proposal to the Union of all Chambers of Commerce that the Union should come out against introducing the lump sum.
The Chamber of Commerce in Sosnowiec also resolved to come forward with a proposal that the keeping of a turnover book be reintroduced, which should be accepted as credible when assessing the tax.
—o—
A new instalment of the property tax.
The Ministry of Finance has decided to proceed to collect this year a new instalment of the property tax [podatek majątkowy] still owed from the old assessment.
Taxpayers of the first category will pay 1 per cent of the value of their property as it was assessed back in 1924.
Taxpayers of the second and third category, that is, merchants and artisans, will pay 0.6 per cent of the assessed property.
The last date for paying the property tax is the 10th of December [grudzień].

Our “Yizkor”

[Editorial — 15 years since the World War.] We have had, then, many “Yizkors”. A Yizkor after the World War, a Yizkor after the millions of victims who fell on the battlefields, — a Yizkor after the innocently perished young lives, cut down before their time, a Yizkor after the rivers of blood and tears, after the terrible devastations, epidemics, hunger and so on and so forth — who can count them and who can reckon them up...
And finally our own Jewish “Yizkor”, a Yizkor that cries out and demands perhaps even more strongly and loudly than all the other Yizkors, because no people, it seems, paid for the World War with as much blood as we did, as many tears, as much pain and suffering as the ancient martyr-people.
And on this great day of remembrance, when the whole world draws up an account, a total of all the victims, of the millions of destroyed souls, of the treasures of human labour and the wealth gathered through generations — we too come with our account and draw up our own total in our martyr-history.
Who will answer us for this account of blood and tears, where is our Jewish reward for the thousands of myriads of Jewish lives lost, for the seas of trouble and pain and for the ruins and devastation that the great storm caused our people?
Great is the list of our losses, of our damages, and how ridiculous, how paltry the gains look, the “mshtayns” [?] won, the achievements, in comparison with our enormous loss!
Wherever you cast your eye — everywhere graves, tombstones, ruins without measure. And even now, 15 years after the war, our wounds have not yet healed, our tears have not been wiped away and our ruins have not been rebuilt...
The war wound still bleeds on our body, but even more terrible are the after-pains that the war has left us; everywhere, in every country and in every town, lawlessness, brutalisation, cruelty and bestial brutality rage, of man against man and even more — of man against Jew. All Europe, and especially its eastern part, is flooded with a wave of hatred of man, of chauvinism and ugly antisemitism. One is seized with horror reading about the refined murders committed day after day on helpless people, on women and infants. Conscience has vanished from human hearts. The image of God has been wiped away and the wild beast has broken loose — murdering, running wild, carousing, gnashing its teeth and holding its devilish ball...
And the most terrible thing is that people have sunk so low that nobody reacts any longer even to the most terrible crimes, committed day in, day out by the unleashed and enraged beasts, and for every misfortune, may it never come, everybody has one excuse: the war atmosphere is to blame, the demoralisation...
But what is being done to combat this so-called “war atmosphere”, to root out the dangerous demoralisation? Nothing, or almost nothing; on the contrary, there are people and even whole groups who strive to make the war atmosphere even more unbearable, who add fuel to the fire, fan the sparks of war and deepen the demoralisation still further.
On the 15th anniversary of the war, let this too be remembered among all the “Yizkors”.
Ch. L—n.
Olkusz

General meeting of “Dobroczynność”.
[Olkusz — charity.] On Sunday afternoon the annual general meeting of “Dobroczynność” [the charity society] took place in Olkusz, in the premises of the “Artisans’ Union”. The chairman, Mr. Blum, gave a report on the year’s activity, which reads: “Dobroczynność”, which was founded on his initiative, has achieved a great deal for the poorest strata of Jewish society; and he called on those assembled to support the brethren in distress with all means. A report of the audit committee was delivered by A. Paluch, which the meeting took note of.
The budget for the current year was set at 9,000 złoty.
Elected to the new board were: Dr. Chain, B. Weislfisz, A. Glikstein, Abrahamle Karner, Akiba Kuzma, A. Paluch, S. Unger, S. Stark, M. S. Szwarcberg and H. Gliksman. As deputies: Arie Kuperberg, Meir Szerman, Paltiel [?] Gutfel and Alter Ratner. Audit committee: L. Pres, L. Goldberg, H. Żeriker and J. Frenkel. Mr. A. Blum was elected honorary chairman by the general meeting.

Dąbrowa

Smashed the window panes in the municipal court.
[Dąbrowa — crime.] In the local municipal court in Dąbrowa a trial took place against a well-known thief, who had carried out a series of thefts among the local merchants.
After the court procedure was finished, the thief started “settling accounts” with her husband (lit. “her man”), who — according to her expertise — had not conducted the trial properly. The judge called her to order several times, but the “woman of valour” did not obey and went on with her scandals.
The judge then turned to a policeman to lead the “wench” out of the hall. When this happened, the thief took her revenge and smashed all the panes of the entrance door.
—o—
Loans for building purposes.
[Dąbrowa — municipality.] The building committee of the local magistrate has received at its disposal a sum of 200 thousand złoty for building purposes.
According to a resolution of the local town council, such a loan must not exceed 10 thousand złoty.
Until the 10th of this month, until Sunday, there is time to submit declarations to receive such loans.
Łódź merchant says he is going to Dąbrowa — and disappears

[Dąbrowa — disappearance.] The Łódź merchant Herman Deichner has disappeared these days in a mysterious manner.
Deichner had only a short time ago moved [?] from Łask. A few days ago he told his wife that he was going on business to Dąbrowa, where he would spend several days.
His wife waited for him a whole week and, seeing that he still did not come back, she enquired among the Dąbrowa merchants she knew why her husband was staying there so long.
From Dąbrowa, however, she was answered that he had not been there at all and nobody had seen him there. Greatly alarmed, Mrs. Deichner reported the matter to the police, who have undertaken an energetic investigation of the mysterious affair.
Deichner had a large sum of money with him, and there is therefore a suspicion that he was murdered somewhere.

Sport

R.K.S. Radom — "Hakoach" 2:0.
The final match between the Radom champion R.K.S. and the Częstochowa champion "Hakoach" ended in a defeat for "Hakoach". "Hakoach" had, above all in the first half, many chances to score goals, but because of the helplessness of the forwards they were not used; only Szychek gave satisfaction, playing with great ambition from start to finish. Rotenberg in defence — good. The rest were weaker.
From the very start "Hakoach" had a slight superiority, and many chances were missed by Gutman and Jankielewicz. In the 24th minute, through the fault[?] of Kakatek and Wekselman, the outside left gets the ball, passes it to the inside left, the inside left to the centre forward — he to the inside right, who shoots it in lightning-fast and unstoppable. "Hakoach" had many more chances to equalise, but did not succeed, because they were too slow against the Radom men, and in the end the guests managed, 3 minutes before the end, to improve the result to 2:0. Referee Mr. Błaszczyk — not decisive[?].
Kolejowy (Katowice) — "Maccabi" 2:5.
It would be worth the "Maccabi" management giving the team a holiday, since it seems to be overtired. For I have not seen for a long time a team (drużyna) playing so apathetically and without ambition as "Maccabi" did recently against Kolejowy. The exceptions were Kleiner, Piekarski and Rozik. A special chapter is due to the goalkeeper Kimelman, who of the 5 goals let in may put 3 on his conscience. The guests presented themselves very well; the centre half stood out with his fine heading game and the inside left, a dangerous shooter.
In the 15th minute Kleiner gets the ball from Piekarski and scores the first goal. To this Kolejowy retaliates with 3 goals, then Saber[?] uses the opportunity and it is 3:2. The guests attack powerfully and score 2 more goals.
Referee Mr. Chmiel.
"Maccabi" — "Zagłębie" 2:1.
"Maccabi" turns out in a weak line-up with many reserve players, but thanks to the young players it acquits itself well. Szach played well, who[?] was fielded again after a longer time. The goal for "Maccabi" was scored by Piekarski, for "Zagłębie" by the centre forward. Referee Mr. Chmiel weak.
"Hakoach" 3 — "Zagłębianka" 4:2.
A fine victory of the second "Hakoach" over the strong "Zagłębianka". Goldsztajn, Szwarcbaum and Szywek of "Hakoach" stood out, and Nej[?] of "Zagłębianka". Referee Mr. Steiger good.

"Kraft" (Dąbrowa) — "Stern" (Sosnowiec) 1:1.
The friendly match between the two above-mentioned clubs aroused interest in Dąbrowa. The match was very interesting because of the very fine technique displayed by the "Kraft" players, who attacked the opponent's goal, but without success. In the 44th minute "Stern" manages [printed "lungt"] to exploit a mistake by "Kraft", and it remains 0:1 in favour of "Stern" until half-time.
