For various reasons the second half was played for 30 minutes, and it remained 1:1. The best on the pitch: Judel Stawski, Wolf Goldblum, Sz. Kanaruk and goalkeeper Moshe Malgowicer. Referee Gutszprach. Ch. G.
"Samson" — "Jutrznia" 2:3.
The reserve team begins to play, but "Jutrznia" immediately takes over the initiative. "Samson" does not get a word in[?] in the first minutes. In the 15th minute the referee awards an 11-metre kick against "Samson", and Aniśman uses it and manages to score a goal; in the 30th minute "Samson" scores an equaliser, and about 6 minutes later a second goal. In the second half "Samson" plays somewhat more sharply, and the referee awards an 11-metre kick against "Samson", and Aniśman manages to score a second goal [against] "Samson". [Then] the 3rd goal is scored. Referee Feder not good.
"Maccabi" (Königshütte) plays with its fists.
The sports club "Shimshon" in Magdoszet[?] invited the sports club "Maccabi" of Königshütte to a friendly match. The "Maccabi" players, seeing that the match would end in "Shimshon's" favour, played brutally, so that several "Shimshon" players were injured. On the 4th of this month "Maccabi" announced a return match. The "Shimshon" players did not want to go, and only after an assurance from the "Maccabi" board that the players would no longer play brutally did they go. But this time too the same thing happened. "Maccabi", seeing that they could not come away with a win, started to beat. The spectators also beat with sticks, so that the "Shimshon" players barely came home alive. Let this be a warning to other sports clubs that they[?] should not play with the Königshütte "Maccabi". K. Ts.

Clouded Horizons

[Editorial — economy; the crisis and taxes in Zagłębie.]
(The crisis. — The tax question. — What ought to be done at the present moment?)
Our region is considered one of the richest corners of Poland. The "Residence" [the central government in Warsaw] knows this perfectly well, and that is exactly why we are taxed considerably more heavily here than in other provincial districts.
The government knows that our material situation is considerably better than elsewhere, and therefore it makes stiffer demands on us. It is not for nothing, then, that we cry out every time that the taxes are unbearable, that we are burdened with them too heavily and too hard.
But when business is going, when the wheel [?] is turning, the taxes turn along with it, and one steers [?] through somehow. It is worse, however, when business begins to come to a halt, when the situation turns bad, when a crisis sets in — and then there is no longer anywhere or anything to take from, and then it is bad, bitter, very bitter.
Actually, the crisis in the country is no longer news; it has reigned everywhere for quite some time already, but during the time it was everywhere it was hardly noticeable here, or we felt it little. True, we only began to feel it little by little later on, and indirectly at that — the commercial world was [?] dragged along. On the other hand, those who had nothing to do with export within the country, those who traded here locally, i.e. in Zagłębie and Upper Silesia — them the general crisis in the country hardly harmed at all, and at best very, very little.
Now, however, the situation has changed here locally as well; the severe crisis has reached us here too, and directly at that, so that now not only the small and the weak feel it, but precisely the strong, the big ones.
The factories are beginning to work less; many workers are being cut back and dismissed, so that we already have to record an ever-growing number of unemployed. If that is how the big factories, the big industry, look — then how can small-scale manufacturing look in such a situation, the kind that the weakest wind can bend, ruin and break? And when manufacturing begins to totter, when the worker and the clerk lose their posts, one surely understands how far this affects the world of merchants and artisans. The merchant has no one to bring his goods to, and when he does bring them, he does not know to whom he can give [on credit] and to whom not. The same is true of the artisans: they too have no one to work for; on top of that, for the very same reason, credit terms are becoming harder, so that he is soon crushed and the real crisis arises. The crisis from which it is hard to wriggle out.
And here the hard question mark arises: what is to be done? How does one save oneself from ruin in these hard times? How does one manage to push through the severe crisis with one's bones intact?
At first one does not notice that the times are hard — and that too only those with whom things are still [printed "gakh"] turning as usual. But if one looks deeper, if one examines the situation with full clarity, one comes to the conclusion that the situation is not at all cheerful [?], and one does not see it improving either; on the contrary, the horizons are clouded. And when one begins to study it, one sees that X and Y have gone under, and that quite large firms have ceased to exist altogether, and this has to be reckoned with. Be that as it may, we must be fully aware and take seriously what is happening in our times.
The tax question is one of the worst problems. There are times when one has not only nothing to pay the bill of exchange with, but literally nothing to buy a piece of bread for the children — and the tax must be paid; and no sooner has one paid one tax than the second tax is already standing at the door, so that we are crushed by the terrible tax screw, which, God forbid, does not grow any smaller, regardless of the fact that the economic situation in the whole country is worse.
However much people did not want to talk about this matter, and however much they did not want to act in this field, one still cannot steer away from the question and say that every word is wasted. No — one must not make light of the matter, which is simply a question of life.
One must surely demonstrate to the proper authority that the economic situation has become considerably worse and that the crisis reigns on all fronts; and therefore one cannot, in such hard times, be taxed as heavily as at the time when there was no crisis. A government must surely take into account the interests and the situation of its citizens. We know that in the high windows they do not want to know about any of this; on the contrary, for them everything is good and fine, and industry is flourishing, and small manufacturing and the merchant and the artisan are doing good and fine.
But one must not accept that; one must show that these are mere illusions and not reality — life, after all, has to reckon with pure reality; otherwise one fools oneself and others, and no good comes to anyone from fooling.
Had we sound economic and professional institutions, such an action would have had to be carried out through them; unfortunately they limp everywhere and on all sides, so that one cannot rely on them to take their members under their protection and defend them properly. And if not they, then there is truly no one to represent the community as one whole, as a single unit, for here it is not a matter of an individual, of a private person. Here it is not a matter of defending somebody's "I", somebody's egoism.
In the present case the powerful representation must come forward — one that would be close to the community and would be able to speak in its name, to defend, to request and to demand.
Unfortunately we do not have this sound public representation, and therefore the tax question remains at a dead point, so that everyone makes his own Sabbath [acts on his own], everyone tries in his own name to do what is in his power — and therein lies precisely the reason why the community cannot attain what is due to it, what it so badly needs.
Selekt.
Figures That Teach Something.

170 thousand unemployed are to be found in our Poland today. And this at the time of the „economic improvement“ so widely advertised by the Prime Minister.
So within the space of 1 year unemployment here has risen from 118 thousand to 170, i.e. by more than 50 percent.
These are figures according to the official data of the Ministry of Labour.
In fact, however, one must reckon the number of unemployed as larger by half. The Ministry of Labour takes its figures on the basis of the official [illegible/doubtful word] labour offices; of thousands more unemployed in all trades, branches and enterprises only the trade unions know; nor do the thousands of „hidden ones“ enter the number registered at the Ministry — those who are not enrolled in the trade unions and do not go to register even at the unemployment office, and about whom nobody really knows anything except they themselves.
But even if we do not paint the colours blacker than the Ministry of Labour does, the figure is already large enough for a country like Poland, which is only counting the first decade of its life since its rebirth. Even relying on the official figure given by the Ministry, and reckoning a minimum of only one family member for each unemployed person, we already have an official figure of 340 thousand souls who have no employment in Poland and are exposed day after day to hunger and want. That amounts to more than 1 percent of our population of 30 million.
And what is the situation of the lucky ones who do have work? What do the same data of the Ministry of Labour tell us?
Over 82 percent earn less than 150 zł. a month; from 150 zł. a month to 300 zł. a month only eleven and a half percent earn, and only six and one tenth percent are the really lucky ones, who earn here from three hundred to a thousand zł. a month. Above 1000 zł. not even 1 percent of the working people earn. Two tenths of a percent is the number of the very luckiest of the lucky here in Poland, who earn more than 1000 zł. a month.
So 82 of every 100 unemployed [sic; read: workers] do not earn even a minimum of subsistence.
This is how the situation looks in the bright colours of the official report of the Ministry of Labour. In fact — the cost of living keeps rising, wages stay the same, unemployment rises.
And if it goes on like this at the pace so far — who knows where and to what we will really come.
L. M.
The Three Tears... (A Tisha B'Av Picture).

The night of the seventh to the eighth of Av was very dark; the half moon, which had appeared after sunset at the western edge of the sky, seeing Jerusalem's agony — how old men, women and children were rolling about in Jerusalem's streets with parched lips and lips dried up with hunger — wrapped itself in [sic: "and"] the black clouds, as a mourner wraps himself in a dark sackcloth, and would not shine...
Not a single star wanted to be a witness and see how in Jerusalem's streets heaps upon heaps of carcasses, dead and living, were lying — how in Jerusalem's streets death and scraps of life were mingling...
Between the first and the second wall of the capital Jerusalem stood, with their last strength, the Jewish fighters, holding fast in their weakened, trembling hands the heavy shields, spears and bows.
Twelve legions they were. Tens of thousands of weakened, starved bodies, sunken bellies, protruding, [doubtful word] chins[?], and glowing eyes.
Twelve legions corresponding to the twelve tribes of Israel. Each legion with the banner of its tribe at its head. — Twelve banners fluttered, black and dark, in that dark night of the seventh to the eighth of Av...
It was quiet in the camp. As quiet as a house remains from which a corpse has just been carried out. A heavy despair had found its place in their hearts and pressed down and stifled every sigh and every tear that wanted to tear itself out from there.
All at once lightning fell into the camp. It was not lightning from the sky, for during the whole time that the enemy had stood around Jerusalem's gates the sky had put on a leaden armour, as if wishing in this way to hide its transparency — it was lightning from the eyes of Yohanan, from the eyes of the supreme military commander, who with weak steps, leaning on the shoulders of his two deputies (adjutants in the foreign tongue), approached the camp.
Yohanan took in the whole camp with his gaze and with his fire warmed all the chilled, weakened hearts.
At the head of the camp Yohanan stood like a finely planted fir tree.
The deputies unrolled before him a fiery Torah scroll.
Fiery letters flew like birds over fiery parchment, and Yohanan began to read in his lion's[?] voice, which made the whole camp tremble:
— „Reuben, my son, thou art my firstborn, my might and the beginning of my strength“ — tribe of Reuben, the Torah bears witness about you that you are the first strength in the camp. Will you, tribe of Reuben, make the Torah, as it were, into a liar and let the enemy into the city?
From thousands of hearts a „No“ burst out.
Yohanan read on:
— „Simeon and Levi are brethren“ — stout-hearted brothers Simeon and Levi, for the sake of one sister of yours you destroyed Shechem and turned it into ash and dust — will you let the enemy into the city and hand over tens of thousands of your sisters to shame?
— „No“! — thousands of hearts stammered out.
— „Judah“, the supreme military commander of Israel, Yohanan, read on: Judah, from whom kings were chosen for Israel and whose throne was hallowed, as it were — will you let the enemy into the city, so that a stranger may defile the throne hallowed by God?
— „No“! — thousands of hearts thundered out with pride.
Thus Yohanan asked tribe after tribe, and thus tribe after tribe answered.
— Whoever of you is afraid, whoever of you is faint-hearted, whoever has married a young wife, whoever has built a house and not dedicated it — let him leave the camp!
No one stirred.
Then Yohanan took the fiery Torah scroll and went with it from tribe to tribe, and the camp swore by God and by Jerusalem not to surrender to the enemy — — —
Very dark was the night of the seventh to the eighth of Av. On Jerusalem's walls stood watchmen. Every fifty paces — a watchman, and to drive the drowsiness from their eyeballs and the hunger that gnawed at their hearts, they called to one another:
— Watchman, what of the night! Watch—man, what of the n—ight!
And somewhere in the middle of the city a mother lay hunched on the ground, like a wild hyena lying in wait for its prey, and with glazed eyes, bulging[?] with the madness of hunger, waited for her two-year-old child to fall asleep..
„A—a—ah, what a feast this will be! The pot is already boiling on the kindled fire, the little neck[?] is stretched out.. the knife is sharp.. it gleams so... — A—a—ah, what a feast this will be! Meat.. and red wine... red as blood — — —
On the northern side of Jerusalem's walls the traitor crept among the bushes and palm trees.
And perhaps Ben Merodach was no traitor at all? Perhaps he simply had such a soft heart and could not eat[?] his own child — his own flesh and blood? — Perhaps. Who knows? — The wailing of the jackals, the shrieks of the hyenas deadened his steps and thoughts — — —
One after another the Roman soldiers came into Jerusalem through the breach in the northern wall that Ben Merodach had shown them, and with the dawn of the eighth of Av, which appeared at the eastern edge of the leaden sky, the proud, wild voices of the Roman legions echoed through Jerusalem's streets:
— Israel is defeated! Israel is put to shame! Israel is a mockery! —
The fire of the burning Temple melted the leaden armour of the sky, and above the Temple an opening appeared[?].
Through the opening, three tears of the Almighty, as it were, fell into the burning fire and extinguished the fire, which wanted to burn the Western Wall as well.
The three tears were „Eikhah“ „yashvah“ „badad“ [„How doth (the city) sit solitary“, Lamentations 1:1].
Józef Zełkowicz.
What Is Being Done There After All? (They keep on conducting "high politics." — Jewish money is up for grabs. How do the members react?)

[Będzin — Kehilla; opinion piece.]
Say what you like, but I with my simple common sense cannot possibly understand what is going on here. I do not know what sort of thing it is, the present Jewish kehilla of Będzin; it is some kind of riddle, a sphinx, something impossible to understand and grasp.
Here everyone knows from all sides that everything there is rotten, that what was built up over a series of years is systematically going under; not only is nothing real being created now, but the good and healthy things that existed before are being destroyed one by one. And one asks: why, under the prevailing conditions, must such a large staff be kept? Why is it not reduced, when there is no work for them? Why must such a large budget be maintained when it could be reduced? Why must a city of Jews be burdened with such a large establishment [etat] when it could be cut down?
Such and similar questions are asked by the householders in town, and there is no one to give them an answer, no one to exchange a word with them. And it is characteristic that at a time when wonder eats us up and we do not understand why the former[?] Jewish kehilla must now have such a large staff, along comes the freshly baked Agudah president with a brand-new method of enlarging the office staff: thus a fresh official has now been taken on, one of their own people, a person close to the "court." And the question arises: what is going on here? What is happening in our kehilla board, which apparently has already lost all shame and no longer reckons with anyone? Otherwise Jewish money would surely not simply be up for grabs! Otherwise they would surely have reckoned that a president cannot engage his own people merely because one needs him to be there [printed "דארף", probably a misprint for "דארט"] and so that he should have something to milk... It is unheard of — that one should be an autocrat to such an extent, ask no one and reckon with nothing! Is Jewish money really so ownerless that one's own brothers need not reckon with it? Can partisanship really blind an honest man to such an extent that he no longer sees anything true?
Why are fresh people needed now in the office of the kehilla administration? What kind of work has been added that the existing staff could not cope with?
It is unheard of, what goes on there; one would never have imagined that a few people would dare to lead a city around by the nose like this, and that both the other board members and the whole city would not react to it properly. The entire activity there consists only of playing politics and more politics; nothing but tricks are performed for whole days and nights, and in the end it all comes out of the city's pockets.
Two years ago they went after the secretary of the Jewish kehilla, saying he was dangerous, that he was a stumbling block, that one could not pull off with him all the escapades that anyone might fancy — and they gave him ten thousand złoty and sent him away... The second time, against the will of the city, they took on as cantor a Jew who had not yet [—?] to be one; for the post they had already favoured him with four thousand złoty as severance pay. Afterwards they engaged the present cantor together with the choir conductor, who impressed the city; but then they realised that this was no good — that there should be peace and quiet in town is no business. So they began to introduce quarrels between cantor and conductor, and the well-aimed bullets hit the mark exactly: they began to bite one another, and the desired results were achieved; the quarrels between cantor and conductor broke out, and things reached the point where the kehilla removed the conductor, and he is being paid out three thousand złoty. Of course, afterwards they will look around to see how things stand in the world, and then they will know whom to go after [?] again and whom to set against one another.
It makes the same impression as the Russian government before the war, which was interested in the people having something to occupy themselves with, so that the government would be left in peace; therefore it incited the Russian population that the Jews wanted to uproot it and that pogroms must be made on them.
Our kehilla providers too play politics about everything the world stands on, so that we should have something to busy ourselves with and forget about them; and meanwhile, meanwhile they run an economy that God preserve and save us.
What is the meaning of this — taking people on and removing them, and giving severance pay of thousands and tens of thousands of złoty? They throw the money about as though it were a spring that never runs dry.
The same is certainly true of the hiring of the official just now. As soon as the city says that this man is not needed and the Agudah board members see that they must capitulate, they have reckoned that he will at any rate receive a few thousand złoty. So what are they putting into this business?
Here, then, is the eye with which they look upon public money, which is collected from Jewish pockets. Try, out of curiosity, to make a test with the collectors [inkasenci]: you will hear how hard it is for a Jew to pay those few złoty of tax [etat], and how many times such a Jew has to beg the sequestrator not to take away his bit of bedding.
Such lawlessness there has never yet been; no Jewish leaders have ever yet allowed themselves to ride so mercilessly on the backs of the Jewish people. And therefore there must be one slogan, one unified demand: dissolve the present board.
— This is what must be done at the present moment, with full awareness and seriousness.
R. Let.
A Husband, a Maid — a Wife and a Lover

A true story that happened in one of the nearby summer-resort places.

As many nights as summer has, so many piquant dacha stories and bits of gossip get told. But all these stories are worth nothing compared with the true story that has just happened at one of the summer-resort places — and this is how it happened:

On one of the streets of Sosnowiec, in a fine, spacious house, lives the young couple Ts., who have been married all of 8 years. But what do even 8 years count, when you married for love and all the time since the wedding you have, thank God, an abundant livelihood — you really live like turtle-doves, happy and content. As usual they keep a pretty maid, Madame does not dip her hand in cold water, and at home it is delightful: the food is ready on time and every corner radiates [?] a woman's touch.

Indeed, not a summer goes by without her, God forbid, failing to observe the sacred wifely "commandment of the dacha". In the 8 years since her wedding she has already been to nearly all the spas, and she always took along new, modern clothes, no worse than other lady dacha-lovers.

This summer, however, she decided something... and unexpectedly told her husband: "I'm not going anywhere; I've had enough of those dachas with their weird dishes" — she can "do the dacha" around the resort places quite close [?] to home, and take the maid along too, who will see to it that every moment she has a fresh, tasty "potrawa" [dish]. For "certain" reasons the husband tried to talk her out of it and specifically urged [?] her to go to Krynica or Sopot. But she dug in her heels and stuck to one thing: "I don't want to go anywhere except the Olkusz area" — and having no choice, the husband had to give in.

The husband, being lonely by himself in town, used every Friday — and so too last Friday towards evening — after finishing his business, to buy a little bag of sweets and set off, full of longing, to visit his wife. Coming into her lodgings he found only the maid — the wife was not there. To his question "Where is Madame?" the maid answered curtly: "Gone for a walk in the woods." The husband then suggested to the pretty maid that she walk through the woods with him to look for his "wandering" wife. The maid obediently followed the master's order.

When they did not find her, however, they sat down for a while to rest a little, tasting the... sweet things he had brought from town. Suddenly they heard human footsteps and right after saw before them — her... his own wife... and how, off to the side, a young man was sneaking away among the dense trees.

Seeing this scene, he raised a hue and cry at his treacherous wife; she in turn shouted and made a racket at him — why was he having ugly dealings with the servant girl...

The voices were so loud that even the trees trembled...

Many dacha-goers came running together in alarm and, having learned the story, tried to make peace between the inflamed husband and wife. But no peace came of it: the little wife left the dacha in shame and now sits sulking at home.

The quarrels between husband and wife repeat themselves several times a day, and the word "get" [divorce] hovers like an evil spectre over the formerly peaceful house...

And the sworn "eternal love" is in great danger...
Zman Pleitatenu — The Season of Our Bankruptcy...

[Feuilleton — a satirical tale.] By S. Rozenshteyn [S. Rozensztajn].
(A topical little story)

Old Count Radziwiłł, so they say, used to say: "Live you should among gentiles, but trade you should with Jews"...
And indeed, at harvest time merchants from every corner of the country would come to the shtetl, dressed in holiday clothes and in an expansive mood, and stroll into the old castle, where the count himself conducted all the transactions over a glass of liquor, which he did not dislike at all; more than once the count was a guest of the shtetl's respected grain merchants or brokers, especially on a Sabbath eve or a holiday eve, and could not stop praising the delicious Jewish fish with which the Jewish housewives used to honour him.
Money, presumably, the count never lacked, and so he would lend a certain sum to the Jewish inhabitants of the shtetl, especially to pious Jews who, moreover, ran bigger and safer businesses — not because he could not find other safe places, but because the Jew would pay him a much higher interest than the English or foreign banks.
In summertime the count would dash over to his residence-shtetl, and through the whole shtetl and the surrounding area the news would spread lightning-fast that the count had come.
The count's debtors would start gathering the interest due from them for the past year, dress up in holiday finery and set off to the castle, where the count received all the parties concerned.
Thus days and years went by. The principal was almost forgotten; the main thing was to pay the interest.
And it came to pass one day that a foolish whim seized the count, and he sends a messenger to Reb Moshe the timber merchant, that he should kindly bring in within 5 days the 2,000 roubles borrowed 15 years ago, together with the interest for the past year.
Reb Moshe was left in great embarrassment: where does one suddenly get such a sum of money? His whole fortune is scattered to the seven winds; what is to be done? After long deliberation it is decided that Reb Moshe should run over to the Rebbe and seek his counsel.
The old one, of blessed memory, hears him out, wrinkles his brow, closes his eyes for a while and says: Go home, Moshe, and make a holiday at home; see that your so-and-so [wife] prepares a feast fit for a king, and God will help.
Reb Moshe does not understand what the Rebbe means by this, but he is afraid to ask again — lest, God forbid, the Rebbe be angry... He, of blessed memory, noticed how the long-time Hasid stands there astonished, so he claps him on the shoulder and says: Never mind, don't fret, the count knows that you are God-fearing and devout in the word of the Lord, and a holiday is a sacred day for Jews.
Reb Moshe drives home content and tells his wife what the Rebbe said. Even the wife does not understand what it means to make a holiday in the middle of an ordinary Wednesday, but if he, long may he live, says so — he surely knows.
His wife Feige was a capable Jewish woman; she quickly got everything ready and made a holiday. Reb Moshe combed out his majestic beard, put on the silk kapote, paced back and forth across the room and waited, not knowing himself for what...
Suddenly a noise was heard, and two white horses harnessed to a splendid carriage stopped at Reb Moshe's yard. Reb Moshe and Feige at once rushed to the door and saw before them the count stepping out of the carriage. With pounding hearts they bowed deeply before the great guest and greeted him humbly. The little children huddled in a corner and, out of fear and joy together, looked up now at the guest and now at father and mother, and could by no means understand what was going on...
Reb Moshe carefully took the count's coat off him and invited him into the room; the count stopped on the threshold of the room, seeing its festive appearance, and exclaimed, stammering: Excuse me for disturbing you on your holiday.. but... tell me, Moshe, what holiday do you Jews have today?
Reb Moshe was left dumbfounded by the question and did not know what to answer. He was angry with himself for not having asked the Rebbe yesterday what to answer in such a case. But in the middle of speaking Reb Moshe collected himself and suddenly blurted out, not hearing himself what his mouth was saying:
— Today, dear sir, we have a great holiday.. Zman Pleitatenu ["the Season of Our Bankruptcy" — a pun on Zman Cheirutenu, "the Season of Our Freedom"; Yiddish pleite = bankruptcy, flight from creditors]..
The count opened his eyes wide and somewhat laboriously repeated the name of the holiday: Zman Plei-ta-te-nu... ha, ha, ha! And I, old fool, thought I already knew all the Jewish holidays — and at that he began counting on his fingers: Wielkanoc [Easter] (Passover), Zielone Świątki [Pentecost] (Shavuot), Trąbki ["the Trumpets"] (Rosh Hashanah), Sądny dzień ["Judgment Day"] (Yom Kippur), Kuczki ["the Booths"] (Sukkot), Święta Tora ["Holy Torah"] (Simchat Torah), Ostatki ["Carnival"] (Purim) — and that's it; and here you go, yet another holiday... Zman Plei-ta-te-nu... ha, ha, ha!
But Reb Moshe did not lose his head; lightning-fast he poured a real glassful of pure "ninety" [90-proof spirit] and asked the count to drink l'chaim...
The squire did not need to be asked twice and downed one glass and two, and Feige had already set before him a fine portion of fish and saffron challah for the blessing over bread, at which the count went into great raptures and relished it greatly, and all the while did not stop repeating to himself the new holiday "Zman Pleitatenu"... never knew what a fine holiday it is...
It goes without saying that the squire no longer mentioned the 2000 roubles with the interest, for such a pious Jew as Reb Moshe would not, God forbid, desecrate a holiday by taking or giving money. He took a very fine leave of Reb Moshe and Feige and even of the little children, and Reb Moshe escorted the squire to the carriage, which had waited for him the whole time; and already sitting inside, the count repeated: "Zman Pleitatenu, never knew of such a precious holiday, ha, ha, ha"!
As he rode, the squire noticed through the carriage window how Reb Berl the textile merchant, from whom a thousand roubles were also due to him, stood in his shop with a yardstick [arshin] in hand, measuring off a piece of goods for a peasant woman. It struck the count as very odd that such a pious Jew as Berko should desecrate so holy a holiday, so he told the coachman to stop. In his great surprise the yardstick fell out of Reb Berl's hand and he leapt toward the count, but the count cried out almost angrily: Listen here, Berko, how come such a pious Jew as you desecrates a holiday? If so, I no longer have any trust in you, and immediately you shall pay me back the thousand roubles due to me. There, you see, Moshko the timber merchant is a truly pious Jew. Go and see how he keeps all the holidays; why, today is Zman Pleitatenu and you make nothing of it...
Reb Berl at once grasped what it was about and answered with a smile:
— True, dear sir. Zman Pleitatenu is indeed a holiday, a great holiday, but for the time being each of us celebrates it separately, that is, as he wishes: today Moshko celebrates it, tomorrow Shlomko, the day after tomorrow — I. We will all celebrate it... Without Zman Pleitatenu we could not exist at all...
The squire, pleased with Reb Berl's answer, waved his hat in the air, and the two white steeds set off at a gallop toward the castle gate.
The Seduced Girl (15)

[Literature — serialized novel; installment 15.]
Dr. A. Weissman.
(A novel of Jewish life in the Old World, based on historical facts.)
15.

"So it was you, then, who was the coachman. And I did not understand where you had come from, like a good angel, back then when I found myself in great trouble."
"What you count as trouble, He who is in Heaven sent to me as good fortune. From then on I began to hope that your heart would change towards me, and now... what shall I do with myself, Mania? When you push me away, you take all my hopes from me."
And Jan burst into tears.
All the colours changed on her face; Jan's tears aroused in Mania even more disgust for him than before, when he had fallen on his knees. Mania did not know what to do, and various thoughts tangled in her head.
And Jan did not stop talking.
"Mania, have pity on my life; without you I cannot live. Even if you had not renounced Ludwig, I would not have given you up to him, even if it cost me my life."
Mania said to him angrily:
"Tell me, Jan: on the one hand you kneel before me, weep, beg me for pity, and on the other hand you regard yourself as my master — 'I would not have given you up,' you say, as though I were some object without a will of its own that anyone may do with as he pleases. I must tell you, Jan, that what I want or do not want is my own affair, and no person whatsoever can force me to anything against my will."
"That means I cannot even hope for anything, and I may go away now with nothing. If so, we shall say goodbye, only..."
"Wait, Jan, just let me collect my thoughts... It is I who must beg for pity. Begging for pity befits a woman.. just wait..."
————
Jan sat back down in his place.
"You need not beg me for any pity," said Jan. "You need only order, command. Everything will be done."
"But can I be sure that you will not pass my request on to anyone? For no one may know but the two of us."
"I swear to you by my whole life that I will not pass it on to anyone."
"If so, I ask you to free me from these thick walls, and once we are on the other side of the monastery, let me find my parents there, with whom we shall travel home together; for with you alone — I must tell you the truth — I am afraid to travel: you have become wild."
"I ask you," Mania went on, "whether you are able, whether you will decide on such a thing or not — do not tell anyone about my plan, because, as I have learned here, if they only notice that I am thinking of running away, they will lock me up in the cellars of the holy graves that they showed me."
"It cannot be; they are only frightening you for nothing."
"You are mistaken. In the name of piety they are capable of anything; I feel they will do it if I try to run away from here. I was told that there, in the cellars, there are special punishment rooms, and that many Jewish girls are locked up there, who were lured there with kind words."
"Old wives' tales. I too am a pious Christian and would not do such things."
"Well, enough — tell me your decision at once, one way or the other."
Jan hesitated for a few minutes and then said:
"What is all this good for? Convert, then say that you are my bride, and they will free you at once. Don't think that I will force you to marry me; if you do not want to, I will not compel you. Just convert, and you will be completely free. They cannot force you to become a nun; that you can do only of your own free will."
"Thank you for the advice, but no one will ever get me to convert by force. No one has yet made me do anything by force, not even my own parents, whom I love so much. I must tell you frankly: you know Chaim, after all; you know how he loves me, and you will not deny that he is a very decent man — no one can say a bad word about him; for me such a bridegroom would have been happiness. But do you know who ruined the match? — My own parents. They kept on so much at me that I must become Chaim's bride. Then, when my parents saw that I would not obey them with kindness, they started with harshness: that I would never live with them again, that Chaim was my good fortune, and that if I did not become Chaim's bride they would no longer want to know me. Day and night they did not stop threatening, as is the way when the parents like the match and the child does not want it. All this, Jan, I tell you as an example: no one will get anything out of me by force, not even the nuns with their cellars of graves. If you can free me from here as fast as possible — even right away — good; if not, say that you cannot, that you are afraid, that you are a coward."
"Not true — no one will say of me, Mania, that I am a coward. But I ask you: how is it done? You know that I am, first of all, a pious Christian, and it is terrible to take such a sin upon myself. Why, they will stone me, everyone will turn away from me, and they will be right: a Christian should do such a thing? I shall be cursed in both worlds. They will find out at once that this is my doing, and if they catch us my punishment will be more terrible than yours; no penance will help me. On the contrary — you give me advice how I should do it."
"You know the monastery better, and the walls through which one comes and goes from here; I can find no way here. But why are we talking so much about it? If you cannot carry out my plan — enough; the two of us have nothing more to talk about."
Jan was silent again for a few minutes and then said:
"I have a plan: your parents will rescue you from here — I will see to that. First of all I will let them know where you are."
"Very good; nothing more is needed."
"May God forgive me the great sin that I take upon myself. But I want to ask you: what will happen when I free you?"
"What do you want to happen? What can I tell you now? I myself do not know what will become of me."
"But I know."
"What can you know?"
"I know that when you come back to your parents they will again talk you into marrying Chaim, and then, oh, your not wanting to will no longer help; they won't even ask you any more whether you want to become Chaim's bride; your parents will no longer be afraid that you will run away with a shaygets [a gentile]."
"Why are you tormenting me? You torment me more than the nuns who are holding me here. Are you afraid that I will marry Chaim? Believe me, and I swear to you, that I myself do not know what will become of me; I am not thinking about that at all, I am thinking of only one thing: how to get free as quickly as possible, and then we shall see. Time will show everything. I beg you, Jan, if you truly love me as you say, ask me nothing and just listen to my request, if you are willing and if you are able. You are, after all, as you say, a pious Christian and a pious man; when such a man does something, he does not ask in advance and does not demand to be paid beforehand. Free me, Jan, and you will see that doing good is never lost."
Mania suddenly fell on her knees and, with tears in her eyes, kissed his hands and begged him to free her.
In his eyes Mania now looked more beautiful than ever.
"Calm yourself, Mania," said Jan. "I will do everything, even if it costs me my life."
Suddenly the door opened and in came "Sister" Maria.
When Sister Maria came in, she still found Mania kneeling before Jan.
"Woe is me, woe to the eyes that see this!" cried Maria, wringing her hands and staring piously with her eyes. "In a monastery, in such a holy place, must I see such a sinful scene, which falls like a stain of shame on all of us!"
The Sister caught her breath from agitation and [sic: "bin vayter"] went on to address the young couple, who stood as pale as the wall:
"I do not blame Mania so much, for as long as she has not yet been sanctified among us she is still sinful; but you, Jan, a pious Christian, should commit such an outrage? The walls of the monastery now lament and weep over this great disgrace."
"Sister!" Jan gathered his strength and said. "Sister, nothing bad at all has happened between us. We love each other, we have declared our love, and soon we shall have our wedding."
On hearing the word "wedding" Sister Maria softened a little and said to them in a calmer tone:
"But children, you must know that in a monastery there is no place for declaring one's love. The holy walls of the monastery have never to this day seen such scenes or heard such words. You, Jan, will have to take upon yourself a penance which the monastery will impose on you, so that you first wash away your great sin."
Jan sighed, and Mania could barely keep herself in her place and kept straining to tell the Sister that Jan was lying, that they did not love each other and were not getting married. But Jan, recognising in her face that she wanted to do something terrible, shot her an angry look, so that they both understood what a dangerous step she wanted to take, and she kept silent with bitten lips.
"Well, Jan, you have spent long enough here; you may go now."
"Farewell, my dear bride!" said Jan, and went out of the room.

The Old-New Lament (Shabbat Chazon Thoughts)

By Ben Amotz.
The people of Israel is steeped in a sea of troubles. "All her people sigh" — sighs and groans are heard throughout the camp of Israel. Jewish livelihoods are torn away, Jewish existences are shattered, "they seek bread" — people look for a livelihood and do not find it, all gates are locked to us, we are like sheep among a pack of hungry wolves, every day the troubles grow greater and the number of sheep — smaller...
"Better off were the slain of the sword"; the shame is great, no credit is given, the ground under one's feet is shaking and one looks for a way out.
— To jump from the 4th floor...
And the chain of troubles grows longer with new links, a wailing and a lament, people weep by day and by night.
— "She weeps sore"...
———
In the Będzin synagogue, on 20 Tammuz, a congregation of Jews gathered. A solemn mood. Everyone's face is turned toward the bimah, on which the cantor, wrapped in a tallit, is preparing to hold a memorial in honour of the 25th yahrzeit of a lofty, idealistic creator.
After the memorial the audience is told of the deeds of the great man and Jew.
But suddenly there is a tumult. Sticks are raised high; a "kstsan"[?] felt the urge to take revenge in the little sanctuary and thereby desecrated its holiness...
And the prophet laments over this: "Mine eye, mine eye runneth down with water, because the comforter that should relieve my soul is far from me" — my eyes shed tears like water, seeing how the youth, on whom we place our hope that they will be our comforters, are distancing themselves from the holy Jewish traditions and organising brawls in our holy place...
———
At a meeting of barber-masters in Sosnowiec.
The barber-masters of Zagłębie gathered to discuss their economic situation. With great bitterness several Jewish barbers spoke, pointing out how great their sufferings are as Jews and as citizens. Two days a week their shops are closed — we do not want to work on the Sabbath — they argued, and on Sunday we are again persecuted by the police..
Then the floor was taken by one of "our brethren, the children of Israel", who sharply rebuked the Jewish barbers for their "chutzpah" — that the "związek" [the union] should intervene with the authorities so that they allow them to open for a few hours on Sunday.
— What do you want? Perhaps to make Poland into Palestine?
— If you do not want to work on the Sabbath, you have, after all, the option of emigrating to Palestine..
And the several Jews, hearing the words of this "żydek" [little Jew], recalled the words of the prophet:
— "All mine enemies have heard of my trouble; they are glad" — my enemies heard how a Jew speaks against his own brothers and rejoiced, but we could not answer, "for my sighs are many, and my heart is faint".
— Full are my sighs, and my heart aches.
———
The hall of the Sosnowiec district court is packed full. A very interesting trial is taking place. For the judges themselves the trial has a special significance. They did not believe that such a thing could happen among Jews.
And the indictment is read:
In the Niwka beth midrash Jews had gathered to pray. During the morning (Shacharit) prayer one provoked and incited the other, but when the Torah scroll was taken out a real fire flared up; Jews — not Romans — threw themselves upon the scroll and
— tore it to pieces...
The presiding judge of the court takes up the sentence and repeats it once more:
— The Torah scroll torn to...
Like a shadow I shuffled out of the courtroom; every human glance pierced me as if with spears, and to the tune of Eikhah the words tore themselves out of my bleeding heart:
— "Oh, what has befallen us. Behold, and see our reproach"..
———
Already 2000 years since the destruction of the Second Temple. We have wandered through all parts of the world, eaten at "strangers'" tables, served every idolatry, and
— nothing has changed for the better..
The same troubles as in that time; in the Jewish street there rage with full force groundless hatred, falsehood, licentiousness, lawlessness. One wants to swallow the other alive, our possessions [?] are desecrated by our own people, the spiritual leaders bow down basely before the golden calf, and the heart yearns and quietly whispers the prayer:
— "Renew our days as of old"..
The Mirowski Family (A Novella)

Salomon Mirowski sat in his study over the account book, lost in thought, smoking one cigar after another.
He was thinking about how his business had lately been going very badly, how he was being pushed little by little off the edge of life, to which he had — clinging tightly — wanted to hold on at all costs these last years.
Out of habit Mirowski turned again to the balance book, like a drowning man clutching at a straw, although he knew the answer would come out the same:
— The catastrophe is unavoidable!
For the first time, surely, since he had come to awareness, Mirowski now slackened the reins of his thoughts, which had been charging at him like rampaging forces, ever more strongly, with the single intention of tormenting him.
He buried his head between his shoulders and, as if in resignation, let it drop onto the table.
And the thoughts ran off without any order, like wild steppe horses let loose into freedom by their owners after a long yoke, which it is now impossible to rein in.
Some thought flashed through his mind:
Salomon Mirowski gathered his last bit of strength, pushed away from himself all the tormenting thoughts that had been plaguing him without end, in order to clear the way for the one — as it seemed to him — saving thought.
He pictured to himself clearly what it was about, and remembered that today, early in the morning, while still lying in bed, he had thought a great deal about how it was still possible to save the situation — one only needed to obtain somewhere good and cheap credit for his business dealings.
Mirowski began to consider the plan calmly and with a settled mind, from all sides and in all its details, and came to the conclusion that with the improvement in the business conjuncture that seemed about to set in in his line of trade, it was possible to crawl out of the crisis and perhaps even get back on his feet.
A barely noticeable little smile appeared on his lips at this last thought...
— A cheap and good creditor — that is where the key to the solution lies.
He now ran through in his mind all the people with whom he had lately stood in business relations and who could come into consideration for his transactions, and on none of them did he pin any hopes.
On one of them, Steinberg, he lingered longer.
Mirowski felt ashamed of his own thoughts:
— After everything that has happened between us — he thought — he cannot possibly go and propose anything like that to him.
He remembered how years ago, when his Rózia was still younger, he could not bear the regular sitting-in [at his house] of Moshe Steinberg in particular; though, to tell the truth, he had thought about him more than once, and quite seriously at that: a modern young man, knows several languages, grammar and Bible, and a good businessman besides — had it not been that, as the devil would have it, he — Steinberg, that is — became a frequent visitor, and, as it seemed to Mirowski, as though Steinberg felt secure here, once tried to lend him an interest-free loan — very politely, even, but...
He sank his gaze into the book of accounts.
From the adjoining salon came the striking of the old chiming clock — an inheritance still from his grandfather — with its tone, by now hoarse and melancholy with age, which now echoes through the large, already quiet rooms even sadder, more gnawing...
Instinctively he tore his gaze away from the big book with small figures.
And although Mirowski had a clock standing before him on the writing desk, he nevertheless always liked, and especially at night, whenever he happened to sit alone until late, to hear from it [the old clock] itself what time [?] it might be by now, as if he would not trust another, and perhaps also to listen closely to its sound, which — it seemed to him — had changed a great deal, as if the clock, too, felt what had lately been going on here and was trying to adapt itself to the gloomy mood around.
— Three... five... eight... eleven... twelve — he counted quietly, as though afraid to miss even a single tone; at twelve he remained quiet, listening with half-closed eyes to its last sound, which modestly, as if not wishing to disturb the surrounding calm, rolled across the open [?], sleeping rooms ever quieter, weaker, until it died out entirely somewhere there in the corridor.
He gave a full shudder.
— Yes, he could not have done otherwise — he went on spinning his interrupted thoughts — he, Salomon Mirowski, the respected Jew and wealthy man of the town, could not bear it then, and on one occasion declared to him:
— You have... with me, for the time being, Mr. Steinberg... nothing... to hope for... You understand, I believe!...
He still remembers it very well, and also that his voice must have trembled badly as he said it, because Steinberg seemed frightened of him and, like a guilty man, tried to defend himself:
— I meant nothing bad by it, but if you, Mr. Mirowski, take it amiss, I am very sorry. In any case I will not be the first to begin speaking to you again about anything of the kind. But if you should have a request to make of me, you may, regardless of all this, turn to me.
Mirowski began to smoke the cigar more hastily.
The rings of smoke wound through the air ever denser, forming whole [?] coils, and Mirowski stared into them stubbornly, as though seeking in them some answer about bygone years, which now seem to him so strangely alien...
Mirowski would have sat like that for a long time yet, lost in himself, had it not been for his wife, who came in and interrupted his reflections.
— Why don't you go to sleep, Salomon, it's already past twelve o'clock? — she asked; — have you forgotten that you have to leave early tomorrow morning!
— Right away! — he answered; — yes, were you at young Steinberg's office about the protested bill of exchange? — He finished the last half-sentence quietly, as if he were ashamed of his own words, lowering his eyes at the same time into the book with small figures.
She moved closer to him, laid her delicate white hands — which in the half-darkness of the room paled more delicately still — on his shoulders, and looked him straight in the eyes.
— I — she drew out the words, like little whimpering [?] children who know they have done wrong and want to be forgiven all the same — I cannot go to his office; I was even halfway there already and turned back; I cannot!...
She reminded him once more that it was already late, asked whether the maid should bring in a glass of tea, and when she received in answer a shake of the head, as a sign of no, she slipped, as it were, out of the room — with a "good night" already in the doorway.
Mirowski remained alone with his thoughts.
In the chaos of thoughts and reflections, which now flew through his mind like short, chopped-off sentences, not always clear — one kept demanding an answer of him without end.
— All this now depends on me — the thought tormented him stubbornly, like a gnawing worm.
He tried to put together [?] a plan for the next day: — tomorrow he will be at Steinberg's, will try to begin the conversation just like that, about the protested bill and other business — and drop a hint that he may ask him for his daughter's hand, etc.
Mirowski closed the book and stood up with a brow cleared of the wrinkles that had lately furrowed so often his broad and clear mind, like people who after a long struggle with themselves have decided on an important step and feel the full seriousness it entails; he cast a chance glance at the clock standing on the table, took a few steps and remained standing in the open door.
From the adjoining salon came again the hoarse, melancholy sound of the old heirloom clock. — Now it is already very late, and so the old clock did not want to wake the sleepers and struck only one, as if to do its duty by the house and as a sign that it alone is always awake..
A knock on the door from the kitchen side interrupted Mirowski's dreams. — His daughter had come back from the theatre — he realised.
He strained his hearing in order to catch a few short phrases that carried here through the long corridor.
A strange grimace appeared on his somewhat twisted lips. — Adolf again — he thought bitterly — he doesn't even know why, but somehow he can't stand him, and at the same time, against his own will, a comparison forced itself on him between the two: Adolf and Steinberg.
Mirowski felt the need, which had been tormenting him for a long time already, to talk things over with his Rózia, and also to put his present plan to her. He felt guilty for everything she was going through; he knew that she was not indifferent to Steinberg, and that if not for him, she might already be happy today...
He went into her room and found her distraught, evidently from strong emotions just lived through, for he noticed on her matt-white cheeks two tears which she had not managed to hide from him..
In the conversation with her he felt helpless today; he asked — stroking her hand — about the play that had been performed today, and immediately, without any connection, asked whether she had not met again at the theatre — Steinberg? And whether she would not want him to meet with him tomorrow?
She tried to control herself.
— Yes — she answered — we saw each other; the whole time he looked at me with pleading eyes and waited, evidently, for me to begin the conversation, but, Father, we cannot, we are of the Mirowskis.
* * *
He barely dragged himself back to his study. Doubled up with pain, he dropped into the armchair. His head, gone pale, he let fall helplessly onto the table like one condemned to death; his temples pounded without end, as if with hammers, and in his mind a turmoil and jumble of seething thoughts: the downfall unavoidable... the only rescue lost... and above all, the words of his daughter rang in his ears:
— Father, we cannot, we are of the Mirowskis!...
Sosnowiec — 1929.
L. Kerner

The Jews in Zurich

[Jewish world — Switzerland; on the Zionist Congress in Zurich; letter.]
(A letter from Zurich).
By N. Weldler.

Swiss Jews in general are not unknown to Congress-goers. Since the Zionist Congress is now taking place for the first time in Zurich, it is worth saying something here about the life of the Jews there.

Individual Jews could already be found in Zurich in earlier centuries too, but until the time of full emancipation, up to the seventies of the last century, great restrictions on Jews still existed in Zurich.

When all the restrictions were abolished, the first to move to Zurich were the Jews who had lived in the Swiss villages of Endingen and Lengnau in the canton of Aargau: these are the Guggenheims, Balens [?], Wylers, whose family names already show that their forebears came here from somewhere else, and the Dreyfuses, whose name points to Alsatian origin.

The Alsatian Jews are the second element among Swiss Jews, if one speaks of the old-established ones. South German Jews came to Zurich from the border towns, such as Baden. Only in the 1890s did an immigration from the East begin — caused not only by the bad economic situation in Poland, Romania and Russia, but above all by the pogroms.

The first decade of the 20th century, which was rich in persecutions of Jews, increased the immigration of Jews to Zurich. During the war many Jews came in again, but they could not settle in here, both for economic reasons and because of the immigration restrictions, and after the war they left the city.

As everywhere, here too an antagonism between Eastern and Western European Jews can be noticed. But still not as strong as in other countries. For if only the Eastern Jew manages to climb up the social ladder and "become a mensch", then his brothers from the West are no longer ashamed of him.

The old-settled Zurich Jews are few in number and so they have necessarily had to mix with the Eastern Jews; to the credit of the Endingen and Lengnau Jews it must be said that apostasy is not widespread among them and that there are not so many mixed marriages among them as among the Jews who immigrated later, although on the other hand they keep themselves at a distance from other Jews.

There was no exact statistic of the Zurich Jews until recently. Only after the war, when the German Jew-haters wanted to afflict Switzerland too with antisemitism, did the Zurich community begin to investigate the structure of the Jewish population there. The work, however, was not carried out. On the other hand Sally Braunschweig, on the basis of the 1920 census, has written a monograph on the Zurich Jews, which appeared for the Congress. According to the figures he gives, Jews in Zurich made up 3.2% of the total population in 1920. Of them, 45% were Swiss citizens and 55% foreigners. Recently, however, the ratio must have changed. This can be seen from the lists of newly admitted citizens. The number of naturalised persons would have been much larger even earlier, had it not been for the 1920 ban on granting citizenship to Eastern Jews before they had lived 15 years in the country.

Nevertheless one cannot speak of antisemitism in Zurich. Here it has a quite different character than in Germany. The Italians in Switzerland are not treated any better than the Jews.

The Jews in Zurich form no fewer than three communities. The first is the liberal Israelitische Cultusgemeinde, the second the Israelitische Religionsgesellschaft, and the third — the "Agudat Achim" of the Eastern Jews.

Each community has its own cemetery. Recently, under the influence of Zionism, people have already begun to complain strongly about this fragmentation. There are now 4 Zionist associations in Zurich: the local Zionist organisation, the Zionist club, the Mizrachi and a Zionist women's association. The Zionist youth, too, has its own groups here, and it is hoped that it, the youth, will spread national consciousness among the old-established Zurich Jews and bind them more closely with the Jews of the whole world.
What's new in Zagłębie? — Będzin: Director of the power station paralysed at a meeting

Friday, 3 Tammuz [recte: Av] 5689. Piątek 9 sierpnia 1929 [Friday, 9 August 1929].
Będzin
Director of the power station paralysed at a meeting.
Last Friday, during a board meeting of the municipal power station (elektrownia), the director of the power station was suddenly struck by paralysis and stopped speaking.
The doctors who were called established that the paralysis is a serious one and the condition is hopeless.
The office of director is being filled by the deputy chairman of the city council, Mr. Jakub Erlich.
The funeral choir is active again..

During the school holidays, when children are out in the fresh air, the funeral choir is [?] active — made up of children whose lot it is to study at the local Talmud Torah..
This Tuesday we again saw, at a funeral, how the choir walked in front and naively[?] sang "Tzedek lefanav yehalekh" ["Righteousness shall go before him"]..
This time a smaller number of Talmud Torah children went along, because only the children wearing shoes were delegated to the funeral, whereas the barefoot children were kept away from the "holy work".
A fire in Plesner's house. — A horse and a cow burned

On Wednesday before dawn a fire broke out in a stable in Plesner's house on Kołłątaja Street. The fire spread with lightning speed to the surrounding stables and sheds, and in a moment everything stood in flames.
The first help was given by the tenants of the house; then the firemen from Koszelew arrived, and when the fire was already almost extinguished the Będzin firemen arrived...
The fire hurt poor Reuven Dąbek: his little horse, from which he made his living, was burned, and Moshe Lazeks's[?] cow was burned too.
Kołłątaja Street and the Old Market will be brighter
The magistrate is installing 11 new electric lamps on Kołłątaja Street and on the Old Market; of these, 6 lamps will be on Kołłątaja Street and 5 on the Old Market.
They got scared...

Our stand against the leaders of the kehilla, for having engaged the new officials Kaminer and Freilich, has had the proper effect. Last Sunday the kehilla board held a meeting at which it was decided to dismiss the officials after a month's time.
A policeman — a forger of bills

The policeman Górski had a fancy for a few jewellery articles. For that purpose he took goods from the jewellery dealers Balimowski[?], Weinsztok and Neuman and "covered" them with forged promissory notes (bills of exchange).
So that the swindle would be done properly, the policeman, who bore the number 319, changed it to 139...
These days the policeman was sentenced to 6 months in prison.
"Take my son from me too" — so cries a [?] community-tax payer

In the course of the week the community (gmina) collectors distributed the demands to pay the community tax ("etat") for 1928.
The tax commission worked over the tax roll very "thoroughly" and "taxed" with larger sums whomever it could — even madmen...
These days the community collector witnessed such a scene: a taxpayer on the Old Market has a mentally ill son, and this son was assessed 40 złoty of community tax. When the collector handed over the reminder slip, the father shouted:
— "Let the 'davores'[?] take my son as well"...
The tram stop
[The tram stop] on Kołłątaja Street has been moved. The stop is at house number 36 on the same street.
The Czeladź City Council Thinks Big... A Resolution to Take a Loan of Half a Million Zł.

[Czeladź — City council.]
At the last session of the Czeladź city council a resolution was adopted to take a loan in the sum of half a million zł. The loan is to be used to build a municipal slaughterhouse and to regulate the streets of Czeladź.
At the session an important resolution was also adopted: to open free courses for artisans.
A Bloody Wedding in Dąbrowa. One Guest Was Murdered

[Dąbrowa — Crime.]
On Bartar [?] Street in Dąbrowa a wedding took place on Sunday at a local Christian family.
Around one o'clock at night several unwanted guests came into the wedding, who also wanted to make merry.
At first there was an exchange of words, then blows began to fall, until people went for knives.
The result was terrible: one of the guests received several severe wounds and died on the way to the hospital.
Sosnowiec — A Horrible Act of Revenge by a Deceived Husband. Victim of a Dacha Romance

[Sosnowiec — Crime.]
The residents of Piaski Street were alarmed early on Sunday morning by terrible wild cries that were heard from the Kozak family.
When the door of the apartment was opened, the following horrible sight was seen: on the floor, in a pool of blood and without signs of life, lay 20-year-old Zosia, the wife of Ludwik Kozak.
Not far from the victim stood her husband in a frenzied state, with a bloodied razor in his hand...
At the screams of the neighbours the police arrived and took the severely wounded woman, in a dying condition, to hospital, and the murderous husband to the police station.
At the station the murderer calmed down only after several hours and gave explanations as to why he had committed the terrible deed against his young wife.
The husband related that he had sent his wife to a dacha in a nearby village. There she became acquainted with a young man, fell in love with him and had intimate relations with him.
When she came home she did not forget her “kochanek” [lover] either and corresponded with him. A love letter fell into his hands, and after an exchange of words he threw himself upon her with a razor and inflicted 13 wounds. The husband has been arrested.
Penny by Penny Adds Up to a Large Sum... The City Administration Must Cover 3 Million Zł.

[Sosnowiec — Municipality.]
The local magistrate did not regularly pay the instalments to the Ulen company, and a sum of 3 million zł. has accumulated.
Because of this the magistrate applied to the Bank Gospodarstwa Krajowego [National Economy Bank] for a loan for that sum.
The bank agrees to give the loan only on the following conditions: 1 million the magistrate is to pay in the course of this year, and in the following years smaller instalments.
At its last session the city administration considered the conditions and resolved to delegate President Marczyński to obtain more favourable conditions.
A Terrible Accident on 3 Maja Street

[Sosnowiec — Accidents.]
On Saturday at midday a motor vehicle running on the Sosnowiec—Katowice line ran over a railway worker who was walking on 3 Maja Street.
The victim was taken in a hopeless condition to the hospital at Pekin.
A Midwife Punished

[Sosnowiec — Courts.]
Behind closed doors, the trial of the midwife Hrynkiewicz, who had engaged in illegal operations [abortions], took place at the local district court. The midwife was sentenced to 2 months in prison.
A Hooligan Attack on a Jewish Worker

[Sosnowiec — Crime.]
At Federman's bazaar on Dekerta Street the worker Dawid Wierbski is employed by the Jewish butchers there. On Tuesday morning, being tired from his work, he lay down to sleep on a yard cart belonging to the local watchman.
While Wierbski was sound asleep, the yard watchman ran up to him and gave the young man a blow with a shovel.
The blow was so strong that the shovel broke into several pieces and the young man remained lying unconscious.
In this condition he was taken to the Jewish hospital, where he was given medical help.
The hooligan attack by the watchman, who makes his living from Jews, has caused bitterness, and they have resolved to demand of Mr. Federman that he remove the hooligan.
The Editor of “Kurier Zachodni” Sentenced to 2 Months in Prison

[Sosnowiec — Press, Courts.]
The Endek organ “Kurier Zachodni”, which is a full sister of the “Dwa Grosze”, has to this day not had a single lawsuit from Jewish society, upon which the paper pours pitch and brimstone.
But no sooner had the paper attacked the ławnik [alderman] Hauke [?] than the latter at once sought satisfaction and sued the paper's editor at the district court.
This week the trial took place, and the editor of the above-mentioned paper was sentenced to 2 months in prison.
A policeman unintentionally shot his comrade — for this he is punished with 2 months in prison.

On 19 March, in the police barracks, a policeman unintentionally shot dead his comrade.
The policeman stood these days before the District Court, which sentenced him to 2 months in prison.
—o—
For a "guest performance" on the tram he will sit a year in prison.
Yosef Geisztat [?] of Kraków came to Zagłębie, where he began to "give guest performances" on the trams. He took whatever he could lay his hands on: watches, travel bags, and also from breast pockets...
From a Christian passenger Geisztat tried to pull out a wallet with money, but this did not succeed, and he was handed over to the police.
These days Geisztat stood before the local District Court, which sentenced him to a year in prison.
A car ran over a Jewish woman.

On Monday, on Magrzeżewer [?] Street [probably Modrzejowska Street], the fruit-seller Zlate Wandersman was run over by a car; she suffered several serious wounds and is being treated in the Jewish hospital.
— Perhaps the police will at last see to it that cars do not race like devils through the commercial streets?
—o—
Sosnowiec will have a main police station.
The police precincts in Sielec and Pogoń, which have existed until now, are being converted into police stations (komisariaty).
The station in Sosnowiec will be the main station and will bear the number 1, Sielec — number 2 and Pogoń number 3.
Session of the Chamber of Commerce.

On Monday a session took place under the chairmanship of the vice-president of the commerce section of the Sosnowiec Chamber of Commerce, Mr. Chalewicki [?]. After discussing the agenda it was resolved to delegate the vice-president Mr. Chalewicki and councillor Kwiatek to the congress of the Polish chambers of commerce, as well as of Czechoslovakia, Bulgaria, Yugoslavia and Romania, which will take place in Poznań on the 25th of this month.
—o—
Killed by electric current.
On Monday at 10 in the evening a 15-year-old Christian boy was repairing a car. While working he used an electric lamp. Through carelessness the lamp came into contact with the electric current, which killed the boy on the spot.
—o—
From the court.
On Tuesday another trial took place in the municipal court which, regrettably [?], again brought out some pretty "flowers" concerning the activity of the "Tog editors" and their helpers.
Before the court stood Messrs. Zachariasz, Grinfeld, Fajner and others, who together washed the dirty laundry in the kettle that was, so to speak [?], called the "editorial office"...
The harshest sentence, however, went to the innocent Mr. Fajner, who was sentenced to 2 weeks' arrest.
—o—
A cloudburst.
On Tuesday at midday a cloudburst passed over Zagłębie, lasting barely an hour.
The rain damaged the tram line on Żeromskiego Street; because of this, tram traffic was disrupted for a long time.

[Będzin — circus.] Staniewski’s circus, which has come here for a few days, is enjoying colossal success; every performance is well attended. The programme is a good one. The acrobatic numbers in particular are first-class.
The circus stays until Monday; Saturday and Sunday — 2 performances.

The magistrate’s “wagon” wanders around the town.
[Będzin — municipality and taxes.] The Będzin magistrate (town council) has concluded that during the present crisis it is the most suitable time to collect arrears of municipal taxes.
A “wagon” goes along with the bailiff (sequestrator), and whoever does not settle his tax debt has his household goods taken away.
—o—
Excursion of “Hakoach”.
[Będzin — sport.] The gymnastics and sports club “Hakoach” in Będzin is making an excursion to Olkusz on Sunday.
Those who wish to take part in the excursion must come to the “Hakoach” premises at 5 in the morning.
—o—
Don’t eat cucumbers.
[Sosnowiec — health.] In Sosnowiec a child in a Christian family fell ill and died within a few hours.
The doctors established that the child fell ill from eating cucumbers.
—o—
When they snatch the bills of exchange and send no goods
[Commerce — bills of exchange and the law.] Also on the agenda are many disputes between merchants and buyers, because the wholesalers (hurtownicy) accept the bills of exchange but do not send the goods to the provincial merchant, and nevertheless the bills are put into circulation.
The provincial merchant does not know what to do in such a situation. He cannot redeem the bills, since he has received no goods for them; and it often happens that the wholesaler does not want to redeem the bills either, and demands that the buyer do it, and afterwards, when the bills have been paid, he will send the goods.
This is illegal. The wholesaler has no right to deceive the buyer and snatch the bills from him with the promise of sending the goods, and in the end put the bills into circulation and not send the goods. In such cases the buyer can go to court against these wholesalers for extortion (blackmail).
A merchant who does not send the goods because he does not trust the buyer must return the bills at once; he may not make use of them.
In such cases the injured parties can bring a suit against the merchants in the district court. One need not wait until the bills fall due. As soon as one receives a notice from the bank about the bill, one can go to court with the suit.
—o—
If the creditor goes bankrupt and the bill is in other hands.
[Commerce — bills of exchange and the law.] Many merchants are mistaken in thinking that if the merchant or manufacturer from whom goods were bought on bills of exchange has gone bankrupt, one may absolve oneself and not pay the bill.
They think that if the creditor, to whom the bill was given, does not pay, the drawer may meanwhile not pay either.
This is ridiculous and false.
The drawer cannot rely on the fact that his creditor is bankrupt and that he will no longer receive goods from him on credit. He is obliged to pay the bills to whoever presents them to him for payment.
—o—

[Będzin — crime.] Yesterday the (female) collector of “Express Zagłębia” was standing on Małachowskiego Street waiting for a tram to Sosnowiec. While she was lost in thought, a certain[?] thug ran up to her and snatched a briefcase with money from her.
