Jews as Co-Builders of the Economy in Poland

[Poland — economy; the Jews in the Polish economy.]
It is a fact that the field of economic life in Poland is becoming ever more strewn with Jewish casualties, and it is no wonder that the Jews have lost a whole series of economic positions. The economic conception of the leading Polish circles is driving the Jewish population, thanks to the étatist policy [state control of the economy], towards impoverishment and economic ruin. It is enough to glance at the Jewish street of any small town in Poland you choose to see the poverty that literally strikes the eye, and the fruitless chase after daily bread. Every clear-thinking person will understand that the overwhelming majority [as printed: "the oppressing humanity"] of the Jewish population does not eat its fill and is going under in hunger and want. The emaciated faces of the Jews in the provinces and the rags on their children should serve as a "memento mori" for Jewish public workers.
The Jewish people is being gnawed by an economic disease, which every day carries off thousands of victims from the economic surface and fills the broad Jewish street in Poland with them. And if that is so — and we have no reason to doubt this truth; these are not empty phrases — then one must approach the diagnosis of this disease with a clear, cool mind and quickly seek the means that would halt and cure it.
The faulty preparation of Jews for the various trades causes the Jewish population always to be hit harder and faster in its earning possibilities during a prolonged or passing economic crisis. Bound up with this faulty economic adaptation is also the artificially created and cultivated economic separation of the Jews in relation to the other peoples living in the country. In certain trades there is a hypertrophy [excess] of Jews, which was brought about[?] by circumstances and tradition, and other peoples are now pushing into these trades, at a time when the Jews have neither other conditions nor the proper preparation to choose other trades for themselves — trades to which Jews are not admitted owing to various restrictions for religious-national reasons. Let us tell the truth: from the perspective of Poland's ten-year jubilee [ten years of independence], the Jewish people has to this day not found a possibility of closer cooperation with Polish society.
It is a fact that the Jewish population in general relates to the Polish state positively, with a genuine desire for creative cooperation. It is also a fact that the Jews want a strong and rich Poland, because their material well-being, not to speak of other elements of social life, is organically bound up with the well-being and the development of the state; and if so, the mentality of Polish society and government must be ploughed over from the ground up in the direction of a matter-of-fact understanding of the actual situation of the Jews in Poland.
It is a sad truth that in certain social circles a false assessment of the Jews as citizens and as co-builders of Poland's economic development has taken root; there prevails the false conviction that the Jews are an element that supposedly burdens the well-being and the economic development of Poland, and that they must therefore be pushed out of all fields of economic life.
This opinion, however, is false for this reason alone: that the purely human economic distress of the Jews in Poland contradicts such a view. And besides, looking at the matter quite objectively, some forget that by destroying the Jewish economy one at the same time undermines the foundations of the state, because a hungry and naked citizen is no source that strengthens the state treasury.
Society and the Polish government must open their eyes and soberly understand that the Jews in Poland have constitutional rights to work and to live. People of good will who have a feeling of social responsibility must take up this question, and above all the government must not evade it; it must remember the old historical truth that a contented citizen is a firm point of support for the strength of the state, while a hungry one serves as a breeding ground[?] for upheavals and anarchy.
The help and intervention of the government will not, however, suffice; Jewish society itself must place the question of rescue at the head of its tasks. It is simply a vital necessity to convene a general Jewish economic congress in Poland with a controlled platform, for one single purpose: let us save ourselves, by our own efforts, from want and ruin, while it is not yet too late!
G. D.
A Letter from Bystra

[Letter from a resort — Bystra.]
Bystra is a very beautiful place with about 200 permanent residents; it has very good, mild air, a beautiful forest and all the necessary things a health resort calls for: good water, water for bathing and also a so-called „plaża“ [bathing beach].
The health-insurance fund (Kasa Chorych) has a splendidly beautiful villa here; apart from that there is no permanent doctor here, only from Bielsko a doctor comes once a day (and not every day either) and receives patients for about 2 hours, together with a dentist. The connection with Bielitz [Bielsko] is very convenient. Besides the railway, fine buses run frequently; there are also fine hotels and „dancings“, where people „shimmy“ on all sides. There are already about 20 boarding houses (pensions), among them 3 Jewish ones and one „Jewish-Catholic“, i.e. of Jews who are not particular about meat with milk...
Prices in the Jewish pensions are between 12 and 14 złoty. The Christian pensions are mostly occupied by our brethren, the Children of Israel. There they are mostly hungry, yet they push their way in there, where people still point fingers at them.
Statistically there are about 1300 guests here, of whom, no evil eye, 80—95 percent are our brethren, and a good number of them „genuine“ Jews too. Of course the majority are of the fair sex, who, poor things, work hard all year and must come here to spend a whole summer, so that at least a trace remains — a bit of „tan“ on the behind. Most represented, according to information, are Sosnowiec, Będzin, Katowice, Kraków, Bielitz, a little also Dąbrowa, Częstochowa, Zawiercie, Łódź, and even Warsaw.
The public is divided into two categories: 1) those who rest, i.e. lie on the deck-chairs (leżaki) and on the meadows and stroll a little; 2) those who want to live it up — sing, dance, play cards and enjoy all the pleasures of this world at full steam.
The pensions, especially the Jewish ones, have their own specific guests, namely: „Kuchnia Domowa“ [„Home Cooking“] — a Galician „fine Jew“, lehavdil like in the old days R' Berishl Weiss (Berish Kodesh) with a minyan, a rabbi or a rebbe, according to the dirt — kosher even for the most scrupulous of the scrupulous; the owners, real restaurateurs, declare all other Jewish pensions „treyf“.
2) The pension „Graner“ is already arranged for all kinds of Jews, the more pious and the intelligentsia.
3) The pension „Podlanka“ (Frenkel) is no less kosher than „Kuchnia Domowa“, only much cleaner, very elegantly and neatly furnished; it caters to the whole Jewish intelligentsia, and consequently the guests come only from the better class.
As a curiosity the following case may serve: for a certain time the bigwigs of Będzin took their meals at the pension „Podlanka“. Once they suddenly found out that it is kosher there — and they turned yellow[?]...
Ger ve-Toshav [„Stranger and Sojourner“].

A Letter to the Editor.
1.
Esteemed Mr. Editor!
We have the honour to ask you to publish the following letter in your esteemed newspaper:
For about 2 years now we have been drawing the attention of the Będzin rabbinate to the fact that the town of Będzin is supplied with 30 percent foreign meat from various places, whereas the rabbinate forbade us butchers to bring from those places even a single kilo of meat, because it is not kosher. It goes without saying that we had to submit to this prohibition and even sign it. If it happened that a butcher broke the prohibition, he was summoned to the rabbinate and his butcher's stall was banned.
But what is forbidden to us is permitted to other Jews, namely: the sausage manufacturers may quite freely bring meat „without any fear of prohibition“ from all places, use it and sell it as „glatt kosher“. Several times already we have shown the rabbinate with facts that the sausage manufacturers bring meat from Łazy, Poręba, Gejdwecke[?], Gołonóg etc., where one does not know whether it is completely kosher, or deveined, or whether the treyf meat has been removed — which borders on compromise. After long and hard effort we managed to get the rabbinate to issue a prohibition on the sausage of the partners Becalel Kuperwaser and Icze Ber Fatasz, and [to announce] at the afternoon prayer in 2 minyanim[?] of Jews that the sausage is not under the rabbi's supervision. But that did not last long.
Meanwhile, however, the following case occurred: the feldsher of the slaughterhouse was walking in the street and, seeing a strange cart with meat, he took it into the slaughterhouse for inspection. It turned out (the butcher Jakub Rozenholc happened to be present) that very much treyf meat was found there, not deveined, pieces of udder still with milk and fat, which cannot be deveined at all and are as treyf as pork. The butcher Jakub Rozenholc was beside himself and ran to the rabbinical judges (morei hora'ah) to hand over the matter, but they began sending him from one to the other. Finally he managed to find the supervisor (ne'eman) Szalom Baruch Lewowicz, who also saw the fact. The rabbinate, however, at once began to look for a dispensation, on the grounds that R' Becalel Kuperwaser deveins the meat. But the butchers answered at once that long practice in Kuperwaser's factory has shown that as soon as he receives meat, no matter from whom, the worker or helper, even a gentile lad, immediately soaks the meat. Nobody checks for deveining or for treyf.
Seeing that the rabbinate takes no clear position on these facts, we are compelled to bring the matter to the knowledge of the whole Jewish population; perhaps in this way the situation will come to an end.
Respectfully,
The Master Butchers' Association in Będzin.
(Stamp and chairman of the section)

Esteemed Editors!
We, the undersigned summer guests from Leśniów (near Żarki), ask you to publish the following lines in the columns of your newspaper:
For quite a long time now the local summer guests have been witnesses to various outbursts and incidents against the Jewish summer guests. Lately the attacks are frequently repeated and in an ever sharper form, so that they threaten the very stay of Jews here. We are simply not safe when it gets dark. To be outside the house means catching a stone or a bucket of water from some lowlife or other. Last Friday night, when a group of summer guests was sitting in the clearing (polanka) at 10 o'clock in the evening, they were attacked by a group of hooligans who, armed with sticks, threw themselves at the public, which consisted mostly of women and girls, who went into spasms from fright. There are a few lightly wounded; the attackers could not be caught because of the darkness that reigns here at night.
We therefore find it necessary, through the medium of your esteemed newspaper, to make the public of summer guests aware of the above facts, and at the same time we ask the gmina (municipality) in Leśniów: perhaps it is already time that, out of the money collected every year from the Jewish summer guests, a policeman and some lamps should be put up, so that there will be no room for various hooligans?
We are sure that you will publish our letter; we thank you in advance and sign
Respectfully,
A group of summer guests.

Flourishing and Decline.

[Sosnowiec — Kehilla; charity and mutual aid; opinion.]
(How must we relate to institutions that bring benefit to society, and to those that do not?)
Not long ago we had a notice about it, and now we are being told the same thing once again: that the Jews of Sosnowiec, and precisely the well-to-do among them, want to take revenge on the Gemilut Chesed (interest-free loan) fund because a certain number of people were given too high an assessment ("etat").
But, for heaven's sake, how unbalanced these people are, how irrational these complaints are! What does it mean to take revenge on a Gemilut Chesed fund — on an institution set up to rescue a person just as he is about to lose his balance, just as he is about to go under? What, then, is this downtrodden person guilty of, if someone has wronged[?] you? What kind of justice is that? On whom are you going to take revenge? On the poor, careworn Jew? What does he owe you? And what will you achieve by it if you help bring down this institution of bright light — apart from [harming] the few people who look forward to the loans that keep people on their feet?
Of course, that is not the point; the state of this useful institution is not, God forbid, at such a level — and yet one cannot understand how people would be helped if they brought it down to that bitter level.
It is a rare thing, how unbalanced we are. At every opportunity we go at things with the left hand to the right ear. No one tries to get rid of the Jewish kehilla because it is good for nothing, because it is rotten through and through, because we get nothing from it, because it does absolutely nothing for us. In that case we do not try to protest in any way whatsoever; no one makes an effort to replace the leadership; no one cares whether bad should become good, whether something helpless should become useful and effective — yet it is considered a radical remedy to disrupt the existence of another, useful, popular institution.
Why, then, go by such crooked paths? Whom will the destruction of a useful institution benefit? Let us suppose that no such institution existed in Sosnowiec and people had to be helped — those who can be saved with a small loan must not be allowed to fall — would you not, at a given moment, support such people out of your own pocket? Quite certainly you would; so surely it is more convenient for you when it is done on your behalf, when you discharge the duty by paying your monthly pledge there.
No one, therefore, will doubt the necessity of the Gemilut Chesed fund, let alone in the present crisis, when so many downtrodden people come asking to be rescued with a loan. On the contrary, understanding people, mature in public affairs, should see to it that the scope of this institution is broadened, because lately more and more downtrodden people have begun to use it; evidently the crisis is taking firmer root among us, and people need rescue.
This matter really ought to be discussed more broadly and the question considered seriously. After all, we are a people of "merciful sons of the merciful"; we do not let anyone fall as long as we have the strength to support them. And from precisely this standpoint one ought to see to it that our Gemilut Chesed fund receives broader powers — by which we mean that it should be able to grant more and larger loans. For this, the assistance of the city is needed, and the warm attitude of respected citizens.
The institution unquestionably deserves that people take an interest in it. Let its activity be examined; let it be seen whether it needs broader powers, whether it must take up larger premises; and when all this is confirmed, let Jewish Sosnowiec not remain indifferent to so useful an enterprise, which was created with so much toil and effort.
We must, once and for all, render ourselves a clear account; we must make clear to ourselves and want to understand that institutions — whatever they may be — as soon as they bring benefit to society, a sacred duty lies upon us to maintain such institutions and to give them every possibility to prosper as well as possible. When, on the other hand, we realise that we have institutions that bring no benefit, then it is one of two things: either one must go in there and look into everything, investigate, establish order and bring it to a proper, useful condition, so that it brings benefit to society; or, if not, it should be declared incompetent and useless, and in that case society should rid itself of it — because, after all, one must remember that public money is not, and must not be made, a matter of lawlessness (hefkerut).
As for our kehilla board, we all know what state it is in, how low it has fallen and to what extent it accomplishes nothing for society. We know very well that beyond collecting the budget ("etat") they are capable of nothing there; and therefore it is self-evident that when the members are taxed with sums that are too large, it must provoke indignation — especially when we do not see the kehilla give anything to anyone, accomplish anything for the common good, for the benefit of Jewish Sosnowiec, where everything is in such a lamentable condition, in such a dreadful state, that it is better not to speak of it, because one's face turns red with shame when one has to speak of every detail. And therefore it would indeed be high time for our Jewish kehilla board to be dissolved.
That is what must be demanded, and for that serious steps must be taken.
Dr. Papuri.
Little Feuilleton: My Bookkeepers...

[Feuilleton — a humorous letter on the tax burden.]
Dear brother Jacob!
Your "letter" with your "picture" we have received; I am very glad that together with many of your landsmen you are planning to come to us in "Europe" to visit the "graves of the ancestors"... Long may they live indeed, our dead! In their merit you over there, in your faraway America, remember in passing us, the living, as well — although I must tell you the truth, dear brother, that here it has lately become hard to tell a living man from a dead one... Apart from the tax inspector and the "sekwestrators" [bailiffs] of the Magistrate [municipality] and of the tax office, you don't see a single customer nowadays.. It is "sianokos" [haymaking season] — they mow, they keep on mowing...
In one thing, you see, little brother, I am well off: the bookkeeping. My tax accounts are, thank God, in perfect order: the "zeznania" [tax declarations] lie separately, the "nakazy" [payment orders] — separately, the "przypomnienia" [reminders] — separately, the "odwołania" [appeals] with the arguments — separately, and — the most important thing of all — the "pokwitowania" [receipts] separately. I won't boast to you, but wake me in the middle of the night and I will find you at once, for example, the 2nd "zaliczka" [instalment] of the "podatek obrotowy" [turnover tax] of the year 1926.
I'll tell you the truth: if only they had such order at the tax office as I have, we too would look better. Just recently, for instance, our executor [bailiff] suddenly bethinks himself and, out of the blue, brings me fresh tidings — what is it? I owe, he says, a "zaległy podatek" — "stale tax" they call it. — Meaning? — A few years back, when demanding from me the turnover or the income tax ("abiratowy" [sic] or "dochodowy"), he made a mistake of 20 groszy; he had, he says, a headache at the time, so he made a mistake in the calculation — and so would I kindly now pay the sum with the interest — 15 gulden and 80 groszy... What do you think? I had to pay him, and I even wished him good health and a calm head in future, because a few more headaches and — "a gentile's mistake is permitted" — I'm finished, a "hat-maker" [i.e. bankrupt]... So, dear brother, I still pray for the welfare of the government.
And my bookkeeping is in order for a very simple reason: I have my own "urzędnicy" [officials], "tax officials" it's called. You surely remember my elder boys, may they be well, Motele and Berele — today they are already "boyen" [? boys], no evil eye. And although they have been through university, and one is a qualified "economist" and the other a "humanist" (and with kosher Polish diplomas, too), they are as far from getting government posts as I am from... making a living. So I thought it over and sat one down on the turnover tax and the other on the income tax, and they work for me in the "business" — may it be no worse in future. Work, thank God, I don't lack... Besides that, for the "appeals" I also have an only daughter, Chayele is her name, a "maturzystka" [holder of the matriculation certificate], who has just finished commercial courses; she writes "pragies" [? petitions] with "appeals" — I tell you, the best and finest lawyers aren't worth a thing next to her, for who else knows Daddy's "arguments" as well as she does?.. True, the appeals have never helped me yet, but I promise you: whoever is to blame, she truly is not.
As you see, dear brother, the children and I are provided with work over our heads. The only worry is a livelihood. First heaven, then your dollars — and I'll be provided with a livelihood too.
In expectation of your dollars, with which I must pay the latest instalment of the turnover tax, I sign with greetings and love,
Your brother Shmulik.
I Wish I Had Been a Woman...

[Feuilleton — humour; the position of women.] By M. Mendelson.
All over the globe, wherever the human species is to be found, the accepted opinion is that the "male sex", i.e. the man, is countless times happier than the woman; that he, the man — "the one who wears the trousers", as they say — with his muscles and his spirit, with his position and his build, is top of the heap, the boss of everything, the crown of mankind, while she, the woman, is a blessing in vain, not worth a kopeck, a poor unfortunate creature.
Such a false notion has been rooted since ancient times in the psyche of mankind, among men and women alike, and that is why we men send off every day to Him Who Lives Forever the blessing "who has not made me a woman" — such praise and thanksgiving. And since such masculine greatness has been poured out upon our heads, on the other side too a jealousy of us men has been aroused among the women: they are emancipationists, suffragettes, they fight for equality, they begrudge us our manhood, and they, the women, want to be as happy as we men are...
Well, to stand up and argue it out with the woman and prove to her that it's woe and alas for our manhood — that I won't undertake, because, first, however many words I use, she will always have nine times as many, so that she will always end up in the right; and second, it simply doesn't bother me that she lives in error. On the contrary, let her think that we are happy, let her really want to be equal to us, and let her too taste all the "joys" that we men have...
So, as I said, it won't help, nor will it pay, to show the woman her mistake, especially when she sees how we fuss over her so, how we don't even let her bend down, how we run after her and melt for a smile of hers, for a wink of hers — she really thinks that we lack nothing at all, except a bit of headache and a few troubles. And this is exactly what amazes me: how can it be! Why should we men fool ourselves and others, persuade ourselves and others that we are the happiest of all, while — whoever else may not know — we do know very well how deep our "trade" lies in the ground, how far gone we are in utter troubles; so why on earth is it so?
Truth is truth[!]: we too once had better times, times when it was worth envying us. But all that was once, yes, once — when there did not lie upon our heads all the modern inventions like: little bills of exchange, little protests, little gmilus-khesed loans, taxes, and so on and so forth; when all sorts of little bailiffs, little sequestrators and plain little briefcase-gents were not forever whirling around us; when the man in the house was still a man; when "and he shall rule over her" had not yet heard of any modernization; when the wife still had in mind the home, the kitchen and the husband with the children — back then the blessing "who has not made me a woman" was still topical, and we menfolk could really swagger and praise and thank the great Creator for having created us men. But today?
Today things are bitter and nasty in the "men's branch", so bitter that any woman of today is a thousand times better off than us menfolk with all our "joys", "rights" and privileges; and although it is not in my nature to envy anyone, I nevertheless envy the woman of today, who lives such a good day with such a good night — first at her father's expense and then at her husband's — and more than once I say to myself: I wish I had been a woman!
Yes, with all my male consciousness and subconsciousness I wish I were a woman, even though my brain capacity would suffer a great deal, my intellect would shrink considerably, and many good qualities and virtues would then vanish from me — and yet it is all worth it, because what comes out? That we are strong and clever and we rule the world — while she, the weak woman, rules over us, and makes us weak and sick, grey and old, and wears out our few years?
So I want to be a woman, a modern woman, and it goes without saying that my comrades — the women of the whole world — would not be ashamed of me; like all of them I would not dip my hand in cold water; like all of them I would live free and carefree, letting the husband work like a donkey to make money for my toilettes, fashions and make-up contraptions; at home too I would harness the husband to run the household, while I myself would run to the shops, to the tailor, out for a stroll, to every amusement — in a word, I would live and love everyone, as long as it was not my own husband, that dupe; for however much the husband wears himself out and however much money he gives, he is still a dupe, a miser, a scoundrel, a tyrant, a murderer, and on such a man it is a mitzvah and a duty of every modern woman to take revenge, so that he will have plenty to tell about!
And had I been a woman, I would surely also have been pretty and forever young, though I am already well on in years and my face is old and "so-so"[?] too; because, first, today, thank God, there is a whole industry for making the woman pretty and young! Second, nowadays there are no ugly women at all; the proof: show me even one woman who doesn't consider herself, if not a "consummate beauty", then at least an "average beauty"!
And what difference does it make, pretty or ugly! And even if ugly — so what? Isn't the ugliest and silliest woman better off today than the cleverest and strongest male person? So what do I have to lose? And what kind of risk is it anyway?
I therefore say quite firmly and resolutely, quite openly and loudly, that "without wavering and without regret" I am ready to swap places with the woman — and would that we all meant it as seriously as I mean this wish and desire:
I wish I had been a woman!...

For Shabbat Nachamu

Nachamu, Nachamu! [Comfort ye, comfort ye!]
Be comforted, payers of the market tax,
stall-keepers [straganiarze], bill-twisters,
what is the "halia" [hala — the market hall] to us, who needs the "halia"?

the municipal in-laws led you to the wedding canopy,
the sworn "benefactors" and intercessors,
who are ardent suitors for your votes,

swear by beard and sidelocks,
but whether the promises will be kept —
who knows? who knows?
Meanwhile — do be comforted!

pay your tax instalments regularly,
console yourselves that in a year
you will have to pay twice as much.

Console yourselves, young wives, that at the dacha [summer resort]
you can do as you please,
and your husband, the dim-witted golem,
will send you ever more money...

Be comforted, sportsmen [sportowcy]! The Częstochowa luck is something of a consolation for the defeats by "Sosnowiec" and Radom.

Be comforted, city of Sosnowiec! The magistrate [city council] has presented you with a sewer system; it will not be stingy with taxes on you; you will have plenty to sing and tell about...

Dr. A. Weissman — The Seduced Girl (a novel of Jewish life in the Old World, based on historical facts), instalment 16

Sister Maria stayed. Her face changed all at once. All the anger went out of it, and a sugar-sweet expression spread over her face.
— My child! — she said in a slow tone.
— You will be happy when you marry Jan. He is a very decent and honest young man, and a devout Christian besides, a believer; he is nothing like today's young people, he is quiet, calm, and you will be happy with him.
— Sister, I am terribly tired, leave me alone.
— This is the first time I see a girl get bored and tired of talking about her beloved bridegroom.
— Have pity on me, Sister, and leave me alone.
Sister Maria shrugged her shoulders, her face again twisted into an angry expression, and she now said sternly:
— You are too capricious, Mania, you do not want to value our kindness to you. Nobody here lives as well as you do, everyone loves you, and you do not make use of our kindness. Another girl in your place would consider herself the happiest of all if such a decent young man as Jan were found to free her from the convent.
Mania started.
— Are there then still others in the convent as unhappy as I, who want to be freed?
— You understand nothing, my child, you do not know our sisters. There are some here who renounced all the pleasures in the world in order to be in the convent, and there are also some who sit in silence, sing prayers and long for the moment when they can be freed in the way you can be freed — by marrying Jan, who loves you so much.
— And without love I cannot get free of this place?
— It is hard, my child, very hard. I myself promised you only yesterday to free you, but it has been decided here that we may not take such a great sin upon ourselves.
Mania's patience snapped; she jumped up and screamed in a voice not her own:
— But what do you want of me? Tell me, by what right do you rule over me? Did I sell myself to you? I do not want to be here with you any more, I do not want to know your convent or you. How much longer will you torment me with your kind words? Let me go! I may do with myself what I like, I have a home, I have parents, what do you want of me? Let me go!
— Oh my God! What do my ears hear? Unhappy one, your own ears do not hear your words.
The Sister began crossing herself and went on:
— It is not you, Mania, who speaks such words — some demon has entered into you and blasphemes our convent. May the one God have mercy on you and make your heart pure. You must first prepare for baptism and then marry Jan, and you speak such words. No, my child, we cannot, we may not let such lost little lambs go; we only want your good — for what else is our convent for, if not to do good for sinful people? Remember, Mania, that you yourself will thank us afterwards; and now you speak with such anger — it is lucky that nobody but me hears it. Lie down, then, and better be silent and wait for your happy day of baptism. — Good night, my child!
With these words Sister Maria made for the door.
— Don't leave me alone! — Mania begged — or let me go completely free!
— Calm yourself, Mania; after tonight you will know whether you are free or not; we shall see each other again tonight.
And with these words the Sister left Mania's room.
That same night Mania waited a long time for Sister Maria to come and free her, until she fell asleep from exhaustion.
She saw terrible dreams in her sleep, and in great fright she woke with a start and suddenly saw before her the elder Sister Irena with several more sisters, who held lit candles in their hands — just as on that earlier occasion when they had led Mania into the cellars to show her the holy graves there.
— Come, my child! — Sister Irena addressed Mania in a stern tone.
— Where to? — she asked in a voice not her own, but she received no answer from anyone.
And Sister Irena, arm in arm with Mania, accompanied by the sisters with the candles in their hands, left the room and went along the same way by which they had earlier gone with Mania to the cellars of the holy graves.
— Where are you taking me? — Mania asked in a trembling voice. But no one answered her. Her voice was drowned by the quiet prayer-chant of the sisters with the candles in their hands, who did not stop singing prayers the whole way.
— — —
In the great cellars where the holy graves were, there were also several rooms which were called "cells". There lived the most pious sisters, who had bought themselves a good name with their constant prayers, their faithfulness and their devotion to the cloister.
Into the hands of these pious sisters newcomers who were very stubborn and did not want to convert were quite often handed over.
The sisters would never stop talking at length to the newcomers, to convince them of their error, and that only devotion and faith of the spirit can save their sinful souls.
Into the cellars they would also transfer those who, it was feared, might run away.
When these were in the cellars, it was easy to deny that they were in the convent, because the cellars were the safest place, which no private person could enter or even learn about at all.
The cellar buildings stood quite apart on the large grounds of the convent, and not all of the convent's permanent residents had the privilege of passing near them.

What's New in Zagłębie?
(Date boxes: Friday, 10 Av 5689 — Piątek 16 sierpnia 1929 [Friday, 16 August 1929].)
Będzin
How magistrate officials collect tax debts
A pogrom scene in the Old Market.
On Wednesday afternoon a scene took place in the Old Market that can serve as an illustration of how a sequestrator (bailiff) of the local magistrate collects tax debts.
A magistrate "wagon" drove up to the little shop of the widow Lichtig, and the sequestrator, accompanied by a policeman, set about the job of emptying out the little bit of iron goods that the poor family owns. Mrs. Lichtig and her 6 children, seeing that they were about to be ruined entirely, began to scream and weep. The desperate voices brought together the surrounding neighbours, and also many people, who began to use every means so that the distraint should not be carried out.
The wailing also called out the neighbour Mr. Abraham Hampel, who wanted to go into the shop in order to find a way out and ease the terrible situation.
But the policeman, who was standing at the entrance to the shop, resisted and did not let Mr. Hampel go in. When Mr. Hampel nevertheless insisted on going inside, the policeman whipped out his naked sword and threatened Hampel. The latter, seeing that he faced certain danger, ran off and intervened by telephone with the magistrate that the terrible distraint against the desperate family be stopped.
A few minutes later a second sequestrator indeed arrived, who accepted an instalment in the sum of 50 zł., and the distraint was not carried out.
As we are informed, the first sequestrator, who had come to carry out the distraint, expressed himself with the words: "All the Jews should be killed"...
The scene made a shattering impression, and among the assembled crowd one heard various comments addressed to the magistrate and to our city councillors.
A New Director at the Jewish Gymnasium.

[Będzin — Education.]
On the strength of the recommendation of such scholars as Professors Schorr and Bałaban, the management of "Yavne" has engaged as director Dr. David Einhorn, long-time director of the Jewish gymnasium in Przemyśl.
Dr. Einhorn is known as a great scholar and, above all, a nationally-minded Jew, and it is to be expected that he will bring the school to a high level.
The school building, which was built by the philanthropist Mr. Fürstenberg, is being entirely completed these days, including the interior fittings, and next week the school will already be operating in the new, splendid building.

The residents of Rybna Street complain about the lamentable state in which the lane finds itself.
Because of the water-main works in the nearby lanes, deep channels of water and mud have formed in several places.
The sun bakes, and from the "homely swamps" there rise unpleasant smells, and it goes without saying that the swamps are also a nest for various dangerous bacilli.
Discovered after 25 Years.

[Będzin — Crime.]
The local police have arrested a well-known bandit who in the year 1904 committed a murder beyond Łagisza. The man has been wanted for 25 years already.

[Będzin — Market.]
On Tuesday a brawl broke out in the Old Market among several Jewish greengrocers. In the brawl a Jewish woman "distinguished" herself and fiercely attacked her opponents with crates, boards and other similar implements.
Some of the participants in the brawl were taken, covered in blood, to the police station.
"Evening Lessons" in the Aleksander Shtibl.

Because of the great interest aroused by the study of the chapter [of Pirkei Avot] every Sabbath by the well-known head of the yeshiva, Rabbi Shmuel Silberstein, the yeshiva committee has decided that in the Aleksander shtibl evening lessons are to be taught every evening by the above-mentioned head of the yeshiva.
The opening takes place next Tuesday, the fifteenth of Av.

He vanished in front of the prison
[Będzin — crime.] A well-known thief was being led to the local prison escorted by a policeman. On coming close to the prison building he vanished — “and is no more”...
Czeladź abolishes the post of vice-president

[Czeladź — municipality.] At the meeting of the Czeladź town council the “club” of the “Mieszczanie” [burghers] put forward the following 2 motions: 1) because of the economic crisis the post of vice-president [deputy mayor] should be abolished, in order to save an expense of several thousand zł. a year, and 2) that the salaries of the ławnicy [aldermen of the town board] be reduced from 100 to 50 zł. a month.
The first motion, to abolish the vice-president, was adopted by a majority of votes; the vote on the second motion, however, could not take place, because the P.P.S. [Polish Socialist Party] members broke the quorum of the meeting.

Accident on Zuckerman’s ramp

[Dąbrowa — Medicine.] An Important Invention in Medicine by a Local Doctor
The local doctor Giefielski [?] has succeeded, after a great deal of work and many experiments, in making an invention that may be of very great importance in making a diagnosis in complicated illnesses, when with the means known until now it is difficult to find out what the patient is suffering from.
As is known, it happens in very many illnesses that it is hard for the doctor to make a certain diagnosis, and in such cases it is hard to cure the illness. Needless to say what misfortunes this leads to, and how important in medicine is the problem of finding a means that would make it possible to establish the correct diagnosis in a more certain way than until now. Many scientists are occupied with the question, but no sure means in this field has yet been invented.
Now the local doctor A. Giefielski has succeeded in making the invention thanks to which it will be possible to make the diagnosis even in such cases where until now this was not possible.
It is a known rule in medicine that with every illness the weight of the blood changes. Dr. Giefielski went in this direction in his research and experiments and, after much effort, constructed an instrument for weighing blood specially for diagnostic purposes.
The instrument is a very simple one and can be used quite easily. One need only take one drop of blood from the patient, weigh it on the instrument, and according to the weight the drop of blood has, one can establish the diagnosis of the illness on the spot.
These days Dr. Giefielski patented his invention at the Warsaw Patent Office under number 10611, and although this has not yet been officially published, a German firm has already turned up that wants to buy the invention.
In Polish scientific circles they are convinced that the new invention is of very great importance, and it is to be expected that it will be widely adopted.

[Olkusz — Sport.] Olkusz: From the Gymnastics Festival
On Sunday the gymnastics festival (Turnfest) took place, organized by "Postęp" with the participation of Będzin's "Hakoach". At half past 7 in the morning the train arrived with the "Hakoach" drużyna (team), and accompanied by their band they marched through the town to the Resursa on Żuradzka Street, where they rested. At half past 2 in the afternoon a march-past (defilada) took place in the market square before the initiators of the excursion, and afterwards the march into the woods to "Szarga Góra" [?], where gymnastic exercises and other entertainments took place. At 7 in the evening "Hakoach", accompanied by the local youth, marched back to the train with timbrels and dances. In the evening there was a dance.
The Rabbi (may he live long, Amen), on learning that the entertainment would take place on a Sunday within the Nine Days, endeavoured with the initiators to have it postponed, but without success.
—o—
[Olkusz — Municipality.] Personal Notes
The Jewish ławnik (alderman) and decernent (department head) Mr. A. Blum has laid down his mandate as ławnik because of the hostility of some Christian councillors. After the holidays the election of another ławnik in his place will take place. The Jewish councillors held a consultation about a candidate for the place of the resigned ławnik. For the time being nothing definite has yet been decided. A. B.

[Sosnowiec — Institutions.] Correction
Mr. Reuven Binensztok, who chaired the last general meeting of the Sosnowiec "Linat Hacholim", asks us to publish the following correction:
1) It is not true that anyone of those assembled protested against me as chairman, and 2) [it is not true] that the motion of Mr. Jungster to express no confidence in the present administration was adopted; on the contrary, a considerable majority was for expressing full confidence in the present administration.

[Sosnowiec and Będzin — Trade and taxes.] The small-trader commercial councillors of the Sosnowiec Chamber of Commerce have resolved to launch a campaign for an amnesty on the tax arrears of 3rd- and 4th-category commercial enterprises up to and including 1927. Therefore the Będzin Small Traders' Association calls on all taxpayers — 1) who in their time submitted petitions to have their tax arrears remitted and whose petitions have not been dealt with to this day, and 2) the impoverished[?] taxpayers whose tax arrears ought to be remitted — to register immediately, in their own interest, at the Association's secretariat.

Drunkards make merry
[Strzemieszyce — Incidents.] On Wednesday a group of drunkards in Strzemieszyce "made merry" by accosting every Jew who passed by, whom they "honoured" with blows. As a result a fight broke out between the drunkards and several Jews who put up resistance. A mob soon gathered, among them dark elements who incited to excesses, but thanks to the energetic intervention of the police no serious incidents occurred.
—o—
Victims of thunder and accidents
[Strzemieszyce — Accidents.] On Monday a terrible storm passed over Strzemieszyce, accompanied by heavy thunder and lightning. A Christian was killed by the thunder [i.e. lightning] and several persons were injured.
On Tuesday a car ran over a young man who was riding a bicycle; the result was that the young man was taken to hospital in a moribund state.
—o—
The young generation of the Ger shtibl "rejoices" on Tisha B'Av..
[Będzin — Hasidim.] In the big Ger shtibl in Będzin the young "Hasidim" observed this year's Tisha B'Av according to a new rite: they no longer made use of the old prickly Tisha B'Av "meteors" [probably the burrs traditionally thrown on Tisha B'Av], but of banging with ersatz (toy) revolvers. Afterwards a bloody brawl took place in which Mr. M. Krel was injured, having tried to react to the young people's insolent deeds.
—o—
Agitation in Orthodox circles against the mikveh sheet.
[Będzin — Press and controversy.] In the course of the week many people from Orthodox circles came to us at the editorial office, among them some who are very far from any party strife and known in town as honest Jews, men of Torah learning.
The delegations expressed to us their bitterness against the insolent people of the "mikveh sheet", who in their last issue used the most disgraceful words and expressions against such authorities as Dr. Weinzieher and the well-known patron Mr. Fürstenberg.
We — the people declared — have not come to defend the honour of the above-mentioned, but how much insolence and impudence must one possess to desecrate the honour of a person who is one of the few philanthropists who make no distinction as to who the needy one is, a man who supports with the most generous hand all local institutions and those outside Zagłębie too.
The whole Jewish community must react and voice the sharpest protest against the unbridled youths who with their dirty hands have touched the printed word...
—o—
A secret agent chases a thief and shoots dead a young Jewish man.
[Będzin — Incidents.] Yesterday towards evening Jewish Będzin was shaken by the terrible news that a secret agent had shot dead a young Jewish man.
The tragic incident happened in the following circumstances:
In Kościuszki Street a secret agent was chasing a bandit. The bandit turned into Sielecka Street, whereupon the agent fired after the bandit. At that very moment a worker of the firm "Jakub Gutman", 27-year-old Ajzyk Zuchter[?], was walking home from work, and a revolver bullet struck him in the heart and he fell dead on the spot.
The tragic victim lived at Zawale 38 and leaves an orphaned wife [a widow] with 2 small children.

One Must Learn to Walk!

In former times people believed that children had to be taught to walk. How often the children were tormented while being taught this skill. The whole family took part in the mitzvah of teaching the child to walk. Everyone considered it his duty to stretch out his arms and make the child take a few steps. "All by itself, all by itself the child walks" — Mama would sing, and everyone helped. And not only people helped the "cripple" to stand on his feet; whole machines were invented, baby walkers, "stoyakes" [?; standing frames, Polish stojaki] were bought to help the child get up on its little feet.
Today this system has been abandoned. Today we know that no child needs to be taught to walk, just as no animal needs to be taught to walk. Who, after all, teaches the chick, the goose, the calf and the dog to walk? When the time comes it walks, and there is no need to teach it. But if no child in the cradle needs to be taught to walk, the grown-ups, the adults, must be taught the art of walking.
And a very great art it is; since ancient times people have been taught to walk. For soldiers, marching, placing the foot, was always the first and hardest skill that had to be learned. It had to be, because if each one placed his foot the way his mother had taught him, it would be impossible to lead an army: one would climb onto the other, one would stumble over the other's step. And at a critical moment, when one had to run forward or back, there would be more victims of their own feet than of a foreign sword.
Once only soldiers were taught to walk; today everyone must learn the art, because today we all find ourselves on a battlefield. Today the street is a war zone. And the bigger the city, the more destroyers it holds, the greater the danger of moving from one's place; one must look in all directions, one must not forget for a single moment that one is in the street, where cars fly, where motorcycles leap, and where every minute there is the danger of falling under the wheels of a tram or, what is even worse, of being crippled.
Yes, one must learn to walk. Just in these days accidents have happened. Several people were killed by cars. Certainly the driver is to blame first of all. He must pay attention, he must signal, he must always be alert, sober and watchful. But it is not always he alone who is to blame. It often happens that someone runs straight into the arms of death, and however much the driver rings and manoeuvres, it does not help him; the person runs straight into death. This is seen especially here in our streets. When someone hears a car's signal, the first movement he makes is to pull back. He wants to jump backwards, and that is usually his misfortune, because the driver tries to avoid him and therefore drives behind him, reckoning that at that second the person will take a step forward and so make room for the car. But when the person takes a step back instead of forward, he naturally falls under the wheels, and the catastrophe is complete.
"To teach the children of Judah the bow" [2 Samuel 1:18] — one must teach the public to use arrow and bow, so it used to be said. Today it must be said: one must teach the public to walk. One must take the public by the hand and show it how to place a foot, how to cross the street, how to avoid a car, a tram, etc. Such courses must exist everywhere today.
But first of all, before anyone comes to us with the art of walking, let us learn ourselves, let us be careful, let us remember the rule: never back! Better to stay standing in place than to start running and get flustered. This lesson is important, because it is a matter of danger to life.
Ch. Landau.

On the 31st of this month the term of the labour agreements in the Upper Silesian coal industry expires. The workers have sent the mine managements a notice that they wish to conclude an agreement on new conditions.
On Improving Rail Communication and Conditions on the Warsaw–Radom–Kielce Line.

In connection with the frequent robberies on the Warsaw–Radom–Kielce line, which are easily carried out because the night trains are made up of carriages with an indirect [?] exit, the Sosnowiec Chamber of Commerce has turned to the Ministry of Communications with a memorandum asking that carriages with a corridor system run on the line.
The Chamber has also turned to the Ministry of the Interior asking that police travel on the night trains, in order to safeguard the lives and property of the passengers.
Celebrations in Katowice in Honour of the President of the State

On Sunday the President of the State, Mościcki, was in Katowice, where he took part in the celebration of the 10th anniversary of the Polish uprising in Upper Silesia.
The President was accompanied by Ministers Kwiatkowski and Prystor.
From early morning crowds of people streamed to Katowice. For this purpose the railway directorate in Katowice put 50 special trains into service. The number of participants reached 50 thousand people.
After the march-past, speeches were made to the crowd from a balcony of the municipal theatre by Minister Kwiatkowski and the president of the insurgents (powstańcy), Dr. Pawlek [?].
In the evening a festive academy took place in the theatre, at which those present sent telegrams to Marshal Piłsudski and to the Minister of the Interior, Składkowski.
Afterwards a reception (raout) was held.
A Letter to the Editor.

Esteemed Mr. Editor!
We have the honour to ask you to give room to our letter in reply to the "kashrut guardians", the Master Butchers' Association in Będzin, for which we thank you.
In the last issue of the "Zaglembier Tsaytung" the butchers' association came out against us, saying that they had learned of a "terrible" kashrut scandal: on a cartload of meat that was going to our sausage factory one or two pieces of unporged meat had been found...
The "scandal"... actually happened several weeks ago, and we believed that after the rabbinate had laughed at their "secrets" they would not have the nerve to publish a lampoon against us and against the local rabbinate, in which they write that "the world should know that Bezalel Kupferwasser is nothing but a feeder of treif and the rabbinate is false... (incidentally, perhaps even bribed), and only thanks to the well-known master butcher was the scandal uncovered"; and he indeed — as they write — ran out of breath from one member of the rabbinate to another, who, incidentally, have known him for many years as a "glatt kosher" Jew...
And this very "Jew" also established [that there was] an unporged piece of meat.
It is even beneath our dignity to answer attacks from such people, but nevertheless we wish to explain the following: that their hatred of us actually stems not from our buying Sosnowiec meat, but from our not buying that same Sosnowiec meat from them... (from several local butchers, who more than once have sold us foreign meat as local slaughter).
And now, concerning the whole matter of foreign meat, we once explained to the rabbinate that in no town does the prohibition of "outside meat" (basar chutz) apply to sausage manufacturers as well, and if it were introduced here we would without any doubt be the first to agree; but if the ban came into force, half of the local sausage businesses, which have their factories in Sosnowiec, Dąbrowa, Częstochowa, Wolbrom..., would have to close.
We presented the matter as it stands in reality, and the rabbinate recognized our complete sincerity.
Concerning the piece of unporged meat we will add that this simply cannot happen; every child knows that every piece of meat is carefully examined by the porger (menaker) Bezalel, and besides that a special trustworthy supervisor (ish ne'eman) is on duty in our factory during working hours.
With these explanations we wish to draw the attention of the butchers that they will not succeed by such means in compromising [us] before Jewish society, which can only smile on reading your "kashrut scandals"...
Respectfully,
Bezalel Kupferwasser,
Itshe Ber Patasz [?].

On Saturday a return match took place between the 2 Jewish workers' clubs mentioned. The play in the first 15 minutes was on the whole interesting thanks to the fine play of both sides. The field, however, is fully dominated by Gwiazda, which constantly attacks the opponent's goal and in the 20th minute scores the first goal through Tuchsznajder.

This arouses discontent among the spectators, who demand that the Gwiazda players leave the field in protest. Gwiazda does not do so and plays on. Quick Aid for Zagłębie

[Zagłębie — health, municipality; article.] (Will we have a pogotowie [ambulance / first-aid service]? For what reasons has the institution not been created? Can one wait?)
Several times we have dealt with this question in the columns of our newspaper. In the course of the last few months we have devoted some articles to the matter, pointed out the necessity of creating such an institution — and nothing: it moved none of our "city fathers" in Zagłębie. We showed that the highest time had come for a system of rapid aid to be created in Zagłębie, but nobody tried to do anything about this important matter, and nobody even stopped to consider it from all sides in order to know what can be done here and what cannot.
And it is an old rule that as soon as the author of an article sees that he writes and it has no effect, that he speaks and his words stick like peas to the wall, he loses heart and reaches a decision: rather than talk to the wall, it is better to wipe his mouth as though he had said nothing and meant nobody.
In this case we, too, should have done so: wipe our mouth as though we had spoken to nobody and said nothing at all. For how many times is it reasonable to point to one and the same fact and argue the necessity of the establishment? We already showed at the time that Zagłębie must have rapid rescue, quick aid. In what way, then, is the situation here better than in Warsaw or Łódź? On the contrary, here it is considerably worse and harder, if only because accidents very often occur in factories that are not properly equipped as regards giving rapid aid to the workers. Besides, traffic here is heavy: the trams run quite frequently and the bus service is also quite widespread, and as a sign that this is so, the fairly large number of accidents that occur here in everyday life can bear witness.
True, one does not notice it this way: one glances through the local press, notices an accident here today and there tomorrow, and does not even stop over it all. People are harried and absorbed, and all events pass as if nothing had ever happened.
But it is quite different when one sets about reading all these accidents and events attentively — then a terrible picture emerges. When we study all this, we see that our municipal administrations are committing enormous crimes when they look on at all this with indifference.
Many, many times we have seen accidents that ended terribly tragically only because there is no quick aid, whose task is usually to rescue the unfortunate person instantly.
It is interesting: two weeks ago a young man came into the editorial office and told us that, while walking at night, two unknown young drunkards attacked him and stabbed him in the head. The young man screamed, but as usual, hearing the screams, everyone ran away, and of course no policeman was to be seen; so the wounded man walked with the open wounds, from which blood was flowing, until he reached the hospital, where they agreed to dress his wound (opatrunek) only after he had promised to pay 5 zł.
So the question arises: what would have happened if the unfortunate man had been wounded so badly that he could not drag himself through the streets? What would become of such a person? And how often do we hear that people depart this world only because they did not receive medical aid on the spot? None of this is news, and if we try to study such cases we will come to the conclusion that many people leave this world in this way.
The question therefore arises: can one remain indifferent to such serious events when it is a matter of mortal danger? When it is paid for with human lives? Can one in such a case put up with the fact that our city fathers remain indifferent and do not listen to the heavy human losses?
But the newspaper, above all others, must not remain indifferent to all this; it must fulfil its duty, it must awaken, call and remind that running an administration this way is a terrible crime. And at this moment the author of this or that article must not take into account that he has written and illuminated the matter from all sides and nevertheless [?] his words were not heard. On the contrary, not only must he not let the pen out of his hand until he carries his cause through to the end, but [?] he must fight and not stop calling until his proposal becomes reality and his ideal becomes an accomplished fact.
It must be recognised once and for all that Zagłębie must have a pogotowie in every [?] (place) in order to save human lives in the event of a serious accident; a modus must be found by which one is obliged to rescue the unfortunate citizen on the spot, at the time when every second plays a role in preserving a person's life.
Can there be anything more urgent for a self-government than to provide the possibility of rescuing citizens in the event of an accident? Who else should concern himself with restoring [?] the lives of citizens when sudden circumstances bring them into danger? We have already reached a sufficiently low state that one must speak so many times and give so many explanations about such an elementary matter.
Perhaps now people will at last take to heart that it is no great honour at all for municipal self-governments that one has to speak and write so many times about one and the same matter?
And therefore nothing remains but to ask and demand: create a pogotowie, organise rapid aid, which should be designed to rescue people instantly from serious danger.
Dr. Papuri.
Make Your Children Productive People.

Our children's fate is now the worry of most Jewish parents.
Among other peoples — and not only among other peoples, but also among Jews in other countries, let us say, for example, America, England, France — this is no worry at all. There the growing Jewish generation has open doors equally with the growing generation of the ruling nation. There it has broader possibilities, both political and economic, to settle in, to make a living, to earn not merely bread but also a better life.
True, there too the preparation of the young generation for life does not always follow the right path, which leads to a surplus in certain professions, branches, enterprises, etc. But not always and not everywhere is this the same, and in any case people there do eventually settle down normally, one way or another, and attain a secure existence.
With us, however, the failure to adapt to real life is a mass phenomenon, and this leads to the point that not only is the older class becoming more and more declassed, but the youth too is being raised in a declassed atmosphere, without ground under its feet, without content in life.
And this can be seen in all classes of Jewish society: with the craftsman, the merchant, the shopkeeper and the worker.
Take, for example, a German craftsman, let us say a shoemaker — how does he think of giving his child a livelihood? Not only is he himself a shoemaker, he even boasts: "My Fritz will be the best Schuhmacher in Germany!" The same with the German merchant, scholar, etc. With the German, a child is born already with a prepared existence in life — a ready-made "Schuhmacher", a ready-made "Kaufmann". He does not think that his child will be something other than what he himself is.
With our Jews it is different: a Jewish shoemaker, tailor, tinsmith, locksmith, joiner, shopkeeper, merchant, entrepreneur thinks from the very start not to leave his children the same trade as an inheritance. The very profession from which he himself draws his livelihood — he wants to make of his son nothing less than a doctor, an engineer, a lawyer, a professor, anything but what he himself is, just as if what he is were a stain on the family, a disgrace, a despised trade to be ashamed of.
In this way the young generation is estranged from a life of toil and falls into the category of a declassed element that cannot settle into life, even though it has education, is intelligent, has studied, etc.
It is precisely this weaning, this tearing of the young generation away from work, from its independence, already in early youth, and the dressing[?] of it in a special white[?] shirt, as if it were not created to be, like the father, a "benighted craftsman", a "speculator, a shopkeeper", but an "enlightened 'intellectual'" with "ideal" white fingers — that is a very harmful phenomenon among us.
One cannot separate education from a trade, intelligence from a profession; on the contrary, they must go together. And the more closely they are bound together, the more useful it is for the person concerned. Enough of the self-persuasion that a craftsman must necessarily be "benighted" — he can also be "enlightened".
"Do not estrange your children from your own occupation" — that must be the slogan of Jewish parents.
Truly, hand your occupation down to your children together with education, with a school. That will be all the more useful for him. What later develops out of your child according to his abilities is the child's luck, but you yourselves hand down to him as an inheritance what is real — in your own hands — your own occupation, from which you yourselves draw sustenance.
Yes, the trade and profession by which you yourselves live — that is the most important thing. For, being in your home, living in your surroundings, he is already from early youth better fitted to your branch than to occupations that are as yet only in your imagination.
A. Y. G.
L. Kusman — The Decline of the Horse

[Essay — civilization and technology; by L. Kusman.]
Civilization is merciless. It kills off the finest institutions, thousand-year-old customs, traditions and comforts, and does not shed even a tear over them, nor does it ever[?] set up a monument to them in the squares and parks.
Before our very eyes civilization, with its ever-growing[?] technology, has made a ruin-heap of many beautiful things in which mankind delighted ever since it first drew breath on its way[?]. Only isolated individuals mourn the victims of civilization and of its greatest child: technology. Mankind as a whole triumphs and erects monuments to the victress, not to the vanquished.
Here, before our eyes, so beautiful an institution as the horse has perished. For thousands of years the horse was one of the finest and most useful institutions in human life. The horse was man's most faithful servant and companion. It carried him along all the roads of dry land, dragged his plough and helped him sow and reap, carried the grain to the miller and the water to the baker. The horse was the pulse, the nerve, the life-force of human existence.
Besides its usefulness, the horse was also a romantic figure, to whom the world's greatest poets sang songs and dedicated ballads. The post-chaise, the "troika" — what glorious names in romantic poetry! At the very sound of the words, broad steppes open before our eyes, long roads through forest and field, silver snow and moonlit nights, the trembling touch of the girl at one's side and the hot breath of the horse, the mute, four-legged witness of naive love and youthful dreams.
Can the automobile, or even the aeroplane, replace that? No! The automobile, too, takes loving couples to a rendezvous ("randke"), but love is by now as mechanical as the motor. The hot breath of the mute four-legged witness is missing. The chauffeur in front is too human, or too machine-like[?], for his mute presence to add romance to the sacred trembling.
And what the aeroplane will bring to the domain of love and romance remains to be seen. One does not believe, however, that it will add anything to the beautiful romance. Love itself has wings of its own. It soars with its own motor in the heavenly spheres — [no need] for it still to require steel wings, a gas motor and a pilot.
And even in falling, love has no need of an aeroplane. In case of "motor trouble" it can fall by itself from the greatest height into the deepest abysses with the speed of an aeroplane whose motor has broken down; and when the horse is there, it can only soothe — one can sing to it: "Coachman (yamshchik), do not drive the horses, there is nowhere more to hurry, there is no one more to love..."
Go and tell that to an automobile or an aeroplane — dead souls...
•
An old lover of horses in America committed suicide the other day, because he could no longer bear to watch the grief, the decline of the beautiful and faithful four-legged creature. He hated the automobile with a deadly hatred and fled from it with his horses wherever he could. But the automobile pursued him at every step, until it drove him "into death."
Before hanging himself the man went into the stable, took leave of the horses, his faithful friends in life, stroked and kissed them, and then pulled a rope tight around his neck.
Thus died a man from whom civilization took away the most beautiful thing in life — the horse. His act is a worthy protest against the cruelty of people who so quickly turned their heads away from the four-legged creature that served man in every need and at all times.
If mankind were not so cruel and so forgetful, it ought at least to erect a monument to the martyr of civilization — the horse, which served it [—] in the ploughed field, on the battlefield and on the field of love.
A hero who has [—] for so many thousand[s of years —] so to honour on [—] "bitn"[?] in the world, that [—] stand on all the sq[uares —] "parkans"[?], beside the [—] statesmen, [—] and musicians.
For there is no [—] horse has [—] I [—] raise [—] perhaps [—] "grief [—] that [—] [—] [—]
The Seduced Girl (17)

[Serialized novel — Mania's parents search for their daughter who vanished into a convent; installment 17.]
Dr. A. Weissman.
(A novel of Jewish life in the Old World, based on historical facts.)

And those who lived in the cellars led a prison life. The pious sisters accepted such a life as their lot [?] in this world and expected a good reward in the world to come.
All the sisters, except a counted few, sworn ones, who could be trusted, were informed that the newly arrived Mania was no longer in the convent.
Reb Leyzer [so printed; further on "Reb Zelig"] Sarahs and his wife Hanna, Mania's parents, did not stop standing before the high walls of the convent — perhaps they would learn something about their vanished daughter.
More than once they rang at the gate and begged to be let in to Sister Irena, but they were answered with all sorts of excuses, and the meeting was put off from one day to the next.
When Mania's parents would stand for hours at the gate, a sister would sometimes come out to them and ask why they were weeping. Reb Zelig Sarahs and Hanna would then tell, with tears in their eyes, of their great misfortune and beg to be let in to their daughter.
The sister, too, would answer with tears in her eyes:
"Believe me, this is the first time I hear your daughter's name; she is not with us, you must look for her somewhere else."
But the parents, knowing that their daughter Mania could be nowhere else but in this convent, did not stop weeping before the sister and did not budge from the convent gate.
"Perhaps you do not know — others know."
"What makes you so sure that she is with us of all places? How many convents there are in the world — why do you believe that she is precisely with us? Our convent forces no one to convert and snatches no one; only whoever wishes it of his own good will comes to us."
"She is still a child, what does she know? Just let me speak a few words with her, and if she tells us to our faces that she wants nothing more to do with us, then we will go away from here quietly, we will forget her as one forgets the dead, and we will no longer disturb your convent."
"But do believe me that I do not know, and none of us here knows anything about your daughter. We are already used to such cases. Many of your people come to us asking about their vanished daughters; they run away somewhere else, and it is us they come to ask."
While the sister was talking with Mania's parents, a second sister came up to the gate and joined the conversation.
"Aha! Jews again! I don't understand why they are let in here at all."
"What can one do with them? You don't know the Jews: when they latch on to something, it is impossible to drive them off even with sticks."
Reb Zelig and Hanna nevertheless did not stop weeping and begging to be pitied and told where their daughter was.
"Where are we supposed to get your daughter from?"
"Ask in your own convent, perhaps someone knows."
The sisters, wishing to be rid of Mania's parents, tell them they will inquire. The heavy gate of the convent closes, and the unhappy parents remain standing and waiting.
"Perhaps she really isn't here?" Reb Zelig is seized by doubt.
"What has got into you?" says Hanna. "Where else would she be, if not here? Don't I know whose doing this is? Day and night I argued that no good would come of Mania's friendship with the estate steward's children, and you only beamed with pride when Mania went to the squire and spent her time among the gentry. I shouted at you: what have we to do with them, everyone should keep company with his own kind. This is Aunt Siwiańska's [?] doing; they begrudged us having such a precious child, with whom God blessed us, and they tore her away from us; and as if that were not enough, they want to take the mill away from us too, to lease it to someone else."
Reb Zelig Sarahs sighs:
"Oh, the livelihood. They tear the piece of bread out of our mouths, they take everything from us — and now they want to take our children as well."
"I will not leave this place, even if I knew that I would die here; they will have to carry me away from here dead. No, I will not stir from here; my child is here. Don't I know that Sister Irena and the Siwiańskis are relatives?"
"And what if she is not here after all?"
"Where else would she be? She is here and nowhere else. Didn't the Jew from the inn tell us that when he was standing by the synagogue in the town of Ts—n on the night of Yom Kippur, a britzka sped past with two figures sitting in it; the driver was whipping the horses hard, so that the Jew at once became suspicious."
"Surely, surely our Mania stayed here, but what can be done about it? What can be done?" Reb Zelig did not stop wringing his hands.
"The one God will help us, Zelig. We must not budge from here; if they drive us away today, we will come again tomorrow."
"And what will come of it?"
"They will have to give our child back, they will have to."
Suddenly the convent gate opened again, and a sister appeared who addressed Mania's parents with the words:
"Our eldest sister is waiting for you and has permitted you to come to her."
With the greatest joy and good hopes Mania's parents stepped over the threshold of the convent.
Accompanied by the sister, Mania's parents were led into a front building, where there were old chairs and a couple of small tables.
The walls were almost entirely hung with old holy pictures, and in one corner a lamp was burning.
"Sit down here and wait until our eldest sister Irena comes out to you," the sister who had accompanied them said in a polite tone.
Trembling and with pounding hearts they sat down on a bench that stood by the door.
It lasted a whole hour. Various sisters, dressed in black and in white, came in with bowed and covered heads, so that their faces could not be fully seen; they disappeared through various doors and later came back, and again new ones arrived.
"Who knows how long they will leave us waiting here?" Reb Zelig said to Hanna.
"Perhaps it is taking so long because they have gone to call our daughter? Praised be God that they have at least let us in here. I will not leave until they give our child back — what do they have against us?"
"It must surely be from God. Perhaps He will now have mercy on us at last."
While they were questioning each other, a sister came up and pointed them to a door where Sister "Irena" was waiting for them. Passing from one room into the next, all richly decorated, they finally entered a large hall whose richness dazzled the eyes. Here, on a large chair, sat Sister "Irena", surrounded by several sisters dressed in white and black garments. Except for Sister "Irena", all were standing, and Mania's parents too were left standing.
