Our Panorama

[Zagłębie — satirical feuilleton; small-town kehillas.] (Not all dozors [members of the kehilla board] are incompetent. — A Chełm wisdom. — Punishment of a Hasid, a "traitor". — It is not a lawless world. — A Tseir may not romance. — A shtetl split into 4 parts. — The power of Y"Sh [spirits] occupies a kehilla. — Messianic times. — Democracy wins. — Jews pray at dawn.)
It is a clear thing that in every rule there is an exception. Among us it is almost an established fact that today's kehilla representatives are incompetent, good-for-nothings, without any initiative — but along comes Modrzejów (Mandzhev) and says: "Stop!" In this respect we are an exception; we in Modrzejów have dozors who are real antiques, and it is truly worthwhile that their names become famous and that their deeds be immortalised too.
The Modrzejów kehilla needed to buy a boiler to heat the mikveh. [—] For this purpose [—] a meeting was held, at which four dozors were [del]egated[?], [—] the four sons of the Haggadah, [who sh]ould carry out the transaction of [buyi]ng [the b]oiler[?].
[The emissar]ies of the community[?] said the "prayer for [the road]"[?] [—] and went off into the [wide wo]rld[?] to look for an "antiseptic"[?] [—].
[—] King Solomon said: "[There is nothing new under] the sun"[?], there is no [—] [—] [—], with the [—] [—], there happens the [—] [—] the well-known [—] who [—] [—] [b]ought[?] a trump[eter][?] [—] at the moment [—] [—] [—] [—] [—] [—] [—].
[—] spiritual" of the Modrzejów kehilla.
With faces shining with joy the dozors returned from their mission abroad, convened a meeting and announced to the public what a bargain and what a precious vessel they had acquired.
A few weeks later some curious people asked one dozor: where is the vessel? Where?...
— It will come any day now...
— — — — — — — —
Are you curious to know the end of the boiler story? The end is the same as what once happened in Chełm, only differently veiled. The people of Chełm at least brought home a trumpeter, while the Modrzejów people are still waiting for the boiler...
———
We have another neighbouring shtetl which deserves — in our opinion — first prize for its practicality. In no shtetl are the inhabitants as practical as in Czeladź. All the inhabitants, Jews and Christians alike, are engaged in practical matters; even the local town councillors realised: what is a vice-president good for? How many "darmozjads" [freeloaders] are there anyway? They held a meeting about it and — "heyda!" [off with it].
"Practical" too are the local Gur Hasidim. And when it actually happened that one of their Hasidim, at his father-in-law's suggestion, travelled to Aleksander [the Aleksandrów court], a trial was held in the shtibl and the judges handed down a verdict:
— to give [him] l[ashes?]... according to the old custom.. and precisely during the Nine Days...
A similar ruling was also received by the leader of the "Tseirei Emunei [Yisrael]". The leader — more precisely, the gabbai — suddenly became romantically inclined and... "you can guess the rest"... so he was brought before the "green table", from which a ruling came out:
— Zrika, expulsion from the society; it is not a lawless world after all — that at the time of the Knessia Gedola a "Tseir" should stroll with a girl, and precisely behind the cement works [?]!...
———
In fairness we should have printed the report from Sławków right after Modrzejów, because the Sławków report also begins with "Here it is boiling like in a boiler". The only difference is that in the Modrzejów boiler lie four dozors and in the Sławków boiler "lies" a rabbi..
The Sławków kehilla lived in peace and tranquillity. But no rest was fated for it: the rabbi dies, and as a result the shtetl undergoes an upheaval and a split. The kehilla is split into 4 parts and on each part sits the rabbinical throne..
The most active part are the shochtim, who influenced the butchers; the latter in turn recruited a few "people" [toughs], and they don't give a fig for the whole kehilla..
First of all they engaged a rabbi who — disregarding the many protests of the gmina [municipality] and the Hasidic public — came to Sławków and began to exercise the rabbinate...
So that the "business" should make progress, this part performs deeds that are very apt to recruit new members.
"To enlarge the business", every Sabbath a "Kiddusha Rabba" is held at the rabbi's; worn-out Jews snatch a few "95s" [shots of 95-proof spirit] and revel in having lived to see the golden age, when for a "glass" one can rinse one's stomach with a quarter-litre of schnapps and also get a loan from the "Gmilut Hesed" fund...
The "mizner"[?] [perhaps: minority] side, those who had brought the rabbi here, tried to take a further step towards victory, but here they got "scalded"...
They went into the beit midrash and took a Torah scroll out of it. When the shtetl learned of this, everyone's ambition was aroused, especially among the Hasidic public, and people ran[?] into the beit midrash to the holy war...
According to the "latest" reports we have received, on the "battlefield" there remained smashed... tables, split.. zhupitses [long coats] and torn.. hats.
The fire also caught the female sex: they tear at each other's wigs, the men at the beards, the police write up reports, and there it is "a holiday in the middle of the week"..
— The old men are even pleased with the holy war; they see in it a sign of the coming of the Redeemer..
———
That these are Messianic times is also "proved" by the "miracles" occurring in Strzemieszyce. In the local beit midrash, on Shabbat Nachamu, tables, candlesticks and other similar "flying devices" flew up in the air.
The "miracles" happened because of an order by a dozor who greatly longs for the old government, for the "Tsarist regime", and cannot bear the "democratic" arrangements — that a dawn minyan should pray in the beit midrash.
The order hit the "hungry" public hard, and it undertook a counter-action against the dozor:
— "We made him and we'll erase[?] him.."
But the dozor has a side: his four sons, who threw off their jackets and set about defending their father's honour...
"Democracy" won, the dozor capitulated, and the dawn-Jews of Strzemieszyce make Sabbath kiddush at 10 o'clock in the morning.
———
The Jews of Olkusz have no such "freedom". On the Sabbath they hold up the Torah reading there, and in the process "secrets" are revealed — who has eaten in a non-Jewish restaurant...
There is in Olkusz a moreh hora'ah [rabbinic decisor], who is a great scholar and an even greater pauper.
So the community thought it over and found a solution: they raised [the fee for] slaughter by 20 groszy, and the surcharge was to go to the moreh hora'ah.
But the result is the reverse: the community pays and the moreh hora'ah gets nothing of it; and why? — the dozor doesn't want it, and calls him a "knak-nisl" [nutcracker; a nobody].
On the Sabbath during prayers there is a "va-yitz'aku" [an outcry]. The public gnashes its teeth: how can this be?..
The dozor, by the way a handsome Jew, does not remain in debt and uses "pretty names" towards the "recalcitrants". The latter do not keep quiet either, they tell about "green lunches", and in the shtetl it is cosy...
Ben Amotz.

On Browarna Street frequent quarrels take place between a girl and her stepmother. The cause of the quarrels is that the stepmother does not want to give the girl anything to eat, in order to get rid of her.
The „faithful“ father, too, stays neutral for the sake of domestic peace, and is thus forced to agree with his „woman of valour“.
Last Friday evening the stepmother locked the door and did not let the girl into the flat. The girl then opened the cupboard which stood in [—] and took out of it the Sabbath dishes...
Matchmaker's Fee Paid with... Blows.

[Czeladź — matchmaking; incident.]
Matchmaker's fee paid with... blows.
Late on Sunday evening the residents of Bytomska Street in Czeladź were alarmed by cries of „Stop thief!“...
Down the street ran the young man S. Blach, and after him Akiva the matchmaker with a battered hand. Both „guests“ were taken to the police station (komisariat), where the matter became clear.
Akiva the matchmaker had arranged a bridegroom for Blach's sister, whose engagement contract (tnoim) was written last week, and the matchmaker came to demand his matchmaking fee.
The in-laws, however, argued „po chupie“ [after the wedding canopy]... and one word led to another, until the matchmaker came out with [coarse] language. For that the bride's brother paid him with lashes.
A Mysterious Murder in Maczki.

[Maczki — crime.]
A mysterious murder in Maczki.
At the railway station in Maczki a railway official was found murdered. According to conjecture the murder was an act of revenge, for the victim had been lured out of his carriage in order to kill him.
In Uncle's Ways...

[Press — Agudah; satire.]
In uncle's ways...
The editor of „Yud ha-Kadosh“ [„The Holy Jew“], R' Meshulam Kaminer, has been sentenced to 2 weeks' arrest for paying the typesetters with uncovered cheques.
According to this uncle's system the „editorial office“ of the local Agudah mikveh-sheet is run as well. There is hardly a typesetter, distributor or printing-house owner left who has not suffered financial losses at the hands of the „Vayakhel-Pekudei editors“ [a pun on the Torah portions: they „gather“ and „count“ — but do not pay].
On the Eve of a General Strike in the Zagłębie Coal Mines! — Workers Refuse, in Protest, to Come Up out of the Pit

[Zagłębie — Labour and mines.]
The Class Union (Związek Klasowy) of mine-workers recently presented a demand to the mine managements that an 8-hour working day be introduced, i.e. that the working time, including going down into and coming up out of the pit, should take no more than 8 hours.
In connection with this demand a conference of representatives of the union and of the industrialists took place on Tuesday. The conference brought no positive result whatsoever, and the workers' union decided that if their demand is not met, a general strike in all mines will be declared tomorrow, Saturday the 24th of this month.
At several coal mines it has already come to misunderstandings: at the "Saturn" the workers demanded to be released at half past nine in the evening. Because the overseer did not allow this and declared that their working time ends only at 10 o'clock, the workers stayed down below in protest for a whole night.
The next morning the management of the mine hung up a notice that the mine is no longer operating.
Such incidents have also occurred in other mines. Order is being kept by the police.
"If They Won't Let Us Live, Let Us Both Die" — A Love Tragedy in Dąbrowa

[Dąbrowa — Tragedy.]
On Szosena[?] Street in Dąbrowa the Christians Rozinska and Rechowicz live as neighbours. Rozinska has a daughter, and Rechowicz a son. The children fell in love and swore each other "eternal faithfulness".
The girl's parents, however, were not pleased with their daughter's sweetheart and prevented her from going out walking with him.
Last Sunday, when the 21-year-old Rozinski [sic] wanted to go out for a walk, where her beloved was waiting for her, her parents barred her way and did not let her out.
Then the girl snatched a glass of vinegar essence and drank half of it.
The "kochanek" (lover), on hearing the news that his beloved had attempted suicide, drank a small bottle of poison with the cry "let us both die".
The poisoned couple lie side by side in the local hospital.

Sosnowiec — Chulent Held Back over 30 Groszy...

[Sosnowiec — Daily life.]
In honour of Shabbat Nachamu Mrs. P. prepared a "fiery" chulent and handed it over to the maid to carry to the baker.
The maid took the chulent and also 30 gr. and carried out her mistress's order.
But Mr. Baker, in honour of Shabbat Nachamu, had raised the chulent price and demanded of the maid that she bring another 30 gr.
On coming home the maid forgot about the surcharge, and the baker decided to put a sequestration on the chulent...
On Saturday at midday, while the company sits at the table waiting impatiently for the tasty dish, at that very moment the maid comes back and relates that the chulent has been "confiscated" because of the 30 groszy...
— Gevalt, it's Shabbes after all! How can it be? Such a wealthy family as S. won't pay the baker 30 gr.?
No arguments whatsoever helped; when the baker received a goblet from the family as a pledge, he released the Sabbath dish...

A Gang of Smugglers Discovered

[Upper Silesia — Smuggling.]
These days a gang of smugglers, who engaged in smuggling tobacco, cigarettes and silk from Germany into Poland, was discovered by several police agents of the border guard in Upper Silesia.
The police received secret information that in a village on the road to Tarnowitz (Tarnowskie Góry) a taxi with smuggled goods would pass through.
The indicated place was watched by the agents. At the appointed hour the taxi arrived, in which there were several smugglers, Christians, but no goods were found in the taxi.
After the arrest of the "passengers" the agents went to the railway station in Tarnowitz, where after a period of observation they arrested another 2 smugglers who had hidden the smuggled goods in the forest.
Meanwhile other agents of the border guard went to Myslowitz (Mysłowice), from where there was information that the chief of the smuggling gang was there.
The smugglers' chief, who was staying in Myslowitz with his sweetheart, who occupied a flat on the third floor at 6 Prebendy Street, on seeing the arrival of the secret police wanted to escape. For this purpose he tied a rope to himself and in this way began to let himself down through the window.
At that moment the agents entered the flat and ran to the window to thwart the escape plan, but it was already too late: the smuggler fell from the third floor onto the pavement, was badly hurt, and is now under police guard in hospital.
In the forest near Tarnowitz 40 kilos of tobacco, 2500 cigars and 2500 cigarettes were seized.
The greatest catastrophe in the last 30 years.

[Upper Silesia — mine disaster; short news.]
All of Upper Silesia is under the heavy impression of the terrible catastrophe in the "Hildebrand" coal mine, which took place on Friday, in which 16 workers were buried to death; of the 7 injured, one has already died as well. Access to the site of the catastrophe is very difficult. Only after the ventilation was restored did it become possible to get closer to the site of the accident and dig out the buried. The work is directed by the mining office of Königshütte (Chorzów) with engineer Badzowski [?] Grosz [?], and the higher mining office in Katowice with its chief Kuszyński [?].
The explosion occurred while blasting a seam of coal with explosive material.
It is the greatest coal catastrophe that has happened in Silesia in the last 30 years.
The last catastrophe, which took place 30 years ago in the "Kleofas" mine, cost 120 human victims.
The President of the State donated 15 thousand zł. for the widows and orphans left behind. Larger donations were also given by Minister Kwiatkowski and the Voivode of Katowice.

In the Land of Israel Blood Is Being Shed

[Leading article — Palestine; the riots of August 1929.]

For weeks and months now a struggle has been going on around the Western Wall. It began when the Arabs started erecting a building behind the Wall, intending to open a passage in the Wall and thereby to desecrate, to make profane, the ancient Jewish sanctuary. But this is only [?] a pretext, a criminal device on the part of the Arabs and of those who stand behind them. In truth, much more serious and deeper matters are at stake. The point is that now, precisely when the upbuilding of the Land of Israel is taking on broad dimensions, when things have reached the stage where the whole of the Jewish people (Klal Yisrael) is to strain its forces for the upbuilding — precisely now the Arabs want to provoke a scandal and bring the question before the wider public. So far, unfortunately, the provocation has succeeded. In the streets of the Land of Israel demonstrations are taking place, and blood is being shed.

And where is England? Where is the great world power, which until today has managed to subdue and pacify the wildest peoples of Africa, Asia and Australia — why is it suddenly so helpless against the Arabs in the Land of Israel? This question is surely being asked by many Jews all over the world, and not only by Jews. Wherein the tragedy lies — that is worth [?] some thought.

The English government did indeed give the Balfour Declaration; it did promise. But at that time the English government was waging a war, was in a difficult position, and was ready to accept help from whatever side it might come. At that time Jewish help and Jewish sympathy were important to it too.

Today the war is long gone, it has long been forgotten; today England has quite different interests; today it matters to England to live in peace with the Mohammedan world, because eighty million of its most loyal citizens, in India, the Sudan and the various islands, are Mohammedans.

In such a situation the English government is in no hurry to fulfil the promises it gave in the Declaration. It is not even in a hurry to fulfil its duty as the Mandatory Power; on the contrary, it seeks every means and uses every opportunity to drag things out.

It is precisely in this policy of the government that the great misfortune lies, and the Arab agitators in Palestine know it, and that is why they permit themselves so much. But the latest events have already filled the cup to overflowing; such provocative insolence could not have been expected, and this has already filled the cup to overflowing.

In the Land of Israel blood is being shed! The news has gone like fire through the entire Jewish world. Everywhere a Jewish pulse still beats, regardless of the party and tendency to which it may belong, the news has aroused deep mourning, bitterness and protest. In our history we have become accustomed to bloodshed. There is no corner of the world where Jewish blood has not been spilled. The holy soil of Jerusalem is soaked enough with Jewish blood; but all that happened in the grey old times, or in countries in the hands of wicked rulers, of dark despots. But that this should happen in our time, under the protection of the "merciful kings" — nobody expected that. And that is why the resentment is so great, that is why the protest carries so mightily throughout the world.

An old Indian legend tells that the lion, the king of beasts, comes out of its mother's womb dead. But when the mother sees her cub dead at her feet, she raises such a cry that all the trees in the forest tremble, and from that cry the cub awakens to life and grows into the mighty lion before whom all the beasts of the forest tremble.

The "lion's whelp Judah", too, looks in the world as if it had been born dead: somehow everything with it happens so slowly, so sleepily; somehow it is so helpless. But when it raises its voice, when "the voice is the voice of Jacob" is heard in the world, all the beasts of the forest tremble, and even the English lion will have to wake up and be shaken out of its phlegmatic calm and indifference.

In Jerusalem blood is being shed. It is very sad. We have no words to express our grief and our anger. But we do not lose heart; in this case too we believe in the ancient "In thy blood live" which the prophet proclaimed. And we send our greetings to the heroic defenders of Jewish honour and Jewish right. If until now the Wall was called the Holy Wall, the Wailing Wall (the Wall of Tears), it now becomes the Wall of Blood and its holiness is doubled, because blood is stronger than tears.

Sh. Y. S.
The Cry of Woe of the Jewish Traders in the Old Market. Delegations to the Kielce Voivodeship Office

[Będzin — Economy; trade evicted from the Old Market.] In the last few days announcements of the Magistrate [the municipality of Będzin] appeared throughout the town, announcing that from the first of next month [1 September 1929] trading in the Old Market [Stary Rynek] will be cleared away, and therefore no more places in the market will be leased.
The market stallholders [the print has „צי“, probably a misprint for „די“, "the"], seeing already that "the Angel of Death is already standing at their heads", no longer relied on the hollow [?] promises of the communal workers, who had assured them that "they may rest easy, the market will not be broken up", and began to storm and knock on the doors of those who have the power to ease their sad situation somewhat.
In this connection a crowd of Jewish women traders went to the chairman of the City Council, Mr. Fürstenberg [Szymon Fürstenberg], and with tears in their eyes begged him to intervene so that the decree be annulled and their existence not be shattered.
On Monday [26 August] Mr. Fürstenberg conferred with the President [mayor] and the Vice-President, acquainted himself with the whole matter, and on the initiative of Mr. Rubinlicht a large consultation took place on Monday evening in the premises of the Merchants' Association, with the participation of representatives of the merchants, the artisans and the petty traders, in order to find a way to solve this painful question.
Dozens of traders with their wives and children also came to the meeting to learn about their bitter fate in the future.
At the meeting the sad picture was only now properly displayed. Before the "onlookers" the helplessness of our communal guardians was laid bare. A long list of sins was enumerated at the meeting; people sought the one to blame for the danger to the hundreds of Jewish families who have been placed on the brink of ruin.
The merchants' representatives threw the blame on the petty traders' representatives, and the latter in turn on the artisans, but all admitted that the situation is now catastrophic.
The meeting was chaired by Mr. Rubinlicht, who declared that on the part of the Magistrate no step whatever had been taken to have the market cleared away. The initiator is the Voivode [provincial governor], who takes the position that the market does not meet the necessary regulations and demands that it be removed. Mr. Rubinlicht proposes that at today's meeting the question be dealt with objectively in order to find a way to ease the situation.
Then Mr. Fürstenberg takes the floor and says: in the question of driving the Jewish trade out of the Old Market, the blame lies with 1) the previous City Council, which agreed that the Magistrate should build market halls, and 2) the interested organisations, which through their indifference neglected the question. We stand — says Mr. Fürstenberg — before an accomplished fact. The Voivode, following the many interventions of the hall [?] owners, has issued an ordinance that the market be cleared; the knife is already at the throat, i.e. the market will definitely be cleared of trade, and an action must be started with the aim of having the deadline for clearing it extended for a certain time, until the Magistrate builds trading stalls in the halls in the European manner.
Messrs. Gutensztajn, Lewin, Rus, Szwajcer, Rynski, Altman, Flak, Erlich and Brauner also spoke on the question, stressing its urgency. In the end Mr. Fürstenberg's opinion was accepted.
It was immediately decided to draw up a memorandum with which a delegation, made up of all the interested organisations, is to travel to Kielce.
On the proposal of Mr. Gutensztajn it is decided that the Presidium of the City Council should also travel as a second delegation.
To draw up the memorandum a commission of all the organisations was elected, which held a meeting on Tuesday afternoon [27 August] on how the memorandum should be worded.
At this meeting, however, the whole situation became clear: the boil has been "lanced" and the terrible "secret" was uncovered.
As we are informed from a reliable source, the Voivode did not at all issue on his own initiative any ordinance that the market be driven out; rather, the chief initiators are [print: „in“] the municipal administration, which urged [?] in Kielce that the ordinance be issued.
On Tuesday evening the delegation of Mr. Rechtman, D. Gitler (petty traders) and H. Altman travelled to Kielce, to the Voivodeship Office.
The International Congress of the Chambers of Commerce in Poznań

[Economy — Poznań; international congress.] On Sunday [25 August 1929] consultations began in Poznań of the representatives of the chambers of commerce and industry of Poland, Czechoslovakia, Greece, Yugoslavia, Romania and Turkey. At the international gathering 100 delegates of the Polish chambers of commerce and more than 40 delegates from Czechoslovakia assembled. The other countries sent smaller delegations.
The congress was opened by the Vice-President of the Chamber of Commerce in Poznań, Dr. Dżażdżyński [?]. On the presidium were President Grossmann of Prague, Mr. Steratoulas [?] of Athens, Dr. Ilieska [?] of Constantinople, Councillor [Ratmann] Kostica of Belgrade, President Garamski [?] of Sosnowiec, and the President of the Łódź Chamber of Commerce, Mr. Geyer.
In the name of the absent Minister of Commerce the greeting was given by the department head [print: „דעפארטאמענטס-צוזאמענפאר“, apparently a misprint] Dąbrowski, who pointed to the benefit that all the represented states can draw from a direct understanding among themselves. In the name of Foreign Minister Zaleski the gathering was greeted by Dr. Bertagi [?]; as host of the city of Poznań and president of the National Exhibition, President [mayor] Ratajski gave a greeting.
A long lecture on mutual economic relations [print garbled: „נעגענזייטיגע“] was delivered by the director of the Warsaw Chamber of Commerce, Dr. Wartalski [?]. Then the director of the Poznań Chamber of Commerce, Dr. Waszka [?], discussed the possibilities of cooperation and put forward a draft statute for a so-called Union of the Chambers of Commerce of Central and Southern Europe, in order to develop economic relations and bring them onto an international forum. The cooperation is to take the form either of meetings of the allied "chambers" or of correspondence. The union of the "chambers" is regarded as already founded.
After the discussion of the draft, the Polish Union of Chambers of Commerce gave a luncheon for the participants of the gathering.
From the World of Sport.

„R.K.S.“ (Radom) — „Sosnowiec“ [printed „Sakhnaviets“ in the headline] 4:2 (0:1).
Sosnowiec had a great sporting experience on Sunday at the match between „R.K.S.“ (Radom) and „Sosnowiec“. The match drew about 2000 spectators to the „Wiktoria“ sports ground.
The public did not behave calmly, so much so that this forced the referee to change his decision many times. Already in the first minutes „R.K.S.“ carries out an attack and scores the first goal through the centre-forward. „Sosnowiec“ does not lag behind and answers with fine counter-attacks, but without success. So the play becomes very sharp on both sides. „R.K.S.“ attacks the „Sosnowiec“ goal, the latter want to strengthen the result, but the „Sosnowiec“ defence is well disposed and cancels out all the offensives of „R.K.S.“. The „Sosnowiec“ attack also plays with great „bad luck“, and up to the first half the result is not changed.
In the second half „Sosnowiec“ takes up a strong tempo and has a slight superiority over the opponent, but all the sorties end without success. In the 25th minute the referee whistles a corner for „R.K.S.“. Here great chaos breaks out on the sports ground, because the public wants an 11-metre kick. The referee, being terrorised by the public, is forced to change his decision, and „Sosnowiec“ equalises the result by scoring. 2 minutes later Bergel shoots the 2nd goal, and shortly afterwards the 3rd goal is scored. But „R.K.S.“ does not lag behind either and attacks the „Sosnowiec“ goal; from the left wing of „R.K.S.“ the second goal is shot. Shortly before the end „Sosnowiec“ increases the result with one more goal; the final result stays 4:2 in favour of „Sosnowiec“. Referee: Mr. Rauenzweig of Częstochowa.
After the match the points table stands as follows:
„R.K.S.“ 6 points, „Sosnowiec“ 6 pts., „Hakoach“ 0 pts.
Because of this a final match will still take place between „R.K.S.“ and „Sosnowiec“ for the title of champion of the Kielce voivodeship.

Problems of Education.

(Summer is over. — The youth of yesterday and of today. — The difficult school and education question.)
1.
So, summer is over; the public has finished bathing, the children are coming back from the dachas [summer cottages], and the young people, who had grown lazy, are beginning to get used again to their everyday occupations.
In town we now meet little carts bringing back the things and the bedding [“lezhakes”, from Polish leżak — loungers/mattresses] from the dachas.
And say what you will — I don’t know how it is with others, but with me, when I meet these things with the bedding, it gives me something like a pinch in the heart; the soul grows murky when we remember that another summer has passed and that this summer’s sun will no longer warm our bones, and after summer — as everyone knows — comes autumn, which lies so heavily on everyone’s heart and demands so much strength for the future and for the hard, long winter that we must welcome...
But it can’t be helped; such is man’s fate: we must adapt to nature, however capricious she may be.
My heart also aches for the tiny, helpless little children when I see how they are all brought back to the smoky, dusty town from the beautiful treasures of nature where they had been — some under the branching, age-old green trees, some in the valleys and on the high mountains — where they breathed in the beauty of nature and lived with the rustic simplicity that so glorifies the little muscles and develops the soft little bones.
Today it is not as it was decades ago, when people hardly concerned themselves with children; today it is a different world: people devote themselves to the little ones, occupy themselves with them day and night, and think only about how to beautify and improve their lives. The children, the school youth, the teaching body — that is a quite separate world, a world of its own, into which grown-ups cannot penetrate.
The children are the generation of the future, on whom we look, or ought to look, with so much reverence and with full, understandable seriousness. How often do we, their parents, envy the children when we see what ceremonies are made for them — while we ourselves grew up and our parents hardly knew when it happened. Who paid attention to us, and who cuddled and played with us? From childhood on we were talked into believing that we were already grown-up people and that it did not become us at all to play, to laugh and to romp. When we remember what our childhood years looked like, we envy today’s children, and we would surely like, if only for a moment, to be transformed into the true, simple, healthy, beautiful [printed “sheyge”] and innocent childhood years, in which we might know the taste of cosy childhood amusement that we never saw with our own eyes.
Who ever gave a thought to children in the old days? The parents were busy with their businesses, and the children were “handed over” to the cheder, where they had to stay from early till late [unclear word in print: “ahgs”?], and with that the matter was disposed of for a whole term. And when the between-terms came — Sukkot or Passover time — they again considered which cheder to give the children to, and once the decision was made, the question was again settled for half a year.
But it never occurred to our parents that this question was a matter that had to be considered with deliberation and should take time and effort.
Today all this has changed thoroughly; we live in other times, and the education question is one of the hardest problems in our life. We would like to bring up our children as modern people and good Jews, and that is so difficult under the conditions in which we live: there is no proper school here, and the teachers here are not suitable; besides, chaos reigns in many schools, so that one doubts whether one can send this or that child there at all.
And then — how many difficulties do many parents meet who, for material reasons, cannot educate their children. After all, we do not have from the government such schools as would suit our spirit, and if we want such schools we must maintain them on our own shoulders, and that is of course no easy matter. Moreover, the economic situation of the Jewish middle class has lately become so hard that a Jew who has 2—3 children to send to school is left helpless when he remembers how much school fees he has to pay; and that is no trifle: it ruins the parents, it makes a big hole in their yearly budget, and however much such parents may wish to have their children educated, they must nevertheless give it up. This is one of the hardest questions in our educational system, one that absolutely ought to be dealt with from every side.
The writer of these lines knows several such parents who cannot pay the tuition for their children, and sending the children to school free of charge will not suit them, even if they were to be accepted — so imagine in what a hard situation such families find themselves.
One knows that educating children must cost money; one knows that everything is burdened; unfortunately it grows harder and harder, at a time when abroad, in the cultured countries, the education question is constantly being made easier. Abroad, as soon as a citizen merely wishes to continue his children’s education, the money question will not stand in his way. On the contrary: for getting an education all doors are open to every citizen. We too are, after all, in the centre of Europe, and Poland too plays a role as a cultured state — so why should we not also receive the same possibilities of educating our children as exist in other cultured states?
Unfortunately we find ourselves in a very hard situation in this field, and we do not see that the situation will improve in our favour; on the contrary — the more we delve into the matter, the more we think about the question, the more we see the future in anything but bright colours, which causes much pain to those who want to see modern, free schools and want them to produce fully intelligent people who will at the same time remember to which people they belong.
Y. Sh.
A Short Feuilleton — A Conversation.

[Zagłębie — short feuilleton, humour.] A Conversation.
There we sit, the three of us, on the "Górka" [the "little hill", an outing spot] on a bench: I in the middle and on both sides of me — two young men from Sosnowiec.
We had gone there with the kosher intention of uniting with the dear "splendours" of nature, of sitting under the clear sky and smelling the rich odours that drift over from the nearby lane.
But opposite us, on the sandy little hill, there was an exhibition, or a laying-out, of naked female bodies, roasting themselves in the sun. At once all our thoughts were captured by this strange picture.
My right-hand neighbour speaks up:
— Do you see that pair lying stretched out right there opposite us?
— Well, of course we see...
— You see how they have uncovered their legs right up to the groin, their whole arms and more pieces of their body, and only the head with the face have they covered.
— Well, we see; after all we are not blind, and not Hasidim either.
— So what is your opinion about it?
— An opinion, no less? — my left-hand neighbour asks back — what has an opinion to do with nakedness?
— Well, I do have an opinion — answers the right-hand one.
— By all means, let's hear it.
— I think it is an ugly impudence, if not more...
— With that I do not agree..
— That means you have an opinion too.
— If you force me to think. I hold, you understand me, that just as all the planets, our earth among them, are round, so everything is a wheel that turns back [galgal ha-chozer]. The little wheel has kept turning from Adam and Eve onwards, until people came back to today's style. Afterwards the little wheel will turn further, people will again begin to cover themselves: first a fig leaf, then something more, until they come back to the crinoline.
— Aha, what profound wisdom! — answers my right-hand neighbour — but tell me, my dear fellow, if it is a wheel, why is it only Eve who turns? Why do those Adams over there — just look — go about in long white trousers, in socks, with a shirt covering them up to the neck, only the sleeves rolled up to the elbow? If it is only nature, then both sexes ought to be subject to its laws!
My left-hand neighbour is silent and the right-hand one talks on:
— That is why I hold that they have bared themselves precisely for us, for male eyes...
— Now, now, you are already talking like an "Ernstman" [?] —
— No, simply like a man...
— But they do go to a separate women's corner, so as to be protected from a stranger's eye.
— You don't know the female nature: they themselves also look with male eyes; their own nakedness awakens passion in them.
— Hm... it seems to me you are babbling a bit...
— Is that so? Have you ever seen in a kitchen how a woman tastes the dishes she cooks? She tastes them with her husband's palate. Think it over and ask no more questions.
— Now that is real philosophy.
— Everything is simpler than your little wheel that turns.
— Well, and what is your opinion? — both my neighbours asked me.
— I have no opinion, only a proposal.
— Namely?
— Let us move over on the bench with our backs to the "plaża" [beach] and with our faces to the Modrzejów [?] lane.
Argus.
What I Heard, What I Saw.

[Będzin — feuilleton: "What I Heard, What I Saw".] Submitted for print by Ben Amotz.

Sad greetings.
A few Jews stand in the street. Their eyes express grief and pain; melancholy, worried, they cast glances back and forth, searching for "yesterday" and see no way out.
One of them holds open a Jewish newspaper that announces in Kiddush-Levana letters [huge type]:
— Bloody Friday in Jerusalem!
40 Jews killed and slaughtered, hundreds wounded!
— Oy vey, the Jew is not granted even a crumb of joy. How long ago was it at all? Only 8 days ago the same newspaper drummed out the news of the new bright epoch beginning for the Jewish people, the historic day in Zurich on which the Jewish Agency was concluded, a jubilee of joy, millions of dollars in donations for the Land of Israel, new bright prospects, mass emigration, a Jewish majority, and so on and so on..
And all at once a black, dark cloud arrives and covers all our hopes with Jewish blood; hearts turn to stone, breath is choked, and eyes grow dark from the terrible news that keeps arriving.
— "9 Jews killed, 120 wounded, state of war in Jerusalem."
— And I am quite pleased — pipes up a little Jew with a pointed little beard — how long must one wait? We must find out once and for all where we stand on the Land of Israel question; let the British power see that the Jewish people, too, demands its historic rights, even if it has to cost new martyrs...
— "Co za zebranie na chodniku?" [Polish: "What's this gathering on the pavement?"] — suddenly a policeman's voice was heard, and the conversation was cut short..

A "plebeian" meeting.
At a general meeting of the "Gemilut Chesed" [free-loan] fund. Once, when the "child" was born, it was called a rescue action. But as time went on the enthusiasm cooled, and only the dry name remained — "Gemilut Chesed".
In the street the "people" enjoys making a stir, "and the people murmured"... they whisper, tell stories, and get ready for the moment, the general meeting, when one will be able to uncover the "terrible secrets".
And when the "important" day arrives and people are called to come to the meeting — there is a "retreat", nobody comes, mouths are "shut" and
— everything stays as it was..
...There was a meeting, or rather a "plebeian" assembly, at Kołłątaja [Street] 24. At a specially reserved little table covered with a green tablecloth sat those who had for a while been "drawn by lot"[?] by the board, and they waited for their fate.
Between one item and the next a short break was made, and a neighbour from the courtyard, like a gabbai at hakafot, handed out to the crowd... sweets.
The meeting was conducted in a cosy manner. In the first row sat a few old men, who accepted with love the chairman's order of business, and when needed — they "duchened" [gave the priestly blessing]...

An "evil eye".
A second meeting on the same street; the house number is a different one — number 46. There everything is done with "koach" [strength].
At that meeting it was quite the opposite. The atmosphere is tense, the dissatisfaction very great, and nobody can establish the diagnosis of the "Hakoach" illness...
For some time now an "evil eye" has reigned over the treasury of "Hakoach" [the sports club]...
The matches are well attended, the takings are large, and when it comes to the accounts the "bad eye" comes again and the money disappears.

She is envious..
Toybe [Dove] is her name. True to her name, like a dove she lived quietly and modestly. Although she is already of very advanced age, 90 years old, she still made her living from her "business". She bought and sold [—] [?], and from the profit [drew] her livelihood.
Then the red Angel of Death cast an "eye" on her and cut off her leg.. She can no longer "fly"...
So she sits, one-legged, at Małachowskiego [Street] 9 and curses the devil that runs past her every 10 minutes, and she envies those whom the same Angel of Death has sent away forever..

Shabtai Weiss (Jerusalem)
From Afar...

[Editorial note:] The author of the article, Mr. Weiss, who was counted among the respected and active communal workers in Zagłębie until his aliyah to the Land of Israel, is known to the readers of our paper. Mr. Weiss will now contribute articles to our paper from time to time, chiefly on life in the Land of Israel. The Editors.

From afar I watch[?] you, [—] in Zagłębie; from [afar — —] your deeds and achievements, your conduct and dealings, your dreams and strivings.

For more than ten years I lived in your midst. For more than ten years we fought together for a finer future for the people in its home, for better living conditions and forms of life in exile[?]; for more than ten years we built national positions: in the kehillot, the city councils, in the field of education, in the national and socio-economic organization of the various strata of the people, in the organization of the youth, etc. Ten years of common striving and creating have surely left in me a watchful interest in the further development of your life and its social tendencies, and they give me the right to dwell critically on the phenomena of your public life and to draw great conclusions from these observations.

And so I ask you, brothers in Zagłębie: where has the impetus gone, the Sturm und Drang that carried your social and national work in those ten years of struggle I mentioned? What has become of your esprit de corps, which had then begun to develop so beautifully? Where have the placówki [outposts] gone that were built up with hard toil and struggle? What has become of the national youth, which had then organized itself so well? Why have you stopped halfway? And do you know at all where your road is leading you?

Week after week the "Zaglembier Tsaytung" brings me details of your life and "creativity" in various fields. And from these very details I put together a picture that reveals to me what lies hidden in the decline, what is characteristic in the routine, the face of the fog-shadows. And that face is terrible.

What has become of you, brothers in Zagłębie?

———

Allow me to dwell on a few facts and details that have stayed in my memory from the last issues of this paper, chiefly concerning certain general meetings, since the course and level of general meetings always serve as a barometer of the social development and cultural height of the given community.

At a general meeting of artisans in S. [Sosnowiec?] officials of the organization are torn to pieces and criticized in language that is a rarity even among market women.

At another general meeting, of merchants, the opposition tosses the board or the chairman up and down the way one tosses a play-ball.

To the general meeting of the women's gymnasium[?] in Sosnowiec, which has lived to see the event of receiving government rights [i.e. official accreditation], come all of six persons from among the parents, and this "meeting" elects a chairman, assessors and a secretary; the attendance of the six is described as progress, because last year not even that many came.

The chairman of the Zionist Organization in D. [Dąbrowa?], Mr. G., resigns his chairmanship because of a certain failure. That one can still understand. But this chairman wants to give a textbook example of the concepts of steadfastness and consistency, and he declares in the paper that he (who is supposed to serve the members as a model of activity, etc.) will take no part whatsoever in any Zionist work in D. (Only he will live in D. and take part in Zionist work in London?).

I could string a whole necklace of "pearls" of further similar facts from the series of elections, from the work of the community leaders (parnasei ha-dor) in the kehillot, of the councillors in the city councils, etc. But enough. The situation is too glaring in its social and national decline[?] and needs no further illustrations.

And allow me to ask: if such is your attitude to the matters of everyday reality, to the problems and affairs of the passing hour (chayei sha'ah) that you must bump into day after day, what can you still have to spare in your heart and mind, in your thought and attention, for eternal life (chayei olam), for the royal idea and the crowning work of the Jewish people — the upbuilding of the Land of Israel — which, although "imposed by a decree of Jewish fate on all parts of the Jewish people in the present era," is still regarded by some, out of short-sightedness, as a complex of tasks that lie outside the circle of immediate exile reality?

When indifference runs so deep toward matters that carry the evil urge of local patriotism and of quite [ligende?] ambitions — what can you still feel (I speak of feelings that awaken to deeds) when we in the Land of Israel lay stone upon stone in building the fortress for the Jewish spirit and matter, the last fortress, the new Masada, which shall defy and stand against all the waves that threaten to swallow us?

And when you hear how Jewish energy is creating here in the Land of Israel, through an intensive life of labour and culture, new foundations for the Jewish way of life throughout the whole world, new values, new forms of life for you, yes, truly for you, and surely for your children — are you, in your impoverished[?] decline, still capable of grasping it?

And when we in the Land of Israel choke with grief and anger over the matter of the Western Wall, or when our feet sometimes stumble over other great difficulties that accompany our work — what are you then capable of thinking about?

And yet... one wants to believe in your awakening and your rallying, brothers in Zagłębie.

In an old Jewish book I once read about[?] a tribe in one of the lands of the East whose gaze was always directed toward the future; sunny and bright days used to cast upon the members of that tribe an unusual melancholy and sadness — because after the days of sun must come days of shade and rain; and conversely, on clouded and murky days they would go dancing in a round dance (korohod) — because after the darkness must come the light.

One wants to believe that now that the social and national decline among you in Zagłębie has reached its lowest point, the days of sun and light and of strengthened national work must now return.

Within the four cubits of the last four, five years a piece of Jewish history has been wrapped up[?], which will decide over a large area of our future. For the realization of the Jewish idea of sovereignty a general Jewish front has consolidated. At such a time you, Jews in Zagłębie, have no right to be weak and disorganized. At such a time you must gather all your strength to break the atmosphere of social and national darkness[?]. At such a time you may not stand aside in backwardness and dullness. At such a time your footsteps too should and must be heard on the broad road of Jewish revival.

— I have been told, — "Irena" turned to Mania's parents, — that you wish to see me, that a great misfortune has befallen you and that you want to ask something of me. The doors of our convent are wide open to all unfortunate people who seek help with us. Say what you want, and whatever we can, we will do with God's help to ease your pain, which has brought you to our convent.
Mania's parents, out of great gratitude that she was so kind to them and wanted to help them in their misfortune, threw themselves down to kiss her hands.
— Calm yourselves; tell me, what do you want of our convent?
Reb Zelig and his wife stood as if petrified and could not utter a word.
— Calm yourselves and say what you want of our convent?
— Do you really not know why we have come to you? — Mania's parents barely managed to say.
— I am no prophetess, that I should be able to know. I am a sinful [?] creature of flesh and blood like all people, and everything that God knows is hidden from me, as from all people.
— We have come to beg you to give us back our child, who is here with you in the convent.
Sister Irena looked round at the other [?] sisters, who were standing [—], and answered Mania's parents coldly [?]:
— Is it for this that you have come to us and wanted to see me?
— What else have we to do here? We beg you, have pity on us and give us back our daughter.
— What do you mean, I should give her back to you? I did not take her from you, so I cannot give her back to you. Your daughter is not a small child, not a thing that can be taken and handed back. She came to us of her own free will, and of her own free will she can leave us; we force no one. In vain do your Jews give our convents a bad name, saying that they take your children by force and baptize them. That is a slander.
— Praised be God that I hear from you that she is here, — Chana exclaimed.
— Praised be His dear Name, — said Zelig.
— Yes, she is here, I do not want to deny it to you, although, as I have learned, you were told that she is not here. Your daughter herself asked for this — that you and all others who would ask about her should be told that she is not here, because she has turned away completely from you and from your Jews and no longer wants to know you.
— Woe is me, — Chana began to wring her hands.
— Surely it is impossible that my Mania should speak like that and renounce us.
— And yet you see that it is so after all. When a child [?] renounces his parents and his people, the parents and the people themselves are to blame.
— It is not possible; let me see her and talk with her, and you will hear for yourself.
— I have already heard it from her.
— I want to hear it from her own mouth, I want to see her; more than that I do not want — I want to see her and talk with her; that is my only request of you.
Sister Irena turned to one of the sisters:
— Go and tell Mania that her parents are here and want to see her; let her come here.
Reb Zelig and his wife, hearing these words, again threw themselves to kiss the hands of Sister Irena, and impatiently and full of joy they waited to see their daughter.
Mania's parents were told to wait for their daughter in the front house. They were led again across [—] back [?] into the front house.
Chana thought to herself: if, God forbid, it is true, as the sister said, that she no longer wants to know us, I will weep before her, plead with her; my tears will move her — she is such a good child, after all.
— What are you thinking, Chana? She will go home with us right away. What has she to do here? Praised be God that we have found her and know for certain that she is here.
— Surely I am not worthy to mention His dear Name for the kindness He has done us today.
Various sisters again walked to and fro, and every time the door opened they thought that any moment now they would be called to see their child.
— Why is it taking so long? — Reb Zelig asked his wife.
— Who knows? A child — perhaps she is asleep and they do not want to wake her, may I be her atonement. My heart is breaking. I have not seen her for so long. I would so like to see her — and tears began to pour from her eyes, and she wept quietly.
Reb Zelig could barely keep himself from weeping.
— Calm yourself, Chana, it is not fitting to cry here. She will come soon and we will go home.
— I cannot hold back my heart, I have not seen her for so long. May I be her atonement. Who knows how she looks, perhaps she is not well at all.
— What are you thinking? If, God forbid, she were not well, they would have taken us to her. She will come soon. Believe me, when I remember what is happening at home without me, how things are going at the mill without me, my hair stands on end; but what can one do — a child comes first.
— Is it the mill you have on your mind? And what can happen to the whole house without me? Let it all be an atonement, as long as I see my child again. I accept everything willingly — as long as I have my child.
— It is taking so long and she still does not come, — said Reb Zelig.
— As long as she is well, I don't mind if we wait a little longer. As long as she is well.
Suddenly a door opened, a sister came in and said to Mania's parents:
— I regret that I must tell you, in your daughter's name, that she does not want to see you. I argued with her a great deal, and it did not help at all.
— It is a lie! — Chana cried out in a voice not her own, — let me go to my child, — she cried out in a voice not her own.
In the front house, where more sisters were gathered, there was an uproar. — — — — —

What's New in Zagłębie? — Great Protest Demonstrations against the Bloody Events in the Land of Israel

[Head of the local section; Będzin and Sosnowiec — protests over the 1929 riots in Palestine.]
What's New in Zagłębie?
(Date boxes: Friday, 24 Av 5689 — Piątek 30 sierpnia 1929 [Friday, 30 August 1929].)
Great Protest Demonstrations
against the Bloody Events in the Land of Israel
Jewish shops closed as a sign of protest. — The Sosnowiec kehilla sends protest telegrams to the League of Nations.
The bloody events in the Land of Israel have, as in the whole Jewish world, found a sorrowful echo among the Jewish population of Zagłębie too. The main topic of conversation, regardless of class or political trend, was — the bloody massacres in Eretz Israel.
Many families who have children and relatives in Eretz Israel turned there with telegraphic inquiries, but to this day no one has yet received any answer.
In the Zionist premises
on Sunday evening, with the participation of the Rabbi of Widawa [?], a large youth meeting of Będzin, Sosnowiec and Dąbrowa took place, which decided to organise a demonstration in front of the English consulate in Katowice.
On Monday evening, in connection with the sad events, the kehilla board held an urgent
Meeting in the Gmina [town hall],
at which a sharp protest was adopted and it was decided to organise a mourning demonstration in the synagogue.
The organising committee issued an appeal to the Jewish population, which is called upon 1) to assemble at half past 5 in the afternoon in the Gmina courtyard, from where the procession to the synagogue will be formed, and 2) at 6 o'clock all shops shall be closed as a sign of protest.
In response to this call, and under the heavy impression, hundreds of Jews of all strata gathered at the appointed hour in front of and in the courtyard of the Gmina, and from there was formed the
March to the synagogue.
At the head of the procession walked the members of the local rabbinate, R' Yehoshua'le, R' Dan and R' Henech David. Behind them, in closed ranks, walked hundreds of Jews, and the procession kept growing, so that at the Old Market [Stary Rynek] the number of participants reached into the thousands.
With the exception of a few individuals, all the Jewish merchants at the Old Market
closed their shops.
Everyone left their everyday occupations, and men and women, old and young, hurried to the synagogue to attend the
Memorial service in the synagogue,
— where the crowding was enormous and the heat terrible, and yet everyone stood like a solid wall and expressed the sharpest anger against the English government, which allowed things to come to such sad results.
The memorial service began with the recitation before the reader's desk of the chapters of Psalms from chapter 74 to 79. The first chapters were recited by the old synagogue beadle R' Abraham Kapłan, and the last chapter by the member of the synagogue choir Mr. Danciger, who after the Minha prayer recited „El Male Rahamim“ and „Yizkor“.
In the middle of the memorial service a terrible panic broke out when the „Altitshker“ [?] moreh tzedek R' Yehoshua'le, who had gone up before the Holy Ark to speak from there, fainted. The women in the women's gallery screamed in their manner and raised frightful wails, and it took quite a long time until order was restored.
Later it turned out that R' Yehoshua'le, on touching the electric chandelier, had received an electric shock and had been saved by a miracle.
After the memorial service ended there were delivered
Mourning speeches.
The first to speak was the moreh tzedek R' Yehoshua'le, who called for repentance and for Jewish daughters to dress modestly.
Then Mr. Winadzki spoke on behalf of the Zionist Organisation, comparing the pogroms of old against defenceless Jews with today's heroic self-defence by the Jewish youth in our Land.
Moving to tears was the speech of Mr. Sz. J. Rinski, who spoke on behalf of the Jewish kehilla about the sad events. When Mr. Rinski mentioned the terrible massacre of the 45 yeshiva students slaughtered in Hebron, a wail broke out.
Later, in the synagogue courtyard under the open sky, there took place a
Youth rally.
Speeches were made by Yehuda Preger (Poale Zion Right) and Zelkowicz (Brit Trumpeldor). During the speeches, cries of protest rang out loudly against the English government, which bears great guilt for the bloodbath.
After the singing of „Hatikvah“ there was formed a
Youth demonstration,
which marched, headed by blue-and-white flags wrapped in black ribbons, through the Old Market and Kołłątaja [Street] as far as Sobieskiego Street, where the demonstration was dispersed under pressure from the police.
The demonstrators went off to the premises of their organisations, where it was decided to travel the next day, Wednesday, to Katowice to demonstrate
in front of the English consulate.
From early morning groups of young and older Zionists left for Katowice by every train. In Katowice the demonstrators avoided anything that might arouse suspicion against them and waited in various places for the moment of assembly.
At 12 noon, when the factory whistles began to blow, about 300 people suddenly gathered in front of the building in which the English consulate is located and shouted various words of protest against the English government.
In the consulate premises
two window-panes were smashed.
Police soon arrived on the spot and very politely appealed to the demonstrators to disperse quietly.
This was done, and after the singing of „Hatikvah“ the demonstration was dispersed. Several young people who did not immediately obey the police order were arrested.
On Wednesday
Jewish Sosnowiec expressed its sharp protest.
On Tuesday evening a consultation of all the Jewish national organisations took place in the premises of „Mizrachi“, to discuss how to express the bitter protest against the pogroms on the Jewish Yishuv in Palestine.
Speeches on the matter were delivered by Dr. Melodysta, J. S. Weinryb and others. It was decided to arrange on Wednesday
A protest demonstration
throughout the town: the shops shall be closed at 6 o'clock in the afternoon and a memorial service shall be held in the synagogue.
At 5½ in the afternoon there took place in the Gmina hall
A special meeting
of the kehilla board and council. The meeting was held under a deep impression of mourning. The chairman, Mr. L. Zendel, opens the meeting and gives the floor to Mr. Weinryb, who devotes some warm words to the events, and on his proposal the fallen heroic martyrs in the Land of Israel are honoured by standing.
Mr. Weinryb also proposes to send protest telegrams to Geneva [the League of Nations] and to the English government in London. The proposal is adopted.
Then the chairman of the kehilla council, Dr. Melodysta, speaks: We bow our heads — says the speaker — before our brothers and sisters who fell like heroes defending Jewish honour and Jewish pride, and who showed the wide world that the Jewish people stands ready to make great and heavy sacrifices in every field in order to conquer the Land, which is the Jewish hope and the Jewish future.
The kehilla council member Mr. Chaim Unger (Orthodox) speaks about the colonies destroyed by the Arabs, which had been built thanks to the blood and sweat of the heroic halutzim, and calls for support so that what was destroyed may be rebuilt.
During the meeting a procession to the synagogue was formed with the help of „Maccabi“. At the head of the procession [were] Rabbi R' Menachem Szwarc, the president of the kehilla, doctors, lawyers, a large number of Hasidic Jews, „Hashomer“ with its banner, and thousands of young people, men and women, who demonstrated in closed ranks.
The procession went along Czysta, „Sarawa“ [?], 3 Maja, Modrzejowska and Dekerta [Streets] to the synagogue, where hundreds of Jews — men, women and children — were already waiting. All the Jewish shops, even those of half-assimilated Jews, were closed, except the shops of Manela, Einhorn and R' Meir Wajgsztok.
In the synagogue
there was terrible crowding; the women's synagogue too was packed full. The cantor Mr. Lejchter, accompanied by a choir, very beautifully recited Psalm 79, prayed Minha, and brought people to tears with his heartfelt rendering of „Look down from heaven and see“ and „El Male Rahamim“.
Then Rabbi Szwarc and Dr. Melodysta spoke on the topic of the day. Dr. Melodysta expressed thanks to the Polish consul in Jerusalem, Dr. Zbyszewski, for his humanitarian conduct: wishing to protect and rescue the Polish citizens, he was for that reason seriously wounded by the savage Arabs.
On behalf of „Agudah“ Mr. Berekh [?] Stczesski [?] speaks, who uses the moment to settle accounts with the Zionists for their groundless hatred and with the free-thinking youth. A tumult breaks out; Mr. Szenicki protests against this, shouts of „Bravo!“ are heard, and the unseemly incident regrettably weakens the gravity of the moment.
The closing words are spoken by Mr. Weinryb, and with the singing of „Hatikvah“ the memorial service is concluded.

Będzin — General meeting of the “Gemilut Chesed” fund

On Sunday the annual general meeting of the Będzin Gemilut Chesed (interest-free loan) fund took place in a hall.
How distant the Jewish public's attitude is toward institutions whose turnover reaches tens of thousands of złoty can be shown by the paltry number of members who came to the meeting.
Mr. Bożykowski opens the meeting, stresses the members' meagre interest, and the chair is taken over by Mr. Yitzchok Aharon Landau. The latter invites to the presidium Messrs. A. Gitler, Sh. Lewkowicz, Y. Landau, M. Fröhlich, M. Sendyszew and, as secretary, Mr. Montag.
Reports on the activity and on the treasury are given by the chairman Bożykowski and secretary Montag.
The reports show the enormous importance of the institution, which in the course of its existence has granted loans amounting to tens of thousands of złoty; the donations section, too, holds an honourable place.
The reports, as well as the provisional budget, are adopted.
After a formal clause of the statutes is amended, the “elections” of 5 board members take place.
The few voters had not prepared any candidates at all, and the printed list, prepared in advance, won.
From the “Muse”

The Jewish Dramatic Society “Muse” in Będzin will soon renew its activity in the field of the stage; also being organized are: systematic lessons in Yiddish; a guitar-and-mandolin orchestra; a choir section and a wall newspaper called “Muze-Blat”. — All interested and capable members in these fields can register with the society's secretariat.
Sosnowiec — Suicide of a Jewish girl

In Sosnowiec, on Dęblińska Street, 15-year-old B. poisoned herself with a hefty dose of vinegar essence.
The circumstances of the suicide are tragic. The girl needed a rubber (artificial) leg and she had no money.
When she saw that she had no prospect at all of obtaining the leg, she decided to put an end to her life.
A case of sleeping sickness

The director of Count Renard's rolling mill returned last Saturday from the Poznań exhibition. After eating supper he went to bed. On Sunday morning, when the household tried several times to wake Mr. Engles and he did not wake up, a doctor was called, who established that he was alive.
All the means used by almost all the local doctors to wake him produced no result whatsoever.
On Tuesday 2 professors of the Jagiellonian University were summoned from Kraków, as well as several doctors from Katowice. But none of them succeeded in changing the situation, and as we write these lines Mr. Engles is still asleep.
The doctors explain this as a case of sleeping sickness.
Stabbing over an inheritance

In Wojkowice two Christians had a claim to an inherited estate. The heirs quarrelled day and night, and one of them decided to get rid of his competitor and fell upon him with murderous blows.
The heir was taken to hospital in serious condition.

Because of the latest events in the kehilla, where Mr. Avrohom Liwer was elected president, and the dirty outbursts of the Agudah's “mikveh leaflet” against such authorities as the former Sejm deputy Dr. Weinzieher and the all-round philanthropist Mr. Sh. „Quick“ help from the Sick Fund

[Sosnowiec — health insurance fund.] „Quick“ help from the Kasa Chorych (Sick Fund).
On Monday before dawn Mr. Sh., the clerk at the Tobiasz[?] firm in Sosnowiec, suddenly fell ill and needed urgent medical help.
When the sick man's family telephoned the Sick Fund's emergency service („quick help“), they were asked there for various documents before the patient could receive help.
The patient's life, however, was at risk. Until he would get help from the „Sick Fund“ — and [they] turned to private doctors.

New relief in paying the turnover tax.
The Ministry of Finance has sent out a circular to all finance chambers and tax offices concerning a speedy provisional review of the appeals against the turnover-tax assessments for the year 1928.
Depending on the provisional reviews, tax enforcement must for the time being be limited only to the sums provisionally fixed at the first review of the appeals.
In connection with this, the heads (naczelnicy) of the tax offices must also limit the size of the quarterly „advance payments“ (zaliczki) for the year 1929.

Nothing to Do!

Zagłębie is becoming like everyone else [lit. "equal to people"]: here too the problem of work is growing more acute, here too the general crisis is beginning to show what it can do.
Nothing to do, no work — this is a curse from the Admonition [tokhakha] that has been fulfilled in our time; in antiquity and even in the Middle Ages people knew nothing of this curse. In those times human labour was dear: people paid money for a person, people bought human beings and paid large sums, bought them as soldiers, bought them as servants.
The modern age abolished man as an article on the market. Soldiers are not bought, servants are not bought. Man became free; he can sell the labour of his hands and demand for it whatever price he finds right and fitting.
So it is in theory. In practice it looks different. A man cannot demand for his work as much as he wants, as much as comes into his head. Wages are regulated by the law of supply and demand. If there are many hands looking for work and few people willing to give work, the price of labour falls. Wages also depend on the general state of the market — dearness or cheapness in the country as a whole. They also depend on the world market and on the prices paid for the finished article.
But the greatest misfortune of the modern economy is unemployment. The fact that thousands, or even millions, go about without occupation because there is nothing to do — this fact casts a shadow on society and its order. The curse "and ye shall sell yourselves unto your enemies for bondmen and bondwomen, and no man shall buy you" [Deut. 28:68] — you will sell yourselves as servants and maids and nobody will want to buy — is the worst thing that can happen. And this is the situation we are now in here too.
Why is the number of unemployed growing? It is the result of the crisis: how can factories work when there is no one to work for, when there are no orders; how can one work when there is no credit, when one never sees money before one's eyes, when the bills of exchange received for goods are protested, when nobody pays and cannot pay on time; and he cannot pay because whenever a cash grosz turns up it has to be carried off to pay taxes.
In such a situation the wheels cannot turn, they have to stop, and poverty, which until now was hidden, concealed, drowned out by the noise of the machines, shows itself in the street. It is "free", there is nothing to do, it can go strolling about the town. But when poverty marches, when it strolls — it is bad for the town, very bad.
Nothing to do, no work, people are unemployed — that is what it is called in ordinary language. But people must not be unemployed; society, the government, is obliged to provide people with work so that they can earn a living from their labour ["prace", from Polish praca]. "Nothing to do" is no excuse; there must be work, conditions for work must be created. Nothing good comes of idleness and one cannot live on it.
Zagłębie is becoming like everyone else; we are getting more unemployed, and it is bad, very bad.
Sh. Y. S.
Echoes of the Events in Palestine — Protest Meetings and Memorial Services

During the week protest meetings against the bloody events in the Land of Israel took place in almost all the nearby[?] towns and townlets.
In the Sosnowiec municipal theatre a protest meeting was held by the Left Poale Zion. The well-known labour activist Mr. Zerubavel gave a lecture on the subject in the same hall.
In Dąbrowa a large protest assembly took place in the synagogue. Speeches were given by Dr. Teladista[?], Gotlib and others, and a memorial service was held for the fallen martyrs.
In Olkusz on Sunday at 11 a.m. a procession formed at the "Mizrachi" premises, in closed ranks of Zionists, "Tse'irei Mizrachi", "Hashachar", "Yardenia", headed by "Hashomer Haleumi" with a blue-and-white flag wrapped in black, and entered the synagogue. The synagogue was already packed beforehand with men, women and children. The Rabbi, may he live long, spoke in a weeping voice on current affairs, recalling various epochs of Jewish pogroms and massacres, and with reverence commemorated the martyrs who have now fallen for the sanctification of the Name in the Land of Israel. The cantor Mr. Lejchter of Sosnowiec, with choked tears, recited Psalm 79, "Habet mi-shamayim u-re'eh" and "El male rachamim", at which the congregation broke into weeping. Further speakers were Moshele Szwarcberg, Zhabner[?] (Będzin), Paluch (Agudah), Goldberg and Silberberg. It was resolved to send protests to the League of Nations, the English government and the Zionist Executive, and thanks to the Polish consul in Jerusalem. The impressive protest assembly ended with the singing of "Hatikvah".
In Modrzejów on Thursday, on the initiative of the "Keren Kayemet committee", a protest meeting against the events in the Land of Israel was organised in the synagogue. The entire Jewish population of Modrzejów and Niwka took part. The shops were closed. After the 2nd cantor of Mysłowice, Mr. Diament, recited the appropriate chapters of Psalms and held a memorial for those fallen in Jerusalem, Rabbi Englard spoke on current affairs. Then speeches were given by Lejzer Ginsberg, Isachar Fajner and Aron Frajberg. A resolution was adopted unanimously against the Arab outrages and the disregard [lit. "light esteem"] of the English administration in Palestine, with thanks to the Polish consul general in Palestine. A committee was also set up, which has so far collected 600 zł. To the singing of "Hatikvah" the public dispersed in a depressed mood.
Afterwards a street demonstration formed on the initiative of the sports club "Shimshon", marching through the town with shouts against the English administration in Palestine.
In Strzemieszyce on Wednesday, the fast day, an assembly took place in the beit midrash. The local rabbi delivered a moving eulogy in honour of the fallen martyrs, and a committee was founded to carry out a fund-raising collection. The committee was joined by the most respected local householders; the names of the donors will be published.
In Zawiercie, on the initiative of the Jewish community (gmina), a joint committee of all strata was formed to carry out a quick fund-raising campaign for the victims in the Land of Israel. On Saturday night a meeting of prominent communal workers took place and a committee of the following persons was elected: Cwi Landau (treasurer), Mordechaj Hilel Windman (chairman), secretary; Josef Zabelman, Nachum Israel Szajewicz, Hirszel Haberman, Szlomo Rozenbaum, Ozer Zajfman, Josef Petak. Gustaw Berensztajn, Henich Chwat and Chaim Lewkowicz. The committee hopes to raise a minimum of 15 thousand zł.
It was also decided to observe three months of mourning, abstaining from entertainments, theatre, cinema and the like.
On Tuesday a youth meeting was organised. Messrs. Israel Herman and M. Ch. Windman spoke.
The youth committee consists of: Israel Herman, Jehuda Wigdorson[?], Icchak Buchszrajber, Wolf Wajs, Cukerman, Wygodzki, Blajfer[?], Lustiger, Szyrlowski, Almer, Jakobowicz, Zielonki, Bruziger and Liberman.
The Tse'irei and Poalei Agudat Israel organised a large assembly. A moving speech was given by Mr. Eli' Bruziger, who described the fighting in the Land of Israel and called on all those assembled to show their sympathy fittingly for the benefit of our brothers in Palestine. Then Hirszel Liberman gave a speech, and afterwards a sizeable sum was collected.
———
The events have aroused sympathy among non-Jews too. In the course of the last few days non-Jews came to us at the editorial office and to the community office wishing to enrol as volunteers to fight against the Arabs. One of them donated 5 zł. for a wreath for the fallen heroes.
— The restaurateur Mr. Fryd in Sosnowiec, Targowa 17, is donating 2 per cent of his takings from the 8th to the 14th of this month.
Olkusz. — From the City Council.

At the first post-recess session of the Olkusz city council, councillor Berisz Weisselfisch was elected, almost unanimously, in place of the resigned alderman (ławnik) Mr. Blum; in his place on the city council, Berisz Trapauer enters.
At the same session it was also decided to evict, in the coming days, the inhabitants (Jews only) of the house on the market square at Krakowska and Kościuszki streets, and to give them a total of 2,500 złoty for other dwellings.
A. B.

A father attacks his own son.
For a long time Icchak Neumark traded in partnership with his son Lejbisz. But a few weeks ago the partnership was dissolved, and since then quarrels have broken out between father and son on that ground.
Last Saturday, when the son and his wife passed by the father's house, the father attacked him and beat him murderously. In the brawl the son's wife was also injured.
—o—
Szczekociny.
A Jewish child burned to death.
On Wednesday night a terrible accident happened in the Kanal family. A fire broke out in a cellar from a little spilled spirit.
The flames caught a 9-year-old girl, who was badly burned and died the next day.
Strzemieszyce.

A drunken brawl.
In Frajman's beer-house several drunkards made a row and wrecked the premises. The police who arrived "calmed" the heated tempers.
A play falls flat.
Last Saturday a theatre performance by amateurs from Będzin and Sosnowiec was to take place here.
Because of the events in Palestine the hall was empty, and the poor amateurs did not even have the money for their travel expenses...

From Sports Life.

Hakoach (Bielsko) — Hakoach (Będzin) 2:2
At the above match I was astonished by the fact that at such a specifically friendly match with a brother club, Hakoach [Będzin] happened[?] to display such great ambition, which went as far as self-sacrifice; players such as Rotenberg 3 and Szywek 2 simply risked the integrity of their bodies — and not only of their own bodies, but often also the body of the player from the brother club. Incidentally, a large part of the blame for this lies with the referee Mr. Lichtensztajn, who allowed such a bitter fight as well as coarse behaviour on the part of the Będzin players; he should unconditionally have sent Szywek 2 off the field for his tactless "foul"[?], and likewise Rotenberg — then it would surely not have come to the match being abandoned before the end.
And from us a few words to the players themselves: where did you leave your great ambition when you played for the championship against Sosnowiec or Radom? Where did you forget your self-sacrifice when Jewish sporting honour was at stake? Then your self-sacrifice might have been understandable to us; but this Sunday, alas, against the brother Hakoach of Bielsko, it was understandable to no one.
The course of play was quite interesting and was conducted at a fairly fast pace. Already in the 5th minute Hakoach scores the first goal through Richter. The Bielsko players have a slight advantage, but only in the 32nd minute do they manage to equalise, and soon afterwards they also score the second goal. In the second half the Będzin players manage to equalise through Szymek[?] 2 from a [—]. Gradually it gets "warmer" on the field, and on account of personal scores it comes to [blows?], and the game is abandoned...
"Kraft"[?] — "Hakoach 2" 3:0
The Hakoach reserve team is considerably better technically and holds a slight advantage from start to finish, scoring one goal in the first half through Hampel[?] and two more goals in the second half through Rozen 2 and Goldsztajn 2. Referee Mr. Plesner — good.
M. Z.

"Powstaniec" (Königshütte) had a great sporting event on Sunday in the match against "Samson". 500 spectators attended the match. The play was interesting. In the 20th minute Powstaniec manages to convert a goal; then Samson begins to play and manages to equalise through S. Brener. In the second half Powstaniec plays at a stronger pace and has a slight advantage, but without success; in the 30th minute Powstaniec manages to make a second goal from an 11-metre kick, and Samson equalises through Brener. "Samson" (res.) — "Powstaniec" (res.) 2:1.
