Not Only Mourning — Deeds Too!

[Editorial — Palestine; the 1929 riots; appeal for aid.]
(On the sad events in the Land of Israel.)
The bloody events in the Land of Israel have shaken all strata of the Jewish population; the savage deeds of the half-savage Arabs have roused the Jewry of the whole world. No one could rest, no one could remain indifferent — wherever a Jewish heart beats, it trembled with anger and fear, with hatred and bitterness.
Our humanity somehow became bewildered [?]; people could find no place for themselves. Grief was poured over every face; no one could look another in the face; it seemed as though we were the ones who had been wronged [?], as though we were the guilty ones. We wept, we mourned, we protested; we nearly lost our senses and remained helpless like tiny innocent children, like people without life and without consciousness.
So it was in the first moment. And no wonder, for no one had expected such unheard-of deeds: after all, a Jew in the Land of Israel went out with such security, with such freedom, as in no other country.
Now is not the time, and today is not our task, to search for the causes of all this; instead one must sober up from the terrible despair and become practical. One must begin to take a clear accounting and to know where we stand in the world and what we can do for our brothers in the Land of Israel, who perished for the sanctification of the Name (al kiddush ha-Shem) and sacrificed themselves for the fatherland like true heroes and like valiant men, who did not let a single position fall.
We know that Jewish Zagłębie was shaken by the heart-rending savageries that were played out on the holy soil of the Land of Israel; we know how people went about as if stunned [?] and strained their eyes to hear some reassuring news. We have seen how much strength and health it has cost our brothers and sisters.
And yet, and yet we cannot remain standing on this very spot, mourning and waiting until salvation comes from somewhere. We must take a step further; we must consider the prevailing situation with full seriousness and with a settled mind; we must remember that the beautiful and new Land of Israel, which so impressed everyone and enchanted so many eyes, has been laid waste and utterly destroyed, and those who built all this, who planted the beautiful orange avenues and drained the swamps and made of them flourishing colonies, are now left impoverished and wretched and without a roof over their heads.
And therefore, therefore we must comfort those who have remained alive and have the hope of rebuilding the present ruins. And therefore we must hasten, first of all, to send them material help.
Let Jewish Zagłębie hasten to carry out a great fundraising campaign, which will make it possible to ease the troubles and the hunger of our unfortunate brothers and sisters in the Land of Israel.
Let relief committees be created in Zagłębie whose only purpose is to collect money for the unfortunate in the Land of Israel. Let the committees in every town work together; let no partisanship reign in this field; let their only aim be to send bread to the hungry and to save the lives of the sick. It seems that here partisanship must vanish, that every Jew must be rescued, whatever trend and outlook he may belong to.
So let us set to practical work; let the committees be created now, and let the campaign be carried out in a planned way, for with good organization and diligent work every Jew will come with his donation and will want to have the privilege of helping his unfortunate brothers and sisters in the Land of Israel.
In the meantime our editorial office also undertakes to accept donations, which we will publish in the columns of our paper.
Let Jewish Zagłębie not discharge its duty with mere tears and protests; let it not merely refrain from remaining indifferent to the bloody calamities — but let us show deeds, activity, devotion and love.
Let Jewish Zagłębie, together with Upper Silesia, prove that it knows how to come to the aid of the unfortunate with an open hand.
R. Let.
In Moments of Despair and Hope.

[Essay — the August 1929 events in the Land of Israel; protest and mourning.]
Hearts are pounding... Jewish hearts are pounding — here is fresh news. Perhaps it is quiet, perhaps the murderous hands have already dropped, perhaps they have already had their fill of cruelties, of warm human blood...
— Perhaps there is already an end to the robbing, raping and murdering!..
Hearts are pounding.. the eyes are popping[?] out of one's head — a fresh report — a whole Jewish family butchered!
— An orphanage attacked and little innocent lambs murdered!
— A Jewish colony burned, and yet another colony!
And such lines run one after another, such reports flash without end, without measure, and an inner voice asks: perhaps tomorrow it will be better, perhaps tomorrow it will already be quiet!..
But — tomorrow — still graver, still more bitter, still more cruel.
— An end to everything. A ruin-heap of everything.. the finest sons slaughtered, the finest gardens burned... and the hills and valleys of Zion have soaked up the blood of our holiest, and the hills and valleys of Zion have wept in the nights and lamented the destruction, the Third Destruction.
* * *
A dream..
For thousands of years it has accompanied us, given us a goal in our dark life.
A dream, a sweet dream, that gave us courage and strength to go on dragging our heavy and hard life all over the world.
A dream that we dreamed awake, and it seemed to us that any moment now the beautiful dream would come true! that any moment now it would cease to be a dream, a legend, and become a beautiful reality, a reality dreamed of..
And deep in our hearts we carried the holy dream until it became our soul, our meaning, our goal.
And now, now the wild ones have come out of their clay[?] lairs and lay their beastly hands on everything that is holy and dear to us; they hack down our young, beautiful lives, young stalks, buds not yet grown, they lay waste and annihilate forty years of work in blood and sweat, they reach out with their filthy claws to tear from our hearts the only thing we possess, the only thing that has remained to us, the only thing that gave us strength to drag the chains of a two-thousand-year exile — the dream of our Land of Israel.
And what is our life worth without this dream?
And what goal do we have when the idea of our Land of Israel is robbed from us? What meaning does our life have then?..
* * *
England! The great British Empire, which reigns over almost three parts of the world, has deceived us. Deceived us shamefully, and we, the "wise and understanding people", let ourselves be deceived.
We heard a kind word from rich Aunt England, and we believed; England wants to make us a nation, England wants to give us a land, and we believed. England will be our protector, and we were happy; England will redeem us from exile, England is for us the true saving angel.
— And now? Ah! How bitter is the disappointment!
Now they sit there in the royal palaces and with a deathly-cold gentlemanly calm issue devastating orders; and there they sit, the ice-cold [?] ministers, calmly smoking their pipes over the ruins of Jewish property, which flickers on the ruins of the bloodied fields of the Land of Israel, where our martyrs lie and convulsively breathe out their souls.
And even now they sit in their blue and golden salons and go on giving their lying promises, and meanwhile people are butchered there and young souls slaughtered.
And surely now too they are sitting, our protectors and providers, thinking how to provide for us — but instead of [going] with cannon and bayonets against the savage murderers, they are thinking about new thousands of missionaries to catch our souls.
* * *
— Jabotinsky!
Did he not warn us a thousand times, that brilliant, great mind!
— They will slaughter you like sheep — he cried — and you will not even have anything to help yourselves with, anything to defend yourselves with!
— Jabotinsky!
— England is harassing you — he pounded on the table — England is fooling you and you believe blindly; you must demand, insist, and not bow down submissively; you must have a battalion, you must have self-defence that will rescue you in time of need. But his voice was a voice crying in the wilderness. Almost alone he stood in his struggle, and few, very few understood him. Few, very few listened to him. And how tragic it is that his own people, who fought him so[?] sharply in the Land of Israel and shouted at him "Imperialist! Militarist!", now see how gravely they sinned against him; only now do they see and understand what this great fighter meant by his militarism.
Let us all bow our heads before the great, luminous spirit, before the sage who foresees what is to come, who warned us not to entrust all our property, our lives, to wild Arabs wrapped in an English police uniform — nor even to a uniform in which a genuine British soul is found; they too want to drown us in a spoonful of water. Only ourselves, by ourselves must we protect ourselves; by ourselves, with our modest strength, must we defend ourselves; by ourselves must we fight. True, small and modest is our strength, but great is our spirit, great is our ideal — and therefore strong will be our struggle and certain will be our victory.
* * *
Hearts are pounding! But no! One heart is pounding! All of Jewry now has one heart, and that heart is pounding; it is as if all the partitions between us suddenly fell down, as if we had all been kneaded together into one lump of dough. And this gives us, in our present dark moment, a ray of hope. Never before have we all gone out to struggle as now; never before have we all had, as now, one thought, one goal, one will.
And the rabbis of Poland, the most pious of Jewry, come and decree a fast; and pious Jews come to say Psalms and fast for the soul of the free[?] pioneer who fell for the sanctification of God's Name defending the Western Wall; and English Jews come, already assimilated in the third or fourth generation, and open their money-granaries and give for the beaten, for the robbed; and in New York a Jewish mass of some fifty thousand heads pours out into the street, and fifty thousand Jewish mouths protest and cry out, and this cry fills the space of the whole globe up to the seventh heaven.
And because our seventeen-million people is now one soul, and because one great ideal now unites us, and because we all now stand in one struggle — the victory must be a just and a holy one.
— And to you, pioneers! Fighters and builders who now stand in this desperate struggle with the sword in hand, defending the Wall, the eternally standing Wall — we say to you from far and from near, from the whole great world: wherever there is a Jewish heart, it beats for you and with you; and the murderous bullets that are aimed into your hearts strike the heart of your whole nation; and the blood that you shed for our existence, for our great cause, will be forever hallowed by us; and a whole people will mourn for your souls, a whole people will say Kaddish.
L. Goldsztajn.
In the Hard Days

[Lyrical prose on the riots (in Palestine); by "Algiz".]
(Moods).
In the hard days the heart thirsts for a word. Deep and earnest and calm and full of light let the word be.
In the hard days the heart calls for a prophet. Come, man, carry your faith into our dark world, announce to us with your clear voice: the day of terror will pass, the flood will vanish from our earth, the sun will shine again on liberated hill and dale, and your [?] flowers, like innocent children's eyes, will bathe in warmth and light.
Come, man, and announce to us with your sure voice: love will again reign in the world, people will press one another's hand in friendship, and the reflection of blood will no longer lurk in their eye.
Come, man [?]!...
In the days of terror the heart longs for a miracle. Stones, heavy as eternity, press on man's breast. Under heavy stones the tormented heart flutters and trembles and is afraid to hope, and longs for a hope, and sends a prayer into the silence.. whither?
* * *
Somewhere tender fingers weave the music, somewhere between high, desolate yellow-red walls, over damp, deep courtyards, over narrow, crammed-together alleys, and it rises into the sparkling air, and meets up there with the rays of the sun, with the fragrance of distant fields, with the breath of the fresh wind, and it rings and sings and reaches the ear like a consolation.
Lull me, you singing greeting from an unknown hand. In your language there is so much youthful joy, in your hurrying tones a loving playfulness is woven; you are — like the young wind in the field, you are — like the restless wave on the gold-sprinkled sea; the heart will hurry along with you, swim, float somewhere far away, where there is healthy joy.
But no.
Through the tones a groan already sounds. From somewhere a scream comes flying. Who calls there in mortal agony? Who begs for mercy in merciless hands.
The music screams and calls and rages and storms and roars. Darker is the sky, stone is the earth, lead is the air, and in the uncanny distance rings the voice of vengeance. Rings the voice of blood.
I hear a people drowning [?] in its own blood, I hear a wild hellish pain screaming from one end of the world to the other.
Is this the voice of my people?
* * *
My little town is empty, as if dead; deserted the streets; desolation — in the houses; orphaned lies the great market. And green [?] grasses begin to sprout on it; abandoned, the old synagogue looks out with its little panes gone green.
It is still. No sound, no voice, no cry. Dead is the town. Above, a clear sky, below, bright streets, and in the bright stillness terror strides about and looks with mute eyes out of every house, out of every corner.
It is still in the town. Only from time to time black crows come, circle over the roofs, scream, screech, call with a hungry voice, let themselves down by the broad road, there where a heap of bones lies.
The crows peck at the white bones, turn them, throw them right and left, but the bones are already dry. The earth has soaked up the blood, wild birds have pecked out the flesh, the marrow...
Where are you, brothers? Where have you rested your head?
*
By the rivers of Babylon the exiles sat and lamented; on the trees by the bank they hung up their harps; the enemy came and demanded a song — and wrath flared up in the proud hearts of the vanquished [?]. The flame of wrath scalded the poet's heart, and the wonder-song was created, full of pain and gall and hatred, which is stronger than death: "By the rivers of Babylon"..
For two thousand years the song has rung. And its mighty tone has not died away, and still it stirs the soul with words forged of steel.
Who will sing the song of our present-day terror? Who will forge the song of our present-day wrath? Who will pour together all the pains with all the abysses of our torment into one mighty chord? Who will come and tell what screams and burns and bleeds in our tormented soul?
Where is he — the man [?] with the wonder-word?
Too full is the cup, too poisonous the drink, there is no strength left.
Who will sing us the song that shall set our soul free?
Problems of Education. — The heder of old and today's school. — The teaching staff. — Safeguarding children's upbringing.

[Article — education; serial, part II.] (The heder of old and today's school. — The teaching staff. — Safeguarding children's upbringing.)
II.
The question of education has always been a difficult one. From time immemorial the upbringing of children stood at the very top of a Jewish father's and mother's concerns. And when the bein-hazmanim [the break between heder terms] came, the father did not deal in any trade at all; his only "trade" was the question of how to provide for the children so that they would grow up fit for God and for people.
The Jew knew that a melamed was someone who was no longer good for anything, a ne'er-do-well, and therefore parents in those days knew that they had to keep their children under their own supervision, so that it was a duty to "examine" the child every Sabbath, and by that yardstick the abilities of the melamed were measured.
From those times until today we have come a long way. The heder has become a school and the melamed — a teacher who has certain qualifications, and parents have become sure that they can entrust their children there. This has led to a state where parents do not concern themselves at all with the question of their children's education; they consider their duty done by picking as good a school as possible, and with that the matter is settled. People take no interest, do not care to know how the subjects are taught, both religious and general; they are content that the child moves up a class every year.
But if one begins to draw a parallel even between a secondary school of former times and today's, one sees here too an enormous change. It is not now what it used to be. There is no longer the sense of responsibility and the idealistic way of thinking of before; today a private school is a business like all other businesses, and one looks only to "get as much profit as possible from it, just as in any business, and of course the institution suffers from it, because in this case one naturally tries to have as few expenses and as much income as possible. Moreover, people take no proper interest in the children at all. One comes officially to "get through" the lesson and goes back again. Not once does one consider the psychology of this or that child, the abilities or lack of abilities of this or that pupil, in order to know how to continue further study. On top of this, every school is ruled by a peculiar kind of self-rule, with whatever and however it pleases. Nobody ever tries to take the pupils or the parents into account; they simply do what is better and more convenient for themselves.
Many schools, both private and communal, even have parents' committees, but which of the parents takes the trouble to come into the school to find out how things look and how matters stand with the fate of his child? People think that as soon as the child is sent to a school, there is no further need to take an interest, and no need to come into the school to find out how things look there — at a time when this is so important, so necessary.
Parents have no idea that for a school it is simply a cure when the teachers see that there are people who take an interest both in the school and in the children. Things reach the point of sheer absurdity because the teachers see that everything in the school is ownerless and that they can do undisturbed whatever they like.
Everyone knows that a school is in fact also an educational institution; that means that the pupil, boy or girl, must know not merely the lesson, but must also be brought up in the school — and why should we fool ourselves: are the children really brought up there? Does anyone take an interest in how the pupils behave outside the school? What they read, what friends they have and how they spend their free time? This, in our view, is to a certain extent more important than learning the lesson by heart. Upbringing, after all, sets its stamp on the development and future of the child.
We often see in the cinemas many children at such films that we are astonished. We cannot understand how and who let these children into films that are harmful to them; such films after all corrupt the soul and the spirit of the child.
A terrible demoralisation prevails in every sphere of our life, and that is precisely why great attention must be paid to the educational sphere of our children; otherwise they run the risk of being demoralised at every step.
Without doubt the most important role today is played by the school, which the child enters in his earliest years, so that the process of development takes place in the school; therefore great attention must be paid to the children throughout, from the very day they cross the threshold of the school.
It is very, very important that parents should always stay in contact with the schools. Many schools even have parents' committees, but they take very little interest either in the schools or in the education of their children. One must therefore have such committees not merely on paper; they must be organically bound up with the school. This will be of great benefit in every respect: many shortcomings will be remedied, which will not allow children to be demoralised, and the school staff will be more keenly aware that there is a committee standing on guard and seeing to it that the school is kept at the proper level.
Let us remember at all times that the school is the true house of upbringing, which must be the guide for our children, in whom we wish to see the humanity of the future.
If we remain indifferent to our educational institutions, it means that we remain indifferent to our children, who thereby have the opportunity to become demoralised — which is dangerous in today's modern times.
Let us not forget for a single minute that the dearest and holiest thing is our future, which we must guard like the apple of our eye.
Y. T.
The Zagłębie Polish Press on the Events in the Land of Israel

Besides the telegraphic and telephone reports about the bloody events in the Land of Israel, the Polish press is printing longer articles about the conflict between the Jews and the Arabs over the Western Wall.
Z. N.[?] "Pogroms against Jews in Palestine," writes the "Kurier Zagłębia" (No. 226).
"The attitude of the British government to the Zionist demands in Palestine has changed radically in recent years. At the last Zionist Congress in Zurich one of the speakers publicly complained that in the British Parliament the tendency has lately prevailed to place the interests of the permanent inhabitants of the country above the 'interests of the past' and historical right, i.e., that in London — to the great annoyance of the Zionists — they have not forgotten that the majority in Palestine consists of Arabs, and that it is to them, and not to the Jews, that Palestine belongs." (?)
The author of the article takes up the cause of the Arabs, who, in his opinion, do not wish to be held in contempt and to have the right taken from them to remain masters in their own country. And he passes on to the main cause that led to the bloody events.
"The events at the Western Wall are one of the proofs of the [?: 'iberlikhn' — supra-personal/overt] struggle between the Arab population and the Jews in Palestine. On the Arab side, at the head of the struggle stands the Supreme Muslim Council in Jerusalem, which is quite influential in the whole Muslim world.
With the help of this council the Muslims exert pressure on the British administration in Palestine and demand majority rights for themselves as the actual masters of the country."
In conclusion the author points out that the bloody events in Palestine are only the beginning of further terrible actions by the Arabs against the Zionists.
"It is characteristic — the article ends — that the Jewish-Arab conflict grew sharper together with the conclusion of the 16th Zionist Congress in Zurich and the enlargement of the Jewish Agency, which the non-Zionist groups are entering. The latest phase of Jewish policy has, it seems, hastened the outbreak of the recent events in Jerusalem."
In the Christian-Democratic "Polonia" we read:
"The struggle that has begun in Palestine is a prelude to further terrible events for the Zionists. The Jewish dreams of building a land of their own are nothing more than an unattainable illusion; because of her own interests and in order to safeguard the route to West India [sic; presumably India], England must pay more regard to the sentiments of the Arabs than to the Jewish demands. Ironic sounds the fact that the Palestine events took place during the rule of the socialist government headed by MacDonald. MacDonald did after all promise that his government renounces every imperialist policy, and in this spirit negotiations are already being conducted on an agreement with Egypt.
The Arab-Jewish conflict therefore compromises MacDonald's policy. The near[?] future will show whether England will keep her promise of a Jewish national home in Palestine or not."
The socialist "Głos Zagłębia" gave a small notice about the bloody events. The notice is distinguished — on the model of the Warsaw "Robotnik" — by great "love" for the Zionist bourgeois...
S. Shtroykh.
A Mother's Heart

[Literature — humorous story.]
By Yosef Marshelik
Mrs. Pitsel married off her first daughter in a jiffy, practically with a whistle. A young man came to the house for the third time and spent time with her daughter; she waited until the oaf gave the girl a kiss, and ran in with a great shout:
"Well, children, mazel tov — may it be in a lucky hour!"
At that moment she called her husband:
"Isidor, come in and wish your eldest daughter mazel tov."
Whether the young man really meant it or not — he let himself be led to the slaughter.
That very same evening he was "engaged", and a month later — a married householder.
That is how Mrs. Pitsel packed off her first son-in-law, and she thought the second would come to her just as easily.
But that, it seems, was not her destiny.
A young man came to her younger daughter — quite a fine young man — once and a second time, and spent time with the girl. Both times Mrs. Pitsel peeped through a gap in the portières, but saw nothing. Both times the young man sat at one end of the sofa, her daughter at the other end of the sofa, and they talked. They talked about books, writers, education... A whole evening they sat and talked. Mrs. Pitsel nearly [—].
To tell her daughter to "draw" the young man in, to entice[?] him, somehow did not seem proper to her. How does a mother herself speak like that to a nineteen-year-old daughter? But she could not keep silent either, and as soon as the young man left the second time she asked her daughter:
"Tell me, I beg you, how can one sit a whole evening with a person and just talk?"
"What else, then," the girl wanted to know, "does one do?"
To that Mrs. Pitsel of course knew what to answer, but she only said:
"Nothing, nothing..."
And added, as if speaking to the wall:
"Such a lump of a golem, a grown girl!"
Two days later the young man came again and again took his place at the other end of the sofa. The girl again sat opposite him, and both, as the first two times, talked. They talked about books, writers, education.
Mrs. Pitsel decided that today it must come to an end.
"Even if I knew," she said to her husband, "that I would drive him away forever, the salmon [i.e. the dolt], tonight I'm putting an end to it."
She waited until half past seven, peeped, hoped, but heard nothing at all. Finally her patience burst. She went in and said:
"Young man, I am a mother and — — —"
"And evidently a very devoted mother," the young man cut in.
She liked that at once.
"Good that you understand," she began anew, but again she did not manage to finish; the young man immediately cut in:
"A mother," he said with feeling, rising to his feet, "a mother is the best friend. Without a mother a person is no person... I know it... I grew up a complete orphan among strangers... More than once my heart longed, yearned, pined to fainting for the soft, tender caress of a mother's trembling hand; more than once in the stillness of the night, still as a child, I lay with open eyes and thought —"
Mrs. Pitsel was moved to tears and began to wipe her eyes even before she heard what the young man, as a child lying whole nights with open eyes, had thought.
"And I thought," the young man continued, "how pleasant, how good, how wonderful it is to have a mother... a mother!.. A trifle, you'd think — a mother!... The most beautiful word in our language, said the great philosopher Socrates, is 'mother'.. Ma-a— Mmmother!.."
His voice trembled now and it was evident that he was deeply moved; his two listeners were both weeping.
"Speak on.. speak as much as you like... your words are a balm for a mother's heart," Mrs. Pitsel begged him, catching the young man by the sleeve.
He obliged her.
"All the beauties, all the sweetnesses," he went on, "are hidden in this one word: 'mother'... Take the encyclopaedia.. the word 'mother' occupies 53 whole pages in it.. Everything that has ever been written about mothers is there... Then comes the word 'father', with 34 pages... But that is not yet everything one finds in the encyclopaedia.. You find there — — — — — —"
He reached into his breast pocket, pulled out a printed sheet of paper, and began to read from it:
"Where does rain come from?.. In which century did Alexander of Macedon reign? What is soda water made of? Where does—"
Suddenly he flung the sheet of paper away and said:
"But enough. As I have already explained to your daughter, the encyclopaedia is a regular school, a set of thirty volumes for — — —"
Mrs. Pitsel stood up, wanting to say something.
"I know, I know," he blocked her way, "you want to say that you can't right now, that right now you're short of money, but that's no excuse. Education comes before everything, and nobody is asking you for money; take the books, you'll pay later — when you can, and I can assure you that —" Mrs. Pitsel did not want to hear any more; she ran out.
Outside her husband, Mr. Isidor Pitsel, was waiting for her.
"Well?" he asked.
She fell upon him:
"Golem! Ninny! Idiot! Why are you silent? You're a father, after all — go and throw him out!"
Dr. A. Weissman — The Seduced Girl

[Literature — serial novel.]
Dr. A. Weissman.
(A novel of Jewish life in the Old World, based on historical facts.)
19.
In the village where Mania's parents live it is now quieter than usual. Few guests come to the white house, where the steward lives with his old-maid daughters, nieces and aunts. Everyone is somehow afraid; everyone avoids the house where a terrible drama took place, a drama that has not yet ended, and everyone was afraid that he might be mixed up in that drama, which could perhaps end very ugly for those taking part in it and for those who come to the white house. Chaim, the young man who loved Mania to death, did not sit with folded hands. From the letter of Mania's that had been handed to Dvora, Chaim learned that Mania was begging to be rescued and that she was locked up somewhere in a room, a kind of prison. Chaim was an educated young man and had many friends among Jews and among Christians, especially liberal, progressive Christians, who are no soul-snatchers and are opposed to Catholicism and its dark power. Chaim had got Mania's little letter out of Dvora, because Reb Zelig and his wife were not at home — they were searching for Mania. After consulting his friends, well-known lawyers and important politicians, on good terms with those who hold power, Chaim submitted a complaint to the government against Ludwig, the Sichojańskis [?] and the monastery, that they had abducted a Jewish child, a young girl, from her parents, and are holding her locked up in a convent against her will by force, and want to convert her and compel her to marry a man she does not want — probably for indecent purposes. He asks the government: since the girl Mania, whom the band of bandits abducted, is his, his bride [?] of long standing, that it, the government, the Polish authorities, should apply its power to free the girl from her abductors and return her to her parents and to him, her lawful bridegroom. The petition was accepted where it needed to be, and steps were taken to fulfil it as quickly as possible. Naturally this was done quickly and in secret. Secret police agents were instructed to investigate the whole story quickly and secretly, and to do what was necessary if it should turn out that the matter was true.
Rumours had been going around that the Catholic convents were carrying out various deceptions with Jewish girls. The Polish authorities placed the investigation of the matter in the hands of Captain Stanisław Branicki, a progressive policeman and a mortal enemy of the Catholic convents and the Jesuits.
When the Polish authorities set about investigating the affair of Mania, at the request of her bridegroom Chaim Braunstein of the small town of K., the Polish authorities handed the whole matter over to Captain Stanisław Branicki. He was appointed as the "head", the superior of all the secret agents who were dealing with the matter.
It did not take Branicki long to find out that the whole story about Mania was true through and through. He also soon found out that she was locked in the Catholic convent and shut up in the cellars.
Stanisław Branicki immediately sent a report to the police minister of L. that the stolen [?] Jewish girl was shut up in the convent and that the whole story given by the Jew Chaim Braunstein was true.
Stanisław Branicki soon received an order to free the imprisoned girl at any price and to arrest those guilty of the shameful affair.
Despite the fact that all these things were done quietly and in secret, rumours were nevertheless floating in the air that something was being done, something was being investigated [?].
That is why the former [?] guests avoided the house. When the regular residents there occasionally met their acquaintances and asked why they did not come, they were brushed off with the answer that they were busy and had no time.
The village feldsher [medical orderly], Ludwig's father, at once answered the steward's two aunts:
"My wife and I do not come to you because of the story of Mania's running away."
"What do you mean — what do you have to be afraid of here?"
"Afraid we are not, but still we do not want suspicion to fall on us, because we cannot yet know how this story will end."
"How can it end? She wanted to run away, so she ran away. Well, your son ran away with her; who could have refused such a great good deed as leading a lost, innocent child to baptism?"
"I am not responsible for my son. I too like to do a good deed when it is done the way it should be — quietly, calmly, so that not even a dog knows; and here half the world already knows. The Jews will keep quiet, will they, as soon as they know where she is?"
And the feldsher began to tell, with cruel relish [?], how he and others, in years gone by, had led more than one "Jewess" to baptism in the convents — and all hush-hush. Their souls have long been in the Christian paradise; and here, with Mania, there is something of a stir. It is seething in all the villages and towns, and God alone knows with what scandal this story will end.
"So what is to be done?" the aunts asked, trembling.
"There are only two ways: either she is returned to her parents in such a way that she herself suddenly turns up in the village at home, or she is taken away from the convent somewhere further off, so that no one will find out any more."
"It is easy to say — return Mania to her parents. How much fright it costs us, and how does one give up such a good deed? How can one take on oneself so great a sin, and hand such a dear, pure soul back to the demons, the Jews? And what will I be able to say to Sister 'Irena'?"
"Do as you see fit. 'Moja chata z kraja' — that is: 'my house is off to the side' — I am not getting involved."
"Why do you pretend not to know? After all, your son took the biggest part in the story."
"My son? What about my son? He is a person in his own right. I am not responsible for him. Well, what does he as a young man have to do with various girls? I believe that in the affair with Mania he was not looking for any good deeds; her conversion meant little to him. In Mania he was looking for a pretty girl and nothing more."
"Nothing more, you say — you, his own father? That is a great sin!"
"I told you, didn't I, that I will not pay for my son's sins. Everyone pays for himself."
"If that is so," the aunts thundered and crossed themselves, "if that is so, then Ludwig must not be let into a respectable house!"
"As you wish. I will be glad if you do not let him into your house any more. He is the son of a plain feldsher and has no business pushing his way up to the high windows among the lords. My grandfather [?] was a plain man, and so am I. What has my son to do with such people? I let him study in the schools, so in his own eyes he has become a regular lord."
"You speak to us with too much impudence; you are mocking our house!"

"The World Asks an Old Question"

[Essay — reflections; philosophical feuilleton.] L. Z. [Lamed Zayin].
Do you know the song?
Of all the songs I have [?] heard, it is this song that has made the deepest impression on me.
I doubt whether there is another song, in whatever language, that expresses all the helplessness, all the mysticism and all the world-sorrow that people feel, the way this old song does.
The whole song consists of six lines, three of which are only a tune, without words, yet a whole library of philosophical books could not say more than these six lines:
The world asks an old question:
Bam, tray-lay lay-lay, bam?
One answers with the old excuse:
Bam, tray-lay-lay-lay bam!
Still there remains the old question:
Bam, tray-lay-lay-lay-bam!
Who is the poet of this little song, whose tormented soul sought to express human despair almost without words?
Nobody knows. Perhaps the song never had any particular author at all, but welled up from the heart of the people. All the undefined, unclear, clouded questions of existence, of the world, of God, of human destinies sought expression. People pondered, asked, searched, and finally came to the melancholy conclusion:
Still there remains the old question:
Bam, tray-lay-lay-lay bam!
The years pass over us; without mercy time removes the individual. The older [?] one grows, the greater the sorrow grows [?], seeing how the threads of love, of blood, of friendship, which lit up the past years, snap one after another; one by one, one by one they go, until we follow them. Millions have gone before us, millions will come and go. As individuals we must all vanish. And yet, unbroken, the thread of life goes on spinning. Its beginning is somewhere in the deep, dark past, and it draws on through millions upon millions [misprinted] of forms and individuals towards something higher.
With great effort we trace our evolution out of the past, always hoping to infer from it our rising, higher development in the future. Whence? Whither? Here reason gets stuck. The broader view, the source, the goal, the purpose of it all — that is hidden from us. We have not even reached the point that could give us the hope that we shall one day be able to answer it. But we have learned to ask. Of all living creatures on earth, man is the only one born with a "Why?" on his lips. This very "why" is the source of all sciences and of all faiths. The question is there. But when it comes to giving an answer —
Still there remains the old question:
Bam, tray-lay-lay-lay-bam!
Our grandfathers and great-grandfathers tried to answer the old question with faith; they only covered it up, but did not answer it. Then we came, the people of today's world, and dismissed them. Bah! We will do it better, we will do it with science. We took telescopes and looked deep into the heavens and discovered that the sky has no floor [?]. We took things and crumbled them, and ground them, and burned them, and discovered that we are unable to make nothing out of something, just as we are unable to make something out of nothing. And we investigated the force that animates everything, right up to the point from which all that exists emerges. Yet when it comes to the essential point, when we want to know something of the plan, of the goal, of the "why" and the "wherefore" —
Still there remains the old question:
Bam, tray-lay lay-lay-bam!
True, in seeking the primal source and searching for a plan, science has discovered tremendously interesting things. It has drawn up a list of the wonders of the world around us, has examined other worlds beyond our world and then, turning to itself, it examines its own intellect, which comprehends all these things. Something new it has not created; it only discovers the things that have always been. With effort, slowly, it lifts bit by bit the veil from the wondrous order. It uncovers the marvellous bonds between matter and force. It finds that there is a unity in all the things it sees and feels and grasps. The same material and the same force reveal themselves in all kinds of forms. One thing is chained to the other, one thing feeds [?] the other, and the motion goes on without a beginning and therefore also without an end.
And then, when science has over thousands of years fathomed all this —
The world asks an old question:
Bam, tray-lay-lay-lay bam?
Science answers that it does not know.
One cannot reproach science for not knowing what it cannot know. Science is merely a method of looking at things as they are, and not as one persuades oneself they ought to be. It does not settle for simplifications and does not accept things it cannot prove.
But the "old question" concerns precisely the things that cannot be proved, and yet these things surround us on all sides. The spark that is called life science has not explained. And not only in the higher creatures, but not even in a small grain.
Take, for example, a grain of wheat. You put it into the earth, it rots, sends out roots from itself into the earth, and green leaves sprout up out of the earth, towards the sun, and then it brings forth an ear with many other grains of wheat, just like the buried grain was.
The man of science can take a grain of wheat, grind it, and boil it, and analyse it, until he knows exactly the various materials of which it consists. Then the chemist can come, put the materials together and artfully produce a grain of wheat that would be in every respect like the grain that brought forth the ear. When the chemist buries his grain in the earth, it too will rot like the first grain, but it will not send out any roots into the earth, nor any ear up towards the sun. Why? The chemist answers that one component is missing; the spark of life is missing. That he did not put into his grain.
And what exactly is this spark of life? What does it consist of? Where does it come from?
The chemist answers that he does not know.
Still there remains the old question:
Bam, tray-lay-lay-lay, bam!
From our grandfathers and great-grandfathers we heard that there is in man a soul, and that it comes from lofty places, and comes pure, whole, and strives towards its source, from which it was taken, only that it is often corrupted by the lusts of the body, of matter.
We, the people of today's world, have dismissed this. Bah: a soul — who has ever seen a soul? With science we search through every corner of the human body and find no sign of a soul.
But the scientists who seek to discover the origin of man and his development from a lower stage to a higher one — the scholars who call themselves anthropologists and ethnologists — find that wherever there is a race of people, or a group of people, they always reveal certain strivings, create certain principles and customs, which cannot always be explained by the material appetites of the body. There is always a striving towards godliness, towards goodness, towards refinement and towards beauty. Not among all races is this expressed in the same way, but the inclination [?] is there among all. One calls it conscience; or one calls it the aesthetic sense, or one calls it religion. It makes no difference by what name one designates it, but the thing itself is there.
Our grandfathers call it the soul. So science cannot quarrel with our grandfathers about it; on the contrary, it confirms the grandfathers' assertion: mankind strives only higher and higher, and becomes ever better, wiser, more experienced and nobler.
But up to where? And to what end? What is the purpose of all these things?
One asks, and asks the "old question," and seeks to answer it, but — oh, woe is me!
Still there remains the old question:
Bam, tray-lay-lay-lay, bam!
Representatives of the whole world pay honour to a Jewish industrialist

[Economy and industry — Germany; report from the Leipzig fair.]
(Letter from the Leipzig fair).
By Z. Haber.
(Special for the "Zaglembier Tsaytung").
At the Leipzig fair, which opened on 25 August, representatives of states and of economic enterprises from the whole world gathered in order to pay honour to the Jewish industrialist Philipp Rosenthal, who is now celebrating fifty years since he founded his factory.
There are only very few enterprises in the world that have so famous a name as Philipp Rosenthal's porcelain factory. There is not a single country in the four corners of the earth that does not carry Rosenthal porcelain. There is not a single magnate in the world, not a single reigning monarch, who does not take great pride in owning Rosenthal porcelain. The great ships from every corner of the world write in their prospectuses that meals aboard are served on Rosenthal porcelain. Dr. Eckener related that in the last storm over the ocean a hundred Rosenthal plates were broken on the Zeppelin.
In a word: Rosenthal porcelain means, all over the world, comfort, wealth, luxury and fine taste.
Who is Rosenthal?
The answer was given by the great number of prominent personalities from the whole world who gathered at the present Leipzig fair, of which Rosenthal is vice-president, in order to pay him honour; this was told to us in their speeches by the famous leaders of the world economy, this is told to us by the beautiful book that has just appeared about "Rosenthal and his work", and about this Rosenthal talked at length with your correspondent, the writer of these lines.
Philipp Rosenthal was born 74 years ago in a small German town, in Werl. His parents were small dealers in glass and porcelain, respectable householders, but not rich. At 17 Rosenthal went to America against his parents' will, and there he suffered very hard. He literally served at every menial job there: he was an errand boy, a labourer's helper, ran the lift in a hotel, rode from village to village with the post, until he worked his way up to a post as salesman in a small department store. There they soon recognised his clever business head and handed him the management of the porcelain department.
Rosenthal, however, held this post only for a short time. He saved up a few dollars and travelled to visit his parents, who would not let him go back to America any more.
So Rosenthal began to manufacture on his own. His work consisted in buying white porcelain and painting it with various decorations. Here his tremendous artistic sense showed itself, which made him famous all over the world. He began with a single worker, and after a year he already employed sixty workers, who worked day and night to keep up with the orders.
Some years later he began to make porcelain himself, after his own models. He not only personally influenced the models of the greatest artists who worked for him, but also travelled himself from country to country on all five continents, chose merchants with a good artistic sense and entrusted them with the sale of his porcelain — which he knew how to adapt to the taste of each country.
Little by little he got so far that today there is hardly a city in the world where there are not his own branches, or at least where large firms do not sell Rosenthal porcelain.
At the same time one must not forget that almost all over the world there are state porcelain factories, which were bound up [?] not only with a great old tradition but also with state capital, against which Rosenthal had to wage a struggle.
Nevertheless he succeeded in competing with these very state porcelain factories and in establishing himself to such a degree that today he has the largest porcelain factory in the whole world and is reckoned, after Krupp, the greatest industrialist in Germany.
And at the present Leipzig fair state representatives and representatives of all the largest economic enterprises of the whole world paid honour to the greatest economic genius of the 20th century, the Jewish industrialist Philipp Rosenthal.

Greater Poland, Lesser Poland and Upper Silesia

[History — Poland and Silesia.] (A bit of historical research.)
(Specially for the "Zaglembier Tsaytung")
Where does it come from that the Poznań region is called Greater Poland, while Galicia — Lesser Poland?
The newest Polish historical research explains it aptly.
As is known, the Poznań region (the basin of the Warta river) was the cradle of the Polish state. The name of the state, Polska, comes from the fact that the said region has numerous fields (pola). "Polska" (Poland) meant, until the 13th century, only the Poznań region. The population there was called: Polanians.
The Poles a thousand years ago — like all other peoples — consisted of separate tribes, which only with time, thanks to being neighbours, became united into one great Polish people. The strongest of the tribes was the said tribe of the Polanians (today called "Poznańczycy"). It subdued the other tribes, such as the Vistulans, i.e. the inhabitants of Kraków and its surroundings, the Ślązacy (in the old historical documents: Ślężanie), the Mazovians (the inhabitants of the Warsaw area), the Kujavians [?], the Sieradzians and others.
The residence of the first Polish kings was Gniezno (Gniezna). In the year 1039 the Czechs invaded Poland and occupied Poznań and Silesia. Casimir the Restorer moved the residence to Kraków, where it remained until the end of the 16th century.
On the old maps of Poland the inscriptions were in Latin. At the place [?] that marked the Poznań region stood Polonia Maior, i.e. the older Poland, while at Galicia there was the inscription Polonia Minor, i.e. the younger Poland. The words "maior" and "minor" have several meanings in Latin: the first — older (a majorat, for example, means an inheritance that passes to the eldest son); it also means greater, a greater one. "Minor" means younger and smaller. More often "maior" means greater, "minor" — smaller. From this it came about that it was rendered into Polish incorrectly as: the greater Poland (Poznań) and the smaller Poland (Galicia); later this became Greater Poland and Lesser Poland.
The name "Galicia" we find already in medieval documents. To understand it we shall briefly relate a little Ruthenian-Russian-Polish history. So:
In the 9th, 10th and 11th centuries the state that stretched from Moscow in the north to Kyiv in the south was called "Rus". It consisted of very many small states, or better said principalities, such as: Moscow, Suzdal (printed "Sodzal"), Vladimir, Kyiv, Lutsk and others. The princes "tested their strength" from time to time. When in the 12th century one of the princes ordered Kyiv destroyed and, assuming the title of Grand Prince, transferred it to his residence Moscow, "Rus" finally split into 2 entirely separate worlds with opposed cultures: north-eastern Rus, later called "Rossiya" (Russia), out of which there developed [?] the later mighty Muscovite state, which for hundreds of years subjugated [?] the neighbouring states in western-southern Rus (today called Ukraine). The latter later, together with Lithuania, concluded a union with Poland.
One of the princes of the latter state, even before the said partition, tore away from Poland the region of Lemberg, Przemyśl, Czerwień and others, the so-called Czerwień region, in Polish Ziemia Czerwieńska, and founded there a separate principality, which for several hundred years — with small exceptions — was under the despotic rule of Ruthenian princes. From the residence Halicz (a small town not far from Stanisławów) the whole principality was called Halichia. Since in the Ruthenian as in the Russian alphabet the consonants (spółgłoski) "g" and "h" have the same sign, it was wrongly read "Galicia". Later the name passed also to the regions west of eastern Galicia.
When Casimir the Great reconquered the region for Poland in the year 1340, it was called Eastern Lesser Poland.
After the third partition of Poland in the year 1795 the Imperial and Royal Austrian government, not wishing to recall the Polish historical name Lesser Poland, preferred to revive the medieval name Galicia.
Silesia.
The main river of Silesia, the Oder (Odra), flows out of the Sudetes (the mountains that separate Upper Silesia from Bohemia), runs through all of Silesia and falls near Stettin (Szczecin) into the Baltic Sea. The direction of the stream is thus from south to north. The part of Silesia that lies along the upper course of the river (not far from the source), or southern Silesia, is therefore called — Upper Silesia, whereas the part lying along the lower course (nearer to the sea), i.e. the Breslau region, is called — Lower Silesia.
As regards state affiliation, all of Silesia, Cieszyn Silesia too, belonged to Poland from the beginning of the Polish state. When King Bolesław Krzywousty (Wrymouth) before his death divided the Polish lands among his sons, he assigned Silesia to the eldest son, Władysław II. The latter, wishing to have power over all of Poland, waged war with his younger brothers, by whom he was then driven out of the country. The intervention of the German emperor had so much effect that Władysław's children afterwards got Silesia back. And from then on the Silesian Piasts had sympathies for Germany.
At the end of the 13th century, when Poland was split into separate "dzielnice" [provincial duchies], there were also 12 separate principalities in Silesia. Some of the Silesian princes declared themselves "lennicy" [vassals] of the Czech king, some on the other hand — of the German emperor. Casimir the Great strove to unify the Polish state; since he saw that Poland would have no joy any more from the Silesian Piasts, he thought it over and in the Visegrád treaty, year 1335, renounced all of Silesia in favour of the Czech king John (the son of the German emperor Henry VI [sic] of Luxembourg).
Among the said Silesian principalities, which fell away for several hundred years, were also the following: Oświęcim, Zator (Muterer [?]) and... Siewierz (the historians describe: Siewierz on the Przemsza, not far from Olkusz, so indeed our Siewierz, which lies several kilometres north of Będzin). The last 3 principalities became Polish provinces again in the 15th century: thus the Bishop of Kraków, Zbigniew Oleśnicki, bought the Siewierz principality for his "biskupstwo" [bishopric]. Later King Casimir Jagiellon bought the Oświęcim principality, and his son John Olbracht (printed "Abracht") — the Zator principality. The remaining Silesian principalities, on the other hand, stayed with Bohemia until the year 1620. In that year the Czechs — as is known — suffered a great defeat from Emperor Ferdinand's army and fell for 3 hundred years under the rule of the great Habsburg monarchy; all of Silesia thereby becomes an Austrian province.
When Prussia turns from an electorate (elektorstwo, i.e. a principality that takes part in electing the "Roman Emperor of the German people" — so all the monarchs of the Austrian monarchy were called) into a separate kingdom in the year 1701, and the disciplined, well-organised Brandenburg-Prussian army makes successive conquests of foreign lands, it finally annexed all of Silesia in the year 1790 [sic]. Maria Theresa, the Austrian queen, declares war on it. Frederick the Great, the Prussian king, wins great victories, so that in the Peace of Breslau he receives all of Silesia. Maria Theresa forms a coalition of states against Prussia and starts the Seven Years' War (1756—63). Prussia wins again, the "Habsburg" peace [sic; i.e. Hubertusburg] recognises anew Silesia's belonging to Prussia, and so Prussia (today called: Germany) holds it in its possession until the year 1919, when Poland reminded the world of its historical rights to Silesia.
G—t.
What's New in Zagłębie? — Będzin

[Będzin — trade; the Old Market.]
[Friday, 1 Elul 5689 — Piątek 6 września 1929 (Friday, 6 September 1929).]
Będzin
More on the Terrible Fate of the Traders in the Old Market.
As we have already written, last week a delegation went to the Kielce voivodeship office, where they interceded for the deadline for liquidating the trade in the Old Market to be extended.
The delegation returned home with the promise that the voivode would come to an understanding with the local magistrate (town council) on the question.
Only on Saturday morning did the delegates learn that the starosta (district head) had received an order[?] that the trade in the Old Market be liquidated on the first of this month.
On receiving the news, the councillors (ratmani) Lewin and Gitler interceded with the mayor (president) to hold back the decree. The mayor declared that extending the deadline is not within his competence; he is only the one who must carry out the regulations of the voivode, who, relying on the circular (okólnik) of Minister Składkowski, issued on 28 październik [October], number 174, [ordered] that by 1 wrzesień [September] 1929 all markets must be cleared of public trade.
Because the site at the market halls does not yet meet the necessary arrangements, the deadline has been extended by 1 month, i.e. if by 1 październik [October] the trading places on Modrzejowska Street are ready, the Old Market will be cleared of the market stalls.
This small reprieve, however, applies only to the dealers in manufactured textiles, haberdashery, shoes, etc. The worst fate falls on those who trade in fruit and other foodstuffs. For them the extension does not apply, and the magistrate no longer wants to lease their stalls.
On this matter the chairman of the town council, Mr. Fürstenberg, together with Councillor Mr. Lewin, interceded with the mayor several times in the course of Tuesday[?], to obtain that the extension should apply to this sort of trader as well — but without success, and at any hour they are liable to be chased off by the police, because, as we are assured, the starosta has sent such an order to the police.
On Wednesday the writer of these lines conferred with the mayor about the fate of the poor fruit dealers and asked that they should not be made an exception in this respect.
The mayor told us that he is not able to ease the matter, and only the voivodeship can grant an extension. The main blame — says the mayor — lies with the representatives of the merchants' and artisans' organisations, who made light of the matter and did not do the least thing to have the regulation annulled for a certain time.
At the end of the conversation the mayor told us that the magistrate can intercede for the deadline to be extended only if all the traders in the market come forward with a memorandum stating that they are ready to carry out the order, but only once all the necessary arrangements are ready at the new trading place.
But at a time when work is being done from various sides against the cause, the magistrate can do nothing to help, and everything depends on the police.
For lack of premises a large number of Jewish children are being pushed out of the schools.

As we have already written, certain changes have come about in the current school year. In school no. 2, headed by Mr. Rapaport, only boys study, and in school number 4, headed by Mesdames Szancer and P. Wira [?], only girls study. The boys are taught by male teachers and the girls — by female teachers.
In the 3 "powszechne" [state elementary] schools about 2 thousand children are enrolled, among them some 800 boys and 12 hundred girls; but because the school premises available until now are not suited to such a number, the inspector gave the "good advice" that the girl pupils of the 6th grade [oddział] should be sent away from the school and should content themselves with the evening courses.
A fire caused by lightning.

On Friday night, during a rainstorm, lightning struck Birsztajn's [?] smelting works. The lightning started a big fire, but thanks to the great rescue effort only the roof burned down.
The same lightning had earlier struck the flat of Szlama Szarf, where only the installation and the telephone wire were damaged.
Resigns as a member of the kehilla council.

The member of the kehilla council Mr. Chaim Szajn has submitted, through the gmina [the Jewish community], a request to the starosta [district head] that he accept his resignation as parnas [community councillor].
The reason for the resignation is that the administration consists of people who are not fit for it, and therefore they cannot properly fulfil the community's functions.
A Christian donates 5 zł for the victims in the Land of Israel.

The Christian Mieczysław Pająk of Będzin came into our editorial office and handed us 5 zł for the victims in the Land of Israel. For the same purpose the Christian challenges Mr. Burstein, Kołłątaja 27 [to donate as well].
In honour of the start of the new school year.

On Tuesday, the day the new school year began, hundreds of children from the powszechne [state elementary] schools and the secondary schools gathered in the synagogue to take part in a divine service in honour of the day.
Owing to the absence of Cantor Wszupowicz [?] the ceremony was conducted by Mr. Danciger, and instead of saying a few words to the children about the bloody massacres in the Land of Israel and about the present Jewish mourning, the school orchestra played several numbers...
Enlarging the cemetery.
Next Thursday, on the proposal of the local moreh-tsedek [rabbinical judges], the ceremony of enlarging the cemetery with the plot of land that was bought several years ago will take place.
The Rabbi's (may he live long) leave extended.

The local rabbi applied to the kehilla heads with a request that his leave be extended by another month.
Needless to say, the request was granted.
Wronged merchants must register.

We have been asked by the Merchants' Association to announce that the merchants who were badly wronged in the assessment of turnover for the year 1928 must report from Sunday the 8th to the 12th of this month at the secretariat of the Merchants' Association in order to register.
A cart wheel broken — but a child saved from certain death

[Będzin — road accident.] Five-year-old Yosele Mandelbaum wanted to run across Saniczewska [?] Street. At that moment a car came speeding along, and the child found himself in great danger. The driver, seeing the danger, hastily swerved the car to the side and drove up onto a cart. The result is that a wheel of the cart was broken, but the child was saved.
Meeting of “Hakoach”

[Będzin — sport; Hakoach.] Because of the events in Palestine (Eretz Israel), the general meeting of “Hakoach” [the sports club] has been postponed to today, Friday, at 8 in the evening. On the agenda: election of a board and other important items.
A desecration of God's name by a Czeladź landlord

[Czeladź — community; prayer houses.] In the house of H. Holzdorf the Radomsko (Radomsker Hasidim's) shtibl has been located for several years. The landlord, however, had a mind to evict the shtibl. To that end he took out the Torah scrolls, put them into the beys-medresh (study house) and locked the room.
Those concerned had no other recourse than to turn for help to the police, which ordered that everything be put back in order.
“Gordonia's” response to the events in Palestine

[Zionism — youth movements; Gordonia.] In connection with the events in Palestine, the Zionist pioneering youth organisation “Gordonia” is convening, this Sabbath and Sunday, a conference in Łódź devoted to the newly created situation in Palestine and to the tasks of the Zionist youth at the present moment for Zionism and for the Jewish community (Yishuv) in Eretz Israel.
To the conference, which will serve as a great Zionist manifestation and will proclaim a pioneering aliyah (immigration) to Palestine, the following were delegated by the Zagłębie “Gordonia” branches: M. Haspel, D. Liwer, D. Sapirsztejn (Będzin), H. Mękarski [?], Y. Szpring [?] (Sosnowiec) and Magerkiewicz (Dąbrowa).
Sosnowiec — A non-partisan relief committee formed for the victims in Palestine; collection campaign already under way

[Sosnowiec — community; relief for the victims of the 1929 riots.] (Section heading: Sosnowiec.)
On the initiative of the presidium of the kehilla board and council, a meeting was called in the gmina (municipal hall) to found a committee to carry out the relief campaign for the victims in Eretz Israel.
80 persons were invited to this important meeting. But no more than 32 came.
A sharp discussion developed over the question of the “egg not yet laid” [i.e. money not yet collected] — where the money collected should be sent.
On this question 2 proposals were put forward: 1) that the money be sent directly to the Va'ad Leumi, and 2) to the Central Committee at the Warsaw Jewish kehilla. The second proposal obtained a majority, and the funds collected will be sent through the local Jewish kehilla to the Central Committee (C.K.) in Warsaw.
The committee, which the kehilla representatives join automatically, has also been joined by: Markus Hamburger, Naftali Bachmajer, Levi Jungster, Yisroel Mikhl Berkowicz, Menachem Szereszewski, Borukh Secemski [?], Julian Ajbeszyc, Yosef Goldberg and Motl Hachman.
The collection campaign has already begun, and it goes without saying that it will meet with the greatest success.
A young Jewish man drowned

[Sosnowiec — drowning.] Last Sabbath afternoon, 20-year-old Itshe (Icek) Aszpitz [went] to bathe in the Brynica on the way to Szopienice. Some young Christian acquaintances were also bathing in the water, to whom the drowned Aszpitz wanted to show that he was a good swimmer. But unfortunately, as soon as he went into the water he went down into a deep spot and drowned.
A few hours later the dead body was taken out and brought to his parents.
Hooligan attack on a Jew

[Sosnowiec — antisemitism; violence.] On Monday evening Mr. Yitskhok Dafner was attacked on Targowa Street by several hooligans, who beat Dafner and wounded him.
—o—
“Malbish Arumim” prepares for a winter campaign
[Sosnowiec — charity.] The board of “Malbish Arumim” [society for clothing the poor] has already undertaken a campaign to clothe a large number of children for the winter. For this purpose the institution has already ordered 200 pairs of shoes.
On importing foreign goods

[Sosnowiec — trade; chamber of commerce.] We are asked by the local chamber of commerce to announce that the Minister of Commerce has changed part of the decisions of the Central Import Commission and has introduced one representative of the Sosnowiec chamber of commerce.
In this connection, firms belonging to the Kielce voivodeship that wish to import prohibited goods from abroad this quarter must immediately submit the said applications to the local chamber of commerce.
Together with the required documents, 10 zł. must be enclosed as a “municipal” fee.
—o—
An election committee in the dock
[Czeladź — elections; court.] During the election campaign for the town council elections in Czeladź, the election committee of a workers' list issued an election appeal in which a candidate of the “BPIBE” [?; probably BBWR, the pro-government Non-Partisan Bloc] list was insulted.
The committee accused the candidate of having been a deserter at the time of the Bolshevik invasion of Poland.
Last Monday the election committee, 8 persons in number, sat in the dock at the local district court.
Owing to the absence of an important witness, the trial was postponed to another date.
—o—
When it's hot you drink, and when you drink you get drunk
[Sosnowiec — drunkenness; police; short sketch.] On Wednesday a scene played out on Modrzejowska Street among several drunks who were carrying on a lively conversation among themselves. The dispute was a very “hot” one, and from words they moved on to deeds.
The scene ended with the drunks lying beaten to pulp in the street like carcasses, and the police had a hard task taking the “in-laws” off to the police station.
Modrzejów — A Terrible Accident

[Modrzejów — Accident.]
Six pupils of the gymnasium set out on an excursion to Tychy. The car in which they were travelling ran up onto a tree and overturned. The result was that 2 pupils were killed and the rest were seriously injured.
Correction

[Correction.]
Mr. Meir Weinstock asks us to correct the report that his shop was open during the protest demonstration against the events in the Land of Israel; it was not reported correctly.
— Mr. Manela asks us to correct [the report]: when he was asked to close his shop, he did not grasp the situation for a moment, but immediately afterwards he closed the shop.

Relief obtained for the fruit and vegetable traders

[Będzin — trade; the Old Market.]
As is known, the voivodeship granted an extension (prolongation) to the traders in the Old Market of Będzin, with the exception of the fruit and vegetable traders, who had to leave the Old Market at once, and this threatened them with ruin.
In this connection Mr. Fürstenberg travelled specially to the voivodeship office, where he finally obtained that the extension should apply also to the fruit and vegetable traders.
—o—
Będzin kehilla assigns 2,000 zł. for Eretz Israel.
At Wednesday's meeting of the Będzin kehilla board the proposal of the president[?], Mr. Prajwer[?], was adopted to assign 2 000 zł. for the benefit of the sufferers in Eretz Israel. The sum is being sent directly to Eretz Israel.
At the meeting the following synagogue committee was also elected: G. Rechnik, B. Pelk, A. Liwer, Sh. Szlesner, L. Bożykowski and Y. Sztajcer.
—o—
Three suicides in one day.
In the course of yesterday three young people committed suicide, ending their lives.
The worker Szyrla of Sosnowiec had been ill with tuberculosis for a long time. Seeing no improvement, he threw himself under the tram near the power station[?] in Małobądz. The wheels cut off his feet and inflicted severe wounds on his body.
— In the Sosnowiec jail a drunkard was locked up, and there he hanged himself.
— In Zagórze the 26-year-old Chana Trajman committed suicide by drinking 2 small glasses of vinegar essence.
—o—
A "tactful" answer..
Yesterday the "Agudah" activists R' Avraham Liwer and R' Moshe Eliezer Altman called on R' Mendel Damb in Będzin, asking him to contribute for the sufferers in Eretz Israel.
Because the collectors were furnished with a stamp of the "United Relief Committee", Mr. Damb refused to give them anything for this purpose, giving as his reason that apart from the "Agudah" not a single other trend is represented on the committee.

Będzin Has Responded

[Będzin — the 1929 riots in Palestine; relief campaign. Article.]
Będzin has responded. A commission has been formed to help the victims in the Land of Israel.
It responded a little late; decent towns have already collected large sums and have already sent them to the Land of Israel. In such a case, in a time of need, quick help is double help. But better late than never. Therefore one may expect that the help will be great, that the public will give with a full hand — for in this misfortune there is after all a piece of luck: that now too, as in moments of misfortune and terror, it is a matter of Klal Yisrael, the whole Jewish people. It is not the affair of any party but of the entire community; the whole Jewish Yishuv in the Land of Israel has suffered; the enemy made no distinction between the old and the new Yishuv; he dared to strike Jerusalem as well as the colonies; he attacked the yeshiva students as well as the halutzim (pioneers); against all and everything that bears the name Jew he raised his hand — and therefore we too cannot and must not make any distinction: we must give our help to all those who suffered as Jews.
Help must be given in need; a brotherly hand must be stretched out — bread to the hungry, a garment to the naked, and not to disown our own flesh and blood. That applies only to the help in the critical hour, in the first days, when all doors are shut, all roads are blocked, when "none went out and none came in", when perhaps even for money one cannot get anything to buy on the spot and bread has to be brought from afar, from abroad.
But by giving bread to the hungry and a garment to the naked one has not done one's duty. The damage the enemy caused must be repaired; the ruins must be rebuilt. Twelve colonies have been destroyed; how great the destruction in the towns is, is not yet known, and for the time being it cannot be assessed. "After a fire one becomes rich," says the folk saying, because only then does one see how much one possessed and how much one has lost. In ordinary times one does not know how to value and appreciate what one has. The same holds for the community. In normal times one does not know how to value and appreciate what a Jewish Yishuv, a Jewish colony, a Jewish kvutza means. Only after the fire did one see how much one possessed and how much one had lost — and the Jewish heart trembled.
I cannot forget the words I heard in those days, when the terrible tidings came from the Land of Israel, from a woman: passing by in the street, I saw her standing and telling what she had heard as "butcher-shop news"[?], and she burst out: "I tell you, God forbid, the end has come, the Jews are perishing!"
That is how the simple Jew reacted to the events: the Jews, God forbid, are perishing. It is possible and even probable that all year round this woman takes no interest at all in the Land of Israel and is even annoyed when someone talks about it — but in a moment of misfortune she felt her heart torn, that the Jews, God forbid, are perishing. The woman certainly did not know that she was repeating the words of the lamenting prophet, who cried out at a similar moment: "Wilt thou make a full end of the remnant of Israel?" — do you wish to destroy the remnant of your people Israel!
The Jews, God forbid, are not perishing. On the contrary, precisely at the moment of danger they have shown great vitality, and this energy and strength are evident throughout the whole Jewish people. Feverish activity is under way in the Jewish camp; everyone is doing what they can and more than they can. Help is rushing in from all sides. We may hope that Zagłębie too will do what it can and more than it can. Będzin has responded, and it will surely not shame its name and its standing in the Jewish world as the great Jewish town, the old "city and mother in Israel", the fourth[?] kehilla in Congress Poland.
Sh. Y. S.

The 2nd Annual Jewish Tennis Championship of Poland

[Sport — tennis; Tarnów.]
At the end of September the second annual Jewish tennis championship of Poland will take place on the tennis court of the Jewish sports association "Shimshon" in Tarnów. The event enjoys special sympathy among the members of the Jewish tennis clubs in Poland, as it gives everyone the opportunity to take part in the championship contest. The world federation of Jewish sports clubs "Maccabi", under whose patronage the championship contests are organised, last year founded a silver challenge cup for the club that wins the greatest number of points; last year the cup was won by the Jewish sports club "Shimshon" in Tarnów, which will defend it this year in the championship contests.
Interest in the event is very great; clubs from the most important places in Poland have already registered, among them also some of the most outstanding tennis players in the country, so that the level of the players will be very high and it will be one of the most important events in the Jewish sporting life of Poland.
The organisers of the tournament are making every effort for the event to turn out as impressive as possible. Technically the tournament has the best organisation: megaphones will be set up on the court, through which the public will be informed immediately of the course of play and the result; there will be a special stand for the press of the city as well as of all Poland, which is to announce its participation in the tournament. The organisers are also providing free lodgings for participants who wish to take advantage of them, in order thereby to secure the largest participation of Jewish tennis players in the tournament.
In a word, this year's championship will be an event in Jewish tennis in Poland and will faithfully reflect the state of this branch of sport in the Jewish sporting community of the whole country.
Myszków.

[Myszków — the events in Palestine; memorial and relief collection.]
In connection with the events in the Land of Israel, protest meetings were held here in Myszków, as well as a relief campaign, in the following order: in the craftsmen's school a memorial (hazkarah) was held for the fallen martyrs; Mr. Leibish Szojmer gave a speech in which he honoured the memory of the martyrs and protested against the English officials in the Land of Israel who with their policy brought about the sad events. The speaker then called on all those present to take part in the campaign for the victims.
A committee was founded at once, comprising: Yehuda Strachlitz, Chaim Baum, Reuven Diament, Leibish Szojmer, Bunem Epsztein, Fishel Winter, Avraham Turner, Yosl Majtlis, B. Turner and A. Szywek. Secretary: H. Tatarka.
Last Sabbath, by agreement between the committee and the local religious judge (moreh tzedek) Rabbi Yosef Epsztein, no prayers were held in any minyan, and all the Jews of Myszków gathered in the great beit midrash, where the moreh tzedek (may he live long) delivered an ardent sermon, lamented the death of the fallen martyrs and called on the public to donate for the Jewish victims in Palestine. During the moreh tzedek's speech many people wept; afterwards the cantor recited El Male Rachamim.
The next day the committee held a collection, which went very well; a sum of 800 zł was collected, which was immediately sent to the Central Relief Committee in Warsaw.
It is worth noting that all the Jews of Myszków came, except a few "Agudahniks", who found it fitting to use the occasion and demonstratively did not come to the prayers. This insolence aroused great bitterness and agitation among all the Jews assembled in the beit midrash.
L. Sh.
