[Sport — Zagłębie; football.]
"Samson" (Modrzejów) — "09" Mysłowice 2:3 (1:2).
In connection with the 20th[?] jubilee celebrations of "09" Mysłowice, various sporting events took place. Among others there was also a match with "Samson" for a diploma, which "Samson" indeed won. At a very fast tempo, only in the 17th minute does "Samson" (Zajdler) score the first goal. "09" wants to equalise but only succeeds in the 23rd minute. Shortly before the end "Samson" scores the second goal through Frischer.
In the second half "09" equalises. "Samson" does not lag behind and in the 20th minute scores the decisive goal through Szlezer, and the result stays 2—3 in favour of "Samson". Bendzinski and Hapciim[?] stood out in particular. Referee Hetka[?] weak.
"Ż.K.S." (Czeladź) — "Aryeh" 0:5.
"Aryeh" suffered a very heavy defeat in its first appearance for the Class B championship title against the "Ż.K.S." of Czeladź. The large score alone shows that the forces were not equal. "Ż.K.S." surpasses its opponent both physically and technically by a whole class. Only in the 18th minute does the referee award an 11-metre kick against "Aryeh", and Zbyszek converts it into a goal. "Aryeh" goes on playing without organisation, and in the 32nd minute an own goal falls against "Aryeh". A few minutes later the centre forward shoots the 3rd goal. The first-half result stays 0—3 in favour of Ż.K.S.
In the second half the "Aryeh" attack plays a little more, but without calculation; this is exploited by the opponent, which already completely dominates the field, and Zbyszek scores 2 more goals.

To the Będzin match-goers!
It must be stressed here that what has been happening lately on the sports ground of Będzin "Hakoach" brings no particular honour to football in general and to Jewish sport in particular. I do not want to touch here on the brutal play we have lately noticed among the Hakoach men, especially against Jewish teams — the players are not to blame; the whole blame lies with the Podokręg [sub-district football association] and with the match-goers. The Podokręg is to blame in that for "Hakoach" matches against a Jewish team it appoints a referee who has not the slightest notion of the rules of sport, and therefore the sports ground is turned into a battlefield. But the chief culprit is the Będzin public with its reactions to the referee's decisions. The public has under no circumstances the right to react to any decision whatsoever of the referee. Only the captain of one team or the other has the right to react.
The public must take account of its reactions, for if there is no end to it, one may expect various unpleasant surprises...
I therefore appeal, in the name of the honour of Jewish sport, to the esteemed match-goers: keep calm and do not hinder with your heckling the referee in fulfilling his duty and the players — in playing.
A. Wrocławski.
Self-Interest in the Guise of Communal Concern

[Będzin — kehilla; polemic with the Agudah news-sheet.]
(One must know how to veil the lie. — Jews who cannot grasp this.)
A few weeks ago, when the Agudah parnassim in Będzin saw that this was a golden opportunity "to save Judaism" and to snatch a fat morsel — to obtain a president of their own for the Jewish kehilla board — they stopped at nothing; they did everything in the world to make the little deal succeed. And after that our Agudah politicians had it in mind: they would [?] show everyone the fig, they would secure their position, and then they would manage to carry everything through just as they wished and just as they needed.
True, "garangim" [?] they are not, these political "kierowniks" [leaders], and they did it in great secrecy, hush-hush, so that God forbid no one should find out about it; even the rabbi, who is a guest in town, was summoned in the deepest secrecy from Otwock, in order to have the required number of votes. The thing was thus prepared in advance, the plan calculated, and the itinerary succeeded systematically and perfectly.
And then, when it was already a fait accompli, when we learned whom we had got for our president, we took the floor on the question and said: true, the man is a simple householder, a serious Jew, but that is still far from giving him the right to become the president of the entire Jewish kehilla. Surely — we said then — Jewish Będzin cannot be represented by a Jew who cannot utter a word of Polish and has no notion at all of Europeanism, worldliness, public life, and after all is said and done cannot even utter a word of plain Yiddish, a true mother tongue. This is, after all, a Jew who all his days never stuck his nose out of Będzin, and even here at home never involved himself in communal affairs, so that he never had anything to do with the public and never came into contact with it; and had he not been compelled from the high windows there to accept the office, he would not have dared to do so, because he does not feel himself up to it.
And discussing the question in this way we pointed out how far our kehillas are falling; we drew a parallel between the Jewish kehilla of a few years ago and today's, and we came to the conclusion that our prestige keeps falling ever lower and lower. We dwelt on the time when Dr. Weinzieher was president and did everything in the world to raise us higher and higher. Who does not remember with what self-sacrifice the man worked so that we should get a synagogue that would look decent, like other people's; and for that very synagogue he had to endure persecution — not, God forbid, from such "free elements" as the [?] doctor himself, but precisely from the Agudah parnassim, who would by no means allow us to have a synagogue in the town; and when the doctor with other "free elements" stood rock-firm that the synagogue must be completed, whatever it might cost, the "skurniks" [?] then cried out that painting every little bird costs Jewish blood.
And when they drove out the doctor, who saw that it had at last become too cramped for him there, that he would not and could not adapt himself to the pettiness and intrigues, and in his place came Mr. Fürstenberg, who also had no small merits regarding the synagogue — we saw in him then the iron hand that was so badly needed at the time. It was a pleasure to watch how quickly salaries were created in those days, which were indeed paid out first of all only to the clergy; but he too did not impress, and so one kept falling step by step, ever lower [?], until it led to the level of R' Avrahamele.
After our newspaper appeared with the above-mentioned article, the following week the Agudah sheet came out in language — may God guard and save us — such as one hardly hears, such insults and coarse words, even among the worst Jewish market-women and professional beggars.
Well, had the "writers" of that sheet been clever, they ought to have understood that it is wiser to hold one's tongue between one's teeth precisely when a not-so-pretty piece of work has been done. But they think they must always defend those who pay them their Rosh-Hodesh money — and with that they have ruined [literally: slaughtered] everything.
Their insults aroused so much indignation in the town that genuine Hasidic Jews, who know nothing of the various lies, came to us at the editorial office and cried that a newspaper which honestly and sincerely serves Jewish interests must not allow a clique of ignoramuses, who monopolize themselves as a Hasidic "łobuzeria" [rabble of hooligans], to insult with the worst abuse the finest and noblest people in the town, the philanthropists and patrons, who never refuse to support any undertaking, whether it is for the common people or for Hasidic Jews.
We answered the distinguished delegation that they should not take it to heart, and that it does not befit us at all to polemicize with sold souls who go about in the conviction that, speaking in the name of the Torah, they may commit the worst wickedness.
And indeed we did not want to polemicize with the clique of sold souls — who, when they are paid for it, will not even print a ban issued by their own rabbinate; we merely gave a short note about the intervention.
And here the "writers" rolled up their sleeves and began telling those who pay their monthly money that everything the "Zaglembier Tsaytung" writes is vanity and lies, that no Jews have any access there — and here is the proof: they cannot look at the place where a Jew has stood.
It goes without saying that these threadbare phrases go into our left sidelock [i.e. we don't care]; but by chance a letter reached us, which was printed by us last week, in which such Hasidic Jews as R' Mendel Damb, R' Wolf Werdiger, R' Tuvia Tenenbaum and others take up the defence of the honour of Dr. Weinzieher and Mr. Fürstenberg.
What will these "perfect saints" of the "Tsaytung" say to the Jews who do not know that one must hold to the lie and say that the lie is truth and justice, as long as one only says that everything is done in God's name? Or perhaps they want to keep to their rule that Jews are not Jews as soon as they will not submit to their dictatorship?
To tell the truth, conscientious people from the "Agudah" have explained to us more than once that this very sheet quite often leads them astray with its scribblings, with which they frequently do not agree; but that is no longer our affair and does not concern us at all.
With today's article we only meant to characterize in brief strokes in what manner people want to work for the common good at a time when what they have in mind is their own benefit, little earnings and little livelihoods...
That is how the "good deeds" of the uninvited parasites who forced their way in look in reality — parasites who watch for every opportunity to ride on the people's back, however ugly and abhorrent that may be.
R. Les.
A Time Will Come...

[Będzin — education; feuilleton.]
(Dedicated to the opening of Fürstenberg's gymnasium in Będzin)
By Ben Amotz.
...And the time will come when grandfather and grandson will stroll along Sobieskiego Street, and during the walk the grandfather will tell the grandson old stories about the growth and greatness of the town, how the town looked when the grandfather was at the same childhood age as the grandson.
— Do you see, my child, this edifice, the three-storey building with the wide windows and the garden around it?
— Of course I see it, grandpa, that is Fürstenberg's gymnasium, my mummy told me.
— Right, here is the Jewish gymnasium; but let us sit down on the bench and I will tell you who built this colossal building, and also what there is in it.
...It was — if I am not mistaken — in the year 1928. That same school, which was called by the distinguished name "Yavneh", was a tenant in Z—s's house on the third floor. The material situation of the school was very bad, the deficit grew, and, as today, the parents took very little interest in the state of the educational institution.
But the situation was much worse, and the worry of how to obtain a building of its own still greater, because the school inspector of the time did not want to grant the school public rights on the ground that the school was housed in alien [rented] premises.
At that time there was a Jew, a "Datsh" [a "German" Jew] — Szymon Fürstenberg was his name — a Jew who, thanks to his great energy and commercial talents, had risen to a high rank and played a great role in the industrial world.
This Fürstenberg was not like today's rich men, who merely advise that others should give; he supported all Jewish undertakings with substantial sums. Although he was far from Hasidism, he gave away tens of thousands of złoty for Agudah purposes.. But that is not what I am driving at; I want to tell you precisely how the splendid school building came into being.
It happened when the school's board of trustees found itself in a desperate situation, and in that hour of trouble this same Fürstenberg came forward and said:
— Gentlemen, I will build a building for the school!..
Naturally, the news was given various interpretations. The dreamers took the words as a deliverance. The "logical" ones, on the other hand, smiled sarcastically and thought to themselves:
— "The same promise as that when the Messiah comes, rolls will grow on the trees."
But, my child, the "dream" came true. True, it took a little while, various obstacles arose, between a "yes" and a "no" the whole building "wobbled", but the power of the human "I" won, and when the building was finished they quietly struck out the 4 letters Y—V—N—H and wrote for generations the words that you see engraved here on the tablet:
— "8-class Co-educational Gymnasium named after "Mr. and Mrs. Szymon Fürstenberg"" [Szymonostwa Fürstenbergów].
And now we will really take a walk through the gymnasium: I will show you what is there and what one man created with his own strength for you children. Yes, my child, today's children, with all the various comforts that are made for them, ought also to have a little diligence, as we had in our childhood years.
I remember when I studied in the heder, we pupils sat on the ground; the heder room, four by four [cubits], was sunk in a sea of dirt and mud; the whole week the rebbe traded at the fairs, and when Thursday came, the day of "examination", the rebbe honoured our emaciated bodies with thirty-nine lashes; and when the rebbetzin lay in childbed we pupils had to replace her in the housework.. We had to watch that the "broth" should not be spoiled [?]; and if it was, our faces were soaked with red broth [blood]..
— You see, here on the ground floor there is also a second school, a Hebrew Froebel school [kindergarten]. Once, when the school was founded, the Jewish spark glowed here more than today. Hebrew is treated like a stepchild; to fulfil a duty, the little children are fed a coffee-spoonful of Hebrew, and this "system" greatly impresses your mothers, who are enraptured by everything that is alien to Jewishness: foreign languages, foreign songs and foreign traditions..
— Just take a look how spacious and bright the lower classes are; look at the necessary comfortable hygienic facilities for the children, at the huge hall for gymnastics; and when the children finish the gymnastics lesson they refresh their little bodies under the shower and afterwards they sit down at the buffet...
— Grandpa, the whole house and all the rooms are for the school?
— Yes, my child, everything you see was made especially for the school. There are 56 rooms here — do you hear? — fifty-six rooms take up this splendid two-storey building. Believe me, Yankele, when I stand here on the first floor and look at the glass dome up high, at the [?] of the architecture and the whole brilliant appearance of the inner and outer form of the entire space, I get the urge to become a child again and run into the school...
— Grandpa, do they also learn Humash, Rashi and Gemara here?
The grandfather's face grew more serious at the child's question; it seemed that the naive words had touched the depths of his soul, and almost involuntarily a deep sigh tore itself from his breast.
— Yes, my child, among us Jews there is no balance. In every field, especially in education, there is still no force that would issue a law that the Jewish child should be brought up as a Jew and a human being.
The Jewish child is tossed between two warring camps, the extreme right and the extreme left: if the extreme-right camp prevails, the child is clamped into the narrow four cubits of halakha; and if [?] the extreme-left camp prevails, the Jewish boy is turned into a "man of the world" and a "kaddish" sayer...
— In such a healthy building, my child, Jews with healthy souls must be brought up; the Jewish spark must burn like an eternal light in our long life in exile.
The whistle of the siren broke off the grandfather's thoughts, and from the loud voices of the pupils there resounded an echo of the grandfather's words:
— A Jewish soul, a Jewish fire...

Problems of Education

[Zagłębie — health and education; serialized article, part III.] (The sad state of our hygienic education. — How should the question be solved radically?)
III.
Our first two chapters of “Problems of Education” attracted the attention of a respected Kraków doctor who has a large practice among the population of Zagłębie. The writer of these lines received a letter from the said doctor, who writes: “I read your ‘Problems of Education’, which are highly important and topical. I cannot, however, remain indifferent to the neglect of your sisters and brothers, sons and daughters.
You must absolutely devote — writes the doctor — one chapter to hygiene in your ‘Problems of Education’ column, because the apathy of your citizens towards hygiene belongs entirely to the field of education.”
In an accusing letter the said doctor enumerates for us a whole series of sins of neglect and slovenliness. He says that children and adults come to him — and precisely not from the poor class — who are terribly dirty, so much so that he cannot examine them, whereas in other districts even the poorest are clean and tidy.
More than once have we dealt with the question of hygiene in the columns of our paper; more than once have we said that we do nothing in this field; more than once have we accused our local self-government bodies of criminal indifference.
But a Kraków doctor does not know in what conditions we live; he does not know that we have no bathhouse at all; he does not know how crude and petty all this still is with us.
Let us not fool ourselves; let us say it openly: do children and adults here really have the possibility of getting a bath every week? They do not have that possibility even for money, and all the more so not without money.
After all, we have self-government bodies in Zagłębie with budgets of millions — so why should our town councils not arrange matters so that popular hygiene takes up a broad place in our life?
The police make sure that in food shops the salesmen wear white coats — so why does no one see to it that, first of all, that salesman has a white [clean] body under the coat?
Why is the population not given the possibility of having baths every week for themselves and for the children, if not entirely free, then at least for a few groszy? This is surely no less important than compulsory schooling, to which so much attention has been paid in Poland in recent years.
“I would appeal — writes the doctor in his letter — for the doctors to speak about this question in the batei midrash [study houses]. One cannot allow such a state of lack of culture and backwardness.”
We already wrote at the time that every Sunday the doctors should hold lectures in the largest halls, with free admission; the self-government bodies should publish free periodical [?] brochures in Yiddish and Polish.
This is certainly very important; but what turns out? That first and foremost one needs institutions for the people, and in these we are, unfortunately, so poor. Where is the population to bathe? All in the few bathtubs we possess, where admission costs one złoty? Is a middling family of several persons able to spend several złoty every week on bathing?
It would be right to dwell on this question; one must not wait until the situation becomes serious and has undesirable consequences. First of all one would need to give everyone, adults as well as children, the possibility of getting a bath every month, and to get it for little money; and once that is in order, one should then prepare the population and explain to it the necessity of bringing up children in hygienic conditions.
When the doctors now explain to the children in the schools the necessity of keeping the body clean, the children laugh and say to themselves: he's fine, he has a bathroom at home, he can bathe, wash and take showers — but we, how are we to do all that? How can we get to such an “operation”? And indeed, for the children and for the children's parents this is a question that simply cannot be solved as long as we do not have the necessary bathing facilities; not every such family can afford it materially.
We would therefore say, as the doctor reproaches us, that this hygiene belongs to the “problems of education”, and we must see to it that this problem is solved.
When we sometimes run into epidemic diseases, people start to storm and make a racket and investigate where it comes from. Would it not perhaps have been better to avoid the danger from the outset and to get used to the thought that we must live in different conditions, that we must see to uprooting the dirt radically, and that hygienic education should take its place?
The councillors in the municipal administrations of Zagłębie must see to it that this urgent matter is dealt with as soon as possible at one of the next sessions. The doctors, for their part, must see to interesting everyone, so that the question is finally settled as quickly as possible — and only then will it be possible to set about popularizing the idea among the broadest strata of the population.
Hygiene still stands at a very low level with us; what everywhere is a matter of course, an urgent necessity that one cannot even imagine having to talk about, is with us still at the stage of crudeness, at the stage of preparing the population and creating the necessary institutions for it.
Y. Sh.

[Poetry — the Western Wall.] Western Wall!
I have always carried your name in my heart.
And your image stands before me always:
before my eyes.
Whether I walk, worried, on my way among people,
or eat my bread alone in my room.
— At night, when my soul goes to plead before heaven,
then you come with quiet steps to my window
and your spirit steals through the cracks into my room
and I feel how your soul hovers over my head
and your humming stillness singes my ear
and from the bookcase the greying stones look out at me,
and stream and comfort together
with their calmed sorrow:
“My child,
bear your fate and your suffering
and be still
and be great in your silence”.
Then I want to drown my sorrow in the sea of your faith,
to hide my anger in your grass-grown cracks
and I cannot...
Western Wall!
With thirst I have drunk courage
from the refreshing springs,
from the legends woven around you,
I am your child, raised to nestle my head
in the lap of your traditions and legends —
you wanted to teach me
the secret of bearing suffering.
— There he goes, an insolent one, the Roman,
among slain brothers,
there he raises the crowbars against you, Wall,
there your ash-grey body trembles,
as a ray of the sun trembles
when huge shadows fall upon it.
All in vain the Roman waits for your end,
your peaks strain towards heaven and smile
in sorrow, in hope, into the distant future...
— You taught me, the weak one, to bear suffering and keep silent,
to look the enemy in the face and smile,
and when the last smile sprouts
on my sealed lips...
I shall wrap myself in your tallit of sorrow
and in the blue of the heavens that are above your head.
And I...
Oh, Wall, I cannot!
The torments of hell that thresh my body —
it is not they that are terrible to your child...
And if I know the taste of a thousand-year dog,
let me also know the taste of a one-hour lion...
It happens that I curse my fate, torn apart,
and like a wounded lion I cry out against the enemy;
it happens that the enemy tears out of my heart
a word of despair,
and my soul is drowned in anger.
And I cannot overcome my wrath...
Y. D-ki.
Moses Mendelssohn and His Bride

[Essay — Jewish history; Moses Mendelssohn bicentenary.] By Moshe Feinkind.
(For the 200th birthday of the great philosopher).
A.
One of the ugliest people in the world, so they say, was the great Jewish philosopher Moses Mendelssohn.
Short, hunchbacked in front and behind, his face overgrown with hair, and on his head he had to wear a wig...
His gauntness and his hunched back came from the hunger he suffered at the home of his poor father, the scribe R' Menachem Mendel, and then [?] in Berlin during his studies.
And when he came of age, it was therefore hard for him, despite his very great learning and greatness, to make a match; the girls avoided him.
But it was not his "Philosophical Conversations", which Lessing published without Mendelssohn's knowledge, nor his "Phaedon" and other works, with which he had won such renown, that brought him a bride — it was only his sample collection of ladies' fabrics, which Mendelssohn issued as bookkeeper to the manufacturer R' Isaak Bernhard in Berlin, that made him popular in the ladies' world, thanks to which he came to a match. It is told that during a walk in the street with his friend Lessing, they overheard a conversation between two strolling ladies who were talking about the latest patterns of ladies' fabrics issued by the Bernard firm [sic]. In the course of it the ladies greatly praised Mendelssohn as the author of this sample collection.
Hearing this characteristic conversation about the Jewish philosopher, already famous by then, whom people called the "German Plato" and the "Jewish Socrates", Lessing envied Mendelssohn for being very popular even among the ladies.
This "sample collection" on the one hand, and his "Conversations" on the other, brought it about that Mendelssohn came to a bride to his taste.
B.
The rich Hamburg banker Gugenheim had a very accomplished daughter, an only daughter, for whom he was seeking a suitable bridegroom.
Learning of Moses Mendelssohn, he travelled specially to Berlin to make his acquaintance. Gugenheim invited Mendelssohn to his home, and Mendelssohn indeed did not need much persuading and travelled to Hamburg to visit the rich prospective in-law.
Fromet Gugenheim, the bride-daughter [?], made use of this visit and conversed with him about philosophy, metaphysics and also about the latest fashions. The conversation between them stretched out in length and breadth, and Mendelssohn found great favour with the banker, i.e. with the daughter's father, and with his entire household.
Mendelssohn even understood the Hamburg banker's intention, and he liked Fromet well too, but out of great modesty he lacked the boldness to speak of a match either with him or with her.
The banker, too, could not get a word out of his daughter's mouth as to whether he pleased her, and it already looked as though Mendelssohn would leave with nothing.
But when taking leave of Miss Gugenheim, she stops him at the last moment and asks him whether it is true, as is written in the Talmud, that forty days before a child is born it is proclaimed in Heaven "the daughter of So-and-so to So-and-so", i.e. every person's match is determined.
Mendelssohn, the great sage of the world, understood the meaning of her sharp-witted question and answered that what is written there is a holy truth, for, as he remembers, before he was born he was shown his bride, who also had a hump just like his; he then fell at the feet of the Master of the Universe and begged Him for mercy, that He take pity on such a gentle being and not disfigure her with a hump — better to lay her hump upon him, and thereby set his bride free. That is why he has a hump in front and behind...
Hearing this answer from Mendelssohn, and perceiving in his words a hint that she had been destined for him by Providence as his bride, Fromet Gugenheim declared her love to him, and she became his bride..
C.
Fromet Gugenheim was already a girl of mature years when she married Moses Mendelssohn.
Indeed, she was not beautiful, but she was highly educated and clever; besides her blue eyes, the Jewish philosopher was greatly impressed by her gentle character, and therefore he honoured and loved her so much.
Influenced by her, Moses Mendelssohn began to keep a more or less modern house, but the traditional Jewish way of life had to be preserved in the home. That was his demand and his ardent wish. But his Fromet was not very pious; she did not give her children a Jewish religious upbringing, which was then also the sad reason why all of Moses Mendelssohn's children abandoned Judaism after his death and converted to Christianity.
The Seduced Girl (20)

[Serialized novel — Jewish village life, a Jewish girl held in a convent; installment 20.]
Dr. A. Weissman.
(A novel of Jewish life in the old world, based on historical facts.)

"Forgive me, I don't mean to insult anyone. I am talking precisely about my Ludwig, who has become too much of a squire [pritz] for me and forgets that his father is a poor village feldsher [barber-surgeon] and [?] his mother works hard on our little bit of field, while he [—] [?] carouses. He has become an idler. He forgets that I can no longer work so much; I myself am to blame for sending him to the schools. He has become a great squire."
Angry, and without so much as a "goodbye," the [?] young ladies [panny], the "[squir]esses" [?], left the feldsher's, and the "white house" fell sad and silent.
———
In the village it was quiet, sad and gloomy. Above all, the village was saddened that the clatter of the wheels in R' Zelig's mill was no longer heard. Ever since he and his wife had driven off to look for Mania, the mill had stood still. The stock of grain had run out. Old Żybek [?] did not know what to do. He went to old Dvora to ask her what to do next about grinding the rye and wheat, and she answered him:
"Whatever we grind, whatever mills — to us it is all the same now, so long as our Mania is not found."
The old gentile Żybek stopped the wheels of the mill with a groan, and all at once it became quiet. A deathly stillness reigned in the mill. Old Żybek, who over many decades had grown used to the noise of the mill, said quietly to himself, looking at the wheels:
"Lived and died. Hush, quiet as in a cemetery. Soon I too will die; everything must die."
Żybek locked the mill and moved over to his master's in the house, climbed up onto the stove, and would lie there snoring for hours on end, until old Dvora would shout at him to climb down.
"What am I to do when the mill stands? I can't live without work, so I lie on the stove and snore."
And old Dvora sighed.
"You're right, Żybek, it's hard to knock about without work when one is used to working."
And Dvora would comfort him that her son and Chana would come back and bring Mania with them, the mill would start running again, and the village would be cheerful again.
Hearing this, the old szlachcic [impoverished Polish nobleman], dressed like a beggar, who these last few nights had begged to be allowed to sleep in the house at Dvora's — hearing this from Dvora, asked Żybek to tell him the whole story about Mania, of which he had heard so much in the village. Żybek told him the whole story in brief, each time [—] [?] Dvora, who confirmed his words.
Meanwhile Jan passed by in the stillness. Seeing that the mill was standing, he set off for the house of R' Zelig Sarah's [Zelig son of Sarah].
"I'll tell them straight away," Jan said to himself, "I'll tell them openly that they should let Mania marry me, and then I'll free her from the convent."
When Jan came into the house of Mania's parents, he found only Dvora, sitting by the table like a half-sick woman, while the old mill-hand Żybek lay in the kitchen smoking his pipe [lulka] with makhorka — that kind of tobacco — and the poor szlachcic, who had begged a night's lodging, sat beside him, half asleep, supposedly, listening attentively and watching everything that went on.
Dvora took fright on seeing Jan, for it had been a long time since she had seen anyone come to their house.
"Where is your son, with your daughter-in-law?" Jan asked.
The unknown szlachcic moved closer to the people talking.
"Where should they be?" Dvora answered with a sigh.
"Are they still looking for Mania?"
"What else? How can we live without her?"
"When will they come home?"
"God alone knows."
"They surely won't go searching for Mania forever; the mill can't stand idle forever, and the whole house will turn into a ruin."
"What are we to do, when God has punished us?"
"It's a pity they're not here. I can't bear to watch your suffering; I could help you a lot to find Mania — I know where she is..."
"Ah, ah, so this is the lad," the unknown szlachcic muttered to himself.
"What comes of it? My son writes to me too that he already knows where she is, and still they won't give Mania back to us."
"What? They already know?" Jan asked in surprise. "Then why doesn't he take Mania home?"
"They say that Mania wants to stay there and doesn't want to know us."
I don't believe it.
"And has your son already seen her and spoken with her?"
"No; they at the convent say that Mania doesn't want to see her parents."
Jan jumped up from his seat.
"That's a lie! She begged me so to take her out of the convent. She wants to go home."
"I know the sisters in the convent tell lies."
"Where are your son and your daughter-in-law now? I urgently need to see them."
"Where should they be — over there, in the little town by the convent."
"What are they doing there, if they won't give them Mania?"
"They're looking for ways at least to meet her, to hear from Mania what she will say. When she sees her parents, it's surely impossible that she won't want to know us."
Jan sat for a few minutes without a word. He had already begun to take his leave, when suddenly he took old Dvora by the hand and said to her:
"Tell me that you won't refuse me what I am going to ask of you, and I will bring you Mania from the convent!"
"Ah, ah, now he's come out with it!" muttered the unknown szlachcic.
"If you can bring that off, you know how grateful we would be to you. Whatever you ask we will give you, everything we own. But you know we are not rich."
"I don't want any money."
"What then?" Dvora asked in surprise.
"I ask only one thing: that you should not be against her marrying me. I will live with her right here in the village, and she won't become a stranger to you."
"What are you saying, Jan?" Dvora cried out in fright. "What are you saying? I don't understand — are my old ears hearing right?"
"What is there not to understand? I am asking you to allow your granddaughter to marry me. I have loved her for a long time, and when I marry her I will guard her like the apple of my eye."
Jan waited for an answer. Dvora seemed to have frozen, and it was hard for her to utter a word. At last she said to him:
"As soon as she marries you, she surely can't remain a Jewish child."
"Certainly not."
"Then what difference is it to us if she stays in the convent?"
"There she will lead the life of a prisoner, and here, when she marries me, she will be free, and the convent won't be able to keep her any longer."
"Woe is me for her!" Dvora burst into tears.
"Tell me, Jan," Dvora suddenly asked him, wiping her eyes, "why do you want to marry Mania?"
"Because I love her," Jan answered.
"And you won't be ashamed before your own people to marry a Jewess?"
"No, because I love her too much; I can't live without her."
"Then why do you treat her so badly?"
"How?"
"You are holding Mania like a pledge: if they give her to you as a wife, you'll free her; if not, she stays locked up and shut in, under arrest. It's something like a story in a storybook about murderers who seize people as hostages so they'll be paid money, and if not, they'll kill the captive. How can you talk of loving her when you behave like this? I'm already an old woman, yet I know that when you love someone, you act differently. First you free the person, and afterwards you talk, and then one can give an answer. Right now my son is not at home, and I don't know at all what to tell you. The only thing I can tell you is this: if you truly love her, you shouldn't wait for a reward; you must first of all free her as quickly as possible, bring her home, and afterwards we can talk. I think Mania too must be asked first whether she wants to marry you."
"She won't be against it. I'm only afraid that when I free her, you'll then right away marry her off by force to a Jew. Can you assure me that you won't do that?"
"Without my son I can assure you of nothing. I can only tell you that neither to a Jew nor to a Christian will we marry her off by force. Whatever she wants, she will do with herself."

A Doctor's Prescriptions

(Dedicated to the medical advice columns). — By B. Kovner.
I have a nasty nature, I do: I love reading in the newspapers the advice, or the answers, that the doctors give to the readers of those newspapers.
And since it is hot now, and writing respectable things doesn't come easily, and one has to write something, it occurred to me to copy out the doctors' prescriptions for my readers, so that my readers may see how certain newspapers "lead their readers into the bathhouse" [i.e. take them for a ride] — what sort of prescriptions their doctors write for their health.
Let us begin:
Yakel of Nshikheve[?] ["Bite-ville"]: — Dear Doctor, what does one do when something bites me so? Ever since I got married — it is already the 13th year — it hasn't stopped biting me; I tear pieces of flesh off myself. Give me some advice.
Answer: — Every married man has to scratch himself: some more and some even more, depending on what kind of wife one has, and what kind of mother-in-law... There are three remedies, or three prescriptions: get a divorce, or run away wherever your eyes will carry you, or go on scratching. The last remedy is the cheapest. You can scratch yourself with your nails, with a fork, with a nail or with a grater.
If you follow my advice, you will certainly be helped.
Shifra Chaya: — I am a young wife, only 30 years old; one moment I feel cold and the next I feel hot; may I bathe in the Przemsza?
Answer: — No, my dear lady, you must first learn to swim before you go bathing; it would be a pity for such a young wife as you to drown. Meanwhile, for the time being, follow my advice: when you feel cold, smear your body with lard and cover it with feathers, and you will get warm. And if you feel hot, lie down on a big block of ice and stay lying there until the ice has completely melted.
Asher Lemel: — You inform me that a cough is tormenting you. It depends on what sort of cough is tormenting you: if you have time, come over to me, I will listen to you cough, and from the sound of the cough I will know what to give you. And if you have no time to come yourself, you can send me a sound of your cough packed in cotton wool. Make a good parcel, so that the cough doesn't fall out — it might still get broken.
S. Y. Shimel: — I am losing weight; I have stabbing pains in the left side of my shoulder; my hair is falling out and there is a whistling in my ear — sometimes in the right and sometimes in the left. What should I do[?]? I am still a young man, I am still[?].
Answer: — My advice is that you should get married already; that will save you. A man like you, with so many virtues, need not worry about finding a bride.
Yes, marriage will drag you out of all your troubles! You will simply forget that you are ill. And if you don't want to tie yourself down for good, there is another remedy: pop over to Krynica for a couple of months, "nisht gedazht"[?] [probably "nisht gedakht" — "may it not happen to us"].
Noach Tsimel: — Dear Doctor! Two weeks ago a little boy was born to me: he keeps crying and crying; he just cries, it doesn't stop for a single minute; my wife and I cannot close an eye. What shall we do? Answer, dear Doctor.
Answer: — The best advice is to stop up the child's little mouth.
Yona Hopke: Dear Doctor! What should I do, as my nose is blocked?
Answer: — The only thing you can do is — talk through your nose.
Dovid Podel: — What should I do, as one of my eyes keeps twitching? It just twitches and twitches.
Answer: — See that the other eye twitches too; a thing must be systematic.
Yisachar of Będzin: — Doctor, when my wife keeps her mouth shut everything is fine, but when she opens it, a not at all good smell comes out of there... What should she do?
Answer: — Let your wife drink a plate of perfume at every meal, and if that doesn't help, hang a padlock on her mouth and seal the padlock with seven seals.
Mendel: — Doctor! My wife is very ill, she has been lying in bed for two months now. Doctors have already cost me some three hundred dollars, and it doesn't help; she's only getting worse... Professors have found out that she has a superfluous vein [ader] in her heart. What should I do?
Answer: — It's nothing at all! She got the superfluous vein not long ago, because this year was a leap year, there is a superfluous Adar... There is Adar and Ve-Adar [pun: Yiddish "ader" = vein, "Adar" = the Hebrew month doubled in a leap year]. It's nothing at all; wait a few more weeks, let us say until Rosh Hashanah, and if it doesn't go away, you will have to get another wife.
Naftali Shnepsel: — I have a lot of lime [calcification], enough to supply a whole town; I also have a terrible headache, and my stomach bothers me, and my knees ache as if broken, and when I breathe I get stabbing pains in my sides, and every moment I feel as if I am about to faint. What should I do?
Answer: The healthiest thing for you is: to die! Then you will be rid of all your ailments in one shot; but if you don't want to die, there is a second remedy: go on suffering the way you have suffered until now.
Hershel Fefferholtz [Pepperwood]: — Dear Doctor! What does one do, as I sneeze so much? Of the 24 hours that a day has, I sneeze away no fewer than 20. It wears me out; I cannot eat, cannot sleep, cannot go to the theatre, cannot talk to people. What does one do? Answer me, dear Doctor.
Answer: — Try eating a lot of hot chickpeas [arbes], salted and peppered; if that doesn't help, sneeze little by little into the wide world on your own [pun on "talking into the world" — talking nonsense].
Talpiot

(Pictures from the Land of Israel)
By Israel Kalisz.
Every Sabbath, right at twilight, I used to visit the antechamber of Jerusalem — Talpiot. Talpiot lies on the road to Hebron. A narrow road, but rich in many-coloured landscapes.
Here on one side is a valley in which Arabs live[?], at the foot of the Mount of Olives, and from a distance it seems as if the old Arab houses with the domes on their roofs were part of those tombstones that stand in the cemetery on the Mount of Olives.
Down[?] from the Arab settlement lies the site of the historic "Siloam" (Mei ha-Shiloah). To the right stretches the quarter — Mekor Chaim, which the Keren Kayemet founded for the petty bourgeois of Jerusalem who are unable to settle on their own money. Some of the Mekor Chaim residents earn their living by supplying milk to the residents of Talpiot, and some have businesses in town.
The quarter "Mekor Chaim" lies in the Valley of Rephaim, the place where King David won a final victory over the Philistines.
And around the Valley of Rephaim stand the rocky Judean Hills, like proud, armoured walls that guard the capital, Jerusalem.
Along the narrow road to Talpiot many camels trail, with their high, outstretched heads, loaded with stones, and on the very top of the back sits an Arab boy with a flute in his mouth, piping. And the little blackish donkeys, in which mystical longings lie hidden, are turned toward the setting twilight sun that dips far, far beneath the mountains of the Judean Hills.
Near Jerusalem, which the mountains encircle, sunset does not last long. Night falls quickly. I walk all alone, in good spirits and cheerful. I take to observing the sunset over the mountains that ring the Valley of Rephaim. I forget that night is about to fall and that I will be left all alone in an Arab area. Something — the Arab boy with his melancholy tune awakened in me a homely feeling, of the Sabbath "Bnei Heichala" mood, of my childhood years in my home shtetl on the Vistula.
Suddenly I hear a pleading voice, uttered[?] with a timid expression: — "Khawaria, karesh sa'ahz khahadiau!" (Sir, how late is it?).
I turned around and saw the Arab boy stretching on the camel's back and yawning. Out of great weariness he asks what time it is.
The darker it grew over the Talpiot sky, the more mysteriously the echo of the camel bell answered, disturbing the divine stillness of that twilight.
And now Talpiot can already be seen from afar. The little palaces with terraces on the roofs, the verandas built in Oriental style with half-moon-shaped domes on top, and the metal Stars of David over the doors.
The planted little gardens with their various flowers now give off their scent after the thirsty August dew, and the electric lamps, scattered through the corners of Talpiot and shining like the seven branches of the Menorah, burst into the dark night. All this bears witness that Talpiot is the most beautiful quarter of Jerusalem.
And just as the little palaces of Talpiot are beautiful, even more beautiful and splendid are its "small fry" — the so-called "shovavim" (rascals, łobuzy), in the very middle of the street where the cars drive they play football, and when it happens that a ball rolls under a car, "he" stops the driver with the well-known vulgar exclamation of the Land of Israel:
— "Donkey. Stop!.."
And these are, all told, 8-year-old children.
In the first house, which stands on the narrow road by which one arrives from Yemin Moshe, lives a citizen who comes from Poland, from Ciechanów. All day long he works for the government, in the "Department of Public Works", and in the evening, at the hour that is neither day nor night, he busies himself in his little garden, waters it, pulls out the wild growths, etc. And when it is already quite dark, "landslayt" (fellow townsmen) gather there, one drinks tea with bananas and they debate various questions.
And "he", the citizen of Talpiot who comes from Ciechanów, listens, takes it in and keeps silent, for his motto is that in the Land of Israel one must talk little and do more...
A little further on, the main street, which leads out to the Hebron highway; on this street lives the very "cream". Here is a one-storey house belonging to the widow of Eliezer Ben-Yehuda, from that balcony a ringing and splendid Hebrew is always heard. A little further — the house of Prof. Dr. Joseph Klausner, on which is engraved in letters of the Jewish alphabet — "Judaism and Humanity". Who does not know them, the noble citizens of Talpiot, Joseph and Fania Klausner?
And in a side lane of Talpiot there, where one can already see in the distance the bare rocky mountains stretching toward Bethlehem, there, in that place, there is a small sanctuary, or, as they call it in the Land of Israel — a "Temple in miniature": that is the "Ein Harod Company" (Plugat Ein Harod).
There a new life is being woven, a life whose symbol is — building. This life is full of content; it is a life without shame or disgrace. They, the builders, do not split hairs; they say that by "avodah" one means not prayer but real labour — and their modest singing after a whole, hard working day echoes in the darkness of the night far over the quiet and modest little houses of "Mekor Chaim" across the way, which lies in the lap of the "Valley of Rephaim".
* * *
And today! Terrible fighting at "Talpiot", Klausner's library desecrated, eight killed, the Ein Harod Company in flames..
Your noblest brothers went into battle and fell there, and you, Grandfather Israel, sit with folded hands!
They Went to Claim an Inheritance and Paid for the Burial...

Who doesn't know that nowadays nobody pays bills of exchange.. Babies in their cradles already know that whoever holds a protested bill flutters [?] about with it happily. The merchant has already grown used to not paying and not getting paid, but to go and collect a debt and still have to pay on top — to go, that is, after an inheritance and pay for the burial — that is something new.
Such an encounter was had these days by the creditors of a certain textile merchant, B.
Like all merchants, our merchant — after the wedding, all of about two years ago — took a lively dowry, with a young wife into the bargain. And not an ugly wife at that. What does a young man do with a dowry, and a dowry in "lokshn" [noodles; apparently slang] at that? — he rents himself a little shop. Fresh, and well provided with the "big things" in his pocket, he sets out into town to "sniff around". Sniffed here, sniffed there, so long and so wide until he had sniffed out a "bundle": a bit of "novelties", a "kreml" [?] of "sheyblers" [?], a few pieces of lining (podszewka) and a bit of stiff linen. At first there were some "lokshn" and the rest "tsimmes". Later, when business was going, after the first bills had been honoured, the young man [sentence broken off as printed]. Having already learned only "handwork", i.e. only written things [promissory notes], the young man felt himself in clover, became a "buy-all", took whatever he could get. Winter goods and summer goods. And a bit of furniture — has he turned apostate?! [i.e. is that a sin?] So Mr. B. indeed furnished himself like an emperor: a "jadalnia" [dining room] with a "sypialnia" [bedroom], sideboards with "pomocniks" [serving cabinets], dressed himself like a monarch, lived like God in Odessa — and how he lived.
When Mr. B. realised that he had already somewhat overshot the measure [?] for his person, that his debts already reached some 40 thousand złoty, he took his wife aside; the couple talked the situation over and it was agreed to pull a "knack" [a deliberate bankruptcy]. What's the big deal [?] — everyone may, and I may not! And so it was: one fine morning B. took to his heels, turned the bit of goods into cash, locked the shop with a thick bar, and "the child is not" — gone, and go talk to his cap-peak [daszek; i.e. try and find him].
Seeing that the shop was not operating, there began a rush of creditors. Coming into the house, everything went dark before their eyes; instead of opening their mouths, instead of falling upon their debtor, they were left open-mouthed, they were left dumbfounded. On the couch (kasetka) lay the beautiful wife tearing the hair from her head: "Jews, give me advice, I am miserable. My husband, the robber, has left me with a tiny child, a desolate agunah [abandoned wife]. Have pity, dear people, find him. Maybe he went off with a 'kochanka' [mistress]." The young wife pours out tears, sighs and sobs [?]. The creditors stand with folded hands and staring eyes, shrugging their shoulders: what is one to do? How can one let such a young, radiant little wife perish? One would need the heart of a Tatar. So several creditors came together in a meeting and resolved to support the "desolate agunah".
Now the "desolate agunah" had quite a bit of work: every day lying on the couch and weeping over her bitter fate, cursing the robber who had left her an agunah with a tiny child. And later, when the creditors are on the other side of the door — collecting the love letters that arrive poste restante from her husband. And meanwhile the pretty young wife plays her role on the couch well, as the "desolate agunah".
Thus did Zagłębie creditors go to claim an inheritance and paid for the burial...
Amei ha-Arets and Amei ha-Arats [Ignoramuses, of Both Kinds]

[Feuilleton — Jewish folk humour; anecdotes.] In the light of Jewish satire and folk humour.
By Yosef Zelkowicz [Józef Zełkowicz].

It is remarkable [?] that "Teach your tongue to speak clean language" and "Keep yourself far from what is ugly and from what resembles ugliness" are accepted among Jews to such a degree that every learned man will guard himself against letting an indecent word out of his mouth — but when it comes to mocking and joking about an am ha-arets [ignoramus], the joke forgets every kind of limit, and they tell each other such things that, in other circumstances, not only would the teller never bring such words across his lips, but [printed "gur"] he would not even want to listen to them...
Here are some examples of such anecdotes, of the more printable kind:

A little pshetl [a small exegesis].
In former times there was a custom that the bes-medresh lads would come every Sabbath after the meal to the rabbi of the shtetl, to talk Torah with him, and on that occasion the lads would recite to him the novellae they had devised in the course of the week.
In one such shtetl there lived a "shveyger" [?], a coarse fellow, who had a son of some twenty-odd years, and this son insisted on doing just as the other lads did, that is, also going in to the rabbi and reciting his own [printed "zeyge"] novellae to him.
But since he was an ignoramus of the first order, he hired a melamed to teach him some little pshetl.
First of all the melamed began to teach him a bit of the rules of good manners, and told him this:
— When you come in to the rabbi on the Sabbath, you kiss the mezuzah with your right hand and say: "Gut shabes, rebbe." And only later did he set about teaching him this pshetl:
It is written: "And there was darkness and slipperiness, and the angel of the Lord pursuing them" — it will be dark and slippery, and God's angel will chase after them. So here is a difficulty: if it is dark and slippery, how will the angel be able to chase them?...
A second difficulty: Noah's sons were called Shem, Ham and Japheth — why is it not written what their father was called?... And a third difficulty: it is written that Joseph did recognize his brothers but they did not recognize him, because when Joseph went away he had no beard, and when the brothers came to him he did have a beard; so here is the difficulty: why did Joseph not shave off his beard?..
These three blockhead-difficulties the melamed hammered into his head over half a year, and in the end, when the lad came in to the rabbi as was proper, he went and so, in a hurry [?], mixed everything up:
— "Gut shabes, rebbe, may it be dark and slippery for you, and may the angel shave off your beard!. So here is the difficulty: how will he see? — The answer is: the father commanded to kiss the mezuzah with the right hand..

He is well provided.
When Tisha b'Av falls on the Sabbath, it is postponed to Sunday; the law, however, is that Tisha b'Av is only [printed "gur"] postponed, to the extent that on the Sabbath one may eat, wash and wear shoes, but "private matters" [marital relations] must be refrained from on that Sabbath as on Tisha b'Av, or, as the Shulchan Aruch puts it: "private matters apply."
In many small shtetls there was a custom that when Tisha b'Av fell on the Sabbath, the rabbi had the above-mentioned law announced in the synagogue and in the bes-medresh, that "private matters are forbidden."
There stands in the synagogue an arendar [leaseholder], who kept his leased tavern in the village open on the Sabbath because he had made a "deed of sale", and he hears the rabbi announcing about the "private matters"; so he asks someone what this thing "private matters" is. As it happened, he came upon a joker who explained to him that by "private matters" is meant an arenda [leasehold], and that this is precisely what the rabbi is announcing: that on this Sabbath one may not keep the arenda open...
— I am allowed! — the arendar cried out.
— What do you mean, you are allowed? — the rabbi asks him, — are you not a Jew? — When it is said "private matters" are forbidden — they are forbidden!
— Rebbe — the arendar answered him — for the Sabbath private matters I have, after all, a special permit [?]... Have you already forgotten, rebbe? You yourself made me the "deed of sale" and told me that I am allowed!...

The women polished it off
A butcher, a great boor who, however, had a lot of money, bought himself into pedigree: he took the rabbi's son as his son-in-law.
He laid on a wedding fit for a king, with all kinds of pastries, a lot of fish, a lot of meat and drink in abundance of every sort.
To the wedding, for the rabbi's sake, came all the prominent householders of the shtetl, as well as the rabbi's family, and the butcher felt greatly elevated by this, so much so that he decided to hold grand sheva brakhot as well, with fresh pastries, wines [?] etc.
At the first sheva brakhot the rabbi gathered with his circle, and before they washed their hands for the meal, the rabbi discussed the question why, at mayim acharonim [?; by sense: the washing before the meal], when one washes one's hands to eat, there must specifically be "koach gavra" [human force], that is, one must wash specifically with a vessel and pour the water, and not dip the hands in water, whereas for mayim acharonim [the after-meal washing] there need be no "koach gavra".
The butcher sits and hears once "koach gavra" and again "koach gavra", so he asks quietly, so that no one should hear, what sort of thing this "koach [printed "koh"] gavra" is?
— "Koach gavra", explained the one he had asked, is chernukha [nigella] (caraway). And the rabbi, he went on to tell him, holds it against you that you did not sprinkle the rolls [bulkes] with caraway...
The butcher was deeply hurt by this, and to appease the rabbi he excused himself thus:
— Don't take it amiss, in-law, that I did not sprinkle the rolls with any koach gavra; I had in fact provided myself with plenty of koach gavra, only the women polished it off on me before the wedding, on the earlier pastries...
What's New in Zagłębie? — Będzin: A Non-Partisan Relief Committee Created for the Victims in the Land of Israel

[Head of the local page; Będzin — Relief for the victims of the 1929 riots in the Land of Israel.]
What's New in Zagłębie?
(Date boxes: Friday, 8 Elul 5689 — Piątek, 13 września 1929 [Friday, 13 September 1929].)
Będzin
A non-partisan relief committee created for the victims in the Land of Israel.
At the very height of the fire, during the bloody slaughter of our brothers and sisters in the Land of Israel, nearly all kehilla leaders stood on guard and relief committees were created. An exception in this respect was our Będzin, where the kehilla leaders are very "busy" with the behind-the-scenes[?] mouse-scurrying around the gmina [the community board] and took no interest whatsoever in the question of creating such a relief committee. Even more vexing is that at the meeting in the Merchants' Association the official kehilla was not represented..
And the initiative to create a relief committee was taken up by the local Zionist organisation, which on Sunday called a meeting in the premises of the Merchants' Association.
Invited to the meeting were all Jewish political, economic and philanthropic organisations, societies and institutions, except for the local "Agi" [Agudas Yisroel], which, as it turns out, has a very good "sense" and stayed sitting at home...
Present were: representatives of non-partisan Hasidim, the "Agudah" and all the Zionist groupings.
Mr. Nota Landner opens the meeting with a short introduction on the important purpose of the meeting and hands over the chair to Mr. Sz. Fürstenberg. (Mr. Landner! Why did you not propose honouring [the memory of] the fallen martyrs?..)
Invited to the presidium table are Messrs. M. Rozenzaft and Y. Wygodzki, and the meeting proceeds to the single main point — electing a committee that should start working at once, because time is pressing.
The mood is serious; everyone feels the great duty that must be fulfilled towards the destroyed Yishuv. But the seriousness soon vanishes, tempers flare, and only then does one see how great our fragmentation, party strife and helplessness are, even at a time when the whole Jewish people must hurry with help as one man.
The cause of the chaotic situation were the "Agudah" politicians, well known to us, who are capable of harming the most vital[?] interests of the whole of Klal Yisroel as long as the prestige of their party shop[?] is not diminished. This little band of wreckers and destroyers cannot agree that the collected money be sent to the Central Committee in Warsaw, to which all of Polish Jewry sends it; rather, they want the money to be deposited in a local bank until news comes from the Land of Israel that the "Agudah" is represented in sufficient[?] numbers on the distribution committee there.
Such declarations were made by Messrs. Skórnik and Ryński, and seeing the bitterness of the assembled public, they put forward compromise proposals: that the money be sent to the "Lema'an HaKotel" [For the Western Wall] committee, or alternatively handed over to Fürstenberg and Rozenzaft.
Reb Mendel Rozenzaft then took the floor and said: "I do not know what people are arguing about here; I, as a long-standing communal worker, trust the Va'ad Leumi [National Council] in Jerusalem that the money will be distributed in the best order to those who suffered damage in the destruction."
These true words did not impress the Agudah leaders either, and Mr. Ryński expressed himself: "He doesn't know what he is talking about"...
A number of people speak out against the "Agudah" proposal, reproaching the Agudah representatives that their only aim is for such an important action to be broken up because of party ambitions. The chairman, Mr. Fürstenberg, too, turns several times to Messrs. Skórnik and Ryński, asking that they finally give up such trifles, so that the relief for the spilled blood may be carried out with the greatest success and bring honour to the Będzin Jewish kehilla.
But it did not help at all, and the Agudah representatives, seeing that the meeting was proceeding to elect a council and an executive, left the meeting.
Then a council and a board were elected unanimously.
The Campaign to Root Out Jewish Teachers. The Wronged Teachers Break Off Their Lessons.

For several years a systematic campaign has been waged against the Jewish teachers of the so-called „powszechne“ (general elementary) schools. Various reforms are supposedly being introduced in these schools, whose only aim is to reduce the Jewish element among the teachers of the said schools.
The same system of uprooting has lately also been applied against the teachers of the evening courses for Jewish artisans and commercial employees, who work all day and attend the evening courses in their free evening hours.
The evening courses for Jews have developed very nicely; hundreds of young Jews study there, and the pupils have almost grown together with the Jewish teachers, who treat the courses with special affection.
The first step of the local school authority, the „Dozór Szkolny“ (school board), was from the outset to „cast an eye“ on the number of Jewish teachers. And at the evening courses they increased the number with... Christian teachers. But they did not stop at that point and went further, if only to cover up the Jewish face entirely...
This week a mixing system was introduced at the evening courses, i.e. the pupils of the Christian schools were sent in to the Jewish pupils, and „of all the stones one big stone was made“...
Naturally, the Jewish teachers, Messrs. Rotenberg, Eisenberg, Grossman and Wiesenfreund, could not tolerate such an act, and in protest they broke off the lessons.
Tragic Death of a Poor Jewish Woman.

On Monday at 7 in the evening, not far from the tram depot, 38 [?]-year-old Chawa Pelcmacher, an alms collector from Zawiercie, was killed by the tram.
The tragically deceased was walking with her husband, a well-known figure of the beggars' world, from Dąbrowa to Będzin. And as she was about to cross the tram line she met her death.
On Wednesday evening she was buried at the expense of the Jewish kehilla.
Ceremony at the Cemetery — Postponed.

The Rabbi also turned [?] to the rabbinate about this in a letter, in which he stresses that he would not envy whoever changes the will of the Rabbi.
Cooperative Bank Strengthened with Large Sums of Money.

In recent weeks various versions have circulated in the town concerning the financial situation of the Cooperative Bank.
In connection with the rumours that were spread, and also in order to establish the bank's real situation, at the request of the bank management the well-known instructor of the Auditing Union, Mr. Michelson, was called in from Warsaw; over 3 days he carried out a thorough inspection of the bank's activity and established that: 1) the crisis that has arisen in the bank is a consequence of the general crisis prevailing in the country, 2) the bank is not exposed to any risk whatsoever, 3) the shortage of money exists because the bank has granted large long-term loans, and 4) owing to the rumours that were spread, larger sums of deposits were withdrawn.
On Sunday a meeting of the board was held under the chairmanship of the president, Mr. Fürstenberg, and at the meeting the instructor Mr. Michelson presented the above-mentioned report and at the same time announced that, in order for the bank to resume its normal activity, the Auditing Union will provide a sum of 50 thousand złoty in the form of a rediscount.
Then Mr. Fürstenberg declared that for this purpose he too is giving 50 thousand złoty.
At the meeting a directorate was elected to run the bank's operations. The directorate consists of Messrs. Fürstenberg, Hampel [?] and Goldsztajn.

Sensational trial of Jewish merchants at the Sosnowiec District Court

[Sosnowiec — court.] Last Wednesday a sensational trial began at the Sosnowiec District Court over a large smuggling affair, in which a number of Polish and Jewish merchants and several senior customs and railway officials are accused.
In the dock sit: Dawid Fiora[?], Bernard Grajcer and his son Jankiel, Eli' (Eliyahu) Fiora, the head (naczelnik) of the Sosnowiec customs office Medyński, the inspector Klimas, the customs official Chomczyk[?], and the Katowice merchants Urbach, Ehrenstein and Gottreich, the railway official Zahar[?] and the railway storekeeper Zadras[?].
Interest in the trial is very great; admission to the courtroom is by entry ticket only.
The persons listed are accused of illegally bringing colonial goods in from abroad, causing the State a loss of 348 104 [348,104] złoty.
For the trial, which will last several days, 146 witnesses have been summoned.
During the first day of the trial the indictment, which runs to 32 pages, was read out. Then the accused were given the floor; they did not admit guilt.
Appearing for the defence are the best lawyers from Warsaw, Messrs. Herling, Goldsztajn, Peruszyński[?], Brokman, Wasserberger and Krzemuski[?], Pawlak[?] of Sosnowiec and Farelli[?] of Będzin.
In the course of yesterday no more than 10 witnesses were heard, among them the chief witness Chilecki[?], who plays a large role in the indictment.
The hearing of the remaining witnesses will probably last until Tuesday.
The verdict is expected[?] on Wednesday or Thursday.
—o—
Meeting of the council of the merchants' associations.
On Wednesday evening a meeting of the council of the merchants' associations of Zagłębie was convened at the premises of the Będzin Merchants' Association. On the agenda was a discussion of the institution's position on the turnover tax, which is determined by the Chamber of Commerce.
Attending the meeting were representatives of the Będzin Merchants' Association and of the small traders, and delegates of the Dąbrowa Merchants' Association. The Sosnowiec merchants' associations, on the other hand, did not find it necessary to delegate their representatives to this important meeting.

A guest from Eretz Israel in Zagłębie.
In connection with the events in Eretz Israel, there arrive here today the leader of the Zionist pioneer (halutz) organisation, Magister Pinchas Lubianiker, and David Schmetterling from Eretz Israel, who will give a lecture this coming Saturday night (motzaei Shabbat) in the large hall of the Będzin "Hitachdut" on the subject "The task of Jewish youth at the present moment".

Autumn Manoeuvres

The military autumn manoeuvres are already ending. The soldiers are beginning to march back from the field to the barracks; that is why the political autumn manoeuvres are now really beginning. The political armies have already marched out onto the field. One can already see how the army is grouped.
On one side, the government army of the „Eynsl“ („the One“ — list no. 1, the Nonpartisan Bloc for Cooperation with the Government, BBWR). This army keeps its plans secret and is under the command of experienced military men, equipped with every good thing and with real strength to hold out in a longer struggle. Experts say, however, that the strategic position of this army is not a favourable one.
A second army, under the command of the Endek (National Democratic) „field-marshal“ Trąmpczyński, manoeuvres with much display, even brandishes its sword, but no great importance is attached to it. This army is regarded in part as one tacking between the government army and a third army — the most important in the present manoeuvres — the army of workers, peasants and, in support, also part of the bourgeoisie. This army was finally formed last Saturday and sent out a joint ultimatum:
— We are not coming to the conference with the government. We do not believe that any conference with you whatsoever can bring any positive benefit; besides, we do not believe you. We demand: lay down your arms — resign.
One must admit that the Left in the Sejm has never until now taken so sharp a stand against the government. It is already clear now that the final moment of decision is approaching in the 3-year conflict between the government camp and the Sejm.
The „Robotnik“ declares openly that the P.P.S., which has placed itself at the head of the Sejm opposition, has now sharpened its tactics.
— You have worked in the sweat of your brow — writes the „Robotnik“, addressing the Sanacja — to deepen and sharpen the political and social struggle in the country. Listing the government's sins, up to Col. Sławek's threats of breaking bones, the paper asks that the Sanacja press shed no tears and not pretend to pity the opposition for its manner of struggle.
— „We say openly that the liquidation of the present regime is a necessity not only from the standpoint of socialism, or of the democratic doctrine and its [—], but also, seriously[?], in the interests of Poland as an independent state. We strive to liquidate the present regime in a legal and peaceful way; that is why we are measuring ourselves in a parliamentary struggle. We threaten no one with „breaking bones“ and not with any „attempt on the state“. The question whether the regime will be liquidated „peacefully“ depends not on us but on the other side. If the leaders of the colonels' clique[?] — concludes the „Robotnik“ — will render an account of the ideological and moral bankruptcy of their [?], they must hang out a white flag.“
The „Głos Prawdy“ also has its say on the newly created situation. That confident, aggressive, „bone-breaking“ tone is gone; the „Głos Prawdy“ reckons only with the P.P.S., because of its leading role, and assures that the government does not take the Left's refusal to heart. Especially when the P.P.S. goes arm in arm, with its left hand, with the socialists of the national minorities, and with its right hand — with the Ch.D. [Christian Democrats], the N.P.R. [National Workers' Party] and „Piast“. As for the fist that the Left is now showing us — concludes the „Głos Prawdy“ — „we want to see this fist not only in the salon but also on the battlefield“.
The political autumn manoeuvres have thus begun with a very interesting exchange of notes between the sides. The „Robotnik“ [calls on] the opponent to capitulate and hang out a white flag, and the „Głos Prawdy“ answers: „Let us first see on the battlefield“...
N.
Great Material Losses of Zagłębie Jews during the Bloody Events in the Land of Israel

In the Land of Israel it is already quiet, and the Palestine mail that reaches us brings sad greetings from the Jewish settlement there that has been laid waste. Among the victims there are also natives of Zagłębie, who have been completely ruined, and yesterday's rich men have to turn to the relief institutions to get a little food and a shirt on their backs.
Mr. Złotnik of Dąbrowa has received a letter from his family in Be'er Tuvia saying that of their goods and possessions, which were worth over 14 hundred pounds, a mountain of ashes has been left: the Arabs attacked the colony of Be'er Sheva [sic] and burned it down entirely; afterwards they slaughtered several Jews, wrapped the cut-up bodies in Torah scrolls and set them on fire.
We have received a heart-rending letter from Mr. Zyndel Weissmark, who left Będzin for the Land of Israel 9 years ago, where in the course of time he rose to a certain standing, owned a woodcarving factory in Haifa and lived with his family quite comfortably.
But in the recent events Mr. Weissmark was left naked and destitute; his fortune, amounting to about a thousand pounds, went up in smoke; his household goods, among them also a complete trousseau for his daughter, were plundered by the Arabs. Mr. Weissmark, who wanders about with his family naked and barefoot, without a roof over his head, has sent us the following letter to the Rabbi of Będzin, the kehilla leaders, his former good friends and his comrades in Będzin, that they should help him out of his critical situation.
[The letter, in Hebrew:]
With God's help.
To the honourable great Rabbi of the holy community of Będzin, may he live long and happily, and to the honourable Town Council of Będzin.
Honoured Rabbi!
In connection with the terrible riots, of which you have surely heard, that passed over the towns and settlements of the Land of Israel, I have suffered greatly; I have been turned from a rich man into a poor and destitute one, from a factory owner into one lacking bread and shelter. Since a wicked hand [—?] set fire to my factory with its machines, to my house and my property, my belongings and my furniture, I was left naked and destitute, without food for a single meal. I therefore beseech my honoured dear friend the Rabbi to call a meeting of the council, and especially of these acquaintances of mine: Messrs. Yeshaya Pisztenberg [Fürstenberg?], Yaakov Gutman, Izydor Sercz[?], Grundman, Szymszon Rozenblum and the rest, with whom I worked together on all the town's affairs and on various charitable matters, that they may deliberate on my terrible situation and come to my aid, so that I can rebuild my factory and earn my living by the labour of my hands.
Needless to say, while I was in Będzin I took an important and active part in all the town's affairs and never shirked my duty. The honourable Rabbi of Będzin visited me and my factory about three years ago, accompanied by the son-in-law of the Rebbe of Sokołów.
Being sure that the town of Będzin will come to the aid of the victims of the riots, and believing that my share through the Zionist Executive will be very small, since many are those who were damaged and impoverished by the riots, I therefore ask the honourable Rabbi and the council, if they wish to raise me from my lowliness and poverty, to send me their support in my private name. For if the money reaches the Zionist Executive, my share will be very small and I shall not be able to do anything with it, small or great.
With great respect and in expectation of your speedy[?] help,
Zyndel Weissmark.
29 Av 5689, Haifa, may it be rebuilt and established.
The letter bears the stamp of the „Rabbinate Office of the Hebrew Community of Haifa“, who write:
We the undersigned, the Rabbinate Office in Haifa, confirm the words of Mr. R' Zyndel Weissmark that in the days of the terrible bloody events that took place in the Holy Land his factory was burned and all he had was plundered, and he was left destitute. And to this we set our hands, Sunday, 1st day of Rosh Chodesh Elul 5689, Haifa, Land of Israel.
Rabbinate Office of the Hebrew Community of Haifa
Address: Zyndel Weissmark, Haifa, P.O.B. — P.O. Box 253, Palestine, Land of Israel.

Dąbrowa — The Agudah People Won't Give, but Taking They Do Want...

[Dąbrowa — kehilla; relief for the victims in Palestine.] In the hall of the kehilla in Dąbrowa [Górnicza] a meeting of the committee for the victims in Eretz Israel took place on Wednesday evening.
On the agenda were: electing a chairman of the committee and sending off the money collected so far.
The first point, regrettably, provoked a discussion that lasted a whole hour; over the innocent "little chair" a passionate fight was waged, and in the end, on the proposal of Mr. Rechnic, Mr. G. A. Gutman was elected chairman.
When the second point was discussed, the "Agudah" dozór members [kehilla board members] came out with their well-known separatist proposal: that the money should not be sent to Warsaw, but to Eretz Israel, to Rabbis Kook and Sonnenfeld.
The cynical proposal of the "Agudah" aroused strong bitterness among those present, and at the meeting the Agudah people received the proper answer from the parnassim [kehilla board members] Liberman (non-party Orthodox), Suterka and Rechnic, who sharply condemned the Agudah's tactics.
Mr. Liberman in particular came out against them, stressing that it was impudence on the part of the "Agudah", which had made a Sabbath for itself [i.e. gone its own way], founded a separate committee, and in the end they come and give an opinion on where the money should be sent.
Mr. Rechnic puts forward a proposal that the 2 thousand zł. collected so far be sent to the Central Relief Committee in Warsaw, and that the sums collected by the Agudah people be returned to them.
The chairman, Mr. Gutman, supplements the proposal and declares that nothing at all of the collected sum has been touched, but whatever the "Agudah" gave for this purpose he will pay back to them out of his own money.
Mr. Gutman's gesture made a good impression, and it was resolved to send off the 2000 zł.; the "Agudah" can get its donations back from Mr. Gutman.
It is interesting to add that, according to the collection lists, it turns out that the entire "Agudah" took part with 130 zł. (read: one hundred and thirty zł.).
Sławków — A Relief Committee

[Sławków — protest and relief for the victims in Palestine.] Last week a protest meeting against the events in Eretz Israel took place here. The speakers were Messrs. Icchak Ber Makowski on behalf of the gmina [Jewish community], Icchak Astry on behalf of "Mizrachi", Szpigelman on behalf of the Zionist Revisionists, and Mendel Makowski on behalf of the "Agudah".
The cantor, Mr. Stahl, held a memorial prayer for the martyrs, and a committee of the following persons was elected: M. B. Szpigelman (chairman), I. B. Makowski (secretary), Astry (treasurer), Libermensz, Trajberger, Testiler. One thousand zł. was collected, which was immediately sent to the Jewish community in Warsaw; a few hundred zł. more we are sending off this week. The Szajn brothers too responded warmly with their donations.

Unveiling of a Tombstone.
[Sławków — memorial and charity.] Last Friday the first yahrzeit of Dvora Szajn, of blessed memory, took place here, together with the unveiling of the tombstone. The whole town took part, as did the workers of the Szajn Bros. The clerk Mr. Szwimer described the good deeds of the deceased, who had been the "mother" of the poor. After the memorial prayer Mr. Mordechai Ejn [sic; probably Szajn] pledged one thousand zł., the brothers Chaim and Ichel 500 zł. each, and all the relatives together 6000 zł., to build a school in the name of Dvora Szajn. For this purpose a plot will soon be bought.
It is to be hoped that all the local public workers will energetically help to build such an institution at once. Elem.
