And We Thought...

(The great relief campaign for Eretz Israel. — In what manner does the "Agudah" come to help here?)

As soon as the first sad news appeared that Jewish blood was being shed in Eretz Israel, that Jews were being murdered and Jewish goods and property destroyed, we were all shaken. In a single moment we were all on the lookout to catch a latest piece of news about our sisters and brothers in Eretz Israel.
One could hardly wait for a fresh newspaper, and when one did arrive it held terrible things. The police even had to keep order at that moment. And say what you like: at that moment I learned a great deal and even grew taller[?]. In those sad days I saw that we are a people; I sensed palpably that in the Jewish heart something beats and surges, and that we all have one aim in life, one hope, one ideal.
And precisely in these troubles of ours, in the heavy sufferings of our days, we felt that we have behind us a people which, in the sad days and dark nights, commands the unity and the solidarity that a people needs so badly. We felt then that all threads bind us together and that we are one power, one force, one sound mind.
But that was apparently a dream: those were days of intoxication, of mourning, of unconsciousness, of disorientation.
Yet hardly had people sat down at the green table, hardly had they begun to look around — that one must render an account, that one must rescue what has remained alive, that one must provide the widows and orphans with bread and a roof over their heads — than precisely then we again struck the terrible abyss of the Agudah muddle[?].
It is truly impossible to understand that on such an innocent question as collecting donations for the unfortunate sisters and brothers in Eretz Israel no agreement can be reached. And anyway, what agreement is needed here? What is there to quarrel about? The demands of the "Agudah" representatives are simply ridiculous and at the same time sad: that the money should meanwhile be deposited in a local bank, and that only when they receive news from Eretz Israel that a sufficient number of Agudah representatives take part in the distribution will the local representatives deign to agree that the money be sent there.
Do these people take account of their own words? Do they really think it is permissible to make party capital at such a serious time, when help is necessary and urgent? What does it mean, "we will see whether the Agudah is represented in sufficient numbers"? And if not, must such a campaign be wrecked? Are these people in their right minds? What does it mean to make a distinction between Jews and Jews? Between brothers and brothers? Must a distinction be made between one unfortunate Jew and another? Must the Jews of Eretz Israel be classified? Must not the Bukharan be protected in the same measure as the Yemenite Jew, the Sephardi as the Ashkenazi Jew, who all became equally unfortunate and together sacrificed themselves for the fatherland? And he who is sick and needs medicine — must one first investigate his biography, which party he belonged to and what outlook he holds? How are these people not ashamed to make themselves so ridiculous, so banal? What does it mean to make a kind of "swój do swego" ["each to his own" — the slogan of the Polish anti-Jewish boycott], a kind of "my" Jews and "your" Jews?
Last week a Jew came into our editorial office to seek advice. What is the matter, we ask him. He then takes out two leaflets and does not know what to do: since both call for giving money for Eretz Israel, he does not know to which party he should give, for giving to both is beyond his means. Go and make such a Jew understand that even in such holy work some have party intrigues and honours in mind, and that as soon as one does not yield to them, they are ready to turn the whole campaign into a sort of penny-collecting of alms.
Apparently the Agudah has sworn always to place itself in opposition and to be against the people's interests. Excuses for doing so it will always find. One time the straight will not be crooked enough for it, another time the crooked will not be straight enough for it; and when the talk is that everything must be crumbled and everything turned to ashes, there is surely nothing more to discuss.
We still remember with what self-sacrifice these people worked here during the Sejm elections to break the Jewish mandate: although they themselves had no prospect whatsoever of electing a deputy of their own, they did everything so that Zagłębie should no longer obtain a Jewish deputy, and to our great sorrow their work of destruction succeeded completely — and then they showed us their heroism, that they are capable of breaking and destroying.
Now it is the same story again; again they want to show everywhere that they are experts[?] at wrecking and breaking. Yet this is not about any political platform at all — so what is all the noise about? What is the work of destruction needed for now? Who will benefit from the present failure? What are these people after with the present disruption? And on top of that they still have the nerve to ring the bells that nobody wanted to unite with them. With whom are people to unite, when their only aim is to destroy and to harm the people's interests?
So it is in Będzin, so in Sosnowiec, and so too in many other towns. Everywhere we hear the same; everywhere they come to disrupt, to destroy. Who does not remember their "holy and clean work" when Jaffe [Leib Jaffe of Keren Hayesod] came to conduct the campaign for "Keren Hayesod", when they even permitted ordering Jews to work on the Sabbath?
It pains the heart when we see how our own brothers are only out to do harm at every opportunity.
And we thought, during the latest sad events, that one Jewish heart beats, that one Jewish people weeps, that one Jewish union had crystallised which would not allow our holy places, which have stood in the Land since ancient times when Jews were a people equal to other peoples, to be destroyed.
We thought there would not be a single Jew who would not tremble on hearing with what cruelty the savage Arabs tortured and slaughtered old people, young children and women.
We thought that all as one would be beside themselves on hearing in what manner the holy and new Eretz Israel had been destroyed...
So it looked at the first moment, when our hair stood on end; but later our "Agudah" apparently sobered up and saw that this was an opportune moment to break and destroy the great relief campaign, and it set out in all towns and townlets on the path of "making Shabbes for itself" [acting for its own benefit], on the path of crumbling and fragmenting the great relief aid on which the Jews of Eretz Israel are counting so much.
R. Let.

Our Panorama

[From the small towns — weekly feuilleton; Wolbrom, Zawiercie, Czeladź, Wodzisław.] (The provincial towns are a delight. — Life goes on as normal. — "Short" brides of "tall" grooms. — The microbe of today's troubles has been found. — The artisans lose and the "Agudah" wins. — Gerer Hasidim evict the Trisker Hasidim.)
Long may they live, our dear provincial towns — they have breathed a fresh "life" into me. Taking the "provincial mail" into my hand, I expected that every little letter would no doubt be soaked through with bloody tears — how could it be otherwise? Such massacres, such destruction, so many Jewish lives cut short, and of Jewish property and goods — a heap of ruins left.
But I was mistaken: our brethren, the children of Israel, do not despair, do not fall into any mood of hopelessness, and the destruction has no effect whatsoever; the situation has absolutely not changed, everything is as before — the same ambitions, the same quarrels and... the "same" troubles.
Wolbrom is now suffering from an unforeseen "ailment", a "disease" for which no medicine helps; even Professor Einstein with his relativity theory will not be able to cure anything here.
— What?!!
A rumour has gone out about the girls of Wolbrom that they are short of stature... This "discovery" was made by the "Tse'irei Emunei [Yisrael]" in Zawiercie. And this is how it happened:
A member of the Zawiercie Tse'irim wanted to become the groom of a girl from Wolbrom. The "match" took place, the couple liked each other, and the in-laws on both sides began to prepare for the betrothal contract — that is, the bride's father got the dowry ready, and the groom's side got ready to take the cash...
Well, "along comes Gedaliah and makes a mess of it": the Tse'irim, hearing of their comrade's match, held a meeting, put the bride on the agenda — that is, they considered the bride's height — and issued a resolution that:
— The bride is short of stature...
And therefore the match cannot be carried out, because a Zawiercie Tsa'ir must receive, along with the big dowry, also — a tall bride...
———
A second fresh, wriggling discovery was also made by the Tse'irim in Czeladź. The local researchers, who have set up their scientific laboratory in the premises of "Beys Yaakov", came to the conclusion that the "source" of all troubles and calamities comes from "Haynt", "Moment" and the "Zaglembier Tsaytung"...
The discovery was published in the beys-medresh, where "grass"[?] orators called on the holy flock no longer to read the above-mentioned "free" newspapers; instead, every Jew who wants to become holy and pure should enrol in the newly founded "Agudah" and pay monthly dues.
The Gerer Hasidim in Czeladź are not sitting with folded hands either: they have cast an "eye" on the "outpost" [placówka] of the artisans, who gather on Sabbath at dusk in the vestibule of the beys-medresh and hold the third Sabbath meal (shalosh seudos) there.
Such impudence the Gerer could not bear. How can it be? Tailors, shoemakers and house-painters [malarze] should occupy the benches in the vestibule and sing zmires? No! This must not be allowed. And one dark Sabbath evening, while the artisans were sitting holding shalosh seudos, sunk in thought, the Gerer came in "with timbrels and dances", and where mouths had no control, hands "did the work"; after an attack that lasted about half an hour, the artisans were evacuated from the vestibule, and in their place the Gerer sang zmires.
As the "radio" informs us at the last minute, the "events" are expected to follow the weekly Torah portion: after "Tetse" comes "Tavo" — the artisans have received reinforcements and are preparing an offensive to reconquer the vestibule, where the "common folk of scissors and iron"[?] shall continue their melodies...
———
In Wodzisław [printed "Vaidislav"] the same Yente is also found, only she wears a different veil. The Gerer Hasidim of Wodzisław are not fighting the artisans, but "Yedid Nefesh" and "El Mistater".
There is a "Talmud Torah" in Wodzisław. The building is a bequest of a local Jewish woman, who donated the building for the purpose that poor Jewish children should learn Torah there.
And it came to pass that the proprietorship of the "Talmud Torah" was taken over by the honourable gentlemen of the "Agudah", which is led by the local rabbi; and since "Agudah" as such is, after all, Ger, and since in Ger they do not say "Anim Zmiros" after prayers, the rabbi too stood on guard and with his power of speech did not allow the worshippers of the "Talmud Torah", the Trisker Hasidim, to say "Anim Zmiros". Right after "Aleinu" the rabbi pronounced — "Gut Shabbes", and the "Anim Zmiros" was left hanging in the air...
But the "Agudah" did not stop at this point, because the Trisker Hasidim, the regular worshippers in the "Talmud Torah", had yet another "sin" on them: at shalosh seudos they used to sing "Yedid Nefesh" and "El Mistater". This caused great distress to the sharp Gerer, and they said: "come what may" — this disgrace we shall not allow. How can it be? The walls of the "Agudah" should hear "other elements" singing "foreign" zmires...
No sooner said than done: on the Sabbath, at shalosh seudos, while the Trisker Hasidim were immersed in devotion, several young fellows came in with Reb Pintshe at their head (Wodzisław also possesses a Pintshe, a bigger antique than the Będzin one) and...
The rest you can guess for yourselves; the main thing is that the "Yedid Nefesh" and "El Mistater" were evicted...
Ben Amotz.

An Unhealthy Phenomenon

[Będzin — Education.] (Why do they want to replace the Jewish teachers at the evening courses, the "komplety", with Christian ones? One must react to this)
Pedagogy is one of the most interesting and at the same time also the most responsible kinds of work. To be a pedagogue means to renounce the general material notions. A pedagogue, a teacher — no sooner does he take up a post than he becomes embodied in that little world of children, and body and soul he becomes bound up with the methods and with the pupils.
A pedagogue — no sooner does he cross the threshold of the school than he must at the same time also become a psychologist. He must know the psychology of the pupil, he must penetrate into his pupil, he must become embodied in the soul of the child, in the soul of the student.
It goes without saying that, apart from the fact that the effort here is great and hard, it is also a responsible one and moreover one that requires qualification. We know, for example, that there are teachers, men or women, who are sold for whole days to their work — not because all their hours are taken up, but simply because the school is their world and the pupils are their delight. With time the teachers are carried away by this little world of children, and later they no longer know that apart from this little world there is anything else.
This devotion we see mainly among the teachers of the people's schools, or as they are called in Polish, "szkoły powszechne", and thanks to this we meet children there who are attached to their teachers as to their parents. It goes without saying that this has a great effect on the studies and on their abilities; the children's love for their teachers we notice quite often during the performances.
Since compulsory schools have existed in Poland for quite a short time, we therefore have a certain contingent of older illiterates. The Będzin magistrate has therefore set up evening courses, "komplety", where adult craftsmen study in their free hours.
A few Jewish young people were found who, as pioneers [?], took upon themselves the organisation of the evening courses, the "komplety", so that in the course of several years a contingent of a few hundred pupils has been formed, with whom these young people are occupied. It is interesting to note in this connection that both the teachers and the pupils relate to the studies with rare devotion and love.
But this harmony has begun to be disturbed: there is a scheme for the Jewish pupils to get Christian teachers instead of Jewish ones. To this end they began to mix the small number of Christian pupils with the large number of Jewish ones, so that the Jewish teachers could be replaced by Christian ones.
The Jewish teachers, seeing that they were becoming a blind tool in the hands of whoever holds it [sic], reacted to the injustice and broke off the lessons in protest.
As we write these lines the matter has not been settled; it is still stuck at the same dead point. But be that as it may, and however the question is settled, it is outrageous to allow such a policy. Why are they casting eyes on the Jewish teachers and wanting to swap them for Christian ones? If perhaps they are not fit, then this must be justified to them, and afterwards other Jews must be taken on in their place. Let the Christian pupils have their Christian teachers, but the Jewish students must by all means study with Jewish teachers.
After all, one cannot toss about either the teachers or the pupils, who, by the way, are already grown-up young people; and while they study with so much love and devotion under the Jewish teachers, they will gain nothing from the Christian teachers, because, as said, the teachers must know the "physiogabie" [sic; probably psychology or physiognomy] of their pupils, they must delve into their souls; and thanks to this a mutual love has arisen between teachers and pupils.
It goes without saying that such harmony cannot come about between Christian teachers and Jewish pupils, because these are two worlds, two outlooks, two opposed notions.
But whatever may be, and whoever [?] it may be — what complaints can one have against such devoted and capable people, thanks to whom the courses have developed so nicely? Should their only defect be that they are Jews? After all, the pupils too are kneaded from the same dough.
Our city councillors ("ratmener") must speak up on this question; they must unconditionally react to this illogical phenomenon, by which the aim is to wrong people and take away their bread only because they are Jews — regardless of the fact that they are devoted to their work and give the komplety their whole soul.
From the practical point of view, too, the "Dozór Szkolny" [school board] ought not to permit such a strange change, because one must not forget that here we are dealing with grown-up young people who are complete illiterates, and only a Jewish teacher will [?] be able to speak to them, because only a Jew knows and feels the soul, the mind and the spirit of these young people; whereas a Christian teacher will by no means know how to deal with these pupils, to whom he is foreign and distant and for whom he is incomprehensible.
Moreover, it must not be allowed that Jewish young people be wronged only because their sole sin consists in being Jews, and hence brothers of their pupils.
Our communal workers must not allow these young people to be ignored. To such an undesirable [?] and unhealthy phenomenon one must unconditionally react at once and as is proper.
Selekt.
A Good Sabbath to You!

[Poem — the August 1929 riots in Palestine; Britain and the League of Nations.] "Anim Zemirot" — by "Shin".

Today one has no heart to greet the Sabbath with a "Gut Shabbes",
one is ashamed to sing "Anim Zemirot".
One wants to clench one's teeth hard,
one wants to curse — but whom?
Oneself, or the enemy?
One wants to run away like the prophet Jonah,
one wants to sleep it all away like Honi the Circle-Maker —
an empty world — no voice and no answer...
One wants to curse our naivety,
our pleading with the world so nicely,
our weakness, our trust,
our "stroyen" [arranging?], our building —
on all the waters and swamps,
on kind words, false [diplomatic] notes,
on empty talk and promises,
on gentile love and priestly blessings...
One wants to curse our bitter lot:
to take [?] every descent for a merit,
to consider the Tokhecha [the curse] an ascent —
and to make do with "shihe pie" [?]..
One wants to curse, one wants to rail:
at our forever not counting,
at our forever trading in papers,
at our forever letting ourselves be led astray...
* * *
Dear people of mine, forgive me!
Old you are, but you have no sense...
You can be bought off with a smile,
with a little compliment for your Bible.
Beloved people of mine, take no offence,
you are a weak diplomat,
even with Weizmann and with Sacher...
One wants to speak sharp words,
words like knives, words like swords —
to those who deal in our name,
to the signboards on our shops.
One wants, strongly [?], oh, to let out a scream,
but one does not want to hurt oneself —
and you must stifle your voice,
you know, it is a poor remedy..
One wants to punish the "League of Nations",
those pious milkers of peace,
those who today let us be slaughtered
as if today were a yesterday,
as if we lived in the Middle Ages,
and not under English administrators...

One wants to cry out at the top of one's voice
over the freshly brought burnt offerings.
What good are the fine words, the smooth ones,
if at heart the "League" is a rag!
What good is handing out the mandates
if words do not match deeds!
* * *
Oh, Jew, you have been fooled again,
what can one do, oh, dear brothers!
"Noah was a righteous man and blameless" —
we believed in England's trap.
We trusted the Kingdom of Britain,
wanted to get out of the inn of exile,
and we sent our children
to be slaughtered there like cattle...
Oh, Jew, you have been fooled again,
it is an old song among your songs!
* * *
One does not want to weep or lament,
one does not want to preach morals to the world,
have all the appointed ends then run out,
is there no one left to protect us?
You too, Reb Leib, have betrayed us,
to the shame of your diplomats!
You love our Bible, you say,
you bear great love for Isaiah.
That is not worth an onion to us,
better love the people of the Bible!
* * *
One does not want to weep or lament,
but how can one tell oneself a word of comfort?
Great is the pain and the shame,
forever fighting a band of murderers,
forever demanding — forever not getting,
forever consoling oneself with false victories;
forever burying holy dead,
forever calling for fasts!..
One does not want to weep and lament,
yet one wants to say a word of comfort after all:
we are a people of great sufferings,
we shall yet live to see many joys.
But you, world, beware of our curse,
we shall yet make an end of more than one nation.
With a whole people one must not trifle.
Beware, Lion [Arye], of our hatred!
Dr. A. Weisman — The Misled (Chapter 21)

(A novel of Jewish life in the old world, based on historical facts).

"If that's so," Jan burst out, "it won't take more than a couple of days and you will see Mania back home with you."
"If only. May God help," said old Dvora, not believing the "orel" [the uncircumcised gentile].
Jan took his leave and went out of the house with a rush, saying already at the door:
"Soon you will see Mania."
———
At that very minute the unknown szlachcic [Polish nobleman] rose from his place and followed Jan.
"I forgot to take something with me," he said, and quickly went off after Jan.
He had followed him barely a hundred paces. Coming up beside Jan, he laid his hand on Jan's shoulder and said:
"You are my prisoner!"
Jan was badly frightened and was at a loss for words. He soon came to himself and called out:
"Who are you, then? What right have you to arrest me? And what for?"
"Who I am," answered the stranger, "you will learn later. For the time being I can only tell you that I am an official sent by the government."
And saying this, the stranger showed him a policeman's badge. "I have orders to arrest you."
"What for?" Jan asked in a trembling voice.
"Because, according to your own words, which you just now said to the old Jewess, you take part in holding the girl Mania."
"It's not I who hold her, it's the convent that holds her!"
"To the devil with your convent! You are one of those who take part in it."
"But—"
"No 'buts', you are under arrest!" said the secret police agent, and meanwhile chained Jan to himself with a steel chain. "And I advise you not to show any resistance and to come [?] with me; but if you resist, I tell you, you will come off badly. You see this little tool," he said, showing him a revolver, "it will calm you down if you make the slightest move to stand against me! Patah shin — sha! [i.e. quiet!]"
The stranger blew a whistle. It did not take long, and a wagon harnessed to two fiery "chestnuts" sprang up as if out of the ground.
"One I've already bagged," the secret policeman said to two thugs who had jumped down from the wagon, "and as far as I can see, he is the most important one. He will be of very great use to us. Well, lads, why are you standing there like golems? Take him and sit him in the 'cart'!"
The two fellows took "Jan" "by the arms" from both sides to the wagon, hoisted him up the way a demon lifts a melamed, and sat him down in the wagon with a thrust. One sat on one side and the other on the other side next to Jan. The stranger sat down facing Jan. The driver urged the horses on with a "tare" [?], and within a minute they had dragged the wagon with its passengers off like a whirlwind and soon vanished into the darkness of the night.
———
When Mania's parents were told at the convent that their daughter no longer wanted to see or know them, they did not believe it. When they were led out of the convent and the gates closed again before them, they went off to the nearby [?] little town of Z., to inform the rabbi there and the town notables that the eldest sister had herself admitted to them that their daughter was in the convent, and to take counsel on what to do next.
The local rabbi and the respected householders had already told the unhappy parents once that as long as one did not know for certain where their daughter was, it was hard to do anything.
Now the hopes of Mania's parents of rescuing their child from gentile hands grew.
"With what can anyone help us now in our misfortune?" asked Chana with tear-stained eyes.

Będzin — Boy's Eye Put Out with a Board

During the break at the „Cheder Yesodei Torah“ several boys of the cheder were playing in the yard with a board. The 14-year-old Goldberg also took part in the game and received from a schoolmate a blow with the board in his right eye. The unfortunate boy was taken to hospital, where the doctors established that the eye must be removed in order to save the other eye.
In connection with the incident the management of the cheder with the fine name „Yesodei ha-Torah“ immediately turned to the starostwo [district authority] with a complaint, demanding that the carpentry workshops of Moshe Herszkowicz and Icze Radziński be removed by the police.
On the strength of this malicious[?] complaint the owners of the carpentry shops were summoned to the commissariat [police station], where they were informed of the decree, which had been instigated[?] by those who stand at the head of the Agudah cheder...
Trams „Jump“ the Rails

On Saturday night the tram came off the rails on Third of May Square [plac 3 Maja]. The same thing happened at the same spot on Monday afternoon.
Fortunately there were no human casualties; only the tram traffic was halted for about an hour.
Bricklayers' Savage Revenge

On Saturday night several Christian bricklayers forced their way into the flat of Moshe Wekselman on Modrzejowska[?] Street; they stabbed Wekselman with knives and inflicted several serious wounds on him.
The reason for the attack is that the bricklayers had claims against Wekselman concerning the pay for their work.
They Kill Each Other over a Customer...!

The crisis in trade continues, takings are very meagre, and when a customer shows up in the street he is literally „torn to pieces“ by the countless touts and grabbers. The merchants themselves also take part in this „work“, and this leads to street quarrels and brawls.
Such a savage scene took place on Tuesday on Kołłątaja Street, where the ready-made clothing merchants Potaszyński and Mrs. Melcer came to blows. The woman received cruel blows from her competitor, for which he will be called to account in court.
From the Synagogue Committee

The kehilla board and the newly elected synagogue committee held a meeting at which the question of electing a chairman of the synagogue committee was dealt with. Mr. Gershon Rechnic was elected chairman unanimously.
On taking up the office Mr. Rechnic began his activity regarding the arrangements in the synagogue, such as installing ventilators, increasing the number of lamps, etc.
The Gerrer Rebbe Passes Through

On Wednesday morning the Gerrer Rebbe passed through on the express („courier“) train from Marienbad[?]. At the station, as at all the stations, a large crowd of Hasidim welcomed the Rebbe.
On the same train the local rabbi also returned from his health cure.
First They Drank „L'chaim“, and Later One Killed the Other

In a beer tavern in Dańdówka the good friends Gajowski and Młodawski sat comfortably drinking liquor.
When they had become drunk, a quarrel broke out between them over a sweetheart [kochanka], and the „przyjaciele“ [friends] began to peck at each other like roosters.
The tavern owner then threw the drunkards out into the street, where a real battle only now flared up, in the course of which Gajowski struck Młodawski on the head with a board and killed him.
Last Tuesday G. sat in the dock at the Sosnowiec district court, which sentenced him to 6 months in prison.

Large meeting of the relief committee

[Sosnowiec — Palestine, relief.] In connection with the fact that the representatives of the "Agudah" refused to take part in the general committee for the collection campaign on behalf of the victims in Palestine (Eretz Israel), a large meeting was held in the premises of the "Merchants' and Industrialists' Association" at Kahalska [?] 10, with the aim of strengthening and reorganising the committee.
Rabbi Haner [probably Rabbi Hager] also took part in the meeting and delivered a brilliant lecture on the latest events in Palestine.
Rabbi Haner's speech made an enormous impression on those assembled, among whom were a great number of the local Jewish intelligentsia.
Fresh forces were co-opted to the existing committee, and it is to be hoped that Jewish Sosnowiec will not lag behind other towns and townlets and that the collection campaign will bring the proper result.
Jewish linen manufacturer from Kraków commits suicide in Sosnowiec

[Sosnowiec — suicide.] Last week the Kraków linen manufacturer Wolf Königsberger came here on business matters and took a room at the "Hotel Warszawski". In the course of his stay here no sign[?] whatsoever was noticed that Königsberger was carrying about with him such a criminal plan to commit suicide. On Thursday evening he ate supper and afterwards went off to his room on the third floor, where he hanged himself on a window beside his bed.
On Friday at 10 in the morning, when the hotel servant noticed that Königsberger had not yet come out of his room, the matter seemed suspicious to him and he informed the hotel owner of it, who unlocked the door and found the dead body of the hanged man.
A letter was found on the suicide in which he asks that his wife in Kraków be informed of it.
According to conjecture, the suicide found himself in a very critical situation and, finding no way out, he put an end to his life.
Königsberger's father, who lives in Kraków, is a religious Jew and therefore did not want to come to his son's funeral.
The suicide has left (literally "orphaned") a wife with 4 children.
Artisans' protest against the English administration in Palestine

[Sosnowiec — artisans, Palestine.] On Sunday a general meeting of artisans took place in their own premises.
The chairman, Mr. Silberschlag, opens the meeting, and on his proposal honour is paid to the new martyrs in Palestine (Eretz Israel), to the death of the leader of American Jewry, Louis Marshall, and to the members who died in the course of the year, and a protest resolution is adopted against the English administration, which allowed the bloody massacres in Palestine.
The resolution was sent to the Zionist Executive in London.
The chair is handed over to Mr. Eckstein, and reports on the activity and the treasury are given by Messrs. Silberschlag and Secretary Baum. From the reports it emerges that the association has a deficit of about 17 hundred złoty.
Because of the discussion, which dragged on for several hours, the item "elections" was not dealt with, and they will take place at the continuation meeting, which is being held next Sunday.
Killed his own brother

[Olkusz district — crime.] In the village of Targow [?], Olkusz district, a fight broke out between 2 brothers Palik, and one struck the other on the head with a chain and killed him.
The fratricide stood this week before the local district court, where the accused defended himself by saying that he committed the deed because "his brother never wanted to obey him".
The court sentenced him to 6 months in prison.
Simulated drunkenness and took a coat

[Sosnowiec — crime.] A Christian came into Mr. Weissberg's beer tavern and ordered a glass of beer. After drinking up the beer he "became drunk" and took a lady's coat that was hanging in the premises.
The theft was noticed in time, and the "drunkard" at once became sober...
A fight over a little rainwater

[Sosnowiec — brawl.] On Friday towards evening the young men Piekarski and Steinfeld of Targowa Street got the "urge" to wash themselves in honour of the Sabbath with rainwater.
Because each wanted to be the first to grab the "bargain", a fight broke out between them, and the rainwater turned into blood.
Officials of the sick fund before the court

[Sosnowiec — court.] The trial took place at the local district court against Messrs. Znażelski [?] and Juszczyk, officials of the sick fund (Kasa Chorych), who were accused of embezzlement in the books to the sum of 19,286 złoty.
Because the witnesses did not substantiate the accusation, the officials were acquitted.
Threw himself under the train

The unemployed Radławski, out of want and despair, threw himself under a passenger train running from Sosnowiec to Będzin.
The engine driver stopped the train instantly and thus still saved the would-be suicide, who sustained only several serious wounds.

Szuster and Kriger were sentenced to a fine of 9,800 zł. or 490 days' arrest.

Revenge on a competitor...
Last Wednesday, when the merchant Szmul Gut opened his shop, he saw that kerosene had been poured out on the floor. The matter seemed suspicious to him, and the next night he kept watch on the approach to his business.
Around 12 o'clock at night Mrs. Merc, the owner of a nearby business, came to the shop with her two brothers and set about the job of setting the shop on fire.

The police drew up a report, and the arsonists will stand trial.

A relief committee founded.
On the initiative of 'Poale Zion' (united with Z. S.) in Ząbkowice, a meeting was held on Saturday night with the aim of founding a united relief committee for the victims in Eretz Israel.
The meeting was opened by Mr. Uzjel Bugajski, who proposed honouring the martyrs in Eretz Israel and the leader who has just died, Louis Marshall. Then Mr. Josef Hirsz Radal (Agudah) was elected chairman of the meeting and Mr. E. Bugajski secretary. A discussion was then opened on how to conduct the relief campaign in Ząbkowice, and it was resolved that all the residents of Ząbkowice should be given aliyot on the Sabbath of parashat Ki Tavo, so that they would pledge donations for the victims in Eretz Israel. Then the following committee was elected: Urjel Bugajski (Zionist), Abraham Minc, shochet (Agudah), Icchak Dizenhojz (Mizrachi), Henech Goldzilber (Poale Zion), Jakob Goldzilber (Frajhajt), Szlama Bajtner (Poale Emune Israel), Chanoch Klajn (non-party) and Josef Ludn (non-party).

On Order in the Synagogue During the High Holy Days

[Synagogue — High Holy Days.] As our readers know, every year in the town synagogue, during the most solemn prayers of Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur, there occur regrettable unpleasantnesses — disputes, quarrels and even fistfights. All this happens because of the enormous crowding, and above all because of the chaos and disorder, which the synagogue gabbaim, for certain reasons, are by no means able to keep in check.
On the days of Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur the number of worshippers in the synagogue reaches thousands, may they multiply; the crowding is great, and the noise from the worshippers in the second half of the synagogue, by the door, is even greater; instead of reverence for a holy place, there reigns commotion and uproar. Even among the more conscientious and more sensible worshippers in the first half of the synagogue, near the Holy Ark, there are often scuffles [?], which lead to fistfights and later court cases [?], as has already happened even on Yom Kippur. Ordinary people off the street, who are not regular worshippers of the synagogue, occupy the seats of the regular worshippers. If someone pays for one "seat", he occupies instead of 1 place — 4 and even 5 places, for himself, for his under-age children, family and mere acquaintances. The same happens in the women's gallery, from which very often come shouts and the like, which cause interruptions of the prayers and outright disgrace and shame.
It is therefore our duty to draw the attention of the honourable synagogue committee, together with the kehilla leaders, to the need to take appropriate measures in good time (not police measures), so that order in the synagogue during the coming High Holy Days is maintained and is not disturbed by anyone. 1) The first task must be to sell only as many seats as actually exist; 2) not to allow 4 others to be occupied for one paid seat; 3) not to permit under-age children to be brought into the synagogue; 4) not to allow any pushing between the lecterns; 5) to bring order into the women's gallery; 6) not to show any excessive favour to privileged guests who come only for the High Holy Days; and 7) to stop the shouting in the lower part of the synagogue and on the bimah.
We hope that the synagogue committee will take note of our suggestions with gratitude, and that the worshippers themselves will appreciate the seriousness of the High Holy Days and will themselves help to ensure that order in the synagogue is kept in the best possible way.
—o—
A Jewish Mother in Paris Seeks Her Son from Zagłębie
Many years ago the couple Jakub Josef Fajgenbaum, born in Jędrzejów, and Brajndl Cukierman of Kielce were married. After the wedding the couple went to Warsaw. There was no domestic peace between the couple, and they came to Zagłębie, where they were divorced in Będzin; this was in the year 1900.
A year later, i.e. in 1901, the divorced woman left for Paris, leaving her little boy Lejb Ber with his father. Since then the mother has had no news at all of her son, and the son perhaps also does not know where his mother is.
As we are informed, the mother lives in Paris and is a very rich woman; her only aim is to learn what became of her son.
Interested relatives should apply about this matter to our editorial office, where they will receive more detailed information.
Israel Brafman, of blessed memory

[Będzin — obituary.] One of our best and most energetic members has been torn away from us in the bloom of life, at the age of 28.
Great is the grief and deep is the pain as we stand by the freshly filled grave of our dear comrade Israel Brafman, who was one of the best leaders of the National Cultural Organisation "Hashachar", where he stood at his faithful post for 10 years and distinguished himself in its finest work.
There was not a single campaign in which comrade Brafman was not an active co-worker, helping in its development. Beginning with the "Keren Kayemet LeIsrael", where he was secretary for many years, up to the campaigns of the "Keren Hayesod", KPAI [Palestine Workers' Fund], etc.
With the death of comrade Brafman, the Będzin national-Zionist youth has lost one of its best members and faithful sons, who fight for the upbuilding of the Land of Israel.
Alas for those who are gone and are not forgotten!
National Cultural Organisation "Hashachar".

[Sosnowiec — sport.] The Sosnowiec "Maccabi" on Sunday arranged a series of matches in aid of the relief committee for the victims in the Land of Israel. How far the Sosnowiec population has fulfilled its duty, and how "great" the sympathy for the sports club "Maccabi" has lately been, was shown by the quite small number of spectators who were at the sports ground.
The first match took place between
"Maccabi 2" — "Shimshon"-"Kinneret" 1:1

"Maccabi 1" — "Arje Gwiazda" 2:5 (0:2)

[Dąbrowa — merchants, town council, accident.] Meeting of merchants.
On Sunday, in the premises of the Artisans' Association, the general meeting of the "Merchants' Association" took place for the 3rd time. How great the merchants' interest in the institution is, is shown by the fact that although the agenda included the question of electing delegates to the assessment commission for turnover and income taxes, of 200 invited members barely 40 came...
The chair of the meeting is taken by Mr. G. A. Gutman. Reports on the institution are given by Messrs. Rechnic and Szpilberg. It turns out that the association has a deficit; the income does not cover even the rent...
After the reports Mr. Rechnic proposed that under such disastrous conditions and the complete lack of interest of the members he is no longer able to run the association, and the only way out is to liquidate the association.
The proposal is rejected and elections take place, which give the following result: elected [?] were: G. A. Gutman, B. Rechnic, H. Szpilberg, J. Parasol, A. Najfeld, J. Minc, D. J. Prewrawowicz [?] and L. Rechnic.
The constituent session takes place this coming Saturday night.

A letter to the editors.
Honoured Mr. Editor!
I ask you to publish the following letter in your esteemed newspaper:
For 3 months now I, with my wife and child, have been knocking about in the street. I, as a poor porter, have no possibility of obtaining a roof over the head of my unfortunate family. As long as it was warm, it was still bearable to stay[?] in the street, but for some days now the weather has been terribly wet and cold, and my wife and child are already ill from the weather.
For several weeks now I have been appealing to our h[onoured] city fathers about a dwelling for my unfortunate family, but unfortunately they have no interest in the matter, and one sends me on to the next...
I therefore turn, through your esteemed newspaper, to the whole Jewish population and also to the Jewish city councillors: have pity on an unfortunate family and get us a roof over our heads.
Respectfully,
Moshe David Mager, Będzin.

(Hebrew has been introduced in the public schools. — Will the children get anything out of it?)
It is a certain thing that the greatest part of our schoolchildren are brought up in the public schools [szkoły powszechne]; therefore we ought to reckon with them, and we would need to give the educational institutions a little more attention.
After all, every one of us knows that among the broad strata of the population there are all kinds of children, and we often come across very gifted and simply wonderful children — for that reason alone the problem ought to interest us more.
But this is a matter in which we, plain mortals [„flesh and blood“], can have no great say. The teachers have their regulations, their inspectors, and they must conduct their lessons according to the prescribed regulations.
From the present school year, however, something new has come in: they have begun to teach Hebrew in all the schools as a subject, apart from religion, which has existed until now too. It goes without saying that the phenomenon is to be welcomed. But let us take a look at how this function is being carried out.
If we take a pencil in hand and calculate, we will see that in Będzin, for example, we have 40 public schools, in which 2000 children study, and these 2 thousand children, who learn both religion and the Hebrew language, are „processed“ by a total of three people. It goes without saying that no more than one hour, or at most 2 hours a week, can be devoted to it — so the question arises: can three teachers manage to teach 2 thousand children? And can a child get anything out of such teaching? Does such learning not make an impression of ridiculousness? We know, after all, that nothing can come of such teaching, that the child can get nothing out of it. Of course the parents not only are not versed in these matters and give themselves no account of them, but on the contrary, they are sure that their children will learn Hebrew, and many of the parents are certain that the Hebrew of the public school will replace the cheder for them.
These parents really ought to know that this is nothing at all, that it is no more than a medicine in the dose of half a teaspoon, and say what you will — such teaching looks like a kind of toy, because neither can the teachers manage, in so short a time, to teach such a contingent of children, nor can the children learn anything here.
Grünbaum [Yitzhak Grünbaum] fought in the Sejm for Hebrew to be introduced in the public schools for the Jewish children, but he did not reckon that it would simply turn out a caricature. Either — or: either one teaches so that it may be called teaching, so that the children benefit from the instruction; if not, it is better not to begin at all, and one should not lead the parents into expenses and tell them to buy Hebrew books.
If one does mean to teach the Hebrew language, then it must be introduced properly [?]. A number of teachers must be engaged who will be able to teach properly all the children attending the public schools.
After all, there are parents' committees attached to the schools, which are supposed to look at what the lessons look like — so why should they not take an interest in seeing that the teaching proceeds properly and that the children can really benefit from it? There is no sense in teaching in such a way; it looks no more than a kind of fiction — so what is it needed for? Rather than learning in such a way, it would be better to leave things as they were.
There is, after all, no purpose in tormenting pupils for nothing. The children will by no means learn anything if things stay the way they are today.
We do not know how this works in practice in the public [powszechne] schools — whether the heads have the possibility of increasing the number of hours and engaging an enlarged teaching staff, or whether this belongs to the inspector, who possibly must in turn apply to a higher authority; but be that as it may, it is a matter for the committees that exist in every school, made up of the children's parents. On them lies the duty to supervise these lessons and to see that they are arranged in such a way that the pupils really learn the language, and that it is not turned into a kind of decoration giving the impression that they learn there just to fulfil an obligation.
There is no doubt that the children of the public schools, boys as well as girls, would really benefit from that little bit of Hebrew, because the greater number of children, as soon as they leave the walls of the public schools, are already harnessed to carry the heavy material yoke.
The school committees must take note of this and consider well what function they fulfil. If they cannot find their own way in the question, they can also arrange conferences, to which they should invite conscious parents who would help them solve the question.
In any case this is a matter on which one is obliged to dwell and to treat from every side, so that the blame should not fall on those who stand at the helm.
We believe that as long as there is good will and the question is not neglected, something can certainly be achieved; and one is certainly obliged to do something so that it does not stay as it is — neither this world nor the next: one can neither say that Hebrew is being taught, nor say that nothing at all is being taught. To leave it hanging in the air like this is certainly not fair.
Selekt.
The Economic Situation (Business Conditions) in Poland

In the latest issue of the journal "Koniunktura Gospodarcza" we find the following characterisation of the economic situation in Poland.
The sharp crisis that set in in the Polish economy at the beginning of 1929 has continued without a break and persisted also in July of this year. The critical situation expressed itself in a tendency to reduce production and in a worsening of the ability to pay. The limitation of working days in industry covers almost all branches of production. The process of deterioration proceeded at full impetus, but only gradually did it become so bad that industry and trade entered a phase of depression.
Building activity in July was carried on at exactly the same pace as in the months of May and June. Considerably fewer workers were employed in building work this year than in last year's building season. Similar is the situation in the production of building materials. The mineral industry is working relatively well in July, but the brickworks have not reached this year the level of last year's output. The ironworks too have not managed to produce as much as was produced in the last months of 1928. Nevertheless, the situation of ironworks production is not bad at all. After 2 months of standstill in the Polish ironworks, orders increased strongly in July (almost as much as in July 1928). In July the number of workers employed in the metal industry fell considerably. The strike and lockout in the Białystok district contributed to this in particular.
Among other branches, in the textile industry in July they began to halt the further reduction and limitation of production that had prevailed until then. On the contrary, at the beginning of August a partial revival began in textile production. Other branches show no tendency towards strong stagnation.
In the coal industry a "good time" continues without a break, i.e. a great deal is being produced and there is a considerable sales market.
Owing to the usually prevailing tendency of worsening business conditions, efforts are being made to enlarge sales possibilities by strengthening Polish exports, especially in the ironworks industry and partly in the textile industry (chiefly woollen goods).
On the labour market no particular changes have occurred; given the existing tendency to limit workers in industry and the small possibilities for the further development of the building trade, the prospects of a demand for new hands are now weakening.
The supplying of industry and the ironworks with raw materials had to be stopped because of the reduction of production. For the same reason the import of foreign raw materials was also limited. Machines and apparatus for industry are being imported continuously in large quantities.
In the prices of industrial products no general changes in a downward direction have occurred; from the fall in prices it was the textile industry that suffered in the first place, whereas the prices of glass and of some machines rose; the wholesale prices of raw materials did not change.
In percentage terms, the number of protested bills of exchange at the "Bank Polski" fell from 5.81 to 5.37 per cent. But at the same time the sum of protested bills grew considerably (according to the figures of the Main Statistical Office) from 98.5 million zł. in June to 115.8 million zł. in July.
The month of July brought an improvement in the situation of agriculture, and although grain prices fell and a shortage of cash is felt, there are good prospects for an improvement of the situation in agriculture. The good harvest gives good hopes. The easier possibilities of selling cattle, poultry and dairy produce also give partial compensation for the damage the peasants suffered from frozen crops.
The crisis, which struck the textile industry very sharply, will hopefully pass entirely in the very near future.
What Was Heard, What Was Seen.

[Będzin and district — weekly feuilleton, satire.] Caught and handed over for print by Ben Amotz.

On the "Pure Field" [the cemetery].
All articles have their seasons. The Beis ha-Chaim [cemetery] too has its season. "When Elul comes in, joy is increased" [a deliberate twist of "When Adar comes in"] — when the month of Elul arrives, the Beis ha-Chaim comes alive... especially now that the "communication" there has become a comfortable one: the tram has a "przystanek" [stop] there, so one can permit oneself such a pleasure...
The entrance to the Beis ha-Chaim is guarded by all kinds of poor folk, professionals and "respectable" ones [?], who make use of the season: hardly do you take out your purse than they fall upon you like bees: "Petershi" [?], a poor widow with seven swallows [small children]! Give alms to a cripple! A Jewish woman with a deep "kupka" [?] tugs you by the coat-tails: Reb Jew, give something — not, God forbid, for herself; she "cares" for others...
Entering the Pure Field, various voices and wails carry from every corner; everyone has his own "bundle" [of troubles], and here, at the holy place, the bundles are unpacked.
Here stands a girl, a "garsonutka" [?] [apparently a girl with a modern bobbed "garçonne" haircut], laying flowers on a grave; she takes a photograph out of her handbag. When she notices my glance, she wipes the tears from her eyes — after all, it isn't proper to cry — and takes out of the same sakwojażka [handbag] a red stick [lipstick], smears her lips, then licks them off, and takes leave [?] with her [waiting?] cavalier [word unclear].
A little further, a second scene: a Jew, a merchant, has come to "consult" [Pol. radzić się] with his [late] wife: to marry or not to marry? He has come to her for her consent; but she does not answer, so he holds:
— "Silence is as good as admission."

A Fresh Question and an Old Answer.
To a Hasidic Jew, a man who studies Torah for its own sake and not for the sake of politics, come two Agudah men [members of Agudat Yisrael], collecting for the victims in the Land of Israel [the August 1929 riots].
The Hasidic Jew does not refuse, and hands them a donation.
— What? Such a small sum? We did not count on that. Why should we be worse off than the Zionists? They — we are sure — will probably get a bigger donation from you; how can that be? Do they have so little to dig into from the money that is given for Zionist purposes...
— Hm, quite right, you really speak justly, I fully agree with your words; only one small thing will I point out to you, gentlemen, namely: I do not wish to plead that the Zionists are entirely kosher. But be that as it may, it is plain to us that the Zionists have also created something real: dozens of flourishing colonies have been built with Keren Kayemet money. Whereas from your money collections, you "kosher" Jews, there always becomes a "thing hidden from the eye"...
Having received such an honest answer, the "Agudah" collectors snatched up the 5-złoty donation and were out of the house.

The Ice Has Moved...
For years the "fortress" remained untouched. Hosts of Jewish children streamed there, to the purely Polish secondary school, brought a "tithe" to the priests of that place of worship, and hoped to receive a smile from those who stuff themselves with Jewish money.
And the fathers, and even more the Jewish mothers, trembled — God forbid — to utter a word concerning the school; they swallowed a great many bitter feelings and watched how their children were forced to come to the Sabbath lessons and write.
The only comfort for this bit of trouble was that at the end of the school year Zośka or Bronka would receive the matura [school-leaving certificate].
A mere trifle — ma—tu—ra!
And the awaited salvation did not come. The only "Maske"-type [?] in the school, in order to give satisfaction to her bread-givers, took revenge on the "żydowskie uczennice" [Jewish girl pupils] and played them a "kawał" [prank]:
— to stay back another year in the same class.
From this experiment the "fortress" shook, the ice moved, and the Jewish mothers suddenly opened their eyes and saw that:
— Zośka can get the matura in a Jewish gymnasium, which also has "goyish" rights [state accreditation]...

A Gentile's Mistake...
Our likeable town councillors went to Poznań to visit the exhibition [the 1929 General National Exhibition, PeWuKa]. They travelled like the pairs in the days of the Flood — man and wife; and the councillor who had nothing with which to represent himself in the great world took along his daughter, just so as not to be an exception among the "Europeans"...
So our portly councillor, Reb Moshe, strolls along the streets of Poznań, a gold pince-nez on his nose, his face haughty, head held high — not at all like an exile-Jew from Congress Poland.
He was met by some Poznanians, pupils [?] ["sekretarczyks" — word unclear], who conducted the following discussion among themselves:
— "Czy to Żyd?" [Is that a Jew?]
— "Podobny do Żyda, ale..." [Looks like a Jew, but...]
— I'll tell you, my friends, who he is — he is a Ślązak [Silesian].
— Yes, yes, a "Jewish Ślązak"...

The "Agudah" Takes Revenge...
This is no news to us. The revenges of the "Agudah" are very well known to us. Because of the "Daf Yomi" the "Agudah" took revenge and abolished the yeshiva in the Będzin Beis Midrash; because of their politics we lost a second Jewish ławnik [member of the town executive board]; [they] broke up the relief action for the ruined Yishuv in the Land of Israel; and now we face a fresh revenge on their part.
— They are taking revenge on the "Talmud Torah" and refuse to pay the monthly dues.
— What happened?
— The gabbaim of the "Talmud Torah" protested against the young rascals of the "Mikveh-Sheet" [a scurrilous leaflet], in which Mr. Fürstenberg was smeared.
The collector relates that when he comes for the monthly dues to an Agudah man, he gets the answer:
— "Money for the 'Talmud Torah'? Go to Fürstenberg"... We have to pay monthly dues for our "tsatink" [?] [apparently "newspaper"]..
And the Talmud Torah gabbaim are quite pleased with this answer: it is better for us — they say — that the "Agudah" sends us to Fürstenberg; were it the other way round... the Talmud Torah would long since have closed...
Neglect Means Crime

[Sosnowiec and Będzin — opinion; public representation, the turnover tax and the attachment of the county to Silesia.]
(People's representatives must always [?] be on the watch and guard their mission.)
When a bad decree happens to fall upon us, when a heavy tax comes along that ruins the masses, people begin to shout and make a noise until the heavens open. Here they throw themselves upon the representatives, and there the representatives are good for nothing. In short, there is an uproar and a clamour and an agitation, so that one is ready to do who knows what; but how long does all this last? No more than a few hours or days; the heat cools down and one begins to get used [?] to the bad, to the hard.
It goes without saying that it is very bad to get used to the bad; but what is characteristic is that one will never try beforehand to put one's hand into cold water in order to avoid and remove the bad from the very beginning.
More than once we have seen various decrees arise in our everyday life which made Jewish livelihoods harder, and the interesting thing is this: that after the fact it was seen that one had not previously grasped what it was about; and had one known at the time what was at stake and how far it would have bad repercussions in the future, one would have fought beforehand, and every possible means would have been taken not to let the situation worsen.
So orientation, foresight, examining every project from all sides from the very beginning, plays a great role in our life, as the past has already needed [thus: "gebroykht"] to prove to us.
Now too we must look with open eyes at the project that has now been put forward, that the Będzin county [powiat] should belong to Upper Silesia [Górny Śląsk].
At the given moment we cannot pronounce a firmly resolved, decisive opinion on the question; it may be that this will be a disadvantage for us and, who knows, perhaps at some time an advantage. We have not yet given ourselves a clear account of the question, we have not studied it from all sides; but in any case one must not pass over this project with a light conscience, because for us it is a very, very complicated matter on which one must dwell with full awareness and with complete deliberation. We know only that the big industrialists are strongly against the proposed project and are fighting with self-sacrifice so that it should not be realised; and it is possible that it could also ruin our Jewish merchant, who could be swallowed up by the well-organised and trained merchant class of Upper Silesia.
As we see, then, the question must be considered from all sides with full attention and seriousness; but when one sees with what frivolity our representatives treat this important question, the heart truly aches.
For example, we know that last week a meeting of the council of the Zagłębie merchants' associations took place in Będzin, on whose agenda stood the above-mentioned question and [the question] of putting forward candidates to the Chamber of Commerce for the turnover [tax] ("umzats") for the year 1929. It would seem that both questions are so serious and important that any explanation and elucidation is superfluous — and yet Sosnowiec, Jewish Sosnowiec, did not send its representatives to such an important meeting.
What, then, can one call such conduct? What kind of tactic is that, what kind of understanding of the people's interests? Can one really call it mere indifference? Is not such indifference worse than any crime whatsoever? Than any harm to the people, which individuals cannot pay for? Do the representatives understand what mission they have taken upon themselves, when they assess ["shetsn"] such responsibility so lightly?
It is sad and painful when, on such important matters, one has to wake the representatives so that they do not neglect what has been laid upon them, what they understood that they must guard.
Let us take even the less important question, the candidates for the turnover tax: how many victims has this tax claimed among us? How many incorrect assessments arose, owing to which many solid and large firms had to leave the scene entirely? Surely the past years should have taught us something, so that we know how far it is possible to guard the positions to which we are admitted.
And now concerning the second question, where it is in sum [?, "s"h"] a matter of our county being assigned to the Upper Silesian Voivodeship [województwo]. We have already said that we know for certain [thus; "not" probably missing] what results this may bring; but one fact is clear: that its coming into being can certainly provoke a revolution in our world of trade and industry, and this we must certainly reckon with. In any case the question is so important that we should devote time to it. The matter is so important that all citizens should acquaint themselves with it, so that everyone can have a say in the question. For this is an event of the greatest importance.
It is surely high time no longer to remain indifferent to the most important interests and to the most serious questions. We have already paid so dearly for our indifference — let us at least now look with a clear gaze at our future. We surely cannot make light of what is so important, of what means human existence, human life.
Sosnowiec frightens us. Sosnowiec has already now, at the very beginning, shown a rare indifference to the two questions mentioned, which are so important in our economic life. Apathy and indifference to such cardinal questions can be called nothing other than an incomparable crime [printed "peyrbrekhn"], and it must not be allowed to repeat itself, because in that case it would already have become humdrum ("vokhndik"), and humdrumness is a dangerous thing in our everyday life.
We must demand of our representatives in Sosnowiec that they not neglect our interests, that they not regard as a trifle what has such important significance, what is an important event in our grey life.
Let our representatives remember that in the end they are responsible for every mistake they make. True, the responsibility is not a legal and material one, it is only a moral one; but a moral responsibility has much more weight for a people than a legal one. Moral responsibility is the highest expression, which can never be paid for with money.
Let our people's emissaries take this well to heart, let them always carry these "Ten Commandments" before their eyes, for to take upon yourself the mission of being a people's representative and then not to guard it is no trifle, especially when it concerns questions of the greatest importance.
It is high time that our representatives understood the true meaning of being a people's representative, and once they take the office upon themselves they must fulfil it completely.
Let the Sosnowiec people's representatives remember well that they are responsible for every mistake they make; let our people's emissaries remember that the interests of the community cannot be exchanged for private matters that interest only individuals.
The highest ideal for public representatives must be to work conscientiously and not to let slip a single position when it is a matter of fulfilling the mission for the people and its interests.
Dr. Papuri.
Selichot (Jewish Motifs)

By L. Glanc.
Folk creation has, as if on purpose, turned the first night of Selichot into a kind of mystical impromptu celebration, an unexpected, unprepared ceremony.
Precisely on a perfectly plain, ordinary Saturday night, after the traditional Jew has taken heartfelt leave of his Sabbath Queen in the twilight melancholy, something like a black cloud draws near over the Jewish skies and angrily announces the tidings of the "Days of Awe" in the Jewish street — the tidings that one must begin to "gird one's loins" for the Day of Judgment.
Late at night the Jew still sits wide awake and hums to himself, as if it were not meant for him, his usual Saturday-night tunes; and even the oriental idyll "Eliyahu ha-navi, Eliyahu ha-Tishbi" is this time disturbed by nothing at all; after the King-David-like Melaveh Malkah with its artificial optimism, accompanied by melancholy eastern melodies, people even go to rest as on all the nights of the whole year — and hush, it grows quiet in the Jewish houses, quiet in the Jewish lanes too...
And only afterwards, when everyone is sound asleep, the synagogue beadle comes up to the window and knocks three times, sternly, with a special motif of dread: "Arise to the service of the Creator, for that is what you were created for!"
And at the beadle's call great and small, men and women, respond; they quickly throw on their clothes and with a tremor in their hearts run chaotically to Selichot in the deep, sinking night.
— — —
But here in the synagogue, too, everything is unexpected, confused and sudden. On Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur the whole congregation repeats the High Holiday liturgical tunes after the cantor, and often the Jews lead the cantor along the smooth road of the traditional ("skarbowe") melodies. At Selichot, however, it is the other way round: everything runs ahead of the congregation, and it is not yet fully at home in the High Holiday sounds. And that is perhaps why something truly tears in everyone's heart at the Rosh-Hashanah "Yitgadal", which suddenly bores into the ear and announces that it has already begun, that it is coming, on its way — the Day of Judgment — and one must begin to think about something...
The Selichot motifs are therefore reminding, announcing — I would say, if one may put it that way — "proclaiming and making known"..
Almost all the High Holiday liturgical tunes are recalled in the Selichot in one way or another, beginning with the awesome "Yitgadal" and ending with "Ashamnu".
Musically, of course, the most accomplished is the "Yitgadal", which is without doubt one of the finest oriental themes.
Whoever is able to grasp the "Yitgadal" musically will surely admit that in due course it could serve as the foundation for a complex modern Jewish musical work, and that the "Yitgadal" theme is still waiting for its redeemer.
As said, the "Yitgadal" is not a Selichot motif, but an announcement of Rosh Hashanah! The same can be said of "Zekhor lanu" with "Teviyenu", which recall the Rosh-Hashanah Malkhuyot, Zikhronot and Shofarot. At the end of "Va-yikra le-khol ha-amim" the announcement motif already reaches its climax, and a Rosh-Hashanah awe falls on the synagogue as it prepares to welcome the unexpected guest with his peculiar sounds.
But beyond all this the first Selichot also possess their own specific motifs, which characterise them alone and have no equal anywhere at all. Such is, for example, the wonderful "Be-motza'ei menuchah", which is wholly Saturday-night folklore and which tells with its sounds the story of the impromptu celebration: "Be-motza'ei menuchah kidamnukha techilah" — here, on a plain Saturday night, we came to you early and suddenly demanded that you "incline your ear" and listen "to the song and to the prayer". This is an intimate prologue to a difficult drama which will very soon have to be played out between God and man, and which begins musically quite calmly, almost singing, steals up to God so brotherly that [the worshipper] is meanwhile already pouring out his whole bitter heart at "Retzeh atiratam be-omdam ba-leilot"; there the prayer bursts in with such unexpected impetus and caresses itself before the Master of the Universe with special strength and a mystical Selichot grace.
Even more Selichot-like are the traditional ("skarbowe") motifs of "Shome'a tefillah", which represent a synthesis of a love song to God and the complete self-annihilation of man's worth. Here the sounds always had to manoeuvre between the two basic moments: between solemn ecstasy over the Almighty God (Atah moshel be-ge'ut ha-yam, atah bakata ma'yan va-nachal etc.) and the humble self-abasement and nothingness of lowly man (Asher be-yado nefesh kol chai, ha-neshamah lakh etc.). The two contrasting elements find their resolution in the victory of the second moment. The "Shome'a tefillah" indeed ends in weak tones, without ecstasy and faith ("Aseh le-ma'an shemekha", "Eikh niftach peh lefanekha" etc.).
The same can be said of the Selichot "major figures"[?] of "El erekh apayim", which symbolise an artificial faith in a God of mercy. All these cadences, "Va-yikra be-shem Adonai, ki al rachamekha ha-rabim anu betuchim" etc., which are repeated very many times, are also used on Yom Kippur and especially at Ne'ilah. And here one can clearly see the colossal difference in mood. Then, on Yom Kippur, all these cadences are lively, joyful, energetic and bold. One may be physically exhausted from fasting, but in spirit one is winged with hopes, one presses toward the gate, one breaks through gates: "Petach lanu sha'ar"; one has almost nothing left to lose, "ki fanah yom" — and take, too, the piece of the heart-rending "Shema kolenu", which on Yom Kippur is literally transformed into a musical-dramatic scene.
At the first Selichot, however, spirits are still calmer. It is only the prologue, the announcement of the drama and not the drama itself; one still stands at a distance, one trembles, one does not yet know what tone to take with the Master of the Universe, one has only just to begin to plead, and one has been woken suddenly from sleep, unprepared — and who knows whether anything will be achieved, who knows...
And that is why the Selichot are musically never finished. The congregation is still saying the remnants of the Selichot in every corner: "Anenu Adonai anenu", others say "Va-anachnu lo neda mah na'aseh"; people lose their way, something is not sure of itself, and the cantor has already left the lectern; for him the Selichot night is already over. And I would venture to say that precisely on that night, the night of Selichot, we are truly in a confessional mood, fallen — and not in the grandiose night of remorse of "Kol Nidrei"..
