[Eretz Israel — the 1929 riots; letter from Jerusalem.] By Shabtai Weiss (Jerusalem).
One hundred and twenty-six victims have fallen for the sanctification of God's Name and for the sanctification of the Land of Israel — besides more than one hundred and fifty wounded, who are in the hospitals. A bloody milestone on the road of our upbuilding.
For years, for years we have been building and creating in the Land, peacefully and quietly, and suddenly, unexpectedly, a wave of wild, incited Arabs flooded over us — and the bloody wave found us unprepared, but strong and firm as the rocks. It was not only the lives of individual Jews and their property that the enemy aimed at. Against our collective soul he sharpened his spear; our hope of life he wanted to stifle. And the hellish plan ran up against an armoured popular will. Heavy and bitter are our sacrifices, but we did not bend, did not break and did not lose our heads in the bloody days. These days will remain in our memory, and in the memory of our Arab neighbours and English rulers, not only as bloody days but also as days of Jewish heroism, which neither we nor they had suspected before. Not only lamenters will write their dirges over these days; poets and bards too will sing of the heroic stand of the Jewish Yishuv in these very days, from which coming generations will draw courage and pride.
Our wounds are still fresh and painful, and it is still too early to draw, under the bloody lesson we have received, the bottom line that is needed so that the recent events may be transformed by us into that kind of defeat in which lies hidden the kernel of future victory. But some remarks can already be made now on account of that bottom line.
*
Let it be recorded for generations, proudly and boldly: the holy children of the self-defence, of Jewish self-protection, or, as it is called here for short, the Haganah — wherever they were, they rescued the lives and the honour of the Jewish Yishuv. Now we know: Jerusalem, God forbid, was liable to become like Hebron or Safed, on a larger scale. Those two young men who, like Nahshons, leapt into the very midst of the hundred-headed mob of wild and armed Arabs and opened hot fire before the eyes of the English policemen, who had become confused and bewildered — not only scattered that mob and foiled the massacre plan against the densely populated Jewish quarter of Meah Shearim, but also, to a great extent, clipped the wings of the attackers on Jerusalem in general.
This is only one detail out of hundreds of deeds of valour, and it is mentioned here not in order to tie [?] crowns on the Haganah, but so that we may draw from it the proper moral for the future.
It seems that we must beat our breasts with "al het" for having so neglected, and having paid so little attention to, the question of security and protection in Eretz Israel.
"It is an iron law of colonization that a people whose protection and defence have been entrusted to the sons of another people may not dream of true colonization. Defence by a foreign force is not only dangerous in the political sense; it is also bad defence."
"If, in the course of two and a half years, no attacks have lately occurred in Eretz Israel, that fact is no contradiction of our arguments; on the contrary, it confirms them. The attacks did not occur, not because the Arabs 'are afraid', but because immigration has fallen sharply, and with the rise of immigration the dangers rise. And the English garrison, which has been reduced to 3000 men and is permeated with a 'neutral spirit', cannot, to our regret, serve as a sufficient guarantee against this danger. This is as clear as one times one — is one."
These words were written by Jabotinsky in 1925, before the 14th Congress — and now they have come true so bloodily. For one reason or another, only a small part of the Yishuv used to speak of not relying on foreign protective forces and to think of defence by our own forces. The bloody events have brought a radical change in this respect. The question of a legalized armed self-defence has become the concern of the entire Jewish Yishuv and is now the problem of problems. True, the solution is not simple and is not ready to hand. But all political forces will have to be concentrated in order to find an appropriate answer to the question, now that the bloody experience has shown that the protection of Jewish life and property must be handed over to our own forces.
*
The British Eretz Israel administration. For those who live and create in Eretz Israel there is not the slightest doubt that the criminal attitude of this administration, which showed itself so glaringly in the recent events, must be brought to an end. Where did the administration get such a regime of "liberalism", bordering on anarchy, which gave full freedom to the work of all sorts of hotheads among so half-wild a population? Was there here a neglect of British interests out of ill will or out of small-mindedness, or did this administration even persuade itself that by sharpening the antagonisms between the two peoples in the Land it serves higher British interests? — That is study material for the Commission of Inquiry that is to come here, or [?] — it can no longer interest us. For the Yishuv in the Land, which has drunk the cup of blood that this administration let be prepared for it, it is clear that those officials who have become entangled in the local influences, in the game of intrigues conducted by all sorts of clans and forces and pedigreed families with crafty, hair-splitting Levantine cunning — may not and cannot carry out the Balfour Declaration.
All this is clear, but what must be stressed in this connection is, again: our own negligence, our own guilt. If our political leadership, which is in constant contact with the central British Government in London and with the local English administration in Eretz Israel, could in recent years repeat its stereotyped assurances about the good state of our political affairs — it is our own guilt that we were content with the moderate, all too moderate, line in politics. If in the political circles of London it was known with certainty, after an inspection tour by a certain Orient expert in Egypt and in Eretz Israel in the past months of March to May, that in August—September of this year attacks on the Jews in Eretz Israel would take place, as Edwards*) is able to relate in the "Vossische Zeitung" — and our political leadership knew nothing of it, then that is our sin.
*
And now a few words to you, brothers in Zagłębie.
For us in Eretz Israel there are no two opinions: the Jewish people will worthily honour and sanctify the memory of the fallen only when it fulfils the words of the memorial prayer — "and may their souls be bound up in the bond of life" — when the people wraps and weaves their holy souls into the life-work of Eretz Israel; the blood of the martyrs will find its redress only through enormously intensified work for the good of Eretz Israel, work of unusual intensity and of a scope never seen until now. An epoch of Sturm und Drang must now begin for the continuation of the upbuilding of Eretz Israel, an epoch in which a flood of energy and creative power shall consolidate and [expand?] what has been created and exists, and lay further foundations for new positions — that is the Kaddish the Jewish people must say after the fallen martyrs. That, and only that, must be the unequivocal answer of the Jews of the whole world to the recent events.
Among the many telegrams received here from the various centres of the Diaspora, there was one from a far-flung Jewish community, in which the confidence was expressed "that the victims will not have been in vain". We here in the Land believe in this firmly and unshakeably. We believe that there, where buildings of brick were destroyed, we shall now build granite. If, according to our tradition, the lips of the righteous murmur in the grave when the living recall their thoughts, then this is the pure prayer of the fallen martyrs: would that the burning [?] spirit of intensified upbuilding work in Eretz Israel take hold of [?] all, all in the various centres of the Diaspora. In the place of each fallen martyr there must now come, as Weizmann says, a thousand new immigrants. For every pound of Jewish property that has been ruined, 1000 new pounds must be invested. With great and strong deeds in the political, colonizing and cultural fields we must now prove that there is no force capable of diverting our movement and our work, which draw their sustenance from thousand-year-old beliefs and prophetic destinies, from their historic course. Only in this way can the bloody events become part of that power "which ever wills evil and ever works 'good'" — as Goethe expresses it.
Do you feel, brothers in Zagłębie, the burning of that pure prayer? Are you ready to answer substantially, strongly and fittingly the voice of "your brothers' blood crying out to you from the ground"? Are you, at least now, at this time, "sick with identification" — that is, do you feel everything that happened in Eretz Israel as though it had happened among you and to you? Do you, at least now, in the glow of the spilt blood, make a reckoning of the soul that we here are emissaries, sent from the depths of the people to realize its eternal ideal, and that you may not leave us standing alone on the front of work and blood? —
Answer, brothers in Zagłębie.
Jerusalem, Menahem-Av 5689.

"What do you mean, with what?" Reb Zelig argued. "We will go to the great 'ksiondzes' [księża, priests] in the guberniya [province], so that they order Sister 'Irena' to give us back our daughter peacefully. It is none of her business whether our daughter wants to know us or not."
"The great 'ksiondzes' will most likely side with the Sister. With fine little speeches they will turn our heads, thinking that we will grow tired and give up our child. Don't forget, Zelig, that the longer it drags on, the more we are reduced to ruins. The mill stands idle, the house is abandoned, we are homeless wanderers, and we don't even see Chaim. He seems to have already pulled back from Mania and from us. The best thing is for us to go straight to the guberniya, to the governor, and tell him everything — how our child was robbed from us."
"We will first hear what the rabbi tells us and what advice people will give. I think the best thing is simply to go peacefully and plead with the 'ksiondzes'. We are Jews, after all; we must see to it that, God forbid, nothing bad comes of it for the Jews. You are playing with fire with Sister 'Irena', may her name be blotted out! She keeps company with the greatest people; the greatest landowners and counts pay her visits. So what can we poor Jews do? How can we quarrel with her? You see, after all, that as long as we went peacefully, with pleading, with weeping, they did let us into the convent, and we have already found out for certain that our Mania is there."
Reb Zelig Sarahs and his wife came to the nearby Jewish shtetl Ts. and began going round among acquaintances and respectable householders to take counsel with them. All of them, from the rabbi to the town's rich man, said that if Sister 'Irena' does not want to hand over their daughter, it is bad — nobody can do anything to her. All the more so as she says that Mania no longer wants to see her parents.
The whole shtetl Ts. spoke with anger and contempt about Mania, who no longer wants to know or see her parents.
Mania's parents insisted that this cannot be, that Mania should no longer want to know them; that it is nothing but an invented lie — a lie as the cross is a lie — so as not to let them see their child.
"We have nothing else left to do," the unhappy parents said to the rabbi and the householders of the town, "but simply to go to the guberniya and ask the governor to demand that we be allowed to see our child. And if we hear from her own mouth that she does not want to know us, we will sit shiva as for the dead and forget her."
"You will achieve nothing," the rabbi answered them. "They will make you promises and put you off from day to day. Months will go by, you will only tear yourselves away from your businesses, from your livelihood, and you may, God forbid, be reduced to ruins. Trust in God, blessed be He, that He will help you in your misfortune."
"I don't need any mill or any house," Chana answered, weeping. "My husband and I will go into service, and we will not rest until we see our child."
"May God help you, wherever you turn," the rabbi wished them with tears in his eyes.
Mania's parents left the shtetl with a new plan: to stand every day by the walls of the convent and from time to time to shout: "Mania! Mania!" Perhaps she would hear, answer, and also show herself in one of the many windows. "Mania! Mania!" — they did not stop shouting, and Mania did not answer and did not show herself; only from time to time a 'Sister' would appear in the gate and say:
"We ask you kindly to stop walking around here and shouting; your daughter will not answer anyway, even if she should hear."
"We will not go away," Chana answered. "We will not stop calling our child until we see her."
"If you do not stop shouting, we will be forced to drive you away from here by force."
"What are you threatening us with? You have robbed us of our child, you have taken everything from us, and we are afraid of no one. So it is said [?]. What worse harm can you do us than taking away our child? Will you set the convent watchmen [stróże] on us with nahaykas [whips], with harapniks [hunting whips]? Will you set dogs on us — then you will find our dead bodies by your walls. We will not leave this place and will not stop calling our child until we see her!"
The 'Sister' turned pale and vanished in the convent gate, and Mania's parents, in the stillness that reigned around the convent, did not stop walking along the convent walls and shouting:
"Mania! Mania! Your parents are calling you! Mania! Manyechka, our child!"
Mania did not answer, did not show herself.
But instead three riders suddenly appeared on three fiery 'sivaks' [grey horses].

The Gypsies

[Article — ethnography; the Gypsies.] (Their life and customs).
The most secretive people among the peoples are [—] without doubt[?] the Gypsies. A people without a history, without a future. The Gypsies are the only nomadic people who, in their customs, mores etc., have remained unassimilated with the peoples among whom they live as neighbours. The morality, religion and customs of the peoples among whom they live as neighbours are foreign to them and an abstract thing.
The Gypsy's main aim is to live to the detriment of others, or to live at someone else's expense. The more it is possible for the Gypsy to live to someone else's detriment, the more content is [—] nature. [—] his, he steals, not under pressure to satisfy [—] their lust[?] — mostly he steals because it already lies so in his nature; something [—] is already for him a kind of holiness. He [—] tells lies in order to be able to carry out his roguish and terrible [—] deeds (this could be established during the well-known Gypsy "man-eater" trial, which took place not long ago [—] in the Czech town of Kaschitz [Košice]), because he likes it — in a word, his soul torments him into it. This is the inheritance left to him by his forefathers, who also led such a wandering life as he.
"Gypsy" — this word is, among other peoples, a word of insult (e.g. in Upper Silesia the word "Cygan" is used when one person insults another). As Gypsies they are called in Romania, in Hungary, Poland, Italy, Austria and Germany. In the old court records of the 15th century they are called "Egyptians".
The first Gypsies came to Germany in the 15th century through Bohemia. They also came to France by the same route as to Germany. That is why the French call them "bohémiens".
Today no one will any longer deny the assertion of various researchers and scholars that the original homeland of the Gypsies is India. The emigration of the Gypsies to Europe begins in the 9th century. The first stage of their wandering was [—] Asia Minor, Persia and Armenia, [—] a small part of them remained as settlers in the transit camps. But here too, in the countries where they remained, [—] did not assimilate with the native population. [—] in the 12th century to [—]. From [—] they [—] were forced[?] [—] through Europe, and already then [—] from one place to another, because their staying in one place [—] always [—] had to end with something bad[?]. But in order to be [—] they need a strong organisation and further [—] in the same [—] or in another place.
In the Middle Ages we find Gypsies in witchcraft trials. There too the Gypsies are the main heroes. They particularly liked — and still today — to snatch other people's children and afterwards train them as thieves and tricksters. To this day a proverb goes round among the people: "A Gypsy is capable of stealing the child out of its mother's belly", and this has many times proved true. In various medieval trials against Gypsies we find many cases of cutting open the bellies of pregnant women.
It is characteristic that among Gypsies you find no feeling of shame; they are always ready, for a few groszy, to carry out various sexual orgies and other abuses. Sexual intercourse between father and daughter, son and mother, brother and sister is not among the rarities.
In Europe there are now up to 650 thousand Gypsies; the greater part of them live in Hungary. Many possess a wonderful talent for music. In Hungary Gypsy music bands are now very popular and have great success there.

What's New in Zagłębie? — Będzin: The Construction of the Mikveh Is Being Completed

[Będzin — Community.]
What's new in Zagłębie?
(Date boxes: Friday, 22 Elul 5689 — Piątek 27 września 1929 [Friday, 27 September 1929].)
Będzin
The construction of the mikveh is being completed.
This week the kehilla administration concluded an agreement with a building firm from Katowice, which has undertaken to complete the mikveh building.
The work begins next Monday.
Chamber of Commerce Against the County Belonging to Upper Silesia

[Będzin — Economy and Trade.]
The trade section and the board of the Sosnowiec Chamber of Commerce held several meetings in the course of the week, at which the position of the Chamber of Commerce was discussed regarding the plan that the Będzin county (powiat) should, from New Year on, belong to the Katowice voivodeship (województwo).
The members of the trade section and the board spoke out against the plan.
Vocational Courses Are Poorly Attended by Jewish Apprentices

[Będzin — Vocational Education.]
The local magistrate has organised vocational courses for apprentices, craftsmen and commercial employees. But, as we are informed, the tailoring courses are very poorly attended by Jewish apprentices. On the other hand, apprentices come here from Sosnowiec and Czeladź.
We therefore draw the apprentices' attention to the fact that if they do not complete a 3-year supplementary vocational school, they lose by law the right to sit the journeyman's examination and lose the possibility of practising the trade in the future.
The masters, too, who do not release the apprentices (for the classes) face a fine of up to 1000 zł. or 14 days' arrest.
One can still register at the local magistrate.
The "Dyskonto-Bank" Calls a General Meeting

[Będzin — Banks and Cooperatives.]
Next Sunday at 5 in the afternoon a general meeting will take place in the bank's own premises. The only item on the agenda is to change the name of the bank to „Spółdzielczy[?] Bank Kredytowy“ (Cooperative Credit Bank).
10,000 zł. for the Victims in Eretz Israel

[Będzin — Eretz Israel.]
The relief committee at the Zionist Organisation for the benefit of Eretz Israel sent off on Wednesday the first sum of 10 thousand zł.
The money was sent to the Warsaw kehilla.
The "Agudah" Takes Revenge on the "Talmud Torah"

[Będzin — Community and Education.]
Two weeks ago a protest was published in our paper by the gabbaim of the Talmud Torah against the local „Agudah“ sheet, in which Dr. Weinzieher and Mr. Fürstenberg had been insulted in a base manner.
The protest, which was signed by the notables of the town, made the proper impression, and in all Jewish circles there was bitterness against the ignoramuses of that sheet who permit themselves such vile deeds.
Because of this the „Agudah“ took its organ under its protection and, as revenge, decided not to pay its monthly pledge to the Talmud Torah.
On this matter a meeting took place on Saturday night in the residence of the local rabbi, who, having heard the explanation of the Talmud Torah gabbaim, also agreed that their step regarding the protest was a very proper one, and censured the tactics of the sheet, in which the most respected householders of the town are besmirched.
The rabbi promised the Talmud Torah gabbaim that he would intervene so that the boycott against the poor Talmud Torah children be lifted.
A Policeman Asks Whether the Arabs Beat Well... — Terror Methods Against the Jewish Night-Watchmen

[Będzin — Watchmen and Police.]
Terror methods against the Jewish night-watchmen.
The night-watchman Moshe Shimon Sandzer reports the following fact to us:
In the night from Monday to Tuesday the head of the watch company, Mr. Zygmunt, and his assistant attacked Mr. Sandzer and beat him cruelly. At the cries of the victim the surrounding residents gathered, and then the assailants stopped what they were doing.
Mr. Sandzer then went to the police, where he was told that he may not perform his duty as a watchman, and that if Mr. Zygmunt had beaten him, Sandzer should take him to court.
Coming out of the commissariat, Sandzer met 2 policemen, who said: „Well, Shimele, are the Arabs chopping well?“ When Sandzer asked what the question meant, the policemen explained to him exactly that they meant whether „Zygmunt chops well“.
— The same night, on Kołłątaja Street by Gutman's house, the night-watchman Moshe Paska was attacked; one man stuffed his mouth shut and another beat him.
A Lucky Chance

[Będzin — Incidents.]
On Sunday the strong wind tore pieces of tin sheeting off the roof at Kołłątaja 34, and the sheeting tore through the electric wires. Luckily a tram motorman was passing by, who alerted the police about it, and thanks to this human casualties were avoided.
An Excursion of Starosts from All over Poland

[Zagłębie — state administration.]
This week an excursion of starosts [district heads], 22 persons in number, stayed here, with the aim of acquainting themselves with the question of social welfare, the hospital system, the school system and economic activity in Zagłębie.
Also taking part in the excursion were a ministerial delegation and the persons of Dr. Kurczyński, Suski and Lewicki.
The starosts held a conference on the premises of the starostwo [district office], at which the Starost Mr. Koks [?] gave an informative report on the state of the activity of the local self-government bodies in the Będzin district [powiat].
From Zagłębie the starosts travelled on to Upper Silesia.
—o—
“Our Tasks after the Events in Eretz Israel”.
[Zagłębie — Zionism.]
This week there stayed in Zagłębie the representative of the Eretz-Israel “Hapoel Hatzair”, Mr. David Schmetterling of Degania, and the leader of “Gordonia” in Poland, Mr. Pinchas Lubianiker, who lectured in Będzin in the hall of the “Hitachdut”, in Sosnowiec at the “Hotel Polski” and in Dąbrowa in the hall of the P.P.S. [Polish Socialist Party] on the topic: “Our tasks after the events in Eretz Israel”.
The speakers stated that no riots and acts of violence will weaken our faith in Zionism and in Eretz Israel. The only true answer to all oppressions must find expression in a broad Zionism (“Grois-Zionism”), in “persifings”[?] work and in a planned pioneering emigration to Eretz Israel.
—o—
The “Hechalutz” Is Being Organised.
[Będzin — Zionism.]
Many attempts have been made in Będzin to organise the “Hechalutz”, but always without success. Taking into consideration the recent events in Eretz Israel, to which Jewish youth has responded with aliyah to Eretz Israel and with intensified Zionist work, the pioneering youth organisation “Gordonia” has taken the initiative to create the “Hechalutz” in our town.
On Sunday a joint consultation of all Zionist organisations that recognise Working Eretz Israel took place in the hall of the “Hitachdut”, and it was decided to found the “Hechalutz”. The provisional committee consists of: M. Haspel, B. Weisshaus [?] and Tz. Kutner.
—o—
A Dead Woman in the “Przemsza”
[Będzin — accident.]
Near Wiejska Street the dead body of an unknown woman, 35 years old, was taken out of the “Przemsza” [river].
—o—
To the Address of the School Guardians
[Będzin — education, trade.]
We have received a letter from several merchants and shopkeepers dealing in writing materials, who complain about the system that has been introduced in the public (folk) schools, where the teaching staff occupies itself with trading in the above-mentioned articles, and in this way [?] they systematically take away Jewish livelihoods.
Over a Rooster and a Hen Betar Was Destroyed, and over a “Polka” Wig a Woman Runs Away from Her Husband and Children..

[Sosnowiec — family.]
At Bieyska [?] 10 live the couple Baruch Silberstein and his wife Chava. They have been married for 15 years already, and in that time 5 little children have come along.
Baruch Silberstein, a carpenter by trade, does not live in peace with his parents-in-law, the Kritzlers of Piaski. The son-in-law has various money claims against his father- and mother-in-law, which they do not recognise. Because of this, sharp quarrels arose between the couple over various family matters, since the son-in-law Baruch wanted by all means to influence his “woman of valour” so that she too would take a hostile attitude toward her parents; but their daughter resisted and lived, as is proper, in peace with her parents.
Two weeks ago the parents-in-law in Piaski married off a daughter, and the Sosnowiec daughter, Baruch Silberstein's wife, at her husband's suggestion demanded of her parents that they order her a “polka” wig [?].
The demand was not fulfilled, and because of this the daughter Chava was not at her sister's wedding. The father- and mother-in-law, as we are assured, “took their daughter Chava in hand” and prevailed upon her to do no more and no less than run away from home and abandon her children and her husband, their “beloved” son-in-law.
Chavale obeyed what “father and mother bid”, and on Monday towards evening she left home and vanished, leaving her husband with 5 children to God's mercy. The youngest child, who is not more than 2 years old, cries and screams “Mamme-shi!”, but the “faithful” mamme-shi does not answer and takes revenge on her husband..
The abandoned husband has also turned to the police, but as we write these lines Chava Silberstein has still not come back to her little children.
Changes in the Kehilla Budget

[Sosnowiec — kehilla.]
This week the kehilla budget for 1929 was sent back approved by the authorities. The following changes were made in the budget:
Reduced: the subsidy for the Talmud Torah from 7 thousand to 5 thousand, “Mizrachi” from 6 to 5 [thousand], the girls' gymnasium from 6 to 5 [thousand], “Gemilut Chesed” from 5 to 4 [thousand], and for evening courses for workers from 2 thousand to a thousand.
Increased: for the moreh tzedek [rabbinical judge] Schwarz, 500 zł.; for repairing the town synagogue from 8 to 12 thousand; the old Sosnowiec synagogue from 1500 to 3600; the Pogoń synagogue from 3 to 5 thousand; for medicines for the poor from 3 to 5 thousand; the item of unforeseen expenses from 2 [thousand] to 5,600.
The subsidy of 1500 zł. for vocational courses for artisans has been struck out entirely.
New Board of the Artisans' Association

[Sosnowiec — artisans.]
On Sunday the continuation of the general meeting of artisans took place. At the meeting a coalition board was elected, in which representatives of every section are represented.
The board consists of: Y. Rotenstein, M. Dawidowicz, S. Horowitz, Y. Kuziński, Y. D. Langer, H. Szajer, S. Ratmer [?], M. Ekstein, M. Stern, Grynberg, Szmitana, Mendelewicz and Wiślicki.
On the auditing committee: H. Warszawski, H. B. Piekarski and S. Goldkorn.
The artisans hope that the board will work solely along the line of improving their economic situation.

How "Religion" Is Taught in the Public Schools. / The Relief Committee Has Already "Completed Its Task". / From the District Court. / The Trial in the Smuggling Affair. / Is a Commissioner to Run the City Economy?

[Sosnowiec — Education; Sosnowiec — Relief for Eretz Israel; Sosnowiec — Courts; Sosnowiec — Municipality.]
How "Religion" Is Taught in the Public Schools.
With the new school year the time for Jewish studies in the public (powszechne) schools has been increased by one hour, for learning Hebrew and other Jewish subjects.
But how the religious lessons are conducted is shown by an interesting fact which Mr. Gelbhar, guardian (opiekun) of Majerczyk's school, told us.
A father turned to Mr. Gelbhar and complained that in the school under the direction of Mr. Majerczyk the Bible (Tanakh) is studied bareheaded.
When Mr. G. intervened about this with the above-mentioned head (kierownik), the teacher explained to him that it is not proper otherwise. "This is," he says, "a Polish school, where all lessons are held with uncovered heads"...
Comment is superfluous.
—o—
The Relief Committee Has Already "Completed Its Task".
Jewish Sosnowiec has not "distinguished itself" in the relief campaign for the victims in Eretz Israel. To this day a whole 1000 (one thousand zł.) has been collected, and the collection campaign has completely "fallen asleep"...
—o—
From the District Court.
The Będzin president Michel, who is at the same time a councillor (rajca) in Sosnowiec, at a session of the local city council reproached councillor Hauke that during the war he had joined the Austrian border guard and in that post had oppressed[?] the population.
Hauke brought a suit against President Michel. The trial took place at the time in the Peace Court (magistrate's court), which acquitted Michel.
This week the case came up for the second time in the local District Court, which sentenced President Michel to pay 100 zł. or 4 days' arrest.
—o—
The Trial in the Smuggling Affair.
The course of the trial, which began 10 days ago in the local District Court against the merchants accused of smuggling foreign colonial goods into Poland, is very slow. In the course of the week a small number of witnesses, on whom the indictment rests, were heard.
Because of this it is hard to foresee when the sensational trial will end.
—o—
Is a Commissioner to Run the City Economy?
As we are informed, because of the bad economic management of the local city administration a commissioner will be appointed in the person of Mr. Julian Osachowski[?], delegate of the "Bank Gospodarstwa Krajowego".

Bandit Attack on a Factory Director

[Sosnowiec — Crime.]
On Tuesday armed bandits attacked the director of Huldczyński's (Huldschinsky's) factory, Mr. Pantan [?]. The bandits tied up the house watchman and, bound as he was, threw him into a cellar. Then they went in to the director and, terrorizing him with revolvers, the bandits robbed 260 zł.

[Zagłębie — Societies.]
Jewish Society for Knowledge of the Country.
On Wednesday, in the premises of the Jewish Women's (Girls') Gymnasium, an organizing meeting took place of the "Jewish Society for Knowledge of the Country (Żydowskie Towarzystwo Krajoznawcze), Zagłębie Branch".
The aim of the society is to organize excursions to the most important places of the country.
The following board was elected: Dr. Wiederman (chairman), Miss Goldberg (vice-chair), Miss Regina Mejslim [?] (treasurer), Miss Natalia Szyfman (secretary), Miss Brener, and Messrs. Bal and Kampf.

The Year 5689 in Jewish Life

(A brief summing-up.)
The year 5689 was not — as we had strongly believed — a year of improvement and revival, but one of the hard years for us since the war years. Once again we were subjected to pogroms, tormented, and severely oppressed spiritually as well as economically.
In Soviet Russia the Jewish situation has not changed at all. The Communist order has killed off the Jewish shtetl and declassed the three-million-strong Russian Jewry, which now stands before an abyss of destruction. The Bolshevik attempt to transfer Jews to colonisation has failed. Among the resettlers in Crimea and Biro-Bidzhan great discontent prevails, and there are frequent clashes there between them and the former inhabitants. The wild region of Birobidzhan, which was supposedly to bring redemption to the impoverished, declassed Russian Jew, is turning out to be a bankruptcy, and, wishing to save the failed undertaking, the Yevsektsiya is sending special emissaries out into the Jewish world to agitate for the Russian colonisation.
The halutz colonies in the Soviet Union have been dissolved because of their Zionist views. Thousands of young nationalists are being deported to the frozen regions of Siberia and thrown into the prisons of Turkestan. The spiritual oppression and persecution of the Jewish religion, Zionism and Hebrew grow ever stronger; synagogues and batei midrash are being turned into Communist clubs; Jews are forced to work even on the High Holidays; in the Jewish schools of Soviet Russia a new subject named "Anti-Religion" is being introduced, whose purpose is to uproot and stifle every religious feeling in Jewish children. The works of the Jewish classics such as Mendele Mocher Sforim, Sholem Aleichem, Peretz and others, which used to be taught in the schools there, are being withdrawn out of fear that these works are too nationalistic.
Antisemitism in the "free" Soviet Union need not be ashamed of itself either. Jewish workers are persecuted by their Communist "comrades", who spread the slogan "Russia for the Russians, down with the Jews"! The war of extermination against the Jews is waged in all fields, and there is a danger that our brethren in Russia may, God forbid, be wiped out entirely.
Among the antisemitic countries are to be counted Yugoslavia, where blood-libel incitement took place in the village of Petraia-Sala [?]; Bessarabia, where serious antisemitic excesses took place; Hungary, where the "bearers" of culture and light, the local students, organised anti-Jewish street demonstrations.
Lithuania, too, has "honoured" us with pogroms and blood-libel incitement, and Jewish property was robbed; in the course of this the 40-year-old Dor [?] Schachtel also fell victim.
In Romania a good change has come about in the government's attitude towards the Jews. The former antisemitic government fell in the last parliamentary elections, and democratic elements have taken the helm of the state. The policy of the new government gives reason to believe that Romania will at last be permeated with the spirit of equality towards all its citizens, without distinction of nationality and religion.
In Eretz Israel the difficult economic situation which had oppressed the Yishuv for several years has been completely liquidated, and the country has entered a new period of work and upswing. After long years of stagnation and depression a large emigration has begun again, which is going to Eretz Israel today under the name "Fifth Aliyah". The Dead Sea concession has been finally signed and Novomeysky has already begun the exploitation of the "Dead Sea". The first preparatory works for the port in Haifa have also begun, which will bring a blessing to Eretz Israel.
Parallel to the economic upswing in Eretz Israel goes the spiritual development; it is truly astonishing to see how the Yishuv of 160 thousand souls cultivates the Hebrew book, newspaper and theatre. The Hebrew publishing houses are working intensively, enriching our book market with new Hebrew publications. The well-known Hebrew art theatre "Habimah" has at last found a place of refuge in Eretz Israel and is staging historical plays with great success and applause. The Technikum in Haifa has been turned into a college and this year produced its first graduate engineers and architects.
In the political sense Eretz Israel has gone through a severe crisis. We believed that the new High Commissioner Chancellor, known to us for his sympathies for Zionism, would put the Balfour Declaration into effect, but we were bitterly disappointed. The sad incident on Yom Kippur at the Western Wall over the little partition that was meant to separate men from women aroused a great storm and bitterness throughout world Jewry. The desecration of the Jewish holy places was answered by the Palestine government with the "status quo" and, what's more... with permission to break a passage door through by the Wall, through which the Arabs could stroll freely and disturb the worshippers. The Jewish petitions, memoranda and delegations to London had no success, and the Arab provocations and acts of violence continued until the tragic Friday, 23 August.
Still fresh in our memory are the latest sad events in Eretz Israel. The barbaric attacks on the Jewish Yishuv, the innocent blood shed in the streets of Hebron, Safed, Jerusalem, Haifa and Jaffa, the 130 Jewish victims who fell at the hand of the Arab murderer, demand of us not despair, dejection, an "Eikhah" mood of lament, but strengthened, strenuous Zionist activity and intensive work for Eretz Israel.
Here in Poland the Jewish situation has grown much worse.
This year anti-Jewish excesses and riots took place in the Polish university cities of Lwów and Poznań. The excesses were "justified" by the pogromists with a medieval libel that Jewish schoolgirls had mocked a Christian procession.
In our Zagłębie no special news [?] occurred; Jewish life went on in its usual course. In the three neighbouring towns of Dąbrowa, Będzin and Sosnowiec city-council elections took place, which brought only very small changes in the make-up of the councils. In Będzin we did indeed win a victory by getting 16 Jewish councillors elected, who however have little influence in the local city council. In the Jewish kehilla great stagnation prevails, and apart from attending to the dead it shows no sign of life whatsoever.
A little vitality, a bit of festivity in our drab, hard life was brought by the poet Leib Jaffe, who stayed in Zagłębie on the business of Keren Hayesod. His visit turned into a great Zionist demonstration. The Eretz Israel campaign was very successful, and every Jew contributed his share for Eretz Israel generously. We were also visited by the representative of the Eretz Israel Histadrut ha-Ovdim (Workers' Federation), Mr. Ben-Zvi, who conducted with great success the campaign for the Palestine Workers' Fund (Kapai). It should also be mentioned in this column that the Będzin "Yavneh" was moved for the new school year into a building of its own, erected by the esteemed patron and national activist Mr. Fürstenberg.
———
The year 5689 was a year of public upswing. Many congresses, conventions and assemblies took place, whose aim was to strengthen Jewish life. The Jewish Agency was created, which almost all Jewish forces in the upbuilding work of Eretz Israel have joined. The 16th Zionist Congress ratified the enlargement of the Agency.
The "Agudah" convened a "Knessiyah" in Vienna, which rejected joining the Agency, so that the "Agudah" remains outside the Jewish camp that is building Eretz Israel.
In Beuthen [Bytom] the first world congress of Jewish artisans assembled. There were also world conventions of the Jewish gymnastics and sports associations "Hakoach" and "Maccabi". The Jewish national woman, too, held congresses in Hamburg and Zurich, and even the "Benot Agudat Israel" made progress, holding conferences in Łódź and in Vienna...
———
On the threshold of the new year we wish ourselves that in the year 5690 the true redemption of the Jewish people in its land, Eretz Israel, will at last come.
Mordechai Hampel.
The Head Office in Jerusalem

[The Head Office in Jerusalem sends a New Year's blessing to the editors and readers of the "Zaglembier Tsaytung".]
Dear Mr. Editor of the "Zaglembier Tsaytung", Będzin.
For the New Year we wish you, your esteemed collaborators, your newspaper and its worthy readers, men and women, a heartfelt "May you be inscribed and sealed for a good year".
We take this occasion as our duty to express to you and your collaborators our deepest thanks for the attentive attitude and the sympathy that you have shown in the columns of your esteemed paper towards our National Fund and the land-redemption work in Eretz Israel.
We permit ourselves to hope that your attentiveness and sympathy will now grow even greater because of the latest events in our country.
For you must know that the Jewish Yishuv in Eretz Israel, which was attacked so grievously in the very midst of its peaceful and cultural work, has nonetheless not lost its courage. It now awaits the answer of the entire Jewish people in all the lands of the Diaspora, whose most sacred duty now is not only to cover the holes and mend the cracks in our national edifice, but also to exert itself far more in order to enlarge and strengthen that edifice.
Not merely help for those who suffered during the bloody events — for them the Palestine government must and is obliged to care, the government which did not know how to provide in time for the peace of its citizens and the security of their lives and property, entrusted to it already by the power of the mandate of the League of Nations.
Build we must at this present moment, and far more intensively, energetically, broadly and strongly than at any other time; and to build means first of all: to enlarge the Jewish national land holdings!
The problem of the Jewish National Fund has now been recognised as a highly topical one. Both the Zionist Congress and the "Jewish Agency" have recognised in so many words the immediate necessity of creating a sufficient land reserve in Eretz Israel and of raising for that purpose 1,000,000 pounds in the course of the next two years.
We are therefore certain that you, like all other friends of the Jewish National Fund throughout the world, will now considerably increase your moral support for that Fund.
We open our appeal to the Jewish people in the year 5690 with the words — build and create!
With Zion's greetings,
Natan Bistritzky, Z. Katler.
The Seduced Girl. — Dr. A. Weissman

[Dr. A. Weissman. 23. The Seduced Girl. (A novel of Jewish life in the Old World, based on historical facts).]
The three riders suddenly galloped up to Reb Zelig Sarah's and his wife Hanna.
Mania's parents were at first frightened to death when they saw the three riding heroes[?] coming straight at them.
They thought that someone had come to destroy them, to murder them.
When they, the riders, were already beside them, Mania's parents recognised two of the riders.
One was their acquaintance and friend Haim Braunstein; the second was none other than Jan Sichiański! The third was a stranger whom they had never yet seen.
— Look, look, Zelig! Look who is here! Haim!
— Sholem aleichem, Haim! What are you doing here? Eh? And you, Jan, what?
— I have come to look for you, Reb Zelig! — said Haim, and jumped down from his horse like a hero. — I looked for you and found you! Praised be He! And good that you are here! Here is exactly where you should be; you must not leave this spot until this evening, when you will have Mania back with you; do you hear, Mania, Mania, back with you!
— Amen, Master of the Universe! — cried Hanna.
— Good, amen, merciful Father in heaven! — said Reb Zelig. — But tell me, Haim, how do you know that this evening we will have our Manieczka with us?
— If you are told yes, it is yes! You see, here is Pan Jan Sichiański, you know him after all.
— Some question, whether we know him! Well, well! Of course! He is, after all, something like our forest warden from our village!
— Yes, good. He will help us free our Mania this evening.
— So, so? Oy, I begrudge him the good deed. That an uncircumcised one should thus redeem[?] the exile...
— Don't be afraid, he will not redeem the exile. He does it not of his own good will, but because he must, in order to save his "skóra" — that is, his skin — by helping.
— And who is the third one, also an "uncircumcised"? Will he help us too?
— Ah, yes! I have the honour to introduce to you Mr. Stanisław Branicki, the chief secret agent of the police of the Polish government! — Haim waved his hand towards the third rider, who had until now remained sitting on his horse, listening to the conversation.
— It is an honour! — replied Branicki, jumping down from his horse and approaching Mania's parents with even, measured steps.
He bowed deeply to Hanna and to Reb Zelig, who were trembling with surprise.
— Oy, Haim, who is this? The governor? — whispered Reb Zelig.
— Go on, go on, Zelig! This is the "second to the king"! — stammered Hanna.
— Ah, no! This is the head of the secret policemen of the government! Him, him we must thank for the work.
— Oy, a gentile redeems the exile! — said Hanna, and burst into tears.
— He has earned the World to Come! — exclaimed Reb Zelig with a deep sigh. — No small thing, "redeeming captives"!
— Do not cry, madame, — Branicki said in plain German, — today we shall free your daughter! And you, Jan, — he turned to Jan, — get to work and see that everything is ready at five o'clock in the evening. Do you hear? Exactly five, when we all come at once.
Jan rang at the gate. The gate soon opened, and Jan vanished through the gate, which soon closed again.
— Tell me, Haim, this is surely your work too? — asked Reb Zelig.
— A little — yes. Don't ask; I have not rested, not eaten and not slept since Mania was abducted, until God helped me reach my goal!
— You have earned the World to Come, Haim, — said Reb Zelig, — but tell me, do you know that Mania renounces us and does not want to see us? Oy, what is to be done?
— Who talked you into such a lie? Surely the Mother Superior of the convent? Don't believe it! Mania is begging for mercy, that she be freed, that she be saved. As proof you have her letter to you!

On the Threshold...

...And a trembling feeling ran through the whole Jewish people... A strong, heavy darkness covered Jewry.. As if through a mighty thunderclap the Jewish people awoke and saw itself in a critical situation... on the threshold.
Where does such a powerful sound come from? And where does such a lament, such a groan pour out from?... How is it that from the narrow, cramped and dark Jewish synagogue lane one hears together, as if mixed, the voice of might and the voice of weeping?...
Is this perhaps a minute in which the Jewish people passes through pain, suffering and grief to might?...
Or is this perhaps a day on which the Jew wishes to sound forth into eternity his unartificial spiritual strength?...
On the threshold...
A day [it is?] when old weeks pass away, when old months dissolve in mists.. It is a day on which old forms, which seemed[?] to be cast in hard steel, suddenly vanish, and there appears a new day, a new form, a new life, a new year... Behind us the familiar, dark past, and before us a fog-shrouded[?] future..
On the threshold...
Yes, on the threshold we stand today with a worried face, and our mind's eye wants to tear through the dark mists and peer into tomorrow, into the future...
And from the narrow, dark Jewish lane there pierces out today, together with the sound of the shofar, together with the voice of might, together with the voice of certainty, courage and a fine future — a voice of weeping, groaning, servility and a dark past...
But that is how it is with us Jews: on the day of Rosh Hashana, the day on which we begin a new year, a new world, a new life — on that very day we remain for a while alone with ourselves and in our thoughts leaf through the bloody history of our past year, and there we read of our sad economic and spiritual situation in exile, there we brood over our struggle in Eretz Israel, there we remember that only thanks to our firm unity, our solidarity, can we stand up against the strong... And a weeping is heard in the Jewish heart when it remembers its homelessness, its strangeness in the whole world...
But at the same time, on the day of Rosh Hashana, together with the weeping, the sound of the shofar is heard too, the voice of might, of strength, of courage...
How are we to understand this?
Yes, it is the sign of our sure hope...: "And it shall come to pass in the end of days"... Better days will come.. A better year is already appearing..
That is the eternal refrain to our old and sad song of exile.. That is the refrain which accompanied our forefathers after the great Destruction; the same refrain encouraged them in Spain; the same refrain was the source of their consolation in all the hardest moments, and the same refrain also gives strength to endure among the gentiles [printed: "in der goyim"].
And so it is today too, on the threshold — on the threshold of the new year we come with broken hearts into our synagogues, where we simply drown in our own tears when we see our situation today; then a trembling seizes our soul and we bow our head, then our breath stops and we see our powerlessness.
And a flash[?] goes through our whole organism when we remember that today the Book of Remembrances is opened and today one more thing happens.. "and it reads itself, and every man's hand has signed it." All people are judged today, all — not only the weak and the small; all, the great and strong as well.
And so, sadly, we look around today on all sides for help. In spirit we see ourselves today tiny, like young sheep, "kivnei maron". And with fear we look at the deeds of the past year and with dread we look into the future: what will happen today? What verdict awaits us?
But the sound of the shofar encourages us today and fills us with trust... The sound of the shofar recalls that Isaac let himself be offered up as a sacrifice.. For his ideal he wanted to sacrifice his life — his only child; the future of the whole people Abraham our Father wanted to sacrifice to God... And we today?.. But the sound of the shofar encourages us and fills us with a strong faith in our great ideal; it brings us closer to our God, it reminds us of the day when at Mount Sinai we became a whole people, it raises our soul today too to all the great Jewish ideals and... Together with our groaning and weeping over our fresh martyrs, from the narrow Jewish synagogue lane the sound of the shofar is heard — the voice of our might, of courage, of prospects of a fine and strong future...
Today, as the last ray of the old year has passed and the first ray of the new year has appeared, as we stand on the threshold, we are filled with pride and honour, both born of our painful past. Both of them, pride and honour, unite today with our tears, and our soul, cheered by the sound of the shofar, is set trembling today, because a new year stands before it today; today our soul is full of vows for an honest, beautiful and strong future.. a future which shall be great and mighty as once, thousands of years ago; a glorious future on our own soil, a crystal-clear future, of which only our once-strong past dared to dream...
The sound of the shofar gives us this promise today... The sound of the shofar, mixed with our tears, wakes us today and encourages us...
And we must not remain standing with folded[?] hands at a distance! We must promise ourselves today that such a future must be created...
And what we promise ourselves on so great a day shall be fulfilled...
On the threshold...
A Little Feuilleton — Let It Go to Its Rest!

I have that sort of nature: when I have to part from someone or something, it costs me my health and heartache. I see a train carry off someone close to me, or an acquaintance, and it is as if a limb had been torn from my body; I say goodbye to someone and I quiver like a little child. A nature like that — it really isn't nice!
And so too when I part from an old year: somehow as though my most intimate friend, with whom I spent days and nights, were being robbed from me, for who knows whether I'll be able to get used to another.
But I confess and avow that the departure of this year touches me exactly as much as last year's snow. Oh, so to speak[?], what a friend he was to me, and what have I to regret about him!
A shlimazl of a year. Wherever I turned, everything turned away from me; I'd just lift the morsel to my mouth and it always fell for me butter side down.
I bought bills of exchange — they "took flight" from under my hands; I tried to chase after them — I "slipped" myself; and if I did send my missus to a dacha, she came back to me unrecognisable (by now I have recognised her).
Well, never mind — if only I'd had some luck[?] in public life; but there too everything fell for me butter side down.
That I would become a town councillor (Ratman), or even a vice-president, was certain in my mind; I had even had two kinds of visiting cards printed.
Well, and what came of it? Walking yesterday in one of the local lanes, I nearly broke a leg.
That I would become a whole "cooking-spoon" [bigwig] in the kehilla I certainly didn't doubt, since the kehilla decree was supposed to be "extended" to our Zagłębie any minute.
All my hopes melted away, like the Reich's "understanding" plans.
And if I do by luck become a board member of some institution or other, everyone there — may it not happen to Jews — has gone deaf, and what can I achieve there, when it's all the same as talking to the wall!
Well, I ask you: if in general and in particular I've fared like a sinner in the world to come, then what indeed have I to regret about the old good-for-nothing year? Let it go to its rest — I don't miss it one bit.
Talye.
When a Year Goes Away... (A Bit of Soul-Searching) — by Dr. Tsvi Kohen

[Essay — Rosh Hashana eve; soul-searching.] By Dr. Tsvi Kohen. (A bit of soul-searching.)
Erev Rosh Hashana.
In my childhood I used to have on this day a quite special interest, a peculiar task, an original mission.
With impatience I would wait on this day for the sun to set and for the sunset shadows to wrap house and yard, street and market, and when the west began to play in colours I would go out to the field and stand and watch how the sun goes down today.
I wanted to see the death throes of a year — how a year dies! What does its last day look like? And on the last day — the last hour? How does the sun set on this day?
And an eeriness would then come over me, for I felt as if a great corpse were lying right before me: a year is dying and I hear its last death-rattle groans. And the sun labours so hard, and the whole sky is flooded with such a melancholy redness, and in a moment a dead man will stretch out before me — such a great departed one, a year.
And shadows, camps of shadows, hurry from all sides and cover and wrap and guard and shelter the departed.
A year has died.
•
Today I no longer look for and no longer wait for the setting of the sun when a year goes away.
I want as far as possible to avoid the mood of dying, but precisely for that reason the mood of dying pursues me and seeks me out. And although I already know well enough that the sun does not die in colours at all on the eve of Rosh Hashana at dusk, and that the sun has no last days at all, and that the last day of a year is our own notion — because we have last days, because the number of our years is limited, and because after a certain number of years we go away and leave everything behind...
And although I already know that nature has no weeks and no months and no years, that this is all our invention, our concepts — because we have only a little bit of lifetime, we count it and weigh it and divide it and measure it like a poor man his few pennies, for yesterday we came and tomorrow we go, one with a few years more, one with several years less — still such a melancholy mood comes over me on the eve of Rosh Hashana at dusk..
And a cold shudder passes through our bones...
———
Erev Rosh Hashana.
A year gone, a year of life; properly translated it means this: a year of running, drudging, working, a year of staring with the eyes, flapping with the soul and splashing with the hands as in water, a year of torment, chasing, running about, borrowing, worrying, pushing, fretting and spinning in the great cauldron-pit that is called life... What is the sense of it all?...
And what is the whole chase in life? What does one chase after, and for whom? Really not for oneself. Rarely does anyone attain something for himself, and when he does attain it he is already old and gets no more pleasure from it. But those [most people] attain nothing. They gather money — it remains for heirs, who as a rule squander it far more easily than the one who gathered it; they leave books behind — these become popular and famous only after death. In one's lifetime there are too many living people who cannot allow their friend and colleague to rise above them; one works for the community — the community is never grateful to you while you live, and you have only the hope of being entered into the book of public servants after your death, that is, then, when it is actually of little consequence to you anymore, when the last day of this foolish, giddy life comes...
And what? When? What was achieved?..
Erev Rosh Hashana.
And what is the sense of being a Jew; how long will we still suffer like this?
How long is the limit and the measure? And what hopes do we have?
Each year it gets worse, each year we go further downhill, outwardly and inwardly.
Outwardly it is indeed today a world of culture, of civilisation. Outwardly all people today are indeed modern, but a Jew is truly not liked, one is ashamed of a Jew; the Jew in Europe is a kind of castor oil. When one really must have him, when one already needs him, one swallows him like a Parisian pill, improved and dressed up: "The Jew is almost no Jew at all."
Outwardly people are indeed cultured and civilised and modern, but for the Jew they have cultured troubles, civilised sufferings and a modern Inquisition.
And inwardly?
Who does not know the ruin we have inwardly? The ruin that grows greater and greater each year.
Inwardly everything Jewish is dying away; inwardly everything withers and wilts, although we still make a noise and although it keeps seeming to us that we are constantly singing, that we are even reviving.
Inwardly Hebrew is a dead language for millions of Jews; Yiddish for other millions — "an ugly jargon" spoken by the benighted masses. Jewish aspirations for yet other millions — utopias that will never be fulfilled.
Inwardly the whole source of a new revival withers and wilts — already dried up and parched, and it no longer gives the youth any courage. There is no longer any spiritual ideal that awakens faith and hope.
Inwardly it is chaos (tohu va-vohu). Jews have never yet had such a time.
It is a time when in everyone the question begins to peck:
— What will become of us if we keep going down and down like this?
And every year we stand on this day and keep shouting "Let the year end together with its curses" — away with you, year, with your curses!
Every year the same refrain, every year like this...
When a year goes away, we see it off:
— Away, away, be gone already with your curses.
But what if the curses have no end? And what if one year surpasses the other so far that our whole life is one great curse?
— What will be the end?
And I no longer go to see how the sun dies in colours and the year expires, but the last rays of the departing year give me no rest and awaken and call forth in me, wherever I am, only — the old eerie feeling...
And the old question stands before me alive again. The same question that I always used to ask my father, only with more bitterness:
— What will be the end of the Exile?
A year gone, again a year comes — will we again, as today, stand next year on the eve of Rosh Hashana like fools and see off the year sarcastically and bitterly:
— Let the year end together with its curses! Be gone already, year, with your bit of gall and bitterness!
Or will something change this year in our wandering and roaming?
Let us live and see!
Yitzchok and Shmuel Maftir.

[A Rosh Hashanah story.] By A. D. Egoz.
(A tale connected with the maftir of the first day of Rosh Hashanah.)

They were fine and respected householders. One is called Reb Yitzchok Maftir, and the other — Reb Shmuel Maftir.
They are two brothers, twins, the children of Mordechai the shopkeeper and Basya the shopkeeper's wife, who have long been dead.
The two brothers got the nickname "Maftir" as soon as they were born. They grew up with the nickname "Maftir", and to this day they are called by that name.
They got this nickname because their coming into the world is connected with the maftir of the first day of Rosh Hashanah.
This is how it happened:
Their parents, Mordechai the shopkeeper and Basya the shopkeeper's wife, were childless for some fifteen years after their wedding. They travelled to doctors, to "good Jews" [Hasidic rebbes] and, to make the distinction, to sorcerers, but nothing at all helped, and the couple remained childless.
Mordechai the shopkeeper was never a rich man; he barely earned enough to get by, but they were content with little. As long as there was bread with krupnik [barley soup] and a garment to cover their nakedness, they were satisfied.
The only thing that embittered their life was their childlessness. A child is, after all, a comfort in a house; a child drives away gloom and brings joy. Not to mention after a hundred and twenty years — then, after all, a child comes [to the grave]. A son says Kaddish and, if he is able, studies a chapter of Mishnah. A daughter at least lights a yahrzeit candle, and [if?] she is faithful to her father and mother, she hires someone to say Kaddish or to study Mishnah. But when one dies, God forbid, without children, one is simply forgotten; no one even comes to the ancestral grave, and it is as if one had never been in the world at all.
This constantly gnawed [?] at the minds of the unhappy couple, and they suffered great torments from it, which were truly unbearable.
There were times when Mordechai and his wife Basya agreed between themselves to divorce peacefully: they would split everything they owned half and half and part as good friends. Perhaps — they said to each other — they were not the right match; perhaps if he married another woman and she another man, both would be "built up" [blessed with children], and it would be as the saying goes: better four in joy than two in sorrow.
But as soon as they came to the rabbi intending to write a get [bill of divorce], they both regretted it. They had a very good life together, and when it came to the point, they could not part; both would have a good cry and go back home, with hearts both glad and broken.
Next door to their shop was Zerach the shopkeeper. Zerach had a great abundance in his shop, and he was doing very well. He took in good money and earned well, while Mordechai would be waiting for a bit of takings.
Zerach the shopkeeper lived in comfort in every respect. He had children, a fine apartment. He was counted among the most important householders in town, meddled in kehilla affairs and had a big say in the community, while Mordechai and his wife lived in a poor apartment and all their property consisted of a single goat and a few household goods.
Zerach the shopkeeper had his "seat" in the beis medrash by the eastern wall and used to get the finest aliyos and honours, while his neighbour, Mordechai the shopkeeper, prayed in the same beis medrash way at the back, and the fat aliyos never reached him.
The two neighbours were always quarrelling over matters of livelihood, and very often they cursed each other.
One day Mordechai and Basya heard that somewhere in Poland there was a "good Jew", a mighty miracle-worker, who literally makes the dead alive, and especially in the matter of childlessness he is a very great "expert".
Hearing such a tale, Mordechai shut his little shop, took his Basya along, and they went to that "miracle-worker". He heard them out and said to Mordechai:
"God willing, next Rosh Hashanah, on the first day, have yourself called up for maftir, and the Almighty will help and your wife will bear you a male child."
Mordechai and Basya had great faith, and they fantasized that, God willing, they too would soon be blessed with it. They imagined how their little boy would grow up, how they would take him to the beis medrash, where he would answer "Amen", say Kedushah and drink a little of the Kiddush wine together with all the children in the beis medrash. After all, all that is missing is the Rosh Hashanah maftir, and that, God willing, will come.
Just before Rosh Hashanah the two shopkeeper neighbours, Mordechai and Zerach, had a bitter quarrel, and it came literally to knives.
Rosh Hashanah came; they finished praying Shacharis and sold the aliyos. When they came to maftir, our Mordechai, the childless one, began to "bid up". Someone offered five gulden for the maftir — he gave six; someone called out "nine" — Mordechai bid "ten". He was determined to go even as far as hundreds of gulden. What won't a father do for a child? Even if he had to sell the hut [?] and pawn the bedding — the thing must be done. A child, a Kaddish, is no joke!
And his neighbour Zerach sits there the whole time and smiles. Then he goes up onto the bimah and says to the gabbaim: "The maftir is not for sale; it belongs to me, I have a chazakah [established right] to it."
There were Jews in the beis medrash who knew for what purpose Mordechai wanted to buy the maftir, and they began to plead with Zerach to let him have it. But he holds to one thing: he has had a chazakah on the maftir for three, four years already, and he will on no account let it go.
So it reached the rabbi, and the rabbi began to talk to Zerach: "Reb Zerach, you have, no evil eye, children — may they be healthy; let another Jew also have a drop of joy; perhaps the maftir will really help and the unhappy souls will be revived — why should you be so stubborn?" But Zerach does not budge.
Zerach was so obstinate that he declared: "Blood will be spilled, and the maftir is mine!"
Meanwhile a great uproar arose in the beis medrash, and the end of it was that they called up Zerach for maftir, not Mordechai.
Coming down from the bimah in triumph, the maftir-holder muttered proudly: "Maftir he wanted!"
The grief of Mordechai and his wife was truly beyond measure. A bad man, a villain, comes along and kills off their only child, for whom they have been waiting fifteen years!...
But the end was that Basya, that very same year, gave birth to twins, two little boys, who were named "Yitzchok and Shmuel", after the two children of barren women of whom the Torah reading and the haftarah of the first day of Rosh Hashanah tell.
And Zerach's wife miscarried that year, and she never had any more children.
The town saw in this the hand of God and His just judgement, giving the childless joy for their sorrow and punishing the unjust one for his unjust conduct.
And the two boys were given the nickname "Maftir", because but for the Rosh Hashanah maftir they might perhaps never have come into the world.
For the People.

[Literature — a poem for Rosh Hashanah.] By M. Aronson.

In heaven's expanse many angels hover,
they are drawn in fright towards that place
where the book of death and life lies open
and a hand writes there the fate of man.

And prayers rise, mingled with tears,
to heaven's expanse, where God's Shekhinah shines;
the quiet wish of each one can be heard:
"Inscribe us, God, in the book of life, today."

To this wish I join my own prayer,
as part of the people, as an individual and as a Jew;
not for my own life do I pray now, God forbid,
not for my own happiness does my song ring out!

What is a man, if not born for death?
Life is, after all, only a passage.
Therefore I do not pray for my own years,
that the Creator let me live long.

An individual dies — a people must live forever;
therefore I pray for my people in this hour of pain:
guard it, God, and sustain its long striving,
may eternity be forever its own!
A Mother's Love.

[Literature — a folk tale.] (A little folk tale)

1.
Once there was a mother.
She had a child, and she loved the child dearly, very dearly, with the whole strength of a mother's love.
Then suddenly the child fell ill, ill, very, very ill, and the young mother could not call any doctors, because poor, very poor was the young mother.
And — one night the child died. Trembling all over, the young mother remained standing by her child's cradle when she saw her child without a soul.
The child lay stiffened, a dead one in the cradle, like a little angel.
The mother began to scream terribly, to beat her head with both her hands and to tear out her hair...
— My child!.. My child...
She screamed and screamed; people, neighbours came running together and comforted her.
And all at once she tore herself away from the house and out into the open, and began to run about the streets like a madwoman...
She ran and ran.
— My child! My child — — —
She got lost in deep forests; over mountains and valleys she climbed and ran and ran.
She grew tired, was left without strength, and beside a mountain she fell down in a faint.
Beside her an angel appeared from the mountain, and the angel spoke up:
— Mortal! What longings have driven you here? Speak!
— W-h-o a-r-e y-o-u — stammered the mother in a voice choked with tears.
And the angel answered:
— I am the angel of longings; say, weak creature, what do you long for?
And the young mother fell at the angel's feet, wet them with her tears and quietly pleaded with him:
— I am a mother, a mother am I; a child of mine has died; I want you to give it back to me, to bring it back to life — I want my child back!
And again the angel said:
— Mortal! Ask riches of me — I will give them to you; ask of me anything you want — I will give it to you; but alas, what you ask of me I cannot fulfil — it does not lie within my power!
— You must — the mother wailed still more.
— Then you must go to the angel of death.
— Show me the way — the mother begged the angel of longings.
And the angel of longings showed her the way and said to her:
— Look! The way to the Angel of Death is not a long one; on the contrary, it is very short, but very dangerous to pass along; the whole way is strewn with thorns, and you will meet bad, wicked people; one has to endure a great deal until one gets through it! So, mortal, will you go there?
And in mad wildness the young mother burst into hysterical laughter, and between laughter and weeping answered the angel:
— Whether I will go? Ha-ha ha, I am a mother, a mother am I; a child of mine has died, and I want my child back!
And she went away.

2.
Night fell. A storm, a great storm held sway in the night.
And the young mother ran on and on. Again she climbed over mountains and valleys, she was pricked all over by the thorns and many times fell to the ground, picked herself up and ran on and on — — — — — — —
— — — — — — — — — — — —
In the darkness of the night the storm tossed her hair about and played with the folds of her torn dress. With a feverish cold the storm stabbed her body and lashed her sunken cheeks with big raindrops.
And the mother kept cleaving the darkness of the night, wrestled with the storm and did not feel the pains of her wounded body.
— My child, my child — she pleaded, as if with the storm, and ran on to reach her goal.
— Stop! — a voice was heard behind her shoulders — stop!
— Who are you? — she answered, trembling.
— The Angel of Death! — the voice answered her out of the darkness of the night.
She fell on her knees before him and kissed his bony ankles.
— I am a mother; you have taken my child's soul; I want you to give it back to me, to bring it back to life.
And the angel of death answered coldly and harshly:
— You know, mortal, that whatever comes to me never returns again; but if you wish, young mother, I will give you back your child's soul.
And the mother rejoiced greatly, and for great joy burst into still harder weeping.
And the Angel of Death went on speaking to the mother:
— But before I give you back your child's soul, I will first show you what your child would have had to endure in the course of its life; and everything it would have had to go through in its life — come and see; and afterwards, if you still want to take your child's little soul with you, you may.
The angel went ahead with his heavy steps, and she, the young mother, with a trembling heart, followed him humbly like a little dog [?].
In the air young and old souls fluttered.
— Stop — said the Angel of Death, raised a red, broad [?], bloody curtain and went on to say to the mother: — Look!
And long, long the mother stood by the raised curtain and looked, looked; her eyes grew ever larger, and streams [?] of tears ran down her sunken cheeks.
— Well, mortal! — the Angel of Death asked the mother, letting the curtain fall — do you want your child's little soul back now? Then take it.
— No, no, I don't want it, I don't want it — the young mother screamed wildly — no, no!
— Then turn back.
And the mother, after all her sufferings, after all her torments, returned home alone, without her child's little soul...

3.
Like a madwoman the young mother burst back into the house, threw herself over the cradle, and rocked her dead child to sleep as if with a [—?] melody.
A. Moszkowicz.
