Whither Goest Thou, Sosnowiec? (What Does the Total Look Like When Drawing Up the Balance Sheet for Rosh Hashanah?)

[Sosnowiec — essay; New Year stock-taking.]
So it is Rosh Hashanah already, and we have grown a year older... And as usual, we Jews have an old custom of living by reckoning — of giving ourselves an account of where we stand in the world, drawing up the balance and seeing how credit and debit look, who has remained indebted to whom.
I think and think and can find no answer, for what will come out when we draw up the total — since apart from debts we will have nothing to enter on our account.
All year long Jewish Sosnowiec has distanced itself from its public interests; all year long we have sinned against our duties to the people. A dangerous policy of destruction toward the community has been pursued among us, so that what we possess is systematically going under and nobody cares; none of us tries to give a clear account in order to see that our public prestige keeps falling and that we are becoming, as a community, ever poorer and poorer.
There is no need at all to dwell on each institution separately: all of them grew paler in the course of the year, and we have no flourishing [?] institutions to record. Take the Jewish financial institutions in general — the banks, which flourished a few years ago, no longer play their brilliant role; the party institutions: Zionists, Mizrachi, artisans — have fallen asleep and show no signs of life; the economic institutions — where are they and who sees them? The philanthropic and cultural societies — who knows of them? The only Jewish hospital that still shows [?] signs of life does so only thanks to a few respected people who were found, to whom the institution is dear and precious and who are frightened of nothing — otherwise padlocks would already be hanging there too. And so it goes on and on: one position is lost after another.
Our "Gemilut Chasadim" (interest-free loan) fund ought to have flourished. Surely there are people here to support such an institution, especially when it is in the hands of respected citizens whom the town trusts — so why is this useful people's institution in such a state? But why speak of this institution in particular, when everything is sinking and about to go under?
Our public [lit. mankind] has completely forgotten that there is a community, that there is a society. We have somehow become terrible egoists: everyone looks out for himself, is immersed in his own four cubits, and beyond that nothing in the world interests him; let everything turn upside down, let the world go under — nobody cares. People are so sunk in egoism that nobody minds that the economic situation is again beginning to totter and that the results could be terrible — that does not interest anyone either. Our Jew is interested only in today; as for tomorrow — he says — let God worry. That is where the danger lies.
Do people here really not understand that, living in the twentieth century, when everything has made such enormous progress, when America can speak with Europe and one part of the world flies to the other with terrifying speed — in such a period one must not stay behind, and one must then strive to find one's bearings with lightning speed? Do people not understand all this, or are we simply so apathetic and indifferent, as if it did not concern us? Such a game is dangerous to the point of losing one's balance, to complete downfall. This thought, this idea, ought to be popularised at every step so that people here understand the danger of missing the opportune moment, the consequences of lagging behind the times.
We now live in conditions where every second plays a role, where every day turns into a period and often into a whole epoch. One must reckon with all this, one must give an account of all this — otherwise we stay behind until we can no longer catch up, until we can no longer catch our breath.
It goes without saying that living in such a time one must go with the current; otherwise one is washed off the surface and ceases to exist. And we — not only do we not go with the current, but on the contrary, we keep going backwards, and so it is in every field of our life.
Let us draw a parallel between Sosnowiec and our sister town Będzin, and we see that whereas Sosnowiec formerly stood considerably higher than Będzin, both nationally and culturally, we now find ourselves in an incomparable process of decline.
Będzin, for example, thanks to its patron Fürstenberg, obtained a unique building for the Jewish gymnasium, for which all Poland envies it; now a modern orphanage is being built there on a grand scale [lit. with a broad gesture], something the like of which Sosnowiec cannot even dream of. When [Leib] Jaffe came to Będzin, Będzin could boast of the success of the "Keren Hayesod" campaign.
And now let us take the smallest example we have to record. At a time when Będzin had already managed [?] to send 10,000 zł. to Warsaw for the unfortunate brethren in the Land of Israel, our Sosnowiec tore its hand from its heart and collected 1000 — read: one thousand — zł. Small towns, we have read, gave more than Sosnowiec. Well, is that not a disgrace for a town like Sosnowiec? And why fool ourselves — we all know that materially Sosnowiec stands a whole heaven above those little towns that collected a thousand zł.
That is the degree of degradation, indifference and apathy Sosnowiec has reached: it cannot compare itself even with the small towns of Poland.
And as we enter the new year of life and stand at Rosh Hashanah, we Jews have the old tradition of giving ourselves a clear account: what have we accomplished in the course of the year, what merits have we brought the community, what have we done for society — and then we can give the honest but sad answer: nothing! Sosnowiec has done nothing for the community; Sosnowiec has remained in great debt to society, because it has achieved nothing for anyone; it has done nothing in the field of philanthropy, economy, nationalism, culture or any social work whatsoever.
And therefore the question arises: Sosnowiec, what has become of you? Whither goest thou, and what goal do you have in life, when nothing interests you?
Dr. Popuri.
Letters from Home.

[Feuilleton letter — Zagłębie; Rosh Hashana 5690.]
My friend R' Shlomo, may his light shine.
By the time you read this little letter of mine, the year 5689 will already be on its way to its eternal rest, and we will already be making the festive preparations to welcome the new guest, the New Year.
Sadly, very sadly we look after the departing year; long, long will we remember it. The Jewish people, scattered and dispersed, was enriched in the past year by a long list of martyrs, who perished only because they too wanted to live in the same conditions and enjoy the same rights as the wild Arabs...
Among the nations of the world, New Year's Day is — a year [sic] of carnival orgies. With us, the day of Rosh Hashana is — a day of fear, a day of soul-searching, a day of drawing up the sum total and of serious reflection: — "What will happen next?"
I do not mean a "soul-searching" between man and God, about our lack of piety, the licentiousness and the demoralisation that reign in the Jewish street — let our "Torah-loyal" folk worry about that. What I do mean is a bit of soul-searching about our political and communal work, about the fine deeds of our various communal workers who busy themselves a whole year over the public charity pennies, about our public delegates of various colours, about those who preach in the very name of Klal Yisrael and act just as is needed[?] for their own interests, for their own pockets.
5689! A whole round year you whipped us, tormented us, inflicted harsh torments on us; with seas of Jewish tears and rivers of spilled blood your baggage is filled; tens of thousands of Jewish families were ruined under your rule; to the Angel of Death you handed dictatorial power, and with his many thousands of destroyers he "strolled" around the globe, and in every corner where there was any human community at all they wrought ruin, and humanity sighed bitterly:
— Oh, what a bitter year!...
* *
The days of forgiveness, pardon and atonement are beginning, the days when the Jew avoids offending anyone even with a true word. Faithful to this tradition, I too want in today's little letter to "keep silent" and not write at length about what I have hinted at regarding the abuses, the squandering and the other calamities that have become so entrenched in our little world; I only want, R' Shlomo, may his light shine, as you close the books and draw up the annual balance, to talk with you, as one man speaks to his friend, about the state of our political and communal affairs at this serious moment.
In the political field we have achieved nothing at all. Above all, this "article" has gone completely bankrupt at the present moment; political sense and education are superfluous — what for? why? It is enough to possess a little chutzpah, to know how to flatter right and left, to become a kehilla "cooking ladle" [a busybody who stirs every pot], and then, then everything goes automatically, and one makes a career..
About our city councils, too, I have nothing to write; there we have living automatons sitting, whose only task is no more than to sit in the armchairs and raise their hands... The voters are, after all[?], very satisfied with their "work", because it is worse when they become active and talk in a language nobody understands..
———
Communal life in Zagłębie did make "progress" during the past year. Once, years ago, we were "poorer" in this field. Rarely, very rarely did it happen that illegal deeds took place in any communal institution, and when such a thing did happen — the heavens opened! The culprit was isolated from the institution and no longer dared to touch a communal matter.
Then came the year 5689 and changed the "fanatical" system. New "reforms" were introduced according to which one may do things that ought not to be done, rake in public money with both hands, falsify books, and only then rise to greatness.
The "reforms" became very popular here and in our neighbouring towns. It has already come to the point that "there is not a house where there is not one dead": there is hardly a single Jewish institution, whether financial, cultural or communal, that is clean of dirty deeds, but — hush, quiet... And many times it is precisely the "heroes" who receive the laurel wreath...
———
In the "cultural" field, too, we have gone "forward". This step did cost quite a lot of effort and time, but it was worth it, if only so that the nations of the world cannot reproach us that we Jews are cowards and that we fear a blow as a demon fears incense...
For a "cultural victory" we must thank the Jewish football clubs, and "Hakoach" in particular. The latter team rose last year to a very high level[?]. The team no longer waits for non-Jewish players to honour them with blows; rather "each swallowed his fellow alive" — they hack at each other, and, as experts assert, it is foreseen that "Hakoach" will receive the first prize for their heroic deeds at the matches...
The "Muse", too, did good "business" this year at night on the Old Market. The business went very well, until an evil eye, God save us, was to blame, and the till was suddenly left as after the burning of the chametz..
———
Philanthropic deeds? Not to sin — you will not find, I tell you, R' Shlomo, another region where so many beggars would establish themselves[?] as there are in Zagłębie. The local Jews have "rich hearts", they[?] hold by the saying "whoever stretches out a hand is given": he who stretches out his hand, he receives. You can see every month how the shops are flooded with collectors, preachers (maggidim), "editors" and plain beggars, and all receive a regular monthly allowance...
But best of all the Zagłębie magnates distinguished themselves in the latest relief campaign for the Land of Israel: their hearts were truly soaked[?] with grief, rivers of tears they "shed" over the great number of martyrs, and out of great "grief" they simply "lost" their strength and "could not" touch their cash-boxes...
— — — — — — — —
A young little angel knocks with his wings at the window, and I see how on his crystal-pure forehead the initials of the New Year are engraved in golden letters:
— Tapen[?] rak[?] tzlecha..! [the initials of 5690 (TaRaTZ); probably meant "let it be only success".]
— If only, sweet mother!
Your friend, who wishes you and all Klal Yisrael a good inscription and sealing,

What Is Happening in Zagłębie? — Będzin: The Kehilla Budget Approved

[Head of the local section; Będzin — Community, budget.]
What Is Happening in Zagłębie?
(Date boxes: Friday, 29 Elul 5689 — Piątek 4 października 1929 [Friday, 4 October 1929].)
Będzin
The kehilla budget approved.
This week the kehilla budget and the establishment schedule ("etat rozkład") for the current year came back approved.
In this budget the Ministry made the following changes: the kashrut stipend for the moreh-tzedek (rabbinical judge) Lewental in Czeladź was reduced. The item of 1,500 zł. as a supplementary stipend for the members of the rabbinate, so that they would supervise kashrut in the slaughterhouse, was struck out entirely. The item for renovating the synagogue was raised by 400 zł.
—o—
[Będzin — Charity, orphans.]
90 Hungry Orphans Wait for Help.
The situation in the orphans' shelters ("ochronki") of the charity society is catastrophic. The 90 orphan boys and girls are suffering hunger, because the baker has stopped supplying bread, the milkman — milk, and the butcher — meat. The income is minimal, the deficit grows larger every day, and there is a threat that this useful institution, where so many children have their home, will be closed.
In order to save the situation, the management of the institution, in agreement with the local rabbinate, has decided that the first pledges (nedarim) made by those called up to the Torah on Rosh Hashana, Shabbat Shuva and Yom Kippur shall go to the orphans' home.
The campaign has been organized properly, and the fate of the 90 children depends on Jewish society.
—o—
[Będzin — Synagogue, High Holidays.]
About Order in the Synagogue.
In connection with the remark in our paper that the kehilla leaders should find means to ensure order in the synagogue during the Days of Awe, a meeting took place on Sunday [29 September 1929] in the premises of the community ("gmina"), at which the chairman of the synagogue committee, Mr. G. Rechnic, reported on the matter and explained the plan he has regarding it.
Present at the meeting was the writer of these lines, who proposed that the system of hired ushers be abolished and that order be kept only with the help of the synagogue's own and "flis"[?] worshippers.
The proposal was accepted, and a committee was formed with the above-mentioned task. It is also to be hoped that every worshipper will appreciate the seriousness of the moment and help ensure that exemplary order reigns in the holy place.
—o—
[Będzin — Taxes, Rosh Hashana.]
"On Rosh Hashana It Is Written..."
The local "Urząd" (tax office) decided to convene the assessment commission, so that it would come to assess the turnover for 1929 during the days of Rosh Hashana.
Because of this, the Jewish members of the assessment commission officially notified the Urząd that, on account of Rosh Hashana, they will not come to the sessions.
—o—
[Będzin — Crime.]
Because of His Mother's Sins He Shoots Her Lover.
In the house at Przeczna [?] Street 19 lives the Christian woman Brzywcza [?], some thirty-odd years old, who had a lover. Her son was angry that his mother was going down evil paths and decided to take revenge on the lover. On Sunday [29 September 1929], when the lover came out of his mother's flat, the son greeted him with several revolver shots and killed him.
—o—
[Będzin — Theatre.]
Guest Performances of Ida Kamińska.
The famous actress Ida Kamińska will soon come here for several performances with a first-class ensemble which she has organized.
The repertoire: "Secrets of the Tsarist Court Ladies" and "Panna Maliczewska"[?].
—o—
[Będzin — Trade, municipality.]
Judgement Day for the Market Stallholders Came Before Rosh Hashana.
Yesterday morning the hundreds of Jewish families who draw their meagre livelihood from conducting their trade at the Old Market received a terrible "welcome". When they came out with their bundles of goods to the Old Market, they found police there, who prevented them from unpacking the goods and chased them away.
The men and women traders, seeing the ruin, ran wailing to the Magistrat (town hall), stormed the doors of our city administrators, and the uproar in Kołłątaja Street was great.
After lengthy intercession by the alderman ("ławnik") Goldsztajn and councillor ("Ratmann") Klajnman with the mayor, it was obtained that the decree would be postponed for another month, until the time when the Magistrat sets up stalls ("budki") for the traders on the square where the market halls are.
The voivode, however, did not want to agree to this, and because of that hundreds of Jewish families have lost their livelihood.
—o—
[Będzin — Accident.]
A Drunkard Falls off a Tram.
On Sunday [29 September 1929] around midday, the 42-year-old Ferdyn [?] fell off a tram in Kołłątaja Street; he was seriously injured and taken to hospital.
—o—
[Będzin — Workers, meetings.]
General Meeting.
The commercial and office employees are holding a general meeting next Sunday [6 October 1929] in the evening in the premises of Poale Zion (united with the Z.S. [Zionist Socialists]).
—o—
[Music — Warsaw.]
Concert by Miss Tenenbaum in Warsaw.
Next Sunday [6 October 1929] at 3 p.m. the pianist Miss Fela Tenenbaum, a graduate of the Berlin Academy of Music, will give a concert in the Warsaw Philharmonic, accompanied by the Philharmonic Orchestra.
The concert will at the same time be heard on the radio.

Sosnowiec: The Trial Against a Number of Jewish Merchants Has Ended. Fiora Sentenced to 2 Years’ Arrest / Sosnowiec Councillor Wolf — Elected Mayor (President) of Zawiercie / Another 2,000 for the Land of Israel / Festive Dedication of the Pogoń Beit Midrash / Collision of a Tram with a Motor Bus

[Sosnowiec — trial and customs; followed by four news items: Zawiercie, Palestine fund collection, the Pogoń beit midrash, a tram accident.]
Sosnowiec
The Trial Against a Number of Jewish Merchants Has Ended. Fiora Sentenced to 2 Years’ Arrest
On Wednesday evening the Sosnowiec trial against the merchants Dawid Fiora, B. Grajcer, J. Grajcer, E. Fiora, Urbach, Erensztajn, and against the officials of the local customs office Madejrk[?], Banach, Chamsik and others, who were accused of bringing dried fruit in from abroad illegally, came to an end.
The trial lasted 2 weeks. 130 witnesses were heard; 16 were excluded from the hearing. The defence was undertaken by the well-known Warsaw lawyers Messrs. Sterling, Goldsztajn, Brakman, Wasserberger and Senator Peuszyński[?], and by Parelli, Pawlek and Kszymuski of Sosnowiec.
Hearing the witnesses took 10 days. On Monday, after the examination of the witnesses was completed, the prosecutor took the floor and delivered a forceful 3-hour indictment speech against the accused, demanding punishment for each of them.
In the course of Tuesday the defence counsel spoke. A great impression was made by the long, substance-rich speech of advocate Sterling, who demolished the accusation entirely.
On Wednesday the prosecutor spoke again; then at 12 o’clock a recess was declared and the court withdrew to deliberate.
The verdict was supposed to be announced at about 6 o’clock. By then the courtroom was packed with the families of the accused and with mere onlookers, but instead of at 6 o’clock the court came back out only at 8 o’clock.
In a tense atmosphere the presiding judge reads out the charges once more and announces the verdict:
Dawid Fiora is found guilty of smuggling and is therefore fined 590 thousand zł. plus 59 thousand zł. in court costs. The fine may be commuted to 2 years’ arrest; the other accused are acquitted.
After the grounds of the judgment, delivered by the presiding judge, the prosecutor takes the floor and declares that he is filing a cassation appeal against the guilty party, and demands that Dawid Fiora be arrested at once.
Against this demand the defence counsel Parelli speaks out, saying that the law does not provide for Fiora to be arrested, since there is no fear whatsoever that Fiora will fail to appear for the hearing of the cassation; had Fiora — says the lawyer — had any intention[?] of fleeing, he would have done so before the trial.
The representative of the Ministry of Finance also associates himself with the prosecutor’s view and demands arrest for Fiora.
The court holds a short deliberation and decides to release Fiora from arrest against bail of one hundred thousand zł.
Mr. Fiora, who lies ill at home, is being guarded by the police.
—o—
Sosnowiec Councillor Wolf — Elected Mayor (President) of Zawiercie
On Tuesday the Zawiercie city council held a session at which the municipal executive was elected.
Elected mayor (president), with 19 votes, was the alderman (ławnik) and Sosnowiec city councillor Jerzy Wolf (N.D. — National Democrats). Among the 3 aldermen Mr. B. Hegdiler was also elected.
The post of deputy mayor is still vacant.
—o—
Another 2,000 for the Land of Israel
The relief committee for the Land of Israel has been reorganised. At the head of the committee stands Mr. Markus Hamburger, who has drawn a larger number of the nationalist youth into the collection drive; during the past week they collected 2 thousand zł., i.e. up to today a sum of 3 thousand zł. has already been sent to the Central Committee in Warsaw.
The collection drive is still under way.
—o—
Festive Dedication of the Pogoń Beit Midrash
At the present time, when all the kehillas in Zagłębie are not creating even the smallest thing, the small Jewish community of Pogoń has managed to build in the course of one year a magnificent beit midrash, of which the Jews of Pogoń may be proud, and also to immortalise the communal workers Messrs. Dawid Zweigenhaft and Moshe Yosef Friedman, who set to work with tremendous self-sacrifice, and thanks to whom the dream came true.
The dedication ceremony, however, which was celebrated last Sunday, looked — thanks to the disorder on the part of the inexperienced ushers — like an election meeting. In the women’s gallery the majority were Christian women, and the same was true among the men; during the greetings the crowd of Jews stood on the benches, the women chattered loudly, young men preached morals[?], and little by little the holy mood vanished and only the chaos remained...
Also contributing to the chaos was the “editor” of the Agudist mikveh-sheet, who preached that “in the Land of Israel nothing is left any more, all the colonists and the whole Yishuv have already been wiped out”... These shameful words naturally provoked a great storm, and the audience would not let him speak any further.
———
The beit midrash is beautifully decorated, a festive mood prevails, and everyone waits for the most important guests — the Torah scrolls, which are being brought here under a wedding canopy from the shtiblekh; the orchestra plays, the festively dressed crowd, and especially the hosts of the celebration, clap their hands and break into a dance.
Mr. Friedman opens the ceremony, Rabbi Schwarz cuts the ribbon and hands the chair over to Mr. L. Bauszykowski. Delegates of a number of institutions are invited to the presidium, and the Sosnowiec cantor with his choir sing “Ma Tovu”, “Mizmor Shir Hanukat” and the Polish anthem (the Jewish anthem — no).
After the orchestra plays “Boże, coś Polskę”, the martyrs in the Land of Israel are first honoured, and the cantor recites “El Male Rachamim” for the martyrs and for the deceased members.
Then come the greetings: Rabbi Menachem Schwarz and the rabbinical judge (moreh tzedek) Avraham Yehonatan Stark speak on the topic of the day. Rabbi Schwarz turns to the women, asking them not to come bareheaded to the prayers on the High Holy Days. On behalf of the Sosnowiec kehilla and the Zionist Organisation Mr. Y. M. Wajgryb gives greetings; on behalf of the “Gemilut Chesed” loan fund — greeting[?] — Mr. Bauszykowski; the guest Mr. Ch. Kupferminc; from “Tze’irei Mizrachi” — Jungster; and Mr. Glirman[?] (“Hashomer”).
A storm breaks out when the “editor” of the mikveh-sheet begins to preach; he repeats what the Communists say, that “in the Land of Israel we have nothing any more, because the little we had there has also been destroyed”...
Against these base words of informing, the representative of the Sosnowiec kehilla board, Mr. Itshke Zaks, protested sharply, saying: “You liars, are the slanders you have spread so far still not enough for you, that you still dare to come here to a Jewish celebration and provoke? How much money has the ‘Agura’ [read: Agudah] given for the Land of Israel?!”
The audience was greatly incensed at the despicable performance and stormily took[?] the floor away from him.
A report on how the building came to be is given by Mr. D. Zweigenhaft, who says that the initiators set about the building with barely 800 zł. “People regarded us — says Mr. Z. — as dreamers, and here we stand before an accomplished fact: we are celebrating the dedication of the beit midrash, which cost nearly 50 thousand zł.”
After the “dry” speeches the crowd turned to a glass of liquor, and then to dancing, which went on until late into the night.
Because of the establishment of such a splendid house of prayer, all the Hasidic shtiblekh in Pogoń have been closed.
—o—
Collision of a Tram with a Motor Bus
On Tuesday, on 3 Maja Street, a tram ran into a passenger motor bus operating on the Sosnowiec—Mysłowice route. Luckily the passengers and the driver escaped unharmed, but the bus was smashed to pieces.

A plot of land consecrated for the cemetery

Yesterday morning a large plot of land, situated at the front of the cemetery on the road to Czeladź, was consecrated.
Present at the ceremony were the local rabbinate with the Rav at its head, the moreh-tzedek of Czeladź, the rebbe R' Yitzchak Menachem Rosenberg, the gabbaim and members of the Chevra Kadisha, the dozores (kehilla board members), "pri nisim" [?] (probably: parnasim, community elders) and a large crowd of Jews.
The cemetery and the plot were circled 7 times, while the appropriate chapters of Psalms and "Yoshev be-seter" were recited.
After the hakafot were completed, the cantor Mr. Wszpowicz [?] and the choir chanted El Male Rachamim for all the departed in the cemetery and for the martyrs in the Land of Israel.
During the memorial prayers the crowd, numbering several dozen people, showed "great awe" — but towards something else: the little bottles of brandy... as [?] each one tried to outdo the other and grab one more glass... and so voices like "Give a bit of brandy", "Me a bit of sweet", "I haven't had any lekach (honey cake) yet" etc. drowned out the words "the souls of the martyrs who fell and were slain"...
— Where are the manners!
—o—

Both Days of Rosh Hashanah in Zagłębie

[Zagłębie — holidays; community life.] This year's Rosh Hashanah passed quietly in Będzin. The Great Synagogue and all the houses of prayer were full of worshippers. Thanks to the fine weather the public went out for a stroll in the afternoon.
The second day of Rosh Hashanah coincided with the Socialist Youth Day, and the youth organisation "Frajhajt" ("Freedom") held a torchlight procession through the streets at the close of the holiday. Among the many transparencies, slogans stood out strongly, such as: "Honour to the fallen halutzim in Eretz Israel" and "Down with the Arab effendis and their allies. The torchlight procession was supposed to go out into the street in the evening, but because the police at the last moment permitted demonstrating only before it grew dark, the demonstration set out a little earlier.
———
In Sosnowiec the holiday passed very peacefully; even in Old Sosnowiec, the nest of "war", it was quiet. All the "war-waging" forces shook hands and made peace. Left outside the peace-loving camp is the "Fiks"...
———
Stormy and lively it was in Dąbrowa. From the local Pilica (Pilitzer) shtibl Hasidim came out, some without teeth, some with blackened eyes, and the "lucky ones" got away with dry blows...
The "holy" war broke out for the following reasons: in that shtibl there is a Hasid, R' Yosef Szywek [?], who has been leading the Shacharit prayers before the lectern for some twenty-odd years.
Times change, and the Shacharit leader too has changed and become more modern, but he did not want to give up his hazakah (established right).
The Pilica Hasidim realised that the Shacharit leader with the hazakah was not acceptable and decided that someone else should lead Shacharit. In order that the Shacharit leader with the hazakah should not lead the prayers, they announced that prayers would begin at 9 o'clock, while "upstairs" it was confided as a secret that prayers would begin at 8 o'clock, so that the Shacharit leader with the hazakah would be late...
And so it was: when Mr. S. came to the shtibl, he already heard someone else saying "Ha-Melekh". At this Mr. S. became very angry. How could it be! To play such a "trick" on him — and he dealt out blow after blow.. His rival he gave black eyes, and on Ejnik [?] Rozenberg, who raised objections, he fulfilled "blunt his teeth": with a single blow 2 teeth were at once rolling on the floor.. and finally he also honoured Messrs. Lubling and Grajcer with dry blows..
———
Not even a week has passed since the dedication of the newly built beit midrash was celebrated in Pogoń, and already the local congregation has split. The split came about because the "common folk" were "offended" that the "notables" had grabbed the eastern-wall seats and left them "na tamim ostatki" [Polish: the leftovers]. Because of this the "breakaways" made a separate minyan for themselves and prayed there.
The gabbaim of the beit midrash even forbade the shofar blowing, but the opposition argues: "neither of your sting nor of your honey" — we do not begrudge you the seats, but do not judge [?] us.
———
A treat for the antisemitic newspapers was provided by Madame Holcdorf of Czeladź. In the house of Mr. Holcdorf there is the Radomsko shtibl, which the landlord has a strong desire to evict. For this purpose he took the Torah scrolls home to himself several weeks ago, and with the help of the police the Torah scrolls were taken back into the shtibl.
On the second day of Rosh Hashanah the "woman of valour" Mrs. Holcdorf "purified" the gabbai, Mr. Berman. The latter again ran with this "find" to the police station, where the number of reports against the "heroic" woman has grown...
———
On the second day of Rosh Hashanah "Hashomer Hatzair" held its traditional meeting, at which Mr. Avraham Chlewicki [?] spoke on "The situation in Zionism and in Eretz Israel", Cwi Fergricht [?] — on "The situation in the Hashomer Hatzair movement", and Yechezkel Fridman gave a report on the activity of the past year.
Olkusz — From the Court

[Olkusz — courts.] At the session of the Sosnowiec District Court held in the local court, the trial took place of Senior Constable Aleksiejew for shooting dead, while an eviction was being carried out at his home, the bailiff (komornik) Jaroszewicz.
The trial aroused great interest. Despite the limited number of admission tickets, the court building, the corridor and the whole square were packed with the curious. The "accused was defended by Advocate Pawełek of Sosnowiec; the prosecutor demanded 15 years' imprisonment. The defence counsel delivered a 2-hour defence speech and asked that the accused be acquitted, or alternatively be given the mildest punishment. During his speech many women wept. Above all he relied on the fact that his client had committed the murder without a sound mind. At 9 in the evening, amid great tension, the court pronounced the verdict, according to which the accused is sentenced to 3 years' imprisonment, commuted to 3 years in a reformatory; the prosecutor and the defence counsel announced that they are lodging an appeal.
—o—
Eruvin Made Already.
[Olkusz — community.] After a break of 50 years our town has received eruvin again. The Jewish town councillors carried the eruv project through the town council, and afterwards it was approved by the Voivodeship; Mr. Yosef Szwarcberg took a particular interest in the eruvin.
As is reported, 50 years ago the ban on the eruvin was issued by the then Governor-General Gurko while passing through Olkusz.
A. B.
Żarki — "He Does Not Give for Goyim"

[Żarki — relief for the victims in Eretz Israel; Agudah.] Here [in Żarki] a relief committee for the victims in Eretz Israel was founded. Various strata of the town were represented on the committee, except for the "Agudah".
The campaign went off successfully; no one refused to give for the victims in Eretz Israel, except for a few Agudah people.
When members of the committee — very respectable householders, by the way — asked a certain Agudah man [for a contribution] for this purpose, he answered in these words: "For goyim I give no money".
The Proclaimed Tishri Campaign for the Keren Kayemet

[Będzin — Zionism; Jewish National Fund.] In connection with the proclaimed Tishri campaign for the settlement of Eretz Israel, the KKL (Jewish National Fund) in Będzin organised at the "Nowości" a lecture by Comrade Wielopolski on the topic "The recent events in Eretz Israel and our task at the present moment".
The introduction was given by the representative of the local KKL committee, Mr. Nute Landner, who gave a survey of the recent events in Eretz Israel and emphasised the difference and the character of the events in Eretz Israel compared with the various pogroms that took place in the lands of the Diaspora, and the courageous, proud defensive struggle of our halutzim in Eretz Israel. The entire overflowing audience honoured the fallen heroes and martyrs by rising. Then Mr. Landner gave the floor to Mr. Wielopolski, who delivered a detailed lecture on the recent bloody events in Eretz Israel, analysed the causes of the events that took place, and expressed the opinion that what happened in Eretz Israel cannot be understood as a political struggle between the Arabs and the Jews; rather, the main causes are more economic, and they were organised by the effendis and muftis.
With great bitterness the speaker dwells on the treacherous role of the "Bund" members and the Reds, who declared solidarity with the Arab murderers who threw themselves upon workers' kvutzot, where the type of a Jewish socialist workers' life is being created.
The lecture made a strong impression on the whole audience, and the entire time an extraordinary silence reigned in the hall.
Then Mr. Landner gives the closing word, appealing in the name of the KKL with a warm call to the Jewish population to support the Keren Kayemet and to strengthen our Zionist funds.
Mr. Landner also mentions the loss of the young comrade Israel Brasman, of blessed memory, who was an active worker for the KKL, and the whole audience honours his memory by rising. With the singing of "Hatikvah" the lecture is concluded.

Strzemieszyce.
On Sunday a meeting of representatives of all the existing minyanim was held in the premises of the gmina [local council], with the aim of sending off the money collected for the victims in the Land of Israel. The first to take the floor was Mr. Lipszyc (Agudah), who proposed that the money be sent half to the Warsaw kehilla and half to the Agudah. Mr. Wajdband (Mizrachi) proposed that the "Agudah" receive no more than 10 per cent of the collected money, because its followers had not given it either. Mr. Zinger came forward with a proposal that, since the Va'ad Leumi distributes the money only to Zionists, at least the local money should be distributed to the local pious Jews. Only after a sharp fight did they come to an agreement: of the 630 zł. collected the Agudah receives 27½ per cent and the rest is sent to the Warsaw kehilla.

Small Remarks on Big Matters

The economic system.
We often see the police drawing up reports for small, insignificant disorders, while on big and important matters — we see — nobody even stops. We see this quite often, and indeed we have written about it more than once.
It goes without saying that our house-owners are still far from knowing how to observe the regulations and to keep order as it should be kept.
But it is even more astonishing when those who issue the proper regulations do not observe them at the very moment when they themselves must fulfil them. For instance: we see that whenever a heavier rain passes, the 3rd of May Square [Plac 3 Maja] together with Małachowski Street [ul. Małachowskiego] is flooded, and on „Magdushever" [?] Street it is downright terrible; there poor people are utterly ruined, their dwellings are flooded, and their whole bit of bedding, with the bit of merchandise such a family owns, is destroyed. This is unheard of; such enormous damage must not be allowed. Whoever else may do so — but a self-government [the municipality] surely must not allow this to happen over and over without end. It must, after all, bear responsibility towards its citizens, all the more so when it concerns people who are not rich, those who occupy the cellar dwellings.
The same is true now with the laying of the pipes in the ground. Deep holes are dug across the streets; work is begun everywhere and finished nowhere. No account is taken of the narrow, cramped streets where the traffic is heavy; the dug-up streets simply stand there in the middle of the work and nobody hurries to finish. This is unheard of — how can a whole town be left in such disorder? Moreover, one is covered in dust from the excavated earth. And what will happen when rain comes — we will bathe in the mud. Why should the Magistrate [town council] permit such unheard-of disorder, which incidentally also hinders carting to the shops? Could one not see to it that half or a quarter of a street is done, and as soon as the work is finished everything is filled in properly, and only then go on to the next stage? Can traffic be stopped in whole quarters of the town? That means treating the citizens and their interests lightly, and a municipal self-government must absolutely take this into account.
Our shame in the world of commerce.
And again we have to speak about what we have already spoken about so many times, and which once seemed to have reached its culmination point and to belong to the past already. Unfortunately, we now see that the root is stuck deep in the ground and it is impossible to eradicate what is so unseemly, what brings so much shame on the Jew that we blush with disgrace more than once.
It concerns the „fine and aesthetic" trade of the „rufers" [touts who pull customers off the street into shops]. Not long ago we saw here how things went on [?] solely thanks to the energetic activity of one such heroic „rufer". This kind of touting has become a sort of profession: the more brazen such a rufer is and the more heroism such a „ruferke" [female tout] displays, the better their chances of getting better posts with higher salaries.
Terrible things are told about what goes on between the rufers, the ruferkes and the merchants. It is a special trade that one must know. One must know how to behave, one must be clever [?] towards them, otherwise one is risking one's life — and that is no trifle for a penny. And a stranger passes by, and when he watches such a street scene he is astonished; he asks himself what this is, and where in the world he is. For a moment it seems to him that he is somewhere in Asia — such a terrible impression it makes on a foreign onlooker.
And at such a moment we ask ourselves: where are we, and how can these deeds be permitted? How is it allowed, how does one endure so much shame and humiliation? How much antisemitism and antipathy does such a trade create? With how much contempt does one regard the Jewish merchant and Jewish commerce at such a moment? How many bitter words are then said at our address — at Jewish trade and commerce?
Nor is it any wonder, because it must disgust, it must provoke bitterness and antisemitism, for — say what you will — this is not seen among any other nation or tongue, in any healthy branch of trade.
Perhaps one might set about removing and uprooting this ugliness — such merchants who see the damage it does to Jewish commerce, to the decent Jewish merchant? Perhaps our „merchants' associations" might intervene, not allowing the Jewish shopping streets to be flooded with such a dangerous atmosphere; perhaps they would see to it that such ugly orgies are no longer played out, which only bring poison and venom into Jewish commerce, which is unhealthy and abnormal as it is.
— It is high time that we reacted to these intolerable deeds.
R. Let.
Little Feuilleton.

[Będzin and district — humorous feuilleton for Shabbat Shuva and Yom Kippur.] Machzor — a new edition in honour of Shabbat Shuva, by Ben Amotz.

"Shuva Yisrael" — return, O Israel!
A splendid word it is — Jews,
O leaders, turn your faces to the public!
O parties, turn to peace!

"Shuva Yisrael" — a golden counsel,
it should have been heeded long ago;
we show[?] one another the shoulder —
oh, let us finally return!

To unity, to work, to the Jewish word,
to the mutual responsibility of one Jew for another;
to return from here and there —
our spirit must wander no more.

We nibble at foreign pastries[?],
we live by wild foreign customs,
we sway to the left and to the right
and forget ourselves in the middle.

We lack a centre for our soul
that is drowning in assimilation;
we lack, in our struggle for existence,
a spiritual centralisation.

Everyone goes his own way
and lives by his own "idea",
has his own "one mustn't" and "one may",
and for him there is neither law nor judge.

Everyone airs opinions and "teaches" the town
and considers himself a full "authority":
one in the synagogue, another in the bathhouse,
and a third is a "posek" in "business".

What one declares kosher the other makes treyf,
because he believes in a different "explicit text"[?];
Jewish spirit, straying wanderer,
return to your first root.

You stray there, you stray here,
you sell yourself to every nation,
you know not what, you know not whom,
and you create only imitation.

Shuva Yisrael — return, O spirit!
Throw away the foreign stage-wings;
we must say boldly, as Jews:
a spiritual ingathering of the exiles!

Who swings kapores, and with whom.
The magistrate — with the market tax,
the councillors — with the voters,
the dozors [kehilla board members] — with the community,
the urząd [tax office] — with the merchants,
the merchants — with the bills of exchange,
the outpatient clinic — with the Jewish sick,
the youth — with morality.

Al chet shechatanu ("For the sin we have committed").
The city fathers beat their breasts, "for the sin we have committed": we built market halls.
The Agudah — for the sin that we wrecked[?] the campaign for Eretz Israel.
The "Bund" — for the sin that we made a match with the Arabs.
Kehilla grabbers — for the sin of "dealings of the hand": we lent a hand to public pennies.
"Hakoach" — for the sin we committed "with a strong hand"...
Well-known councillors — for the sin we committed "with foolish speech": our "speeches" in the city council were "ni be ni me" [neither here nor there].
The tax-assessment commission — for the sin we committed: we used to run to meetings, raise our hands and increase the Jews' troubles.
And for all of them, world-golem, forgive us, pardon us, grant us atonement.

I beg forgiveness
a) Of my creditors. May they forgive me.
b) Of my landlord, because I don't want to move out of the flat.
c) Of my summer-resort lady ["datshnitse"], whom I suspected while she was in Rabka.

And Chaim handed R' Zelig Mania's only [?] letter, which Dvoyre had received one day after her flight.
"Ah, Zelig, what did I tell you? Ah yes, it is a lie, a falsehood and a deceit, what 'Irena' said!"
"Yes, Chana! Here — read! Look, a marvel [?], Mania's handwriting, as sure as I am a Jew!"
"Oy, may I be an atonement for her!" — Chana took the letter and began to kiss it and weep — "and we were lying here and knew nothing!"
"Well, Mr. Chaim, it is getting late," Branicki spoke up. "Jump up onto the horse and ride quickly to the village and tell Sylwester in my name to see to it that aunt 'Fanny' and the other 'aunts', the conspirators, and the whole gang come to the convent no later than four o'clock, and you be back here at the same time; I will stay here and see that meanwhile no harm comes to Mania's parents. I have a whole troop of mounted police here in the little wood. They are ready for anything. And you, R' Zelig and wife, walk about here and have no fear. Here is a whistle for you; should anyone attack you, just give a whistle — and the lads will be here in the blink of an eye!"
"Must we still keep shouting 'Mania, Mania!'?" Chana asked.
"No, not necessary!" Stanisław Branicki answered with a smile.
A minute later both Chaim and Stanisław Branicki had vanished.
"Well, Chana, what did I tell you? Ah yes, we have a great God in heaven, a 'God who works wonders'!" R' Zelig said in a chant.
"Certainly we have a great God! But let us not forget Chaim too!" Chana answered.
"Of course. He is only a messenger of God, blessed be He," R' Zelig answered.
———
It was an autumn evening. An autumn wind was blowing; around the walls of the convent whistled and rustled [?] the kind of wind of which village folk say that "demons are dancing".
Jan Siwiański was received by the eldest sister, Irena, as soon as he entered the convent. He told her that today at about five o'clock in the evening Mania's baptism must take place, and his wedding to her straight after the baptism, because Mania could no longer be kept locked in the convent even one minute. She is planning to escape, the Jews want to take her out by force, her parents are circling the convent and keep shouting: "Mania! Mania!" The baptism must take place today no later than five o'clock — the earlier the better — and right away the wedding too, and then everything will be done with, lost, and people will heed the Jews as much as the cat.
So Jan spoke to Irena in sharp words, "from the teeth outward", as the saying goes. Of course, as the reader already knows, it was all a staged affair, according to Stanisław Branicki's plan to catch the "thief" — that is, the "convent" with the "sisters", with all the participants in the conspiracy — red-handed. Jan did it to save himself from disaster, since Stanisław Branicki had given him his word that no harm would come to him.
Sister Irena at once agreed to Jan's demand and only asked:
"Well, and the aunts and nieces and the other in-laws will be here in time?"
"Yes, all that has been taken care of, they will be here in time, I expect them here any minute," Jan answered, "and where is Mania?"
"Bring Mania up!" Sister Irena ordered two sisters, "and take her into the green room!"
The two sisters at once carried out Irena's order.
Sister Irena was now in her brightly lit, richly adorned room; she was dressed and hung with several golden crosses, polished diamonds and brilliants: a regal sight! After all, Mania — a Jewish daughter — must be baptised and her soul saved!
Mania too was now in her room — the green hall. She was wearing white silk clothes; her black, beautiful locks hung down over her sad, white face.
Her face was sunken, her black eyes shone more than usual, as with a person who has not long ago endured a great deal.
The convent became bright and lively. The "sisters" ran hither and thither like poisoned mice, the cloister bells began to ring, and soon the Siwiańskis arrived, the aunts and the nieces. Aunt Fanny was in seventh heaven with great joy and her face beamed with happiness; she kissed Sister Irena and embraced her out of great bliss. Just think — such a good deed, such a good deed! And she, Fanny, had lived to take part in such a good deed! Lucky her!
Jan asked to remain alone with Mania for a few minutes; his request was naturally granted at once. So what? What if he takes "liberties" [?] with the "holy" Mania too early? So what? Is that some great worry? Is that the sisters' and Irena's worry?!
But Jan took no liberties with Mania at all, not by a hair. He was careful and controlled himself, the gentile lad. Although, to tell the truth, he now found her a thousand times more beautiful than she had ever been. Apparently her heart told her that an end had come to her troubles even before he, Jan, told her so.

The Lights That Went Out at "Kol Nidre".

[History — Łęczyca; the Kol Nidre night of 1656.] By Moshe Feinkind.
It happened in the critical year 1656.
The Swedes, together with the Brandenburgers, were waging war on Poland and seized the town of Łęczyca, the so-called "a city and a mother in Israel".
It was just the eve of Yom Kippur, and all the Jews had gathered for "Kol Nidre" in the new synagogue, only just built.
Outside the cannons thundered, the flaming shells flew through the streets, and their whistling and howling accompanied the loud weeping of the congregation while the cantor recited "Kol Nidre"...
Suddenly, all at once, every light in the synagogue went out, and it was pitch dark.
The tumult grew great. The weeping and wailing grew louder still; the congregation remained standing in fear, as if turned to stone, in their places, and each said whatever he could still say — one Psalms, one the confession, one said [a prayer] and took leave of life.
And so the congregation stood in the synagogue, trembling as one, until daybreak, until the roaring and thundering of the cannons stopped and the Swedes left the town...
But the Jews had a bad foreboding because of the lights that had gone out at "Kol Nidre"; their hearts prophesied to them — a bad year.
* * *
The "Confederates", led by King Jan Kazimierz — who in 1652 had confirmed to the Jews of Poland the rights they had held before — having driven the enemy out of the town, at once set about slaughtering the Jews on the second day of Sukkot.
The remnant of the Swedes who were still holding out in the "castle", hearing the heart-rending cries of the thousands of Jews being slaughtered, quickly abandoned the "castle" and, out of fear, they too surrendered to the Poles.
The king himself in fact [?] wanted to spare the Jewish population of Łęczyca. He "did not want to soil his hands with innocent Jewish blood, but the local population, accusing the Jews of friendly relations with the Swedes during the siege, incited the soldiery, and three thousand Jews perished, whose dead bodies found their grave in the canals around Łęczyca, into which they were thrown.
The small children, on the other hand, who had by chance remained alive, were then dragged by force into the churches, forcibly converted there and handed over to the peasants.
But those bloody heroes did not spare the synagogue either; it was burned together with six hundred Torah scrolls, leaving in the town no trace of anything that had ever belonged to Jews or come from Jews...
Almost all of Łęczyca went up in smoke then, and of the Jews not a single survivor or refugee remained...
* * *
After that cruel slaughter, for a long time no Jew wanted to set foot again on the threshold of Łęczyca, where Jews had settled soon after the First Crusade.
Only after the royal "universal" [decree] issued by Jan Kazimierz on the 20th of June [czerwiec] 1657 in Częstochowa, under which all Jews were cleared of the accusation that they had stood on the side of the Swedes during the war with Poland — only then did the Jews let themselves be persuaded and began to resettle in Łęczyca, receiving back from the king all the privileges they had held there, as well as the right to rebuild the synagogue, which was not permitted to be larger or higher than the former synagogue had been.
So the king expressly stated to the Jews.
From that time on, on the first day of Chol Hamoed Sukkot, the holy memory of those thousands of martyrs is commemorated in the Łęczyca synagogue. An "azkara" (memorial service) is held for them, on which occasion the tragic events there in the year 5416 (1656) are read out from a "pinkas" (communal register), mentioning a large number of names of those who perished for the sanctification of God's name; and then a "kiddush" with honey cake and brandy is held in the synagogue...
There was also a marble tablet with a Hebrew inscription that hung on the town wall next to the synagogue, on which the Jewish tragedy of that year was inscribed; but when the walls were taken down in 1830–34, that tablet was unfortunately lost.
A Young Man from Dąbrowa at a Celebration at Abu-Kishk's (A Letter from the Land of Israel)

[Land of Israel — letter; the Sharon: a wedding at Sheikh Abu Kishk's, Jewish–Arab relations after the 1929 riots.]
The colony committee received an invitation from Sheikh Abu-Kishk to come to his brother's wedding. (The wedding was on Friday, 20/9.) Because relations between us and them are now strained, he invited the Jews specially for Monday, 23 September, so that it should not come to any clash. This is the same Abu-Kishk, the well-known leader of 1921, who organised the attack on Petah Tikva and was sentenced for it to 15 years of hard imprisonment. But today we have him to thank that our region, the Sharon, came out of the present disturbances smoothly, without any damage.
All the colonies — for example Petah Tikva, "the mother" of the colonies, Kfar Saba, Magdiel, Ein Hai, Ramatayim, Gan Haim, Ra'anana, Herzliya — agreed by telephone that we would all go to the wedding, each colony would bring him a gift, and we would meet at Bukharia [?]. At half past nine in the morning we were at the appointed place. There all the representatives of the colonies listed above were already waiting with their gifts. At the head of all the guests was Avraham Shapira of Petah Tikva. At a quarter to ten the cars set off for Abu-Kishk's; from afar we see how the Arabs await us, and Abu-Kishk's horsemen ride out to meet us.
At the spot we are received by the sheikh himself with the bridegroom and his retinue; he first greets Mr. Avraham Shapira, who presents the gift from Petah Tikva, consisting of 3 fine sheep, a sack of rice, a box of sugar, coffee, tea and salt; then he introduces all the representatives of the colonies, and each representative gives him a gift. The sheikh thanks us and invites us into the reception room, where we are asked to sit down, and Abu-Kishk and his brothers, dressed in holiday clothes, treat us to cigarettes; then lemonade is served to drink, and black coffee in tiny little cups, after the Arab fashion; meanwhile the correspondents snatch a chat with the bridegroom, who is barely 15 years old.
The bridegroom's uncle relates that their tribe numbers a hundred men, apart from women and children, who do not count. Their influence is very great; the whole surrounding area is under their sway. It is a fact that even today agitators from the muftis come to them every day, urging them to attack the Sharon, but Abu-Kishk answers: "I live with the Jews in peace and have nothing against them; I gave my word in the year 1921 that I would no longer attack the Jews, and so I keep my word; the Jews got me out of Acre, and I do not want to break my word."
The bride is not seen; she is together with the women, who are in a separate courtyard enclosed by a high wall.
The photographers are at work: Abu-Kishk is photographed with Avraham Shapira shaking hands, then Jews and Arabs mixed together, all the committee members [?] with the Abu-Kishk brothers; the Arabs begin to dance with swords, wave handkerchiefs, hold one another by the belts and dance a "hora" together with our brethren. After that we are invited to eat. I want to note that early in the morning Abu-Kishk had sent for the Petah Tikva shochet, who slaughtered several sheep and was also present at the koshering.
The dishes at the "table" consisted of pitas — a kind of bread that tastes like leather soles; then roast meat was served on large platters, roasted the way it was in olden times; no cutlery was given; everyone ate with his hands, and the bones of the meat were thrown on the ground. At the end rice was served; among the Arabs that is the most precious dish. We eat the rice, on Mr. Avraham Shapira's instruction, with our hands, like dumplings. Over the drinks Mr. Avraham Shapira makes a speech in Arabic; he thanks the hosts in the name of all the colonies for their hospitality and wishes that we may always live in peace. To that we all responded with applause and shouts.
Then Abu-Kishk replies. He thanks all the colonies, listing every one of them by name, for the honour we have done him. This day — he says — he will always remember; it is one of the finest days of his life. He wishes that this day may be the key to peace between Jews and Arabs in the whole Land of Israel. These last words drew a storm of applause from all of us. We lifted him and the bridegroom up high. Then he invited us to the horse races he had arranged for our sake. Avraham Shapira, a Jew of over 60, galloped with the sheikh on horseback. It was a beautiful sight. The Arabs race on their horses like devils [?] and wave their handkerchiefs as they go. At 3 o'clock in the afternoon, when Avraham Shapira gave the command "Comrades, home!", we took leave of the sheikh and of all his brothers and relatives. In an elevated mood we left Abu-Kishk's.
The impression was a very good one, especially at the present time, when a boycott propaganda against the Jews is going on among the Arabs — Jewish neighbours are invited to a celebration at an Arab leader's. This is proof that not the whole Arab people is against us; only the ringleaders and the agitators are guilty of the disaster that befell the Jewish Yishuv.
It is also worth noting that Abu-Kishk had doubted whether the Jews would come to him.
Naftali Rechnitz, Tel Aviv.

What's New in Zagłębie? — Będzin: The Sad Fate of the Jewish Traders in the Old Market

[Head of the local page; Będzin — Trade, City Council.]
What's New in Zagłębie?
(Date boxes: Friday, 7 / 7 Tishrei 5690 — Piątek 11 października 1929 [Friday, 11 October 1929].)
Będzin
The sad fate of the Jewish traders in the Old Market.
Extraordinary session of the City Council.
Our readers already know that on Thursday, the day before Rosh Hashanah, the "execution" [enforcement] was carried out against one hundred and fifty Jewish traders in the Old Market [Stary Rynek], from where they were driven apart by the police, and since then they have lost the livelihood they had until now.
The traders' fate had been sealed several months ago. The Magistrate [municipal board] warned them, announcing through street posters that trading in the Old Market would be stopped, but until today our councillors treated the matter very lightly and did not give a thought to starting any action whatsoever so that the "operation" on the dozens of poor Jewish families should not be carried out in the way it was last Thursday.
Also to blame for this are the individuals well known to us, who swim upside down ["shvimen kapoyer"] in every time of trouble, give all kinds of "advice", and the result is the reverse: instead of helping with something substantial, they make the situation worse, until there is no longer any favourable way out.
In this question, too, such interested persons appeared and with their "activity", so to speak[?], made the hard position of the helpless traders even worse.
The echo of this cry of woe came on Sunday evening in the premises of the "Merchants' Association" ["Sokhrim Fareyn"], where, on the initiative of the small traders' representatives, a large meeting was held on the question of the Old Market.
The meeting turned into a rally; our city fathers and other "public activists" made speeches, and people cursed and insulted one another no end ["on what the world stands"]...
After the personal accounts, which brought no great honour, it was decided that a delegation of 3 persons should intervene with the City President [mayor] to have the matter changed.
The delegation of the councillors Mrs. Ratner, Goldfeld and Hampel[?] conferred the next morning with the City President, who promised them that on the Magistrate's part he would help to have the term for trading in the Old Market extended.
On Monday evening an extraordinary session of the City Council was called, which was to decide that until such time as trading places are built on the site of the "Polyes", trading should continue as until now in the Old Market.
To the session, naturally, all the councillors came, Jewish and non-Jewish, but when the latter learned what it was about, they left...
The same "tactics" were displayed by our "allies", the councillors and the aldermen ["lavnikes", ławnicy] of the P.P.S. [Polish Socialist Party]. They stood in the courtyard of the "Piast" and did not want to go into the hall... The entreaties of some of the Jewish councillors, who stressed that the session had a purely formal character, did not help. The "socialists" were stubborn and by no means wanted to fulfil the wish of the Jewish councillors. They left so that there would be no quorum and the question could not be dealt with..
But the "socialist" move did not succeed. In the hall there was a quorum, and the session, chaired by Mr. Ehrlich, took place. Besides Jews, present in the hall were the alderman ["lavnik"] Żebrowski and councillor Garczarczyk[?].
The chairman opens the session and reads out the motion, which says: "The City Council instructs the municipal administration to build trading places on the 'Polyes' site, and to intervene with the Voivode [provincial governor] that it be permitted to trade in the Old Market until the proper places are ready."
The motion is adopted unanimously, and a delegation of the councillors Mrs. Ratner, Dr. Rechtman and Vice-Chairman Yakov Ehrlich is elected, to travel together with President Michał[?] to Kielce.
The delegation was in Kielce on Wednesday at 9 in the morning and was received by the Voivode only at about 1 o'clock at noon.
The question was first presented by President Michał and then by the councillors Mrs. Ratner, Dr. Rechtman and Ehrlich.
At first the Voivode rejected every proposal for a prolongation, but after the delegation's explanations the Voivode declared that he was not acquainted[?] with the whole matter, but that within 7 days he would send a delegate to familiarise himself with the matter on the spot. Meanwhile he ordered that the trade of the market-stall holders ["markshteyer"] be permitted again.
Since the site where the "Polyes" are located is not yet suitable for such a number of traders, it is to be hoped that the term will be prolonged until the trading places are made ready in the best order.
The news that the term had been extended aroused great joy among the desperate traders, and they wished one another mazel tov...
A murder at a T.U.R. party

Last Sunday, on the holiday of the socialist youth organisations, the local "TUR" [Workers' University Society] held a party in the hall on Góra Zamkowa [Castle Hill].
In the middle of the festivities, when the participants were drunk[?], a quarrel broke out among the guests. From words they passed to deeds and a regular battle developed, during which revolver shots rang out.
The result was that a certain Roman Szmuter of Mysłowice was hit by several bullets and fell dead in the hall.
The murdered man had come here to Będzin together with his fiancée and, on learning that a dance evening was taking place on Góra Zamkowa, he went with his fiancée to enjoy himself — and met his death.

A young man in the role of a midwife

Mrs. Dwora Lustiger of Pogoń came here for the holiday to her mother, with whom she also intended to spend the time of her confinement. Her husband, too, was supposed to come here for the holiday.
On the first day of Rosh Hashanah, when the husband did not come, the woman, uneasy, set off home to Pogoń to find out why her husband had not come.
Walking along Kościuszko Street, next to Zuckerman's railway siding (bocznica), the woman was seized by strong labour pains, and the birth followed at once. By chance Mr. Jancze Lustiger was passing, and seeing the situation the woman was in, he performed the necessary work of a midwife with a shoelace.
At that moment a passenger car drove by; Mr. Lustiger forced the driver to stop, and in the car the new mother and her newborn baby girl were taken to the institution of the "Linas haCholim".
"They are picking money up in the streets"

On Sunday, the second day of Rosh Hashanah, the alley where the Gerer shtibl [prayer house of the Ger Hasidim] stands was "flooded" with small change, and children were kept busy picking it up.
The money had been spilled by a beggar who, on his way home from prayers, let it drop[?] on the ground...
Trade in foodstuffs in Upper Silesia — permitted

As is known, the authorities in Upper Silesia had been preventing traders from selling food products.
Following the intervention of the local Merchants' Association, permission to trade in the above-mentioned articles has been granted.
The articles, however, must be packaged.
Będzin students at foreign universities organise

Under the chairmanship of Magister Mr. Lewin, a meeting of 25 Jewish students studying abroad took place last week at the "Merchants' Association". Before proceeding to practical organisational matters, Mr. Herzinger gave a report on the recently held congress of Jewish students from foreign universities. Instead of discussing objectively the course of the conference and its substantial results, the reporter expressed his regret that the majority at the congress had consisted of nationally-minded students, who had honoured the fallen martyrs in the Land of Israel by standing, and who had protested against the persecution of Hebrew in Soviet Russia...
The report, which bore a tendentious character, provoked a heated discussion lasting several hours, in which Messrs. Frenkel (Liège), A. Erlich[?] (Haifa), Welgrin (Prague), Wrocławski (Brno) and others took part. All the speakers sharply condemned the destructive conduct of some delegates — Mr. Herzinger among them — who had come to the conference in order to push through "prozela-gic"[?] demands. After lengthy debate a resolution was adopted by a majority of votes expressing no confidence in the Będzin delegate Mr. Herziger [sic] for his improper conduct at the congress.
After the first, stormy part of the meeting, late at night, they proceeded to organisational matters. Mr. Frenkel spoke on the significance and tasks of the students' organisation, which is to embrace the young people studying abroad. It was decided to set up at the local "Ognisko" a special section and secretariat of Będzin students at foreign universities.

Sosnowiec: Activity of the Chamber of Commerce / Visit of a ministerial commission / Sequestrator sentenced to 3 months' prison / Budget lists — to the Magistrate / Workers demand coal / A big fire / Today's youth... / A bandit attack / A theatre performance / Donations at the editorial office

[Sosnowiec — Chamber of Commerce; followed by short local items; and at the end, donations received by the editors.]
The finance and tax commission of the local Chamber of Commerce held a meeting at which the list of candidates for the assessment commission was fixed.
The above-mentioned commission decided to apply to the Ministry of Finance with a request that a second appeals commission for turnover tax be set up at the Izba Skarbowa (Treasury Office) in Kielce.
The Chamber of Commerce also considered the new government[?] draft concerning liquor-serving[?] licences and adopted a resolution to intervene so that the draft be amended.
—o—
Visit of a ministerial commission.
During the week a ministerial commission stayed in Zagłębie concerning the question of regulating wages in the local industry.
The commission acquainted itself with the material specially prepared on the question by the labour inspector, and only after acquainting itself with the industrial establishments will the commission issue its decision.
—o—
Sequestrator sentenced to 3 months' prison.
The sequestrator Henryk[?] Gryfs collected several hundred złoty from taxpayers, which he took for himself.
For this Gryfs sat in the dock of the local district court, which sentenced him to 3 months' prison.
—o—
Budget lists — to the Magistrate.
The kehilla administration has decided that right after Yom Kippur the budget (etat) lists will be handed over to the Magistrate (town hall), from where the budget will be collected by sequestrators.
—o—
Workers demand coal.
During the week the workers at Hulczyński's factory, numbering 1,000 men, twice stopped work because the factory owners refused the demand of the workers, who are asking for free coal for the winter.
—o—
A big fire.
On Sunday evening, from an unknown cause, a fire broke out in the storehouses of Cukerman's house on Sienkiewicza Street. The fire was large and threatened the surrounding buildings. The firemen who arrived from Zagłębie and Upper Silesia saved the threatened houses; all the storehouses burned down.
While the police were dispersing the crowd[?], 10-year-old Heniek Abramczyk fell from a gate[?] and broke an arm.
—o—
Today's youth...
In the local district court, behind closed doors, the trial took place of 16-year-old Julian Ralki, who had wanted to commit rape upon a young woman in the Żarki[?] forest. The "gem" was sentenced to a month in prison.
—o—
A bandit attack.
On Sunday at 10 in the evening two bandits entered the flat of Mr. Birnbaum at 10 Chmielna[?] Street and demanded money from Birnbaum. Mr. B. began to scream with hysterical cries, which frightened the bandits and they vanished.

A theatre performance.
The local "Hashomer Hatzair" is arranging a performance at the municipal theatre during the coming Chol Hamoed. The programme includes Hebrew and Yiddish one-act plays.

From the Yom Kippur Just Past

[Review.] Yom Kippur has passed. Thanks to the cool weather, the fast was easier. The synagogue was filled to capacity at "Kol Nidrei"; the fans were working, for otherwise the walls would have "wept" from the stifling heat. The congregation took pleasure in the [prayers] — "Kol Nidrei", "Avinu Malkenu" and the Selichot brought comfort to the soul. The cantor, Żopowicz [?], was at his best and his voice resounded; the choir, under the new conductor Mr. Frenkel, is still a little [unpolished], but one may hope that under a conductor such as Frenkel it will rise to a higher level. No "incidents" occurred anywhere, except in the second Radomsker shtiebel, where there was a small "scuffle" over the prayer-lectern before "Kol Nidrei". Before Musaf, in nearly every synagogue and house of prayer a memorial was recited for the Jewish martyrs in the Land of Israel, which drew tears from the eyes of the worshippers.

The Power of Money, Given with an Open Hand — Do We Know How to Value It?

The power of money — given with an open hand. Do we know how to value it?

[Sub-heading: When public life declines, when the state of public institutions grows more dismal.]

The question arises: what of Sosnowiec? Sosnowiec, which before the war stood higher in civic importance and even surpassed Będzin — now, on all sides, one hears of it neglect and a criminal indifference toward the sharpest and most urgent questions. And when we ask Sosnowiec, "Where are you going, and what will become of you?", its citizens answer: "For you Będziners it is well; you are cultured, you have a mecenas (patron)"... Would that it were so. We are far from flattering anyone; we are not among those who dispense unwarranted praise. But the real truth must be properly valued.

And so the question arises: how do we value the merits of such a patron? With full awareness, a clear conscience and a whole heart we answer: no, we do not value sufficiently the high merits and fine deeds of Mr. Firsztenberg. A man with an open hand — right and left; a man who supports everyone in need of support, so handsomely and with understanding — and the town takes no notice of it. We cannot properly value the [deeds] of this man with a heart of gold.

The man took upon himself the initiative and the idea of building a magnificent edifice for the Jewish gymnasium — not in miniature format, but large and impressive, with a broad [façade], with the most comfortable halls in the latest modern style. One stands and marvels when beholding these buildings. And when representatives of the authorities enter, they will feel respect and reverence before it all.

Moreover, the school has become recognized by the government: it obtained government rights on the basis of the new building — in place of the one it had before, in which it struggled under the harshest conditions. So splendid a building has been erected that not everyone can afford the ready conveniences, the various classrooms, the well-lit halls, and the gymnasium hall with its perfected apparatus. Now the beautiful courtyard is a world unto itself, "spacious".

Mr. Firsztenberg did not content himself with building the beautiful monument and handing it over to the school administration; he continues to give money, has all the furnishings made at his own expense, brings in the furniture, provides the lamps, and does not cease — from the largest thing to the smallest. His unbreakable will and his selfless love for the gymnasium are evident in everything. A whole building, finished and fully built, which seems to say to the passer-by: come and enjoy, behold its beauty and grandeur. In such quiet, modesty and devotion the beautiful building was erected — and almost no one takes notice; not even a house-dedication has yet been held. This must not be allowed: a dedication must be held properly, and the town, the parents and the public must express their appreciation and their sympathy to the patron for the beautiful monument-project given to modern Będzin.

And one more thing: it would be fitting to open the gates of the gymnasium for a time, so that entry be free to all — so that people may behold the beautiful institution. Let people see how great is the power of a generous heart and a good will. We must be fully aware, we must know how to value at its full height what the man has created: the town demanded a proper building in which to educate people, good and national Jews — and to that end the man created a monument that will bear his name for generations.

In Poland too they "laugh": the government sets heavy taxes, and the small merchant cannot "laugh" — he must hold on. The petty trader, with his tiny means and tiny income, is charged so large a tax that he cannot pay it.

Humanity advances so much nowadays — and yet with us [—] the body of the state [—]. The middle class is the [backbone] of every state; and it would be right to understand, with reason and level-headedness, that the middle class must be helped first of all. It must not be left to fall: whoever wishes to work and earn a piece of bread — he should be given the possibility.

When a man is once charged such heavy taxes, he says to himself: "I will pay, so long as I do not [—]"; and he sells his last little property in order to pay — until nothing is left to him, and his health and his rest are lost. And this must be appreciated. With such an income a man reckons: where is he to take it from, when there is no merchandise? [—] He is forced to sell his last in order to pay the tax — and in the end the government has nothing more to collect from him. A man invests much toil, loses his health and his livelihood — and thus the middle class declines.

These taxes drain the middle class in Poland: a man sells his last, collapses, and it seems there is no longer any remedy. Just as the state [rests] upon the middle class, so must it give it the possibility to survive. The high time has come for the state to take the middle class into account and to help it — before it is too late.
